Kongsberg to arm Polish K2 tanks with remote weapon stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:46:20 UTC
15:46:20 KST

- Kongsberg signed a contract worth about NOK 700 million ($75 million) with Hyundai Rotem to supply PROTECTOR RS4 remote weapon stations for Poland’s K2 program.
- The stations will equip K2 tanks, armored recovery vehicles and combat engineering vehicles, with first deliveries for integration starting in spring 2027.
Norway’s Kongsberg will arm Poland’s new K2 tanks and their support vehicles with its PROTECTOR RS4 remote weapon stations. The contract, worth about NOK 700 million ($75 million), was signed with South Korean tank maker Hyundai Rotem.
The stations will go on three versions of the K2 built for the Polish Armed Forces: the main battle tank itself, the K2 armored recovery vehicle and the K2 combat engineering vehicle.
Kongsberg will begin shipping the first stations to Hyundai Rotem for vehicle integration in spring 2027. The deal also includes a support package covering initial spare parts, training for Polish crews and other services needed to keep the systems running once the vehicles enter service.
A remote weapon station lets a crew fire a roof-mounted machine gun or automatic grenade launcher from inside the armor, using a joystick and a screen fed by day and thermal cameras, so no one has to stand exposed in an open hatch to engage a target. The RS4 can carry a 12.7 mm (.50-caliber) heavy machine gun, a 7.62 mm or 5.56 mm machine gun, or a 40 mm grenade launcher. Its stabilized mount lets the gunner shoot accurately while the vehicle is moving. Kongsberg has delivered more than 20,000 PROTECTOR stations to armies around the world, and the U.S. Army’s Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station, known as CROWS, belongs to the same family.
“This contract further strengthens the long-standing cooperation between KONGSBERG and Hyundai Rotem Company and confirms KONGSBERG’s position as a leading supplier of advanced remote weapon systems for international defence programmes,” said Kjetil Reiten Myhra, president of Kongsberg’s Defence Systems division.
The order is tied to the second executive contract Poland signed with Hyundai Rotem in August 2025, a deal worth about $6.5 billion that covers 180 more K2 tanks and 81 support vehicles built on the K2 chassis. Under that agreement, 116 tanks in the K2GF configuration are being delivered in 2026 and 2027, and the first 28 of them reached Poland in August for the 16th Mechanized Division. The remaining 64 tanks will be built to the upgraded K2PL standard, which adds an active protection system and an anti-drone system. Sixty-one of them will be assembled at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice between 2028 and 2030.
The 81 support vehicles, due between 2029 and 2031, are 31 armored recovery vehicles, 25 combat engineering vehicles and 25 armored bridge layers. Kongsberg’s contract names the recovery and engineering versions but not the bridge layer. The recovery vehicles tow damaged tanks off the battlefield, and the engineering vehicles clear obstacles and minefields under fire. The RS4 stations will let their crews defend themselves without leaving the protection of the hull.
Kongsberg and Hyundai Rotem first agreed to work together on remote weapon stations and unmanned turrets in September 2022. That was shortly after Poland placed its first order for 180 K2GF tanks, which was completed in November 2025. Poland already buys heavily from both companies, fielding hundreds of South Korean K2 tanks alongside Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile in its coastal missile units.
The first RS4 stations are due at Hyundai Rotem in spring 2027. K2PL tank deliveries begin in 2028, and support vehicle deliveries start in 2029.

‘Most dangerous thing’: Netanyahu government's LGBTQ record, from Hamas comparisons to 37% cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:43:53 UTC
15:43:53 KST

A 37% cut to government funding for LGBTQ services, proposed legislation restricting recognition of transgender people and discussions of sexual orientation in schools, and inflammatory remarks by coalition lawmakers are among the findings of a new report examining the outgoing Israeli government's record on LGBTQ rights.
Published Thursday ahead of Israel's October 27 election, the report by the Aguda, the Association for LGBTQ Equality in Israel, reviews legislation, budget decisions, government policies and statements by elected officials since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government took office in December 2022. It describes repeated attempts to restrict LGBTQ rights alongside public campaigns that successfully blocked some of the proposed measures.
The organization warns that even legislative initiatives that failed to advance could serve as the foundation for renewed efforts in the next Knesset, Israel's parliament. At the same time, the report acknowledges several legislative achievements that expanded legal protections for LGBTQ Israelis during the government's term.
The first proposed change emerged before the government was even sworn in. Coalition agreements included a commitment to amend Israel's anti-discrimination law to allow business owners to refuse services on religious grounds. A bill introduced by lawmakers Ohad Tal and Moshe Solomon sought to enshrine such exemptions in legislation.
The proposal triggered widespread public opposition, prompting Netanyahu to pledge that LGBTQ rights would not be harmed. The legislation was subsequently shelved.
According to the report, however, additional proposals affecting the community followed. One bill, introduced by lawmakers Avi Maoz and Limor Son Har-Melech, sought to require that sex markers on official government documents be determined exclusively by biological criteria. The organization warned that the measure could prevent transgender people from changing their registered sex to reflect their gender identity.
Another proposal by Maoz sought to prohibit discussions of sexual orientation and gender identity in schools from first through eighth grade. From ninth grade onward, such discussions would be permitted only with the school principal's approval, parental notification, consent from 75% of parents and the individual student's agreement.
Son Har-Melech also introduced legislation intended to expand the authority of the state religious education council. According to the Aguda's analysis, the measure could allow the council to circumvent protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in religious schools.
A policy document published by the Yachin Center, which participated in developing the proposal, stated that "the right to educate for a life of Torah and commandments takes precedence over any other right."
The report notes that the proposal did not advance beyond its initial submission to the Knesset, but warns that it could provide a basis for future legislation.
LGBTQ funding slashed by 37%
Beyond the legislative proposals, one of the report's central findings concerns government funding for LGBTQ programs and services.
In 2024, the budget of the LGBTQ Advancement Division within the Ministry of Social Equality fell from a planned annual allocation of 38 million shekels to approximately 24 million shekels, a reduction of roughly 37%.
Funding allocated through a government program supporting local authorities, designed to finance LGBTQ activities and services across Israel, was also reduced, from 21 million shekels to just 10 million shekels.
According to the report, budget uncertainty intensified in 2025. Although a 24 million-shekel allocation for the division was presented during state budget discussions, the Ministry of Social Equality subsequently informed LGBTQ organizations that it had no available budgetary source to finance their projects.
In a letter sent to the Knesset Committee on the Status of Women and Gender Equality, the ministry stated that "this amount was never promised."
The consequences extended beyond the budget figures. In July 2025, the ministry terminated its agreement with the Aguda, under which dedicated services had been provided to LGBTQ people in Arab communities, adults aged 50 and older, and LGBTQ individuals with disabilities.
The report also found that new agreements sent to local authorities in September included further reductions, with activity budgets in major municipalities, including Haifa and Beersheba, cut by more than 90%.
The Aguda warns that these decisions threaten the continuity of essential services, particularly for LGBTQ people living outside Israel's major metropolitan areas or requiring specialized assistance that may not be available elsewhere.
Laws that passed and equality measures that failed
The report also examines legislation that was not explicitly directed at the LGBTQ community but could, according to the organization, have broader consequences for its rights.
These measures include a law expanding the government's ability to depart from the attorney general's legal opinions and legislation allowing religious courts to arbitrate civil disputes with the consent of the parties involved.
The organization argues that such changes are particularly significant because many LGBTQ rights in Israel are not explicitly guaranteed by legislation. Instead, they have developed through court rulings, legal interpretations and administrative policies, making them potentially more vulnerable to changes in the legal system.
The report also addresses an amendment expanding the possibility of gender-segregated academic education to postgraduate degrees, without establishing specific arrangements for transgender and nonbinary students or faculty members.
Meanwhile, several proposals intended to strengthen equality protections failed to pass. These included legislation to prohibit conversion therapy for minors, ban discrimination in housing, establish civil marriage and recognize victims of hate crimes for compensation purposes.
A bill prohibiting housing discrimination was rejected in a vote of 53 lawmakers against and 33 in favor. Another proposal establishing compensation for hate crime victims was defeated by 56 votes to 40.
Despite these setbacks, the report identifies three legislative amendments that expanded LGBTQ rights during the government's term.
Two involved recognition of same-sex partners under laws governing benefits and rights for the families of fallen IDF soldiers and those of hostages and missing persons. The changes followed the death of Maj. Sagi Golan and a public campaign led by his partner, Omer Ohana, for equal recognition of bereaved same-sex partners.
A third amendment added sexual orientation and gender identity to the grounds of prohibited discrimination under Israel's Student Rights Law.
Comparisons to ISIS, Hezbollah and Hamas
A separate section of the report examines statements made by government ministers and coalition lawmakers about the LGBTQ community.
Among the examples cited are remarks by lawmaker Yitzhak Pindrus, who described the LGBTQ community as "the most dangerous thing to the State of Israel," compared it to ISIS, Hezbollah and Hamas, and called for action to "prevent this movement altogether."
The report also refers to a recorded statement by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who said that his supporters "don't care about gay people" and suggested that measures against the LGBTQ community would therefore not harm him politically.
Justice Minister Yariv Levin, meanwhile, described a proposal to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity as "unnecessary and even harmful." The coalition subsequently rejected the proposal.
The report also documents statements by coalition lawmakers who expressed support for LGBTQ rights and opposed discrimination and violence against community members.
According to the organization, only three members of the 120-seat 25th Knesset openly identified as LGBTQ, while Netanyahu's 37th government included no openly LGBTQ ministers.
Nimrod Gornstein, chairman of the Aguda, said the findings reflected a pattern that began even before the government took office.
"Even before the government was sworn in, we saw an attempt to legitimize discrimination against LGBTQ people," he said. "Throughout its term, the community was repeatedly forced to confront attempts to restrict its rights, undermine its recognition and erode the services it receives from the state."
Gornstein said the inflammatory statements made by certain lawmakers reflected the broader political climate surrounding the community, but emphasized that public opposition and LGBTQ organizations had succeeded in blocking many of the initiatives.
"The extreme statements made by Knesset members about the LGBTQ community are an extreme expression of the climate that has developed," he said. "At the same time, the Israeli public and community organizations managed to stop a significant portion of these measures."
He added that the organization would work with any future government willing to advance equality, while continuing to challenge policies it believes threaten LGBTQ rights.
"The Aguda will continue working with any government that acts to promote equality, but will not hesitate to fight when the community's rights are under attack," Gornstein said.
He concluded by linking the report's findings to the upcoming election. "This report documents the choices politicians made regarding the LGBTQ community. In the coming election, the public will make its choice."
The Aguda warns that although several restrictive proposals failed during the outgoing government's term, they could return to the legislative agenda in the next Knesset, leaving the future of LGBTQ protections and government-funded services unresolved.
The Ministry of Social Equality did not respond to a request for comment.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Shukri Hussein and Ikram Kouachi
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Yemen’s army said early Thursday that the Houthi group targeted Al-Rayyan International Airport in the city of Mukalla, the capital of Hadramout province, for the fourth time within hours.
The army’s official spokesman, Maj. Gen. Majed al-Nuzaili, said the “Houthi terrorist militia targeted Al-Rayyan International Airport in Mukalla for the fourth time,” according to September Net, a website affiliated with Yemen’s Defense Ministry.
In a statement, Nuzaili said that “targeting airports aims to impose a blockade on the Yemeni people,” the website reported.
Al-Rayyan is one of Yemen’s most important civilian airports, serving millions of people in Hadramout and other provinces.
The Houthis had not immediately commented on the attack.
On Wednesday, the group attacked Al-Rayyan Airport in eastern Hadramout province with three drones. 
According to an Anadolu correspondent, this was the first attack on the airport since the resumption of military escalation last July.
The state-run Saba channel also reported that the Houthis had targeted Aden International Airport in southern Yemen with a ballistic missile, without providing further details.
Local residents told Anadolu they heard a loud explosion near the airport.
The developments come amid the internationally recognized government’s ongoing military offensive against the Houthis in southwestern Yemen.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several other provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Hong Kong watchdog warns of hacking risks from flaws in web programming language
Cybersecurity watchdog urges website operators to install updates immediately to fix two critical PHP flaws that could let hackers take over servers
A Hong Kong information security watchdog issued an “extremely high risk” warning on Thursday morning over two critical flaws in a widely used web programming language that could allow hackers to execute code remotely and take control of servers.
The warning followed similar alerts from governments and cybersecurity agencies overseas, which urged website operators to install updates to fix the vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language.
The Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) said a remote attacker could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code on a targeted system.

Musk announced the timeline for the release of Terafab chips and Optimus robots
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Musk announced the timeline for the release of Terafab chips and Optimus robots
Kyiv • UNN
The first Terafab test chip is planned to be produced in May or June 2027, with mass production by the third quarter of 2028. Tesla is also preparing Optimus deliveries and the launch of Cybercabs in new cities.
Elon Musk claims that his ambitious Terafab chip manufacturing plant project is "progressing rapidly" and will be ready to produce its first chip by May or June 2027, with a large-scale launch planned for the third quarter of 2028. UNN reports this, citing Gizmodo.
Details
As the publication notes, these are "fairly unusual timelines, but they fit Musk’s penchant for strange plans and inflated promises regarding delivery-date forecasts." Musk announced the project for a giant chip manufacturing plant in Austin, Texas, in March, claiming that it would produce chips for both terrestrial and space use. But chip manufacturing plants are known to be complex and expensive to build, especially in the United States rather than in places such as Taiwan, where there is already relevant expertise. Bringing a plant into operation alone can often take several years. But Musk is promising a tighter timeline for his plant.
We will begin commissioning the equipment in the first half of next year, and hopefully, if everything goes well, we will produce our first test chip, just to see whether we can produce any chip at all, around May or June. But actual production will begin at the end of 2028, which is lightning-fast by chip-factory standards
The project is a joint venture between two of Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, which are also actively discussing a merger, the billionaire said during the first company’s earnings call. It turns out that the companies have not yet decided how to divide the costs of Terafab.
Musk said that a merger between Tesla and SpaceX was under consideration21.10.26, 10:56 • 5166 views
"We need to figure out the relative allocation between SpaceX and Tesla in terms of who pays for what at Terafab, but it will not be less than tens of billions in capital equipment by the beginning of 2028, and then it will probably be more than $100 billion in the long term," Musk said during Tesla’s earnings call.
Musk said that Terafab, once operational, would become an "incredibly important asset, if not a necessary asset" for scaling up Optimus, the company’s humanoid robots, which are significantly behind Musk’s stated timelines. Early production has finally begun "on a high-volume line" in Fremont, California, Musk said during the call, but Tesla will still need "probably at least a year, perhaps a little more" to reach its previously stated goal of producing around 20,000 robots per week.
The electromechanical design, particularly of the robots’ hands, is a huge challenge, but Musk claimed that he expects it to be resolved by the end of 2027. That is when customers can expect Tesla to begin delivering Optimus. The first customers will be industrial companies whose work requires "dangerous, repetitive tasks, things that people really don’t want to do... such as working around the clock," Musk said.
During the call, Tesla executives also shared timelines for the release of other products. The company’s two-seat robotic taxis, Cybercabs, will be available for customers to purchase by the end of this year, Tesla Vice President of Automotive Engineering Lars Moravy said, although Musk noted that the "vast majority" of Cybercabs would be owned by Tesla and offered as "transportation as a service." Cybercabs are currently available only in Austin, Texas, but Tesla executives said they plan to introduce the service in more cities by the end of 2026, starting with a launch in Dallas in November.
"I think Tesla will ultimately perform the majority of passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely, and you can come back and look at this forecast," Musk told analysts.

Estonian diplomat: Trump, Putin and XI unlikely to agree on new world order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

Estonian diplomat: Trump, Putin and Xi unlikely to agree on new world order
Diplomat Jüri Luik told ERR that expectations are high for a possible meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China, but they lack the power to establish a new world order.
Asked by host Liisu Lass why the Americans continue to overlook the fact that Putin supports Iran and shares intelligence with the country, Luik said it was very difficult to say.
"It seems to me that this stems from President Trump's personal understanding of how the world works. Trump has repeatedly said: We give the Ukrainians coordinates, information and weapons — so why should I criticize the Russians for doing the same in Iran?" Luik said.
"But privately and behind the scenes, the Americans have repeatedly signaled that this must stop. There is no doubt that there may be a much broader dimension here involving cooperation between Iran and China. At the moment, it seems that much of the targeting information provided on various U.S. bases in Arab countries may actually have come through Iranian-Chinese cooperation," Luik added.
Trump has proposed meeting with Putin and Xi Jinping in China to discuss Ukraine. Could such a meeting produce an agreement establishing a new world order?
Luik does not believe so.
"I think that if this meeting takes place at all, it will be a big show that all three will probably enjoy. But Trump has said something very important: He has said that if such a meeting takes place, he is willing to attend, but he wants to discuss nuclear nonproliferation. This is an important issue because the Americans have long held the view that there is no point in discussing nuclear weapons solely with the Russians," he said.
Luik noted that although China's nuclear arsenal is currently not comparable in size to Russia's, the situation could be reversed in 10 years.
"So the Americans would like the Chinese to accept some multilateral restrictions on their nuclear weapons. The Chinese have said: We have so few weapons that we don't want anything to do with this. Trump has now put the issue on the table and it is entirely possible that the Chinese are not actually interested in such a meeting if the Americans really insist on discussing nuclear arms control," Luik said.
"As for Ukraine, let's be honest — what are they really going to discuss? And as for somehow establishing a new world order, I don't believe these countries have the power to do that," he added.
There is growing talk that the U.S. is preparing to present Ukraine with a new peace plan. Luik said he could not say what its main provisions might be.
"We don't have access to any precise documents. Judging by public sources, there is a whole range of different agreements on the table, starting with those concerning the reconstruction of Ukraine's economy. Then there is the so-called territorial issue, which is certainly the most difficult," the diplomat said.
Luik acknowledged that security guarantees from European countries and the United States are of crucial importance to the Ukrainians.
"The Americans say these would be guarantees similar to Article 5 [of the NATO treaty] — which would be a very, very significant step if the Americans ultimately agree to provide them. Because just as important as resolving this conflict is, of course, ensuring that a similar conflict, war or invasion never happens again in the future," Luik said.
Luik estimates that four or five different agreements are under consideration.
"In some ways, this is also the kind of situation in which experienced diplomats would certainly relish working day and night. But these agreements are currently being discussed within a very narrow circle. In that sense, the group of people working on them is indeed very small," he added.

Israel’s IWI arms Thai soldiers with anti-drone rifles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:33:11 UTC
15:33:11 KST

- Israel Weapon Industries has delivered its ARBEL anti-drone fire-control system to Thailand, installing it in existing Thai rifles by replacing their lower receivers.
- The system is operational day and night, and Thai military officials are discussing an additional ARBEL order with IWI.
Israel Weapon Industries has delivered its ARBEL anti-drone system to Thailand’s Ministry of Defence, where the computerized fire-control kit is now fitted into rifles already in Thai service and is in operational use by day and by night.
Thai military officials are already discussing a follow-on order with the company, after IWI finished the integration work and trained Thai soldiers on site.
IWI sells ARBEL either built into a complete IWI rifle or installed in a customer’s existing weapon, and Thailand chose the second option, with the company’s team carrying out the conversion in the country by replacing each rifle’s lower receiver with the ARBEL unit. Thai troops therefore keep the rifles, ammunition and optics they already know, while gaining the ability to engage small drones with them.
ARBEL does not detect drones or point the rifle for the soldier, but instead controls the exact moment each shot is released. The first round fires mechanically, as with any standard rifle, and while the soldier keeps the trigger pulled, the system releases follow-up rounds at the cadence that gives the best chance of a hit, leaving the shooter free to concentrate on tracking a small drone that flies fast and erratically at a distance. The rifle still fires normally if the battery runs flat, and the kit uses standard 5.56 mm ammunition and works with any optic, from red dots and low-power variable scopes to thermal and night vision sights.
“Small tactical drones have become a direct and growing threat to soldiers on the battlefield. We developed the ARBEL ADS to give soldiers an effective means of defending themselves against this evolving threat, while providing armed forces with a critical tactical advantage in an increasingly complex battlespace,” said Ronen Hamudot, vice chairman of SK Group, IWI’s parent company.
The system weighs about 400 grams (14 ounces), and IWI quotes an engagement range against aerial targets of up to 450 m (490 yards) in daylight and about 250 m (270 yards) at night. The current generation was unveiled in February 2025, when IWI introduced ARBEL versions for its ARAD rifle, any 5.56 mm AR-15-pattern rifle and the NEGEV light machine gun ahead of the IDEX exhibition in Abu Dhabi.
Speaking to The Defence Blog in July, IWI chief product manager Adam Fraser described ARBEL as a soldier’s last line of defense against small tactical drones, mainly first-person-view (FPV) attack drones, and said it is meant to work as one layer alongside detection systems and electronic warfare. IWI said its demonstrations had shown attacking drones brought down within 10 seconds with only a few rounds, against targets flying at up to 60 km/h (37 mph) at ranges beyond 100 m (330 feet), and the company estimated at the time that the system was fielded or in procurement in 10 to 15 European countries.
Thailand gives ARBEL its first announced operational customer in Asia, and IWI said several other Southeast Asian countries are at different stages of buying the system, with more deployments in the region expected within months.
“As Southeast Asian militaries place greater emphasis on counter-drone capabilities, Thailand’s adoption of ARBEL ADS reflects this growing operational priority. We see rising demand across the region for solutions that can help soldiers meet this challenge,” said Doron Korol, SK Group vice president for the Asia-Pacific region.
IWI, based in Kiryat Gat and best known for the Uzi submachine gun, the Tavor bullpup rifle and the Negev light machine gun, is the main small arms supplier to the Israel Defense Forces and Israel Police, and its weapons serve with military, police and special forces units in more than 60 countries.

War update: 187 clashes on front line over past day, Pokrovsk sector remains hottest

Over the past day, Ukrainian Defense Forces aviation, missile forces and artillery struck three clusters of enemy personnel and equipment.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, the Russian invaders launched two airstrikes using six guided aerial bombs and carried out 47 shelling attacks on Ukrainian troop positions and settlements, one of them using multiple-launch rocket systems.

Attempts to break through the Ukrainian defenses were repelled in the Lyman sector, where Russian forces launched nine assault actions, including near the settlements of Kolodiazi and Zarichne as well as toward Hlushchenkove, Derylove, and Lyman.
In the Sloviansk sector, the enemy launched two attacks near Ozerne and toward Mykolaivka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, the enemy conducted no offensive operations.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, seven attacks were recorded. Russian forces conducted offensive operations near Kostiantynivka and toward Novopavlivka.
In the Pokrovsk sector, the enemy launched 21 attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near Sofiivka, Dobropillia, Bilytske, and Molodetske as well as toward the settlements of Vilne, Kucheriv Yar, Hannivka, Svitle, Krasnopodillia, Serhiivka, and Muravka.

In the Huliaipole sector, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian positions 11 times attempting to advance toward Rizdvianka, Dolynka, Hirke, and Yehorivka.
In the Orikhiv sector, the enemy made two attempts to attack toward Pavlivka.
In the Dnipro River sector, the Russian invaders conducted one assault.
In the Volyn and Polissia sectors, no signs of the enemy forming offensive groups were detected.

Russians may face complete blocking in ChatGPT, Claude after IPO — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:32:53 UTC
15:32:53 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. AI developers Anthropic and OpenAI could potentially block all users of ChatGPT and Claude from Russia and other countries after going public, Russian company MWS AI told TASS.
This could happen because the companies will need to "reduce operational costs," Tech Lead at MWS AI's Applied Solutions Center Ivan Kopylov said. "Companies are already banning access to ChatGPT and Claude from Russia, China, and several other nations, but they are not always strictly enforcing these restrictions yet," he noted.
Mass bans of corporate Claude users are already visible in certain countries where users access the AI via alternative platforms, the expert said. Individual users are less affected so far, he noted. "Before going public, platforms find it beneficial to showcase maximum reach in terms of paid subscriptions," Kopylov said.
Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been actively preparing for their IPOs for a long time. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, spends billions of dollars on infrastructure and AI training, and submitted a draft registration application for an IPO to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in June. The financial community expects the company to rake up to $100 bln at a $2 trillion valuation.
OpenAI also filed a preliminary application with the SEC in early summer, but its IPO could be pushed back to 2027. The company is competing with Anthropic at the same time and aims to secure investor commitments before its rival goes public - Anthropic could launch its IPO as early as November 2026.
"After an IPO, investors look not only at user growth but also at expenses, cash flow, and profit margins. If a user generates less revenue than the company spends on serving them, expanding that user base only increases losses. This is particularly evident in AI: every single query requires computational power, so even a free user generates ongoing operational costs," Kopylov added.

California's largest state-worker union stages first strike

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Thousands of California state employees staged a one-day statewide strike on Wednesday over pay, healthcare and remote work, marking the first such walkout for California's largest public employees union in its 44-year history.
The Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, which represents more than 100,000 working people employed by the State of California, is seeking salary increases totaling 20 percent over three years, higher state healthcare contributions and department-level remote-work policies based on operational needs.
Workers rallied in Sacramento, San Francisco, Oakland and Los Angeles, nonprofit California news outlet CalMatters reported.
"We're making noise on the picket line and sending a clear message to the State: we won't be silenced because state workers deserve fair bargaining NOW!" said the union in a post on Facebook.
Union President Anica Walls said workers needed a contract that would allow them to afford groceries, childcare, rent and other necessities, according to a statement reported by San Francisco public broadcaster KQED.
About 95,000 employees were eligible to strike, while fewer than 5,000 designated essential employees were required to continue working under staffing requirements determined by the labor board, according to the union.
Some motor vehicle offices and state parks had modified or limited operations ahead of the strike, CalMatters reported. The Department of Motor Vehicles had warned that offices could face delays or close early, the outlet reported, citing a department spokesperson.
The union has accused the California state government of negotiating in bad faith, as workers' collective bargaining agreement with the government expired on June 30, according to local media.
The state had sought to stop the walkout, arguing that it put pressure on negotiations and threatened public health and safety, KQED said. ■

Feature: Vietnamese diners develop growing appetite for Chinese cuisine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:30:59 CST
15:30:59 KST

HANOI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The spicy aroma of mala hotpot drifted from the Chinese booth at the second Cultures of the World Festival in Hanoi earlier this month, drawing a long queue of Vietnamese visitors curious to sample its fiery flavors.
The scene was one sign of a growing curiosity about Chinese food in Vietnam, where diners are discovering not only familiar hotpot and dim sum but also the cooking traditions of different Chinese regions.
For some young Vietnamese, the attraction begins with the heat.
Pham Linh Dan, a 19-year-old university student in Hanoi, said she eats at Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao two to three times a week and has also tried several other Chinese-style hotpot restaurants.
Dan, who describes herself as a fan of spicy food, said what draws her to Chinese cuisine is not simply the level of heat, but the way different spices build the flavor.
"Chinese food is not just spicy in an ordinary way. It combines spices such as cinnamon and star anise, which create a kind of spiciness that is different from what we have in Vietnam," she said.
The distinctive taste has also made her curious about the culture behind the food.
"It makes me like Chinese food even more and want to explore more of Chinese culture and cuisine," Dan said, adding that Sichuan would be her first choice if she had the chance to travel to China for food.
That enthusiasm is also reflected in the performance of larger Chinese restaurant brands in Vietnam.
According to data released by Super Hi International, Haidilao generated about 57 million U.S. dollars in revenue in Vietnam in the first half of 2026, up 31 percent year on year and accounting for more than 10 percent of its global revenue.
But the appetite for Chinese flavors is no longer confined to Vietnam's major cities.
In central Vietnam's Nghe An province, a newly opened restaurant specializing in Jiangxi cuisine has also been drawing local diners as well as visitors from neighboring areas curious about Chinese food.
Nguyen Thu Hien traveled about an hour from neighboring Ha Tinh province to Nghe An and took the opportunity to try Chinese food for a change.
"Before trying it, I thought Chinese food was quite spicy and a little oily," Hien said.
After tasting the dishes, however, she said they were less oily than she had expected and thought the flavors had been adjusted for local diners.
Pham Thi Nhu Quynh, who had previously traveled to southwest China's Yunnan Province and eaten Chinese food there, offered a different perspective.
"I think the food is quite authentic, still oily and spicy," Quynh said, adding that it was neither too sweet nor too spicy for her taste.
For Quynh, seeing more Chinese regional cuisines appear in Vietnam also carries meaning beyond the meal itself.
"I think it is also a way to convey culture, especially food culture, and gives Vietnamese people more diverse choices," she said.
For Wang Shixiang from the Jiangxi Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam, the spread of regional Chinese cuisines to more parts of the country carries a broader cultural meaning.
"We hope to use food as a bridge to preserve and promote Chinese culinary culture, bring Chinese cuisine to the world, and help more people learn about China and fall in love with Chinese flavors," Wang said. ■

S. Korea freezes key rate at 3.00 pct to evaluate impact of back-to-back rate hikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:30:49 CST
15:30:49 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's central bank froze its key rate on Thursday, pausing its monetary tightening cycle to evaluate the impact of back-to-back rate hikes in July and August.
Bank of Korea (BOK) Governor Shin Hyun-song and other monetary policymakers decided to leave the benchmark seven-day repurchase rate unchanged at 3.00 percent.
The unanimous decision was in line with market expectations. According to a Korea Financial Investment Association survey of 100 fixed-income experts, 93 percent predicted the rate on hold.
Shin told a press conference that the central bank needs to prolong its tightening cycle despite the pause, stating that the consecutive rate hikes in July and August gave the BOK policy room to maneuver according to domestic economic conditions.
Expectations ran high for the BOK to resume its rate-hiking path later this year or early next year amid the still high inflationary pressure and the continuous household debt growth.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.9 percent in September from a year earlier, decelerating from an increase of 3.1 percent in August.
The headline inflation, however, stayed above the central bank's mid-term inflation target of 2 percent for 13 straight months.
Petroleum product prices jumped 14.8 percent last month amid the continued Middle East conflicts.
Despite slowing household loan growth, total debt kept an upward trajectory for a seventh consecutive month.
Debt owed by households to deposit-taking banks totaled 1,198.9 trillion won (906.1 billion U.S. dollars) at the end of September, up 0.6 trillion won from a month earlier.
It marked a significant slowdown from the 3.5 trillion won expansion in the previous month, affected by a slump in retail stock investments and a reduction in newly completed housing.
The BOK said in a statement that the domestic economy maintained strong growth led by exports and investment, but it cautioned that inflation remained high at around 3 percent.
The bank explained that housing-related loans continued to increase while the pace of growth in housing prices in Seoul and its surrounding areas accelerated again.
The overall South Korean economy showed a robust recovery thanks to soaring exports of semiconductors used in the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Outbound shipments surged 83.5 percent in September from a year earlier, while the daily average exports more than doubled.
Revised gross domestic product (GDP) data showed that facility investment climbed 6.3 percent year-on-year in the second quarter.
After shrinking 0.1 percent in the fourth quarter of last year, real GDP rebounded 1.8 percent quarter-on-quarter in the first quarter of this year and beat expectations with a 0.6 percent expansion in the second quarter.
The current account surplus from January to August totaled 279.2 billion U.S. dollars, a more than fourfold expansion compared to the same period last year.
Backed by the strong fundamentals, the central bank raised its 2026 growth outlook from 2.6 percent to 3.3 percent in August. ■

One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:23:55 UTC
15:23:55 KST

Finland, Germany and Lithuania share the euro and the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate, but with September inflation at 2.7%, 3.3% and 6.1% respectively, they show how one policy meets different price realities.
Three countries share one currency and one central bank rate, yet their inflation rates differ by more than twofold.
In September, annual inflation was 2.7% in Finland, 3.3% in Germany and 6.1% in Lithuania, according to Eurostat’s harmonised index (HICP), published in October. The euro-area average was 3.8%. All three face the same European Central Bank (ECB) deposit rate of 2.50%.
An energy shock felt unevenly
The common thread is energy. Eurostat data show energy prices across the euro area rose 18.9% in September, adding 1.71 percentage points to inflation, almost half the headline figure. Excluding energy, euro-area inflation was 2.3%.
How that shock plays out depends on a country’s energy mix, tax choices and the strength of its domestic economy.
Lithuania: energy, taxes and wages
Lithuania sits at the top of the range, and food is not the reason. Eurostat figures show food, alcohol and tobacco inflation at 0.5%, while energy prices jumped 33.0% and services inflation reached 6.9%.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) attributes the surge to elevated energy prices amid continued import dependence, strong domestic demand and higher excise duties. Policy added to the pressure. From January, Lithuania raised the VAT on residential heating, hot water and firewood from 9% to 21%. The government’s draft budget estimated that the heating change alone would add 0.5 percentage points to inflation.
Pressure has spread beyond fuel and heating. Eurostat data put Lithuania’s core inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, at 3.9%. The Bank of Lithuania expects average wages to rise 9.4% in 2026, and the European Commission links services inflation to strong pay growth and an 11.1% rise in the minimum wage.
Higher wages may leave many workers better off on average. But pensioners, benefit recipients and low-income households with large energy bills are more exposed. There is also a second-round risk. Labour-intensive service businesses can pass higher wages into prices, keeping inflation elevated after the energy shock fades.
Finland: cushioned and sluggish
Eurostat figures show Finland faced a similar energy shock, with energy inflation at 13.1%, yet headline inflation stayed at 2.7%. The European Commission says Finland’s relatively low reliance on fossil fuels softened the blow. Statistics Finland found that cheaper electricity and owner-occupied housing costs restrained its national consumer price index, even as petrol, diesel and heating oil pushed it up.
Domestic price pressure is weak. According to Eurostat, core inflation was 1.4% and services inflation 1.7%. The Bank of Finland forecasts 10.4% unemployment in 2026, while the Commission expects GDP growth of 0.8%. Statistics Finland reports nominal earnings rose 3.5% year on year in the third quarter, or 1.2% in real terms.
That combination helps explain why another rate rise may seem overly restrictive from Helsinki.
Germany: a spike concentrated in fuel
Germany falls in the middle. Eurostat data show energy inflation at 13.4% and core inflation at 2.5%. Germany’s statistics office, Destatis, found motor fuels up 37.1% and heating oil up 74.9% in the national index. Excluding those two items, inflation was 1.8%.
Wage pressure is moderate. Negotiated wages rose 2.9% year on year in August, and the Bundesbank projects the same average for 2026. Eurostat puts services inflation at 2.8%.
Policy also muddies the picture. Existing federal measures lowered electricity, gas and district-heating prices, and a new fuel-tax cut took effect on 1 October, so it is not included in September’s figures. National interventions can shift measured inflation monthly without changing the underlying European shock.
What a single rate means
The ECB raised its deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.50% in September, arguing that the Middle East conflict was keeping inflation above target and that the full effects of the energy shock had yet to emerge.
Subtracting national headline inflation from the ECB rate gives a rough real-rate proxy: minus 0.2% in Finland, minus 0.8% in Germany and minus 3.6% in Lithuania. This simple calculation based on ECB and Eurostat figures is not a true measure, since households and firms act on expected inflation and face different borrowing costs.
The policy tensions differ by country. Finland’s weak growth and high unemployment argue against tightening. In Germany, the rate is easier to defend given core inflation of 2.5%, but September’s acceleration was driven almost entirely by fuel and heating oil. In Lithuania, the rate looks loose against 6.1% inflation, though higher rates cannot reverse a VAT increase or lower imported fuel prices. They work by weakening demand and curbing second-round effects.
Transmission also varies. ECB research finds that policy works faster and more strongly where variable-rate debt and household leverage are more common, and Lithuania is among the countries relying on variable-rate mortgages with short reset periods.
Yet a recent study covering 2000 to 2025 suggests output and inflation responses to monetary policy are less uneven than often assumed, as some structural differences offset each other.
Sources: Eurostat, ECB, IMF, European Commission, Bank of Lithuania, Bank of Finland, Statistics Finland, Destatis, Bundesbank.

According to the Woodland Police Department, the collision occurred at around 9:38 a.m. on October 20 near Locust and Clover streets. The man was examined by medics at the scene and taken to a hospital, with police describing his injuries as minor.
He was identified as Antonio Moreida, a Woodland Community College student and a volunteer with the advocacy group NorCal Resist. Speaking at a city council meeting, Moreida said he had been recording agents and reading out a license plate when the SUV drove directly into him.
DHS rejected that account, saying ICE did not hit a pedestrian. A spokesperson said the individual jumped onto the vehicle’s hood, the driver braked, and the person slid off. The department added that ICE immediately contacted emergency services and local police.
Woodland police said they have reviewed footage from several angles, including the interaction leading up to the collision, and that the actions of both parties are under review. The findings will be sent to the Yolo County District Attorney’s Office. Police noted that the department did not take part in the federal operation and, under California law, does not engage in civil immigration enforcement. U.S. Representative Mike Thompson, who represents the area, said local law enforcement had confirmed ICE was operating the vehicle and called for accountability, saying no one is above the law.
Three days earlier, Long Beach police found a man handcuffed and bleeding in ICE custody after agents requested help over vehicle vandalism and a person needing medical aid. The man was identified as Ricardo Gonzalez, a former city employee. U.S. Representative Robert Garcia said agents broke the arm of the resident, a U.S. citizen. Mayor Rex Richardson said ICE does not belong in the city and that the activity undermines public trust. Neither ICE nor DHS publicly commented on the incident.
In April, ICE agents shot and wounded Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez during a traffic stop in Patterson, California. Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons said the man was wanted in El Salvador in connection with a murder and had tried to run over an officer. His attorney said ICE may have acted on bad information and that videos showed his client trying to avoid officers.
In March, video of plainclothes ICE officers detaining a woman at San Francisco International Airport as her young daughter watched drew outrage from local officials. Residents later protested outside San Francisco police headquarters over officers’ presence at the scene.
The most serious cases came in Minneapolis in January. An immigration officer shot and killed Renee Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen, in her car on January 7. On January 24, a Border Patrol agent fatally shot Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old ICU nurse at a Veterans Affairs hospital. The killings sparked sustained protests and clashes between demonstrators and law enforcement, and the Justice Department later opened an investigation into Pretti’s death.

U.S. Army tests artillery shell that hunts moving tanks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:21:22 UTC
15:21:22 KST

- The U.S. Army fired three prototype XM1180 hit-to-kill 155 mm shells at a tank target at Yuma Proving Ground to test a new image-based seeker.
- The seeker will next undergo GPS-denied testing and be integrated into the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile, with firings planned within months.
The U.S. Army fired three prototype tank-killing artillery shells at a tank target in the Arizona desert at Yuma Proving Ground. The Army used the tests to check a new seeker that builds an image of the target area and steers the 155 mm round into an armored vehicle, including one that has moved since the shell was fired.
The rounds belong to the XM1180 Cannon-Delivered Area Effects Munition (C-DAEM) Armor program. They were launched from a 39-caliber cannon in different configurations, so the team could evaluate the seeker’s performance on each shot.
Yuma Test Center personnel ran the firings together with Project Manager Combat Ammunition Systems, the U.S. Army’s DEVCOM Armaments Center at Picatinny Arsenal and Raytheon, which builds the GPS-guided M982 Excalibur shell that the XM1180 is based on. Col. Alicia Johnson, who heads the ammunition program office, traveled to Yuma with her leadership team to watch the tests. They were the second phase of a series of guided test vehicle firings meant to prove the shell can find targets on its own.
Lovjoat Singh, a test and evaluation engineer at DEVCOM Armaments Center who planned and ran the firings, explained the two steps of the test.
“It will be an open loop test then following a closed loop test. Open-loop test means the seeker is going to be seeking a target but not actually acting upon it. Then closed loop is actually using the seeker to guide to a target,” said Singh.
The seeker gives the XM1180 a different job from the Excalibur, which flies to a fixed GPS coordinate and was never designed to hit a vehicle on the move. The new shell keeps much of the Excalibur’s design but swaps the payload for an armor-piercing warhead and adds the terminal seeker. As a result, an artillery battery tens of kilometers from the front can attack tanks and armored vehicles that a forward observer can no longer pin to a single grid point.
“It’s a cool new technology that basically creates (an) image of the target area and it’s able to find the target in that area. It should be able to use the image to guide to target,” said Casey Scharenbroich, an evaluator with the U.S. Army Operational Evaluation Command who was on site to judge how mature the technology has become.
“It would be a huge advantage on the battlefield for commanders, allowing them to engage targets that have moved or are on the move with this munition,” Scharenbroich said.
The Army also expects the seeker to reduce collateral damage, because the shell guides onto a specific vehicle instead of saturating an area. That is the main difference from cluster rounds such as the Cold War-era DPICM, which scatter dozens of bomblets and leave unexploded ordnance across the battlefield.
The XM1180 program dates to 2018. The Army fired its first guided test vehicle at Yuma in February 2024, when the shell identified a target and handed guidance over to its seeker, and the program reached Technology Readiness Level 6 ahead of schedule. Army officials have since said they want future rounds to share data with one another, so that several shells fired at a column of vehicles do not all strike the same tank.
The seeker is now headed for a second, newer program. Yuma test officer Ashley Lochetto said the next steps are testing the seeker without satellite navigation and fitting it to the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile.
“Our intent is to conduct GPS denied testing of the (seeker) along with integrating it into the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile,” said Lochetto.
The Extended Range Artillery Projectile effort is the U.S. Army’s push for a maneuvering 155 mm shell with deployable wings that can strike moving targets such as self-propelled howitzers, rocket launchers, infantry fighting vehicles and tanks beyond 65 km (40 miles) without a rocket motor. General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems joined General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems and BAE Systems on the program in June. The Army is aiming for low-rate production in fiscal 2029 and initial operational capability in fiscal 2030. Separately, the service is pursuing a new rocket-assisted 155 mm projectile for the M109 and M777 howitzers.
The C-DAEM Armor guided test vehicle series will continue through fiscal 2027. The first XM1230 firings with the new seeker are scheduled at Yuma Test Center within the next few months.

Taiwan legislative hearing discusses abolition of Control Yuan

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Control Yuan member Yeh Yi-jin (葉宜津) warned lawmakers Wednesday against paralyzing the Control Yuan before amending the Constitution, arguing that such a move would be unconstitutional.
The legislative hearing focused on the potential transfer of the Control Yuan’s powers and the mechanisms needed to facilitate the change, per CNA. National Taipei University professor Chen Chih-hua (陳志華) proposed transferring its investigative and audit powers to the Legislative Yuan to better fulfill the body's intended functions.
Retired Ming Chuan University professor Chi Chun-chen (紀俊臣) argued that the Control Yuan’s perceived poor performance stemmed from personnel issues rather than structural flaws, per UDN. He suggested adopting Sweden’s parliamentary ombudsman system, under which ombudsmen investigate public authorities and courts nationwide, as a possible way to transfer the Control Yuan’s powers to the legislature if lawmakers proceed with its abolition.
Yeh said she respected lawmakers’ desire to abolish the Control Yuan but argued that paralyzing the institution before its formal abolition would be unconstitutional, per Liberty Times. She said the body had processed 89,791 public complaints, conducted 65,503 disclosures of civil servants’ financial information, and produced 1,484 investigation reports, emphasizing that it continued to carry out its constitutional duties.
Yeh also rejected the ombudsman proposal, arguing that lawmakers were already burdened with existing responsibilities and lacked the capacity to act independently of their political parties. She questioned whether the public would accept having four ombudsmen under the legislature oversee public authorities nationwide.
At a legislative hearing in July, Fu Jen Catholic University professor Yao Meng-chang (姚孟昌) argued that transferring the Control Yuan’s powers to the legislature would concentrate too much power in one branch of government, per CNA. He recommended introducing greater democratic legitimacy to the institution by allowing its members to be elected.
In June, rejected Control Yuan nominee Chen Yung-hsing (陳永興) proposed constitutional amendments to transform Taiwan into a “modern democratic state,” per UDN. He suggested transferring the Control Yuan’s investigative and impeachment powers to the legislature.
KMT lawmaker Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) previously said that, while investigating the military’s dashcam procurement, she found that the legislature’s lack of investigative powers limited her to requesting information rather than questioning Ministry of National Defense officials, per UDN. She also noted that when Sun Yat-sen (孫中山) conceived of the Control Yuan, its members were elected rather than nominated by the president.

U.S. Army tests smoke screen built to blind enemy radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:12:00 UTC
15:12:00 KST

- The U.S. Army has field-tested a portable module that releases coated fibers to hide soldiers and vehicles from enemy millimeter-wave radar.
- DEVCOM CBC handed the radar-blocking smoke system to the Army’s CBRN defense portfolio office for further testing before fielding.
The U.S. Army has developed a smoke screen that hides soldiers and vehicles from enemy radar as well as from enemy eyes. The Millimeter Wave Screening Obscuration Module releases a cloud of coated fibers into the air, and that cloud blurs the radar signature of everything behind it. Engineers at the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Chemical Biological Center (DEVCOM CBC) at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, demonstrated the module in live field trials in August. The center then handed it to the Army office that will test it further and prepare it for fielding.
Battlefield smoke has worked the same way for generations: it blocks what the enemy can see. The Army’s Cold War-era generators, such as the M56 Coyote and the vehicle-mounted M58 Wolf, were built to defeat the human eye, optical rangefinders and early infrared sights. Those screens do almost nothing against millimeter-wave radar, the type used in many modern fire-control radars and missile seekers. A platoon hidden in a dense cloud of conventional smoke can still show up clearly on an enemy radar screen.
“Different sensors are designed to operate across distinct regions of the electromagnetic spectrum,” said Dr. Jill Harland, a research scientist at DEVCOM CBC.
Visible-light cameras work on extremely short wavelengths, while thermal imagers and radars operate on progressively longer ones. Particles that block a camera are simply too small to interfere with a radar beam, so the center’s scientists had to rebuild the obscurant around the radar band itself. Their answer is about 30 pounds (13.6 kg) of specially coated fibers, which a portable device releases into the air, where they hang like thousands of tiny shields and scatter the incoming radar energy.
Every vehicle, weapon or soldier gives a radar a distinct signature, a numerical value the radar uses to detect and identify the target. During the August trials, the team set up several targets, watched them on radar and then released the fiber cloud around them to measure how quickly the cloud formed and how far the signatures dropped.
“We used radar to observe the cloud formation and show the degradation of the radar signatures of each of those targets,” said Michael Smith, a mechanical engineer at DEVCOM CBC. “As the cloud formed, the signature dropped and we got our obscuration that way.”
Smith said the moment the team watched those signatures fade on the radar screens during live dissemination was a defining one for the developers.
“Our objective is to buy Soldiers critical time on the battlefield, improving survivability directly accomplishes our core mission,” said Smith.
The radar module comes from the same team at the center’s Smoke and Target Defeat Branch that developed the M75 Screening Obscuration Module. That suitcase-sized smoke generator can be run by one soldier, and the Army has tested it at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah since 2018 as the successor to the Coyote. In November 2025, the center mounted an M75 on an unmanned ground vehicle at Aberdeen to conceal soldiers during a simulated wet gap crossing. At the time, the center said the next generation would add infrared and radar obscurants, and the millimeter-wave module is that radar piece now leaving the lab.
The Army is also looking further ahead. In January, Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground asked industry for ideas on a multispectral version of the module, one infantryman could carry and that would screen troops and combat vehicles from ultraviolet, visible, infrared and radar sensors at the same time. Its stated goal is a cloud that forms within 95 seconds, stretches 204 m (670 feet) long and 12 m (40 feet) high, and holds for 12 minutes.
The Millimeter Wave module now moves to the Portfolio Management Executive for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense, which will run the additional testing required before the system is issued to Army units.

‘I received death threats’: Israeli actress Sarai Givaty sues Francesca Albanese over Nazi comparison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:11:55 UTC
15:11:55 KST

Israeli actress and model Sarai Givaty has filed a 500,000-shekel defamation lawsuit against Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, accusing her of distorting comments from a television interview and comparing them to arguments used by Nazi officials to justify the murder of children during the Holocaust.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday at the Jerusalem Magistrates' Court through the Israeli legal advocacy organization Shurat HaDin and attorney Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, alleges that Albanese shared a selectively edited video of Givaty that went viral, exposing the actress to online abuse, death threats and damage to her professional reputation.
At the center of the dispute is an interview Givaty gave in September 2025, during which she discussed how the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, massacre had changed her worldview. She spoke about growing extremism, referring both to the far right and to radical Islam, and the need to confront radicalization
During the interview, Givaty said: "I feel sad for every child in the world who cries. I do. But I also understand that if we don't act, that child will grow up to be a terrorist."
According to the lawsuit, her comments referred to the dangers of children being exposed to hatred and extremist indoctrination. Her lawyers stress that she neither advocated violence against children nor suggested that they should be killed.
Nearly a year later, a 23-second excerpt from the interview began circulating online, accompanied by what Givaty's lawyers describe as a partial English translation that omitted the broader context of her remarks.
On September 19, 2026, Albanese shared the clip on X and wrote: "The children will grow up". She continued: "This was also the argument that Nazi officials gave, during the Nuremberg Trials, to justify why they had killed children during the Holocaust."
The post quickly spread across social media, accumulating more than 2 million views, tens of thousands of reposts and approximately 93,000 likes. According to the lawsuit, the comparison was subsequently circulated by media outlets and social media accounts around the world, amplifying what Givaty describes as a fundamentally false portrayal of her remarks.
Givaty argues that Albanese's reference to Nazi officials and the murder of children presented her to a global audience as someone who supported or justified killing children in Gaza. The lawsuit specifically challenges the use of the words "justify" and "killed children," arguing that their inclusion created the impression that Givaty's original comments amounted to an endorsement of lethal violence against minors.
Her lawyers contend that the comparison went far beyond legitimate criticism of her political views and instead falsely associated her with arguments used to defend atrocities committed during the Holocaust.
Givaty says the consequences were immediate and severe. According to the lawsuit, she received dozens of abusive messages, including direct threats against her life, after Albanese's post spread online. She claims the publication damaged her dignity, personal security and reputation, while also threatening her career in Israel and internationally.
The lawsuit argues that such allegations are particularly damaging to an actress and model working in the international entertainment industry, where producers, talent agencies and commercial brands may be reluctant to associate themselves with someone publicly portrayed as supporting the killing of children. Givaty maintains that the accusations could cost her professional opportunities and commercial relationships.
"As a mother, I am appalled by this false comparison," Givaty said. "People may disagree with my views, but they cannot attribute statements to me that I never made and present me to millions of people as someone who justifies killing children. I will not remain silent in the face of those who seek to harm Israel and smear it around the world."
Attorney Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, founder and president of Shurat HaDin, accused Albanese of using her international position to spread defamatory claims against Israelis.
"We are fighting back against the international campaign of lies," Darshan-Leitner said. "Francesca Albanese is waging a venomous antisemitic campaign against Israel and is responsible for spreading yet another defamatory accusation against its citizens."
Darshan-Leitner said the lawsuit was intended to hold Albanese personally accountable for her public statements, despite potential legal questions surrounding her status as a UN-appointed expert.
"For the first time, we can sue this Israel-hater over her hateful statements and make her pay for her actions," she said. "We will not let her hide behind her immunity."
Albanese is an independent human rights expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, rather than a salaried UN employee. Questions of jurisdiction and possible immunity could become central to the legal proceedings. No court has yet ruled on the allegations in Givaty's lawsuit, and Albanese had not publicly responded to the case at the time of reporting.
For Givaty, the lawsuit is an effort to challenge a comparison she says falsely transformed her comments about extremism into an apparent justification for killing children, with consequences extending far beyond the original interview.

Boreal said in a statement that new information confirmed in recent days indicated that AI was used during the writing process, contradicting the author's previous assurances.
A US judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties for Facebook's handling of user data, reducing an initial assessment of $219.5 billion in a case involving political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica nearly a decade ago, CNBC reported.
The ruling follows a September jury verdict in New Mexico that found the social media company liable for more than 43 million violations of the state's consumer protection law.
The case stems from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which the company improperly accessed personal information from 87 million Facebook users. Meta is Facebook's parent company.
The European Commission on Wednesday opened formal proceedings against Booking.com to investigate whether the online travel platform breached the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA) by failing to adequately address fraudulent listings, phishing scams and advertising transparency.
The investigation will assess whether Booking.com properly identified and mitigated risks associated with fake accommodation listings, including non-existent properties, impersonation fraud and non-compliant offers, according to a statement.
The EU executive will also examine whether the platform took sufficient measures to prevent fraudulent listings from appearing on its service and protect consumers from potential scams.
US artificial intelligence company Anthropic introduced Claude Duet on Wednesday, a proactive AI agent designed to independently manage tasks on behalf of users.
Powered by Claude Opus 5.5, the assistant targets professionals and small business owners, offering daily briefings and handling tasks ranging from scheduling meetings to preparing financial forecasts and building web applications.
"Claude Duet comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said in its announcement.

Cookies and weapons: Women in Yemen’s Taiz find ways to help the city’s defence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:06:28 UTC
15:06:28 KST

Cookies and weapons: Women in Yemen’s Taiz find ways to help the city’s defence
Amid growing threats, a grassroots aid effort has transformed into an initiative to get more ammunition to the front.
Taiz, Yemen – As Houthi fighters tighten their siege on the government-held southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz, women who initially organised food deliveries for soldiers defending the city have begun raising money to buy weapons and ammunition.
The initiatives have emerged spontaneously since the resumption of fighting in early September in the western countryside of Taiz governorate, between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed armed group.
At first, women volunteers came together to bake cookies for fighters on the front lines.
The aim was “to strengthen the relationship between the supportive social base and the members of the national army and pro-government popular resistance forces stationed at the front lines in defence of their besieged city, which is subjected to daily shelling in preparation for an invasion,” said Amira al-Saghir, an activist involved in the campaign.
The cookie-making initiative attracted widespread participation among women volunteers, drawing encouragement and support on social media. It coincided with a broader community campaign to supply fighters with food and other basic necessities, as well as weapons, with people contributing from districts and villages across the governorate.
In Yemen, a conservative country and the poorest in the Middle East, the vast majority of women do not participate in active fighting in the civil war, which began in 2014. Instead, these initiatives allow women to take part in what they see as the defence of their city against an invading force, and support for the men who are fighting.
After nearly four years of relative calm following a United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022, Houthi forces launched a major ground offensive in western Taiz in early September. The armed group rapidly captured territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic port city of Mocha on September 10 , expanding its presence around Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital shipping route.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God, subsequently advanced towards other parts of Taiz governorate, taking control of key routes into the provincial capital and effectively surrounding the city. Government forces have since launched counteroffensives, with control of some areas remaining contested.
The renewed siege has severely restricted the movement of people and essential supplies into the city, triggering shortages of food, fuel, and medicine.
From cookies to weapons
As the fighting intensified, the women’s initiatives expanded. What began with baking cookies and organising food convoys to supply arms kitchens gradually evolved into efforts to buy ammunition for fighters.
Women involved in the initiatives told Al Jazeera that they felt they had been “forced” to act because of the risk of their city falling to the Houthis.
The change began as more rural districts began falling to the Houthis, leading to some donors making their contributions conditional on part of the money being used to buy ammunition for fighters.
Al-Saghir believes the shift was encouraged by information and criticism circulating on social media suggesting that government fighters in Taiz lacked sufficient ammunition to continue defending the city and surrounding front lines.
The initiatives soon took off, encouraging more women to get involved. Among them was Huriya Wabel, a humanitarian activist.
“After we saw that those [Houthi] militias … are waging a war of extermination against our city, we felt that we had to take a serious stand to support the army, not just with food and clothing, but with weapons as well, especially since a siege has been imposed on Taiz and supplies can no longer reach it easily,” Wabel told Al Jazeera.
“We also found many civilians who wanted to participate in the fighting alongside the army in defence of the city, but they did not have weapons,” she added. “So it became incumbent upon us to help by focusing more of our activities on this aspect at this stage.”
Defending their city
For Khadija al-Majidi, the move from providing humanitarian supplies to delivering military equipment is a response to the growing threat facing Taiz.
“When the enemy reaches the gates of your city and imposes a complete siege on it in preparation for storming it by force, and everyone in it – including you, your children, and members of your family – is threatened with being killed, captured, or displaced … then what do you expect from us?” the activist told Al Jazeera. “Did you expect us to carry flowers for the criminal who came from the farthest reaches of the country to destroy our city and kill us?”
When Al Jazeera spoke to al-Majidi, she had just returned from the fighting around Jabal Sabir, the mountain overlooking Taiz from the south.
It was al-Majidi’s second trip to the front that day, delivering ammunition and other military supplies, which she valued at $3,000, to the commander on the front, along with winter clothing, shoes, food, and other necessities.
She said that after more than 10 years of living through Yemen’s devastating war, she no longer felt afraid to visit active battlefronts.
“Repeated visits to the front lines play a major role in removing fears, given what we see on the ground of the heroes’ courage and bravery in defending the city and their confidence in victory,” she added.
As fundraising expands, the women’s department of Taiz’s Supreme Council for Popular Resistance launched a campaign on October 8 , aiming to equip 10,000 pro-government fighters with rifles and ammunition.
The council has called for contributions from Yemenis across the country and abroad to support the initiative.
The campaign reflects the state of the fighting in Taiz, with government forces facing daily Houthi attacks, as they try to conduct their own counter-attacks.
But the longer the siege continues, the more difficult the military and humanitarian situation becomes in the city.
Al-Saghir and al-Majidi both explained that while many of the donations they receive come from Yemenis living abroad, people on the ground are also giving whatever they can, despite the humanitarian crisis in Taiz.
Al-Saghir said one woman whose husband was fighting in the army donated a wedding ring, while al-Majidi recounted stories of other women donating their gold jewellery.
Al-Majidi recalled a woman arriving at her home carrying envelopes containing Yemeni and Saudi currency.
The woman had written on the envelopes, “God willing, we will win. Buy ammunition for the heroes with this.”

EC announces by-election for Madhya Pradesh Rajya Sabha seat
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission of India (ECI) announced that the by-election to the Rajya Sabha seat from Madhya Pradesh, vacated by former Union minister L Murugan following his resignation, will be held on November 12. The counting of votes will take place on the same day, according to the commission’s press note shared on Thursday.The vacancy arose on October 14, when Murugan resigned from the Rajya Sabha. His term was scheduled to continue until April 2, 2030.According to the schedule announced by the ECI, the notification for the by-election will be issued on October 26. The last date for filing nominations is November 2, while scrutiny of nomination papers will take place on November 3.Candidates will be able to withdraw their nominations until November 5.Polling will be held from 9 am to 4 pm on November 12, with counting scheduled for 5 pm the same day. The election process is to be completed by November 16, the commission said.
The commission has specified the procedure for marking preferences on ballot papers, directing that only the integrated violet-coloured sketch pens supplied by the returning officer can be used.The ECI said in its press note, “No other pen shall, under any circumstances, be used in the above said election.”
The commission has also said that observers will be appointed to monitor the election process and ensure that it is conducted freely and fairly.“Adequate measures for close monitoring of the election process by appointing observer shall be taken to ensure free and fair election,” the press note stated.
