IN BRIEF
- A lawsuit is seeking compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were allegedly exposed to harmful content.
- Meanwhile, a judge in the US state of New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion for misleading consumers.
Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers.
The suit filed in the Federal Court on behalf of eight applicants seeks to recover compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were exposed to harmful content or developed an addiction to social media, law firm Minter Ellison and Litigation Lending said in a statement.
The Federal Court in Sydney issued a suppression order on Monday stopping publication of details of the claim and the identity of the applicants, court documents show.
"We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement.
Litigation Lending Services said it was funding the class action for Australian families who "would have no practical means of pursuing these claims against a global technology giant".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia," Minter Ellison partner William Nolan said in a statement.
The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and big tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.7 billion (roughly $25 billion) in the United States to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users.
Meta ordered to pay US$25 billion in New Mexico
News of the Australian lawsuit came shortly after a judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay US$25 billion ($35.2 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in US President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.
New Mexico attorney general Raúl Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against a company in US history.
"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said.
"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.

U.S. Air Force tests shipping military cargo by rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:02:12 UTC
15:02:12 KST

- The Air Force Research Laboratory flew cargo pods aboard a SpaceX Starfall capsule on Oct. 20 to test rocket delivery of military supplies.
- The pods carried survival gear, medical equipment and trackers, with sensors measuring heat, shock and vibration during launch and reentry.
The U.S. Air Force has sent military-style cargo into space and back aboard a SpaceX Starfall capsule as it tests whether rockets could one day deliver supplies to troops anywhere on Earth within hours.
The Air Force Research Laboratory flew its own cargo pods inside the capsule on a commercial rideshare launch from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20, packing them with satellite trackers, batteries, survival gear, a water desalinator and emergency medical equipment to see how they would hold up through launch, spaceflight and the plunge back through the atmosphere.
The flight was part of Rocket Cargo, an AFRL project studying whether large commercial rockets can move materiel around the world on tactical timelines, and the capsule carried sensors that recorded the temperature, shock and vibration the cargo experienced along the way. Engineers paid particular attention to how electronics and survival equipment came through the ride, and they also checked whether a UNI-PAC III life raft would fit inside the capsule for future tests, which hints at missions such as dropping rescue kits to downed aircrew or stranded sailors far from any base.
“Any day you launch a rocket is a good day, but today was more than just another big rocket launch,” said Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert, Department of the Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL commander. “Today’s launch was another demonstration of how AFRL is partnering with industry to burn down risk, collect hard data and deliver war-winning technologies for the operational force.”
Starfall is SpaceX’s new uncrewed reentry capsule, a squat disk about 3.1 meters (10 feet) across that weighs roughly 2,100 kg (4,600 pounds) and can bring back up to 1,000 kg (2,200 pounds) of payload under parachutes, with recovery planned in the Pacific Ocean. SpaceX flew the first Starfall demonstration in June, and regulatory documents describe the capsule as a way to support both rapid point-to-point cargo delivery and a commercial market for products made in orbit and returned to Earth.
The Air Force’s ambitions for Rocket Cargo are much bigger than a single capsule, since AFRL says the concept stands apart from other fast-delivery efforts because a large rocket could carry tens of tons per launch to places with no runways or roads. The service has said it wants rocket-delivered cargo to reach almost any point on Earth within about an hour and a half and eventually to move loads comparable to a C-17 transport, and in June it awarded Colorado-based Geneva Technologies $4.3 million to help design the rocket cargo system.
AFRL sees uses ranging from resupplying forces in contested areas and expeditionary operations to rescue missions, disaster relief and responding to chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear incidents, and it is working with a long list of companies to get there, including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Sierra Space, Anduril, Inversion Space and Outpost Space. In August, the Air Force expanded Blue Origin’s role in the program with a study contract now worth about $13 million.
“This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force,” said Adam Remaly, director of the AFRL Technology Transition Office.
AFRL plans further tests with commercial rockets and reentry capsules as it gathers data on how cargo survives the trip, and it is also looking at how the military could benefit from commercial investment in capsules built to return products manufactured in space.

The memoir traces Congress MP’s journey from her childhood in post-war Italy to her relationship with former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and the personal losses that shaped her life and relationship with India.
Memoir revisits childhood, Rajiv Gandhi and family tragedies
The book recounts Sonia’s early years in Italy, her romance with Rajiv Gandhi while they were associated with Cambridge, and the assassinations of her mother-in-law, former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and her husband.Born in Italy, Sonia Gandhi was 19 when she met Rajiv Gandhi in Cambridge, England, in 1965. The couple married on February 25, 1968.She went on to become the longest-serving president of the Congress party.

2026-10-22

15:00:52 KST

Recommissioning 14 Dock at Devonport will allow legacy submarine defuelling to restart, paid for from the £7.1 billion going into the naval base over the next decade under Project Royal Oak, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress the department has made in re-establishing a safe and secure defuelling capability at Devonport Dockyard.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As part of Project Royal Oak, £7.1 billion will be invested in HMNB Devonport over the next decade. Part of this investment is being used to complete the 14 Dock recommissioning programme, which will enable the recommencement of legacy submarine defueling activity.”
Defuelling at Devonport stopped in 2004, and the submarines that have decommissioned since then have been held afloat with their fuel still aboard, tied up in the Hamoaze and requiring crews, monitoring and maintenance for decades after their operational lives ended. Restarting the capability is the step that unlocks the rest of the dismantling process, since a boat cannot be broken up until its reactor fuel has been removed.
The Submarine Dismantling Project has been running since 2011 and demonstrated the later stages at Rosyth, where Swiftsure was taken apart as the trial vessel and the work was completed last year. The Devonport boats have been waiting on the defuelling step, and the Public Accounts Committee and the National Audit Office have both examined the cost of storing them.
Project Royal Oak is the wider rebuild of the naval base infrastructure that the submarine flotilla depends on, and it covers dock recommissioning, deep maintenance facilities and the shore support the Astute and Dreadnought classes will need through their lives. The programme was mapped out this year at around £26 billion across the naval bases, with Devonport taking the £7.1 billion share.
Devonport’s role is changing as Faslane consolidates the operational submarine flotilla, with the Plymouth base holding deep maintenance, refits and now the disposal pipeline. This publication reported recently that the Navy is looking to accelerate the Devonport submarine upgrades, and that more refit work is being done at Faslane while the Devonport docks are rebuilt.

‘This used to be paradise’: How intensive farming is destroying Europeans’ favourite swimming spots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:00:37 UTC
15:00:37 KST

'Green sludge' is appearing on Europe's shorelines as warming waters, sewage and agricultural runoff fuel the growth of toxic algae.
“I remember our beautiful beach before the pollution,” says Brittany resident Jean Hascoet, who leads the local campaign group Baie de Douarnenez Environnement. “Now, with thousands of pigs near our town, everything is different.”
Across France and Spain, Europe’s shorelines are being choked by toxic algal blooms. Scientists are clear on the cause: decades of chemicals leaching into waterways. Poorly handled human sewage, as well as fertilisers and excess manure from ever-expanding factory farms, are to blame.
Seas warmed by climate change are further fuelling the rapid growth of the algae which disrupts delicate ecosystems, killing off fish and plant life. Some types can also cause nausea, vomiting and rashes in humans – prompting hundreds of swimming bans across the continent this summer.
Climate investigations outlet DeSmog visited some of the worst impacted spots in Europe, speaking to fishers, swimmers and business owners whose livelihoods and wellbeing depend on healthy waters.
‘Spain’s sacrificial zone’: Farming threatens a protected lagoon
“You’ll never see me swimming in that water again,” Fina says.
The 84-year-old from Murcia lives with her husband on the beachfront at Los Urrutias, on the west coast of Spain’s Mar Menor, Europe’s largest saltwater lagoon. Rotting seaweed piles up on the shore, giving off a foul stench.
“This used to be paradise. The sea was teeming with seahorses,” Fina says.
The last decade has seen a sharp increase in sea life-choking algae in Mar Menor – a hotspot for Spanish and international tourists.
Despite being granted ‘legal personhood’ by the Spanish government in 2022, giving it rights to protection and restoration, the lagoon remains under stress from agricultural runoff.
Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, is reliant on nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus to grow. Intensive farming in the Mar Menor region provides a ready supply of nutrient-rich manure, slurry and fertiliser runoff.
Studies estimate agriculture is responsible for around 85 per cent of the nutrients entering the lagoon, with urban sources making up the rest.
“The land can’t accommodate it all,” says Pedro Luengo, a biologist and spokesperson for the campaign group Ecologistas en Acción in Murcia. “We’re a sacrificial zone.”
Even to the east of the lagoon, furthest from the farmland, local authorities must work hard to preserve an artificial paradise for tourists. In the first three months of 2026, they collected more than 4,000 tonnes of algae from Mar Menor’s shores and nearby water – roughly the weight of 1,000 elephants.
But it hasn’t shielded those who rely on the lagoon for their livelihood.
“We used to catch far more gilt-head seabream and prawns. Now the catch is much smaller,” says Rubén Albaladejo, a fisherman from Lo Pagán. “The Mar Menor is a drain into which everyone dumps their rubbish and waste.”
Rising water temperatures are further hindering the reproductive ability of these species: “We’ve reached 30 degrees – something we’ve never seen before,” says Albaladejo.
Scientists warned in August that human-caused climate change added around 2°C to peak Mediterranean sea temperatures and around 1.4°C in Western European seas, according to World Weather Attribution. The Mediterranean averaged a record 27.07°C in July.
Spain’s environment ministry is funding eight projects with more than €11.5 million to cut livestock pollution, including new ways of treating pig slurry and moving sheep to open pasture. They are part of a €675 million national programme to recover the lagoon, but by the end of 2025 only about 16 per cent of that budget had been spent.
‘The Lough is dead’: Fishers in Northern Ireland face their worst ever year
Two thousand kilometres away in Northern Ireland, Declan Coney has also seen Lough Neagh – the UK’s largest lake – devastated by blue-green algae every summer since 2023.
“Fishing was instilled in me – generation after generation,” Coney says. But “this year has been the worst ever for fishing. The Lough is dead.”
Trout and eel numbers have fallen in recent years, in part due to the oxygen-depleting algae whose weight forces Coney’s fishing nets shut, so fish can’t swim inside.
Since the 2000s, the lough has been besieged by invasive zebra mussels. By hogging phytoplankton, these mussels deprive other species of a vital food source, as well as attaching to fishing nets and ripping them.
“There’s no money [in fishing],” says Coney, who has been working on the lake since 1975. “It’s not a livelihood anymore.”
As in Spain, Lough Neagh’s algal blooms are the result of decades of nutrient pollution. Northern Ireland’s livestock sector has grown rapidly, supported by government expansion plans since 2013: poultry numbers have risen by a third, and pigs by 74 per cent.
Earlier this year, nonprofit Watershed Investigations and UK newspaper The Guardian found evidence of cattle, pig and human faeces in samples of water from the lough, which spans nearly 400 square kilometres and provides 40 per cent of Northern Ireland’s drinking water.
Regulations aimed at improving Lough Neagh’s water quality, including reducing phosphorus and nitrogen levels in animal feed, and limiting manure application, need to be strengthened and better implemented, a report by the Office for Environmental Protection concluded in April. It notes positive investment and efforts from farmers but says more on-farm support and oversight is needed.
Mary O’Hagan lives on the north-west of the lake. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she set up a wild swimming group, and found that the cold water had huge benefits – from improving mental health to relieving chronic pain.
“In my 30s, I didn’t have much of a life, I wasn’t looking after myself. Swimming in Lough Neagh changed my life completely,” O’Hagan says. “We had a community.”
But after the second year of the blooms, she felt forced to shut the swimming group down.
“It was like Armageddon. To see the shores covered as far as the eye can see in pea green sludge was horrendous,” she says. “I couldn’t in all good conscience organise swims where people would be exposed to bacteria, algae, or god knows what else.” Blue-green algae can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and skin irritation.
‘More animals than people’: Manure run-off poisons Brittany’s beaches
Brittany, in northwest France, faces its own deadly battle: sea lettuce algae has been linked to as many as six fatalities on the region’s beaches since the 1980s. When it breaks down, it can produce hydrogen sulphide – a lethal gas that smells like rotten eggs – which can cause blocked airways and fluid to build up in the lungs if inhaled in large quantities.
Locals here are vocal about their suspicions of the cause. Near the tourist town of Saint-Brieuc, one resident has scribbled “les cochons” – the pigs – across an official sign warning about the danger and symptoms of inhaling toxic gas from the algae.
“We have many more animals than people,” says environmental author Yves-Marie Le Lay, who wears a protective mask at his local beach when algae growth reaches dangerous levels. Although Brittany’s peninsula covers just five per cent of France’s surface, its 6.8 million pigs account for 58 per cent of the country’s total population. “We have a manure problem, it all ends up in the rivers.”
France’s national audit court, the Cour des comptes, found in 2021 that more than 90 per cent of the nitrogen in the affected bays comes from agriculture.
Environmental activist Fabrice Hamon is uneasy about the coming months. On his local beach, Plage de Penfoul, E. coli forced a partial swimming ban in 2025. This summer’s drought now means that harmful excess nutrients have built up in the soil of nearby fields treated with manure.
“Right now there’s a build-up of bacteria in the fields,” Hamon says. “All it takes is a heavy downpour and, bingo. It’s a slow-acting poison: little by little, ecosystems are being degraded by the build-up of pollution linked to intensive farming.”
Hamon is working on a system to monitor for the bacteria in around 20 rivers that flow onto local beaches, so that tourists and local beachgoers can check for warnings through an app called La Météo Bacterio.
Elsewhere in Europe, citizens can report the presence of blue-green algae through the Bloomin’ Algae app by the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology. The app is available in the UK, Belgium, Greece, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Norway.
‘The sea was dead’: Baltic blooms flourish in record heat
Citizen science projects like Hamon’s could become vital in the battle against pollution in Europe’s waterways.
In northern Germany, volunteers led by the Schleswig-Holstein branch of the environmental nonprofit Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland (BUND) are collecting water samples twice a month from local rivers to help pinpoint sources of pollution and help cut nutrient runoff into the Baltic Sea.
Jürgen Leicher, the group’s deputy chairman, has been sailing these waters for 40 years, and says this year’s algal blooms are the worst he’s ever seen.
Temperatures in Germany broke records for three consecutive days in June, reaching almost 42°C. Satellite images of the Baltic in August show vast algal blooms swirling towards the coast. Algae grows quicker and lasts longer in warm waters, as higher temperatures allow it to digest and reproduce at a faster rate.
“You feel really afraid when you sail for hundreds of miles through a yellow-brown dirty sea,” says Leicher. “All the way through this algae, the sea was dead. You see no birds, no mammals, no fish. It’s so empty.”
Isabel Seeger, marine conservation expert at Deutsche Umwelthilfe, says the source of the problem is clear: “Our current agricultural system, which is reliant on high fertiliser consumption and manure from mass livestock farming, is the biggest cause of eutrophication in the Baltic Sea.”
The intergovernmental body HELCOM estimates that agriculture accounts for up to 90 per cent of nitrogen and up to 80 per cent of phosphorus in diffuse nutrient run-off into the Baltic.
Despite decades of intergovernmental efforts to reduce nutrient pollution, such as placing strict limits on agricultural fertiliser inputs, the Baltic is struggling to recover from the environmental damage combined with rising temperatures.
Each year, when algae dies it sinks to the seabed, taking large amounts of phosphorus with it. That phosphorus is released back into the ocean in future years – a dangerous feedback loop that gains speed as the sea warms.
Ultimately, though, scientists say that nutrient pollution must be slashed to limit the recurrent harmful algae growth – and that means transforming agricultural practices.
“The science is clear on what needs to be done,” says Professor Friedhelm Taube from Kiel University (CAU), who spent 12 years advising Germany’s Ministry of Agriculture.
Governments should support farmers to use less nitrates-heavy fertiliser; plant catch crops like grass clover that absorb some of the excess nutrients from soils before they run into rivers, lakes and the sea; and reduce the number of animals farmed to one livestock unit per hectare – a technical term that translates to just one dairy cow or roughly three pigs – on limited land, he says.
For campaigners in Murcia, the choice is just as stark: “Either we wreck the Mar Menor or we transform the agricultural model,” says Luengo.

China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
As Beijing prioritises development of the technology, a China-led committee aims to dictate how it is built
China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority.
The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC).
The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a technical director with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases.
“The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group.

Serious risks at EU borders, fundamental rights agency warns

06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

The Ceuta migration crisis put human rights at the bloc’s external borders to the test, the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights warned in a report Thursday.
The Vienna-based agency warned that there are serious risks to fundamental rights at the bloc’s external borders and the sudden arrival of thousands of migrants to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in July “put the balance between protecting fundamental rights and safeguarding the EU’s external borders to the test.”
In late July, more than 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in the space of 48 hours, leading to questions about how the EU should deal with sudden mass movements that may be engineered or used against the bloc. In her State of the Union address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised a European emergency response framework, which she said should allow for “time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures.”
Advertisement
Greece has called for a measure suspending asylum applications in emergency situations — something that could amount to pushbacks, which are banned under international law. Several countries have thrown their support behind the idea, while others question whether this type of measure should be taken at the level of the EU, rather than in national capitals.
In its report, the agency said any emergency measure should comply with EU and international law, both of which guarantee the right to seek asylum and the principle of non-refoulement — a “cornerstone of refugee protection,” it added.
At a meeting of EU leaders last week, von der Leyen said the Commission would come up with a proposal for the emergency framework before the end of the year.
“We will always uphold our values and fundamental rights, but we will never compromise on protecting our borders,” she said.
The agency’s report also highlighted other fundamental rights concerns at the EU’s external borders, including the implementation of rights monitoring mechanisms as part of migration reforms, restrictions on search and rescue organizations, and investigations into rights violations at the borders.
According to the agency’s numbers, 12 EU countries opened 322 preliminary criminal investigations between 2020 and 2025, but only nine of those resulted in a conviction.
Gaps in those investigations “lead to a perception of impunity, which risks undermining the rule of law, one of the fundamental values on which the Union is founded,” the report stated.

The world is $365 trillion in debt, and the interest bill is climbing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:59:52 UTC
14:59:52 KST

The world is $365 trillion in debt, and the interest bill is climbing
Protests in Europe have highlighted debt squeeze, with France now paying more to borrow than Italy and Greece.
Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks, angry at rising living costs, low wages, unaffordable housing and underfunded schools.
Protests in France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal have sometimes descended into clashes, looting and fires, although many protests have remained peaceful.
France has been at the centre of the unrest. More than 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry, amid weeks of student protests over education and living costs.
The unrest has turned the spotlight on a fiscal squeeze that governments are struggling to control. Years of heavy borrowing have left many European countries deeply in debt, and that debt is getting more expensive.
France’s borrowing costs are the highest since 2002, and the more governments spend on interest, the less they have for the schools, hospitals and pensions that protesters want.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at how governments borrow, where France ranks among the most indebted countries, and the trillions that governments spend on interest.
How do governments borrow money?
Governments borrow money much like people do, but instead of going to a bank, they sell bonds.
In return, the government pays the buyers interest and promises to repay the full amount on a set date.
A 10-year bond is a loan the government pays back after a decade. Its yield – the return investors earn for lending – is the most closely watched measure of how much markets trust a country to manage its debt.
Here’s how it works:
- The government borrows money – An investor pays €100 for a 10-year bond.
- The government pays interest – Every year for 10 years, the investor receives a fixed payment. At 2.5 percent, that’s €2.50 a year, or €25 in total. At 5 percent, it’s €5 a year, or €50 in total.
- The government repays the loan – After 10 years, the investor gets the original €100 back.
What happens when borrowing gets more expensive?
When bond prices fall, yields rise, making borrowing more expensive. Like a family facing a higher mortgage rate, a government then spends more on interest and has less money for essentials, such as schools, hospitals and roads.
Ten-year borrowing costs for major European economies have not been as high as 5 percent since the early 2000s, shortly after the euro was launched.
During the eurozone debt crisis of 2010 to 2012, only struggling countries such as Greece, Italy and Spain paid that much or more, and yields above 7 percent pushed Ireland and Portugal into bailouts.
France now pays around 5 percent to borrow for 10 years, compared with 3.41 percent for Germany. The widening gap shows investors want a higher return for lending to France.
The chart below shows 10-year borrowing costs across the euro area and the UK. France now pays more than Italy and Greece, two of the countries hit hardest by the eurozone debt crisis. Only the UK, which is outside the euro, pays more.
Which countries are most in debt?
The United States has by far the largest government debt, at $41.4 trillion, or 127 percent of its economy, or gross domestic product (GDP). The US benefits from borrowing in dollars, the world’s dominant reserve currency, which supports global demand for its debt. But its borrowing capacity is not unlimited.
China follows with $22.5 trillion, or 104 percent of GDP, while Japan owes $8.7 trillion and has the highest debt ratio among major economies, at 199 percent of GDP. The UK’s debt stands at $4.4 trillion, or 102 percent of GDP.
France ranks fifth globally, with debt of $4.2 trillion, or 118.5 percent of GDP. That is more than Italy’s $3.7 trillion, although Italy’s debt is larger relative to its economy, at 138 percent. Germany owes $3.5 trillion, just 65 percent of GDP.
The IMF projects France’s public debt to rise to 121.8 percent of GDP by 2030, complicating efforts to put the country’s public finances on a sustainable path.
The table below ranks countries by government debt. Use the search box to find yours.
The $3.3 trillion interest bill
Global debt, including that of governments, households and companies, rose by $10 trillion in the first half of 2026 to more than $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance (IIF). That is roughly $44,000 for every person on Earth. Much of the increase came from emerging markets.
Paying for that debt is costly. Advanced economies paid more than $3.3 trillion in interest on their government bonds over the past year. That is more than the world spends on defence ($3.1 trillion), artificial intelligence ($2.6 trillion) or clean energy ($2.3 trillion).
For the public, rising interest costs mean less money for services such as schools, hospitals and pensions. Governments may have to raise taxes or cut spending to cover the bill. Higher government borrowing costs can also push up interest rates on mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

‘Stupid talk’: France rejects Trump’s attempt to blame unrest on migration

Unknown Publisher

‘Stupid talk’: France rejects Trump’s attempt to blame unrest on migration
The US president has turned his attention to France, but his comments appear to have been dismissed by French leader Macron.
Paris, France – As France reels from violent clashes during protests, riots and looting, the blame game is on.
One argument making waves across the political spectrum – and across the Atlantic – is that migrants and open-border policies are responsible.
“If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished,” United States President Donald Trump said at the White House on Monday. “When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred – that’s not about school. That’s about people coming into the countries that hate the country.”
French President Emmanuel Macron has since slammed “stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders”, but did not name Trump. Speaking during a visit in Qatar, he said there was no evidence of foreign interference behind the riots.
Young student protesters in France were unimpressed by Trump’s intervention.
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old student at the Paul Eluard high school near Paris, one of the first to witness protests, called it “stupid talk”.
“They can think whatever they like. We’re focusing on the main subject, which is the students’ demands,” Narjissi said. “The far right has to say these kinds of things because they base their politics and political programmes on instilling fear.”
Emmanuel Dupuy, president of the Institute for European Perspective and Security Studies, a think tank on diplomacy and political analysis, said Trump’s argument was aimed at American voters.
“It’s an artificial argument used as a political tool in the context of midterm elections,” he said. “They are trying to argue that what is happening in France would happen in the US if Democrats get elected.”
Trump’s comments came after largely peaceful high school student demonstrations in France descended into chaos over the weekend when rioters attacked city halls and looted stores, marking the most violent unrest in France in years.
More than 2,000 people were placed in police custody – the vast majority of them minors – and thousands of businesses were ransacked. Accused of letting the situation spiral, French authorities imposed partial and temporary curfews in certain cities across the country, including in areas of Paris.
While concerns over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes and teacher shortages were at the fore, the protest movement quickly catalysed wider discontent over the cost of living and social unease.
Italy, Albania and Spain have seen similar demonstrations.
French authorities have not linked crime with migration. The state does not share the identities of people arrested and sent to trial.
Under constitutional laws aimed at equality, it is illegal to collect data on ethnicity and race.
Both far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen and politicians from the centrist bloc, including Macron and Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, have accused hard-left groups of fomenting disorder.
The wave of protests seems to have struck a nerve across the European bloc, too.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was now “clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on immigration”, posting on X a video showing buildings burning in France.
Without explicitly referring to events in France, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk also weighed in. “Poland will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, nor will it pay for them,” he asserted on X a day after the mass demonstrations and looting in France. “We will be uncompromising on security.”
Dupuy said the origin of those who joined the violence was beside the point.
“These protesters were high school students; then professional black bloc and looters joined, too – whether they came from a third or fourth generation of former migrants is irrelevant,” he said. “Eventually, this is a problem of integration, not immigration.”
Vance attacks ‘Western liberals’ in Europe
The US is in campaigning mode as it gears up for key elections in early November that will determine who dominates Congress.
With all eyes on midterms, Republicans seem eager to capitalise on unrest in Europe to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement and its tough policies on immigration and border measures.
“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” US Vice President JD Vance said on X. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”
Some critics have argued that Trump is trying to divert attention from the US’s cost-of-living crisis. Costs are rising in the US amid the Iran war he launched and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has sent energy prices to new heights.
What is happening in France, Trump said, should be a cautionary tale for American voters.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said, doubling down at a rally in the US state of Kansas.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,572,790 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:57:02 UTC
14:57:02 KST

Russia has lost 1,572,790 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 22.
The number includes 2,250 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,439 tanks, 25,594 armored combat vehicles, 165,641 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,447 artillery systems, 2,229 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,719 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,997 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

U.S. and Israel prepare for a new war with Iran

- President Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” as plans for renewed strikes take shape.

The United States and Israel are moving toward a new war with Iran within days, as President Donald Trump said Washington is no longer negotiating with Tehran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” while U.S. troops pull out of exposed bases across the Middle East and Israeli fighter jets rehearse a strike on Iran at the edge of its airspace.
The troop withdrawals, embassy staff cuts and large-scale air activity over the region closely resemble the buildup that came just before the war began in late February, and they put the next round of fighting on a timeline measured in days rather than months, with the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections now less than two weeks away.

The remarks mark a sharp turn from Trump’s pledge on Oct. 8 that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, and they come as Washington and Jerusalem finalize plans for what officials described to The New York Times as a short but intensive operation against Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals. Options presented to Trump include strikes on tunnel entrances at nuclear sites such as Pickaxe Mountain and on the strategic islands of Kharg, which handles most of Iran’s oil exports, and Qeshm, NBC News reported, while officials quoted by the Times said there is a chance he could order strikes before the end of this month.
On the ground, the U.S. military has quietly moved troops out of bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait in recent days, two U.S. officials and two people familiar with the matter told NBC News, and one official said getting forces out of harm’s way is part of planning as Trump weighs restarting major combat operations. The State Department has ordered staff reductions at the U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on the kingdom including strikes on civilian airports, and chiefs of mission at several other posts across the region have been told to operate with fewer personnel, in moves that sources compared directly with the drawdowns at the start of the war in February.
“We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness,” a U.S. Central Command spokesperson said.
Israel has already rehearsed the opening move of a new campaign, sending dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft along a route through Syrian and Iraqi airspace consistent with a strike on Iran and turning them back only as they approached the Iranian border, Axios reporter Barak Ravid reported, citing sources who described it as a massive power projection operation. Israel told Washington the flight was an exercise and a show of force, but the sortie was followed overnight by large-scale tactical aircraft activity over the region that defense writer Tyler Rogoway said looked like a dry run for a large integrated operation, in which commanders put much of the real strike force in position to rehearse before the order to execute is given.
Such rehearsals also force Iran to switch on its air defenses as if a full attack were coming, which lets U.S. and Israeli intelligence detect, classify and pinpoint radars and missile sites that would have to be suppressed, destroyed or avoided on the first night of an offensive, Rogoway noted, and that kind of targeting picture is far sharper when Iranian crews are on high alert than during routine surveillance.
Tensions are climbing at sea as well, after the naval arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its forces hit four vessels it accused of illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf and that three more ships struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that continued provocations could bring a wider response against U.S. bases in the region. Iran’s neighbors are bracing for the fallout, with Saudi Arabia already under a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign that has led Britain to send Royal Air Force Typhoons to guard Saudi cities and Türkiye to prepare forces for deployment to the kingdom under its new defense pact with Riyadh and Pakistan.

Websites go dark as AI exposes critical security flaws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:56:45 UTC
14:56:45 KST

Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites as they raced on Oct. 22 to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP.
Wiz, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws, estimated that PHP code helps run about 70 percent of the world's websites — from online stores and news outlets to government services.
It called the flaws "among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history".
PHP programmers released a fix on Oct. 21, and the U.S. National Security Agency told organizations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline.
Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online.
Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, called the discovery "quite devastating."
It could allow "attackers to get into your servers without any authorization, without any username or password," she told AFP.
"Once they are in the servers, they can do anything they want" — from stealing sensitive information to modifying website content — she added, urging institutions to "take it seriously."
Increasingly powerful AI models can spot weak points in computer scripts that have gone unnoticed by humans for decades.
That has heightened fears over cybersecurity risks, with the number of software vulnerabilities found worldwide in 2026 on track to roughly double last year's record total.
Government-run sites in countries from Australia to the Netherlands were among those that went dark, while insurance firms, transport operators and media outlets were under emergency maintenance.
Japan's prime minister advised businesses to act to protect themselves "with great urgency," while South Korea's government also instructed organizations' tech departments to update their software.
"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.
Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP's code.
OpenAI said on X it considered the flaws "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory."
The discovery "marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact," it added.
Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.
Ethan Mollick, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School who studies AI, said companies he talks to are struggling to keep up with the pace of patches needed to guard against AI-driven cyberattacks.
"Now consumers are going to have the same experience of getting everything updated often and fast," he wrote on X.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP's developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Details leaked online on Oct. 20, a day before the planned release of the fix, prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them.
In France, local government websites, including one for the Paris police, were made inaccessible at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, the interior ministry said.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, warned users they could see outages on its sites while it addressed the flaws, and said it had deliberately taken many of its supporting services offline until they could be safely patched.
Popular apps, including a Pokemon sleep tracker, were also temporarily taken offline while the fix was implemented.

New Astangu-Mäeküla nature reserve to cost Tallinn up to €5.5 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:55:00 UTC
14:55:00 KST

New Astangu-Mäeküla nature reserve to cost Tallinn up to €5.5 million
Tallinn plans to establish the Astangu-Mäeküla nature reserve in the Haabersti district, with the purchase of privately owned land in the area set to cost the city up to €5.5 million.
The creation of the Astangu-Mäeküla nature reserve has been discussed for years. The city restarted the process five years ago after 45 people submitted a proposal to establish the protected area.
Tõnis Bramanis, one of the authors of the proposal, justified the need to protect the area partly by pointing out that it is home to one of Estonia's most important bat swarming sites.
"This is Tallinn's most species-rich amphibian habitat and, at the same time, the one in the best condition as far as we know. There are reptile habitats, various species of bumblebees and more than 40 species of butterflies. It is a very important part of Tallinn's green network," he said.
The proposed area will be 148.7 hectares, slightly smaller than the 157.7-hectare nature reserve first put forward. Bramanis said he saw no problem with the reduction.
"Much more important is that, for the first time, the draft specifically sets out options for acquiring properties and developing a support measure for landowners, which, in my opinion, makes the proposal considerably more credible," he said.
Attorney Indrek Veso, whose clients include one of the landowners in the area, is critical of the establishment of the nature reserve.
"Protecting such a large area is also unjustified because the Nõmme-Mustamäe Landscape Protection Area is located right next to it. We are going to have quite a lot of protected areas concentrated in one part of the city. In my opinion, this is neither justified nor proportionate, especially since the values supposedly being protected there are difficult to understand and grasp," Veso said.
Landowners will also face a number of additional restrictions within the protected area.
"Activities such as logging and property development will be prohibited — the main activities associated with the normal use, management and improvement of real estate," Veso added.
Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said reaching compromises with landowners has generally gone smoothly.
"Considering how many landowners there are — around 50 — naturally, when negotiating with 50 owners, there are different points of view. But I would say there have been no categorical objections where a landowner has said that under no circumstances would they agree to the establishment of the nature reserve," he said.

Ukraine’s access to Starlink a decision for Elon Musk, Rubio says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:54:12 UTC

Ukraine’s access to Starlink a decision for Elon Musk, Rubio says
US secretary of state says White House not to blame for reported speed limits on internet services in Ukraine.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio says decisions about Ukraine’s access to Starlink are in the hands of its parent company, SpaceX, and CEO Elon Musk, not the White House, in response to claims it was involved in restricting Kyiv’s access to satellite internet services.
Rubio’s comments on Wednesday may increase scrutiny of US decision-making to potentially throttle the high-tech system, which allows Kyiv to intercept incoming projectiles and target Russian launchers.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered a slowdown of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on for defence against Russian missile attacks.
The Journal quoted one person as saying Musk, US President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand and two people as saying Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown.
The Reuters news agency has quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter as saying the decision ultimately came from the White House.
This version was also confirmed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy but denied by the Trump administration.
‘Missions disrupted’
Zelenskyy adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on the Telegram messaging app on October 14 that SpaceX had imposed a limit of 160 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) on Starshield services. That affected guidance systems for drones that Ukraine uses to intercept Russian drones flying at far greater speeds.
“Our defence forces received no prior warning regarding this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence confirmed the resumption of services on October 15.
Rubio told reporters during a trip to India on Wednesday that he was not aware if the administration knew about the decision beforehand but said it was “irrelevant”.
“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” he said.
Musk had previously said on X that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS (President of the United States).”
Trump, asked by reporters on Wednesday whether Musk ordered the slowdown, said he did not know who did it but “I was not involved.”
Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Tuesday also portrayed the Starlink cutoff as a commercial matter.
“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” he said.
One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX’s Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon.
Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield while Zelenskyy has said both services had been disrupted in Ukraine.

Tesla's profit drops as it explores a possible merger with Musk's other public company, SpaceX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:53:00 UTC
14:53:00 KST

Tesla reported a decline in third-quarter profit, but generated more cash than analysts expected, leaving investors with a mixed picture as it explores a possible merger with Elon Musk's other big company, SpaceX.
Tesla reported lower third-quarter profits on Wednesday as Elon Musk's electric vehicle maker ramped up spending on artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous transport.
The electric vehicle maker reported third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $787 million (€701 million), or 22 cents per share, down 43% from the year-earlier period. Besides marginally lower car sales, Tesla saw a drop in revenues from regulatory credits and energy generation and storage.
Revenue was essentially flat at $28 billion (€24.9 billion), falling slightly short of the company-compiled average analyst forecast of $28.3 billion.
Excluding certain items, though, earnings per share of 48 cents beat Wall Street analyst expectations by 3 cents.
One standout for the quarter was Tesla's $1.5 billion (€1.3 billion) in free cash flow, a measure of cash generated after subtracting investments needed to keep the business running.
Given heavy spending on artificial intelligence, analysts had expected Tesla would report it had burned through cash, not generated it. However, free cash flow was still down 62% from a year earlier.
"It seems Tesla is taking a more capital-efficient approach, delaying longer-term projects to be able to self-fund their AI growth," said Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein, calling the unexpected positive cash flow the big surprise of the quarter.
Tesla is rolling back its annual spending forecast
The company also reported more than doubling capital spending from a year earlier to $4.7 billion (€4.2 billion) for the quarter, but analysts had expected a far bigger increase.
Tesla cut its full-year 2026 capital spending forecast to about $20 billion (€17.8 billion), from more than $25 billion (€22.3 billion). Chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said the company was managing its spending efficiently and planned to fund it mainly through operating cash flow.
Besides robotaxis and AI, Tesla is investing heavily in Musk's "Optimus" humanoid robots as well as developing Terafab, a chip manufacturing project in Austin, with SpaceX.
On the positive side, Tesla reported strong demand for its paid driver-assistance software, with more than 75% of new vehicles delivered in North America including a paid subscription sign-up.
The company calls the feature Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in North America. Despite its name, the software requires active driver supervision and does not make the vehicle autonomous.
Tesla's automotive gross margin, excluding regulatory credits, also improved. For the three months through September, it reached 18.1%, up from 15.4% a year earlier.
Tesla had previously reported delivering 486,532 vehicles last quarter, a rise from 480,126 in the prior three months, but down 2% from a year earlier.
The modest rise in deliveries from the previous quarter did not translate into higher net profit.
Musk said Tesla was aiming to produce about five million vehicles a year by around 2030, compared with approximately 1.65 million produced in 2025.
"After many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth," Musk said.
The company has faced questions about the rollout of its robotaxi business, which has fallen short of Musk's earlier ambitions.
In Texas, where Tesla has focused its robotaxi launch, more than 800 Tesla vehicles are registered for autonomous service, according to FSD Database.
Tesla shares were down 3.2% in after-hours trading after climbing 3.6% during the regular trading session.
SpaceX merger talks add to questions over Tesla's future
Questions about Tesla's future loomed larger with talk of the potential SpaceX tie-up. The companies have a combined stock market value of about $3.5 trillion (€3.1 trillion).
In a SpaceX conference call after that company reported earnings on Tuesday, Musk said both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to explore a possible merger. He said no terms had been agreed and there was no guarantee of a deal.
Merger speculation and SpaceX's strong results helped lift shares in both companies on Wednesday. Forbes estimated Musk's wealth at $1.013 trillion (€902 billion) at 10.30am New York time, putting him briefly back above the trillion-dollar mark.
Musk said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and satellite infrastructure, including space-based computing.
Musk declined to discuss the possible merger further on Tesla's conference call.

Kenichi Yoda, Princess of Asturias laureate: "Ghibli is closely tied to its time"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:49:09 UTC
14:49:09 KST

The new president of the legendary Japanese studio argues for pursuing beauty even when depicting horrors such as war. Yoda, Ghibli's figurehead in Oviedo, says they will keep tackling contemporary themes and concerns, just as its founders did.
A former reporter for the Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun, where early in his career he covered stories on the Ghibli animation studios, it seems highly unlikely that Kenichi Yoda (born 1974) imagined he would one day go on to head the company he had focused on as a culture journalist.
His rise to the summit of the legendary temple of animated cinema came on 22 June, when he took over the presidency from Hiroyuki Fukuda. His interview with 'Euronews' takes place 48 hours before he accepts, on behalf of his studio, the 2026 Princess of Asturias Award for Communication and Humanities.
The ideas of two of its creators, the late Isao Takahata and his colleague Hayao Miyazaki, together with the work of the roughly 200 people employed by the company, remain one of the main gateways into Japanese culture for millions of people around the globe.
That was the case with 'Marco' and 'Heidi' in Spain. The anime series were broadcast between the final throes of Francoism and the Transition to democracy, at a time when Ghibli had not even been conceived by this pair of film-makers, who met in a trade union while both were working at the Toei Doga studio in the 1960s. Those series were probably, with the exception of landmarks such as Akira Kurosawa's films, the first contact an entire generation of Spaniards had with the Land of the Rising Sun.
Yoda laughs when asked whether they see themselves as a tool of soft diplomacy or Japanese 'soft power'. "I think each work exists only because its directors and animators devoted themselves to it with care. We are very happy that, as a result, people all over the world watch it. But we are not doing it for diplomacy," the president says.
Ghibli and the terrible beauty of war
In 2026 it is inevitable to ask Yoda about one of the themes that most often recurs, alongside environmental protection, friendship or the strength of his female characters, in the scripts produced by his studio: armed conflict.
Takahata, a communist sympathiser, was an outspoken defender of Article 9 of his country's constitution and a convinced pacifist, whereas Miyazaki imbibed war from childhood: his family's company manufactured parts for military aircraft on the fascist side in the Second World War.
Both men bear witness to this obsession in animation classics such as 'Grave of the Fireflies', through 'Princess Mononoke' and 'Howl's Moving Castle', and up to 'The Wind Rises'. Is it still possible today, in a Japan allocating unprecedented shares of its GDP to its Self-Defence Forces and a Defence White Paper championed by far-right politician Sanae Takaichi, to go on making pacifist films?
Yoda sidesteps the issue with finesse. "How to address war is a very important topic for Studio Ghibli. Of course, it is better if there are no wars. But what I find admirable about Miyazaki as a director is that he too has been fascinated by the weapons used in war, or by fighter planes, by their beauty as objects, as forms. Of course, he has not the slightest sympathy for war. But there is in him a feeling he cannot resist: the attraction of those things as objects. And that is, in a way, something very human," he argues.
We also ask him about one of the studio's most quoted lines, spoken by the lead in 'Porco Rosso' (1992), in which he pronounces in a cinema that he would rather be a pig than a fascist. Would a line like that fit into a contemporary script room, whether at Ghibli or another studio? Once again, the executive chooses to dodge the question: he says he is very pleased that one of Emmanuel Macron's favourite films (recalling a statement the French president made during an official visit to Japan) is 'Porco Rosso', according to the interviewee.
The question of artificial intelligence also hangs over the Covadonga room at the Reconquista Hotel, where the Princess of Asturias Foundation traditionally lodges its laureates. It surfaces in connection with the famous viral clip of Miyazaki (source in Spanish) from 2016, in which he cuts down two developers from another company when they try to sell the genius a kind of proto-AI to be used in his drawings. "It is an insult to life itself," he snaps at them.
"Ten years on, in every interview without fail I am asked what Studio Ghibli thinks about AI," Yoda explains with resignation. "It is very difficult to predict how it will evolve, and I think we are all living in that uncertainty. But if there is something we can say right now, and I say this also in a personal capacity, it is this. Imagine two restaurants: one where the food is made by an AI and another where it is made by people. I would undoubtedly choose the second."
His team signals that we should end the interview, but the former journalist tells us he wants to add one last point. "Listening to your questions, I have realised that Ghibli is very closely bound up with its time (...) We debate every day what the studio can do in this era and what kind of era we are living in. In that sense, I have the feeling that we are creating something with restraint," he says.
"There is great honesty towards the act of artistic creation," he continues. "It is not a business plan: it is about thinking seriously about what response the studio gives to its time. That is now the studio's day-to-day reality. And it has probably always been that way." The next decade will show whether, after Miyazaki's generational handover, still active at 85, the emblematic studio manages to maintain its creative independence and ideals, having captivated millions of children and adults far beyond the Japanese islands.

DARPA wants smart nuclear reactor for space and bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:44:36 UTC
14:44:36 KST

- DARPA awarded SpaceNukes an agreement to ground-test a Kilopower nuclear reactor with active, autonomous control rods under its Fat Cat program.
- The team behind the 2018 KRUSTY reactor test will run the new test with Los Alamos National Laboratory.
The Pentagon’s top research agency wants a nuclear reactor that can run itself, and it has hired the team that built America’s last space reactor to prove it can be done. DARPA has awarded Space Nuclear Power Corporation, a small Los Alamos, New Mexico, company known as SpaceNukes, an agreement to build a Kilopower reactor with self-adjusting control rods and switch it on in a full nuclear ground test, the company announced on Oct. 21.
DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, was created in 1958 after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, with a mandate to make sure the United States would never again be caught off guard by a rival’s technology. The agency does not build weapons itself; it funds high-risk ideas that the military services and industry consider too uncertain to pay for, and its bets have included the ARPANET network that grew into the internet and early stealth aircraft research. The new work falls under a DARPA program called Fast Capacitance, or Fat Cat, run by program manager Tabitha Dodson in the agency’s Defense Sciences Office, which is looking for ways to let reactors operate on their own for national security missions.
The reactor at the center of the project has already worked once. Between November 2017 and March 2018, engineers from Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA ran a test called KRUSTY, short for Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology, at the Nevada National Security Site, powering up a reactor built around a solid cast uranium-235 core about the size of a paper towel roll. Sodium heat pipes carried heat from the core to Stirling engines that turned it into electricity, and the reactor ran at full power for about 28 hours while engineers deliberately cut power, shut down engines and disabled heat pipes to see whether it would keep going, which it did.
That test used a passive design, in which the reactor’s own physics kept it stable without moving parts adjusting the reaction. The new version will add active control rods that move to raise or lower the reactor’s output, giving it the ability to change power on demand and respond quickly to shifting needs, which SpaceNukes says opens the technology to a much wider range of missions. A reactor that manages itself matters most in places where no operator can reach it quickly, such as a spacecraft, a base on the Moon or a remote military outpost, where power needs can change suddenly and a human may be minutes or hours away.
“There is no substitute for demonstrated technology when American national security objectives are at stake,” said Andy Phelps, CEO of SpaceNukes. “This award lets us advance the work begun in the KRUSTY program and bring another tested capability forward for the nation.”
SpaceNukes is essentially the KRUSTY team reassembled as a company. Chief technology officer David Poston and chief operating officer Patrick McClure led the reactor work at Los Alamos, chief engineer Marc Gibson ran the program at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, and the company holds a license from Los Alamos for the Kilopower design. Gibson will lead integration of the new test hardware at the company’s workshop in Medina, Ohio, and the program will move through design, procurement and integration stages before the reactor goes critical in a joint test with Los Alamos.
“This award recognizes the maturity and continuity of the team that designed, built, and tested KRUSTY in 2018,” said Patrick McClure, chief operating officer of SpaceNukes.
The project lands as Washington is pushing hard to get reactors into space and onto military bases. A White House policy memo in April directed the Pentagon and NASA to compete designs for space reactors, with an orbital demonstration targeted as early as 2028 and a reactor on the Moon as early as 2030, while on the ground the U.S. Army has committed up to $2.2 billion to build nuclear microreactors at five military bases. The KRUSTY reactor was designed to deliver between 1 and 10 kilowatts of electricity continuously for at least a decade, and the DARPA test will produce flight-relevant hardware that has actually been run on nuclear power, along with the engineering basis for reactors that can control themselves.

Israeli forces and illegal settlers carried out 23 attacks and violations against Palestinian farmers, their lands and crops, as well as solidarity activists, across seven governorates in the occupied West Bank within 12 hours on Wednesday, a Palestinian commission said.
The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said in a statement that the incidents were recorded between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. local time (0300–1500 GMT), coinciding with the ongoing olive harvest season.
According to the commission, 10 incidents were documented in Nablus, six in Ramallah and Al-Bireh, two each in Salfit and Hebron, and one each in Qalqilya, Jenin and Bethlehem.
The violations included shootings, physical assaults, arrests, preventing farmers from harvesting olives, theft of crops and equipment, and the burning and bulldozing of agricultural land.
The commission said a Palestinian farmer was shot in the hand with live fire while harvesting olives in the village of Osarin in Nablus governorate.
Another farmer suffered severe breathing difficulties after being sprayed with pepper spray in the Wadi Abbas area of Qarawat Bani Hassan in Salfit governorate.
In the town of Nahalin, southwest of Bethlehem, Israeli forces attacked farmers and solidarity activists in the al-Habla area, arresting an elderly woman and several activists, including Brad Lander, a Democratic candidate for the US Congress, according to the commission.
Israeli forces also confiscated harvested olives during the incident.
The commission also reported the arrest of a Russian solidarity activist while participating in the olive harvest in the Christian town of Taybeh in the central West Bank, and a young Palestinian man while harvesting olives in Kafr ad-Dik in the north.
Israeli violence
In Nablus governorate, illegal Israeli settlers set fire to agricultural land in the town of Burqa, while Israeli bulldozers levelled olive-planted land in the Rajmanat area of Madama, the commission said.
Illegal settlers also attacked olive pickers near Jalud School and opened fire towards them before Israeli forces arrived and physically assaulted the farmers.
In Beit Furik, illegal settlers threw harvested olives onto the ground and seized crops at gunpoint, forcing families to leave their fields.
Similar incidents involving the theft of olives and agricultural equipment were reported in Qaryut, Awarta and Tell, while farmers were expelled from the Wadi Abuwayn area of al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya.
The commission said Israeli forces also pursued farmers in the al-Jiza area of Beita, preventing them from harvesting olives and opening fire in their direction.
In Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorate, farmers were prevented from accessing their lands in the al-Harayiq area of Deir Jarir.
Farmers, journalists and commission staff were also expelled from agricultural land in Turmus Ayya after Israeli forces declared the area a closed military zone.
Landowners were prevented from harvesting olives in al-Mughayyir, while illegal settlers brought livestock onto olive-planted land in Burqa and Kafr Malik.
Daily struggle
In the southern Hebron governorate, armed Israeli settlers opened fire towards olive pickers in the Birin area, while farmers and activists were prevented from harvesting in Idhna, according to the commission.
In Qalqilya governorate, illegal settlers cut down olive trees in the town of Farata, east of the city.
Meanwhile, farmers in Deir Abu Daif, east of Jenin, were forced to leave their lands despite having obtained prior coordination and approval to access them.
The commission said the incidents reflected a combination of direct attacks, military closures, arrests and crop confiscations that have turned access to farmland into a daily struggle for Palestinian farmers.
It warned that expelling landowners and targeting solidarity activists and journalists undermines efforts to protect the olive harvest and document violations.
The commission called for effective measures to ensure farmers’ safe and continuous access to their lands and accountability for those responsible for the attacks.
Attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their agricultural lands have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began in early October and provides a vital source of income for thousands of Palestinian families.
According to Palestinian figures, approximately 750,000 illegal Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, across 194 settlements and around 400 settlement outposts.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian territory are illegal under international law.
Palestinian, Israeli and international human rights organisations have repeatedly accused Israeli authorities of failing to prevent attacks by illegal settlers or hold those responsible accountable, despite repeated assaults on Palestinians, their homes, farmland and property.

"Such programs can help young people develop professional skills and acquire the qualifications they need for employment," Kalandarova said.

BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China on Thursday released a five-year plan to accelerate upgrading of its industrial foundation capabilities, in a further step toward building an innovation-driven manufacturing powerhouse.
The document, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and other government departments, calls for integrated efforts in technological breakthroughs and their application, addressing weaknesses in China's industrial foundation systematically, and achieving a comprehensive upgrade toward stronger innovation, greater self-reliance and higher quality.
Industrial foundation, the bedrock of manufacturing competitiveness, covers a range of areas including core components, basic materials and foundational software, as well as related talents, market conditions and the policy environment.
While China has built the world's largest and most complete industrial system over the past decades, its industrial foundation remains a weak link, experts said.
"The most critical issue is that China's industrial foundation is large but not strong," said Zhou Ji, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering. He pointed to a structural imbalance, namely an oversupply of low-end products alongside a shortage of high-end ones.
Vulnerabilities and risks persist particularly in areas like integrated circuits and industrial software, Zhou noted.
As China pursues high-quality economic development and advances its new industrialization drive, the strengthening and upgrading of its industrial foundation has become increasingly critical.
According to the plan issued on Thursday, the weaknesses in China's industrial foundation will be significantly alleviated by 2030, while China's overall industrial foundation capabilities will reach internationally advanced levels, thereby providing strong support for building a modern industrial system anchored in advanced manufacturing.
A new cohort of single-champion manufacturers and "little giant" specialized enterprises in the industrial foundation sector should also be cultivated by then, the plan says. ■
