World Insights: Protests reflect France's economic, fiscal dilemmas
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:42:58 CST
14:42:58 KST

PARIS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- France has been shaken by a wave of protests that began in classrooms and spilled onto the streets. What started as student anger over crumbling schools, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages has escalated into violent unrest in several regions.
Soon other groups, angered by soaring energy bills, a cost-of-living squeeze and deteriorating public services, joined the protests. Beneath the disorder lie deeper, intertwined pressures: feeble growth, shrinking fiscal room for manoeuvre and a welfare model under strain, all of which highlight the acute economic and fiscal challenges confronting France.
COST-OF-LIVING SQUEEZE
Soaring fuel prices are one of the drivers behind this concentrated outburst of public anger.
Buffeted by turbulence in global energy markets, French energy prices have kept climbing. The rise has not merely lifted household bills for transport and everyday living; it has also rippled through supply chains and production costs, pushing up prices across the wider economy and further tightening family budgets.
Data released by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) on Oct. 15 showed that France's consumer prices rose by 3.1 percent year-on-year in September, up from 2.4 percent in August. The acceleration was mainly driven by faster increases in energy prices, which surged 21.3 percent year-on-year in September, up from 16.7 percent in August.
For French residents who rely on cars for daily commutes, fuel is an unavoidable routine expense. In 2018, a fuel tax hike triggered the nationwide "yellow vest" movement. Years later, fuel prices becoming the focal point of public discontent once again demonstrates that certain long-standing issues affecting people's livelihoods have not been fundamentally resolved.
Sluggish economic growth has further eroded citizens' ability to cope with the rising cost of living. According to INSEE data, the French economy contracted by 0.2 percent in the first quarter of this year, posted zero growth in the second quarter, and household purchasing power per consumption unit declined by 0.6 percent in the second quarter.
LIVELIHOODS VS FISCAL CONSOLIDATION
High public debt and rising borrowing costs leave the French government with limited fiscal leeway to address social grievances.
INSEE data indicates that by the end of the second quarter of this year, France's public debt stood at 119 percent of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Meanwhile, yields on government bonds have continued to climb. French radio station Europe 1 reported that the yield on France's 10-year government bonds exceeded the symbolic 5 percent threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. Rising financing costs will increase the government's debt servicing burden, squeezing space for other public expenditures.
The French government estimates that interest payments on public debt will rise from 79.2 billion euros (88.96 billion U.S. dollars) this year to 91.2 billion euros next year.
Substantial social protection spending also complicates fiscal consolidation efforts. Data show that in 2024, French social protection benefits expenditure accounted for 31.9 percent of GDP, higher than the European Union average of 27.3 percent. As population aging accelerates, spending on pensions, healthcare and related areas faces sustained pressure.
The French government finds itself in a dilemma: on the one hand, in response to rising energy prices and calls to improve public services, it needs to provide subsidies, adjust taxes, and increase public spending; on the other, heavy debt burdens, rising interest expenses, and pressures for fiscal consolidation constrain its ability to expand expenditure.
UNREST-FUELING ECONOMIC RISKS
The protests and violent riots have damaged shops, public buildings, and infrastructure across France. The government estimates that around 3,000 businesses nationwide have been directly affected, with economic losses likely to reach hundreds of millions of euros.
In the longer run, persistent social unrest could also undermine consumer and investment confidence, dragging down an already fragile French economy. The OFCE, an independent economic research institute affiliated with Sciences Po in Paris, released a report on Oct. 14 forecasting that the French economy would grow by 0.4 percent in 2026 and 0.5 percent in 2027, noticeably below the eurozone average. If social unrest intensifies further, it could place additional strain on economic performance.
At the same time, social turmoil creates greater political headwinds for fiscal consolidation. As the 2027 presidential election approaches, debates over public services, social welfare, fiscal austerity and governance are growing increasingly fierce.
Divergent views among political forces on the root causes of social conflicts and their solutions make it harder for the government to build consensus to cut spending and rein in deficits.
On Oct. 19, Gilles Moec, chief economist at French insurance group Axa, told French daily Le Monde that while France's debt problem was serious but manageable, political instability could significantly aggravate the situation.
The deep-seated economic and social contradictions behind these protests cannot be resolved solely through short-term measures. Striking a balance between easing livelihood pressures, restoring economic growth, and managing public debt remains a long-term challenge for the French government. ■

Colombian frontline police unaware of new AFP anti-drug taskforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:38:51 UTC
14:38:51 KST

Colombia's frontline anti-drug police unaware of new AFP international taskforce
In short:
Two Colombian National Police departments say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce, based in Bogotá.
Five months after the taskforce's announcement, the departments say drug-related intelligence has not been shared and no substance seizures or arrests have been made in cooperation with the AFP.
The AFP says the taskforce is not yet operational, but agreements have been made that would allow it to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".
Two police departments on the frontline of Colombia's fight against cartels say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce based in the South American nation.
In May, Commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the AFP and New Zealand Police would fund an international joint investigations team (IJIT) "to gather evidence about illicit drug shipments".
The team would include AFP officers in the capital Bogotá, working with Colombian, US, INTERPOL and Mexican authorities to curb the flow of drugs through the Pacific to Australia, the commissioner said.
A joint investigation by the ABC and the Colombian newspaper El Tiempo can reveal the anti-narcotics department of Colombia's National Police (PNC) has no recorded data that shows subscribed "protocols, agreements, or procedures" relating to the IJIT.
In a response to a freedom of information request filed by El Tiempo and shared with the ABC, the department said drug-related intelligence had not been shared with the AFP and no "operational activities" such as illicit substance seizures or arrests had been made in cooperation with Australian police as part of the IJIT.
The department also said there was currently only a "letter of intent" outlining a "framework for cooperation and exchange of information", which the ABC understands was signed jointly by PNC Major General Jesús Alejandro Barrera Peña and the AFP in August.
"The instrument does not identify the so-called 'IJIT', nor does it establish specific functions, responsibilities or procedures for this department in relation to said mechanism," the department said.
The letter made no connection between the IJIT and joint drug seizures, destruction of narcotics production infrastructure, disruption of criminal groups or the identification of international trafficking routes, the department said.
The ABC understands the IJIT agreement was made with — and expected to be overseen by — the PNC's Office of International Relations and Cooperation (ORECI) and not the anti-narcotics department.
ORECI coordinates Colombia's international policing efforts by connecting other PNC departments to global counterparts, such as the AFP.
The department focuses on strategic decision-making and intelligence and sits above the anti-narcotics and criminal investigations agencies, which oversee frontline drug and domestic crime policing operations.
An AFP spokesperson told the ABC the IJIT was not yet operational, but an "annex" agreement was made with the PNC in August in addition to the letter of intent that would allow the taskforce to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".
The AFP did not specify when the IJIT would become operational.
In a separate response shared with the ABC, the PNC's criminal investigations department said it had no data that was able to determine whether the AFP was involved, supported, funded or shared intelligence in 174 drug trafficking investigations conducted between January 1, 2025 and October 6 this year.
The department said those figures were collated based on aggregate numbers of cases and investigations outcomes that did not list specific agencies involved.
But the department also said it had no knowledge of Colombian anti-narcotics intelligence being used to "identify, locate, track, monitor or intercept" suspected drug trafficking vessels in the Pacific Ocean or Caribbean Sea as part of the IJIT.
The revelations follow ABC questions posed to the AFP in June about the IJIT's allocated budget, operational commitments and measure of how it would be deemed successful, as part of a separate Freedom of Information request.
In response, the AFP said it had 60 documents that would answer the questions.
The AFP declined to release them, citing national security and international relations concerns, and said at the time that the IJIT was "still in the negotiation phase".
It also said publishing the information would be harmful to relations between Australia and Colombia, or could divulge confidential details regarding how AFP officers operate.
In this year's federal budget, more than $1.16 million was allocated to the AFP for "ordinary annual services" in policing assistance efforts abroad and on Australian external territories in 2026-27.
That figure is expected to rise to $1.4 million next year, before dropping to $1.01 million and $1.03 million in the following two years.
But the budget does not detail how much is set aside specifically for the IJIT.
Commissioner Barrett said 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, have been seized by "local and international" police since January this year and stopped from reaching Australia through the Pacific.
The ABC understands, to July this year, most of the offshore seizures were made in French Polynesia, AFP officers were not physically involved in any interceptions and none were in Australian territorial waters.
The PNC this month announced an Australian-Iranian national, Arash Ebrahimi Far, was detained in Colombia as a subject of an INTERPOL Red Notice for alleged drug trafficking and money laundering, which was not believed to be related to the IJIT.

On October 21, Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that President Donald Trump or anyone in the US government had requested changes to the systems. But a congressional delegation that recently visited Kyiv said the restrictions had impaired Ukrainian air defenses and put American personnel at risk.
Disruptions to the Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of the Starlink service operated by SpaceX on which Kyiv heavily relies to defend against Russian air strikes, has left Ukraine particularly vulnerable since they were first reported on October 13-14.
Russia launched fresh overnight attacks on Kyiv on October 21, killing one person and injuring at least 22 others, including four children, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. Missiles reportedly struck homes, an ambulance station, and a petrol station as diplomatic efforts to restart peace talks continued.
"Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian 'humanism' truly sounds like," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X. "Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will," he added.
Air Defenses Impaired
Dan Rice, a former special adviser to the commander in chief of Ukraine's armed forces and current president of American University Kyiv, told RFE/RL that several separate issues had become entangled in the controversy: intelligence-sharing, satellite speed restrictions, and deliveries of Patriot air-defense interceptors.
Rice said he believed Rubio was referring to intelligence-sharing when he insisted the United States had not interrupted assistance to Ukraine.
"The intel was shared," Rice said, adding that a technical glitch had prevented air-raid alerts from reaching people's phones. "If Secretary Rubio says there was no interruption of intel -- I believe him."
The distinction matters because continued intelligence-sharing does not necessarily mean satellite connectivity was unaffected.
During an October 21 briefing, a Senate Democratic aide who had recently returned from Kyiv said the delegation witnessed Russian drones and missiles approaching the capital with unusually limited advance warning.
The aide said the Starshield restrictions were in effect during the October 13-16 visit and that the delegation's assessment was they had endangered both Ukrainian civilians and US personnel.
Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which can travel at 280 miles per hour or faster, have posed a particular challenge. Starshield speed limits were reportedly initially set at about 60 miles per hour and later at 100 miles per hour, meaning the system could lose connectivity with faster-moving objects.
Rubio Denies US Role
Speaking in Mumbai on October 21, Rubio stressed that Starlink and Starshield are separate systems.
Starlink is a commercial satellite-Internet service that can also be used to guide drones, he said, while Starshield is a specialized defense product sold and operated through the US Defense Department.
Rubio said he had not read The Wall Street Journal report alleging that Musk ordered the slowdown. He denied Trump or other US officials had requested changes or had advance knowledge of the decision.
Neither "the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made," Rubio said.
He argued that the government could not dictate how a private company manages a commercial product, while acknowledging that Starshield operates under different arrangements because it is procured for government use.
Congress Demands Answers
Democrats and some Republicans have called for investigations into the slowdown.
Senator Adam Schiff of California said in a social media post the conflicting accounts warranted a full Senate investigation and called for Musk to testify under oath. Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona also urged Musk to explain the decision voluntarily.
Senator Chris Coons of Delaware said Musk should not have the power to influence the outcome of a war "with the flip of a switch," while Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts warned of the risks of a private executive effectively dictating US foreign policy.
Representative Ami Bera, a California Democrat, said the slowdown had "crippled Ukrainian defenses and endangered innocent lives," calling on Congress to establish who authorized it and hold those responsible accountable. Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania has also called for an investigation.
Separately, a bipartisan group of nearly two dozen House members has urged Trump to press Musk to allow Ukraine to use Starlink to target Russian missile-launch sites inside Russia.
"If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian 'arrows,' it must be able to shoot the 'archer,'" the lawmakers wrote in a letter sent on October 21, arguing that Ukraine needs the ability to destroy the launchers used to attack its cities.
The initiative was led by Republican Representative Joe Wilson of South Carolina and included seven Republicans and 16 Democrats. The lawmakers said granting Ukraine greater access could save lives and give Russian President Vladimir Putin greater incentives to negotiate.
The Senate delegation also raised concerns about other delays in US assistance, including Patriot interceptors reportedly paid for by NATO allies but not yet transferred to Ukraine. The aide said the committee had approved several third-party transfers but had not seen the interceptors reach Ukrainian inventories.

Pentagon extends Raytheon deal for missile defense radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:33:32 UTC
14:33:32 KST

- The Missile Defense Agency extended Raytheon’s AN/TPY-2 radar sustainment contract by two years, raising its ceiling from $2.6 billion to nearly $3 billion.
- The ordering period now runs to Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million obligated at award.
The Missile Defense Agency has extended Raytheon’s contract to operate and maintain the U.S. military’s AN/TPY-2 missile defense radars for two more years, adding $394 million to the deal and lifting its ceiling to nearly $3 billion, the Department of War announced.
The sole-source modification raises the maximum value of the contract from about $2.6 billion to $2.999 billion and keeps the ordering period open until Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million in fiscal 2027 operations and maintenance, research and development, and procurement funds obligated at the time of award.
The AN/TPY-2 is a transportable X-band radar that sits at the heart of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, better known as THAAD, and also serves as a standalone early warning sensor for U.S. ballistic missile defense. The radar can work in two ways: deployed far forward to spot ballistic missiles shortly after launch and pass tracking data to other defenses, or as part of a THAAD battery to track an incoming warhead and guide interceptors to hit it as it descends.
Under the extension, Raytheon will continue to run and support the radars from its facility in Woburn, Massachusetts, and at radar sites in the United States and overseas, where the company’s field teams help keep the sensors operating around the clock. The work combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price contract items, and the Missile Defense Agency at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is also extending the task orders that fund individual radar sites.
The U.S. Army fields eight THAAD batteries, each with one AN/TPY-2 radar, including units at Fort Bliss, Texas, in South Korea and on Guam, while forward-based radars have been stationed at sites including the Shariki area in Japan, Türkiye, Israel and Qatar. The radar is also sold abroad, and in 2020 the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon a production contract worth up to $2.3 billion for seven AN/TPY-2 radars for Saudi Arabia, built with gallium nitride components that extend the radar’s range and sensitivity.
The radars have come under direct fire during the war with Iran this year, and satellite images analyzed by CNN showed that a THAAD radar at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan was apparently destroyed by an Iranian strike in early March, along with damage at radar sites near Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and in the United Arab Emirates. Each AN/TPY-2 costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes years to build, which makes keeping the existing fleet working a priority for the Missile Defense Agency while new radars are produced.
The original contract was awarded to Raytheon on a sole-source basis in 2018 as the radar’s designer and builder, and the extension was likewise issued without competition. The new ordering period gives the Missile Defense Agency two more years to keep the current support arrangement in place before it decides how to handle long-term sustainment of the AN/TPY-2 fleet beyond October 2028.

British submarine hunters delayed by Norway frigate sale
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:30:04 BST
14:30:04 KST

The Royal Navy will not meet its requirement for eight frigates fitted with the Sonar 2087 towed array until 2037 if two Type 26 frigates being built for Britain are sold to Norway, and the government appears to have taken a conscious decision to prioritise defence exports over sovereign capability, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, published its findings following an inquiry that took evidence between March and July this year and included visits to Norway, Denmark and Greenland.
Dhesi said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
The report states: “Analysis suggests (Figure 4) Sonar 2087-towed array equipped frigate numbers could remain as low as five vessels for the next three years. This assumes two Type 26 frigates being built for the Royal Navy are sold to Norway, as the latter has ordered at least five Type 26s for £10 billion—which the government says will sustain 4,000 UK jobs. This reinforces the government’s goal to use defence exports to contribute to its Plan for Change, based around its three foundations of good government: economic stability, secure borders and national security.
However, Norway wants its first ship in service by 2029–30. Based on this scenario the Royal Navy will take until 2037 to meet its requirement for eight frigates to be equipped with the Sonar 2087 towed array sensor. In this case the government seems to have taken a conscious decision to prioritise defence exports over sovereign capability.”
A chart published with the report shows the combined Type 23 and Type 26 anti-submarine frigate line falling to two vessels in 2031 before recovering to eight by 2037.
Norway selected the Type 26 in 2025 to replace its Fridtjof Nansen class, in an agreement the Ministry of Defence valued at £10 billion and said would sustain four thousand British jobs. The ships are being built by BAE Systems at Govan and Scotstoun on the Clyde, and Britain’s own order is for eight.
The committee elsewhere records that the Royal Navy has a requirement for eight of its thirteen frigates to carry the Sonar 2087 towed array, that all five remaining Type 23 frigates are fitted with it, and that HMS Richmond and HMS Iron Duke were both decommissioned in mid-2026.
On the wider relationship with Norway, the report describes the 2025 Lunna House agreement and the Type 26 purchase as “therefore strategically more significant than a conventional defence export”, and says a joint class of British and Norwegian anti-submarine frigates “should improve NATO’s ability to detect and track Russian submarines moving from the High North into the North Atlantic”.
The committee’s recommendation asks the government to set out how major naval export programmes, including the Norway agreement and any future uncrewed maritime systems, will support High North deterrence while protecting Royal Navy capabilities, including an assessment of their effect on British delivery timelines, industrial capacity, shared training, sustainment, interoperability and the availability of critical anti-submarine warfare capabilities.
In written evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence described anti-submarine warfare as a core strength of Britain’s armed forces. The government is expected to respond to the report within two months.

U.S. Navy pays Johns Hopkins to find its subs’ weak spots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:28:03 UTC
14:28:03 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Johns Hopkins APL a contract worth up to $47.7 million to study vulnerabilities of submarines and seabed warfare assets.
- The work supports the Navy’s Undersea Security Program and runs through October 2031, managed by Strategic Systems Programs.
The U.S. Navy has hired the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory to look for weaknesses that adversaries could exploit against American submarines and other assets used in subsea and seabed warfare, under a contract worth up to $47.7 million announced by the Department of War on Oct. 21.
The laboratory in Laurel, Maryland, will provide research and development support for the Navy’s Undersea Security Program, studying both present and future technological and operational vulnerabilities, with work running until October 2031.
The contract went to the lab through full and open competition under a Broad Agency Announcement, and it is managed by the Navy’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive Strategic Systems Programs in Washington, D.C., the office that runs the Trident II D5 missile carried by the Navy’s ballistic missile submarines. About 80 percent of the work will take place at the laboratory in Laurel and the rest in Washington, and the Navy obligated only $50,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at the time of award, with the remaining money to come through future task funding.
Keeping submarines hidden has been one of the core missions of the Applied Physics Laboratory for decades, since the Navy’s work on ballistic missile submarine security began with a 1968 Pentagon directive to investigate how vulnerable the boats were to detection. That effort grew into a long-running program that studies how a submarine could be found through sound, wakes, magnetic signatures, radar and infrared sensors, as well as through predictable patrol routines and lapses in operational security, and the laboratory has supported the Navy’s development of patrol tactics for its nuclear deterrent fleet.
The new contract widens that focus to the seabed, where cables, pipelines, sensors and other infrastructure have become a growing concern for NATO navies. Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, known as GUGI, operates specialized submarines and deep-diving vehicles able to work on the ocean floor, and Western officials have accused Russian vessels of mapping undersea cables in European waters, while several Baltic Sea cables were damaged in incidents blamed on ships dragging their anchors.
The work also comes as the Navy prepares to replace its Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines with the new Columbia class, the most expensive shipbuilding program in its history, and in November 2025 General Dynamics Electric Boat received a $2.28 billion contract modification for advance work on five more Columbia-class boats. The first Columbia-class submarine is now tracking for delivery in 2028, and the new boats are expected to carry the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent into the 2080s.
The Applied Physics Laboratory is one of the Pentagon’s largest university-affiliated research centers, and its defense work has been expanding quickly, with DARPA awarding the lab a sole-source contract worth up to $499.8 million for engineering and research work just a week earlier. The Undersea Security Program contract combines cost-plus-fixed-fee and cost-no-fee work, and the specific tasks the laboratory will carry out over the next five years will be set through individual funding actions by the Navy.

Saturday will see variable cloud cover, with rain expected across most of Latvia during the night.
 However, the weather will become mostly dry during the day.
Light to moderate southeasterly and easterly winds will persist. Nighttime temperatures will fall to between +6°C and +10°C, while daytime temperatures will climb to +12°C to +14°C.

The forum aims to strengthen sustainable cooperation among think tanks, promote the exchange of expertise and develop practical recommendations on key regional development issues.
Discussions are centered on four main areas: high-quality development and joint modernization; sustainable regional integration and the circular economy; innovation and artificial intelligence; and human capital development and humanitarian cooperation.

Inside Ukraine's secret counteroffensive in heavily fortified Donbas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:22:15 UTC
14:22:15 KST

Inside Ukraine's secret counteroffensive in heavily fortified Donbas
Soldiers from the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment Kraken, who go by their callsigns "Cooper" and "Admin," prepare to launch a Darts mid-range strike drone in Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Lisa Bukreyeva / The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: Most of the Ukrainian soldiers and commanders interviewed are identified by their callsigns, in accordance with military protocols.
KHARKIV OBLAST — Ukrainian soldier Oleksandr had already narrowly survived crossing a mine-strewn field and a river in the crosshairs of Russian artillery when the swarm of first-person-view (FPV) drones began hunting him.
"If I'm honest, I was convinced they were going to kill us," the 37-year-old told the Kyiv Independent while chain-smoking cigarettes in the safety of his base in Kharkiv Oblast.
"I was already like, 'everyone goodbye, I love you all, everything is good,' but (the commanders were saying) on the radio, 'don't even think about it, everything will be fine.'"
Oleksandr was part of Operation Vivaldi, which is still ongoing and, until recently, was a top-secret counteroffensive in the Lyman sector in the northern part of Donetsk Oblast.
By pushing forward this spring, Ukrainian brigades under the Third Army Corps aimed to improve defensive positions in the area, which is critical to holding on to the remaining Ukrainian-held strongholds in the Donbas ahead of the winter, multiple commanders who took part said.
As well as liberating 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) of land and 16 villages as of Oct. 14, the operation proved something potentially even more important — that on today's drone-saturated and largely stalemated front line, it's still possible for Ukraine's infantry to advance in significant numbers.
But that does not mean it was easy.
read also
Crossing the river
The first task was making it through a dense minefield. Survive that, and then there was the river to cross. Survive that, and there was a chance the village of Shandryholove could be liberated from Russian forces.
The first group of three soldiers that attempted the crossing barely made it, Battalion Commander Sergii Galchenko said. Two groups that followed were forced to turn back after setting off mines.
"The enemy couldn't figure out where we were."
Those that made it needed reinforcing as soon as possible, no easy task when the few wooden bridges crossing it were destroyed, and Russian drones and artillery monitored the area constantly.
The soldiers initially waded through the water, but used wood and logs to create a makeshift crossing, according to Galchenko.
"We had a very serious problem with logistics when it came to bringing in our own reinforcements," Galchenko, who goes by his callsign "Psycho," said at his command post not far from the front.
The best way to stay alive was to keep moving, not staying in one place long enough for Russian drones and artillery to zero in on their positions.
"The enemy couldn't figure out where we were," Galchenko said.
Galchenko's battalion was assigned to enter Shandryholove from the south and move northward, clearing the central street as they went.
Two tactics proved vital — using drones wherever possible, and using a blockade tactic whereby infantry sneaked behind Russian lines to isolate Moscow's troops from the rear and block their escape.
read also
Taking Shandryholove
Taking Shandryholove — a village only 0.17 square kilometers (0.066 square miles) in size — took more than a month.
"The enemy heavily mined (the area), abnormally heavily, because it understood that it couldn't stop us any other way," Galchenko said.
Anti-personnel mines were everywhere and accounted for 80% of casualties, Galchenko said, without disclosing the total number of Ukrainian casualties during the operation.
To minimize the risk to Ukrainian lives while advancing, the most important thing for the commanders was to rely on drones as much as possible, striking Russian positions ahead of the advancing troops. Soldiers on the ground would then go in to look for survivors.
"We did everything we could to prevent the infantry from encountering the enemy there," Galchenko said.
The silent start
Units of the 66th Brigade advanced northward along the treeline toward heavily mined Shandryholove. The village had long been destroyed by years of heavy fighting in the area.
Oleksandr, who goes by his callsign "Marine," was in the first group of three soldiers to enter.
It was eerily quiet at first. The trio cleared a building as instructed and were approaching a church when they were spotted likely by a Russian FPV drone. A swarm soon followed.
For around four hours, the trio ran in zig-zags through the ruins of the village in a desperate attempt to avoid the drones above, while trying to stick to the concrete streets to avoid the mines below.
All three survived, but were not unscathed — one drone slammed into a door that Oleksandr had slammed shut behind him, peppering them all with shrapnel and dealing each a concussion.
The challenge in liberating Shandryholove was that Russian troops had prepared an extensive underground defensive network, primarily utilizing basements.
With the houses mostly destroyed in the village, it was difficult to assess from drone footage whether there was a basement under all the rubble, according to a company commander of the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade, who goes by his callsign "Ed." He estimated that there were about 50 houses in Shandryholove.
Instead of storming straight into Shandryholove, the majority of Ukraine's troops advanced along the treelines around the village to cut off the Russian troops inside, according to Ed. He said that his 125th Brigade moved roughly in parallel with other Ukrainian units, including the 66th and 60th mechanized brigades, with one advancing at a time and the others then playing catch-up.
What helped initially was that Russian troops in the village had been worn out by the cold weather when the offensive began, with some appearing to have died from exposure, Ed said.
"This really played in our favor," he added.
read also
Beyond Shandryholove
Shandryholove was just one of many such tiny villages that needed to be liberated for the counteroffensive to succeed. In between them, Ukrainian forces advanced along treelines, continuously changing the timing and routes of assaults to keep Russia's troops guessing.
Sometimes the soldiers would move in the dead of night, wearing anti-thermal blankets, while on other days they would switch it up to the gray hour before sunrise or daytime, according to Ed.
The pace of advance varied day to day. Galchenko said that his soldiers from the 66th could advance two kilometers (1.2 miles) in a day, while sometimes it took four days to advance 200 meters.
The vanguard of the advance was made up of soldiers sent usually in pairs to conduct the blockade maneuver, sneaking behind enemy lines to block logistics and prevent Russian infantry from being reinforced or running away to the rear, according to "Judo," a battalion commander with the 60th Mechanized Brigade.
The dense spring foliage in the forest served as a double-edged sword. This helped the infantry hide from Russian drones, but also made it difficult for friendly drones to conduct reconnaissance of the area.
It was crucial for the infantry to serve as the "ears," letting their commanders know where they heard voices and movement.
Galchenko stressed that it was important to enter the Russian positions quietly so the Russian soldiers inside wouldn't have time to warn their higher-ups that the Ukrainians were advancing.
"They knew that the quieter we entered, the more chance that the enemy would not be able to pass on (the information) to his higher-ups."
"We knew that the quieter we entered, the greater the chance the enemy would not be able to pass on (the information) to his higher-ups that we are advancing," Galchenko said.
"Then we have more chance to advance without any (potentially dangerous) moments."
As the 66th and 125th brigades were working on liberating neighboring Shandryholove in spring, the 60th was tasked to move behind the smaller village of Derylove to the south to cut it off so another unit could retake it, Judo said. When trying to infiltrate, the objective was to establish a defensive line inside Russian-held territory by carefully sending in one group after another, he explained.
The commander told his unit that they should only open fire if they were fully certain that they could kill Russian soldiers, waiting until they got as close as five meters.
"The enemy was moving through what he believed was his territory, and our group let the enemy in and completely destroyed them," Judo said.
"Their bodies were then camouflaged, in order for the enemy not to detect our group by finding the bodies of its soldiers from drones."
The soldiers would try to penetrate five kilometers (3.1 miles) into the Russian rear. He admitted that 30 to 40 percent of the time the soldiers would still be spotted by drones, then had to shoot the drones down themselves or rely on their unit to deploy countermeasures remotely.
Despite the risks, Judo said the operation went successfully, with the unit taking "minimal" casualties. He believes that there would have been many more casualties if the positional war had continued and his unit had remained on the defensive.
Evacuating the wounded
Russian troops responded differently to the Ukrainian offensive each day. Russia could react with an extremely heavy barrage of artillery and drone strikes, and by scattering mines, but it could also suddenly go quiet for a couple of days, according to Ed.
Stepping on a mine was the most common cause of injury, followed by FPV strikes, and then gunshot wounds, Ed said.
"On one day there could be up to two mine blasts, and then three days without any," Ed said.
Evacuation proved to be difficult, and the mines that injured advancing troops were also a threat to those that tried to rescue them. They were difficult to spot in the long grass that had appeared with the arrival of spring.
Ed recalled one incident when a soldier was dragging a wounded comrade on a stretcher when it struck a mine, killing the wounded man.
Much has been made of the rapid advances in unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and their potential for evacuations on the battlefield, but during Operation Vivaldi, their slow speed made them prime targets for Russian drones, according to several commanders.
"If Russia sees a UGV, then I will say that there is a very high probability — 90% — that it will try to hit it," Galchenko said.
Galchenko recalled one incident when six Ukrainian soldiers were running across a field to assault a forested area when they were attacked with about 35 fiber-optic FPV drones, 12 fixed-wing Molniya drones, and heavy artillery over the course of two hours.
One appeared to have been killed outright and the other five were injured, one so severely that commanders monitoring the assault via a drone feed thought he was dead. When he regained consciousness, a UGV was sent in to bring him back without the need to send another soldier into an area already the target of so much Russian fire.
After struggling aboard, the wounded soldier made it around 1,500 meters away from the front line when a Russian drone struck, killing him.
read also
Friendly drones
Away from the fighting on the ground, another critical aspect of Operation Vivaldi was Ukraine's middle-strike drone capability, which hammered Russian logistics about 200 kilometers (124 miles) away.
For the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment Kraken, the targets included ammunition depots, repair bases, and fuel storage sites in occupied territories of Luhansk Oblast, according to "Dolyna," one of the unit's high-ranking commanders.
"(Russian troops) were demoralized."
He linked the quieter days mentioned by Ed to successful strikes on Russian ammunition depots which, at least temporarily, deprived Russian artillery of shells.
Perhaps more crucially, these strikes helped deprive Russian infantry of the basic things they needed to survive — food, water, and ammunition.
"(Russian troops) were demoralized," Dolyna said at a middle-strike drone launch site in Kharkiv Oblast.
"It's hard to stay motivated when you are cold, hungry, and have nothing to keep you warm."
Operation Vivaldi
Operation Vivaldi had retaken 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) of territory, including 16 settlements, as of Oct. 14, according to the Third Army Corps. The unit claimed that Russian forces had suffered around 8,000 personnel losses, with over 250 soldiers captured by Ukraine as of this month. The Kyiv Independent couldn't independently verify the claimed battlefield figures.
Ukraine's casualty ratio compared to Russia's has been one to seven, with the majority of Ukrainian losses being injuries while Russia faced more fatalities, Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, the corps' commander, claimed during a briefing, as cited by Ukrainian media Hromadske.
When announcing the end of the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi, Biletskyi said, "four seasons of 'Vivaldi' are over, but the music continues," signaling that the counteroffensive would go on for now.
Commanders believe that Ukraine has already achieved its main objective of the counteroffensive and expect the pace of the counteroffensive to gradually slow, particularly with the arrival of winter.
"(Going on the offensive) is in our blood," Judo said.
"We don't have any intention of withdrawing or retreating. Our only goal is to fight for our territory."

Here's a roundup of our coverage from India on Thursday, October 22:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Google, Mozilla, Apple block certificates by Indian company over security flaw
Bengaluru-based digital identity and cybersecurity company eMudhra has revoked eight intermediate certificates after their private keys were found to be weak, prompting Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft to block the affected certificates.
"Eight intermediate (issuing) CAs in our Global TLS business were revoked because their published keys were weak," the company said, adding that it was investigating the issue.
A certificate authority (CA) is an organization that browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Safari rely on to verify website identities and establish secure connections.
The flaw could have allowed attackers to impersonate legitimate websites using fraudulent certificates and potentially intercept or manipulate supposedly secure online communications. However, no evidence of such misuse has been publicly confirmed.
The flaw originated in a key-generation process in April 2025 that produced weak private keys, the company said.
Media reports citing security researcher Scott Helme said one of the keys was the number four, rather than a cryptographically secure, randomly generated number, while others were also easily guessable.
India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) said it had taken serious note of the incident.
"A special team has been constituted to investigate the matter," the ministry said in a statement on X.
CJP leaders freed after undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday after a Special Executive Magistrate declined a police request to extend their judicial custody by three more days, reports said.
The two leaders at the forefront of the protests calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar following voter-list irregularities, furnished personal bonds and sureties of Rs 50,000 (€470; $530) each.
Their written undertakings promised to maintain peace and not call for protests at Jantar Mantar "till such a time that it is denotified in accordance with law."
The iconic protest site was denotified by Delhi Police earlier in October, months after CJP-led protests culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Das and Ranka were booked for "trespassing" after entering the Jantar Mantar protest site and raising the Indian flag.
The latest CJP protests have called for Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the deletion of voters' names.

German military practices deploying troops to Estonia

German military practices deploying troops to Estonia
The German military, for the first time, is practicing the deployment of additional troops to Estonia as part of the Brave Blue 26 military exercise.
Since last Friday, Bundeswehr convoys from Germany's 4th Logistics Regiment have been visible in Estonia. Similar exercises have previously been held in Lithuania and Latvia, but this is the first time the Germans have been in Estonia.
The Germans have not disclosed how many soldiers and vehicles are moving around Estonia during the 10-day exercise (October 16-27) or where.
During a media day this week, journalists were told that they are practicing bringing reinforcements to German units stationed in the Baltic states in the event of a crisis.
"The strategic deployment to Estonia took place using all modes of transport. We came by land and through the port. We loaded heavy equipment onto a ferry, which brought the cargo to Estonia. The soldiers arrived in Estonia by plane," said Lieutenant Colonel Benjamin Eberhardt, commander of the 4th Logistics Regiment.
Over the course of the exercise, command posts will be established, and communications and logistics will be tested.
The 4th Regiment has previously organized similar exercises every year in Lithuania and Latvia. This is its first time in Estonia. Eberhardt said they had to adapt to the marshy Baltic terrain.
"We were mainly in western Estonia. The Estonian Defense Forces made their military bases available to us to accommodate the soldiers. Outside the bases, we conducted terrain reconnaissance everywhere and familiarized ourselves with the conditions," he said.
The current exercise is in preparation for a major logistics exercise in Lithuania and Latvia next year. It is not yet known when German convoys will next be seen in Estonia.

Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:17:11 UTC
14:17:11 KST

Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.
The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, including bookings in Australia, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.
Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.
Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.
In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.
Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.
Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.
While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.
“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

Drinking tea could lower your risk of stroke, but only if it’s not too hot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:16:03 UTC
14:16:03 KST

Drinking tea three or more times a week is linked to an 11% lower risk of vascular disease, such as stroke or heart attack, a new study suggests. However, burning hot tea was linked to the opposite effect: a 16% increase in vascular disease risk.
Regular tea drinking is linked to a lower risk of vascular diseases such as stroke, coronary heart disease and heart attack, according to a new study.
Tea is made by steeping the processed leaves of Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub native to East Asia. All varieties —including white, green, oolong, black and pu-erh— come from this single plant, with their distinct flavours determined by how much they oxidise.
The beverage is a regular part of the diet in many cultures. From the English breakfast to Chinese tea ceremonies, it is present in the daily lives of millions of people worldwide.
Tea’s bioactive compounds, including polyphenols and flavonoids, have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and endothelial-protective properties that preserve the inner lining of blood vessels and maintain healthy circulation, all of which can help prevent vascular diseases, according to a study published in the Journal of Internal Medicine.
Researchers followed nearly 500,000 Chinese people for an average of nine years, recording their tea consumption and any diseases that developed during that period. They found that those who drink tea regularly three or more times a week showed 11.2% lower overall risk of vascular disease. The strongest association was for ischaemic stroke with a 36.6% reduction, followed by cerebrovascular disease at 19.1%.
The protective associations varied substantially depending on how the tea was prepared and consumed, the researchers found.
Among participants, the median intake was between two and three cups a day; however, the lowest associated risk was in those who consumed six to eight cups daily.
Black tea showed the strongest and most consistent association with vascular diseases, followed by green tea. Researchers attribute this to the fermentation-derived compounds, such as theaflavins, which have anti-inflammatory and lipid-regulating properties.
The temperature and strength of the brew also made a difference. Researchers found that the best combination was moderately strong and non-scalding tea.
Surprisingly, burning hot tea was linked to the opposite effect: a 16% increase in vascular disease risk. Very hot drinks have previously also been associated with a greater likelihood of oesophageal cancer.
Tea is not a silver bullet
The protective association of habitual tea consumption was consistent across most demographic subgroups but was significantly stronger in individuals with obesity, the researchers noted.
Despite these results, the authors warn that drinking tea alone does not protect against cardiovascular disease and that it should form part of a broader healthy lifestyle and complement established prevention strategies.
“This was an observational study and other differences in people’s diets and lifestyles could help explain the findings,” said Dell Stanford, senior dietitian at the British Heart Foundation who did not participate in the study, adding that the results don’t prove “that a daily cuppa protects your heart.”
Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of illness and mortality in the European Union, accounting for one in three of all deaths and affecting an estimated 62 million people.

US Supreme Court reverses Trump administration push to restrict treatment for transgender inmates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:05:30 UTC
14:05:30 KST

The US Supreme Court rejected on Wednesday a bid by US President Donald Trump's administration to immediately enforce a policy restricting gender-affirming care for transgender inmates in federal prisons in a rare win for transgender rights at the nation's top judicial body.
The court denied the Justice Department's emergency request to lift a federal judge's order blocking the Federal Bureau of Prisons from implementing the policy, while a legal challenge to the measure plays out.
The policy, issued in February, prohibits medical and surgical treatments as well as any "social accommodations" such as clothing and hair-removal devices that could be used to alter a person's appearance to align with their gender identity. The policy would still allow for psychiatric services to be provided.
Three transgender inmates incarcerated at federal correctional institutions in New Jersey, Florida, and Minnesota filed a class action lawsuit challenging the policy.
The Supreme Court's brief order gave no explanation for its action, as is common when the justices handle emergency requests. Conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito publicly dissented from the decision.
"This ruling will prevent serious and irreparable harm to plaintiffs and the class while we continue to challenge the government's unlawful efforts to deny medically necessary healthcare for political reasons," said Aditi Shah, an attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union, which helps represent the inmates challenging the policy.
The Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the decision.
Over 2,000 transgender inmates in the US face risk of restrictions
There are more than 2,000 transgender inmates in federal facilities and halfway houses, according to a government figure from 2025.
The new restrictions would reverse the government's prior procedures. The federal prison system has treated people with gender dysphoria with hormones since at least 1992, according to the plaintiffs.
Gender dysphoria is a term for the clinical diagnosis of significant distress that can result from an incongruence between a person's gender identity and sex at birth.
Trump has taken a hard line on transgender rights since returning to office in January 2025.
The president issued an executive order on his first day back in office recognizing only two genders - male and female - and casting transgender identity as a lie. The directive ordered changes across numerous federal agencies, including that "males are not detained in women's prisons" and halting funding for treatments "for the purpose of conforming an inmate's appearance to that of the opposite sex."
In the litigation, the administration has called medical care provided for gender transition "unproven sex-rejecting interventions."
Siding with the administration would cause "immediate and catastrophic" harm, the plaintiffs said in a court filing, noting that "patients who are denied hormone therapy can suffer from increased depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm."
The Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has ruled against transgender rights in key cases since last year.
It backed state laws banning transgender athletes from participating on female sports teams at public schools, including universities. It also allowed the administration to ban transgender people from the military and bar passport applicants from designating their gender identities for the document. In addition, it let states ban gender-affirming medical care for transgender youths.
Washington judge blocks administration's restrictions on federal prisoners
Washington, DC-based US District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the restrictions on federal prisoners in June, concluding that the policy is likely "arbitrary and capricious" and violates a federal law governing agency procedures.
The judge found that the Federal Bureau of Prisons disregarded its own evidence and experience and "reverse engineered" the measure in order to implement Trump's executive order.
"With this opinion, the court has no intention of wading into the culture war being waged against transgender individuals," Lamberth wrote.
On September 18, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit refused the administration's request to lift Lamberth's ruling.
The Justice Department in its filing urged the Supreme Court to allow the Federal Bureau of Prisons to enforce its "decision to prioritize mental-health treatment, while discontinuing medically disputed and unproven sex-rejecting interventions."
The Bureau of Prisons, the filing said, "reasonably considered its prior experience both in determining that such interventions are not medically necessary and in determining that security and prison-administration concerns independently justified a change in policy."

studio thusthat turns the rusty-red waste of aluminum production into delicate ceramics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:05:11 UTC
14:05:11 KST

studio thusthat turns the rusty-red waste of aluminum production into delicate ceramics
with billions of tons accumulating worldwide, the studio explores new uses for one of industry's most overlooked byproducts.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
the vast red landscape behind aluminum
Across the outskirts of aluminum refineries, enormous deposits of rust-colored earth stretch for miles to form strange red landscapes visible even in satellite images. This is bauxite residue, commonly known as red mud, the alkaline waste left behind when alumina is extracted from bauxite ore. More than 150 million metric tons are generated globally each year, adding to stockpiles already estimated at over four billion tons. Most remains in vast storage facilities, despite decades of research into potential uses for the material.
Amsterdam-based Studio ThusThat has been exploring what might become of this enormous industrial byproduct. Its ongoing Red Mud project transforms the residue into finely formed ceramic vessels and experimental building materials, offering an unexpected glimpse of what the waste could become. The finished pieces resemble traditional terracotta, with deep earthy colors and slender forms that seem far removed from the industrial landscapes where their ingredients originated.
studio thusthat turns industrial waste into ceramics
First developed in 2019 at London’s Royal College of Art, the project grew through collaboration with materials scientists at KU Leuven in Belgium. The designers at Studio ThusThat discovered how the residue’s mineral composition, particularly its high iron oxide content, could be adapted for ceramic production. By processing the material and adjusting its composition, they developed recipes suitable for traditional forming techniques, including slip casting. The red mud is used in both the ceramic bodies and their glazes, producing a range of warm reddish tones.
The apparent simplicity of the vessels conceals a fairly complicated manufacturing process. Raw red mud can be highly alkaline and may contain hazardous substances, requiring treatment before it can be safely handled and incorporated into products. Its properties also vary depending on where the bauxite was mined and how it was refined, meaning each new source demands further testing. For Studio ThusThat, the ceramic collection offers a way to make an unfamiliar material tangible, inviting people to reconsider a substance that has long been treated as a liability.
from the tabletop to the coastline
The research has since extended into architecture through a collaboration with London practice Tonkin Liu. Together, the studios explored how red mud could be developed into modular ceramic tiles, with potential applications ranging from roofing to coastal regeneration. The proposed units have shaped surfaces that can collect water or accommodate planting, suggesting a role for the material in landscapes shared with other species. Their modular geometry also allows the components to be combined into larger assemblies.
These architectural studies bring the material closer to the scale of the industry that produces it. Along coastlines, the tiles could potentially support vegetation and create small habitats within waterfront infrastructure, although their long-term environmental performance would require further testing. The proposals remain experimental, with manufacturing partners and larger-scale development needed before the concepts can enter construction. Still, they offer a different destination for a material that currently occupies enormous areas of industrial land.
can architecture absorb the waste of extraction?
For all its potential, red mud presents considerable obstacles to widespread reuse. Processing costs remain high, and many refineries sit far from the industries that might consume their waste. Transporting such heavy material across long distances can quickly undermine its economic and environmental advantages. Regulatory requirements add further complications. According to figures cited by Studio ThusThat, only around three percent of red mud was being repurposed when the research began, despite established methods for incorporating it into construction products.
The team’s ambition is ultimately to see these materials used in architecture, where the quantities involved could make a meaningful difference. There is also a wider contradiction worth considering. Aluminum is increasingly important to renewable-energy infrastructure, yet its production continues to leave behind enormous quantities of residue.
Studio ThusThat’s ceramics offer one small response to that growing accumulation. Whether the material can find a lasting place in construction will depend on what happens beyond the design studio, in the industries capable of using it at scale.
project info:
name: Red Mud
design studio: Studio ThusThat | @studiothusthat
designers: Kevin Rouff, Paco Böckelmann
architectural collaborator: Tonkin Liu | @tonkinliu
scientific collaboration: KU Leuven | @kuleuven
location: Amsterdam, Netherlands; research originating in London, UK
year: 2019, ongoing research

Flights will soon take off from Australia's newest airport. Here's where they're going
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:01:58 UTC
14:01:58 KST

In Brief
- Sydney's second airport opens on Sunday, offering 24-hour flights and new domestic and international routes.
- Seven airlines have signed on, taking jetsetters to both domestic and international locations.
Sydney's second airport is about to open, marking the first new international airport built in Australia in more than 50 years.
Western Sydney International Airport, officially named Nancy-Bird Walton Airport, will welcome its first passengers on 25 October.
Located at Luddenham near Badgerys Creek, about 45km from Sydney's CBD, the airport is expected to reshape travel across Greater Sydney, offering an alternative to Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport and providing airlines access to a 24-hour aviation hub.
From flight routes and transport links to where it's located and how it differs from Sydney Airport, here's everything you need to know.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Where can you fly from Western Sydney International Airport?
Western Sydney International Airport will have one significant advantage over Sydney's existing airport: it can operate around the clock.
Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is subject to an overnight curfew between 11pm and 6am, flights at the new airport can arrive and depart 24 hours a day.
That flexibility has helped attract domestic and international carriers, with seven airlines already committing to operate services from the airport.
Here's where they'll fly:
- Qantas: Four weekly flights to Melbourne and Brisbane from March 2027.
- Jetstar: Four weekly flights to the Gold Coast, three weekly flights to Brisbane, and daily services to Melbourne.
- Qatar Airways: Three weekly flights to Doha's Hamad International Airport from 15 December, with additional services planned in coming years.
- Air New Zealand: Three weekly flights to Auckland from 26 October.
- Singapore Airlines: Daily flights to Singapore from 23 November.
- Fiji Airways: Three weekly flights to Nadi.
- Vietjet Air: Two weekly flights to Ho Chi Minh City from 10 January 2027, increasing to three in March 2027, plus four weekly flights to Bangkok via Vietjet Thailand.
Emirates has also been cleared to add seven weekly flights from the airport but is yet to announce a schedule.
Airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be announced as passenger numbers grow.
How do you get to Western Sydney International Airport?
One of the biggest questions facing travellers is how they will reach Sydney's newest airport.
Unlike Kingsford Smith Airport, which is connected to Sydney's rail network, Western Sydney International Airport will initially rely on road connections and bus services while major transport infrastructure is completed.
A Sydney Metro line linking the airport with St Marys is under construction and expected to open next year.
Until then, passengers can connect to St Marys via a free airport shuttle bus, or travel by express coach, public bus, taxi, rideshare or private vehicle.
If you're driving, the airport is accessible via the new toll-free M12 Motorway and is about an hour from Sydney's CBD, depending on traffic conditions.
An express shuttle service will also connect the airport with Parramatta, Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport.
Current fares are:
- Parramatta: $25 one way, $45 return.
- Sydney CBD: $55 one way, $80 return.
- Sydney Airport: $65 one way, $90 return.
From St Marys, passengers can connect to Sydney's wider rail network, though journeys to some parts of Sydney may take considerably longer than travelling via Kingsford Smith Airport.
State-run bus services will also link the airport with centres including Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown, Mount Druitt and Leppington.
For those driving, the airport has about 6,000 parking spaces available on site.
Where is Western Sydney International Airport?
Western Sydney International Airport is located at Luddenham, near Badgerys Creek, in Sydney's west.
The airport is approximately 45km from Sydney's CBD, 20km from Penrith and 15km from Liverpool.
It sits within the broader Western Sydney Aerotropolis precinct and will become Sydney's second major airport when passenger operations begin on Sunday.
Why is Western Sydney International Airport a big deal?
Plans for a second major Sydney airport have been debated for decades as governments looked for ways to meet the city's growing aviation demand.
The airport is expected to become the centrepiece of the Western Sydney Aerotropolis, a major business and infrastructure precinct that planners hope will drive jobs, investment and development across the region.
When it opens, Western Sydney International Airport will be able to handle up to 10 million passengers a year.
That capacity is expected to expand significantly over coming decades, with airport operators forecasting it could eventually handle 82 million passengers annually.
While flight options will initially be limited, airport operators expect additional airlines and destinations to be added as the airport grows.
Will Western Sydney International Airport make airfares cheaper?
Aviation experts have previously told SBS News that the change will fundamentally alter the country's airfare market and could drive prices down for consumers by opening up air travel capacity.
However with rail links that may not be ready until 2028, getting to the airport could theoretically incur a cost that would be similar or more than the savings on a ticket.

That programme runs on 155mm, the calibre used by the AS90 and by the Archer system bought to replace it.

Residences, shower spas and private lofts: The most luxurious airline experiences ranked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

Think luxury travel is all about the seat? A new ranking of the ‘most outrageous’ luxury airline experiences has found that not all perks begin at takeoff…
What can money buy when you’re travelling in the sky at 40,000 feet?
Beyond the hefty price tag that comes with first-class fares, AirAdvisor has scoured the world’s major international airlines to rank the “most outrageous” individual experiences on offer both in-flight and before takeoff.
The company created a longlist of the "extraordinary premium amenities" currently on offer by airlines and assessed experiences that could only be independently verified through official airline or airport sources.
AirAdvisor’s ranking of the top 10 most outrageous airline luxuries in 2026 excluded private aviation, discontinued amenities, concepts not yet available to the public as well as standard offerings, like lounge access, amenity kits and conventional lie-flat seats.
“Premium air travel has become an arms race," said Anton Radchenko, Founder and CEO of AirAdvisor.
“A lie-flat seat is no longer enough to stand out: airlines are now competing with bedrooms, showers, private lounges and spaces designed for couples or groups.
“What is striking is how scarce many of these experiences remain – often limited to one aircraft type or only a handful of routes.”
The 10 most outrageous airline luxuries in 2026
The research scored qualifying luxury experiences out of 100 across five criteria: extravagance, which had a weight of 35%; rarity 25%; privacy and exclusivity 20%; access scarcity 10%; and beyond-the-seat experience 10%, which looks at offerings such as showers, spas or private apartment-style space.
Here’s how the top 10 experiences ranked:
- 1. Etihad Airways’ The Residence – 98/100: Three-room apartment in the sky
- 2. Emirates’ A380 Shower Spa – 91/100: Shower at 40,000 feet
- 3. SWISS’ First Grand Suite – 88/100: Private loft in the sky for up to three people
- 4. Air France’s La Première – 85/100: Private 45 m² suite before boarding the flight
- 5. Singapore Airlines’ Suites – 82/100: Cabin class with a separate seat and double bed
- 6. Lufthansa’s Allegris Suite Plus – 80/100: Two-person first class suite that becomes a double bed
- 7. Japan Airlines’ A350-1000 First – 78/100: 1.23m-wide suite with a minibar and 43-inch screen
- 8. Emirates’ A380 Onboard Lounge – 76/100: Cocktail bar at 40,000 feet
- 9. Qatar Airways’ Al Safwa First Lounge – 72/100: Thermal jacuzzi before boarding
- 10. Virgin Atlantic’s Retreat Suite – 68/100: Business class suite where four people can dine together
AirAdvisor only considered a maximum of two experiences per airline to avoid the ranking being dominated by a single carrier. The research was also based on information from September 2026.
An apartment, shower and ‘loft’ in the air?
The top spot was awarded to The Residence experience by Etihad Airways, which offers travellers a three-room suite to relax in even before they've reached their destination.
It features a private bedroom, ensuite shower facility and separate living room. Meanwhile, before boarding, travellers can also benefit from home or hotel check-in, chauffeur transfers and a personalised welcome when they get to the airport.
"The Residence achieved near-maximum marks for extravagance, rarity, privacy and the extent to which it goes beyond a conventional airline seat," AirAdvisor said in its report.
Emirates’ A380 Shower Spa comes in second, and is exclusively available to first class flyers. While in the sky, passengers can access a dedicated shower room with a vanity area, changing space and heated flooring.
Rounding off the top three is an experience from a European carrier: SWISS’ First Grand Suite.
Unveiled in 2025 and launched in 2026, this product offers a heightened level of privacy: combining two adjoining first class suites, including the aisle, to create a fully secluded space on long-haul flights. The private area can function as a bedroom, office or meeting room for up to three travellers.
