Marine Le Pen vs Alice Weidel: How the far right wants to reshape the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

AfD leader Alice Weidel unveiled her EU vision in Strasbourg a week after Marine Le Pen did the same in Brussels. Both parties seek to reshape the bloc around national sovereignty but differ on fiscal policy, energy and the extent of reform.
Neither party now advocates leaving the EU. Instead, both want to reshape it into an alliance of sovereign states, with weaker institutions and reduced powers.
If they come to power, their plans could undermine the Franco-German partnership that has long driven European integration and reshape the future of the EU.
Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel unveiled her “New Deal for Europe” at a press conference in the European Parliament on Wednesday, a week after France’s Marine Le Pen presented her own vision at the upscale The Hotel in Brussels.
Both leaders are in strong electoral positions. After a major victory in Saxony-Anhalt's regional election last September, Weidel's AFD party is on track to lead a German State for the first time in history, and is currently leading the polls at the national level. "Our aim is to assume government responsibility after the next federal elections", Weidel said in Strasbourg.
In France, a recent Ifop poll puts Le Pen at 34% to 38% of the vote in the first round of France's 2027 presidential election, despite the recent wave of protests across the country.
Both parties oppose continued funding for Ukraine, criticise the EU’s regulatory burden, reject deeper integration and want to curb the powers of EU institutions.
But they differ on fiscal policy, energy and how far their countries should break from common rules. The AfD goes further, proposing opt-outs that would allow Germany to bypass certain EU policies.
Euronews examines the RN and AfD’s plans for Europe, highlighting the key differences and similarities between two of the continent’s leading far-right parties.
No more money to Ukraine
Both leaders agree on ending financial support for Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s war of aggression.
At her press conference last week, Le Pen argued that France’s strained public finances could no longer sustain aid to Kyiv and called for the lifting of EU sanctions against Russia.
“We obviously agreed to maintain a whole series of mechanisms to train their soldiers, to train their army, to provide them, including aid in terms of equipment, but we can no longer finance Ukraine, so this funding will stop,” she said.
Weidel said on Wednesdayshe wants a peace treaty and called for a “reasonable diplomatic approach,” which takes into account the “security interests of Ukraine and Russia.”
In a recent interview with The Economist, she argued that Ukraine had already lost the war and pledged to end Germany’s support for Kyiv.
Fiscal policy: the sharpest divide
The most significant difference lies in their approach to fiscal policy.
Le Pen wants to harmonise taxes on tobacco, alcohol and large companies at EU level to prevent fiscal dumping across Europe. She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB) revise its mandate to give more weight to economic growth, rather than focusing on price stability.
"As I have always believed, the ECB must rethink its course of action. It is essential that it take into account employment, growth, and innovation, given that the monetary easing policies pursued between 2010 and 2022 were not targeted at future investments," she said last week.
The AfD, by contrast, opposes any transfer of fiscal sovereignty to supranational institutions and claims that the ECB must strictly confine itself to its original price-stability mandate.
"There is a ban on the ECB, the European Central Bank, financing state debt. And what is the ECB doing? It's financing state debt", Weidel said.
Both parties, however, firmly oppose common EU debt and want to cut their countries’ contributions to the EU budget. Le Pen aims to cap France’s net contribution at €5 billion a year. Neither Weidel nor the AfD’s New Deal for Europe paper specifies a figure, instead emphasising the need to “end Germany’s role as paymaster.”
Energy: EU carbon border tax vs freedom to use coal
On energy and climate policy, both parties criticise the EU Green Deal and support nuclear power, but differ in their approaches.
Le Pen rejected the “climate-sceptic” label for her party, backed an EU carbon border tax and proposed tying member states’ contributions to the EU budget to their carbon emissions, thereby incentivising the transition to clean energy.
“The further a country deviates from the [Paris agreement] targets, the more it should have to contribute,” she said.
The AfD paper instead stresses total freedom to choose the national energy mix, meaning Germany must be free to use nuclear power, coal, gas and renewable energy according to the needs of its economy.
"Now we rely completely on an ideological energy transition of wind and solar power. We see this development also throughout Europe, through the implementation of the Green Deal, the building energy law, and above all the ban on combustion engines. This is a blatant disruption of the free market economy," she said.
Le Pen targets the Commission; AfD seeks to weaken Parliament too
Both parties want the European Commission to be stripped of powers and reduced to a “secretariat at the service of countries”, as Le Pen put it.
“The Commission wants to be a State, we don’t want it,” she said, rejecting any EU executive ambitions on security, diplomacy and intelligence. She also wants to abolish the European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee, two advisory bodies representing local authorities and social interests.
Weidel has a similar position. "We don't want a Commission that is not elected to intrude and disturb your private life and [Member States] decision making [process]," she said.
The AfD goes a step further, questioning the legitimacy of the European Parliament and advocating a Europe centred on sovereign nation-states.
One of the most far-reaching proposals in the New Deal for Europe states: “The EP should no longer be elected directly, but instead be composed of delegates appointed by national parliaments.”
Different strategies for change
Le Pen envisages reshaping the EU following elections in Spain, France, Italy and Poland, where far-right parties are expected to win or make significant gains.
Poland’s Law and Justice party could return to power, while Spain’s Vox could join the government alongside the Popular Party. In France, Marine Le Pen could become the country’s first far-right president.
**"**This will be our shared undertaking for the years and, the decades to come. [...] It will not simply consist of undoing what has been very badly done over the past 30 years on the European stage," she said, claiming the new "Europe of nations" will feature EU institutions not exercising any authority over the member states.
The AfD, by contrast, identifies 2029 as the pivotal year for EU reform, when the European elections could deliver a “patriotic right-wing majority in the European Parliament.”
The party also floats disruptive national options should its planned reform of the EU fail. These include making extensive use of opt-outs for Germany in areas such as free movement, defence, taxation, social policy and migration.
"If Schengen [system] is over and it doesn't work, we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," Weidel said, pointing to challenges to free movement amid episodes such as the large-scale arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta last July.
The opt-out on migration would mean that Germany "will no longer participate in any European distribution mechanisms [of migrants] or asylum quotas,” disrupting the bloc's Migration Pact. Berlin currently holds the biggest solidarity quota in the EU and is in charge of relocating 4,555 asylum seekers from frontline member states in 2026.
AFD leaves the door open for EU exit
If far-reaching reforms to the EU’s structure prove unattainable, the AfD’s plan states that "the German people should then decide for themselves," a formulation that could be interpreted as an implicit reference to a referendum on EU membership as a last resort, although Weidel did not raise this possibility at her press conference.
Le Pen, once a strong advocate of France leaving the EU, has gradually abandoned the idea, shifting towards a strategy of radically reforming the bloc from within during her 2022 presidential campaign.
Dave Sinardet, a Belgian political scientist who specialises in far-right parties, considers EU withdrawal an unrealistic scenario.
“Most radical right parties have evolved their position towards the EU in the last years,” he told Euronews, adding that after Brexit no political force is seriously considering leaving the Union.
“On this, AfD is really moving in the same direction that RN has already moved in the past. They are abandoning the ideas as Le Pen abandoned Frexit,” he said.

AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.
Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco.
Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.
The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.
Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.
The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.
“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”
It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”
The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.
Opposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters have begun resorting to direct action and the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.
The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”
It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.
Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”
He said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.
“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”
Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”
He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.
A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.
“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for chicken with citrus and oregano | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

If you look through the window of Piatto Romano between 10am and midday, there will almost certainly be two, maybe three people at the round table trimming vegetables: chicory, artichokes, poppy greens, amaranth. After midday, the crates and trimmings will have been cleared away and the table will now be home to trays of bright-green boiled vegetables and, maybe, baked salt cod. By 12.30pm, everything will have been moved into the small kitchen in time for service, which starts at 12.45pm.
When I first moved to Rome in 2005, Via Bodoni 62 was home to a restaurant called Da Rafaelle, which had white plastic chairs (inside as well) and served traditional Roman food with plenty of offal. We went to Da Rafaelle a few times before it closed in 2009. But, mostly, we went to La Torricella, which is on the other side of Testaccio and serves mainly fish. The owner is Augusto D’Alfonsi and, during lunch one day, he mentioned that he was taking over via Bodoni 62, and that his daughter Francesca would run it. They’d serve traditional Roman food with plenty of offal and it would be called Piatto Romano. This was 2011. My son was born later that year and my memories are not unpleasantly foggy; of the vegetable trolley in the corner, of chicken with red peppers and of Francesca and her father negotiating strongly. I also remember Francesca’s brother, Andrea, starting to be around more, before he eventually took over in late 2013.
Andrea grew up riding his bike along the pavement in front of La Torricella, which his parents had opened in 1973, a few years before he was born. If his lunch didn’t come out of the kitchen at La Torricella, it probably came out of the kitchen at Da Antonio on Via dei Pastini, where Andrea’s maternal grandma cooked, or from the kitchen of his maternal grandfather’s restaurant, Da Giovanni on Via dei Barbieri. As a teenager, Andrea also ate at his paternal grandfather’s osteria, Gran Sasso in Trastevere, and in the various branches of Insalata Ricca, a chain of salad restaurants opened by his entrepreneurial uncle Gino in the 1980s. All the various parts of the family have Abruzzese roots, but Andrea mentions Gino, eccentric and single-minded about history, vegetables and nutrition, as being a particular influence.
The way Andrea continues to evolve Piatto Romano (which for many is the embodiment of an ideal Roman trattoria) would require several columns. For now, though, I will note his singlemindedness about the vegetables he picks up every day from his various sources. The other night, we had courgette greens – a little hairy and very succulent – with Leprino rabbit (typical of the Tuscia area of Viterbo) braised in wine and citrus, which produces a lipsmacking sauce/gravy. And head chef Umberto Mussato, who has worked with Andrea since 2021, has adapted his recipe for this column, but using chicken instead of rabbit. The dish is made even more tasty by the addition of three to five anchovy fillets mashed with a tablespoon of red-wine vinegar, plus a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, which is then left to sit for at least half an hour before it’s served with greens and potatoes, if you wish.
Chicken with citrus and herbs
Serves 4
1.2kg skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (or a mix of legs and thighs)
 
Salt
  
4 tbsp olive oil
  
100-150ml dry white wine
  
1 tsp dried thyme or oregano
  
400ml fresh citrus juice – a mix of orange, lemon, grapefruit, mandarin
  
3-5 anchovies mashed 
 with 1 tbsp good-quality red-wine vinegar
  
A few stalks fresh oregano
Season the chicken with salt, rubbing it into the skin. Working in a heavy-based pan, warm the olive oil, then brown the chicken pieces in batches so as not to overcrowd the pan. Once all the pieces are brown, look at the amount of fat in the pan – I suggest leaving it all in there, but remove some, if you prefer.
Return all the browned chicken to the pan, raise the heat and add the wine, which should sizzle and evaporate. Add the dried oregano or thyme, stir, then pour over the citrus juice. Lower the heat so the pan simmers, then cover.
Leave the chicken to cook for 45 minutes to an hour, lifting the lid to turn the pieces every now and then, then lift off the lid and cook for another 20 minutes, so the sauce can reduce. By the end of the cooking, the chicken should be tender and the sauce thick. (If the sauce needs significant reduction, remove the chicken, simmer hard so the sauce reduces to your liking, then return the chicken pieces to the pan.)
To finish, stir in the anchovies mashed in vinegar and a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, then leave to sit for 30 minutes before serving.

Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

However grim the trajectory might seem, I’ve always believed that sense will ultimately prevail. As the great perils of dismantling the living world become increasingly obvious, even the most rapacious exploiters must come round. Nobody wants to live on a dead planet, do they?
There are – or were – signs that this wasn’t just wishful thinking. Since 2015, mostly thanks to China, the area of the planet being reforested has increased, while thanks in large part to Brazil, the global rate of forest destruction has declined. The area of the Brazilian Amazon forest cleared each year is one-sixth of what it was when records began in 1988. In the past four years, as a result of Brazilian government policy, the deforestation rate has fallen by 71%. If Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is re-elected president on Sunday, the country could reach zero deforestation by 2030. The arc of the moral universe seems to have bent towards justice.
But what my faith in human nature failed to account for was a perverse delight in destruction among a small cohort of the economic elite. There are people who appear to hate life and love death. Donald Trump’s removal of protections on public lands, the small bite – doubtless the first of many – he wants to take out of Yosemite, his assaults on the US National Park Service and the US Forest Service, his trashing of the Endangered Species Act: all are partly a response to lobbying by ranchers, loggers, frackers and miners. But this, I think, is not the primary driver.
More important to him, I’ve come to believe, is a vengeful desire to hurt. I doubt Trump hates the monarch butterfly. I’d be surprised if he knows what it is. But he does appear to hate people who love the monarch butterfly. Destroying the habitats on which this and many other endangered species in the US depend seems to be part of the “retribution” he promised. The New York Times was unable to find evidence that Trump has ever visited a national park. He probably doesn’t hate them either. But seemingly anything valued by the enemy – greens, liberals, socialists, feminists, anti-racists, “bureaucrats” and “blockers” – should be attacked on principle.
Wiping ecosystems off the map is an obvious demonstration of power. Extinction leaves a permanent mark, which is every dictator’s dream. It’s also a highly effective means of hurting those who resist him: the Indigenous people and other people of colour so often on the receiving end of environmental destruction; the regulators; the scientists and the rest of the intelligentsia; above all, people who care.
Caring could be seen as the far right’s meta-target. The “suicidal empathy” theme now crops up repeatedly in videos, newspaper columns and speeches: a professed belief that those who care about other people or species should be destroyed by those who don’t. This belief, by definition, is psychopathic. What exhausts my optimism is that, conned by shallow promises such as the use of brutal methods to address crime, people keep electing those who subscribe to it.
Physically and politically, Flávio Bolsonaro is the spitting image of his father, the jailed coup-plotter, Jair. When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil, he appeared to see ecological destruction as a kind of a holy duty. The deforestation rate rose by 59% in his four years, and attacks on Indigenous people and other forest defenders, as well as invasions by illegal ranchers, loggers and goldminers rocketed. The crudest forms of extractivism – regardless of their costs, or how they might hold back all kinds of progress – were a matter of policy.
The ideology of the far right in Brazil has been described as “beef, Bible and bullets”: violence against those who resist the seizure of their resources, an ultra-conservative evangelism and the expansion of cattle ranching, which is both a potent symbol of far-right machismo and the primary driver of deforestation in the Amazon.
Jair Bolsonaro looked back with nostalgia to the military dictatorship of 1964 to 1985 – which was actively supported by the US government – during which local oligarchs could do as they pleased, and those who opposed them were tortured and disappeared. The warnings couldn’t be clearer, but Brazil seems determined to revisit its nightmares. Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October, and is likely to become president.
If he wins the second round this week, the gleeful rampage of his supporters, catalysed by government policy, threatens not only the Amazon but the Atlantic forest in the south, the Pantanal wetlands, the Pampa grasslands and the savannah habitats of the Cerrado. This is politics as an orgy of destruction. Let’s eradicate our life support systems – that’ll teach the liberals!
Trump has been using all possible means to help Bolsonaro win. He gives the impression of seeing Latin America as the conquistadores did – one big heap of treasure, ready for looting. The region’s far-right demagogues are only to happy to help. Mass deforestation and the sudden ecosystem collapse that is likely to result offers a finality to their politics: there’s no coming back from this. You Indigenous people, you greens, you carers: you’ll have nowhere left to hide. The world will be ours, even if it is a world of ashes.
What might Bolsonarismo teach us? First, it appears there is no limit to the perversity of the ruling class, which would rather there was nothing left to share than cede any fraction of the planet to the poor.
Second, that it possesses all the tools – social and traditional media, the pulpit and the gun – required to make its perversity look like common sense, or at least irresistible, as force is deployed. Third, that the only defence we have against suicidal gullibility is what the Brazilians call conscientizaçao: raising awareness about the relations between exploiters and exploited, and the violence that underpins them. Otherwise all that is good, trusting and hopeful in humanity can be harnessed for a war against everyone and everything.
As for the idea that nobody wants to live on a dead planet, Elon Musk, with his preposterous plans for living on Mars – “Fuck Earth! Who cares about Earth?” – has killed that too. Extending the frontier of destruction, even to the point of human extinction, comes across as a matter of pride. The four horsemen ride again, not in cloaks but in stetsons and denim shirts, driving their cattle before them.
- George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

‘This isn’t greenwashing’: thousands of butterflies surprise experts on restored West Sussex farmland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:06 UTC
14:00:06 KST

An “amazing” abundance of 5,290 butterflies, including rare small blues and dingy skippers, has appeared on land that was barren wheatfields just two years ago.
The speed with which nature has bounced back at Halnaker Hill farm in West Sussex has surprised experts after 133 hectares (330 acres) of intensively farmed land were turned into a commercial nature restoration project.
The farm’s relatively unproductive soils on the South Downs were cropped for wheat for 40 years, but after a final harvest in 2024 the arable land was sown with a special wildflower mix. Seven kilometres of hedgerows have been planted, seven hectares (17 acres) of new woodland created, three ponds dug and 54 hectares (133 acres) of herbal leys seeded, with carefully controlled mob-grazing on existing chalk grassland to improve its wildlife and biodiversity.
Halnaker Hill Natural Capital is a commercial nature restoration project that derives its income from selling biodiversity net gain (BNG) credits, which enable houses to be built in the wider region. Under BNG rules, developers are legally obliged to deliver an increase in nature on new housing estates or by buying credits for nature restoration elsewhere.
The independent ecologist Neil Hulme, who has advised Halnaker Hill on nature restoration and surveyed for butterflies, said he found “clouds of butterflies” on the former wheatfields last summer.
“The speed has amazed me, from a sterile landscape to one brimming with butterflies,” he said. “Despite being tiny, the small blue is very good at sniffing out its foodplant, kidney vetch. I knew it would come, but what I didn’t expect was it to come so soon and multiply so soon.
“Some people are a little bit unsure about BNG and the idea of monetising nature, but projects like this are showing so clearly how BNG can deliver nature by the bucketload. This isn’t greenwashing; this is the real deal.”
As well as seeing a profusion of skylarks, corn buntings, hobbies and dragonflies on the site, Hulme recorded 85 small blue butterflies and seven dingy skippers, which have never previously been recorded on the fields.
Surveys also found 547 small heath butterflies, and scores of common blues and green hairstreaks, alongside eight sulphur pearl moths, a highly localised species restricted to coastal areas of southern Britain and usually observed in ones and twos.
Halnaker Hill farm, which is delivering more than 850 units of BNG, forms part of the South Downs national park authority’s “ReNature” programme, which is tackling biodiversity loss and adaptation to global heating in the region. More than 7,700 hectares (19,027 acres) of land is being transformed into natural havens.
Nick Heasman, the head of natural capital for the South Downs national park, said: “It’s been wonderful to work with the team at Halnaker Hill to bring about real, positive change, demonstrating that BNG can make a big difference for nature, and this survey proves that. Just two years ago this was largely an arable landscape – showing how quickly nature can bounce back, given space, time and love.”
According to Hulme, it is relatively simple for any land manager to boost nature on chalk, simply by scraping off nutrient-rich top-soil and sowing specialist chalk grassland wildflower mixes if the site is not near any existing chalk grassland.
Next year he is planning to reintroduce the rare Duke of Burgundy butterfly to the site, with wild pansies also being sown to attract the Queen of Spain fritillary, a once-rare migrant that is increasingly common visitor to southern Britain.
“Projects like this fill me with optimism,” said Hulme. “If we can achieve this in just two years, the sky is the limit.”

Post by Lithuanian woman in Italy criticising communist youth goes viral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

A Lithuanian woman living in Italy has addressed young Italians on Facebook over their use of communist symbols at protests. Her open letter reached more than 800,000 social media users and prompted thousands of shares, comments and reactions.
“If not us, then who will speak about the true face of communism?” Neringa Budrytė tells LRT.lt.
She says the increasingly visible use of communist symbols at protests in recent weeks prompted her to act.
“These young people romanticise communism, seeing it as an ideology worth striving for: equality, fraternity, economic prosperity for everyone, jobs for everyone, homes for everyone. But that was not the reality. That was the main point I wanted to make,” Budrytė says.
She also wanted to remind young people that under communist rule, protesting and expressing dissatisfaction with the authorities were not permitted.
In her post, she stresses that they can take to the streets and wave those flags today only because they live in a democratic world.
“I wanted them to wake up and understand what symbol they are carrying at these protests and what it means in historical terms. In Italy, there were even young people who brought the North Korean flag to protests.
I do not know whether those are their ideals. Is the North Korean model, or communist ideology, what they aspire to? Why are they carrying those symbols? That was the question I had,” Budrytė says.
She says the first people to respond to her letter were Ukrainian activists living in Italy, who frequently speak out about Russia’s crimes. They began sharing her appeal in their groups, and its reach continued to grow.
“Since the post was in Italian, most of the people I saw sharing it were Italian. So I think I achieved my goal of showing another side of communism. I did not expect it to reach so many people because I am not an influencer and do not have a huge following. I was afraid I would be attacked by an army of bots, but the exact opposite happened. That surprised me the most,” she says.
In the comments, people have spoken about relatives who were deported, while Italians have described what they saw when visiting various countries during communist rule or shortly after it ended.
Others have highlighted gaps in Italy’s education system when it comes to teaching about communism.
“There were testimonies saying that people in Italy are not taught what communist rule was really like. That all their studies end with the Second World War and nothing is said about the Cold War. That communism is idealised because Italy had a different historical experience: fascism existed here, and communists are seen as liberators.
“As a result, some teachers agree with those views and do not discuss communism as a regime that caused enormous harm and countless deaths, and was just as brutal as fascism or Nazism,” Budrytė says.
According to Budrytė, Italy has various communist organisations. Although the Communist Party has no seats in parliament and little political influence, it is actively trying to recruit young people.
“Just recently, I saw an advert inviting people to a communist camp in the countryside. I was personally invited to join an organisation about two years ago, when I was in Milan’s Piazza del Duomo. There was some kind of protest taking place there, too. I stopped by a tent displaying the hammer and sickle to look at their leaflets, and they invited me to join their organisation.
“They stressed that it was not a communist organisation but a new radical communist one, because ordinary communism was too moderate for them. There really is a strong radical left presence, and it is very visible. Now, with these protests spreading across Europe, I think it has found an opportunity to take advantage of the situation and make a comeback,” she says.
Budrytė also points out that the Communist Party is organising a protest in Rome on November 7, promoting it with a quote from Lenin.
“And for those who say that communism in Italy was different and had no connection with the Soviet Union, I do not know how they would explain these coincidences. Why do Italians not choose one of their own slogans when inviting people to protest, but instead use a slogan from Lenin?” she asks.
Budrytė hopes her open letter to young Italians will encourage the emergence of broader initiatives to educate people about communism.
She believes Lithuania could also take certain steps to help achieve this.
“In European countries where communism is viewed through rose-tinted glasses, laws should be changed so that communism is treated in the same way as Nazism and fascism. In Italy, for example, you cannot take to the streets displaying a swastika, but you can freely do so with the hammer and sickle,” she says.

“Hydrofeminism” and leaky saints feature in Everything Moist Seems Alive installation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

“Hydrofeminism” and leaky saints feature in Everything Moist Seems Alive installation
The technical minimalism of artist Boris Acket and the maximalism of fake fashion house Maison the Faux come together in the installation Everything Moist Seems Alive at MU Hybrid Art House during Dutch Design Week.
The multidisciplinary creatives worked with MU to devise the large-scale installation, which fills a dark, cavernous room with kinetic water structures connected by clear pipes and running on a continuous cycle of containment and deluge.
They are overlooked by towering video installations of glistening, oozing humanoid figures called the “leaky saints”.
These are surrounded by marshy candlelit altars and wishing wells, and, several times a day, brought to life by ritualistic choral performances from the Dutch National Opera and Ballet.
Everything Moist Seems Alive was the product of two years of discussion between the creatives on the topic of water, during which they were particularly drawn to cultural theorist Astrida Neimanis’ concept of “hydrofeminism”.
In her 2012 essay Hydrofeminism: Or, On Becoming a Body of Water, Neimanis considered the philosophical, ecological and sociological implications of conceptualising one’s human body primarily as water.
“In this hydrofeminist approach in the sense, we are all bodies of water,” said MU director Angelique Spaninks. “The world is made out of water, and so are we, for at least 60 per cent of our body.”
“Water is like: we need it. We tend to hide it. We want to control it. We use it as something that we need instead of thinking that we are part of it,” she continued. “And all these ideas have culminated into this total installation.”
The leaky saints serve as the most overt visual embodiment of Neimanis’ theory, dripping with shimmering fluid from their eyes, pores and other orifices.
“We lactate. We sweat. We have blood,” Spaninks summarises.
Greek myths and their powerful rivers also influenced the design of Everything Moist Seems Alive, which is broken up into five water structures.
Dubbed “water bodies” by the creatives, they each represent a different form of or interaction with water. There’s The Well, The Womb, The Whirl, The Wake and The Waterfall.
The Womb is a large circular tub in the centre of the space, and represents how everything “gets born in water, some way or another”, said Spaninks – an image that is evocatively conjured in the performance.
The Well is a series of three pumps that draws water from the tub and guides it into the rest of the system, in preparation for a climax that sees the usually dripping Waterfall, representing a dam, turn into a torrent.
The Whirl holds a white cloth that spins and dances with the movement of water, and the Wake slowly drips water onto a hot plate, emitting bursts of steam.
The pipes connecting the structures nod to the sanitation systems that underlie our daily interactions with water, while the gothic 3D-printed metallic ornaments on the pipes were inspired by Paris’ gargoyles, traditionally used to redirect rainwater flow away from buildings.
“We are big believers of ornamentation and the beauty of ‘a lot’ to give some sort of a reaction to mundane bareness,” Maison the Faux co-founder Joris Suk told Dezeen.
“What I like [in Everything Moist Feels Alive] is that it’s a collision of aesthetics. Studio Boris Acket is well known for its quite technical and stylish and minimalistic visual approach to things. We are very maximalist. So just bringing those two worlds together has created a lot of the aesthetics that you see here.”
Acket is best known for his mechanical fabric canopy Einder, which featured on the world tour of music producer Fred Again.
The Everything Moist Seems Alive installation is accompanied by a water bar at the entrance, where visitors can gather and sample three types of water – or choose to feed it to the installation.
The darkened water bar also features a suspended mixed-material sculpture by the artist Roni(a) Johansson that resembles abstracted flesh, with dozens of moist “egg sacs” setting the tone for the installation.
Maison the Faux was founded in 2012 by Suk and Tessa de Boer, both fashion design graduates who have gone on to build a cross-disciplinary practice involving performance art, fashion and costume design and set and interior design.
The conceit at the heart of their practice is that they are “a creative studio posing as a grand couture fashion house”, playing with the aesthetics of fashion and the boundaries between the real and the fake.
This Dutch Design Week also saw students protest against overcrowded facilities at Design Academy Eindhoven. Ahead of the week, we rounded up ten things to have on your radar during Dutch Design Week.
Dutch Design Week 2026 takes place from 17 to 25 October 2026 at various locations across Eindhoven, the Netherlands. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Ukraine, Russia trade strikes after Witkoff talks

Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, wounding at least 15 people, eight of whom have been hospitalized, city authorities said.

The latest round of strikes came after US special envoy Witkoff held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway earlier this week, followed by talks with Putin in Russia on Wednesday.

It was "the closest we've been" to ending the war, US President Donald Trump claimed after Witkoff's meeting with Putin. However, that did not stop the neighboring nations from keeping up a barrage of attacks.

Nearly half of youths in Finland use AI every day, survey finds
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:53:10 EEST
13:53:10 KST

A new survey has found that nearly half of children and young people aged 11 to 17 use artificial intelligence every day.
The survey was commissioned by two organisations working to protect children, Digirauha and the Itla Children's Foundation.
Nearly 80 percent of the pre-teen and teenage survey respondents said they used AI in some form. The most common uses were looking up information and getting help with schoolwork.
Nearly 40 percent of primary and secondary school-aged children said they could not tell the difference between AI-generated images and real photos and videos.
More than half of the respondents said they trusted the information given by AI, with boys reporting slightly higher levels of trust than girls.
Digirauha is a nonprofit aiming to protect children and young people from harms linked to commercial digital platforms. The Itla Children's Foundation aims to promote and support the wellbeing, equality, and position of children and families.
Polling firm E2 Research carried out the online panel-based survey in September. More than 1,000 individuals aged 11 to 17 took part.

Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:52:53 UTC
13:52:53 KST

Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network. However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, though a number of questions remain unanswered.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
What happened in Ukraine?
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News.
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
What are Starshield and Starlink?
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
Is Ukraine using Starshield or Starlink?
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters.
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
Musk and throttling Ukraine's access to Starshield
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X.
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
Intelligence-sharing
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.
Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites.
The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.
Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."
A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.
Rising pressure to end the war
Deliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said.
Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."
Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.
He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.
Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.

India hit out at the UN rapporteurs for bias in a counter-terror report after UN rapporteur Ben Saul described Dawood Ibrahim as leader of "India-based" D-Company criminal gang with terrorist ties
NEW DELHI: India has pushed back against a United Nations special rapporteur’s description of fugitive gangster Dawood Ibrahim’s D-Company as an “India-based” criminal group, flagging “glaring inaccuracies” in a counter-terrorism report. India warned that such factual errors, coupled with a lack of accountability for UN experts, risk undermining the credibility of the world body.Raghoo Puri, first secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, raised the objections on Wednesday during a meeting of the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly, responding to a report by Ben Saul, the special rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism.“My delegation has been pointing out in other forums as well our serious concern at the unacceptable situation of the SR (Special Rapporteur) releasing reports with factual inaccuracies, while not being held accountable for them,” Puri said.
He argued that the publication of reports containing factual errors without adequate accountability left member states with little scope to respond before the findings entered public discourse.
According to news agency ANI, he added, “It is in this context that we would like to point out some particularly glaring inaccuracies as far as my country is concerned.”Puri took issue with Saul's report, which stated that the UN Security Council had listed the leader of “the India-based D-Company” in 2003 for association with Al-Qaeda.“Read in isolation, this line paints a very different picture from the actual reality,” Puri said, rejecting the description of the criminal organisation as India-based.He said Ibrahim and his organisation had been wanted in India in connection with terror attacks since 1993, adding that the circumstances were documented in the UN Security Council's Al-Qaeda sanctions listing.“This is clearly written in the narrative summary of reasons of listing under the 1267 sanctions regime,” Puri said.
“Not mentioning this fact is regrettable, and such incompetence on part of special mandate holders does this organisation tremendous harm,” he added.Seeking to clarify the timeline, Puri said, “Let me correct it for the record. This individual fled India much before the 2003 listing, and it was during this period from outside our country that he was listed for being associated with Al Qaeda and with Osama bin Laden.”Puri also said the UN listing placed Ibrahim in the same country where Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden was found and killed, referring to Pakistan. Bin Laden was killed by US Navy SEALs in a raid in Abbottabad in 2011.

Foreign ministry top official to resign and stand in 2027 election
The top official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Jonatan Vseviov, has said he will resign on Thursday to run in next spring's national election for the Social Democratic Party (SDE).
Vseviov is currently in his second term as the ministry's secretary general and is Estonia's former ambassador in Washington. Previously, he was secretary general at the Ministry of Defense.
Vseviov will submit his resignation on Thursday and will leave his post on November 1.
"I have devoted my entire life so far to protecting and developing Estonia as a diplomat and civil servant. I have had the honor of leading dedicated teams with whom we have shaped Estonia's foreign and defense policy and implemented many of the decisions that have brought us to where we are today," Vseviov said.
"Today, however, I see that protecting Estonia and moving it forward requires more than what I can do as a civil servant. That is why I have decided to leave the civil service, join the Social Democrats and run in the upcoming elections," he said.
SDE Chairman Lauri Läänemets said Estonia's security and its position in the international arena require strong leadership.
"Jonatan Vseviov knows Estonia's security and foreign policy inside out and has extensive international experience. He has shaped Estonia's defense policy, led the Ministry of Defense, represented Estonia as ambassador in Washington and headed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Läänemets said.
Vseviov took office as secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in February 2021. Before that, he had served as Estonia's ambassador to the United States since August 2018.
From 2008 to 2018, Vseviov worked at the Ministry of Defense, eventually becoming its secretary general.
Before being appointed secretary general in January 2016, Vseviov served as deputy secretary general for defense planning, acting deputy secretary general for defense policy and director of the policy planning department.
Vseviov graduated from the University of Tartu with a degree in political science and earned a master's degree with honors in security studies from Georgetown University.
From 1999 to 2005, Vseviov was a member of the Reform Party.

Cuban FM slams U.S. strong-arm diplomacy ahead of key UN vote
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:50:33 CST
13:50:33 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez on Wednesday denounced the United States' unprecedented campaign of coercive diplomacy to pressure third countries to vote against a Cuban-backed draft resolution that condemns Washington's decades-long trade embargo against the Caribbean island.
The draft resolution, titled "Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba," is to be put to a vote at the United Nations General Assembly on Oct. 28, the 34th time for such a vote.
This year's draft resolution is the first to address the fuel and energy blockade imposed by Washington in January 2026, and the "collective punishment" it inflicts on all Cubans, Rodriguez told a press conference.
The resolution is a response to the extreme ramping up of the embargo, which has cost the small island more than 178.7 billion U.S. dollars in economic losses over the course of more than six decades, he said.
U.S. political pressure and economic threats "aim to compel those sovereign states to change their position regarding this draft resolution, to alter a state policy that many of them have, in the exercise of their sovereignty, maintained for decades," Rodriguez said.
Washington's methods, including threatening to impose sanctions and punitive tariffs, suspend cooperation programs, deny visas, and interfere in electoral processes, amount to "genuine political violence, coercion, and blackmail," the minister said.
The United States seeks to obscure the fact that a superpower "is committing an atrocious and ongoing act of abuse against a small, peace-loving nation, an attempt to destroy the nation's very fabric, constituting an act of genocide as defined under the Geneva Convention," Rodriguez added, saying that the debate at the UN General Assembly is not a bilateral matter, as it will address the sovereign rights of all peoples on the planet.
In January, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order imposing sanctions and tariffs on countries and entities that export or supply fuel to Cuba, a move Havana denounced as an "energy siege."
"This is an attempt to suffocate an entire population, to destroy a small nation," Rodriguez said. "What is happening to Cuba today could happen to any other state tomorrow."
A similar draft resolution, presented by Cuba at the UN General Assembly last year, received 165 votes in favor, seven against, and 12 abstentions. ■

Cloudflare sees millions of exploit attempts after PHP disclosure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:46:00 UTC
13:46:00 KST

Cloudflare sees millions of exploit attempts after PHP disclosure
- Cloudflare saw “millions” of exploit attempts after PHP’s critical flaws were disclosed, rising from “thousands” before the announcement to “tens of thousands” and then “hundreds of thousands” within hours.
- PHP developers released urgent fixes on Oct 21 and told users to “update immediately” after AI helped uncover long-hidden vulnerabilities in the language.
- Website operators and governments rushed to respond, with some European sites going offline and Japanese services, including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group and the Finance Ministry, temporarily suspending functions.
AI generated
Cloud services firm Cloudflare saw millions of exploitation attempts after the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the widely used programming language PHP, CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Oct 21.
“In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” Prince said.
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Oct 21 after the disclosure of vulnerabilities in PHP sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
Japanese lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group said it was temporarily suspending some internet services due to emergency measures.
Developers of the PHP programming language on Oct 21 released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying all users were “encouraged to update immediately”.

Collapsed Surrogacy Agency Loses U.S. Civil Case After Court No-Show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:46:00 UTC
13:46:00 KST

Collapsed international surrogacy agency World Center of Baby has been dealt a double blow in Florida, with a judge ruling against its U.S. corporate entity in a civil lawsuit – shortly after another case against the company was filed.
The developments come just over a month after OCCRP published a global investigation into the chaos World Center of Baby left in its wake after announcing it was filing for bankruptcy, including surrogates left unpaid and unsupported, and prospective parents abandoned.
In a decision made publicly available on Tuesday, Judge Thomas Ramsberger in Florida’s Sixth Circuit Court ruled in favor of a U.K.-based couple who brought a case against the agency’s U.S. corporate entity World Center Group Corp and two of its representatives. The complaint was on five counts, including breach of contract and fraud.
The lawsuit accused the company of “a calculated and coordinated scheme” to secure substantial payments for promised services despite its worsening financial and operational problems.
The judge noted that the decision was a default judgement as none of the three defendants — World Center Group Corp, its former listed president Yuri Star, and listed director Malvina Jonas — responded to summons sent to the addresses listed on the company’s corporate documents. The ruling followed an October 5 hearing that the defendants failed to attend.
World Center Group Corp, Star, and Jonas were ordered to recover funds for the couple amounting to $87,415 which they had paid for a World Center of Baby program that was meant to provide surrogate matching, medical coordination, and program management through the birth of two children. In the end, they received none of it. 
The couple, who spoke with reporters, but asked not to be named, said: “Although we have a judgement, we are not yet clear on what our chances of recovery are.”
The case was tried in Pinellas County on Florida’s west coast, because that is where the most recent incorporation documents list an address for World Center Group Corp.
Just before the judgement, a second civil lawsuit was filed in Pinellas County against Yuri Star and World Center Group Corp. by another intended parent who alleges they paid the agency more than $40,000 for medical procedures that were due to take place in Mexico, but did not happen and were not refunded. The plaintiff had been urged to pay the money up front in exchange for a discount, the complaint alleges.
That lawsuit lays out four counts against World Center Group Corp, including fraud and breach of contract, citing OCCRP’s investigation as part of the submitted evidence.
The complaint also alleges that the plaintiff was unaware that the agency did not actually employ medical staff in Mexico and instead used third-party clinics. Former World Center of Baby employees later told the plaintiff that the agency had stopped paying its partner clinics and employees around the time that the plaintiff traveled to Mexico for a clinic visit.
OCCRP’s investigation into World Center of Baby found that the agency’s operations and ownership were difficult to pin down, including basic information such as who owns it, its corporate structure, and what led to its demise.
Star, the former listed president, told reporters during the investigation that he had been hired as a consultant to register the company and knew nothing about it or why it collapsed. He said he was not a shareholder, investor, or beneficiary, and was still owed money for his services.
Star did not respond to a request for comment on the judgement against him.
Reporters were unable to reach Jonas, the listed director. Five employees who spoke with reporters said they had never met or spoken with her and one of the employees claimed her signature was automated.
Ukrainian businessman Vladyslav Natochii, who is variously listed on previous versions of the agency’s website as its founder, owner, and managing director, but is not on the paperwork of the Florida-registered entity told reporters that World Center of Baby had “experienced a severe financial and operational crisis,” and denied wrongdoing.

North Korea to resume propaganda broadcasts, South Korea urges dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:45:41 KST

North Korea to resume propaganda broadcasts, South Korea urges dialogue
North Korea has said it plans to resume broadcasting anti-South Korea propaganda along the armed border between the two countries, as Seoul urged Pyongyang to discuss easing tensions.
Kim Yo Jong, a senior North Korean official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Wednesday that North Korea will place loudspeakers along the entire border, following a visit with top military officials to fortifications along the contested frontier.
Kim warned Seoul of “the most horrible and distressing situation” if South Korea continued what Pyongyang calls interference in the North’s internal affairs.
She added in a follow-up statement on Thursday that North Korea would place “new counter means” on alert along the border, without elaborating, and have its loudspeakers on “standby” within days.
A landmine blast last month that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries has ratcheted up tensions. Seoul accused North Korean troops of deliberately laying mines in the border zone as part of the North’s fortification work.
Kim had denied the allegation, calling the incident a South Korean fabrication. She said North Korean tactical units had taken up new positions, and accused South Korean troops of conducting warning broadcasts and firing warning shots at multiple locations near the border.
Seoul said the warning shots were fired as “legitimate and defensive measures”.
North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications to what is already one of the world’s most heavily armed borders.
South Korea’s Ministry of National Defence urged North Korea on Thursday to discuss measures to ease tension at the border and prevent any accidental military clash, its spokesperson said.
Pyongyang had cut off a military hotline with the South after declaring it would no longer seek dialogue or unification with what it called its “foe”.
Loudspeaker propaganda
Both North and South Korea have historically used loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with South Korean broadcasts featuring K-pop music and news that have long irked Pyongyang and prompted tit-for-tat responses.
The two Koreas are separated by the DMZ, established after the 1950-53 Korean War ended in an armistice.
North Korea has been reinforcing its side of the DMZ with mines, barriers and fencing since 2024 as it seeks to establish what it calls a permanent border with South Korea.

Thursday 22 October 2026 06:45
Thursday, 22 October 2026, 06:45
PHOTO BNR-Ani Petrova
Font size
More than 30 scholars specializing in history, ethnography, anthropology and museology will take part in the academic conference “The Bulgarian Village and Town: Transformations Through Time”. The event will be held on October 22–23, 2026, at the Regional Ethnographic Museum in Plovdiv.
Participants will explore various aspects of the transformations of village and urban life over time-from traditional evening gatherings to concert stages- as well as changes in people’s lifestyles, ways of thinking and forms of communication. Topics will include festivals and rituals, material culture, and places of social interaction, such as markets and railway stations, alongside the economy, art, traditional food, etc. Special attention will be paid to the development of crafts and their role in people’s everyday lives.

According to Ukrinform, the Kherson Regional Military Administration reported this on Telegram.

Contracts have already been signed for the installation of 110 shelters. The first ten mobile shelters were set up in the Kherson district.
As Vitalii Bezgin, Minister for Communities, Territories, and Internally Displaced Persons, reported on Facebook, six frontline regions were selected as pilot areas: Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Kharkiv, and Chernihiv.
A total of 840 shelters need to be installed along school routes. This will require approximately 1.4 billion hryvnias.
Communities in the donor regions have already provided over 800 million hryvnias in co-financing.

UAE formally nominates candidate for UN Secretary-General
The nomination was submitted by UAE President His Highness Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in a letter addressed to the presidents of the UN General Assembly and the Security Council, in accordance with the established procedures for selecting and appointing the organization’s next chief.
In the letter, Sheikh Mohamed highlighted Nusseibeh’s extensive experience within the United Nations, her judgement in addressing international challenges, and her record of constructive engagement.
Nusseibeh previously served as the UAE’s Permanent Representative to the UN from 2013 to 2024. During her tenure, she held several prominent roles, including Vice-President of the General Assembly and President of the Executive Board of UN Women. She also co-chaired processes focused on revitalising the General Assembly and reforming the Security Council.
In addition, Nusseibeh served twice as President of the Security Council during the UAE’s 2022-2023 term.
Her diplomatic work has covered a broad range of international issues, including peace and security, humanitarian action, sustainable development, climate-related security risks, women’s affairs and multilateral reform.
The UN Security Council has been assessing candidates through a series of informal straw polls, with the latest round held on 16 October. The process is expected to continue in the coming weeks as Council members consider candidates for the organization’s top position.
Under the UN Charter, the Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly following a recommendation from the Security Council. The next Secretary-General is expected to begin the role in January 2027.

Taiwan’s National Symphony Orchestra pairs Britten’s bold sounds with Haydn’s surprises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:35:44 UTC
13:35:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s National Symphony Orchestra will explore Britain’s musical heritage through works by Benjamin Britten and Joseph Haydn at Taipei’s National Concert Hall on Thursday.
Conducted by Chien Wen-pin (簡文彬), the concert will feature German violinist Viviane Hagner, who is reuniting with the orchestra for the first time in 13 years. The program marks the 50th anniversary of Britten’s death in 1976.
It will open with Britten’s “The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra, Op. 34,” followed by Haydn’s “Surprise” Symphony. Hagner will join the orchestra for Britten’s “Violin Concerto, Op. 15,” which will close the evening.
“The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra” introduces the distinctive sounds of orchestral instruments. Chien said Britten captured the defining characteristics of each instrument, from the clarinet’s rapid runs to the French horn’s layered, full-bodied harmonies and the trumpet’s distinctive technical flair.
The violin concerto, meanwhile, reflects the youthful energy of Britten’s early compositional period and his willingness to challenge conventional forms. Its opening creates a striking contrast between percussion and strings, Chien said, while its tonal structure pays tribute to Ludwig van Beethoven, connecting the work to the broader classical tradition.
Haydn’s “Surprise” Symphony is one of 12 symphonies he composed during his later years in connection with his musical activities in London. It is best known for a sudden loud chord in its second movement, which helped make the work one of his most popular symphonies.
Chien noted that the symphony’s playful character extends beyond that famous passage. Haydn alternates between sudden bursts of sound and unexpected moments of softness, using shifts in dynamics, melody, and rhythm to give the music its wit and sense of mischief.
The concert will also feature Yang Zhe-yu’s (楊喆宇) “A Dialogue between Wind and Poetry,” part of the One-minute Symphony Project. The initiative is a collaboration between TSMC, the NSO, and the Taipei National University of Arts, designed to nurture young composers in Taiwan.

Russian strikes killed 3 people in Zaporizhzhia and the Zaporizhzhia district, while 3 others were injured. According to the Zaporizhzhia Defense Council, the occupiers launched 862 strikes on 48 settlements in the region over the course of the day.
In the Sumy region, a 74-year-old man was killed as a result of a drone strike on the Velykopysarivska community. Another 5 people were injured in various communities across the region. In particular, Russian drones attacked vehicles in the Sveska and Sumy communities. In addition, an 11-year-old boy who was injured during the October 20 attack required medical assistance.
In the Kherson region, a Russian drone struck a residential building in the village of Biliaivka, Beryslav district, on the evening of October 21. A 64-year-old man was killed in the attack. The prosecutor's office launched an investigation into a war crime.
Strikes on the Kharkiv region and energy infrastructure in the Poltava region
In the village of Lymanivka, Lozova district, Kharkiv region, Russian shelling killed a 42-year-old woman. Four more people were injured, including boys aged 10 and 13, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration.
In the Poltava region, Russian drones attacked Kremenchuk and the Kremenchuk district. In the city, a drone struck a private television and radio company's building, causing a fire.
In addition, a drone strike on an energy infrastructure facility was recorded in the Kremenchuk district. According to preliminary data from the Poltava Regional Military Administration, there were no casualties in either incident.
Fires in the Kirovohrad region and more than 20 attacks in the Dnipropetrovsk region
In the Kirovohrad region, Russian forces attacked the Kropyvnytskyi district on the evening of October 21. The strike caused warehouse buildings to catch fire. According to the State Emergency Service, rescuers localized the fire but continue to work at the site.
Firefighting efforts are complicated by the large area of the blaze and the threat of repeated Russian strikes. According to preliminary data, there were no deaths or injuries.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian forces attacked the Nikopol and Kamianske districts with drones more than 20 times during the night.
In the Nikopol district, Nikopol and the Marhanets, Pokrovske, Myrove and Chervonohryhorivka communities came under attack. In the Kamianske district, the Russians attacked the Pyatykhatske community, damaging infrastructure and causing a fire.
According to the regional authorities, no people were injured in these attacks in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
Rescuers and relevant services continue to deal with the aftermath of the Russian shelling. Information about the damage and the number of injured is being уточнено.

Taiwan issues land warning for Typhoon Champi
