2026-10-22
04:35:31 UTC
13:35:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Central Weather Administration issued a land warning for Typhoon Champi at 11:30 a.m. Thursday as the storm approached, with work and classes on Lanyu and Green Island suspended from noon.
The storm is expected to bring its strongest winds and heaviest rain to Taiwan on Friday and Saturday. Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, and Taoyuan are expected to announce whether work and classes will be suspended Friday at 8 p.m. Thursday, per UDN.
Under existing regulations, authorities may suspend work and classes based on forecast winds, rainfall, and local conditions. The final decision rests with local governments.
Suspensions may also be announced when rising rivers, damaged bridges, flooding, or dangerous changes in terrain affect transportation and the safety of traveling to work or school.
Rain is forecast across the country Friday, with heavy or extremely heavy rain possible in northern and eastern areas through Saturday. The CWA has warned that the storm could slow or linger near Taiwan, potentially prolonging its effects.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said Thursday that he would receive the latest forecasts from meteorologists in the evening before announcing whether work and classes would be suspended Friday, per CNA.
Chiang visited a pumping station Thursday after visiting the city’s disaster response center Wednesday night, where he received departmental reports and called for preparations. He said public safety was the top priority and announced the immediate suspension of all campaign activities.
Chiang said Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, and Taoyuan form an interconnected metropolitan area and that authorities would continue to follow existing procedures. He said differing views on the rules had been raised previously and further coordination with the central government was possible, but the immediate priority was typhoon preparedness.

Could China’s 100-channel single-photon detector enable broadband quantum internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:34:18 UTC
13:34:18 KST

Could China’s 100-channel single-photon detector enable broadband quantum internet?
New design shatters quantum network bottleneck, creating ‘robust and scalable infrastructure’ for large-scale applications, scientists say
Chinese scientists have developed a 100-channel single-photon detector, a breakthrough promising to pave the way for broadband quantum networks.
State-of-the-art single-photon detectors – essential components underpinning photonic quantum technologies – could previously support a maximum of 32 detection channels for photon signals.
Now, a newly developed interconnect scheme by a Shanghai-based team has broken this bottleneck, supporting more than 100 detection channels while maintaining accurate and stable operation.
“This work establishes a robust and scalable infrastructure, paving the way for large-scale quantum photonic applications,” the authors said in their paper.

====================================================================================================

British warship should ‘stand up’ to Russia in north
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:30:39 BST
13:30:39 KST

The government should prepare options for a British state-owned vessel to transit the Northern Sea Route in support of international freedom of navigation rights, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, sets out concern that Russia may seek to turn its control of the route into a de facto monopoly as it becomes more accessible.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its recommendation states: “The government should prepare options for a UK state-owned vessel to transit the Northern Sea Route in support of international freedom of navigation rights, including an assessment of the legal basis, operational risks and potential Russian response.”
The conclusion preceding it states: “As the Northern Sea Route becomes more accessible, Russia may seek to turn its control of the route into a de facto monopoly. A transit by a UK state-owned vessel through international waters could help uphold freedom of navigation rights under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, but this action would need to be carefully assessed against the operational and escalatory risks.”
The Northern Sea Route is a roughly 5,600 kilometre shipping lane running along Russia’s Arctic coast from the Kara Sea to the Bering Strait. Dr Marc De Vore, senior lecturer in international relations at the University of St Andrews, told the committee: “If we do not act to contest Russia’s illegal efforts to territorialise the northern sea route—these are their laws of 2012, 2018 and 2022—we will find after 2030, when the northern sea route becomes navigable all year long, that the Russians have set up a de facto monopoly on transit. They will make money off that, but they could also use it as a form of leverage—for example, if they do not like the level of support that Denmark is providing to Ukraine, they can cut off Maersk ships from sailing the northern sea route. Failing to contest that through freedom of navigation operations will give Russia a tremendous amount of both wealth and geopolitical leverage.”
The report records that in September 2018 the French Navy’s offshore support and assistance vessel Rhône transited the route from Tromsø in Norway to Dutch Harbor in Alaska without informing the Russian authorities. Russia subsequently stated that all foreign naval vessels would have to provide details of any proposed voyage at least forty-five days in advance and carry a Russian maritime pilot, and warned that if a voyage did not comply with Russian regulations it reserved the “right to take extraordinary measures including its forced halt, arrest and in extreme cases elimination.”
Freedom of navigation operations are actions taken by a country to sail or fly through contested international waters and airspaces to challenge maritime claims that break international law. The United States has conducted them in the Gulf of Sirte and the South China Sea, and Britain has done so near the Sea of Azov.
The committee notes such operations carry inherent risks, and in 2021 the Type 45 destroyer HMS Defender exercised its right of innocent passage through Ukrainian territorial waters off Crimea, which Russia had annexed in 2014, and Russia claims to have fired warning shots and dropped bombs near the vessel.
China is focused on using the route, with the sailing distance between Shanghai and Rotterdam approximately 25,500 kilometres via the Cape of Good Hope, 19,500 kilometres via the Suez Canal and 14,900 kilometres via the Northern Sea Route.

Canada unveils $6.2bn plan to shield manufacturers as Trump trade tariffs bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:30:08 UTC
13:30:08 KST

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump tariffs make both US and Canadian industries weaker and reduce choice for households in both countries.
Canada has announced a $6.2 billion (€5.7 billion) package to protect its steel and auto industries from US tariffs, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Washington has permanently altered a trade relationship built over decades.
Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford jointly unveiled the plan on Wednesday, directing $3.7 billion (€3.4 billion) to steelmakers and $1.8 billion (€1.65 billion) to automakers over five years, with $1.1 billion (€1 billion) of the auto funding coming from the federal government in Ottawa.
The announcement came the same day US-owned Cleveland-Cliffs confirmed layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant, underlining the human cost of the trade dispute.
“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage.”
The damage to the auto sector is already visible in the trade figures, as Canadian auto exports to the US have fallen more than 10 percent, while US exports to Canada have dropped more than 20 percent, a decline Carney said hurts both sides of the border.
“Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for our families,” he stressed.
Carney confirmed he spoke at length with President Trump on Wednesday, covering trade, Iran and the Middle East.
He signalled no breakthrough but said Canada remains ready to negotiate. Talks collapsed in August after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€18.4 billion) in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.
For his part, Ford was direct about what the dispute has done to bilateral ties. “No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were,” he said.
US embassy accuses Canada of meddling in midterms
Carney has set a target of doubling Canadian exports to non-US markets within a decade, acknowledging that an integrated North American auto industry may no longer be Washington’s priority.
“Their approach has changed,” he said. “So must ours.”
Meanwhile, the day took a sharper diplomatic turn when the US Embassy issued a statement accusing Canadian politicians of seeking to influence next month’s American midterm elections.
The embassy named Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for discussing retaliatory tariffs targeting Republican states and Ford for running a US television ad featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs, the ad that prompted Trump to walk away from trade talks in October 2025.
Both leaders rejected the allegations. So did independent analysts.
“The implicit assumption that Canada could significantly alter the outcome of the midterms is absurd,” said Daniel Béland, political science professor at McGill University.

2026-10-22
04:28:29 UTC
13:28:29 KST

The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States is scheduled to depart today following a new agreement between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the shipment, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
The tanker is being loaded with 40,000 metric tons of diesel, although Novak did not specify which Russian port it would depart from.
“Further deliveries will follow of course,” Novak said.
“Agreements have been reached between the two leaders. We will fulfill the American needs as well as we can.”
The shipment follows an agreement between Putin and Trump on supplying Russian diesel to international markets.
Russia lifted its own ban on diesel exports on October 9 after reaching the agreement with the U.S. president.
Moscow had previously introduced the export restrictions to address domestic fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The attacks had disrupted refining operations, contributing to shortages that prompted the Russian government to restrict diesel shipments abroad.
The new arrangement allows Russian diesel exports to resume, with the U.S. among the destinations for the fuel.
At a meeting Wednesday, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff thanked Putin for the agreement.
However, the deal has also contributed to worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv, according to the report.
Ukraine has been targeting Russian refineries with drone attacks, while the new agreement provides a route for Russian diesel to reach American markets.
Novak indicated that Thursday’s shipment would be the first of several deliveries under the arrangement.
He did not provide a timetable for subsequent shipments or disclose further details about their expected volumes.

====================================================================================================

Security flaw in widely used software forces Danish websites offline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:28:18 UTC
13:28:18 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Germany’s AfD proposes sweeping EU reforms while keeping euro and membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:28:09 UTC
13:28:09 KST

Germany’s right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party wants to remain in the European Union while substantially reducing the powers of its institutions.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel presented the proposal Wednesday at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, calling for changes to how the EU operates.
“The EU in its current form needs radical reforms,” Weidel said.
Under the plan, AfD would renegotiate EU treaties, reduce the bloc’s budget and transfer greater decision-making authority to national governments.
The party proposes abolishing the directly elected European Parliament and replacing it with delegations appointed by individual countries.
It also wants to limit the European Commission to administrative duties and replace the European Court of Justice with an arbitration court handling disputes between member states.
Weidel argued that the EU had failed to address economic pressures and migration concerns.
“We are experiencing a dramatic loss of purchasing power, galloping inflation, and we still have open borders,” she said.
The proposals resemble those of French politician Marine Le Pen, who also favors remaining in the EU while reducing its authority.
AfD’s announcement comes as the party records strong support in German opinion polls, with projected vote shares of approximately 27 to 30 percent.
Christel Schaldemose, a Danish Social Democrat and vice president of the European Parliament, criticized the proposals as a “frontal assault” on European democracy.
“Europeans must, of course, be able to elect their own representatives and vote us out again if they are dissatisfied,” she said.
Schaldemose also criticized AfD’s positions on Russia, including its opposition to sanctions and support for Ukraine.
“A weak and divided Europe would be a gift to Putin. We should not give him that gift,” she said.

UAE nominates diplomat Lana Nusseibeh for UN secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:28:05 UTC
13:28:05 KST

The race to lead the United Nations now has seven candidates after the United Arab Emirates nominated diplomat Lana Nusseibeh to succeed Secretary-General António Guterres.
The announcement was reported Wednesday evening by AFP.
Guterres, a former Portuguese prime minister, is due to step down at the end of this year after serving two five-year terms.
Nusseibeh previously represented the UAE at the UN for more than a decade, according to Reuters.
“I am running for the post of UN Secretary-General because I believe that we are in a time where there is a need to act with greater speed: to intervene earlier, build bridges between people across disagreements, and carry the work forward until it creates concrete results,” she said in a statement cited by AFP.
Her nomination comes as UN Security Council members struggle to agree on Guterres’ successor.
According to AFP, all candidates faced effective vetoes during an informal vote last week.
The six other contenders are Ecuador’s María Fernanda Espinosa and Ivonne A-Baki, Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu.
Five of the seven candidates are women. No woman has led the UN in its 80-year history.
Several Security Council members have expressed support for appointing a woman, while an informal tradition of regional rotation has also influenced discussions.
To advance, a candidate needs at least nine votes from the 15-member Security Council without a veto from any of its five permanent members: Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States.
The UN General Assembly must then approve the appointment.

Spotify removes millions of AI-generated songs from playlists and platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:27:55 UTC
13:27:55 KST

Spotify has removed 50 million AI-generated tracks from its playlists and recommendations this year as part of efforts to limit low-quality content on the streaming service.
The company also announced that it had deleted more than 75 million tracks from its platform, describing them as “AI slop and spam”.
The term “AI slop” refers to low-quality content generated using artificial intelligence, often produced quickly and cheaply in large quantities.
In a press release, Spotify explained that it identified suspicious tracks through listener feedback, upload patterns, information attached to music files and technology designed to detect AI-generated audio.
The company said it would continue improving its detection systems as artificial intelligence develops.
“AI-generated slop and spam do not belong in your recommendations, and we have made changes to keep them out and protect the listening experience,” Spotify stated.
Alongside removing content, Spotify has introduced measures to help listeners distinguish between music created by humans and AI-generated artists.
These include a verification badge indicating that a human artist is behind the music.
According to Spotify, more than 300,000 artists have received this verification.
The platform has also introduced a separate AI badge to identify artists whose identities are artificially generated.
One example is The Velvet Sundown, an AI-generated rock band that has received the badge.
According to Danish culture publication Soundvenue, the project has more than 100,000 monthly listeners on Spotify.
The band, which has no human members, released the song “Dust in the wind” last year.
The track has since accumulated more than 5 million streams on the platform.

Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:27:50 UTC
13:27:50 KST

Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.
She will be accompanied by Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party.
Turkey is co-hosting this year’s summit with Australia, which is responsible for leading the negotiations.
The annual UN climate conferences bring countries together to discuss international efforts to address climate change and reach agreements on reducing its impact.
During her visit, Queen Mary will meet representatives of Danish companies showcasing environmentally friendly technologies and solutions at the Danish pavilion.
She will also focus on the challenges facing Pacific island nations, including Vanuatu and Fiji, which are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and other consequences of climate change.
Another part of her program involves meeting young delegates from around the world to hear about their experiences with climate change and efforts to support the green transition.
Queen Mary also attended last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, where her program included visits to a cocoa production facility and a research institute working on sustainability.
Her upcoming visit follows a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), published Wednesday, warning that global warming will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
The report attributes this to decades of insufficient climate action.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius compared with temperatures between 1850 and 1900, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees.
Security flaw in widely used software forces Danish websites offline
Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen described the situation as a “global incident” but stressed that it was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she warned that websites could face serious risks unless their operators installed the necessary security updates.
“It can potentially be really serious if system owners do not get a security update done. If that is not possible right here and now, then one must consider going offline,” she said.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP, which powers many websites, online shops and digital portals.
According to Reuters, PHP’s developers identified the flaws Tuesday but released an update to fix them Wednesday at 1:45 p.m.
Bech-Nielsen told Denmark’s public broadcaster, DR, that websites without the update could be exposed to attacks.
“It is in a way positive that we have found these vulnerabilities. But because it is publicly known, there are some who will exploit it,” she said.
Authorities and public institutions in several countries temporarily shut down websites as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected services included websites belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, the Danish Road Directorate and the Danish Meteorological Institute, known as DMI.
Kombit, an organization that manages shared IT solutions for Danish municipalities, also confirmed that Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, had been taken offline.
The ministry said authorities were closely monitoring developments but did not clarify whether further political action would be necessary.
Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.
Danish bishops consider moving Great Prayer Day to autumn when holiday returns
Great Prayer Day could return to Denmark’s calendar in a different season, with most bishops of the Church of Denmark open to moving the public holiday from spring to autumn.
The discussion follows the government’s announcement that Store Bededag, or Great Prayer Day, will be reinstated as a public holiday in 2030, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
The holiday was abolished by the previous Social Democrat, Venstre and Moderates coalition government, with the change taking effect in 2024.
The Ministry of Ecclesiastical Affairs has confirmed that the Church of Denmark will be involved in the reinstatement process. A bill is expected in spring 2027.
Thomas Reinholdt Rasmussen, bishop of Aalborg, suggested that late October might be a suitable alternative.
“Liturgically, it does not really fit into the period from Easter to Pentecost, so perhaps it would be good to place it at the end of October,” he told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Marianne Gaarden, bishop of Lolland-Falster, also expressed openness to changing the date, noting that spring already has several public holidays.
“I like the idea of a prayer day where the focus is on spiritual reflection, and that focus must be preserved. But of course it is possible to consider that it can be moved,” she said.
Bishops in Funen, Aarhus and Viborg are similarly open to discussions, while Helsingør’s bishop, Peter Birch, has not taken a position.
However, the bishops of Ribe and Roskilde favor restoring the holiday to its original spring date.
The bishop of Copenhagen has not commented, while Haderslev’s bishop, Marianne Christiansen, will wait until the government presents its proposal.
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.
She will be accompanied by Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party.
Turkey is co-hosting this year’s summit with Australia, which is responsible for leading the negotiations.
The annual UN climate conferences bring countries together to discuss international efforts to address climate change and reach agreements on reducing its impact.
During her visit, Queen Mary will meet representatives of Danish companies showcasing environmentally friendly technologies and solutions at the Danish pavilion.
She will also focus on the challenges facing Pacific island nations, including Vanuatu and Fiji, which are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and other consequences of climate change.
Another part of her program involves meeting young delegates from around the world to hear about their experiences with climate change and efforts to support the green transition.
Queen Mary also attended last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, where her program included visits to a cocoa production facility and a research institute working on sustainability.
Her upcoming visit follows a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), published Wednesday, warning that global warming will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
The report attributes this to decades of insufficient climate action.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius compared with temperatures between 1850 and 1900, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees.
Severed network cable disrupts departure screens and train information apps across Denmark
A severed network cable at Banedanmark disrupted departure and arrival information at many train stations across Denmark on Wednesday.
The problem also affected the MitTog app, while users experienced difficulties getting updated information on Rejseplanen, Denmark’s journey planning service.
Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, said information about train times was being provided through station loudspeakers wherever possible.
The disruption did not affect information screens for the S-trains, Copenhagen’s suburban rail network, according to railway operator DSB.
Shortly before 1 p.m. Wednesday, Banedanmark’s press office said the damaged cable had been restored.
The company expected information screens and apps to gradually return to normal operation.
New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.
Venstre and other opposition parties expect to be left out of Denmark’s 2027 budget deal
Venstre does not expect to be included in an agreement with the government on Denmark’s 2027 national budget, party chairman Troels Lund Poulsen said after an introductory meeting on Wednesday.
“There is no willingness to listen to our views. It is a budget that has been agreed upon in advance with the government’s support parties. And that is just how it is,” Lund Poulsen said, according to Danish public broadcaster DR.
The government’s support parties are Enhedslisten, the Red-Green Alliance, and Alternativet, a green political party. Both are expected to reach a budget agreement with the government, particularly as it is the first national budget deal since the general election earlier this year.
Lund Poulsen said Venstre would be willing to attend further negotiations if the government invited the party.
Other opposition parties also expressed doubts about their chances of joining the agreement after meeting with Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, a member of the Social Democrats, on Wednesday.
Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, does not expect to receive further invitations, according to its finance spokesperson, Anders Vistisen, who spoke to DR.
The same applies to De Konservative, the Conservative People’s Party.
“That is what I think. Because regarding the wishes we have for the budget, we have not been accommodated,” party chairman Mona Juul said.
The Conservatives were the only opposition party included in last year’s budget agreement, when the government consisted of the Social Democrats, Venstre and Moderaterne, the Moderates.
Liberal Alliance also took part in negotiations on Wednesday. Its political leader, Alex Vanopslagh, does not expect the party to be included in the final budget agreement, according to DR.
Danmarksdemokraterne, another opposition party, also attended negotiations on Wednesday.
The budget negotiations follow a setback for the government on Tuesday, when it had to abandon a proposal to tighten the eligibility requirements for senior pensions after failing to secure support from the parties involved in the negotiations.
The decision was welcomed by Pelle Dragsted, Enhedslisten’s political spokesperson.
“We are very happy about that. It was antisocial to cut the opportunities of worn-out workers to be able to retire,” he said on Tuesday.
Under its budget proposal, the government had planned to save 200 million kroner in 2028, 500 million kroner in 2029 and 800 million kroner in 2030 by tightening the requirements for senior pensions.
Enhedslisten and Alternativet held their budget negotiations with the government on Tuesday.
Danish municipalities shut down IT systems after potential security risk
Kombit, the IT organization serving Denmark’s municipalities, has shut down several of its digital services, either fully or partially, after identifying a potential technical security risk.
The shutdown began Wednesday afternoon and affects services including Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, and the municipal library system, Lars Skov Granerud, Kombit’s press manager, told news agency Ritzau.
“We have been made aware of a potential technical security risk in an underlying element of several of our solutions,” he said.
“Therefore, we decided a short while ago to shut down several of them.”
Kombit does not yet have a complete overview of the situation, Granerud said.
The disruption also affects several municipal systems used by local government employees in their daily work, including systems for processing benefit payments.
Aula has been shut down completely, while the library system is only partially affected, Granerud said.
Kombit has not disclosed which other digital services have been affected.
Unauthorized people have gained access to parts of the computer systems of the Danish department store chain.
Magasin reported the incident in an email to DR, the Danish public broadcaster.
Following the breach, Magasin warned members of its customer loyalty club, named Goodie, that their personal details may have been compromised. The exposed data includes names, addresses, and purchase history.
“We are working dedicatedly with external experts to handle the incident, including re-establishing our access to the systems. In addition, we have reported the incident to both the police and Datatilsynet,” Magasin stated in the email. Datatilsynet is the Danish Data Protection Agency, the national authority that oversees data privacy rules.
Magasin warned that the compromised details could be used to make phishing scams look more believable.
Phishing is a deceptive practice where scammers try to trick individuals into handing over personal information. This often happens through fake emails designed to steal login details for MitID, the official digital identification system used across Denmark for banking and public services.
Magasin stressed in its message to club members that the security breach did not include any credit card information.
“We want to emphasize that we are working to limit the scope of the breach and to ensure that something similar does not happen again,” the email said.
The incident follows a similar alert sent to shoppers a few weeks ago by the British online retailer Asos.
In that case, Asos stated that an unauthorized person managed to enter an employee account. The intruder used that account to pull information from external platforms that Asos works with.
That breach allowed the unauthorized user to access customer names and contact details.
Following the incident, Asos told its customers to be cautious of unexpected phone calls and messages from individuals pretending to work for the company. Asos also reported its security breach to the police.
Foreign workers and older employees fuel Denmark’s job market growth
The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. The competition authorities determined that this practice broke legal rules meant to secure free competition, and they made their official decision on the case back in 2018.
The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. That investigation led to criminal charges against the company, with authorities seeking a fine. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.
The specific legal reasons behind the court decision are not yet known. In a brief summary published on its website, the Maritime and Commercial Court stated that the full ruling will be released within four weeks.
The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.
Denmark warns travelers in France to avoid protests as curfews continue
Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has advised people in France to stay away from demonstrations and large gatherings because of the risk of violence.
In updated travel advice on its website, the ministry warns that unrest and clashes between protesters and police remain possible in major cities, including Paris.
It also warns that authorities may introduce curfews at short notice.
Curfews were imposed overnight into Tuesday in parts of Paris and the northern French cities of Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain.
According to AFP, French police said the Paris curfew began at 11 p.m. Monday. In the other cities, restrictions remain in place Tuesday from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday that the curfews had helped restore calm overnight, according to Reuters and AFP.
He added that local authorities could impose further restrictions if necessary.
“Tonight, new curfews will be introduced where the situation requires it. The decisions will be made locally by the prefects in cooperation with the mayors,” Lecornu wrote on X.
The measures follow a weekend of demonstrations that brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets across France.
Protesters are demonstrating against the high cost of living and what they see as a lack of economic opportunity and security.
The demonstrations were accompanied by reports of vandalism and looting.
According to the Paris Chamber of Commerce, between 300 and 400 shops were vandalized in the capital.
Nationwide, around 2,000 shops were affected, the French Chamber of Commerce told Reuters.
More than 1,800 people were arrested Saturday following demonstrations across the country.
Plans to tighten Denmark’s senior pension rules dropped after political opposition
The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.
Four Danish opposition parties demand broader tax cuts in government plan
Denmark’s Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and Denmark’s Democrats say they will reject the government’s upcoming tax plan unless it includes cuts for people earning less than 58,000 DKK a month.
The four opposition parties will present their demands during tax negotiations with Minister for Taxation and Growth Jakob Engel-Schmidt later this week.
The government wants to remove the top-top tax and intermediate income tax, benefiting people earning more than approximately 58,000 DKK a month.
It also plans to reduce corporate tax by three percentage points starting in 2030.
The four parties argue that lower-income workers should also benefit.
“It is only fair and reasonable that the police officer, the shop assistant, the electrician, and everyone else with a salary below 58,000 kroner also get a tax cut,” Conservative leader Mona Juul said in a written statement.
Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen said his party supports reducing corporate and intermediate taxes but wants cuts for everyone in employment.
Liberal Alliance leader Alex Vanopslagh said “completely ordinary Danes must get more out of going to work”.
Denmark Democrats leader Inger Støjberg called for tax changes that would help families facing higher fuel, energy and food prices.
The government may need support from the four center-right parties to pass its plan.
Its usual parliamentary allies, The Red-Green Alliance, a left-wing party, and The Alternative, a green progressive party, are not expected to support several of the proposed measures.
Government plan would remove SU from 14,000 students living with parents
About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.
An estimated 31,800 higher education students living at home received SU in 2025.
The government proposes ending payments for students whose parents have a combined annual income above 710,077 DKK. This corresponds to an average monthly income of 29,583 DKK for each parent in a two-parent household.
Payments would gradually decline for students whose parents earn between 419,589 and 710,077 DKK annually. The lowest monthly grant would be 500 DKK before disappearing entirely above the upper threshold.
The government initially estimated that 81,000 students living at home across different education programs would be affected. The later decision to reduce grants gradually for middle-income households means the final number could be higher.
Disability supplements and additional support for single parents would remain available regardless of parental income.
The Socialist People’s Party and Social Liberal Party have faced criticism for supporting the reductions.
SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr acknowledged that her party had not proposed the measure but said it was part of the compromises required in government.
Minister calls for talks after report finds major employment losses due to stress
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.
However, the report found no evidence that the number of severe stress cases has increased during the past 15 to 20 years.
Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.
Social Democrat warns foreign labor risks creating master-servant society
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek has warned that Denmark risks developing a society divided between those providing low-paid services and those becoming dependent on them.
“What do we become as human beings if we slowly let low-paid Africans and Asians do everything that is not immediately manageable?” Dybvad Bek said Monday during a budget debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
He questioned whether Danes lose practical skills and the ability to learn when they rely on foreign workers, delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for routine tasks.
Dybvad Bek referred to German philosopher Georg Hegel’s theory that a master becomes increasingly helpless as a servant performs more of the work.
He said individual consumers were not responsible for the development.
“It is up to us politicians to stop the flow of underpaid labor that forms the basis for these services,” he said.
Dybvad Bek argued that goods and services should be priced at a level that allows workers to earn a living wage.
He also warned that Denmark could create new parallel societies if foreign workers remain socially separated from the people they serve.

Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.

More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week

The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.

He said countries could spend time debating scientific facts instead of agreeing on action.

IPCC decisions require consensus rather than majority votes.

Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.

Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, an increase of 1.5 percentage points from the previous year.
Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.

“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.

Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.

Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.

Denmark’s oldest-ever person was a member of the Danish Nazi party
Records show that 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe joined Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation. She says she did so at her husband’s request and did not sympathise with Nazism.
Kirsten Schwalbe, who this week became the longest-living Dane in recorded history, was a member of Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation.
The 112-year-old joined the National Socialist Workers’ Party of Denmark (DNSAP) in August 1941, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
Her name appears in the Bovrup registry, a record of people who were members of DNSAP. Two historians have independently confirmed to the newspaper that the entry matches Schwalbe’s date of birth and address, although her surname is misspelled as “Schalbe”.
Schwalbe has confirmed that both she and her former husband were members of the party, but says she only joined because her husband urged her to do so.
She rejected the suggestion that she had sided with Nazi Germany.
“Not at all. I barely knew what it was, because I have never taken an interest in politics,” she told TV Midtvest when asked whether she had sympathised with the Nazis.
Schwalbe said she found it unfair that she should have to “pay for it” more than 70 years later, adding that “back then, wives didn’t look into such things”.
Membership does not show level of involvement
DNSAP was founded in 1930 and was strongly inspired by Adolf Hitler’s German Nazi Party, the NSDAP.
But Charlie Krautwald, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, cautioned against drawing conclusions about Schwalbe’s level of involvement from the registry alone.
The record shows that a person joined the party, he told Kristeligt Dagblad, but not why they joined, how long they remained a member or whether they paid membership fees.
A person could therefore appear in the registry without having been active in the party.
TV Midtvest has followed Schwalbe for several years and manages an Instagram account about her life. Two of the broadcaster’s employees have also recently published a book about her.
Her membership of DNSAP had not previously been mentioned. TV Midtvest editor-in-chief Marc Killigren Akselsen told Kristeligt Dagblad that the broadcaster had not known about it.
Schwalbe, who lives in Struer in western Jutland, became the longest-living Dane on record on Wednesday, when she reached the age of 112 years and 218 days.

“I don’t know how many it involves, but considering that we have around a handful of million transactions daily, it is a very small part of them,” he said. “We are talking about a couple of thousand in Denmark.”
Customers who notice a duplicate transaction can contact their bank, Pedersen said.

Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Lidl offers the lowest prices on a selected basket of organic groceries among seven Danish supermarket chains, according to an analysis by price-monitoring service Madprisluppen.
A basket containing 22 organic products cost 355.20 DKK at Lidl. The same basket cost 449.60 DKK at Meny, the most expensive chain in the comparison.
Madprisluppen said the Lidl basket was 26 percent cheaper than the one at Meny.
“We want to make it easier for Danes to make room for organics in everyday life, and here price plays an important role,” Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said.
Rema 1000 was the second-cheapest supermarket, with its basket costing only 5 DKK more than Lidl’s.
SuperBrugsen was the second-most expensive, though its total was almost 35 DKK below Meny’s.
The analysis also included Netto, 365discount and Føtex. Prices were recorded from October 9 through October 12.
Products included milk, eggs, vegetables and dry goods. Meat was excluded because Madprisluppen found it difficult to identify comparable products across the chains.
The monitoring service also found that supermarkets carry fewer organic products than they did six years ago. Organic prices have increased, and such products appear in special offers less frequently than non-organic groceries.
Norway to lend 10-meter Viking boat to Danish museum for 10 years
A Norwegian Viking boat will be displayed at Moesgaard Museum near Aarhus under an unusual 10-year loan agreement.
The oak boat is almost 10 meters long and nearly two meters wide. It was among three smaller vessels discovered when archaeologists excavated Norway’s Gokstad ship in 1880.
The Gokstad ship is Norway’s largest preserved Viking ship.
“The boat is a very important cultural treasure from the Viking Age, and it is not an everyday occurrence that we grant permission for such a boat to be taken out of the country,” Kaare Stang of Riksantikvaren, Norway’s cultural heritage authority, said.
The three smaller boats had been chopped into pieces, possibly as part of a burial ritual, according to archaeologists.
The Museum of Cultural History in Norway owns the boat and applied for permission to lend it to Moesgaard Museum for a new exhibition.
Norwegian authorities normally approve loans for no more than three years. Moesgaard Museum must therefore submit a report on the boat’s condition every three years during the loan period.
Stang said Norwegian authorities trusted the Danish museum to protect the boat but emphasized that it must eventually return to Norway.
No arrival date has been announced.
Moesgaard Museum already displays a 6.5-meter Gokstad boat that was used to transport crews and exchange orders between warships.
Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
A new parents’ association has signed a four-year agreement with the City of Copenhagen to establish support groups for families whose children experience prolonged, involuntary school absence.
Such absence is often connected to poor well-being and is considered concerning when a pupil misses at least 20 percent of school for two consecutive quarters. That corresponds to about 10 days per quarter.
The first groups will be funded by Copenhagen and include eight to nine parents who meet approximately once a month, education news outlet Folkeskolen.dk reported.
A family therapist will lead the meetings, with a parent from Forældrekommissionen, or the Parents’ Commission, also participating.
Louise Gielov and Jens Langorn helped establish the association after their family appeared in the Danish public broadcaster DR documentary “Skolens tabte børn,” which showed daily life with children unable to attend school.
The couple received more than 1,000 messages from parents in similar situations after the documentary aired.
The association now has 2,545 members and aims to establish parent groups across Denmark. It also plans to use families’ experiences to promote earlier intervention and broader changes to prevent school absence.
The proportion of pupils with prolonged concerning absence increased from 2.4 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 5.1 percent in 2024-2025.
The association has also secured 7 million DKK from foundations.
Dane becomes first European participant to receive combined flu and Covid vaccine
A 65-year-old Dane will become the first person in Europe to receive a new combined influenza and Covid-19 vaccine as part of a clinical trial Friday.
The trial will examine whether one injection can protect against both diseases as effectively as, or better than, the two separate vaccines currently used, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The first participant will receive the vaccine at Gentofte Hospital.
“We are investigating whether one shot with this new vaccine is just as effective or potentially better than the two shots given today at preventing hospitalizations with influenza and Covid-19,” said Tor Biering-Sørensen, a professor and senior physician at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital who is leading the trial.
About 165,000 Danes have agreed to participate. More than 300,000 people are expected to join over the next two years.
Half of the participants will receive one dose of the combined vaccine. The other half will receive separate influenza and Covid-19 vaccinations.
People age 65 and older in Denmark are automatically invited to receive free vaccinations against both diseases. The Danish Health Authority said about 1.3 million residents received invitations in September.
People with chronic illnesses or other conditions placing them at increased risk are also eligible for the free program.
The vaccines are intended to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization during the winter respiratory infection season.

Hungary is considering a plan to abandon the Russian company Rosatom—the primary contractor for the planned expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant—and has begun searching for alternative suppliers, reports Reuters.
The project, which Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán awarded to Rosatom in 2014 without a competitive tender, is politically sensitive and extremely costly. Climate change has added further uncertainty regarding its future; in August, low water levels in the Danube nearly forced the shutdown of the existing reactors at the Paks plant. The expansion of the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is currently the largest nuclear energy project in the European Union. Finland terminated its contract with Rosatom in May 2022, a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, leading to an ongoing legal dispute between the two countries. Under Orbán’s leadership, Hungary has opposed any sanctions against the Russian nuclear energy sector.
The government, led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, is expected to reach a final decision regarding the Paks Nuclear Power Plant either late this year or early next year. The costs of the expansion project were initially estimated at 12.5 billion euros; however, by the time the first section of the foundation was poured this February, the project had already cost the state more than two billion euros.
A spokesperson for the Hungarian government and Rosatom did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters. When asked whether an assessment of the project could lead to a change in the main contractor, a person familiar with the matter indicated that all scenarios are being considered.
