Israel switches to standard time this weekend: when clocks go back and what you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:14:18 UTC
13:14:18 KST

Israel will officially switch from daylight saving time to standard time overnight between Saturday, October 24, and Sunday, October 25, 2026. At 2 a.m., clocks will move back one hour to 1 a.m., giving residents an extra hour of sleep. The change marks the end of daylight saving time, with Israel remaining on standard time until March 26, 2027.
Here's everything you need to know about the upcoming clock change.
When does standard time begin in Israel?
Standard time takes effect early Sunday, October 25. At 2 a.m., clocks will be turned back one hour to 1 a.m., meaning the hour between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. will occur twice. Israel will remain on standard time until Friday, March 26, 2027, when clocks will move forward again.
Will we gain or lose an hour of sleep?
Because the clocks move backward, we gain an extra hour. For anyone able to sleep in on Sunday morning, that means an additional hour of rest.
Will my smartphone and alarm clock update automatically?
Most modern smartphones automatically adjust to seasonal time changes, meaning users generally do not need to do anything. Alarm clocks set through the phone's operating system should also follow the updated local time.
Anyone unsure whether their device will make the change should check the date and time settings and ensure automatic time and time-zone adjustment are enabled. If the device does not update correctly, users can manually select Israel's time zone, generally listed as Jerusalem, and verify that the correct local time is displayed.
Traditional alarm clocks, wall clocks and other devices without automatic synchronization will need to be adjusted manually.
Why does Israel switch to standard time?
Israel's seasonal clock changes are governed by the Time Determination Law, which was amended in 2013. Under the legislation, daylight saving time ends each year on the final Sunday in October, when clocks move back one hour.
The immediate effect is that sunrise and sunset occur approximately one hour earlier according to the clock. Mornings become brighter earlier, while darkness falls sooner in the afternoon and evening.
How does the switch to standard time affect our bodies?
The transition from daylight saving time to standard time can influence sleep patterns, energy levels and mood, partly because of changes in exposure to natural daylight.
Melatonin, often called the sleep hormone, helps regulate the body's internal clock and sleep-wake cycle. Its production is closely linked to light and darkness, meaning seasonal changes in daylight exposure can affect how alert or sleepy people feel.
Serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation, has also been linked to sunlight exposure. Reduced daylight during the colder months may contribute to lower mood and fatigue in some people, although responses to seasonal changes vary considerably.
How does the clock change affect daily life?
Seasonal time adjustments are intended to better align human activity with available daylight.
During daylight saving time, people benefit from an additional hour of evening light, allowing more outdoor activities after work or school. Standard time, by contrast, shifts that daylight toward the morning, so people are more likely to begin their day after sunrise.
The trade-off is that evenings become darker earlier, affecting everything from commuting and outdoor activities to family routines.
Why not keep daylight saving time all year?
The question has sparked repeated debate in Israel and around the world. Supporters of permanent daylight saving time argue that longer, brighter evenings would benefit families, businesses and recreational activities.
Critics of the seasonal switch also argue that earlier sunsets can reduce the time parents spend outdoors with their children, increase exposure to darkness during evening commutes and create additional economic costs.
However, permanent daylight saving time would also mean later sunrises during the colder months, potentially requiring more people, including schoolchildren, to begin their day in darkness.
Despite repeated proposals to change the system, Israel has maintained its existing arrangement.
What happens in other countries?
Many countries around the world no longer change their clocks seasonally, including most countries in Asia, Africa and South America.
In the United States, proposals to end the twice-yearly clock changes have gained support, although much of the country continues to observe daylight saving time.
The European Parliament voted in 2019 to support ending seasonal clock changes, potentially allowing individual countries to adopt permanent standard time or daylight saving time. However, the proposal has not been fully implemented, and most European countries continue to adjust their clocks twice a year.
When will daylight saving time return in 2027?
Israel will return to daylight saving time early Friday, March 26, 2027. At 2 a.m., clocks will move forward one hour to 3 a.m., meaning residents will lose an hour of sleep but regain longer daylight hours in the evening.

El Salvador launches military operation in Haiti to free four kidnapped aviation technicians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:10:23 UTC
13:10:23 KST

Bukele warned that failure to free the men who have been missing since Sunday’s attack on an armoured vehicle would trigger a far more powerful operation.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele announced Wednesday that he had launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped by gangs in Haiti, warning of a far more forceful response if they are not returned alive and unharmed.
The four men have been missing since Sunday, when gangs opened fire on an armoured vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince. The technicians fled the burning vehicle and have not been seen since, marking the first major attack on the international gang suppression force since it began operating in Haiti.
Addressing Haitian gang leaders directly, Bukele issued a stark ultimatum.
“Today’s attack is nothing compared to what is coming if they do not release the four hostages alive. And do not take our words as empty threats,” he wrote on X, sharing a video of armoured vehicles with shattered windows moving through smoke.
He added that if the men were returned safely, “everything will go back to the way it was before the kidnapping” but stopped short of specifying whether any further action would involve Salvadoran, Haitian or international forces.
Bukele stressed that El Salvador’s mission in Haiti is strictly non-combat. The four men are aviation technicians whose primary role is to carry out medical evacuations, he said, adding that the Salvadoran contingent “consists only of pilots and technical personnel, not to wage war.”
Haiti declares rescue an “absolute priority”
Haiti’s government responded Wednesday evening, saying the abduction of the technicians was an “absolute priority.”
A meeting was held at the prime minister’s office to assess ongoing operations and coordinate with the Gang Repression Force, according to a government statement.
“All necessary resources are being mobilised to achieve this goal,” the statement said. It was not immediately clear whether Haitian authorities had confirmed that the four men are still alive. A spokesperson for the gang suppression force did not respond to requests for comment.
The attack underscores the scale of the challenge facing international forces in Haiti, where gangs are estimated to control around 70 percent of Port-au-Prince. The country is also preparing for its first general election in more than a decade.
El Salvador is one of several countries, including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala, contributing to the multinational gang suppression force, which has more than 2,000 troops on the ground.
The UN originally approved up to 5,550 security personnel and more than 50 civilian staff for the mission in 2025. The force received at least a six-month extension through March 2027 from the UN Security Council.
In early October, El Salvador passed a law extending its own participation in the force for a year, also broadening its mandate beyond medical evacuations to allow the deployment of civilian and military personnel according to the mission’s broader needs.

ADB report calls for action as Asia-Pacific coasts face mounting flood risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:01:34 CST
13:01:34 KST

MANILA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Asia-Pacific coastlines face growing threats as sea levels rise and floods intensify, but investing in resilience could generate benefits up to 20 times greater than the cost, according to an Asian Development Bank (ADB) report.
Annual coastal flood damages in the Asia-Pacific region could increase more than sixfold by 2050 and nearly twentyfold by 2100 without adaptation, according to the Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise-Actions for a Resilient Future released on Wednesday.
Based on estimates across 30 coastal economies, the report estimates that annual flood damages could reach 172 billion U.S. dollars to 199 billion U.S. dollars by 2050 and 520 billion U.S. dollars to 739 billion U.S. dollars by 2100, compared with approximately 27 billion U.S. dollars today.
The report said keeping flood damages near today's levels would require an estimated 9 billion U.S. dollars to 19 billion U.S. dollars a year in coastal protection, an investment that could avoid 178 billion U.S. dollars to 360 billion U.S. dollars in flood damages each year.
According to ADB, over 400 million people in the region live within 10 kilometers of the sea. Coasts are hubs for ports and trade, as well as tourist and heritage spots. Without adequate adaptation measures, larger economies could face some of the highest economic losses in absolute terms, while relative impacts are particularly severe in atoll nations, where annual flood damage could reach 30 percent to 60 percent of GDP by 2100.
In major coastal cities such as Bangkok, Jakarta, Kolkata, and Mumbai, coastal floods that historically occurred once every 100 years could become annual events by the end of the century, said the report. ■

PETERSBURG, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- China and Russia have leveraged more dynamic and resilient cooperation to cushion the impact of external uncertainties and instability, and bilateral ties are entering a new stage marked by greater achievements and faster development, said Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday.
Li made the remarks while co-chairing the 31st regular meeting between Chinese and Russian heads of government with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
This year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination. For three decades, the regular meeting, held every year since its inception in 1996, has served as an important mechanism for implementing the consensus reached by the two heads of state and promoting bilateral cooperation and people-to-people exchanges, no matter how the international situation evolves.
China and Russia have in recent years stood side by side and moved forward together in the face of a complex and turbulent international landscape, Li said.
"This environment calls for continuous coordination and timely adjustment of plans. By advancing all-round cooperation, our two countries (Russia and China) are effectively countering the destructive forces and trends," said Andrei Vinogradov, head of the Center for Contemporary China Studies at the Institute of Oriental Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences.
During the regular meeting on Wednesday, both sides agreed that China and Russia should advance cooperation in key areas such as economy and trade, investment, energy and resources, foster new drivers of development in frontier areas such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology and the digital economy, jointly ensure the success of the China-Russia Years of Education, and strengthen people-to-people and cultural exchanges.
These commitments build on the strong foundation of practical cooperation between the two countries, with economic and trade ties remaining a major pillar of the bilateral relationship.
Data from China's Ministry of Commerce showed that in 2025, China-Russia trade reached 227.9 billion U.S. dollars, staying above 200 billion dollars for the third consecutive year. China remained Russia's largest trading partner for the 16th consecutive year.
The structure of bilateral trade has also continued to improve, with electromechanical and high-tech products accounting for a growing share. Chinese automobiles, home appliances and machinery have maintained strong exports to Russia, while Russia has remained a stable supplier of energy, minerals and agricultural products to China.
"It is noteworthy that the two countries are working not merely to identify new converging interests, but also to explore new development avenues by leveraging the combined potential of their two economies," Vinogradov said.
Bilateral trade maintained relatively rapid growth in 2026. Statistics from China Customs showed that in the first seven months of the year, China-Russia trade reached 159.2 billion dollars, up 26.3 percent year on year.
"Russian and Chinese economies are complementary. This allows each side to pursue its own development path and advance its national interests," said Vladimir Lvovich Nezhdanov, an expert at the Institute of Contemporary International Problems, Diplomatic Academy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation.
"Russia needs a stable and dynamically growing China, just as China needs a stable and dynamically growing Russia. This is a mutual interest," he added.
On the global dimension, a joint communique issued after the 31st regular meeting said that China and Russia firmly uphold the United Nations-centered international system and the international order based on international law. The two countries also support consolidating fair international relations on the basis of mutually beneficial cooperation among sovereign states and oppose dividing the world into rival regions or blocs, it said.
"China proceeds in a steady manner, recognizing that no initiative or policy measure can be implemented without mutual trust," said Nezhdanov, noting a white paper titled "More Just and Equitable Global Governance: China's Principles, Proposals and Actions" released by China in June.
Cultivating mutual trust under the Global Governance Initiative is a practice that major countries, which are willing to assume responsibility for international affairs, have long followed to normalize and strengthen international dialogue, he added.
This year also marks the 25th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation Between China and Russia. Over the years, the two countries have always adhered to the treaty's established principle of non-alliance, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, and stayed committed to equality, mutual respect, good faith and win-win cooperation, making important contributions to safeguarding international fairness and justice and promoting a new type of international relations, and serving as a vital constant amid century-defining changes sweeping across the world, said Xi in May during Putin's state visit to China.
The two sides should deepen multilateral coordination, further increase coordination and collaboration on multilateral platforms such as the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, BRICS and APEC, unswervingly uphold the postwar international order and the authority of international law, unite the Global South, and steer the reform of the global governance system in the right direction, Xi said then.
"Russia-China relations are a truly high-quality model of relations between major countries, delivering benefits and shared interests at every level, from grassroots communities to national governments and the global stage alike," Nezhdanov said. ■

Petrol prices fell 6.5 percent over the quarter, after rising 20.1 percent in the June 2026 quarter, it said.

====================================================================================================

Everyone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:00:07 UTC
13:00:07 KST

In February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in.
This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe, attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling.
Pedestrianisation is one thing; making Oxford Street somewhere anyone actually wants to spend time is another. For weary Londoners and anxious visitors alike, it is a headache in the form of a high street. Its primary associations are crowds, stress, dirt, noise, the tackiest incarnations of consumer capitalism, and crime. At one point during my research I approached a harried police officer in the throng outside Tottenham Court Road tube station and asked if she thought pedestrianisation would be good for Oxford Street, or make her job harder. Both, she said.
This is not to say Oxford Street is an empty, dying high street. At the last count, it receives more than 500,000 visitors every day – equivalent to the population of Edinburgh. It seems reasonable to assume that most of London’s 22 million annual foreign visitors set foot on it at some point. The street generates 5% of the capital’s economic output, and lives in the national imagination the way few others do. “When I was 17, London meant Oxford Street,” sang Everything But the Girl, in their 1988 song of the same name: “It was a little world.” And yet, nobody loves Oxford Street. During the course of writing this article, I haven’t met anyone who will even admit to liking it.
On a Sunday evening in September, I did something I had always carefully avoided doing before and cycled its full length. Even at the end of the weekend, it was overwhelming – with teenagers careening on rented ebikes and gaudy pedicabs parked in the middle of the pavement, blaring music. The pavements were thick with people, in part because the road was still thick with traffic. On another occasion, I watched a late-middle-aged woman perch awkwardly outside Ikea on a narrow black electricity box, in the absence of anywhere else to rest. For most Londoners, Oxford Street is a necessary evil, to be visited with surgical precision before fleeing the scene: a site of crime, grime and perhaps some Christmas shopping. “Who,” wondered the FT’s architecture critic in 2020, “lingers any longer than they have to in London’s worst thoroughfare?”
The grime itself is no joke. In the 1990s, when Oxford Street was known for its huge record shops such as HMV and Virgin Megastore, I remember returning to my south London home on the tube, blowing my nose and seeing a tissue full of jet-black snot. Its narrow streetway and tall buildings on either side create an “urban canyon”, trapping the heavy diesel fumes emanating from its buses and taxis (private car access has been restricted since 1972). In 2014, it was found to have the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. In the same year, the crime had become so bad that the United Arab Emirates warned its citizens to avoid the area for their own safety.
Since then it has become better known for its lawbreaking small businesses, where substantial raids have hauled in counterfeit goods and illegal vapes. This decade has seen the rise of mysterious US candy stores and empty souvenir shops that allegedly thrive thanks to tax evasion. Covid and internet shopping hit Oxford Street hard: vacancy levels soared from 4.5% in 2019 to 16.9% by early 2023, and it was often these businesses that filled the gaps. The current Google Street View images of its shopfronts, taken just two years ago, already look like a postcard from the past.
That Oxford Street has been struggling hurts the reputation of London as a whole. This is in tabloid parlance, “the nation’s high street”, home to the flagship branches of iconic department stores alongside global retail brands. Khan’s gamble is that the pedestrianisation can reverse what he conceded in 2024 was a case of “managed decline”, and will flood the street with life again.
In the offices of East, near London Fields, Julian Lewis and Archie Bashford were seated around a 4ft-long cardboard model of Oxford Street and talking animatedly about bollards. Lewis and his team are public realm architects, devoted not to buildings, but the world beyond them: signage, benches, perches, kerbs, paving, lighting, planters, trees and public art. East have carried out nearly 30 high street redesign projects in as many years, but this is the big one.
The first thing Lewis’s team did after being awarded the contract last year was to dive into the archives. The starting point was a little-known 1932 article in Good Housekeeping by Virginia Woolf. For Woolf, Oxford Street appeared as a “great rolling ribbon … the pebbly bed of a river … washed by a bright stream”. She saw it as gaudy, but also sparkling, thrilling and overwhelming, defined by the restless movement of its messy public. (Her essay also shows us how weird the street has long been – in 1932, it was apparently full of hawkers selling live tortoises.) It was these riverine characteristics that became the starting point for the thousands of material, small-scale design decisions that East are making. The “play of light on surfaces, the subtle reflectivity of a bench or a column” can all help bring out those tendencies, Bashford told me.
The pedestrianisation happening next week will cover 0.6 miles, stretching westwards from close to the Oxford Circus crossing to Selfridges. (Sadiq Khan has expressed his commitment to eventually pedestrianise all 1.2 miles of the street.) The most noticeable transformation will be how much greener it is becoming. The architects’ plan is to experiment with introducing young trees in pots, alongside new places to sit. They will use the test phase – which will last from next week until spring 2027 – to learn about how people respond to the trees. Will they become meeting points? Rest stops? Landmarks for wayfinding? Ideally they will provide respite, Lewis said, “a refuge from the flow of people, which is the river analogy again – maybe that’s optimistic, but instilling some relative calm”.
The pedestrianised zone’s edges will be marked by bollards. Lewis has strong opinions on this subject, and speaks about bollards as if they were people. “Bollards are generally horrible things,” he told me. Too often they seem “apologetic”, he said. “A misaligned, plasticky reflective strip [on a bollard] sends the message: ‘Sorry, I didn’t really mean to be here, but I need to let you know there are some vehicles nearby.’ Instead, they should be saying: ‘I’m happy to be here, because I’m doing a job.’”
An abundance of considerations go into designing the right kind of bollard, including security, maintenance, aesthetics, accessibility, climate, foot traffic, crowd flow and civic pride. Oxford Street’s bollards have to be exactly 1.2 metres apart, for reasons of HVM – hostile vehicle mitigation – but they also need to be helpful and use “the existing language of the street”. They will be made of ductile iron, because it is more resilient than cast iron: it’s springy, and doesn’t crack when you hit it. They are also matt, because shiny bollards are too flashy, and detract from the ambience. “They’re very sophisticated,” Lewis said, and he meant it.
One of the project’s primary ambitions is to better integrate Oxford Street with its neighbours. It is surrounded by four areas with strikingly different identities: Soho, Fitzrovia, Mayfair and Marylebone. “There’s this slightly numb connection to Oxford Street itself, like: where the hell is Oxford Street? It might as well not be there, with regard to the relationship with these incredible centres,” Lewis said. “People want to go to Soho. They want to go to Marylebone. People live in Fitzrovia. Oxford Street does not have a place yet, it’s a non-spatial space, which is unbelievable given how famous it is.”
This is where landscape architecture and design comes in. The noun the architects use over and over is “invitation” – how do you encourage people to do the unthinkable, and linger in the newly pedestrianised space, and move freely in and out of it? The built environment has to invite them to do so. One innovation Lewis’s team wants to explore is outdoor public dining – not outdoor tables for restaurants, because there are barely any on Oxford Street, but continental-style tables to sit and eat whatever you want; takeaway food bought in Soho, or a packed lunch you made at home. “The idea of sitting there having sandwiches at a picnic bench, next to a shop in which you can buy a Prada handbag, is a fantastic kind of paradox,” Lewis said with a smile. “And it’s also very London.”
To understand where the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street came from, you need to acquaint yourself with the work of a Danish urban planner called Jan Gehl. In 2003, when Ken Livingstone was mayor of London, Gehl was asked to spend 18 months researching the flaws in London’s streetscape, and in June 2004 he produced a 120-page report entitled Towards a Fine City for People. Gehl thought there was a huge amount of work to be done. “London comes only after Moscow in the contempt the city planners show for pedestrians,” he said that year. “You never see any children on London streets – what have you done with them all?” The answer is that they have been increasingly shut indoors: driven everywhere in cars or not trusted to play outside – compared both with earlier generations of Londoners, and with most other children across Europe.
Gehl wanted to transform the capital into one of the world’s most walking-friendly cities by 2015. But with the 2004 mayoral election taking place the same month, the radical edges of the final report that was published by Livingstone’s City Hall were sanded down. Gehl’s full recommendations were confined to a “secret document”, distributed to the capital’s decision-makers but never published. Among other things, it recommended the full pedestrianisation of Oxford Street. It has taken 22 years for that dream to be realised. “I see some signs of improvement in London,” Gehl told me recently on a video call from his home in Copenhagen, “but for God’s sake, the tempo and the amount of change have not been impressive.”
Gehl, who is 90, has long sought to turn cities into places that put the people that live there first. His motto is “the city at eye level, and at 5km/hour” – walking pace. Life Between Buildings, his first book, from 1971, was a challenge to the orthodoxy that had shaped postwar urban planning. Rather than judging the city principally by its buildings, its roads or the efficiency of its layout, Gehl asked planners to pay attention to what people actually did in public: where they walked, where they stopped, whether they met, talked or sat down to watch the world go by. These values are now finally at the centre of so much city planning – and it is no coincidence that his organisation Gehl Studio was appointed by City Hall to advise East on Oxford Street’s transformation.
For Gehl, city halls across the world should be looking to Australia. Sydney, Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide have moved dramatically towards pedestrianisation and light rail – they are “more ambitious, daring and faster in making decisions” than their peers in the UK. In Sydney, Gehl said, the rapid transformation of the equivalent of Oxford Street, George Street, is improving the atmosphere in the city around it. With ageing populations, “the end of the shopping era” for cities, and the need to reduce fossil fuel consumption, his once-radical ideas are becoming common sense. “If I am looking back at my professional career, it’s been one big struggle to reclaim public spaces from cars, which in the 1960s filled all of the streets and all the squares – they filled every possible place. We have spent many decades reconquering cities for their citizens.”
What we know as Oxford Street, which has been a street for the best part of two millennia, has always been a stage for the evolving society around it. It was previously called Tyburn Road, and for six centuries formed the processional path to the infamous Tyburn Tree, the gallows at what is now Marble Arch. Thronging crowds would line the route on hanging days, making for a rather different participatory public spectacle than that provided by its window-shopping era.
The evolution of West End neighbourhoods brought stables, barns, abattoirs and breweries, fortifications, countless pubs and coaching inns, and eventually department stores, theatres and music halls. Oxford Street has long been a centre not just of commerce, but culture and social life. Howard Carter gave his first public lecture about the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb at the New Oxford Theatre in 1923, and the most famous punk gigs in history – featuring the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Buzzcocks and more – took place at the (still running, still pleasingly dingy) 100 Club in 1976. Oxford Street’s long list of fallen pubs – the Hog in the Pound, the Jolly Trooper, the Man Loaded with Mischief – today leaves just one survivor, the Flying Horse. At 6pm on a Tuesday in late September, the atmosphere inside the latter was surprisingly gentle and convivial; the dark wood panelling and Victorian fittings offering a calming refuge from the rush-hour chaos outside.
There have been many experiments in recent decades to bring social life back to Oxford Street: tweaks to crossings, traffic restrictions and pavements, and, largely to accommodate more shopping, from 2005 to 2012, one single traffic-free day in the run-up to Christmas called Very Important Pedestrians Day.
One thing everyone agrees on is that a dramatic transformation is long overdue. By the time Khan replaced Boris Johnson as mayor in 2016, London had fallen behind cities such as Paris, Barcelona and Berlin when it came to infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians, and measures to curb car numbers. Then, the systemic shocks of the pandemic, and an electorate voting ever more to the left (and more Green), offered Khan the opportunity and the mandate to catch up.
There are two big structural changes sweeping through the great cities of western Europe that have also shaped Khan’s ability to finally get this done. The first is that the motorcar is no longer king in the modern city. The second is that shopping has been displaced. Even though Oxford Street remains a river bobbing with more than 20 flagship stores, maximal spending is no longer the only consideration. In the age of same-day delivery, out-of-town fulfilment centres, and peer-to-peer secondhand marketplaces such as Vinted, what should replace shopping at the heart of the modern city?
This week, I walked down Oxford Street with Nabeel Khan, CEO of the Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC). His earliest experience of Oxford Street was going to HMV to buy his first CD: 2Pac’s Me Against the World. Today, he is the man in charge of making pedestrianisation happen.
On our walk, the first signs of change were visible: the concrete bases of the new bollards were in place and the old wooden planters – “really poorly designed”, in Khan’s view – had had their dying shrubs removed. Outside the flagship UK store of the US shoe brand Vans, which styles itself as not merely a skateboarding attire shop, but “a space to express yourself” and a “cultural hub”, Khan spoke with gusto about the so-called experience economy.
In city centres post-Covid, there is “this desire, particularly among young people, for human connection,” he said, gesturing through the open concertina doors of the Vans shop, where a full drum kit, guitar and amps had been set up, facing out on to the street. “When you can buy almost anything you want, what’s the one thing that you can’t buy? That proximity to someone else and having that human experience.”
Given that everyone agrees Oxford Street needs overhauling, why has this taken so long? “The West End doesn’t have a single owner,” Khan said. “There are two local authorities, a transport authority, a strategic authority, five business improvement districts, hundreds of businesses and some major landowners.” The maestro trying to conduct this unruly orchestra is now the OSDC, which was created by the mayor. While reporting this story, I noticed the OSDC sought to keep an iron grip on press coverage. Perhaps this is because the local politics around Oxford Street have been fiercely contested for so long.
In fact, angst over vehicle traffic on Oxford Street is about as old as London’s mayor. In 1971, when Sadiq Khan was a baby, so many pedestrians were spilling from overcrowded pavements into the road and being hit by cars that an Oxford Street Action Committee was formed. During one protest calling for cars to be banned, 22 people were arrested. The Greater London Council introduced the first ban of private cars (between 7am and 7pm) the following year, marking the beginning of 50 years of gradual traffic restrictions.
Full pedestrianisation has faced decades of opposition and obstruction, primarily from the Conservative-run Westminster council – continuing when Labour took it over from 2022 to 2026 – but also from taxi drivers, disabled access groups, local residents, smaller traders and local neighbourhood groups such as the Soho Society and Mayfair Forum. The latter worry that plans to reroute buses, delivery lorries and taxis into quiet conservation areas surrounding the street will “destroy” those areas, as Tim Lord of the Soho Society put it. Accessibility advocates and the Licensed Taxi Drivers’ Association argue that pedestrianisation will create a transport desert for older people and disabled visitors. (In a statement, the OSDC admitted that journeys to Oxford Street will change for some, but said that accessibility has been at the “heart” of the planning process. Bus stops, it said, will be no more than about 200 metres from the pedestrianised area; it added that the street furniture was designed with input from specialist disabled groups.)
Khan’s predecessors tried, and failed, to transform Oxford Street. As mayor, Boris Johnson called pedestrianisation the “Schleswig-Holstein question of London traffic”, referring to the infamously complicated 19th-century German constitutional debate, because “everybody in abstract would love to do [it]” until they look at the “actual economic impact”. But by 2016, the tipping point had been reached – all the major mayoral candidates that year proposed pedestrianising it in principle, and when Khan won, he pledged that it would be completed by 2020. For a brief period, City Hall, Transport for London (TfL) and Westminster council appeared to be pulling in the same direction. Polling in 2018 and 2024 has shown about two-thirds of Londoners support the idea.
But the political fight over Oxford Street has often been less about how it is transformed than who gets to decide. In 2018, local opposition to Khan’s pedestrianisation plan crystallised into the creation of Capo, the Campaign Against Pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which stood three candidates in 2018’s local elections, winning more than 1,000 votes between them. Spooked by this, Nickie Aiken, the council’s Conservative leader, used the backlash to nix the plan. Khan was furious, calling Westminster’s withdrawal “a betrayal” and claiming that £8m of public money had been wasted by the scheme’s collapse.
A decade and a pandemic later, it is finally happening because the planning authority is now held by the OSDC, which was established by the mayor’s office. The Better Oxford Street campaign, a coalition of local opponents to pedestrianisation, called this transfer of power a display of “jaw-dropping audacity” by the mayor, with the OSDC superseding the council “and its democratically elected representatives”.
As Jan Gehl observed to me, compared with some city halls around the world, London mayors have limited power. They can’t raise taxes (or introduce rent caps, legislate or control health services), which makes urban change that much harder to achieve. One thing that is under the mayor’s remit though is TfL: after he got the latter to agree to reroute their buses around the street, and with the OSDC up and running, Khan was finally in the driving seat.
What happens next week is just the beginning. The first half of Oxford Street will close to traffic on Monday – but the pedestrianisation process that follows will stretch on for well over a year.
The people behind the project are anxious that the initial testing phase is not misunderstood as a permanent project that has been built cheaply, or half heartedly. The testing process will involve a lot of people standing around with clipboards and measuring things, observing the different ways and places that pedestrians dwell. Even the picnic benches they are installing will be engaging in data collection, thanks to a “beacon”, a sensor recessed into the seat, that will measure how many people sit down, for how long, and the ambient temperature at the time.
There are other problems to navigate. On my first “site visit” to Oxford Street with East’s Archie Bashford, he showed me an example of how not to do public-realm architecture. We were on a little side street behind Oxford Circus station. There stood three vast steel plant pots, each hosting a leafless, skeletal young tree. The soil base was crisscrossed with a lattice of slats, the gaps completely stuffed with cigarette butts. The planters had become giant ash trays, which presumably hadn’t done much for the dying trees. At the root of this miserable scene were security concerns, Bashford explained – the designers had wanted to keep the soil out of reach. I was confused. “Some planters,” Lewis later explained, “are quite conducive to hiding things.” Such as knives.
This might sound like Metropolitan police hyperbole. But the knife threat is not just a scare story: weapons hidden by organised crime groups are often found in “soft landscape”, usually soil, for easy extraction and future use, removing the danger of being caught in possession.
There is a delicate balance to be struck between public safety and a more sociable public realm. The social optimist’s view is that you minimise crime in the public realm not by making it so miserable that nobody wants to visit in the first place, but by overwhelming the minority of people behaving badly with people who are behaving well. The architects at East hope that some forms of crime, such as drug dealing, will become harder, for the simple reason that it will be more visible. “Sometimes you do have to mitigate [criminal activity],” Lewis said, “but I think it’s more successful in the long term to provide an infrastructure that supports social activity, and invites it.”
Another concern is that the new Oxford Street becomes something rather more mundane: a successfully pedestrianised but ultimately disappointing place. An open-air shopping mall, a tourist trap, a hyperbranded open-air events venue, or an empty corridor after closing time. Some observers worry it could acquire some of the same problems that Barcelona’s La Rambla is still tackling. In recent decades the Catalan boulevard has been a tawdry sacrifice to tourists, largely abandoned by local residents. In an effort to avoid that outcome, there has been a great deal of communication between Barcelona and London. Barcelona’s city hall is keenly watching Oxford Street, Nabeel Khan told me, and East’s architects have visited Barcelona to procure their data-gathering seating.
What would success look like in two years’ time, I asked Khan, as we lingered outside Selfridges, occasionally apologising as we sidestepped passersby. “Of course there’s an economic side,” he said. “We want to see retail doing well, we want to see the return of flagship stores. We want to see more people spending time and coming back to Oxford Street: not just first-time visitors, but return visitors.” It should also form the first stage of a wider transformation of London’s entire West End, he added. “We want to see Marylebone benefit from this, we want to see Soho benefit from this. We want to show people that this is how the heart of a global city should feel, should look, should be experienced. That will be success.”
Archie Bashford believes the change in atmosphere will be profound: “Even if we were doing nothing else, and they just shut the street, it would feel amazing and transgressive.” In just a few weeks’ time, visitors will be able to look up at Oxford Street’s glittering Christmas lights without worrying about being run over. People don’t tend to look up on Oxford Street, I’ve noticed, because they can’t – they’d be mown down.
But it turns out, if you gaze above shop-window height, that Oxford Street has a rich architectural history, stretching across styles and centuries, from the modernist Barbara Hepworth statue on the side of John Lewis to the imposing 18th-century Pantheon that hosts Marks & Spencer. It is worth your time to linger, even beyond the fundamental human right to sit down, have a sandwich and breathe some clean air.

As part of a £1bn investment plan, Waitrose has chosen Cricklewood in north London as the location for its first supermarket in eight years.
The upmarket grocer will open the store on Thursday and another supermarket in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, next month. It also plans four smaller stores next year, including a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge).
In 2024, Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, said it planned to open up to four large supermarkets and 100 convenience stores over five years and would also refurbish a number of outlets introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections.
Tina Mitchell, the retail director at Waitrose, said: “Our supermarkets provide the ultimate showcase for everything that sets Waitrose apart – from our unmatched quality and industry-leading welfare standards to the expert service of our partners.”
This year the company – led since January by the former Tesco executive Tom Denyard - also plans to refurbish 29 stores.
After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems which led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. However, the chain is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, which now has a higher share of the grocery market, under some measures, after opening a number of new food-led outlets.
Sales at Waitrose rose 4% in the six months to 1 August. However, its underlying operating profit slid by £7m to £103m as it invested in keeping prices down and improving its loyalty scheme. It was also hit by higher energy costs during the summer heat wave.
Waitrose’s parent company, the John Lewis Partnership – which is owned by its staff – reported a £98m pre-tax loss in the half-year to 1 August, as sales fell at the department stores despite heavy investment in updating the outlets.
The company has been reducing the number of staff it employs directly as it tries to trim costs.
On Wednesday, the partnership announced it had signed its first company-wide union recognition deal. The collective agreement with Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, comes ahead of new rights of union access in workplaces that come into force at the end of this month.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said: “Usdaw already has members working within the business and this agreement will strengthen that presence and help us in supporting and representing members across the partnership. We now look forward to growing our membership and influence within the partnership and to working with the partnership’s management on finalising the details of how the agreement will work in practice.”

A violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paint | Alberto Alemanno
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:00:06 UTC
13:00:06 KST

Last Saturday night, the town hall of Limoges in west-central France was set ablaze. By Sunday, images of the fire destroying a symbol of the French republic, and other scenes of unrest across France, were everywhere, but being used to tell very different stories about what is happening in Europe.
For some, the flames announced a pan-European youth revolt, proof that a single movement was sweeping the continent. Donald Trump, who had already insisted that the French schools protests were not about schools but about migration and Islam, urged Europeans to “close the borders”. The mayor of Limoges saw the fingerprints of an alleged ultra-left insurrection.
I lost count of how many mainly rightwing media outlets were contacting me suddenly. Most were based in India, China, Singapore and the US. They sought voices to validate the idea of a “teen revolt” spreading across Europe, driven by the same grievances and violence.
None of these narratives, each serving a different political agenda, adequately explains what is happening. Europe’s protests have different causes, constituencies and demands. Portraying them as a Europe-wide rebellion erases those differences and makes Europe look ungovernable. That picture is a gift to anyone who wants to exploit the unrest.
What set off the protests varies from country to country. In France, the mobilisation began in schools in mid-September in frustration over longstanding failures to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings and facilities. By the time of the huge demonstration on Saturday, public-sector workers had joined, and the grievances had widened to encompass the cost of living.
In Belgium, meanwhile, students have challenged tuition-fee increases in the country’s French-speaking region and demanded additional teaching hours. Greek students have mobilised over housing costs and access to accommodation, while German pupils have protested against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.
Look beyond western Europe, and the differences become even more distinct. In Albania, student unrest builds on a pre-existing anti-government mobilisation, rather than a standalone youth revolt. In Serbia, students have led nearly two years of largely peaceful protests following the Novi Sad railway station disaster. Their movement centres on demands for an end to corruption, a lack of institutional accountability and political inaction. Now the students are running in this weekend’s election on their own list. This is a battle over power and accountability, and goes well beyond education or generational frustration.
Italian students may occupy schools and shout slogans in French, but the cross-border spread of images, slogans and tactics does not prove a shared organisation. Rather, 24-hour news coverage can turn separate protests into a single story of youth rebellion, creating, deliberately or not, the illusion of a common movement and programme where neither exists.
Rejecting the idea of a single European youth revolt does not mean denying the existence of a shared generational anxiety. Housing has become increasingly unaffordable, public services are under pressure, and the transition into secure employment is uncertain. Eurostat reports that EU house prices rose by 55.4% and rents by 26.7% between 2010 and the fourth quarter of 2024. The 2026 TUI Foundation Youth Study found that 52% of young people aged 16–26 across seven European countries expected to be worse off than their parents, compared with just 25% who expected to do better.
Youth unemployment in the euro area remains substantially higher than overall unemployment. One study of French firms found a sharper decline in permanent hiring among workers aged 21–29 in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. The European Central Bank cautions that the evidence does not yet establish generative AI as the cause. But the uncertainty itself can create a shared sense of insecurity across national borders.
Such anxieties help explain why protests in one country resonate with young people in another, and why images of school sit-ins or street demonstrations can inspire imitation. But they don’t translate into common demands, let alone a coordinated political movement.
France’s demonstrations last Saturday exposed another danger: how quickly violence can overshadow a protest’s message. Most demonstrators marched peacefully, but a minority resorted to violence. Their actions should not define hundreds of thousands of demonstrators, just as peaceful protest should not provide cover for criminal acts.
What happened in Milan showed how the two can blur. A peaceful cost of living march alongside protests over education cuts and race-based reform, was followed by looting carried out by hooded, mostly teenage groups organised partly via TikTok. More than 200 were detained, most of them minors, and the march’s organisers disowned them. Defending public order must go hand in hand with accountability for violence and scrutiny of police conduct.
But when images of burning buildings and looting dominate coverage, peaceful protest and criminal violence become harder to distinguish in the public mind. A single incident can come to define an entire mobilisation.
The misleading narrative of a pan-European revolt has consequences, because it allows images of unrest to be taken out of their national contexts and presented as proof that a chaotic Europe is ungovernable.
This is particularly useful to those seeking to deepen divisions and undermine European democracy: it turns distinct national problems into a sweeping story of European failure.
For the radical right, the idea of a continent in flames proves that open societies cannot protect their citizens, hence the call to “close your borders”. For those on the radical left who celebrate every burning building as the dawn of a continental uprising, the flames prove that liberal democratic institutions are beyond repair. Both need Europe to look ungovernable but neither offers an answer to the disorder it complains about. And both serve the interests of those beyond Europe’s borders who gain from a divided union, from the Trump administration to Vladimir Putin.
President Macron had a point when he lashed out at the “stupid” comments of foreign leaders about events in France. AI-generated images of scenes that never took place in France had been circulating, he said. Macron is hardly neutral, but certain forces clearly have an interest in amplifying images of chaos.
Governments should neither romanticise protest nor use violence as a pretext to dismiss legitimate grievances. They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold perpetrators accountable and address the pressures that leave many young people uncertain about their future.
Europe’s democracies will be judged not by how they withstand these protests, but how they address the distinct grievances behind them and restore confidence in the future. That is how generational anxiety can become a force for democratic renewal rather than fuel for those seeking to portray democracy as broken.
- Alberto Alemanno is the Jean Monnet professor of EU law at HEC Paris and the founder of The Good Lobby

Tied up and tortured: Israel using US-made electroshock weapons on Palestinian detainees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
04:00:05 UTC
13:00:05 KST

The soldiers drag the man into a section of the prison known as Hell’s Wing, a metaphor for its notoriety for acts of brutality. Shoving him violently into a corner, they take a step back before one of them draws his weapon and fires two rubber bullets at his body. The man, a double amputee, collapses to the floor.
After tying him up tightly, the soldiers continue their assault until one of them pulls a stun gun from its holster. The soldier approaches the man, brandishing the gun, before applying it to his body, engulfing him in an electric shock.
This is what Essa* says happened to him during a period in Israeli detention. Today, more than a year and a half later, the scars from the electric shocks remain visible on his body. The close proximity of double scars suggests he was subjected to repeated shocks while in a “tightly restrained” position, says the International Rehabilitation Council for Torture Victims.
Essa, now 43, was arrested in the Jabalia refugee camp in January 2024, where he had been staying since having both feet amputated after an Israeli missile attack on his home. He was held at Israel’s Ofer Prison before being released in October 2025.
According to an investigation by the Guardian and Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism, Essa was likely to have been tortured with a Taser electroshock weapon manufactured by the American company Axon Enterprise, formerly known as Taser International.
The alleged torture is one of a number of incidents that have been linked to the use of Axon weapons, which the company appears to continue to supply to Israel. Three other detainees since released allege they were tortured using Axon weapons between 2024 and 2025.
Human rights groups have condemned allegations of the repeated torture and ill-treatment of detainees held in Israeli detention centres and prisons using electric shock devices, with Amnesty calling for restrictions on exports of such devices.
A spokesperson for the Israel Defense Forces said the abuse of detainees was strictly prohibited and that the use of restraints on detainees was carried out “only in exceptional circumstances that justify their use, and in subject to Israeli law, international law and IDF orders”.
An investigation conducted by the Israeli military advocate general, Itai Ofir, against five Israeli soldiers accused of committing a sexual assault against a Palestinian detainee inside the Sde Teiman detention camp in July 2024 found they had used a Taser weapon while torturing the detainee, leaving him needing hospital treatment.
In November 2025, the UN’s Committee Against Torture reported on allegations of torture, including the use of electric shocks, within Israeli detention facilities and noted that “torture and ill-treatment had escalated sharply since 7 October 2023”.
 
The committee also expressed its “serious concern over widespread allegations of sexual abuse of Palestinian detainees … including allegations of rape … sexualised forms of torture … electrocution of the genitals and anus”.
Despite such concerns, Axon appears to have continued to sign contracts with Israeli entities to supply either the Taser gun or its accessories. As recently as June 2025, the company was showcasing the latest models of its electroshock weapons to Israeli security agencies at a conference in Israel.
Two video clips produced by the Israeli prison service over the past year show a gun that appears to be a Taser electroshock weapon produced by Axon. Both Essa and the three other detainees interviewed say it was the weapon used to torture them inside Israeli detention centres and prisons.
One of the detainees interviewed says he had water poured over his body – which can intensify the torture – before he was given an electric shock with a Taser weapon, during a spell in detention in 2024. He says he still suffers from severe visual impairment, spasms and recurrent fainting spells.
In August 2025, the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs highlighted the torture of detainees at Gilboa prison with electric shocks, before they were dragged to the shower stalls in the prison’s courtyard, doused with water and then shocked again. It did not state the model of weapon used.
 
Amani Al-Sarhanah, from the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club, a human rights group, says: “The use of electric shocks may be just one of dozens of types of weapons that have been used against them [Palestinian prisoners]. We do not actually know what types they are or which companies supply them. Nevertheless, we certainly know that most weapons imported by Israel originate from the United States in one way or another.”
Since October 2023, 92 Palestinians are reported to have died while in detention, but only one Israeli soldier has been tried for mistreating Palestinian prisoners from Gaza, according to a report by a group of Israeli NGOs.
Amnesty says it has published extensively on the human rights risks involved in the use of electric shock weapons and has previously called for such law enforcement equipment to be included in the UN’s Arms Trade Treaty that regulates the trade in conventional weapons.
 
Axon Enterprises and the Israel prison service were approached for comment.

Carminati lift-and-slide windows frame Dubai skyline at Bvlgari Hotel and Resort

Carminati lift-and-slide windows frame Dubai skyline at Bvlgari Hotel and Resort
Minimalist timber windows from luxury brand Carminati’s Skyline Minimal Frames collection were chosen to frame views from the Bvlgari Hotel and Resort in Dubai.
Designed to make the “least possible visual impact”, Carminati‘s Skyline Minimal Frames range includes both windows and doors defined by minimal profiles, natural materials and modern, patented technology.
The frame’s slimness is the result of Carminati’s patented Skyline Minimal Frames construction, where the timber sash is structurally bonded to the glass pane, which reinforces the whole frame.
“With a front-facing profile of just 37 millimetres for lift-and-slide systems and 50 millimetres for all other opening types, Skyline Minimal Frames combines outstanding thermal and acoustic performance with a minimal visual impact, making it the world’s slimmest wooden profile,” said Carminati.
The collection was selected by Milan-based studio ACPV Architects to be integrated into their design for the Bvlgari Hotel and Resort, which reached completion on Dubai’s Jumeirah Bay Island in 2017.
“Our Skyline Minimal Frames range, personally selected by the architects, possesses all the characteristics required for the project,” Carminati said. “The frames provide the perfect setting for enjoying a breathtaking panorama while feeling at the centre of Dubai’s vibrant social life and exclusive luxury.”
“The new resort is the result of refined Bvlgari style, professionalism and taste of its design team,” the brand added.
Carminati’s Skyline Minimal Frames collection offers a range of windows and door products, including Skyline Sliding, Skyline Bifold, Skyline Pivot, Skyline Drive, Skyline NoForce and the Skyline Handle.
Each of the collection’s products is available in a range of styles, from Skyline Modern to Skyline Classic, which can be manufactured entirely from wood or paired with an external aluminium cladding.
For the 158,000-square-metre Bvlgari hotel, ACPV Architects opted for Carminati’s Skyline Sliding lift-and-slide system – combining its sleek 37-millimetre profile with pale oak on the inside and a bronze-coloured aluminium cladding on the outside, chosen for its resistance to coastal environments.
This offered expansive views throughout the hotel, intended to create “continuity between the indoors and outdoors”, along with access to adjacent terraces.
“Large lift-and-slide doors connect the living rooms with expansive shaded terraces, while full-height glazing gives guests the feeling of being outdoors, conveying a sense of luxury associated with greenery, privacy and the tranquillity of the interior,” Carminati said.
The Skyline Sliding system operates through a lift-and-slide mechanism and is available in configurations with two sliding leaves – one fixed and one sliding – among other combinations.
Integrated into the product is the brand’s patented bottom track, designed exclusively for the Skyline Minimal Frames collection.
Its carriages are set entirely into the floor and covered by a flexible belt, which protects the mechanism from dust and allows for “maximum sliding smoothness”.
According to Carminati, the large-scale commission for the Bvlgari hotel involved the development of a bespoke product to meet the project’s specific technical requirements and local building regulations.
With glazed panels reaching up to four metres in height and subject to significant wind loads, the project required a bespoke system: a concealed steel structure between the lift-and-slide doors and the fixed transoms above.
Built around a composite beam, with three welded steel tubes set within the cavity between the frames, it allowed the profiles to stay slim while meeting the structural requirements.
“The structure takes on the challenges of the environment and combines its contrasts in an original and sophisticated solution,” Carminati said.
Carminati was founded in 1894 near Bergamo, Italy, and is still run by the founding family.
The company specialises in architectural timber windows and doors, holds patents on its Skyline Minimal Frames system, and develops bespoke solutions for each project through its in-house technical office.
To learn more about Carminati’s Skyline Minimal Frames collection, visit its website here.

12:56:46 KST

Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.
The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.
Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music and news criticising Pyongyang.
If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.
At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.
The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.
Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.
The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.
The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.
Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.
North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

Addressing recent US threats, Monzon warned that military action against Cuba could trigger a war with devastating humanitarian consequences.
He nevertheless expressed willingness to engage Washington, provided Cuba's sovereignty was respected.
On North Korea's nuclear program, he reiterated Cuba's opposition to nuclear weapons and called for their complete abolition.

US and Israel create plans for 'short but intensive' strikes on Iran after midterms - report
The New York Times reported that American and Israeli military planners have reportedly developed options for an operation against Iran lasting roughly three days
The United States and Israel are preparing for a possible new attack on Iran after the American midterm elections, even as questions persist over whether another military campaign would secure concessions from Tehran, The New York Times reported.
The proposed campaign would concentrate strikes into roughly three days, concentrating operation on nuclear facilities, missile and drone capabilities, and parts of Iran’s energy infrastructure.
US officials and others familiar with the discussions said the United States is also assembling additional forces. Its planned deployment, including three aircraft carriers, Marines, combat aircraft and Special Operations personnel, is expected to be fully positioned by early November.
President Donald Trump has not approved an attack. The Times reported that he has repeatedly held back proposed operations, including one earlier this month that both militaries had prepared to launch.
At the center of the deliberations is a disputed calculation: whether a short burst of military force could achieve diplomatic results that months of fighting and economic pressure have failed to deliver.
Iranian officials have warned that retaliation could extend to data centers, undersea internet cables and regional oil facilities. Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s negotiating team, called expectations of a 72-hour campaign a “fantasy.”
“Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” Mohammadi wrote on social media.

Taiwan drug-prevention lessons reach 50,000 classes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:46:23 UTC
12:46:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Education conducted drug-prevention sessions in more than 50,000 classes last year to help students recognize the dangers of etomidate, CNA reported.
Education Minister Cheng Ying-yao (鄭英耀) said Thursday that etomidate had become the second most common drug encountered by students since 2024, surpassing marijuana and amphetamines.
The sedative, used for general anesthesia, can cause dependence and has been mixed with chemical additives to produce liquid for e-cigarettes, according to the Keelung City Government.
Lessons on the dangers of drugs and e-cigarettes were incorporated into health and physical education courses, and the ministry reached all targeted classes last year. Through September this year, it had conducted similar sessions in more than 48,000 classes.
Cheng said emerging drugs and e-cigarettes were constantly changing in appearance, with some featuring cartoon characters or resembling USB drives and bubble tea. The ministry has stepped up efforts during school visits to teach students how to recognize these products and understand their risks.
The ministry is also considering saliva tests to help schools identify potential drug use early and has coordinated with the National Police Agency on joint procurement. The tests could be introduced after amendments to the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act are passed.
According to the Keelung City Government, inhaling etomidate can cause hand tremors and full-body shaking. Severe cases may result in permanent neurological damage or respiratory arrest.

Eating more ultraprocessed foods linked to hidden brain injury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:45:58 UTC
12:45:58 KST

Eating more ultraprocessed foods linked to hidden brain injury
The study, published in JAMA Network Open on October 15, examined the diets, body fat levels, brain scans and cognitive performance of 8,783 adults aged 35 to 69 who had no history of cardiovascular disease.
Researchers found that participants who consumed the most ultraprocessed foods had 40% higher odds of showing signs of vascular brain injury than those who consumed the least. These changes, detected through MRI, included small areas of damage caused by problems with blood flow and changes in the brain's white matter.
Such damage can develop before noticeable problems with memory or thinking appear and may indicate an increased risk of future stroke and other brain health problems.
The study also found that people in the highest consumption group had, on average, 1.7 percentage points more body fat and a greater volume of fat stored around internal organs than those in the lowest consumption group. Researchers found no significant difference in liver fat levels between the two groups.
Despite the findings from brain scans, higher ultraprocessed food consumption was not consistently associated with lower scores on tests measuring memory, attention, processing speed and other thinking skills.
The researchers noted that the association between ultraprocessed food intake and brain vessel damage was not consistent across all methods used to measure food consumption. This means the findings should be interpreted cautiously.

Venezuela government, opposition reach key agreements in 3rd round of transition talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:43:59 UTC
12:43:59 KST

Laura Gamba Fadul
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Representatives from the Venezuelan government and the 2015-elected National Assembly opposition officially concluded a third round of national transition talks Wednesday, reaching key agreements on political disqualifications and frozen foreign assets.
According to a joint statement signed by Jorge Rodriguez, president of the pro-government parliament, and Dinorah Figuera, head of the 2015 National Assembly delegation, the two sides agreed to review the Organic Law of the Comptroller General’s Office, specifically examining administrative processes surrounding political disqualifications targeting opposition leaders.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate and opposition leader Maria Corina Machado remains the most prominent political figure subject to an administrative ban from seeking public office.
The delegations also agreed to establish a joint commission tasked with coordinating with UK institutions to secure the release of Venezuelan gold reserves currently frozen at the Bank of England.
The conclusions mark the end of the third cycle of negotiations which began a week ago in Caracas and comprised six working sessions, including two plenary meetings, and 15 technical meetings across four working groups.
The dialogue process has progressed through three distinct phases. The first round laid the groundwork for national emergency relief, international asset protection, institutional strengthening, and guarantees for political participation and freedom of expression.
The second round focused on judicial restructuring and democratic reinstitutionalization, establishing a framework to evaluate candidates for the Supreme Court of Justice (TSJ) and outlining steps to reorganize the nation's radio spectrum.
The third round consolidated the electoral and legal roadmap, finalizing technical reviews on political bans and foreign asset recovery.
Announcing the session's conclusion Wednesday, Rodriguez specified that on Oct. 22, the National Assembly will formally swear in the nominating committee responsible for evaluating TSJ judicial candidates. The panel, comprising 12 civil society representatives and 11 legislators, will select the final list of principal and alternate justices.
With the conclusion of this plenary cycle, both delegations reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining structured technical working groups to advance institutional guarantees ahead of future electoral milestones.

KYIV, Oct 22 - Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, a Reuters witness said, and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight, as the two sides kept up a barrage of attacks despite the latest US mediation attempts to end the war.
The Russian strikes wounded 15 people and damaged subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in the Ukrainian capital while also restricting traffic there, Kyiv authorities said. The strikes followed another attack on the city on Wednesday evening that wounded six people.
A Russian strike killed a woman and injured another four people in the Kharkiv region in Ukraine's northeast, Regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
A drone also hit energy infrastructure in the Kremenchuk area in the Poltava region, a local official said on Telegram, without giving details.

In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow after 630 drones were sent towards the capital during the night, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.
In the city of Lipetsk - home to a major steel plant some 400 km (250 miles) south of Moscow - a man was injured as drones hit apartment buildings and a medical facility, Governor Igor Artamonov said on the Telegram app.
Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 after annexing the Crimea peninsula from its southern neighbour eight years earlier, locking the two nations into the deadliest conflict on the European continent since World War Two.
The latest strikes come after US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff held talks this week with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russia's President Vladimir Putin to mediate an end to the conflict.
Zelenskiy said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for three-way talks with Russia and the United States at the level of negotiators to be held as soon as possible, and the Kremlin said Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Kyiv as soon as next month. REUTERS

12:19:46 KST

The Kremlin confirmed Wednesday, Oct. 21, that Russia and the US are discussing the future of sanctioned Russian oil giant Lukoil’s overseas assets, valued at approximately $22 billion, as economic negotiations between Moscow and Washington expand alongside efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov disclosed the talks following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, saying the two governments were considering a broad range of economic projects, including the fate of Lukoil’s international holdings.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The disclosure came as the US Treasury Department extended authorization for negotiations over the sale of Lukoil’s foreign assets until Nov. 21, allowing potential buyers more time to reach agreements that would still require separate US approval.
The developments provide further confirmation that Washington and Moscow are discussing major commercial interests despite American sanctions imposed to restrict Russia’s energy revenues and pressure the Kremlin over its invasion of Ukraine.
Lukoil’s $22 billion foreign assets at center of US-Russia talks
Speaking to Russian state television following Putin’s meeting with Witkoff, Ushakov said Moscow and Washington were reviewing numerous economic proposals, including several major projects.
Among them were discussions concerning US sanctions on Lukoil and the potential sale of its international assets.
‘Capitulating to a Dictator Shows Weakness’ – Republican Senator Slams Trump’s Russia Policy
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov separately confirmed that the US Treasury authorization needed for the sale could be extended if necessary, describing the proposed divestment as a commercial matter.
Lukoil placed its international assets on the market after Washington sanctioned the company in October 2025 over Russia’s war against Ukraine.
US private equity firm Carlyle Group agreed in January 2026 to acquire the assets but subsequently abandoned the deal after it failed to secure regulatory approval. Other prospective buyers have included ExxonMobil.
The portfolio, initially valued at approximately $22 billion, includes oil production interests, refineries and fuel distribution businesses across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia.
US Treasury extends negotiations until November
The US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control extended its authorization for negotiations over Lukoil International GmbH and its subsidiaries until Nov. 21, 2026.
The extension allows prospective buyers to conduct due diligence and negotiate conditional purchase agreements. However, it does not authorize the actual transfer of assets or lift sanctions on Lukoil.
Any completed sale requires separate OFAC approval. The Treasury Department has stipulated that the transaction must sever ties with the sanctioned Russian company, prevent it from receiving immediate financial benefits and keep any proceeds owed to Lukoil blocked until sanctions permit their release.
US Treasury oversees Lukoil asset sale as economic talks with Russia expand
The Lukoil negotiations emerged as Witkoff publicly acknowledged that the US Treasury Department was working directly with Putin’s economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
During Wednesday’s meeting, Witkoff also discussed future US-Russian economic cooperation, while Putin outlined plans for diesel shipments to the US and offered supplies of Russian fertilizer.
The expanding economic dialogue comes as Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine and Washington seeks to revive trilateral peace negotiations.
