Trump administration seeks Supreme Court approval to build Big Bend wall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:19:38 UTC
12:19:38 KST

Trump administration seeks Supreme Court approval to build Big Bend wall
US federal judge blocked wall’s construction on Texas-Mexico border amid an ongoing legal battle.
The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume plans to build a border wall through the Big Bend region of West Texas, as part of its anti-immigration policy to strengthen security on the border with Mexico.
The Justice Department filed an emergency request on Wednesday asking the court to lift a federal judge’s injunction in a lower court that has halted construction while a lawsuit against the project, brought by an environmental group and other challengers, plays out.
The Department of Homeland Security plans include vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology in and around Big Bend National Park.
Big Bend has about 805km (500 miles) of border, and, according to opponents of the project who have sued the administration, accounts for about 1 percent of migrant arrests.
Landscape, historic church
The lawsuit, filed by plaintiffs including the Center for Biological Diversity and a Big Bend-area river guide, seeks to preserve the landscape, protect a historic church, and challenge the federal government’s waivers of environmental and historical laws to fast-track the $1.7bn project.
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an “area of high illegal entry”, requiring additional barriers to control the border.
US District Judge Kathleen Cardone issued an injunction in El Paso on October 2 halting work “until and unless Defendants comply with all applicable laws,” she wrote in her order.
In a later opinion, the judge found that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and Mullin.
The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court to pause or overturn Cardone’s injunction.
The Supreme Court has not yet responded to this appeal.
“Even assuming that the secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction,” the Justice Department wrote.
In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over its potential impact on the park’s landscape and wildlife.

Bukang-i is back: famous shark returns to canal in South Korea hours after being coaxed out to sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:12:54 UTC
12:12:54 KST

A shark that became a viral sensation after getting stuck in a South Korean canal for a month has returned just hours after being coaxed out to sea.
Nicknamed Bukang-i by fans, the 3-metre-long (9.8-foot) female dusky shark was first spotted in the waterway on 18 September.
On Wednesday, workers used nets fixed to floating pontoons to guide the shark free, but it dived beneath a net and returned to the canal in Busan overnight, authorities said.
“The shark is now between the outer net and an inner net installed 30 to 40 metres ... further inside the canal,” an oceans ministry official told AFP.
After it got trapped in September, officials initially opted to wait for the shark to leave on its own – but amid growing concerns for its wellbeing they took a more proactive approach. A fresh attempt to free Bukang-i was under way on Thursday morning, officials said.
Officials spent Thursday morning removing a screen that was potentially blocking the shark’s exit, replacing the net it had swum under and raising an outer barrier, before attempting to guide Bukang-i out again.
Before Wednesday’s effort, authorities had twice tried and failed to steer Bukang-i back to sea, using water jets and then nets.
As each attempt failed, the shark amassed a huge following, drawing more than 1.6m people to the canal for a glimpse.
The affection for Bukang-i has become an industry, with a commemorative soju, a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.
But concerns for the shark’s health are growing.
The canal temperature, now 21C, is near the lower range of what the dusky species prefers, and Bukang-i has not been seen feeding since September.
Choi Yoon, a shark expert at Kunsan National University, told the Hankyoreh newspaper the shark could die within two weeks, due to hunger, colder water and abrasions to its snout and fin.
An oceans ministry official said this week the shark appeared to have difficulty maintaining balance.
Environmental groups have linked the shark’s appearance in the canal to warming seas, saying rising temperatures are pushing warm-water fish northwards, with subtropical sharks following in pursuit.
The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on.

Eisenkot leads Netanyahu as Winter, Hendel-Zelekha may not cross electoral threshold - poll

An N12 News poll published Wednesday evening ranked Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party first with 23 seats, down one seat from the previous poll. A Channel 13 poll published at the same time also put Yashar in first place; however they only received 20 seats.
In both polls, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party came in second, trailing Yashar and falling to 19 seats.
Neither poll found that either of the political blocs would win a clear majority; however, the opposition bloc continued to lead Netanyahu's.
N12 projected that the opposition bloc would win 55 seats and Netanyahu's bloc 51. By comparison, the Channel 13 poll showed Eisenkot's bloc gaining one seat to 52, while Netanyahu's bloc lost one seat to 49.
Whether Ofer Winter's People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha's Reservists-Economic Party cross the 3.25% electoral threshold could affect the balance between the political blocs in the upcoming elections.
Other party numbers remained similar to previous polls
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party remained unchanged at 14 seats, while the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, gained one seat to reach 10, Channel 13 found. In N12, the Democrats remained at nine seats, while B'Yachad gained one seat to reach 15, its highest showing in a month and a half.
In both polls, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu polled at eight seats, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit received seven.
Shas, led by Arye Deri, received eight seats in the N12 poll but seven on Channel 13, while United Torah Judaism, led by Yakov Asher, received seven in the N12 poll but eight on Channel 13.
The Religious Zionist Party (RZP) and Zehut, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, received six seats in the N12 poll, which rose to eight in the Channel 13 poll.
The Joint List, comprising Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad and led by Yousef Jabareen, received nine seats in both polls; however, N12 found that Mansour Abbas's Ra'am was polling at five, while Channel 13 placed Ra'am at 6. In both polls, the Arab parties remained stable, earning the same number of seats as in the previous poll.
People of Israel, Reservists-Economic parties teeter on the electoral threshold
In the N12 poll, the People of Israel party won four seats, crossing the electoral threshold after falling below it in the previous two polls. However, the Reservists-Economic Party remained below the electoral threshold with 2.8% of the vote.
In contrast, the Channel 13 poll reversed the two. The Reservists-Economic Party kept its four seats and remained above the electoral threshold. Meanwhile, the People of Israel party fell below the electoral threshold after receiving four seats in the previous poll.
A pollster for The Madad and Channel 13 News spoke with 103FM about the latest Channel 13 poll, explaining how the results of the two parties could affect the distribution of Knesset seats between the blocs.
Which party will fail to cross the electoral threshold could be significant
Addressing a scenario in which one or both parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, he explained which bloc could benefit from the redistribution of seats.
"In terms of the balance between the blocs, if neither crosses the threshold, eight seats can be redistributed among other parties. However, one scenario is that one fails to cross the threshold and the other does, leaving four seats to be redistributed. Which party fails to cross the threshold could be significant. The side that would benefit more would be what we call the 'change bloc,' rather than the coalition bloc," he said, adding, "That is the conclusion we reached."
He also addressed where the two parties draw their support from and the differences between voters backing Winter and those supporting Hendel and Zelekha.
"People of Israel and the Reservists receive votes from both sides in almost equal measure. The question is when we start counting, whether we use the 2022 election as our starting point and ask where those votes were in the previous election," he explained.
"It is true that Hendel and Zelekha's votes come more evenly from both sides, while most of Winter's votes come from the coalition side. Nevertheless, Winter also took roughly one seat, out of the nearly four he has, from the opposition side, mainly from Liberman's party," he added.

Trump's Netanyahu endorsement crosses a line in Israeli democracy - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:08:43 UTC
12:08:43 KST

Nothing exceptional is wrong with a country’s leader hoping a fellow leader of an allied country wins re-election and stays in power. Some heads of state, whether due to ideology or personal chemistry, work well together, and the desire to continue that relationship is natural.
However, when that desire oversteps its boundaries and becomes a full-blown endorsement, it’s not only inappropriate; it’s also a flagrant example of foreign interference in another country’s election process.
Trump portrays Netanyahu as essential in fighting Iran
That’s what unfortunately happened earlier this week when US President Donald Trump, who until then had reined in his natural tendency to interfere, issued a clear, strong endorsement of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party for next week’s election.
Only five days after telling Newsmax that “in the world of [Israeli] politics, I don’t trust anybody,” Trump, in his usual hyperbolic fashion, posted on his Truth Social feed on Sunday: “To the great people of Israel, Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran...”
Trump portrayed Netanyahu as indispensable to US efforts to combat Iran and intimated that if he was voted out of office, any other future Israeli leader would leave Washington to confront Tehran on its own.
On Tuesday, Trump, in an interview with N12, explained the endorsement, saying, “I decided to express support for Netanyahu because we have a good relationship, and we will continue to do good things together.”
The desire for a loyal and like-minded ally at the US’s side in the justified war on Iran is one thing, but to call on Israelis, faced with dozens of issues that Trump has nothing to do with, to vote for a candidate because it will make the global agenda of America’s president easier to implement is unprecedented and outrageous.
That’s not to say that lobbying and exerting influence in each other’s election process is something new for the United States and Israel.
Netanyahu once said, 'foreigners do not decide the outcome of Israeli elections'
In 1996, although not issuing a formal endorsement, then-president Bill Clinton covertly campaigned for Shimon Peres in his prime ministerial run against Netanyahu, an admission he made in a 2018 interview. Clinton and then-prime minister Peres met in Washington less than a month before the election, which Netanyahu ultimately won.
At the time, Netanyahu bristled at the perceived interference, telling the Knesset that “foreigners do not decide the outcome of the Israeli elections, not the American government, the king of Morocco, or Yasser Arafat.”
“I can’t find an example of any previous Israeli government whose prime minister, on the eve of elections, made a cynical attempt to use relations between Israel and the United States as a party advertisement,’’ Netanyahu added, foreshadowing the posters that have sprung up throughout the country this week, displaying a beaming Netanyahu and Trump.
Fortunately, Trump’s brazen endorsement of Netanyahu is unlikely to have much effect on next week’s election. Despite his actions that have aided Israel in its wars with its enemies and his efforts to secure the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza, Trump is as divisive in Israel as he is in the US.
The endorsement could backfire, undermining Netanyahu’s image as a strong leader and suggesting he is merely a Trump yes-man.
But regardless of its effect, the endorsement was just plain wrong. Israelis alone should decide whom to vote for in their election without the unsolicited advice or veiled threats from another country’s leader, even one as close as the United States.
The Israel-US relationship is much greater than the personal connection between Trump and Netanyahu. Long after they are both out of office, that relationship must stay strong and vital.
One can thank Trump for his devotion to Israel and his attempts to safeguard its security and boost its status in the region. At the same time, one can staunchly oppose his attempts to interfere in Israel’s internal politics.
Israeli voters face no shortage of issues as they decide whom to vote for in next week’s fateful election. The US president’s preference should not be one of them.

Artist and Photographer Raihan Vadra, son of Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, with one of his photographs at Bikaner House, in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)
NEW DELHI: A controversy erupted at Delhi’s Bikaner House after artist and photographer Raihan Vadra, son of Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and businessman Robert Vadra, alleged that the venue’s management asked him to remove around 74 photographs documenting recent youth protests ahead of his solo exhibition, “No Idea Is Final”.Raihan also alleged that he was asked to remove two photographs of the Indian flag, saying he had refused to take them down.
The exhibition opened as scheduled on Wednesday, with around 40 photographs remaining on display while more than 70 were removed, according to a PTI report. The show, featuring wildlife photography, abstract works and images of recent youth movements, is scheduled to continue until Sunday.In a post on Instagram, Raihan wrote, "Five hours ago, the Bikaner House Management forced me to remove the bulk of the artworks displayed in my show "No Idea Is Final", which opens this evening at 7 pm. The photos were of the youth protests in Delhi. Apparently, the content is "objectionable". They also directed me to remove two photos of the Tiranga. I have refused. I will not take down a picture of the Indian flag."
Why were the photographs removed
Raihan told PTI that the management had raised objections to the “political nature” of the protest photographs. He said he was informed at 3.30 pm on Wednesday that the images had to be removed by 5 pm or the exhibition would be cancelled.
According to Raihan, the management said that, given the prevailing political climate in India, it was not the right time to display the images. He maintained that the photographs did not convey a political message and merely documented protests over the preceding six months."I felt it is my duty as an Indian artist, not just because I am doing a show right now, but it is my duty as an Indian artist to document what is going on... They are censoring the work of artists, I don't know what they are scared of. They even went to the extent of removing the picture of the Indian flag," he told PTI.Raihan also said he had shared the exhibition proposal and layout with the management well in advance and objected to the removal of nearly half the artworks less than 24 hours before the opening.A Bikaner House official told PTI that the administration was not authorised to comment on the matter.
Priyanka Gandhi, Congress leaders react
Priyanka Gandhi Vadra criticised the alleged removal of the photographs, describing it as an attempt to silence young voices."I think it's ridiculous. What do you think? He is a young boy but I suppose you know, they are muzzling the voice of the youth across the nation. So it's only expected that they'll do it to anyone," she told PTI."His photographs of the protests, not a single commentary, not a single thing that was either derogatory towards anyone, just a visual documentation of the protest. So, I mean, clearly this is the way they think. It's not a democracy anymore. Today it's him, tomorrow it'll be another artist," she added.Senior Congress leader Pawan Khera also criticised the alleged censorship, questioning why photographs documenting protests had been considered objectionable."When even the Tricolour isn’t safe from the censor’s scissors, perhaps the problem isn’t the art. It’s the regime. Just hours before @raihanrvadra was to open his art show ‘No Idea Is Final ’, 74 artworks - nearly half the exhibition - were taken down for being 'political ' by the Bikaner House. The photographs merely documented protests, and not one was derogatory or inflammatory. So what exactly was the offence?" he said.
Khera further alleged that a photograph of the Tricolour was among the works Raihan had to fight to retain. Congress MP Karti Chidambaram also condemned the alleged censorship, calling the administration's behaviour "obtuse" and "churlish."The Indian Youth Congress Legal Cell also reacted to the controversy, posting on X: "IYC Legal Cell's tweet: YOU CAN CENSOR THE FRAME. NOT THE TRUTH. Saheb dara hua hai (sir is scared)."Raihan said the exhibition would continue with the works still on display and indicated that he could seek another venue if necessary to show the full collection of protest photographs.

TOKYO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese athletes racked up victories across multiple events on Wednesday, the third competition day of the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games.
On the athletics field, 33-year-old Zhou Feifei settled the men's javelin throw F55 contest with his opening attempt, earning the Chinese delegation its 100th gold medal of the Games. His throw of 37.63m set a world record, leaving the rest of the competition as a battle for second place.
In a similar feat, Liang Hongxia won the women's discus throw F11 with one decisive effort, breaking the world record with 42.19m.
In the women's 100m T35, Zhou Xia took gold in an Asian Para Games record of 13.57 seconds, adding to the title she had already claimed in the 200m T35.
"I was so tired after the race that I didn't even look at the big screen. All I wanted was to run a lap of the stadium with the national flag around my shoulders," she said. "Of these two gold medals, the first one is for me, and this second one I'd really like to dedicate to my parents."
In the women's 100m T11, visually impaired athletes raced with the help of sighted guide-runners, with each pair connected by a tether about 10cm long. At 34, veteran runner Liu Cuiqing broke the Games record to win the title.
China's swimmers maintained their strong form in the pool. Eighteen-year-old Zhu Hui won two golds in the women's 100m freestyle S8 and 50m freestyle S8. The youngest member of the Chinese delegation at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, she has since grown into a mainstay of the team.
The men's H1-5 time trial in para cycling was among the first events of the day to finish. Heavy rain fell suddenly during the morning warm-up, but Liu Qiangli braved the conditions to familiarize himself with the course. He went on to post the fastest time in the race, giving China a winning start on the road.
Chinese athletes also topped the podium in para judo, para archery and para fencing. Gu Haiyan, one of China's flagbearers at the Paris Paralympics opening ceremony, was crowned champion in the women's epee Category A final, claiming her fourth gold medal since arriving in Nagoya.
On Thursday, Li Xiaohui will compete in the wheelchair tennis women's singles final, while China will face host Japan for the gold medal in women's wheelchair basketball. ■

Longer bushfire seasons to cost Australia 4.2 bln USD annually, experts warn
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:05:16 CST
12:05:16 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Longer bushfire seasons caused by climate change will cost Australia billions of dollars annually over the next 30 years, experts have warned.
Emergency Leaders for Climate Action (ELCA), a subsidiary of the NGO the Climate Council consisting of former fire and emergency service leaders, said in a report published on Thursday that fire seasons have grown 21 percent longer since 1979, shrinking the window for hazard reduction efforts.
It projected that more frequent major bushfires driven by climate change will cost the nation an average of 6 billion Australian dollars (4.2 billion U.S. dollars) annually over the next 30 years.
Of the projected annual cost, it said 32 percent would come from harm to health and wellbeing, 25 percent from lost trade, 20 percent from damaged businesses and public buildings, 17 percent from lost homes and 6 percent from lost work.
The report said that southeast Australia now experiences 14 more days of extreme fire weather per year than in 1998 and that the number of extreme fire-generated storms recorded from 2004 to 2024 was six-fold higher than the preceding 20 years.
It said that Australia had 10.336 fewer volunteer firefighters as of 2023-24 than four years earlier, while the number of paid positions grew by 433 in the same period.
The ELCA warned that the next two summers would pose a particularly significant risk to communities, with the impacts of climate change exacerbated by the ongoing El Nino event.
"This dangerous double act is setting the scene for record heat, flash drought, and the possibility of worsening bushfires over the coming summers," the report said.
Australia's Bureau of Meteorology said in its latest update earlier in October that El Nino was at near-record levels, with further intensification forecast. ■

The term for the next UN secretary-general starts on Jan. 1, 2027. ■

China Focus: Young tenants, old neighbors: China's care homes try intergenerational living
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:04:55 CST
12:04:55 KST

NANNING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- At a painting class in Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region's capital in south China, lawyer Liang Yinxia lays out art supplies and guides a group of elderly residents through the lesson. On other days, she reads the news with them, takes walks or helps them use smartphones.
Liang is not employed by the care home. Since August, she has lived there, paying part of her rent with volunteer hours.
At Nanning Wuxiang Nursing Service Center, 30 hours of volunteering a month cuts the rent by 500 yuan (about 74 U.S. dollars). Forty hours earns a 750-yuan discount, while 50 hours covers the entire 1,000-yuan rent.
Liang spent four years working in hospital nursing before becoming a lawyer in 2024. The center was near her workplace, and the rent reduction appealed to her.
Applicants must be aged 22 to 40 and meet requirements, including not owning a home in Nanning. The center gives preference to people trained in social work, healthcare, psychology or law.
Other cities have adopted their own rules, as Chinese authorities explore systems of care involving volunteers trading their time for help with accommodation.
In Jinyun County, east China's Zhejiang Province, young people can stay in unused staff rooms at participating care homes and earn rent reductions by volunteering 10 to 30 hours a month. One home has housed 95 young people since the program began in 2024, with 13 living there now.
The programs remain small in scale. Four care facilities in Nanning were selected for similar trials in 2025.
Official data shows that China's population aged 60 and above exceeded 323 million by the end of 2025, accounting for about 23 percent of the national total.
WHAT BOTH GENERATIONS GAIN
Liang had years of nursing experience, but she found that getting to know her new neighbors took time. At first, she struggled to gain their trust. Gradually, residents began telling her about their past.
"The elderly have accumulated a lifetime of experience and wisdom," she said. "You can only appreciate that by getting to know them."
An 83-year-old resident surnamed Li said she now had more people to talk to and participate in activities with. When she fell behind during a video-guided class, a young volunteer explained what to do.
In Jinyun, Wu Weifeng, a young man from neighboring Jiangsu Province, moved into a care home's staff accommodation after taking a hospital job in 2024. He had struggled to find a place to rent.
"At first, I didn't know how to start a conversation. Instead, the elderly residents came over and asked about me," Wu recalled.
The experience has made him more patient with older members of his own family, he said.
At another home in Hangzhou, the provincial capital of Zhejiang, young residents teach older people how to use artificial intelligence tools, while the older residents share memories of the city and stories from their working lives. One young tenant, Qiu Shaoqi, arrived for the free room, but later found he was reluctant to leave.
There are precedents overseas. In the Netherlands, the Humanitas retirement home in Deventer has offered university students rent-free accommodation in exchange for spending at least 30 hours a month with older residents. The arrangement drew international media attention in 2015.
The OECD's 2025 Cities for All Ages report discusses intergenerational housing as one response to loneliness and housing affordability problems, citing projects in Europe and the United States.
THE CHALLENGE OF STAYING
Liang completed 30 volunteer hours in August. In September, work commitments and health problems left her four hours short. The center agreed to let her make up the difference in October.
Social workers and care staff guide the volunteers, with their services recorded and regularly assessed.
"We need to ensure the quality of volunteer services while also considering young people's circumstances," said Huang Zibiao, the center's deputy director, adding that some young people had given up plans to live at the center because their workplaces changed, or the commute became too long.
"Moving in and becoming part of the community are two different things," said Zhang Yingxi, a researcher at the National Academy of Economic Strategy under the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).
Some young tenants may regard cheap accommodation as a temporary solution, making it difficult to maintain lasting relationships with older residents, Zhang said.
There are practical limits, too. The volunteers are not professional caregivers, and care facilities must manage safety, privacy and other risks, said Xia Xuemin, a researcher at Zhejiang University.
In Jinyun, 24 care institutions are testing a volunteer "time bank." Participants can earn points to exchange for care services or daily necessities, or transfer them to immediate family members. More than 1,000 people have signed up.
National guidelines released by Chinese authorities earlier this year encourage localities to develop systems for recording volunteer hours in mutual elderly care programs, with credits redeemable for care services or transferable to immediate family members. Volunteer hours can be recorded, and in some places, saved as credits.
However, several elderly residents at the Nanning center said they valued regular visits and conversations more than occasional group activities. They wanted someone who would keep coming back, sit down and listen. ■

Pakistani Embassy in Tehran, ECO Cultural Institute host exhibit showcasing Pakistan’s rich history
TEHRAN- A Tehran exhibition is offering visitors a journey through Pakistan’s civilizational arc—from its ancient roots to its enduring literary traditions—while spotlighting the cultural bridges between Iran and Pakistan. Titled “Pakistan Through the Ages,” the show was inaugurated on October 20, drawing diplomats, cultural officials and researchers.
Organized by the Embassy of Pakistan in Tehran in collaboration with the ECO Cultural Institute (ECI), the exhibition brings together historical photographs, calligraphy, paintings and visual records from different periods, giving visitors a broad view of Pakistan’s cultural heritage. Its title underlines the country’s historical depth and the continuity of that heritage over time.
The opening also served as a platform for discussion of the two countries’ shared civilizational legacy, the influence of Persian language and literature on the Indian subcontinent, and the scope for expanding cultural and tourism cooperation across the region.
Pakistan’s ambassador to Iran, Imran Ahmed Siddiqui, could not attend the ceremony because he was accompanying a Pakistani delegation led by Field Marshal Asim Munir. His remarks were delivered by Ismat Hassan Sial, deputy head of mission at the Pakistani Embassy.
Some excerpts from the ambassador’s remarks follow:
“There are moments when history comes alive. It is no longer just in books or on screens. It is there in a piece of pottery, a carved stone, a sculpture, a manuscript, a line of calligraphy. Tonight, here in this exhibition, ‘Pakistan Through the Ages,’ we invite the audience to experience one such journey. A journey through time. But, more important, a journey of human connections.
“Our story begins thousands of years before the creation of Pakistan. More than nine thousand years ago, in Mehrgarh, Balochistan, people demonstrated flora and fauna, made tools and built settled communities. Over time, these early communities evolved. New settlements emerged. Trade expanded. Skills developed.
“When Pakistan emerged as an independent country in 1947, it did not begin its story from zero. It carried all these centuries with it. Mehrgarh, the Indus Valley, Gandhara and a rich tradition of Islamic culture. Pakistan was new in its political form. But ancient in the civilizations that shaped it. That, for us, is what makes this exhibition so meaningful.
“Identity is not a single moment. It is a journey. A river that gathers many streams along the way. And every stream leaves something behind. For us this exhibition is an invitation to our friends to seek Pakistan through a wider lens. Not simply as a state. But as part of a culture whose story has, in so many ways, unfolded alongside the story of this ancient land.
“And perhaps this is its special power. Culture can do what politics sometimes cannot. It helps us discover what is shared. It helps us understand our common past and use it to imagine our future.
“So tonight, we celebrate more than the centuries that have passed. We celebrate the possibility of the centuries yet to come. Let us continue this conversation. Let us continue to discover each other. And let us continue building bridges through culture, knowledge and the human connections that have linked our people for centuries.
“History tells us where we came from. But culture gives us the confidence to imagine where we can go. Let’s embark on exploration of linkages awaiting us.”
Other speakers included Ambassador Muhammad Hassan, president of the ECO Cultural Institute; Anoushirvan Mohseni Bandpei, Iran’s deputy minister of cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts for tourism affairs; and Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, president of the Saadi Foundation.
Following the speeches and a video screening on Pakistan’s history, the exhibition was officially inaugurated, and guests toured the exhibition while being served delicious Pakistani snacks.
The exhibition ultimately served as more than a retrospective: it was a cultural-diplomacy platform that connected historical memory with contemporary cooperation.
By pairing archival and artistic material with discussion of shared civilizational heritage, it underscored how Iran and Pakistan can build on centuries of exchange to expand cultural, academic and tourism ties.
As visitors left with a fuller picture of Pakistan’s past, the event also left a clear message: culture remains one of the most effective bridges between the two nations and the wider region.

The purchase stemmed from a memorandum of understanding signed at the 2025 Taipei Aerospace and Defense Technology Exhibition between MarTac, the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, and Taipei-based defense contractor Confucian. MarTac’s Florida-based partner will build some of the boats, with Confucian building the rest, as the deal requires using local workers and sharing technology to ensure China-free production.

The co-produced model has an 8.4-meter-long hull, a burst speed of more than 50 knots (92.6 kph), and a range of up to 600 nautical miles (1,111 km), with a maximum carrying capacity of 816 kg. The coastal drone vessel can also deploy smaller T12 drone boats and withstand signal interruptions, per MarTac.
Coast Guard Administration Director-General Chang Chung-lung (張忠龍) said the T24s and unmanned aerial vehicles will help expand operations, including coordinated investigations and long-range search and rescue. He added that the T24s will also assist patrol vessels as part of the administration’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance network, per Liberty Times.
Flatley said the purchase was made possible through testing by NCSIST and production assistance from Confucian. Confucian CEO James Lee (李志昇) said the Coast Guard chose MarTac not just for its vessels’ capabilities, but also for the firm’s commitment to a reciprocal relationship through local co-production.
Flatley also told Taiwan News that MarTac and Confucian have selected a domestic shipbuilder. He added that MarTac will work alongside it to establish a production line to build, test, and deliver locally produced T24s.

S. Korea holds rates steady after consecutive increases to curb inflation

S. Korea holds rates steady after consecutive increases to curb inflation
The Bank of Korea (BOK) kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3 percent on Thursday, pausing its tightening cycle after two consecutive rate hikes as persistent inflationary pressures, escalating Middle East tensions and strong export growth continued to shape the economic outlook, Qazinform News Agency cites Yonhap.
The decision by the BOK's Monetary Policy Board was widely anticipated by financial markets. The central bank raised its key rate at its July and August meetings, citing the need for preemptive action to contain rising inflation and maintain macroeconomic stability.
Those increases marked the first consecutive rate hikes since January 2023, when the central bank concluded a series of seven straight increases that began in April 2022.
The latest decision to hold rates steady reflects concerns that further monetary tightening could increase borrowing costs and place additional financial pressure on lower-income households. Nevertheless, the BOK has signaled that it intends to maintain a hawkish policy stance as inflation risks persist and economic activity remains resilient.
Consumer price inflation has remained close to 3 percent in recent months, reaching 2.8 percent in July, 3.1 percent in August and 2.9 percent in September. Inflation is expected to remain at a similar level in October, partly driven by rising oil prices amid escalating military tensions in the Middle East.
BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song has indicated that the central bank will continue tightening monetary policy until inflation is firmly on course to reach its 2 percent target.
Meanwhile, stronger-than-expected economic growth has provided further support for the central bank's cautious approach to easing monetary policy. South Korea's economy, Asia's fourth-largest, expanded by 1.8 percent in the first quarter and 0.6 percent in the second quarter.
South Korea recorded a current account surplus of 279.2 billion US dollars in the first eight months of the year, more than four times the amount reported during the same period last year.
Reflecting the improving economic outlook, the BOK raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.3 percent from 2.6 percent in August. The economy could expand by as much as 3.6 percent, supported by robust semiconductor exports and strong demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Market analysts expect the central bank to consider another rate increase at its next monetary policy meeting, scheduled for November 26.
Earlier, Qazinform reported South Korea’s exports doubled in the first 20 days of October.

Mikhail Kukushkin brings more than 20-year tennis career to a close in Almaty
Kazakhstan’s Mikhail Kukushkin has played the final match of his professional tennis career at the ATP 250 Almaty Open, bringing more than two decades in the sport to an end in front of his home crowd, Qazinform News Agency reported, citing the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation.
The 38-year-old faced seventh-seeded Greek player Stefanos Tsitsipas in the second round of the tournament.
The match, held on the central court at Almaty Arena, lasted just over an hour, with Tsitsipas securing a 6-1, 6-2 victory. Despite the defeat, the occasion marked an emotional moment for Kazakhstan’s tennis, as Kukushkin bid farewell to professional competition surrounded by fans, family members and fellow players.
Tsitsipas delivered a confident performance, serving eight aces and converting four break points. The Greek controlled the rallies from the baseline and sealed the victory in straight sets.
However, the match was defined less by the result than by Kukushkin’s farewell to professional tennis. Every point won by the Kazakhstani player was greeted with loud applause from the stands.
Following the match, Tsitsipas spoke about the unusual experience of facing an opponent playing the final match of his career.
Tsitsipas congratulated Kukushkin on his remarkable career, adding that it had been an unusual and somewhat unsettling experience to face an opponent playing the final match of his professional career. He noted that he had never found himself in such a situation before and admitted that it was not easy to realize that his opponent’s career would come to an end just minutes later.
More than 20 years in professional tennis
Kukushkin has left a lasting mark on the history of Kazakhstani tennis. Throughout his career, he achieved notable results on the international stage and remained one of the key players in Kazakhstan’s national team for many years.
In February 2019, Kukushkin reached a career-high ranking of world No. 39 in the ATP rankings. He won his first and only ATP singles title in 2010 at the St. Petersburg Open and also reached several other finals on the professional tour.
Kukushkin became the first Kazakhstani player to reach the fourth round of the Australian Open, achieving the milestone in 2012, and Wimbledon, where he reached the same stage in 2019.
His performances for Kazakhstan in the Davis Cup also played a significant role in his career. For more than 15 years, Kukushkin was one of the leaders of the national team, making a substantial contribution to its results on the international stage.
His decision to conclude his career at the home-hosted Almaty Open added symbolic significance to the occasion. It gave the Kazakhstani player an opportunity to say goodbye to professional tennis in front of the supporters who had stood by him throughout his career.
Tsitsipas, meanwhile, advanced to the quarterfinals of the ATP 250 Almaty Open with his victory. For Kukushkin, the match marked the final chapter of a distinguished sporting career that helped inspire a new generation of Kazakhstani tennis players.

Libyan news channel releases video of the two women freed from captivity

Libya and Niger share a border hundreds of miles long, cutting through the Sahara Desert and connecting with Algeria and Chad on either side. Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime ruler Moammar Gaddafi.
At the moment, two governments are vying for power there: a UN-recognized administration led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah and its rival in the east, backed by Haftar.

Not Just Ukraine Peace Talks – Witkoff Reveals US Treasury Working With Putin’s Envoy on Economic Ties

US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff publicly confirmed Wednesday, Oct. 21, that Washington and Moscow are discussing future trade and economic cooperation alongside negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, revealing that the US Treasury Department is working directly with Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
The disclosure came during Witkoff’s meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, where discussions extended well beyond peace proposals to include Russian diesel shipments to the US, financial arrangements and potential fertilizer exports.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Our Treasury Department is working with you now independently,” Witkoff told Dmitriev during the meeting.
He said the contacts were helping both governments assess possibilities for renewed economic relations, which Washington was also discussing with Ukrainian officials.
The remarks provide explicit confirmation that the Trump administration has been pursuing economic engagement with Moscow, even as the US maintains extensive sanctions imposed over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
They are particularly significant because Washington largely suspended official bilateral trade and investment engagement with Moscow following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, although limited commercial trade continued.
Witkoff reveals direct Treasury talks with Putin’s economic envoy
Dmitriev, the chief executive of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and Putin’s special representative for international economic cooperation, has played a central role in Moscow’s contacts with the Trump administration.
‘Capitulating to a Dictator Shows Weakness’ – Republican Senator Slams Trump’s Russia Policy
Addressing Dmitriev directly, Witkoff praised his contribution to discussions between the two governments.
“You’ve been outstanding, Kirill,” he said.
Witkoff described the economic discussions as an indication of the opportunities that might become available if relations between Washington and Moscow improve.
He also revealed that the US was speaking openly with Ukraine about potential economic developments following the war.
“We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is ended,” Witkoff said.
His comments did not establish whether the Treasury Department’s contacts concerned sanctions relief, investment, banking arrangements or specific commercial agreements.
Nor did he identify the Treasury officials involved or explain what commitments, if any, Washington had made.
The contacts are notable because the US Treasury Department sanctioned Dmitriev and RDIF in February 2022, identifying the fund as part of the financial network supporting Putin’s government.
Treasury also administers and enforces major US financial sanctions on Russia through its Office of Foreign Assets Control.
Witkoff’s comments therefore raise questions about how discussions with Dmitriev fit into Washington’s broader sanctions policy and whether the administration is exploring ways to restore economic relations with Moscow.
US and Russia have had limited trade since 2022
The acknowledgment represents a departure from the sharply restricted economic relationship that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In 2022, Washington imposed sweeping financial and trade restrictions on Moscow, including measures affecting Russian banks, energy imports, technology exports and investment.
The US also withdrew Russia’s normal trade relations status, exposing Russian imports to higher tariffs.
Formal bilateral engagement on trade and investment issues was largely halted, although commerce between the two countries did not end entirely.
According to the US Trade Representative, American goods trade with Russia totaled approximately $4.4 billion in 2025, compared with about $36 billion in 2021.
Against this backdrop, Witkoff’s confirmation that Treasury officials are working with Dmitriev indicates that the administration is considering future economic opportunities beyond the narrow trade that has continued under existing restrictions.
The remarks do not establish that Washington has lifted its broader Russia sanctions or agreed to restore normal trade relations.
Putin confirms Russian diesel shipments, offers fertilizers to US
The economic discussions were not limited to prospective cooperation after the war.
Witkoff thanked Putin for removing Russian diesel export restrictions, saying the decision would benefit American consumers and help ease pressure on global fuel markets.
He said Trump was deeply grateful, particularly because farmers and truck drivers had been affected by higher diesel costs.
Putin responded by claiming that global diesel prices had fallen between 5% and 6% following the announcement of Russian supplies to the US.
He said Moscow was preparing several tankers to begin deliveries, with the first carrying 40,000 metric tons of diesel and scheduled to depart within two or three days.
Additional shipments would follow, Putin said, adding that financial arrangements needed to be finalized to ensure the transactions could proceed.
The Russian leader also offered to supply large quantities of fertilizer to the American market, referring to Trump’s concerns about US farmers.
The discussion revealed that the two governments were addressing not only the political implications of closer economic cooperation but also practical questions about deliveries, payments and trade.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov later confirmed through Interfax that the diesel arrangement was discussed during the meeting and that practical implementation had begun following Washington’s decision to ease certain restrictions.
The diesel deal comes amid criticism in Washington that increased Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue while its military continues attacking Ukraine.
Despite the emphasis on trade, Witkoff said ending Russia’s war against Ukraine remained a central objective of his visit.
He proposed resuming trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, suggesting that technical teams begin examining the next steps toward a settlement.

Hillary Clinton rejects term limits, says voters should decide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:37:53 UTC
11:37:53 KST

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Wednesday rejected the idea of imposing term limits on elected officials, saying voters should decide how long their representatives remain in office.
“I don’t agree about term limits. I think term limits are artificial,” Clinton told journalist and podcast host Kara Swisher, who had argued in favor of some kind of curbs on elected officials, whether they be based on age, years in office, or terms.
“I think voters get to make the choice, and if somebody you and I think shouldn’t be running again, then vote against them,” she added.
Her remarks came amid renewed debate in the US over proposals to restrict how long members of Congress should remain in office.
Representatives serve two-year terms and senators serve six-year terms, but neither chamber limits the number of times a lawmaker may seek reelection.
Supporters of congressional term limits argue that they would encourage political renewal, reduce the advantages enjoyed by incumbents and prevent lawmakers from holding power for decades.
Opponents say such restrictions would deny voters the right to retain experienced representatives and could increase the influence of unelected congressional staff, lobbyists and interest groups.
Introducing congressional term limits would require an amendment to the US Constitution. Such an amendment must secure two-thirds support in both chambers of Congress and ratification by three-quarters of the states, or be proposed through a constitutional convention requested by two-thirds of state legislatures.
US presidents are subject to a separate constitutional restriction under the 22nd Amendment, which generally limits them to two elected terms.
Clinton, the Democratic presidential nominee in 2016, has previously opposed both mandatory retirement ages and term limits, maintaining that voters should judge candidates individually at the ballot box.

Three years into the Gaza war, Israeli commander reflects on the price of defending his country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:30:08 UTC
11:30:08 KST

On Friday, October 13, 2023, we arrived at the staging areas of the 401st Armored Brigade near the Gaza border. Among the tanks, we met Eitan, a lone soldier from Australia who was preparing with his fellow troops for the ground offensive in Gaza. "War is complicated, and we understand that not everyone will come back," he said.
Eitan had a clear-eyed understanding of the reality. The 401st Brigade lost 58 soldiers during the ground operations in Gaza and Lebanon, including brigade commander Col. Ehsan Daxa and Battalion 52 commander Lt. Col. Dor Gedalia Ben Simhon. Many others were wounded in combat, including Daxa's successor, Col. Meir Biderman.
As we walked through the staging area, speaking with soldiers and commanders in the days following the devastating October 7 attack, R. was sitting at the forward command post of the 162nd Division, meticulously planning the ground offensive in Gaza. At the time, he was head of operational planning in the division's operations branch. Three years later, Lt. Col. R. commands Battalion 9 of the 401st Brigade, now deployed in the southern Gaza Strip.
His battalion combat team consists of a tank company, a reserve infantry company, a combat engineering company and a logistics support company. Today, the missions of tank and infantry battalion commanders are almost identical.
"The only difference between us is that I ride in a tank, while an infantry battalion commander rides in a Namer armored personnel carrier," Lt. Col. R. explains.
Active defense
We are standing on the earthen berm surrounding the Etzioni outpost, about five miles inside the Gaza Strip. In front of us is the Yellow Line, marked by concrete blocks that also serve as a physical barrier. Battalion 9 controls the Morag Corridor, which separates Rafah from Khan Younis. Anyone attempting to travel between the two cities will encounter IDF forces.
The 401st Brigade, including Battalion 9, was the first to enter Gaza at the start of the ground offensive exactly three years ago. After two years of fighting in the Gaza Strip, the brigade moved to Lebanon and took part in the ground offensive conducted as part of Operation Roaring Lion. R., who has held his current position for about three months, assumed command of the battalion in Ras al-Bayada, a village in southern Lebanon near the Israeli border.
R., 34, lives in the central Israeli city of Rosh Ha'ayin. He is married to Lt. Col. M., also a career IDF officer, and they have two sons: Alon, 4, and Sahar, 2, who was born during the war. "I managed to make it to the delivery," R. says.
About two months ago, the brigade returned to the southern Gaza Strip, where it has remained ever since.
"Our mission is to defend the area from the Yellow Line to the border, creating a buffer zone between the enemy and the communities in the southern Gaza border region," R. explains. "Because the IDF is here, well inside the Gaza Strip, residents can return to their homes, celebrate the holidays safely and cultivate their land right up to the last furrow. I find that deeply moving."
For him, these are not empty slogans. The battalion commander's sister recently moved with her family to Kibbutz Magen in the northwestern Negev desert, where her husband grew up.
Standing with us on the berm is Capt. A., commander of Battalion 9's Lahav Company. He is 25, from Rehovot and recently married. A. was wounded by fragments from an RPG during the ground offensive in Gaza and returned to combat three weeks later.
"When you work so hard and see the results, when people feel safe returning to their homes, you feel a sense of satisfaction that you've done a good job," he says.
Not everyone has returned, it must be said. Many residents of the Gaza border communities, particularly those that suffered the heaviest losses, remain displaced. Some will never return.
The company commander emphasizes that defense involves more than simply remaining at fortified positions.
"We maintain a presence throughout the area, go out with the tanks, patrol near the Yellow Line and conduct firing operations," he says.
The battalion is also working to locate and destroy tunnels that still exist in the area.
What is absent here are Palestinian homes and residents. The Morag Corridor is deserted, and almost all the houses that once stood in the area have been destroyed. Nearby Rafah has also been completely devastated.
Anyone crossing the Yellow Line is regarded by the troops as an enemy, unless the person is a woman or a child.
"We don't shoot at women and children," the battalion commander stresses, stating what should be obvious.
The Etzioni outpost is undergoing extensive construction and preparations for winter. Cranes are unloading prefabricated structures from trucks. The IDF is becoming increasingly established in the area, and it appears to be there for the long term.
"Even a dentist comes here to treat the soldiers, and God willing, we'll have a physical therapist as well," Capt. A. says.
At a nearby observation post stands a reservist from the infantry company. He does not recognize the battalion commander, who is probably younger than he is.
"If you're finished talking, get down from the berm," the reservist says. "You're exposed to the enemy. God forbid someone should shoot at you."
"We're not finished yet, thank you," the battalion commander replies.
He then assures us: "If there were any real danger, I wouldn't have brought you up here."
On our way back toward the border, we pass through the Regavim outpost, where a combat engineering company from Battalion 601 is stationed under the command of Battalion 9.
Hanging on the dining hall wall are flags bearing photographs of two battalion soldiers killed in the war: Sgt. Nehorai Leizer of Eilat, who was killed in Lebanon, and Sgt. Yisrael Natan Rosenfeld of Ra'anana, who was killed in Jabalia.
Helping farmers
We climb with the battalion commander to the roof of the outpost, which is actually a residential building that remains standing. He points east, toward the Israeli communities along the Gaza border visible on the horizon.
"On the Israeli side of the border, you can see the communities of Sufa, Holit, Kerem Shalom and Nir Oz. It's a reminder to my soldiers of why they're here," he says.
The Battalion 9 commander places great importance on maintaining ties with residents of the Gaza border communities, from working meetings with local security coordinators to volunteer activities in the communities.
"Before a platoon goes home on leave, the soldiers volunteer to help farmers in the Gaza border area with work in their fields and orchards. That, too, helps them understand the 'why.'"
Lt. Col. R. and Capt. A. know the cost of war all too well. Both have lost friends, commanders and soldiers who served under them.
"When Ehsan was killed, I wasn't far from there," A. recalls. "We gathered the company and told the soldiers: 'The brigade commander has been killed, a replacement has been appointed and we are continuing our missions in the spirit of his leadership.'
"When soldiers understand that their commanders are out front, taking risks and sometimes paying the price to accomplish the mission, they understand that they're not alone."
Lt. Col. R. saw another example of that commitment when Ben Simhon was killed in Lebanon, as R. was preparing to take command of the battalion.
"Dor embodied exactly that kind of leadership: leading from the front, standing alongside his soldiers in direct confrontations with the enemy, in the toughest moments, when a commander is needed to make decisions," he says.
When your wife hears that a fellow battalion commander has been killed and knows that you're also on the front lines, what does she say?
"She understands the risks very well and what could happen. She's fully aware of them, and we take that into account.
"All I can tell you is what I always tell my soldiers: 'It's not enough to love this country. You must also take responsibility for its fate.'"

Europe cannot count on American rescue, inquiry told
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
03:30:08 BST
11:30:08 KST

Europe cannot count on the United States returning to the European Arctic as the security partner and ally that Britain and Europe previously relied on, and NATO’s Article 5 is functionally moribund in the American sense, according to evidence published by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined the implications of American policy for High North security as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
Professor David Blagden of the University of Exeter told the committee: “[w]e can talk about the formal aspects of withdrawal or not but, functionally, you would probably say Article 5 in the American sense is pretty much moribund at the moment now anyway. No one really believes that the Americans are riding to the rescue if there were some situation in the Baltic states.”
The report sets out that the American 2026 National Defense Strategy outlined four lines of effort to achieve its America First strategic approach, covering defence of the United States homeland, deterring China in the Indo-Pacific through strength, increasing burden-sharing with allies and partners, and supercharging the American defence industrial base. The committee states that none of these suggest a return to greater engagement in Europe’s defence over the medium term, including the High North, and that where the Arctic is mentioned in the strategy it is in relation to American homeland defence.
The committee was told that “[e]ven if the next US President was a dyed in the wool Atlanticist—Eisenhower 2.0 or something—the US would not have the capacity to pivot back to playing the role it did in Europe and the High North”, largely because the United States perceives the maximum likelihood of conflict in East Asia as between 2027 and 2035.
On troop numbers, the report records a reported plan to cut between 25,000 and 40,000 American troops from the roughly 80,000 currently stationed in Europe, despite congressional provisions in the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act restricting reductions below 76,000 personnel, and notes that significant future reductions in fighter jets, strategic bombers, destroyers, submarines, tanker aircraft and armed drones could also follow.
The Kiel Institute calculated that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons would cost an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Professor Blagden also told the committee: “[t]he caveat, though, to all that glass-half-full stuff is that the UK, for years and years, has been generating SDSR-type documents in which we talk about how far we lean on allies. It has ultimately reached the point where the greatest of those allies has suddenly become unreliable… [w]e cannot just say, ‘We lean on an ally for this. We lean on an ally for that.’ When it comes to the High North, the UK is the major power now. The American cavalry is not about to ride over the horizon and save our fecklessness.”
Ministry of Defence witnesses drew a distinction between American capabilities and American commitments. On capabilities, the department said the United States is making it known to the rest of NATO that “[h]ere are the capabilities we [America] intend not to offer in the future. That is what we think a more European NATO looks like…” On commitments, Brigadier Jeremy Lamb, Head of Euro-Atlantic Security at the department, told the committee that “[w]hat they are talking about, is basing; it is not necessarily what they will make available to the SACEUR (Supreme Allied Commander Europe) in a crisis.”

Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:24:17 UTC
11:24:17 KST

The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.
Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.
But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.
AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.
“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.
Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
The PHP Foundation did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.
“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

US evacuating Middle East bases – NBC

US troops stationed in Jordan, Qatar, and Kuwait are among those being relocated, according to the report. Washington reportedly intends to maintain a limited presence at its regional bases, including personnel responsible for air defenses and security.

House prices down in all Australian capitals in 15-year first
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:14:52 CST
11:14:52 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- House prices fell across every Australian capital city for the first time in 15 years during the third quarter of 2026, according to industry data released on Thursday.
The quarterly house price report from residential real estate marketplace Domain revealed that the combined capital city median house price fell 4.7 percent between June and September, the largest quarterly decline on record, while median unit prices declined 3.5 percent.
The report said it was the second consecutive quarter of falling prices for both property types and that annual price growth turned negative for the first time in over three years.
It noted that house prices fell in the capital cities of all eight Australian states and territories for the first time in 15 years.
In Sydney, Australia's most expensive property market, the median house price fell by 4.7 percent over the quarter to a two-year low.
Perth, capital of Western Australia, recorded a quarterly house price fall of 7.4 percent and a unit price fall of 6.5 percent, both of which were the largest declines of any capital.
Domain attributed the nationwide downturn to lower buyer confidence as a result of interest rate rises, cost-of-living pressures and the federal government's move to wind back tax concessions for property investors.
"What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Nicola Powell, Domain's Chief Residential Economist, said.
"Confidence has become one of the market's biggest headwinds. Higher interest rates and persistent cost-of-living pressures are reducing how much buyers can borrow and their willingness to transact. When buyers expect prices could fall further, there is less urgency to act and greater incentive to wait."
The Reserve Bank of Australia's Monetary Policy Board at the end of September voted unanimously to raise the cash rate target to a 15-year high of 4.60 percent.
The board will next meet to consider the key interest rate early in November. ■

NEW YORK, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A chemical tank ruptured Tuesday night in Toledo, Ohio, leaking toxic glycidyl methacrylate gas into the air, forcing nearly 1,000 residents to evacuate and prompting a shelter-in-place order for over 50,000 people.
The 5,500-gallon tank leaked after a transfer error, Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said at a news conference on Wednesday, adding that authorities were waiting for the chemical to vent out of the tanker rather than trying to "actively stop the leak", which risks an explosion.
At least 35 people were treated at hospitals for minor symptoms like eye or throat burning, a sheriff's deputy was treated after feeling unwell, and schools were closed, local media reported on Wednesday.
The Toledo Fire and Rescue has reduced the evacuation zone to a half-mile radius and lifted the shelter-in-place order.
Glycidyl Methacrylate, a flammable industrial coating and plastic additive that is stored as a liquid and turns into a gas when released into the air, can cause skin, eye, and throat irritation. ■

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index rebounded Wednesday following overnight gains in US equities.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index (TAIEX) rose as much as 962 points to 47,254.93 during the session. It pared gains to close up 594.84 points at 46,887.77, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Turnover rose to NT$833.2 billion (US$25.7 billion), compared with NT$758.7 billion in the previous session. The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$153.48 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
Among the index’s largest constituents, TSMC added 0.62% to NT$2,420, while MediaTek fell 0.24% to NT$4,140. Foxconn gained 3.52% to NT$250, Delta Electronics rose 1.25% to NT$1,625, and ASE added 3.64% to NT$684.
Low Earth orbit satellite stocks advanced after SpaceX reported earnings that exceeded market expectations. Universal Microwave Technology and Win Semiconductors both closed up more than 7%, while Tong Hsing Electronic, Kinpo Electronics, Zinwell, Hitron Technologies, Auden Techno, and Nitech Printed Circuit Board also gained.
Passive component stocks rebounded as investors bought shares that had recently suffered significant losses. Walsin Technology, Prosperity Dielectrics, Taiwan Chinsan Electronic Industrial, Viking Tech, King Core Electronics, and Max Echo Technology all rose by their daily limits.
Industry leaders Yageo and Holy Stone Enterprise each gained 2% to 3%.
High-end printed circuit board (PCB) material stocks advanced amid the ongoing Taiwan Printed Circuit Association (TPCA) Show and tight supply of ultra-low-loss materials used in high-speed AI servers. Ventec Electronics, ShineMore Technology Materials, and Iteq all rose by their daily limits, according to Sinotrade.
In contrast, glass fiber fabric stocks, another part of the PCB supply chain, retreated after broad gains in the previous session driven by the TPCA Show and expectations of higher raw material prices. Glotech Industrial fell 6.35%, Fulltech Fiber Glass declined 4.55%, and Taiwan Glass lost 0.3%.
Concord Securities investment director Liao Chi-hung (廖繼弘) said the rebound lacked broad-based strength. Buying in TSMC near the close accounted for much of the index’s gains Wednesday, according to CTEE.
Liao said the TAIEX could face resistance near 48,000 points, where heavy trading last week left many investors holding shares purchased at higher prices. He expected the index to trade between 46,000 and 48,000 points in the near term before attempting to move higher.
Liao said concerns over AI investment costs and returns, along with competition from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies in the memory market, had weighed on technology stocks. Higher-than-expected US inflation data, elevated US Treasury yields, a weaker Taiwan dollar, and foreign investor selling had also contributed to the market correction.
With the US midterm elections scheduled for Nov. 3, Liao said historical market performance following previous midterm elections offered grounds for optimism about Taiwan stocks. He expected the TAIEX to move higher after the current consolidation, potentially testing 50,000 points in November or December.
However, Liao cautioned that market swings had widened, with more stocks pulling back quickly after reaching new highs. He advised investors to time trades carefully and avoid buying at elevated prices.

A man has been charged after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the Western Australian local government minister, Hannah Beazley.

Electoral staff at Beazley’s Victoria Park office called police after a man caused a disturbance on Wednesday afternoon.
Police said they received reports the man was making verbal threats while in possession of an “improvised martial arts weapon” described as “nunchucks”.
They arrested the 56-year-old man nearby and took him into custody. On Thursday he was charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making unlawful threats and cannabis possession. Nobody was injured in the incident.
The man was refused bail to appear at Perth magistrates court on Thursday.
Beazley was not in the office at the time but told reporters on Wednesday evening her staff were “rattled” by the “confronting situation”.
“He was [allegedly] being very threatening. He did want access to me, I believe, but we don’t know his motivations at all,” the minister said.
Beazley said there had been two staff members in the office at the time. The man allegedly attempted to lean through the security screen but her staff were a safe distance away, she said.
“It’s not the first time I’ve had threats made against me.
“My primary concern is the welfare of my staff, obviously. That was very rattling for them. They called the police.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Hannah Beazley was a friend “because I’m a good friend of her dad”, the former Labor defence minister Kim Beazley.
“This is far too prevalent,” Albanese told Perth radio on Thursday. “It’s not who we are as Australians. We can have our discussions and debates and settle those issues at the ballot box.”
‘A unique and pernicious form of attack’
The governor general, Sam Mostyn, speaking generally on Thursday, discussed the gendered dynamics of threats and abuse directed at women in high-profile positions.
“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC TV.
“I still receive that online. In fact, I was just saddened this morning to see some of the comments on my own Instagram page, in capitals with expletives, once again questioning the very nature of what it is that I do.
“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women … that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”
A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.
Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.
McGowan had spent time with Haines’s staff and she told Guardian Australia they were “all crying together because of the emotion that’s been building up”.
“The people here tonight don’t want violence … but that’s not to say when violence happens in their communities they know what to do about it,” McGowan said.
“There’s a lot of violence in our communities, there’s a lot of violence online … there’s nothing new about this.
“What the attack on Helen has brought to our mind is, this is us. We can’t just pretend that everything’s OK in the regions and we’re doing fine.”
Haines’s chief of staff, Kaz Rourke, said on Thursday that the team was “devastated” by Monday’s alleged attack.
“Helen is adored by her team. She is a remarkable leader, a truly wonderful boss and someone we all care about deeply,” Rourke said in a statement.
