pollinator pathmaker brings buzzing bees back to berlin with foliage-filled artworks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:10:35 UTC
11:10:35 KST

pollinator pathmaker brings buzzing bees back to berlin with foliage-filled artworks
this algorithmically designed garden, created by artist alexandra daisy ginsberg and commissioned by las art foundation, joins art and computation to support pollinators.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Pollinator Pathmaker and LAS art foundation
In 2023, Pollinator Pathmaker sprouted up in front of the Natural History Museum in Berlin, a project in commissioned in part by LAS art foundation, and has continued to bloom each year since it was planted. Full of asters, foliage, and insects, this work is an algorithmically optimized plot of local plants selected to bring pollinators back to the region. Developed by artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg and originally commissioned for the Eden Project in Cornwall, UK, the project has continued to grow, with both large-scale plots at the Serpentine in London and ‘DIY editions’ that anyone can create.
‘They appear as a garden,’ says LAS art foundation curator Sophie Korschildgen, who was instrumental in bringing Pollinator Pathmaker to the green space in front of the Natural History Museum, ‘but Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg is really consistent about calling them editions and artworks because she wants to take this assumption of value that we have when we speak about art—that it’s something to be preserved, that it speaks for our culture, all of these things—and apply it to nature.’ In conversation with designboom, Korschildgen and artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg speak about bringing to life Pollinator Pathmaker’s first international commission, the evolution of the project, and its impact on wild bee populations.
Painting with a Plant Palette (online)
On the driving force for the project, Ginsberg points out that ‘Pollinator Pathmaker began with a question: what happens when we create an artwork for other species rather than ourselves?’ At pollinator.art, the website that hosts information about Pollinator Pathmaker, visitors are met with the question, ‘If pollinators designed gardens, what would humans see?’ Upon pressing the start button, you’re led to a digital garden plot. Through the menu labeled ‘Your garden,’ you can customize your location, the size of your garden, and other factors to generate an ‘artwork,’ which, as Ginsberg notes, utilizes ‘an algorithm to generate planting compositions that prioritize the needs of pollinating insects over human aesthetic preferences.’
The plants that appear in the artwork come from a ‘Plant Palette,’ a curated selection of local plants chosen to attract the most pollinators, chosen based on research conducted by Ginsberg and pollinator and horticultural experts familiar with the specified region. As new commissions of Pollinator Pathmaker arise, so do the region-specific plant palettes available on pollinator.art. In the years since its inception, Ginsberg points out that it ‘has developed into a long-term, distributed living artwork, with planting compositions realised across Europe, alongside commissioned works in the United States. The artworks have been planted by museums, community groups, members of the public and school children, while the project has also expanded into print, tapestry and video works.’
short documentary on Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg: Pollinator Pathmaker
The edition at the Natural History Museum
‘We came on to Pollinator Pathmaker very early in the process, before it was being planted for the Eden Project in Cornwall,’ says Korschildgen of LAS art foundation, the Berlin-based group dedicated to bringing installations and performances to life in dialogue with technology. ‘We were the first international commissioner and partner on the project. Then we also adapted it to Berlin, but more specifically to the continental biogeographic region, because the UK and Germany are different.’
LAS art foundation, a nomadic organization that brings presentations to different sites, such as Ateneo Veneto di Scienze, Lettere ed Arti in Venice and Kraftwerk in Berlin, partnered with the Natural History Museum in Berlin to bring this edition to life. ‘LAS has a research strand focusing on interspecies futures, originally set up together with the Natural History Museum in Berlin and other partners,’ remarks Korschildgen on the collaboration. ‘It’s a multi-year inquiry that had a symposium that produced a publication that is looking at human-nature relationships, but through technology. It asks the larger question: how can planetary computational technology be developed to benefit the natural world rather than extract from it?’
‘Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg’s project Pollinator Pathmaker was such a beautiful concept in that sense because it’s a global series of gardens that are designed by an algorithm (not an AI, that’s important) to benefit pollinating insects. The human role really changes in the setup because the human is the caretaker of this ecosystem.’
Watching the Berlin editions grow
This year, the project has reached a particularly momentous landmark: ‘we reached our goal of being in every district of Berlin with a small edition—there are 20 DIY editions across the city, and 21 editions including the one in front of the Natural History Museum.’ Since 2023, Berlin has come to life with these lush works and their accompanying pollinator species.
Reflecting on how the project evolves over the years and seasons, Korschildgen mentions that fall is her favorite time to see the edition outside the museum. ‘it’s my favorite time because if you were to go, you would see asters across the whole garden. It’s a type called ‘October Skies,’ which means it blooms lilac in October. Right now, in autumn, is the time when you see this almost algorithmic arrangement and formal strangeness of this artwork. It really catches your eye because there are these streaks of asters across this large plot.’
Human, non-human, and tomato agency
Although Pollinator Pathmaker relies on the natural world to take form, Korschildgen emphasizes that ‘The caretaking part is really deeply inscribed in the concept of this artwork, and it’s quite maintenance-heavy. Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg would say, ‘It’s artificial nature for nature,’ emphasizing how it’s an artificial arrangement. It’s not a garden, and it’s also not plants that would naturally grow with each other in this density under these conditions.’
Although the plot is closely maintained, it isn’t impervious to external factors, such as nature and unintentional human interventions. ‘It’s a place where a lot of people spend time because it has benches and it’s a museum that over a million people visit every year.’ Korschildgen mentions that even if a weed could benefit pollinators, the team still removes it to maintain the original planting plan. ‘Sometimes there are also little plants that just seed out that aren’t part of the original planning. And also, rogue tomatoes! For a couple of years, we had rogue tomato plants that were growing because perhaps people were eating their lunch and throwing the bad tomatoes into the artwork.’
Bringing back the bees
Not only is Pollinator Pathmaker a natural beauty and a thought-provoking installation, but researchers are also studying its effectiveness in bringing pollinators back to areas where humans have pushed them out. ‘There was a study at the Eden Project, and there’s also a study on the one that LAS planted in front of the Natural History Museum. Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg also won a UK research grant two years ago to study the project with the University of Exeter and the University of Edinburgh in a village in Cornwall,’ says Korschildgen, referring to the studies underway.
‘In Berlin, especially, we have a wild bee specialist who analyzes the different wild bee species that come to this garden… The average number in areas of the city that are called ‘pollinator-friendly’ is about 30 to 50 different wild bee species in one place. At the LAS edition last year, there were already 83 different species—quite a bit above the average! The study is looking at wild bees specifically because they are indicator species, meaning that when you can see that wild bees are doing well, then you can also tell that other pollinating populations are doing well.’
Seeing the impact of the project in these tangible data points is an affirmation of the core principles that drove Ginsberg to create the project: ‘By questioning whose needs shape the environments we create, Pollinator Pathmaker challenges the assumption that humans should always be at the center of how we design the world.’
project info:
name: pollinator pathmaker
edition: LAS Edition | @las_artfoundation
location: Museum für Naturkunde (Museum of Natural History), Berlin
artist: Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg
curators: Sophie Korschildgen and Carly Whitefield
dates: June 20, 2023–ongoing
This article is part of designboom’s POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things. These stories rethink our relationship with the planet through interspecies architecture, living materials, regenerative landscapes and emerging technologies – learn more here! Tigray resumes daily life amid fears of wider war

Tigray resumes daily life amid fears of wider war
Mekelle’s reopening offers little relief as instability and economic hardship persist.
Mekelle, Ethiopia- In Mekelle, shops are reopening, and banks are resuming services, but residents remain anxious about what comes next. Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters retook the Tigray regional capital on October 4, as renewed fighting raised fears that the region’s fragile recovery could be derailed once again.
Tigray, in northern Ethiopia, is still recovering from the 2020–2022 war between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the region’s dominant political movement. For residents, the return of fighting has brought new uncertainty over jobs, education, security and the future.
Daily life resumes, but hardship remains.
Businesses and financial services are gradually reopening in Mekelle, but many households are struggling to afford necessities. Delayed salaries have left public employees struggling to cover food, rent and school costs, while years of conflict have depleted family savings.
“Things may be reopening, but that does not mean our problems are over. We still have expenses every day, and without our salaries, it is difficult to know how we will manage,” said Gebregziabher, a public servant in Mekelle.
The funding crisis has affected the wider public sector. In March, Tigray’s interim administration said it could no longer cover monthly salaries for about 137,000 civil servants because expected federal budget transfers had not arrived. In April, the regional finance bureau reported an 8.5-billion-birr (about $52,000) funding shortfall affecting salary payments and development projects.
For many residents, the reopening of businesses offers only a partial return to normality. Without reliable incomes and greater security, everyday expenses remain difficult to manage.
Students fear losing more time
For students in Tigray, renewed fighting has revived fears of another interruption to their education. Many already lost valuable study time during the previous war and worry about falling further behind.
In Adigrat, Shewit, a grade 10 student, said uncertainty about classes and security had left him worried about his future.
“I have already lost so much time because of the war. I am afraid that if our education is disrupted again, I will lose another year and fall further behind,” he said.
Some university students have left Tigray for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, to seek transfers to other public universities. The Ministry of Education announced temporary placements at universities elsewhere in the country for students enrolled at institutions in Tigray. More than 5,000 returning students had applied by September 17–18, according to reporting on the ministry’s programme.
Abel, a third-year student at Axum University, travelled to Addis Ababa to request a transfer.
“I didn’t want to leave, but I also can’t keep putting my education on hold. I came to Addis to see if I can transfer to another university and continue my studies. I just want to finish what I started,” he said.
For students who have already lost years to conflict, the uncertainty means more than interrupted classes. It threatens to delay graduation and make an already difficult path to employment even harder.
Border communities fear a wider conflict
Near the Eritrean border, military movements and conflicting accounts of troop deployments have heightened fears that the fighting could spread beyond Tigray.
On October 8, The Associated Press reported claims by a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government that Eritrean troops had entered Adigrat earlier that week and Idaga Hamus the following day. The AP said it could not independently verify those accounts. The conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED separately reported Eritrean troops crossing the border at Zalambessa.
On October 13, Reuters reported that Ethiopian government forces had advanced into Zalambessa, citing people in contact with residents and other sources. The report said it remained unclear whether Eritrean troops or Tigrayan opposition fighters were still present in the town. The differing accounts underscored the difficulty of establishing control of individual towns as the fighting shifted.
The developments have unfolded amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara. On October 8, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, accused Eritrea of sending troops as far as 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopian territory in several areas of Tigray and appealed to the United Nations Security Council to respond.
Eritrea has denied invading Ethiopian territory. Its government said Ethiopia’s accusations amounted to a declaration of war and called on the Security Council to take action against Ethiopia. The competing claims have raised fears that renewed fighting in Tigray could lead to a direct confrontation between the two neighbours.
Ethiopia and Eritrea fought on the same side during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean forces supported the federal government against the TPLF. Their deteriorating relations have added a regional dimension to the renewed conflict.
In Zalambessa, residents are watching developments with concern. One resident, who declined to be named, said the uncertainty made it difficult to know what to expect in the coming weeks.
An uncertain road ahead
On October 16, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, tasked with restoring public services, helping displaced people return and preparing the region for elections. The announcement followed the federal forces’ takeover of Mekelle and other major towns.
The federal government says the temporary administration will help restore stability and pave the way for elected regional leadership. The TPLF has opposed the federal advance, and it remains uncertain how effectively the new administration will operate across the region.
For residents, the immediate concerns are whether salaries will be paid, schools and health facilities will function, and displaced families will be able to return safely.
In Zalambessa, Gebrehiwot said residents knew from experience what another conflict could bring.
“People are worried because we know what war means for this area. We have already suffered enough, and nobody wants to see things reach that point again,” he said.

Canada's Carney visits Turkey in push to ease US trade dependence
ANKARA, Oct 22 - Prime Minister Mark Carney will meet President Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey on Thursday, marking the first bilateral visit by a Canadian leader, as he seeks to deepen trade with other "middle powers" and ease dependence on the US.
Carney and Erdogan are expected to sign a declaration deepening cooperation in four areas including defense and energy, a person briefed on the matter said.
Carney is on a global trade blitz that he hopes will help buffer Canada from a trade war with the US, where President Donald Trump has applied sweeping tariffs and questioned the neighboring country's sovereignty.
NATO member Turkey seeks new investment and collaboration for its burgeoning defence industry, new nuclear power plants and mining sector.
Carney's office said the visit aims “to position Canada as a key partner in trade and investment".
Although trade between Canada and Turkey is tiny – Turkey accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada’s total merchandise trade or C$4.34 billion ($3.09 billion) – bilateral trade has risen by nearly 50% in the past five years.
“This trip is part of the geopolitical necessity of signaling to Americans that we are not sitting around waiting for them,” said Bessma Momani, professor of political science at the University of Waterloo.
In the last year, Canada has signed more than 20 trade deals as part of Carney’s push to double non-US exports in the next decade. He flew to Beijing in January to reset fractured relations with China, striking a deal that slashed tariffs on electric vehicles and canola.
Despite criticism that China is a security risk, given Canadian authorities previously found China had interfered in at least two federal elections, Carney has described China as a “more predictable” trading partner than the US.
However, Canada still sends nearly 70% of exports to the US.
Turkey's crackdown on the opposition since 2024, and arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community have drawn criticism. But Carney has focused less on rights than predecessors.
“Carney will have to walk a very fine line in Turkey between opening new economic possibilities for Canada while trying to maintain Canada’s middle power role in fighting for equality,” said Anna Agathangelou, a professor of politics at York University.
Ankara says the judiciary is independent, denying that investigations or court cases are politically motivated.
At the NATO leaders' summit in July, Carney and Erdogan launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement, where Turkey also agreed to join Canada’s Defence, Security and Resilience Bank as a founding member.
Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis ATRL.TO as well as South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants.
In 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations. Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkey, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry. REUTERS

What is the FDLR, and why does its anti-Tutsi ideology endure?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:02:55 UTC
11:02:55 KST

What is the FDLR, and why does its anti-Tutsi ideology endure?
Four former FDLR officers reveal how its anti-Tutsi ideology took root and endured in Africa.
Musanze, Rwanda – The Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) was built on an ideology that cast the Tutsi as enemies, according to four of its former senior officers, who say they were taught to hate them long before the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi ethnic group.
“In our history and ideology, Tutsis are referred to as ‘snakes’,” said Anastase Munyaneza, a former FDLR major general.
“The analogy is that if a snake bites you, it injects poison and you die. Therefore, it is better to kill the snake before it bites you.”
The former officers say such ideas were reinforced through Rwanda’s political and military institutions before the 1994 genocide and persisted among those who fled into neighbouring Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), after the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) took control of Rwanda in July 1994.
More than three decades later, the FDLR remains a source of regional security concerns, with its presence in eastern DRC a major point of contention between Kigali and Kinshasa.
Al Jazeera met the four former officers, who defected from the FDLR, returned to Rwanda and underwent rehabilitation at the Mutobo demobilisation centre. Their accounts offer an insight into the origins of the group’s ideology, its development in exile, and the networks that have helped it survive.
Where did the ideology come from?
The roots of the anti-Tutsi ideology described by the former officers stretch back decades, to a period when ethnic identities became increasingly politicised and institutionalised in Rwanda.
In November 1959, a Hutu uprising helped bring about the overthrow of Rwanda’s monarchy. The period was also marked by violent attacks on Tutsis, the killing of hundreds and the forced exile of thousands to neighbouring countries.
Before colonial rule, Hutu and Tutsi identities were shaped by social, political and economic relationships. Under Belgian rule, these distinctions were increasingly formalised. In the early 1930s, the colonial administration introduced compulsory identity cards classifying Rwandans as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, reinforcing distinctions that became increasingly rigid.
By independence in 1962, about 120,000 people, mostly Tutsi, had fled the country. Exiles in Tanzania and Zaire who sought to return staged attacks between 1962 and 1967. According to the United Nations, each incident was followed by retaliatory killings of large numbers of Tutsi civilians in Rwanda, prompting further waves of refugees.
By the end of the 1980s, about 480,000 Rwandans were refugees. President Juvenal Habyarimana argued that population pressures and limited economic opportunities made it difficult to accommodate large numbers of returning Tutsi refugees.
In 1988, exiles in Uganda founded the RPF to secure their repatriation, according to the UN.
Lieutenant Colonel Idrissa Bizimana said the exiles who launched attacks against Rwanda were branded “Inyenzi”, meaning cockroaches.
“When the RPF attacked in 1990, we were told that the same Inyenzi had attacked the country. We grew up being taught to hate them,” he said.
Bizimana said they were also taught at school that the Tutsis had come from Ethiopia and had “ruled through hatred for 400 years”.
The former officers say these narratives were carried into the military, where they shaped how soldiers were taught to view Tutsis and their place in Rwandan society.
Major-General Munyaneza said the Tutsis were rarely found in the army because they were not welcome.
“In the army, we were taught that the Tutsi were our enemy,” he said.
He recalled that soldiers had to seek permission to marry and present their fiancees for approval. If a woman was Tutsi, permission would be denied.
The justification, he said, was that a soldier’s in-laws might visit their daughter in the barracks, potentially gaining access to sensitive military information and “passing it on to the enemy”.
What did the army do in 1994?
The former officers say the ideology they encountered in the military was put into practice during the genocide against the Tutsis in 1994.
Munyaneza said soldiers trained members of the Interahamwe militia, which included men who had retired from, deserted, or been dismissed from the army.
The Interahamwe, the youth militia of the then-ruling National Revolutionary Movement for Development (MRND) party, participated in the massacres alongside the Presidential Guard and the army, according to the UN tribunal for Rwanda.
Bizimana said members of his battalion hated the Tutsis, and took part in the killings.
“During the genocide against the Tutsi, the battalion was actively involved in the genocide in the area where it was deployed,” he said.
The killings began after a plane carrying Rwandan President Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira was shot down over Kigali on April 6, 1994. The incident triggered approximately 100 days of systematic mass killings, according to the UN.
Radio Television Libre des Mille Collines (RTLM) broadcast messages inciting violence against the Tutsis, including calls to eliminate those described as “cockroaches”.
How did the FDLR take root in Congo?
When the RPF took control of Rwanda in July 1994, ending the genocide, former government officials, soldiers and militiamen who had participated in the killings fled into Zaire.
In eastern Zaire, the UN refugee agency reported that former members of the Rwandan Armed Forces (ex-FAR) took effective control of refugee camps, particularly around Goma.
“That was where we resumed our military activities,” Munyaneza said.
The former soldiers and militia members continued to organise militarily in exile. Their subsequent activities and alliances helped lay the foundations for the armed movement that would become the FDLR.
Munyaneza said a decisive alliance emerged in 1998, when Congolese President Laurent-Desire Kabila fell out with his former ally Rwanda.
At the time, former Rwandan soldiers and militia members were fighting under the name Army for the Liberation of Rwanda (ALiR). They reorganised under the FDLR name in 2000.
“Kabila asked us to defeat the Tutsis who had attacked him, promising in return to help us defeat the Tutsi-led government in Rwanda,” Munyaneza said.
What is the FDLR?
Munyaneza said the FDLR was officially established in May 2000 by former Rwandan army commanders and politicians. It was the latest name adopted by armed groups that had been operating in exile since 1995.
“The names changed, but the same people remained involved,” he said.
He said the group’s purpose was “to overthrow the Tutsi-led government that had defeated us”, referring to the Rwandan government established after the genocide.
The FDLR’s formation after the genocide has been central to its leaders’ attempts to distinguish the organisation from the forces that carried out the killings.
In an April 2005 interview with IRIN, a news agency affiliated with the UN, the FDLR’s then-president, Ignace Murwanashyaka, denied that the organisation as a whole had participated in the genocide.
“The FDLR is a very new movement, which appeared six years after the genocide,” he said.
Murwanashyaka did not rule out the involvement of individual members.
“If one of us is responsible for this crime, you have certainly heard the allegations, but no one can say that the entire organisation committed genocide,” he said.
The group’s leadership has also faced legal action over crimes committed in eastern DRC.
On July 13, 2012, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for FDLR military commander Sylvestre Mudacumura, charging him with nine counts of alleged war crimes committed in eastern DRC between 2009 and 2010.
In September 2015, Murwanashyaka and his deputy, Straton Musoni, were convicted by a German court for leading a foreign “terrorist” organisation and aiding war crimes committed in eastern DRC.
Who arms and funds the FDLR?
The former officers say the FDLR has relied on a combination of external support and revenue generated through its activities in eastern DRC.
Munyaneza said the group receives financial and logistical support from the Congolese government.
“To this day, the FDLR maintains close ties with the Congolese government,” he said.
Augustin Nshimiyimana, a former FDLR colonel who served as a brigade intelligence officer and later became responsible for external intelligence, described what he said were close operational links between the FDLR, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) and Wazalendo groups, a broad label for local armed groups operating in eastern DRC.
“The FARDC, Wazalendo and FDLR live together, fight together, occupy the same positions and receive the same uniforms,” he said.
The FDLR also raises money through its own activities, according to Munyaneza. He listed roadblocks, taxes imposed on miners and mine owners, cannabis, timber, charcoal and elephant ivory among the group’s sources of revenue.
These alleged funding networks help explain how the FDLR has maintained its operations over decades in exile. Its access to local resources and relationships with other armed actors have also raised concerns about the links between armed groups and the exploitation of eastern DRC’s natural resources.
In July 2026, the UN Security Council sanctions committee listed FDLR leader Brigadier General Sebastien Uwimbabazi and commander Gustave Kubwayo. The listings cited activities undermining peace and security in the DRC and Kubwayo’s role in the group’s targeting of civilians, kidnapping for ransom and illegal exploitation of natural resources.
Is the ideology still alive?
Efforts to address the FDLR have become a central part of diplomatic attempts to ease tensions between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
In February 2025, the UN Security Council called on the Congolese army to stop supporting armed groups, particularly the FDLR.
Under the United States-brokered Washington Accords, signed in 2025, Kinshasa committed to neutralising the FDLR, while Rwanda committed to lifting its defensive measures.
In July 2026, the Congolese government announced that a faction of the FDLR had signed a protocol on disarmament, demobilisation and cantonment.
Rwanda rejected the arrangement, accusing Kinshasa of attempting to evade its obligations under the Washington Accords to neutralise the group.
The agreement marked a new development in efforts to address the FDLR’s presence in eastern DRC, but its implementation and the extent to which it would lead to the group’s disarmament remained key questions.
Munyaneza said the FDLR continued to deny the genocide against the Tutsi. He argued that, although the organisation’s official political narrative was framed around removing what it described as foreign Tutsi, its underlying intentions were different.
Emilien Mpakaniye, a former FDLR lieutenant colonel who was responsible for securing financial aid at the group’s headquarters in eastern DRC in 2008, said the FDLR had also passed its ideology to Congolese armed groups it trained or allied with, describing the organisation as “a coordinator of armed groups in eastern DRC”.
The former officers’ accounts suggest that the ideology has survived through more than the continued presence of armed fighters. They describe a narrative that was taught in schools, reinforced within the military and carried into exile by men who later helped establish the FDLR.
Whether the group can be dismantled, therefore, is not only a question of disarmament. It also raises questions about the persistence of the ideology that shaped its founders, the networks that have sustained it and its influence on armed groups operating in eastern DRC.
“Officially, the organisation does not say that it intends to kill Tutsis; its political narrative is that it seeks to remove what it describes as foreign Tutsi,” Munyaneza said. “However, among FDLR officers, they know that their mission is to kill Tutsis.”

Trump’s diesel deal derailed Ukraine-Russia peace progress, says Czech president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:02:00 UTC
11:02:00 KST

Czech President Petr Pavel speaks during a press conference at La Moneda Presidential Palace in Santiago on April 16, 2026. | Rodrigo Arangua/AFP via Getty Images
Czech President Petr Pavel says a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine was “quite close” – until President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.
In an interview conducted on Tuesday with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which includes POLITICO, Pavel said coordinated U.S.-European sanctions on Russian oil, oligarchs, and other industries were putting Russia “under strain.” But the deal Trump announced earlier this month, in which Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the U.S., gave Russia “time to breathe.”
“It will be much harder now,” said Pavel. “Russia uses this momentum to get out of pressure, and it’s kind of a moral boost for them.”
Advertisement
The White House on Wednesday said Trump “successfully negotiated” the deal in order to supply the global market with “massive amounts of diesel and bring prices down.”
Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to social media that the deal “plays into Russia’s hands” and allows Russia “to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world.” He accused Trump of using peace talks in Florida as a “smokescreen” as the administration pursued its deal with Russia.
Zelenskyy’s criticism was the latest indicator of rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Trump has repeatedly expressed frustrations with Zelenskyy, accusing him of elongating the war. By contrast, of late he has spoken warmly of Putin and said this week that “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine.”
But Pavel offered the Ukrainian president words of support on Wednesday.
“I believe that President Zelensky and the whole of Ukraine is a victim of a conflict,” said Pavel. “So, I would be probably the last to blame Ukraine for being guilty of the conflict. It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia. It was not Ukraine who was threatening Russia.”
He added that Trump shows a more open approach to Russia than any European leader.
Advertisement
“To some extent, he may be attracted by Vladimir Putin as a leader with authority, but I don’t think that … President Trump sees it from a position of a struggle between democracy and autocracies because he’s looking at it simply from the point of view of economic prosperity for the United States,” Pavel added.
Though Pavel indicated concerns about the diesel deal, he declined to say the U.S. had betrayed Ukraine or other European partners.
“I don’t know yet if we can call it betrayal, but I would call it a mistake,” he said. “Because … it’s now giving Russia a new hope: New hope that they can disregard Europe, they can disregard Ukraine, they can focus on making a deal with the United States, potentially with China, and arranging all things up to their priorities and strategies. I believe that it’s clearly against our interest in Europe.”
Pavel also didn’t rule out a future in which European countries would buy Russian oil, but added that it “will take time” before that happens.
“If one day Russia is a country respecting other countries’ sovereignty and borders, why not have regular business with such a country? But Russia is not there yet,” he said.

Far-right Italian general hunts the manosphere vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

ROME — Former paratrooper General Roberto Vannacci portrays himself on social media as a Roman legionary and charioteer. He has declared he prefers women “without skirts” and posted an AI-generated image of a female junior minister with exaggerated cleavage.
None of these projections of masculinity and anti-woke culture are clumsy gaffes. The insurgent far-right star of Italian politics is making a deliberate play to the so-called manosphere to transform himself from an internet provocateur into a heavyweight political force.
For Italy’s first female prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, Vannacci now poses a serious problem as she needs to decide whether he is an asset or a liability. With elections expected next spring, his National Future party is polling at about 8%, making him a potentially crucial factor in building a right-wing coalition.
Advertisement
“It is disgusting to think you can manipulate the image of a woman for such deplorable propaganda,” the center-right junior minister in Meloni’s coalition whose image was manipulated, Matilde Siracusano, told POLITICO. “I don’t think we have ever sunk this low, especially from someone aspiring to be a national political leader.”
Vannacci’s provocations may look like familiar trolling from a politician who has built his reputation on saying the unsayable. But behind them lies a broader political project, tapping into the grievances of young men who feel alienated by feminism and progressive culture.
Emanuele Pozzolo, a National Future parliamentarian who defected from Meloni’s Brothers of Italy, believes young men have become increasingly constrained in their relationships with women.
“I think young Western men are very often almost castrated in their instinct for dealing with women,” he said, arguing that even legitimate romantic approaches risk being treated as aggression.
“The cultural problem is that sometimes everything seems to be harassment, everything abuse, everything violence,” he added, while stressing that genuine abuse must be punished.
Mediterranean patriarchy
Vannacci combines inflammatory online messaging and an alpha-male persona with a political program that promises to restore traditional roles for men and women. National Future even has a name for its preferred social order: “Mediterranean patriarchy.”
Advertisement
Its political program calls for the formation of “strong men” capable of controlling their emotions and passions, protecting women and sacrificing themselves for society. It opposes the recently introduced crime of femicide, condemns feminism, and declares the defense of life “from conception to natural death” and the “natural family” among its non-negotiable values.
The architect of this vision and principal author of the program is Lorenzo Gasperini, a conservative Catholic philosophy teacher from Tuscany, who has opposed vaccines and abortion rights on social media and blamed feminism for violence against women.
The result is a political offering that combines different traditions: conservative Catholic ideas about family and sexuality, older Italian ideas of virility and the much newer online politics of male grievance.
Giorgia Meloni speaks at a press conference in Prague on Sept. 29, 2026. | Milan Kammermayer/AFP via Getty Images
The manifesto seeks to put traditional family values into practice with proposals to pay parents who leave work to raise children, and reward parents of large families with tax exemption and public sector jobs.
Some proposals echo Benito Mussolini’s fascist-era “Battle for Births,” which offered similar incentives while promoting motherhood as a patriotic duty.
Luca Sforzini, a former Vannacci ideologue who has since broken with him, said the Mediterranean label was a clever piece of marketing.
Advertisement
“It’s like talking about the Mediterranean diet,” he told POLITICO. “You think of Italian food, mozzarella, tomatoes, olive oil.” The result, he said, was to conceal a patriarchal model with men above women behind “bucolic, positive images. It’s monstrous,” he said.
Pozzolo rejected the suggestion that the program advocates for male supremacy.
“It is exactly the opposite,” he said. “When we talk about Mediterranean patriarchy, the main idea is to recover, preserve and pass on the responsibilities of being a man within the family and society.” Men, he argued, had a duty to show women respect, love and protection, while rejecting violence or coercive control.
He defended the “without skirts” remark as “extremely funny” — picking up on a reference to Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani advocating long skirts — and not remotely offensive, comparing Vannacci’s ability to connect with ordinary Italians to Silvio Berlusconi’s.
At a recent rally in the Umbrian city of Orvieto, Vannacci defended the Mediterranean patriarchy concept as not “oppression and possession” but “duty, fidelity, sacrifice,” and said it was the family model that had allowed “us to prevail over the last 2,000 years.”
Elisa Ercoli, president of the women’s rights organization Differenza Donna, condemned the program as “a return to the supremacy of the white, cisgender alpha male, and the woman as his handmaiden.”
Advertisement
Appealing to alphas
Vannacci, who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, became a media sensation in 2023 with the self-published book “The World Upside Down,” a broadside against immigration, feminism and homosexuality. In it, he told gay people: “You are not normal, get over it.”
Lionized by fans as a defender of common sense against progressive politics, he received more than half a million votes as a candidate for the anti-immigration League in the 2024 European elections, before founding National Future in February.
Polling analysis suggests that about 62% of National Future’s prospective voters are male, including strong support among manual workers and the unemployed.
Vannacci speaks during the National Future’s constituent assembly in Rome on June 14, 2026. | Filippo Monteforte/AFP via Getty Images
Pozzolo denied National Future was deliberately targeting male voters, insisting the party’s ambition was to reach Italians of all backgrounds who felt unrepresented.
Federica Formato, a lecturer at Brighton University in the U.K., who studies gender and the far right, said Vannacci was “testing the waters” to see whether he can reach a younger male audience, tapping into what she described as the “aggrieved entitlement” of young men.
A career soldier, he has repeatedly portrayed himself through images of physical strength, competition and military prowess. On social media, AI-generated versions proliferate of Vannacci as an ancient Roman in scenes recalling the Ridley Scott epic Gladiator.
Advertisement
For Formato, the Roman imagery projects “virility and hyper-masculinity,” while Vannacci’s army background itself helps construct the image of an “alpha male.”
Humor, memes and deliberate provocation are particularly effective with a younger online audience, Formato said, allowing relatively complex ideological messages to be reduced to instantly comprehensible images. “He is not naive,” she said. “He says things to provoke and get more attention.”
That presents Meloni with a headache. Vannacci’s party is drawing voters from her Brothers of Italy and Matteo Salvini’s League, while offering a more uncompromising platform on immigration, social issues and foreign policy.
Yet Vannacci has opened the door to an alliance with Meloni if she needs his votes. He has described National Future as a natural partner for the center-right, while insisting that any deal must respect his party’s principles. With Italy’s new electoral law offering a parliamentary majority bonus to coalitions winning at least 42 percent of the vote, those votes could matter.
That presents Meloni with an uncomfortable choice: Keep Vannacci outside the coalition, or bring into her government a movement whose appeal rests partly on the grievances of men who believe feminism has gone too far.
For Formato, Vannacci is exploiting a space in Italian politics that has so far lacked a figure capable of turning those grievances into an organized political constituency.
Advertisement
Vannacci, with his promises to restore traditional masculinity, appears determined to occupy it.

Merz’s eastern nightmare is far from over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The weakened German leader wants to overcome humiliating losses to the far right in eastern elections — but the prospect of the AfD’s biggest win yet haunts his chancellorship.
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz leaves after a press conference on the sidelines of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Friedrich Merz has tried to move on from his conservatives’ historic defeats to the far right in eastern Germany, but his biggest test as chancellor — and of his grip over his own party — may still lie ahead.
The Alternative for Germany is pushing to deliver its biggest blow yet to the chancellor’s weakened coalition government by installing the country’s first far-right state premier since World War II in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt when lawmakers vote on the post in December.
Merz’s fellow Christian Democrats in Berlin fear regional members of their own party will help the AfD do this, creating a nightmare scenario for the chancellor. That concern stems from accusations that a group of Saxony-Anhalt conservatives already broke ranks by voting in a secret ballot for the AfD’s candidate for state speaker earlier this month, outraging national conservative leaders.
Advertisement
“The behavior of the CDU parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt with regard to past and upcoming elections is completely unacceptable,” Thomas Röwekamp, a CDU lawmaker who chairs the Bundestag’s defense committee, said. The AfD “wants to annihilate the CDU in Germany” by “forcing us into a debate about how to deal with it in order to divide the party,” he added. “We must not allow that to happen.”
Under pressure from conservatives in Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt CDU leader Sven Schulze announced a plan last week to have his party’s lawmakers leave the chamber during the initial two rounds of secret voting in December, ensuring none can vote for the far-right candidate — or be suspected of doing so. It’s unclear what the party would do in a potential third round, when the AfD would only need a majority of votes cast.
AfD leaders have openly said they are seeking defections from conservative ranks, a strategy designed as much to sow division among conservatives as to win the premiership. That approach seems to be working, at least partly.
Sven Schulze, outgoing Premier of Saxony-Anhalt and member of the German Christian Democratic Union, attends the first session of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since state elections on October 6, 2026 in Magdeburg. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
State conservatives have faced intense criticism for appearing so divided and vulnerable to aiding the AfD that their leaders apparently have no choice but to avoid the vote altogether. “It’s about taking a stand and assuming responsibility, rather than shirking a decision,” Röwekamp said.
Local CDU lawmakers, however, say their approach is tactically necessary. “We have always drawn a clear line between ourselves and the AfD,” CDU state lawmaker Chris Schulenburg said. “We adhere to the principle of distinguishing ourselves on the basis of substance, but not excluding them [the AfD], because, after all, the party is not currently banned, and its parliamentarians were also democratically elected.”
AfD leaders, meanwhile, have rejoiced in the CDU’s disarray.
Advertisement
“This is nothing less than the CDU’s capitulation,” AfD national co-leader Tino Chrupalla said after the state conservatives announced their plan to leave the chamber. “They’re afraid of elections.”
Centrists flirting with radicals
For Merz, whose approval ratings are at historic lows, his party’s conduct in Saxony-Anhalt — and the prospect of a politically explosive AfD victory in December — are complicating efforts to move past last month’s humiliating election losses in eastern Germany and project renewed control as he attempts to focus on core priorities: backing Ukraine and reviving the economy.
Already, center-left lawmakers have attacked parts of Merz’s party as having failed to learn the lessons of Germany’s history, drawing parallels with the Nazis’ rise to power with conservative help.
The co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party Alice Weidel delivers a statement on October 6, 2026 at the Bundestag in Berlin. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images
After local conservative lawmakers appeared to back the AfD’s candidate for the Saxony-Anhalt speaker earlier this month, Social Democratic Party (SPD) lawmakers in Berlin marched in protest past the Brandenburg Gate to a square where the Nazis carried out book burnings. SPD Defense Minister Boris Pistorius sang the national anthem and called the episode the breaking of a taboo that “we haven’t seen in this form for more than 90 years.”
Conservative lawmakers have retorted in recent weeks by attacking the SPD and Greens for letting their Berlin branches enter coalition talks with the Left — a far-left party rooted in the East German communist party— which won first in the city in last month’s election.
But for Merz and his coalition government, the stakes of the December vote in Saxony-Anhalt are far greater.
Advertisement
How the December vote will unfold remains highly unpredictable. Ultimately, the AfD’s candidate for the premiership, Ulrich Siegmund, could win the post with support from Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht, a small, populist-left party that has expressed openness to working with the AfD and shares its Kremlin-friendly views.
Merz is clearly alarmed by the prospect of CDU lawmakers covertly assisting the AfD — an outcome that could trigger his chancellorship’s greatest political crisis yet.
“People who do things like that — members of parliament who extend a hand — there is no place in the CDU for such a choice, and that will not change,” Merz said earlier this month. “The CDU will never elect extremists to public office or government positions anywhere in Germany.”

Ukraine’s foreign fighters battle Russians — and red tape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Members of a Ukrainian Armed Forces battalion take part in a military training exercise in Kyiv on April 10, 2024. | Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images
KYIV — Jordan O’Brien has fought for Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began, including during the 2022 liberation of Kherson and the 2024 incursion into Russia’s Kursk region. But after years of service, O’Brien says he would warn other foreigners against joining up, citing the bureaucratic problems he has faced.
O’Brien, a New Zealander, complained about red tape and a state apparatus that appears to have little understanding and compassion for people volunteering to fight for a foreign country. If that isn't fixed, Ukraine may have a harder time attracting desperately needed recruits, hampering its effort to continue resisting Russia.
“If Kyiv wants more foreign fighters, it needs to fix the ridiculous bureaucratic bias that screws all of us foreigners over who have already fought for Ukraine,” said O’Brien, who has been sentenced in absentia by Russia to 14 years in prison for fighting alongside Ukraine.
Advertisement
As of August, the defense ministry said some 16,000 foreigners from 72 countries were serving in the Ukrainian armed forces, giving crucial help to a 900,000-strong military that is chronically short of recruits.
The volunteers are facing a looming deadline. The Ukrainian parliament last year passed a law mandating that foreigners serving in the military have to file paperwork by Nov. 10 to get temporary residence permits.
“If nothing changes, then after November 10, a significant number of the foreigners defending Ukraine will technically be in the country illegally,” Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan said in a social media post.
That clashes with the official recruitment information given to foreign volunteers, which says their contract "is the basis for legal long-term stay in Ukraine."
“Even though I can prove I was serving in the Ukrainian army, they still make it impossible for us foreigners; none of them have any respect for people who fight for Ukraine, and they treat us like illegal aliens,” O’Brien said.
“I have been in three different Ukrainian units, and all of them have made mistakes in my military contracts or done them in a way that is not legally correct, so when I go to immigration to apply for the residency that I fought hard for, they ended up giving me a fine that I had to pay on the spot because my information was incorrect in my contract,” O’Brien added.
Advertisement
The Ukrainian military ombudsman's office has fielded more than 300 complaints this year from foreign volunteers and their families related to granting combatant status, early termination of contracts at the soldier’s request and ensuring timely medical care.
In a report for the Washington-based Center for European Policy Analysis think tank, an American volunteer said that neither he nor most of his comrades had received their UBD — the document confirming combat participation that opens the door to veteran status in Ukraine.
Part of the issue is due to an uneven transition from paper identification to digital military IDs that has left out many foreign volunteers.
A study by the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper earlier this year found that language barriers are a big problem, especially for Spanish-speaking Colombians who constitute the largest group of foreign service members. The study also found that if a veteran has been discharged from the Ukrainian forces, they can sometimes face deportation.
Kyiv is waking up to the problem.
“We highly value everyone’s contribution and fully recognize the state’s responsibility to uphold their rights and legitimate interests,” said Liudmyla Kalenchuk, head of the soldiers' rights department in Ukraine’s military ombudsman's office.
Advertisement
Last month, the defense ministry started a working group aimed at improving terms of service, legalization and treatment of foreign soldiers and their families. The Ukrainian parliament is also working on legislation to simplify and extend deadlines to legalize the stay of foreign fighters in the country and lift other bureaucratic burdens.
“Many foreign fighters are unable to complete the process of obtaining a residence permit, as they are carrying out combat missions far from their unit’s base and cannot simultaneously gather the necessary documents and visit the migration service,” said Halan.
Kalenchuk argued that legalization problems are not widespread, but did say there are vulnerable categories of service members — for instance, those who lost their passports while serving, including citizens of Russia, Belarus and South Africa.
Foreign fighters
Ukraine opened its doors to foreign volunteers like O’Brien in the first hours of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, when the country's survival was at stake, said Meaghan Mobbs, president of the R.T. Weatherman Foundation, an NGO helping war veterans and their families.
“No one could have predicted either the extraordinary number of foreigners who would answer that call or that Russia’s war of aggression would continue at this scale for years," Mobbs said. "What began as an emergency wartime mechanism became something much larger and more permanent. The system now has to catch up.”
Russia also recruits foreign fighters, many from poorer countries keen to get cash or Russian citizenship. Its North Korean allies are also fighting alongside Russian forces.
Advertisement
Ukraine offers foreigners a freedom-fighting cause, combat experience, deals worth up to $10,000 per month for dangerous front-line duty and the possibility of quitting the three-year contract after six months of service. The pay is the same as that received by Ukrainian soldiers.
About 8,000 foreign volunteers serve in the ground forces, while the remaining 8,000 are dispersed among the National Guard, special transport service and other units, said Kalenchuk.
In its recruitment information, Ukraine says volunteers should be between 18 and 60 years of age, fit, legally allowed to enter Ukraine, andthat military and combat experience is an advantage. Only people who understand English, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian or Ukrainian are accepted.
The flow of foreign recruits is growing, from some 100 a month in 2022 to 600 a month now. About 40% come from Latin America.
Most come to Ukraine to help fight against Russia, while some add that pay and the opportunity to gain combat experience are also motivating factors, Kalenchuk said.
Ukrainian units have differing abilities to receive, train, communicate with and administer foreign personnel.
Advertisement
“Foreign volunteers themselves also vary enormously in experience, capability and motivation. Ukraine has learned a tremendous amount since 2022 about what makes a foreign volunteer genuinely valuable, and those lessons should shape what comes next,” Mobbs said.
Family complaints
As well as red tape linked to residence status, foreign fighters also complain about not being paid, not being given adequate medical care, the lack of official combatant status that gives social benefits and protections, and inadequate provision of food and military supplies, the military ombudsman's office said.
There is also criticism over how Ukrainian bureaucracy deals with the families of volunteers.
More than 10% of the complaints to the ombudsman’s office come from families requesting official confirmation of whether a volunteer is missing or has been killed in action, Kalenchuk said.
“For me, this is where the shortcomings become very personal. These are mothers, fathers, wives and children whose loved ones traveled thousands of miles to defend a country that was not their own. Some families have told us they feel forgotten after that sacrifice — or even maligned when they ask difficult questions or push for answers. That should never happen,” Mobbs said.
According to her, some families have learned of deaths from fellow soldiers, or via social media, before receiving official notification. Families can spend months navigating military units, ministries, diplomatic missions, identification and repatriation procedures, and compensation and benefits under Ukrainian law without one clear pathway or person responsible for guiding them.
Advertisement
Wounded volunteers are entitled to free medical treatment and a special payout in the event of disability. Families of fallen soldiers receive compensation of 15 million hryvnia (€300,000).
“Grief is difficult enough without having to become an expert in the bureaucracy of a foreign country at war,” Mobbs added.
However, she said there is reason for optimism. The Weatherman Foundation helped organize a meeting between Halan, the deputy defense minister, and families of nine American volunteers who were killed or went missing.
“What mattered to me was that she listened. The families were able to explain directly what had happened to them and where the system had failed them. The ministry is now working on administrative and legislative changes, and we are committed to helping turn those experiences into solutions,” Mobbs said.
The ministry will take this experience into account in its work on supporting foreign military personnel and their families, Halan said.
“They are sons of their own homeland, yet in a moment of crisis, they became brothers to the Ukrainian people and soldiers in the Ukrainian army. Therefore, we have an obligation to ensure that their families receive high-quality support at every stage of their interaction with the Ukrainian state,” Halan added.
Advertisement
Unless the country's approach to foreign volunteers changes, O'Brien said he would warn potential volunteers against signing up.
“The military HR system and the civilian departments need significant change because right now I tell everyone to stay away from Ukraine, because you won't be looked after if anything goes wrong and even with a lawyer on my side it's an uphill battle to do anything,” O’Brien said.
But when asked if he regrets fighting alongside Ukrainians against Russia since 2022, O'Brien said no.
“I joined because Russia is a terrorist regime that needs to be stopped,” he said, adding: “I stay with Ukraine because it is the people that I fight for, not [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy or the government or the departments who continue to fuck us over again and again, but the everyday Ukrainians who just want to live in peace.”

Abdul El-Sayed Michigan US Senate campaign hires Jewish outreach director
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
01:58:00 UTC
10:58:00 KST

Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign for Michigan’s US Senate seat has hired a Jewish outreach director in the final weeks of the election season as it pushes to win over undecided Jewish voters as the contentious race enters its homestretch.
Lenore Goldman is a veteran political consultant with Michigan ties whose work has included One Fair Wage, a national movement to raise the minimum wage that has prompted years of back-and-forth in the Michigan state legislature and courts.
She also consulted on Voters Not Politicians, a 2018 Michigan campaign that successfully passed a ballot measure to create a nonpartisan redistricting commission in the state. She has also consulted for Jewish groups, including the Jewish Community Federation of San Francisco.
Goldman confirmed her hire to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency on Wednesday and said she had been with the campaign since September. The El-Sayed campaign did not immediately authorize her to comment further, but she has already attended some local events hosted by Jewish supporters.
The Democratic candidate’s campaign first told JTA in August that it was interviewing for a Jewish liaison position.
El-Sayed struggling to win over skeptical Jewish voters
Goldman enters the campaign at a precarious moment for El-Sayed, who has struggled to win over skeptical Jewish voters in his tight race with his Republican opponent, former US Rep. Mike Rogers.
Recent polls show a tight race, with El-Sayed holding a narrow advantage. A Marist poll released Wednesday put him ahead of Rogers, 50% to 48% among likely voters, within the survey’s margin of error.
Jews have bristled at the former county health director’s strong criticism of Israel, including when he stated earlier this week that the country is “not an ally.” They have also objected to his campaign’s prior association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, whose remarks about Jews have drawn accusations of antisemitism. El-Sayed has since distanced himself from Piker.
Some Jews have criticized El-Sayed’s initial remarks to this spring’s Temple Israel attack, which he has since apologized for. Rogers called his opponent “anti-Jew” in a JTA interview this week.
El-Sayed reaches out to Jewish Michiganders in new letter
El-Sayed is also circulating a new letter to Jewish Michiganders as part of an effort to warm relations.
“I care deeply about the threat of antisemitism to our communities, and I am committed to protecting all Michigan Jews against hatred and injustice,” El-Sayed writes in the letter, which was shared on social media.
A spokesperson for the Michigan Democratic Party, which is named as a sponsor in the letter, did not respond to JTA requests for comment by press time. The El-Sayed campaign also did not respond to a request for comment about the letter.
In the campaign’s final days, Jewish surrogates for El-Sayed are hitting the pavement hard. A new Jewish canvassing initiative led by the progressive voter-mobilization group Seed the Vote aims to engage voters and boost support for El-Sayed. Seed The Vote is working with the Jewish advocacy groups Bend the Arc Action and IfNotNow.
Most of the Jewish canvassers have come from out of state. One Jewish Michigander who is canvassing, Ronit Wagman, said the activists have sometimes experienced hostility from Jewish households.
“People just don’t want to put themselves on a limb and open themselves up to name-calling,” Wagman, who lives in the Detroit suburb of Oak Park and has canvassed in the nearby, largely liberal town of Huntington Woods, told JTA. “So I’m not too surprised that local Jews don’t really want to door-knock.”
In her own family, Wagman said she has supported El-Sayed for a while, but her parents “took some convincing” to vote for him.
The argument that worked on them, she said, was pulling back from the candidate’s remarks about Israel and the Temple Israel attack. Instead, she asked them to consider the prospect of how Jews would fare long-term under what she described as continued Republican attacks on “constitutional democracy and civil rights.”
“Ultimately, we talked about how Jews have been able to enjoy so much safety and security in America because of the protections offered to all people by our constitution,” she said. “And when you start to erode that, nobody is safe.”
Conversations like the Wagmans’ could prove the tipping point for a Jewish population that largely considers itself liberal but has often been troubled by El-Sayed. Jewish organizers for him have also staged a series of small-room meet-and-greets with progressive politicians who are either Jewish or who have close ties to the Jewish community. These figures have made their own pitches for the Senate candidate.
One of those surrogates, Jewish Illinois congressional candidate Daniel Biss, spoke to about 50 people at a private Jewish residence in Detroit on Monday. Goldman also attended the event.
Biss was targeted by far-left activists during his own primary this spring, some of whom accused the candidate of being AIPAC-aligned himself. In fact, he is backed by the liberal Zionist lobby J Street, and he fended off millions in spending that the pro-Israel group dropped in favor of an opponent.
Yet Biss told JTA he had no qualms about supporting El-Sayed, some of whose followers have targeted Jewish Democrats in the state in similar fashion.
“I don’t think it is ever healthy to associate any leader with the ugliest thing that anyone who supports them does,” Biss told JTA. “I absolutely never saw anything like that from Abdul himself.”
He continued, “It is possible to fight for Jewish safety in America with a variety of different positions on foreign policy. I think if we don’t accept that, we make ourselves vulnerable unnecessarily.”
He also told the group that some Jewish concerns about El-Sayed were misplaced, particularly about his language around AIPAC, which spent heavily against El-Sayed in his primary.
The lobbyists also spent heavily against Biss in his own primary and, according to Biss, are fair game for criticism because they used pernicious tactics to hide their ad spending and paid for ads that often obscure their pro-Israel motivations.
“To be a little bit cheeky, I would say you can’t perform an antisemitic trope and then accuse me of antisemitism when I describe the thing you just did,” Biss told the Jewish crowd.
AIPAC announced Wednesday that it would cease endorsing and soliciting donations for its preferred candidates, though its associated super PAC, United Democracy Project, would continue operations. The New York Times reported Wednesday that the lobbyist planned to spend up to $9 million in Rogers's favor in the race’s final weeks.
El-Sayed will campaign in Detroit this weekend with former US president Barack Obama. He and Rogers face off in their final scheduled debate tonight.

The perfect artwork would show us everything we need to see in both the world and the self. Its incredible beauty would offer us the truth in whole, through a display of overwhelming honesty. It would be so free of flaw that it could be examined for an eternity without ever finding any means of improving it. It would be in every aspect as dynamic and vital as the creation it represents. It would, in this way, be a perfect being.
Were we to encounter such a being, we would not recognize it. It would seem to us far less than it actually is. We might appreciate it in a limited way, but we could not fully understand it. Our lack of understanding would cause us to take it for granted. We would give it only some of our attention before cordoning it off to one corner of the mind. Its impact would be limited not by its flaws but by our own.

The Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar denied allegations of immigration fraud in a Wednesday appearance on MS Now, her first interview since federal agents raided her residence last week.

Russia and Ukraine trade strikes overnight as Moscow signals readiness for peace talks
Russia and Ukraine traded major drone and missile strikes on each other's capitals overnight, hours after Moscow signalled readiness to resume US-mediated peace talks. President Donald Trump said negotiations were closer than ever to ending the war, though the Kremlin expressed doubts over Ukrainian and European proposals.
Russia and Ukraine traded major attacks overnight with Moscow's mayor saying on Thursday that 630 drones had been launched towards the region, shortly after a US envoy held talks with the Russian president in Saint Petersburg.
It was "the closest we've been" to ending the war, US President Donald Trump said after his envoy Steve Witkoff's meeting with Vladimir Putin on Wednesday.
The Kremlin indicated it was "in principle" open to the resumption of trilateral talks between the two sides with the United States.
But attacks did not let up in the wake of the visit, with Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko posting on social media that strikes had wounded 15 people in the Ukrainian capital, eight of whom needed hospitalisation.
He said in a separate post that strikes had damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said had restricted traffic between parts of the city.
Ukraine's Airforce posted a warning in the early hours of "more ballistic missiles towards Kyiv" and instructed residents to stay in shelters.
The Russian attacks on Ukraine killed one man in Sumy and a woman in Kharkiv, both in the northeast, as well as three people in southeastern Zaporizhzhia and two in the eastern region of Donetsk, authorities said
Hours after the strikes, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X on that "appeasement, servility and flattery" would not stop Russia's war.

Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that two people had been wounded during mostly intercepted barrages of 630 drones headed towards the region, 163 of which were approaching the capital city.
Witkoff had flown to Russia from a meeting with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, which was aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between Trump and the Ukrainian leader.
Witkoff praised Putin as a "humanitarian" for freeing US citizen Stephen Hubbard, but the Kremlin warned after the meeting that while Moscow was "in principle" willing to restart talks there was little "substance" in Ukrainian and European peace proposals the US diplomat had delivered.

Trump returned to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours – but more than a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands of people killed as Russia's advance grinds on.

Deadly strikes
In Ukraine, Zelensky said that Kyiv also backed resuming trilateral talks.

Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and maintained that Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
Witkoff's ninth meeting with Putin came as Russia continued to strike Ukrainian cities ahead of winter.
Kyiv said Russian attacks killed at least four people on Wednesday – including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
Russian occupation authorities in the Lugansk region, meanwhile, said a Ukrainian drone strike on a phone company had killed two people.

Qatari mediator Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi had said on Tuesday that diplomatic efforts are ongoing to de-escalate regional tensions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that “Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance.”

Heeding ‘agreed arrangements’

‘Almost looks fake’: two Sydney beaches closed after whale carcass washes up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
01:31:15 UTC
10:31:15 KST

A whale carcass has forced the closure of two busy swimming and surfing spots after washing up between Coogee and Maroubra beaches in Sydney – but there are no plans to remove it.
The whale’s heavily decomposed body was found on Thursday morning at Lurline Bay, a rocky cove surrounded by cliffs in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.
It’s believed to be a juvenile humpback.
Local council said nearby Coogee and Maroubra beaches would be closed until further notice to protect oceangoers as whale carcasses have been known to attract sharks.
“We have cordoned off the area to leave this creature in peace and safe from the attention of people,” Randwick Council mayor, Dr Clare Willington, told reporters.
The council has also contacted Surf Life Saving about introducing extra drone patrols, but Willington said it was a precaution as there had not yet been reports of an increase in shark activity.
Willington said there were no plans to remove the whale and that staff were working with Gamay Rangers about a culturally and environmentally sensitive approach to take.
“This is a natural occurrence and in time nature will deal with the carcass,” Willington said.
The Gamay Rangers are an Indigenous ranger team who undertake natural and cultural resource management activities like protection work, conservation, and threatened species management in the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council area.
The whale is an important totem animal to the local Bidjigal people, and Gamay Rangers manager Robert Cooley said previous instances where beached animal carcasses were taken to landfill had distressed his community.
However, Cooley said he was not “super confident” the rising tide would return the carcass to the sea.
“We’re got a reasonably strong north-east wind here and a bit of a swell pushing it back up – so that’s going to be a challenge,” he said.
“We’ll just have to wait and see what happens but the animal is in a pretty advanced stage of decomposition, so if it did go out into the ocean, I don’t think it would take long for nature to break it down.”
If intervention is necessary, the rangers would be discussing plans with cultural advisers, he said.
The whale is believed to be a young humpback, but it is difficult to confirm due to its state of decomposition, Cooley said.
The carcass was first spotted on Wednesday in Sydney’s northern beaches near Manly, where attempts were made to tow it out to sea, which is why there are pieces of rope found with the whale.
The council is encouraging residents and visitors to avoid the area and follow directions from lifeguards and authorities.
It comes as authorities are working to free a large whale found stuck in shallow waters off Turners Beach on Tasmania’s north-west coast.
“Members of the public are asked to avoid the area and not enter the water on the incoming tide due to the anticipated danger,” Tasmanian police said.
‘Almost looks fake’
Curious locals have stopped by Lurline Bay throughout the morning to try catch a glimpse of the whale.
Meeri Pajala, an au pair from Finland who is living in Sydney, said she had never seen anything like this before.
“It almost looks fake to me,” she said. “That skin looks so weird.”
Glenda, a local who did not want her full name published, says she usually watches whales swimming by the coast and was curious when she heard the news.
“My interest is in if it’s newborn, or if it’s juvenile,” she said. “I thought it would be more complete.”
It was nudging up against the rocks as the waves ebbed and flowed but had become stuck in a crevice due to low tide.
To the surprise of many onlookers, it doesn’t seem to have a smell.
