Staff say jobs are moving offshore as NAB sheds workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:59:52 UTC
08:59:52 KST

NAB staff speak out after mass job cut announcement
In short:
Entire teams of National Australia Bank workers are having to reapply for their jobs and compete among themselves as part of a major restructure.
Staff say the writing was on the wall as they witnessed the bank pushing to offshore workers and take up AI.
What's next?
The major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June next year, with 1,500 expected to be out the door before Christmas.
National Australia Bank (NAB) workers have accused the banking giant of a "spill and fill" redundancy strategy, forcing entire teams to reapply for their positions as part of a sweeping restructure.
Earlier this week the major bank revealed plans to slash 2,500 roles by June, including 1,500 before Christmas.
This is about 6 per cent of its total workforce, with corporate roles bearing the brunt.
Several workers who spoke to the ABC on condition of anonymity said the writing was on the wall as the bank pushed the uptake of AI and moved work offshore.
"Until today, it's been a lovely place to work," said Dylan*, who has worked in NAB's technology team for a decade but learnt he could be unemployed by the end of the year.
His team will have to reapply for their jobs in what is known as a "spill and fill" type of workforce restructure, where existing roles are made vacant and current employees have to fight for a smaller number of positions.
There is a two-week consultation period for Dylan's team and, for those being shown the door, their last day will be December 2 or 17.
NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine said in a note to staff he encouraged colleagues to be "thoughtful" and check in on one another, and indicated support would be offered to those "impacted personally".
The bank said in an ASX announcement that the mass redundancies, which are estimated to cost the bank about $300 million in restructuring costs, were part of "actions to simplify its operating model and better align its workforce to prioritise growth and technology initiatives for customers".
The bank declined to comment to the ABC on staff members' claims.
Jobs offshored
The looming redundancies have sparked serious concerns about offshoring among staff, as the banking heavyweight bolsters its Indian and Vietnamese headcount while it cuts staff based in Australia.
A leaked workforce plan seen by the ABC shows Dylan's team in technology, which consists of just under 500 people, is currently 53 per cent Australian-based.
The rest are based in NAB's offices in India (14 per cent), Vietnam (13 per cent), or are external contractors.
But, under the plan, the number of staff would be reduced to 400 by the 2027 financial year while the percentage of offshore workers would increase.
The Australian-based workforce would be cut to 40 per cent, with the Indian and Vietnamese offices upping their numbers to 30 and 20 per cent respectively.
James* resigned last Friday, just days before NAB announced it was going to slash staff, because of fears about the longevity of his business banking role.
He shared an email NAB sent in March, which stated the bank would be "expanding out teams in NAB India" to help in its goal of "focusing on digitising and simplifying processes, including increasing automation to speed up turnaround time" and "investing in our global teams".
James said the messaging in NAB had changed so drastically in the past six months that he no longer felt safe in his job and had left the banking industry.
"People are feeling the anxiety," he said, adding that he had moved to a service-based industry because, "I can't be replaced realistically for the next five to 10 years."
AI concerns
AI is also an issue on everyone's lips.
While there was no direct reference to AI, NAB did refer to "rapid technological change" in its announcement to the market and experts say its impact is clear.
MST Financial analyst Brian Johnson said that for a long time it was politically unacceptable to essentially replace people with AI.
"We're probably approaching the point where it becomes more politically palatable to actually shed staff than perhaps it was even six months ago,"
he said.
"Technology will supplant a lot of functions at jobs. You can just do things better and faster."
Recruiter Clinton Marks from Robert Half said bank redundancies in 2026 appeared to be driven more by cost-cutting and organisational restructuring than direct AI replacement, despite growing pressure on executives to find productivity gains through technology.
Mr Marks said C-level managers were "under great pressure to reduce cost" and that "AI [is] an answer to those questions".
However, he said most organisations were not ready for large-scale AI deployment and he was not yet seeing workers replaced by the technology.
Instead, Mr Marks said, recent redundancy rounds were largely about reducing costs and streamlining operations, while demand remained strongest for workers with skills in cyber security, governance, risk, compliance and AI adoption.
'Wrecking ball'
The union representing bank employees said it was appalled by NAB's redundancy plans and dubbed it a "wrecking ball" to hit staff with the news so close to Christmas.
"Cutting 6 per cent of a workforce will not simplify NAB's operating model or better align its workforce to prioritise growth," Finance Sector Union (FSU) national assistant secretary Nicole McPherson said.
"It will wreak chaos and entrench a culture of anxiety at a bank that seems hell-bent on self-destruction.
"To take a wrecking ball to 6 per cent of one of Australia's largest workforces this close to Christmas is disgraceful and shows that NAB's leadership is completely detached from the lived experience of their workers."
Australian banks, large and small, have been cutting their workforces, with a major restructure at ANZ leading to thousands of job losses in the past year.
Last month, Bendigo and Adelaide Bank proposed cutting 137 jobs as part of an ongoing restructure.
The FSU has also said it had already seen 1,000 jobs cut so far this year at the Commonwealth Bank.
At the Commonwealth Bank's annual general meeting last week, the FSU asked if it could receive assurances workers' jobs were safe, prompting the bank to say there was "no ability to give a blanket commitment", adding that "AI is changing and complementing the way we work".
* Names have been changed to protect workers from potential negative repercussions.

Airbnb scraps check-out chores for guests under new rules

The changes announced on its website apply to bookings made on or from November 20.
What's next?
Some Airbnb hosts have reacted angrily to the changes, with several threatening to move to other booking platforms or change their prices.
Airbnb guests will no longer have to strip beds, wash dishes or remove rubbish when checking out, under new rules to be introduced next month.
The changes have sparked anger among hosts, with some warning the crackdown could drive up costs and push smaller operators off the platform.
The short-term rental platform announced the changes on its website. They apply to reservations booked on or after November 20.
The changes come amid complaints from some travellers about being charged cleaning fees, which can cost hundreds of dollars, while also being expected to complete a list of chores before leaving a property.
The company said while cleaning fees would not be abolished completely, hosts could not require guests to perform tasks that took "significant time and effort or would normally be done by a cleaner".
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb said in a statement.
"So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
Hosts can still ask guests to complete simpler tasks, such as placing used dishes in the sink and gathering used towels.
They will also continue to set their own cleaning fees.
Changes spark anger from hosts
Hundreds of hosts have criticised the new rules on Airbnb's online community forum.
Townsville Airbnb host Nadia Di Martino, who operates three listings from her Kirwin home, said the changes were "infuriating".
"I think that many hosts will either have to increase their prices and then pay someone else to do the whole cleaning," Ms Di Martino said.
She said she did the cleaning herself and did not charge guests a cleaning fee, but asked them to wash their dishes before checking out.
"I don't think it's unreasonable,"
she said.
She said she understood why Airbnb had acted, because some hosts had imposed excessive check-out chores.
But she said she was now considering leaving the platform and renting her rooms to students instead, or would ban the use of cooking facilities.
"I think that I would rather probably just … have permanent flatmates. I think it will be more comfortable for me," she said.
Kendra, a host from South Carolina in the US, warned the policy could drive smaller hosts away from the platform and increase costs for guests.
"It's going to incentivise soulless, basic rentals and raise cleaning and liability costs that guests will ultimately bear the burden of," she said.
Mindy, from New Mexico, accused Airbnb management of being "so out of touch with the people cleaning vacation rentals", while Becky, from Canada, said she had "never been so upset by a policy change".
What does it mean for Australian travellers?
The changes apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform's global policy, including bookings in Australia.
Hosts will still be able to set house rules, including check-in and check-out times, limits on the number of guests, smoking restrictions, pet rules and quiet hours.
Airbnb said guests were still expected to leave properties in a reasonable condition and may be held responsible for damage or excessive cleaning caused by their stay.

the hidden landscape of the digital world: what it takes to keep technology running
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:55:56 UTC
08:55:56 KST

the hidden landscape of the digital world: what it takes to keep technology running
as computational demand grows, architects, engineers, and designers face a more fundamental question: how can technology evolve without deepening its dependence on finite resources?
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
the ‘cloud’ is physical: the hidden infrastructure behind digital life
The digital world is often described as immaterial, a space of information that moves invisibly between devices and across networks. The term ‘cloud,’ for instance, suggests an ethereal space where data like photos, images and more can be stored without occupying any tangible place. In reality, though, these files reside on physical servers housed in data centers, supported by networks, cooling systems, and energy infrastructure. Every search, video stream, and artificial intelligence query depends on systems that consume energy, water, land, and raw materials. From mineral extraction and semiconductor manufacturing to data centers and electronic waste, the infrastructure behind digital life has a substantial environmental footprint.
As demand for computation increases, we need to reconsider how these systems are designed and what their growth requires from the planet and humanity. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centers consumed approximately 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025. The agency projects that this figure could approach 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, driven in part by the expansion of artificial intelligence and other computationally intensive services. These figures reveal the growing physical demands behind technologies that are often presented detached from material reality. They also raise a fundamental question: can the digital economy become more sustainable if the infrastructure supporting it continues to expand?
the material origins of computation
The environmental footprint of digital technology begins before a device is switched on. Smartphones, computers, servers, and networking equipment depend on minerals extracted, processed, and transported through global supply chains. Copper carries electricity and data through physical networks, while other metals and specialized materials are used in circuit boards, batteries, and semiconductor components. Their extraction can require substantial energy and water, while mining and processing can disrupt landscapes and generate pollution. Electrification, transport, and renewable energy systems depend on mineral-intensive supply chains. However, the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure adds another source of demand, particularly as data centers require large quantities of servers and supporting equipment.
Semiconductor manufacturing introduces another layer of environmental complexity. Producing advanced chips involves highly controlled industrial environments, energy-intensive processes, and significant water requirements. A 2023 study examining environmental disclosures from 28 semiconductor companies reported approximately 789 million cubic meters of water withdrawals and 149 billion kilowatt-hours of energy consumption across the companies surveyed. These figures do not represent the entire global semiconductor industry, but they illustrate the scale of the resources involved in manufacturing the components that make modern computing possible.
data centers as physical architecture
Data centers house the servers that store and process the information we access every day. They require a lot of supporting infrastructure, from backup power systems to cooling equipment that prevents the machines from overheating. Where these facilities are built matters. Their location affects the availability of electricity and water, while the design of their cooling systems influences how much of each resource they consume. As more data centers are built to meet growing demand, their impact on local infrastructure becomes harder to ignore. Cooling is particularly important because computing equipment converts much of the electricity it uses into heat. That heat must be removed to maintain reliable operating conditions, creating an additional energy demand. Depending on the facility and its climate, cooling may rely on mechanical refrigeration, air-based systems, liquid cooling, or combinations of different technologies.
Even if a data center uses energy efficiently, it can still put pressure on the local electricity grid or consume water that is already in demand by nearby communities. The impact depends partly on where the facility is built and what resources are available there. A cooling system that works well in one location may be less suitable in another, particularly in areas where water is scarce. The location of a data center, its energy supply, and the way it is cooled are just as important as the technology inside it. These decisions are often made long before the servers start running, but they can determine how the facility affects its surroundings for years to come.
when efficiency is not enough
More efficient servers and cooling systems can reduce the energy needed to run a data center, but they do not necessarily reduce its total consumption. As computing capacity grows and new applications emerge, demand can rise faster than efficiency improves. This is particularly relevant to artificial intelligence, which requires computing power both to train models and to run them for users. As these services become more widely available, the amount of computation they require increases, even as the hardware becomes more efficient.
A data center may use less electricity to process each request but still consume more energy overall if it handles many more requests. The distinction matters when assessing the environmental impact of digital technology. Efficiency gains are useful, but they tell only part of the story. Total electricity consumption, water use, and demand on local infrastructure also need to be considered. The same applies to renewable energy. Using renewable electricity can reduce emissions associated with the power supply of a data center, but it does not address every part of its environmental footprint. The facility still requires land, construction materials, servers, and cooling systems, while the manufacture and eventual disposal of its equipment carry their own costs.
water, heat, and the possibilities of reuse
Water consumption is one of the most widely discussed environmental concerns surrounding data centers, particularly in regions already facing water shortages. Some facilities rely on water-based cooling to prevent servers from overheating, although consumption varies depending on the cooling system, climate, and operating conditions. Choosing where to build a data center is closely tied to the availability of local resources. Cooling systems also involve trade-offs. Air-based cooling, liquid cooling, and other approaches differ in their energy requirements, water consumption, and operating costs. No single solution works best in every setting, making local climate and resource availability important factors in the design of these facilities.
Heat is another part of the equation. Data centers generate large amounts of waste heat, which is usually removed from the building and released into the environment. In some cases, this heat can be recovered and used to warm nearby buildings or supply district heating networks, turning an operational by-product into a potential energy source. A 2024 study examined the potential for integrating data center waste heat into a district heating system in Italy. In the modeled scenarios, recovered heat supplied between 12 and 59 percent of the district heating mix, while gas consumption fell by approximately 11 to 58 percent. These figures represent modeled outcomes rather than measured savings from an operating facility, but they illustrate the potential benefits of connecting data centers to existing heating infrastructure. Unlike cooling, which is primarily concerned with managing the heat generated by servers, heat recovery looks at how that energy might be put to use. Its feasibility depends on factors such as the temperature of the recovered heat, the distance to potential users, and whether demand for heating coincides with its availability.
the problem of electronic waste
The environmental cost of digital technology continues after equipment leaves service. Servers, computers, phones, and networking hardware contain materials that can be recovered, but they also include components and substances that make safe processing difficult. When electronics are discarded without appropriate collection and treatment, valuable resources are lost and harmful materials can enter the environment. The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reported that the world generated 62 billion kilograms of electronic waste in 2022. Only 22.3 percent of that total was documented as formally collected and recycled in an environmentally sound manner. The report projects that global e-waste could reach 82 billion kilograms by 2030.
Data centers regularly replace servers and other equipment to meet performance and reliability requirements. Newer hardware can process more information using less energy per task, but manufacturing it also requires new materials and energy. Whether replacing older equipment reduces the overall environmental impact depends on how much energy is saved during operation and what it takes to produce the replacement. Keeping equipment in use for longer can help reduce the need for new hardware. Servers that can be repaired, upgraded, and maintained are less likely to need replacing as soon as their performance begins to fall behind. When equipment reaches the end of its useful life, recycling can recover some of its materials for future use, although recycling alone does not address the resources required to manufacture new devices in the first place. Extending the life of working equipment, repairing components where possible, and recovering materials when equipment can no longer be used all have a role in reducing electronic waste.
designing for a less extractive digital future
Reducing the environmental impact of digital technology involves more than making servers faster or data centers more energy-efficient. It also means looking at where facilities are built, how they are cooled and powered, how long equipment remains in use, and what happens to it when it is replaced. Recovering waste heat, using renewable electricity, and designing equipment that can be repaired or reused can all help, but their benefits depend on how these measures are put into practice.
For architects and designers, data centers raise questions that go beyond the buildings themselves. Their energy and water needs affect the places where they operate, while their construction and equipment depend on materials sourced from elsewhere. Decisions about location, infrastructure, and maintenance can have consequences long after a facility is built. There is also the question of how much computing we actually need. As artificial intelligence and other digital services continue to expand, improving efficiency will not necessarily reduce overall resource use. The growing demand for computation deserves as much attention as the technologies developed to meet it. The cloud may feel distant from the physical world, but its infrastructure is not. It exists in mines, factories, warehouses, power stations, and data centers, all drawing on resources and leaving an environmental footprint. Recognizing this is a starting point for thinking differently about digital technology, not as something separate from the environment, but as part of it.

US accuses Canada of election interference ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:52:21 UTC
08:52:21 KST

US accuses Canada of election interference ahead of midterms
Washington cites Canadian tariffs, political meetings and anti-Trump ads as evidence of attempted election interference.
The United States has accused Canadian politicians of trying to influence its midterm elections, pointing to Canada’s efforts to push back against President Donald Trump’s tariff campaign.
In a fact sheet released on Wednesday, the US embassy accused Canada of being dismissive of its allegations of election interference.
“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the fact sheet reads.
The two countries have been locked in a trade war since the start of Trump’s second term in 2025, with Canada responding to US tariffs with import taxes of its own.
But the US embassy identified public statements about the tariffs as being attempts to sway the November 3 midterm election.
Among the politicians singled out in the fact sheet was Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly. The fact sheet pointed to comments Joly made in August about responding to Trump’s tariffs.
“We’re also targeting products that will target states in the US. And so we’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” Joly said at the time.
The embassy also took issue with Joly’s meetings with Democratic officials in Boston and Chicago in September. When asked by a reporter what she thought might happen with regard to tariffs if Democrats won the midterms, she said, “That’s exactly why I’m meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates.”
Joly has rejected the suggestion that her actions could amount to interference, saying Canada would never meddle in US elections. She said her meetings with US politicians, both Democratic and Republican, were about building Canada’s economy.
“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the US is to attract investments,” she told reporters on October 14.
The embassy also pointed to Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s calls for retaliatory measures on US products, as well as his government’s advertising campaign against Trump’s tariffs, launched last year.
The campaign, which featured clips of former US President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs in a 1987 radio address, prompted Trump to call off trade talks with Canada in October 2025.
While the embassy laid out several examples of Canadian officials trying to influence US trade policy, it didn’t explain how those efforts amounted to interference.
Other instances of alleged election interference included Liberal MP Anthony Housefather saying he had campaigned in Florida on behalf of Democratic Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, ahead of her primary election in August.
The fact sheet also accused individual Canadians of illegally participating in US elections, naming 11 people who had been charged or sentenced for voting between 2012 and 2024.
The sheet did not, however, present any evidence linking those citizens to a Canadian government effort to involve itself in US elections.
“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way,” the US embassy’s statement said. “Americans decide America’s elections.”
The fact sheet comes a week after US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said Washington was closely watching Canada for signs of interference ahead of the midterms.
“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it,” Hoekstra said in a podcast interview on The Really Big Show, according to The Canadian Press.
The US and Canada have long been allies, but relations have frayed since Trump returned to office.
Not only has the Republican leader triggered a trade war with Canada, but he has also repeatedly threatened to make Canada a 51st state.
There have also been reports that separatist leaders from Alberta had sought support from Trump administration officials ahead of a failed referendum on the province’s independence this week.
Ahead of Monday’s provincial vote, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed concerns about potential US interference in the referendum, saying Canada expected foreign governments to stay out of its elections.
“Our expectation is, to be absolutely clear, on foreign governments, United States included, is we don’t get ourselves involved in their elections, they don’t get themselves involved in our elections,” he told Global News.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Prime Minister’s Office and Global Affairs Canada for comment, as well as the office of Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Industry Minister Joly.

What happened during Witkoff and Kushner’s latest meeting with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:52:00 UTC
08:52:00 KST

What happened during Witkoff and Kushner’s latest meeting with Putin
The latest round of negotiations comes amid growing concerns in Kyiv the US is backing away from its support of Ukraine.
United States special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have wrapped up their latest meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin with the release of a retired American teacher from Russian custody.
On Wednesday, Witkoff visited with Putin at the Constantine Palace in Saint Petersburg, while Kushner attended virtually.
The two special envoys have taken a leading role in conflict negotiations under US President Donald Trump. Their last meeting with Putin came during a trip to Moscow in September.
The latest talks come as the Trump administration intensifies its efforts to secure a peace deal to end Russia’s nearly five-year-long war against Ukraine. The war began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of the Eastern European country in February 2022.
But there are growing concerns in Kyiv that the Trump administration is backing away from its support of Ukraine.
Trump has fostered warm relations with Putin, and critics fear that he may be willing to yield to Russian demands to reach an agreement that would end Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.
Here’s what took place during the meeting:
Putin agrees to resume peace talks with Ukraine and US
The Russian president agreed on Wednesday to resume US-mediated peace negotiations with Ukraine for the first time in months.
A US official told Al Jazeera that Witkoff and Kushner proposed a “trilateral meeting at the technical level” that would focus on guaranteeing the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war had ended. The Ukrainians accepted the meeting when they met with the Americans on Tuesday in Oslo, Norway.
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February, just days before the US and Israel launched their war against Iran.
The Kremlin, according to the Reuters news agency, said the new talks with Ukraine and the US may take place in Abu Dhabi and could start as soon as next month.
Russia frees retired US teacher
Wednesday’s meeting began with a goodwill gesture from Russia: the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher who has been held in Russia for more than four years.
Hubbard, 74, was arrested in 2022 and sentenced to more than six years in a Russian prison after he was accused of being a Ukrainian mercenary. The US has argued the former teacher was wrongfully detained.
Trump, who made a direct appeal to Putin for Hubbard’s release, posted on social media Wednesday that Russia did not ask for a prisoner swap “out of respect for” him.
A US official said Trump spoke with Hubbard by phone and reiterated his “unwavering commitment” to bringing home all Americans who are wrongfully detained abroad.
Hubbard is headed back to the US where he will be reunited with his family.
Putin called a ‘humanitarian’
Witkoff has faced growing criticism after calling Putin a “humanitarian” for his decision to release Hubbard.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Witkoff said to Putin during Wednesday’s meeting. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
That praise for the Russian president sparked bipartisan backlash from US lawmakers and human rights activists, who pointed to accusations of severe human rights abuses under Putin’s leadership.
“WTF, Steve?” US Senator Thom Tillis replied in astonishment on social media. Tillis, a member of Trump’s Republican Party, continued by writing that Witkoff should look up the definition of “humanitarian”.
“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” he said. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian’.”
Tillis’s Senate colleague, Republican John Cornyn, echoed those thoughts.
“Putin is stone cold killer,” he wrote in response to Witkoff’s remarks.
US Senator Mark Kelly, who serves on the US Senate Intelligence and Armed Services Committees, also blasted Witkoff, calling Putin a “war criminal”.
“In what world is Putin a ‘humanitarian?’ He’s assassinated political rivals and journalists, bombed hospitals, and started a war that has intentionally killed tens of thousands of innocent people, including women and children,” Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, said.
But members of the Trump administration defended Witkoff amid the outrage. During a visit to his home state of Ohio, Vice President JD Vance argued that Witkoff had “a job to get done”. He indicated that complimenting Putin likely aided the negotiations.
“I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage,” Vance told reporters.
At a White House event on Wednesday, Trump said Witkoff’s characterisation of Putin was a “good saying” for “that particular purpose”: to release Hubbard.
“But I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other,” the US president said.
Trump, Putin and Xi meeting gains steam
The Kremlin said a possible meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was discussed during Wednesday’s negotiations.
Russian officials said that, if the meeting is confirmed, it could take place next month on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.
“Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday.
“No specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting.”
The three leaders have never before met for a dedicated trilateral visit.

Cargo throughput of Pinglu Canal surpasses 1 mln tonnes in S China's Guangxi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:51:55 CST
08:51:55 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 21, 2026 shows cargo vessels passing through the Madao hub on the Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Cargo throughput of the Pinglu Canal has surpassed 1 million tonnes since its opening to navigation on Sept. 16.
The 134.2-kilometer canal runs from Nanning, capital of south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. It is the first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. (Xinhua/Zhou Hua)

Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment — Vatican

Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment — Vatican
October 22, 2026
Pope Leo XIV will not require further cancer treatment, his doctors announced on Wednesday, after the pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer last week.
The Vatican cited the pope's doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora, as saying the pope's disease was localized and that "no further treatment" was necessary.
This confirms earlier prognoses suggesting the pope's cancer was caught early.
Pope Leo last week underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on October 13 at Rome's Gemelli hospital.
What did Pope Leo's doctors say about his health condition?
The 71-year-old pontiff's doctors said the final histopathology and molecular testing reports on the tissue removed during his surgery were issued on Wednesday.
"The results confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the Holy See said.
The pope's surgeon added that there was "no clinical reason to cancel" the pope's visit to South America.
The ambitious trip, initially scheduled for November 6-17, would take the pontiff to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, involving a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and stops at high altitude.
Pope Leo's transparency around illness breaks with tradition
Leo was discharged from the hospital on Saturday, saying he would resume his activities gradually.
His illness shocked the Catholic Church, stoking concern that any potential prolonged treatment, such as radiotherapy or chemotherapy, could have affected the pope's ability to head the church.
Pope Leo first announced his condition during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, telling followers that he would be having a nodule surgically removed.
The announcement broke away from long-held traditions of secrecy surrounding papal health issues.

Oil prices surged after an attack on an oil field in Saudi Arabia – Brent exceeded $110

Global oil prices rose after a drone attack on the Shaybah oil field in Saudi Arabia, which killed 2 people. The incident heightened concerns about new disruptions to energy supplies amid the escalating conflict in the Middle East. Bloomberg reported this, UNN writes.
Details
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose to nearly $98 per barrel, while the price of benchmark Brent exceeded $110 during trading.

War in the Middle East drives up oil prices
Since the beginning of the year, Brent has risen by nearly 80% due to disruptions in oil supplies from the Persian Gulf amid the war between the United States and Iran, which has been ongoing for 9 months.
Recently, oil exports from the region began to recover and approached pre-war levels. In particular, Kuwait has already restored supply volumes to the level it had before the conflict began.
However, the situation remains unstable. Iran has intensified attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran-backed Houthis continue to launch strikes against Saudi Arabia.
According to Bloomberg, the risk of further military escalation is preventing oil prices from falling, despite the gradual recovery of exports from the Persian Gulf countries.

Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:36:31 UTC
08:36:31 KST

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had confirmed the first detection of flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Pecos county, Texas.
The elk was located on a game ranch and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA said in a statement.
The Texas animal health commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.
“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” Texas wildlife division director Alan Cain said in a statement.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.
The US halted livestock imports from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, but resumed trade in August at an Arizona port as part of a phased reopening plan.
The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.
Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.

Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:32:04 UTC
08:32:04 KST

Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock slid more than 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. 43 cents estimated
- Revenue: $28.05 billion vs. $27.9 billion estimated
Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up.
"I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger.
Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information.
"I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," he said.
Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, according to the earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.
Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion.
Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders.
Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a share, a year earlier, Tesla said.
The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.
Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million.
"We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck.
Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to its forthcoming FSD (Unsupervised) systems around the second quarter of next year.
Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but it's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service."
The company plans to bring Cybercab to cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning.
Musk said the company's driverless Robotaxi fleet will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027. That fleet now includes 362 Model Y Robotaxi, and 449 Cybercab vehicles authorized for driverless operations in Texas, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles,
"It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."
Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, Musk predicted that Tesla "will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."
Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.
Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.
One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.
On Optimus, Musk said Tesla is "making good progress" on the AI systems that control the robots in development. He said there's "still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks."
Musk said he expects current issues around electromechanical design, reliability, usage duration, and AI to be "solved around the end of next year."

Global warming will inevitably exceed the critical threshold of 1.5 degrees – UN
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
02:25:10 EEST
08:25:10 KST

Global warming will inevitably exceed the critical threshold of 1.5 degrees – UN
Kyiv • UNN
The UN forecasts that the 1.5°C threshold will inevitably be exceeded. Under the best-case scenario, warming could be limited to 1.7–1.8°C through drastic emissions cuts.
The world will inevitably cross the 1.5°C global warming threshold compared with pre-industrial levels. Decades of insufficient action against climate change have made it impossible to avoid this scenario. This is stated in a new report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), reports UNN.
Details
Experts emphasize that further government decisions will determine how far and for how long temperatures exceed the critical threshold. Under a favorable scenario, humanity may still limit maximum warming to 1.7–1.8°C.
This does not mean that we are giving up. We can still limit warming to 1.7–1.8 degrees. Every tenth of a degree increases climate impacts such as devastating floods, heatwaves and wildfires
Humanity will have to drastically cut emissions
According to UN estimates, every additional fraction of a degree increases the risk of irreversible changes, including melting glaciers, the release of carbon from permafrost, disruption of ocean currents and the destruction of coral ecosystems.
To curb warming, global greenhouse gas emissions must be reduced by 18% by 2030, by 45% by 2035 and by 69% by 2040 compared with 2025 levels.
At the same time, countries’ current climate commitments envisage significantly smaller reductions — only 5–8% by 2030 and 11–15% by 2035.

Chinese-linked hackers compromise ConnectWise, target hundreds in global attack: Microsoft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:25:00 UTC
08:25:00 KST

Chinese-linked hackers compromise ConnectWise, target hundreds in global attack: Microsoft
- Microsoft said a Chinese-linked group, Storm-0940, used the AI tool ARTEX to breach ConnectWise and target hundreds of organisations worldwide.
- ConnectWise said a China state-aligned group likely attacked its Cloud Backup service and that it has contained affected connections and is restoring services in phases.
- The campaign hit many sectors, including defence, finance and government, and Microsoft warned the hackers gained privileged cloud persistence at many firms despite most attacks failing.
AI generated
A Chinese-linked hacking group used an AI-driven penetration testing tool to compromise IT services firm ConnectWise as part of a campaign that targeted hundreds of organisations globally, Microsoft said on Oct 21.
Based on Microsoft’s analysis and evidence available to ConnectWise, “it appears that a China state-aligned group was responsible for the attack on ConnectWise Cloud Backup”, ConnectWise chief executive officer Manny Rivelo said in a separate statement.
Rivelo said ConnectWise “contained the affected application connections and are restoring services in controlled phases”.
He added that “those actions do not remove unauthorised access that may have already been established within individual customer tenants, which require separate review”.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing regularly denies conducting or condoning cyber-enabled data theft.
The hackers, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940, used an open-source penetration testing framework called ARTEX to carry out the campaign, Microsoft said.
There are multiple tools used to conduct penetration testing, a form of legitimate testing of the security of networks or services.
ARTEX allows users to use any AI model to automate a variety of penetration testing tasks and can be configured to run autonomous tasks including reconnaissance and data exfiltration, Microsoft said.
The attack targeted organisations across a wide variety of sectors, including aerospace, defence, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, think tanks and non-profit organisations, Microsoft said.
While the majority of the targeting was not successful, Microsoft said, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence – or high-level access that could continue even after clean-up efforts – at many organisations in a brief time. REUTERS

Ebola transmission in DR Congo remains active: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:21:37 UTC
08:21:37 KST

James Tasamba
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Ebola transmission in the Democratic Republic of Congo has remained active in more than three-quarters of all health zones affected since the start of the outbreak in May, the World Health Organization's (WHO) Africa regional office said in a situation report Wednesday, as the cumulative caseload neared 10,000.
The disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus strain has affected eight provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, South-Ubangi and North Ubangi.
The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Congo has surpassed 9,600, including 4,646 deaths since the outbreak was declared, according to WHO data.
Of the 66 health zones affected to date, 50, or 75.8%, reported at least one new confirmed case during the most recent 21 days, the report showed.
Ituri continues to account for the largest proportion of cumulative confirmed cases at 72.7%, while substantial transmission persists in North Kivu and Haut-Uele.
The most recent seven-day moving average indicates a modest upward trend, suggesting renewed intensification of transmission, the report said.
WHO said the outbreak is becoming increasingly challenging, marked by an expanding cluster of cases linked to the imported index case in Kenya and the confirmation of a case in Nigeria.
Kenya confirmed another Ebola infection Tuesday, bringing the number of cases to nine.
The report highlighted the widening international dimension and the growing complexity of the outbreak, particularly in Congo, where escalating insecurity, population displacement and restricted humanitarian access threaten to further undermine surveillance and response operations.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) called for global solidarity to stop Ebola after Nigeria confirmed a case in a patient in the capital, Abuja.
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya mentioned the need for immediate, flexible financing, medical supplies, diagnostics, trained responders and stronger community-based surveillance.
Africa CDC is set to convene a high-level virtual meeting of African health ministers on Oct. 28 to assess the situation, strengthen coordination across borders, accelerate support to affected countries and reinforce preparedness throughout the continent.
“Ebola is crossing borders. Our response must move faster, with stronger coordination, greater solidarity and decisive political leadership,” Kaseya said.

Pope Leo needs no further treatment after cancer surgery, doctors say
The 71-year-old leader of the Catholic church has had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery.
Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment for lung cancer after confirming the disease had not spread following recent surgery, the Vatican announced in a statement from doctors.
“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said Wednesday.
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung surgically removed on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Leo was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Polyclinic on Saturday, four days after his operation, and the Vatican said he would gradually resume his activities. On Wednesday, he returned to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with pilgrims.
Found by chance
Additional treatment is generally offered in cases where follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread, such as through the lymph nodes, or if other signs indicate that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumours are caught very early, as the Catholic leader appears to have had, when the nodule was initially found during another unrelated exam.
In an interview with Vatican News on Saturday, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations, and that the pope had not been experiencing any symptoms.
The pope carried on his official business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St Peter’s Square and Wednesday’s longer audience in the square, greeting the faithful from around the world.
“Thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers,” Leo exclaimed to the audience.
It appears that the Catholic leader remains committed to his November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Leo’s lead surgeon told Vatican News that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high-altitude stops.

Nigeria’s first Ebola case matches DR Congo strain, health officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:20:12 UTC
08:20:12 KST

Nigeria’s first Ebola case matches DR Congo strain, health officials say
Bundibugyo strain has now affected four African nations, and become the DR Congo’s deadliest in recorded history.
Nigerian health officials say test results have confirmed the country’s first case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which is behind a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), marking the disease’s first spread to West Africa in the current outbreak.
The case involves a woman who travelled from Uganda to the capital, Abuja, on October 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said.
She was tested for Ebola on October 19 after health officials learned she had recently travelled to Uganda, one of the countries affected by the current outbreak. Officials confirmed the positive result on Tuesday.
“We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo,” Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the NCDC, said on Wednesday.
The World Health Organization (WHO) also confirmed the strain, for which there is neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment.
‘Multi-organ failure’
An unnamed official told the AFP news agency that the woman is a diplomat whose condition has deteriorated into “multi-organ failure”.
Ayoade Alakija, a Nigerian physician who co-chairs a G7 committee for investment in global health, said that it had taken 12 days since the woman fell sick for her to be tested for Ebola, potentially exposing many other people to the infection.
Nigerian authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them healthcare workers. They include the patient’s husband, a Swiss national, who lives with her in Abuja.
Officials are also tracing passengers who travelled with her from Uganda to Nigeria but do not believe she was symptomatic during the flight.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving treatment.
Earlier cases
In 2014, the first Nigerian case, detected in Lagos, raised fears the virus would spread rapidly, but it was brought under control within three months, resulting in 20 infections and eight deaths.
That epidemic killed more than 11,000 people across West Africa between late 2013 and 2016.
The WHO says Nigeria is the fifth country to detect the virus in the outbreak, which this past week widened across the continent, with Kenya in the east reporting nine cases since October 6.
Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director-General Jean Kaseya said on X on Wednesday that the outbreak was “no longer one country’s fight”, and that he would hold a meeting of Africa’s health ministers next week to strengthen the cross-border response and review hospital capacity.
The DRC is the epicentre of the outbreak, its deadliest on record.
There have been more than 9,000 Ebola cases and more than 4,000 deaths there since mid-May.

Anthropic, music publishers square off on ‘fair use’ defence in AI copyright case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:18:00 UTC
08:18:00 KST

Anthropic, music publishers square off on ‘fair use’ defence in AI copyright case
- Anthropic asked a California judge to rule that using millions of song lyrics to train Claude is “fair use” under US copyright law.
- Music publishers UMG, Concord and ABKCO say Anthropic’s AI makes competing lyrics and harms songwriters, citing nearly 120,000 “synthetic” lyric requests in six months.
- The case could affect many AI copyright lawsuits, after earlier Northern California rulings split on whether AI training is fair use.
AI generated
SAN JOSE, California – Anthropic urged a judge in California on Oct 21 to rule that the AI company’s use of millions of song lyrics to train its chatbot Claude is protected as “fair use” under US copyright law, as it seeks to scuttle a lawsuit brought by Universal Music Group and other music publishers.
US District Judge Eumi Lee did not rule at a hearing in San Jose but pressed both sides on the fair use question, which could be key to dozens of other high-stakes copyright infringement cases in the AI era.
Lee also questioned the publishers’ assertion that Claude’s ability to compose lyrics threatens the market for the publishers’ lyrics.
Anthropic lawyer Sonal Mehta of WilmerHale argued that its AI training leads to the creation of transformative new content, putting it squarely under the fair use doctrine.
The publishers’ attorney Matt Oppenheim of Oppenheim + Zebrak responded that Anthropic misuses its lyrics to generate competing content that harms human songwriters.
Oppenheim said Claude received nearly 120,000 requests to generate “synthetic” lyrics over a six-month period. He said large language models like Claude “could overwhelm the market with AI-generated content very easily”.
Mehta countered that AI has not reduced demand for the lyrics, and that the publishers could not identify any specific instances of market harm from Claude or other large language models.
Mehta also said that UMG itself has said that AI is “overwhelmingly a net positive” for the music industry.
Early fair use rulings
Fair use could determine the fate of pending lawsuits brought by authors, news outlets, visual artists and others against tech giants including Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms over their AI training.
Two other Northern California judges who have already weighed in on the closely watched issue have split on whether generative AI training generally makes fair use of copyrighted material, which would shield tech companies from liability for using millions of copyrighted works to train their systems without content owners’ permission.
Now-retired US District Judge William Alsup sided with Anthropic in 2025 on its argument that its AI training made fair use of books. Two days later, US District Judge Vince Chhabria ruled for Meta in a similar lawsuit but warned that AI training “in many circumstances” would not be fair use.
In the case being heard by Lee, music publishers UMG, Concord and ABKCO sued Anthropic in 2023, alleging its use of their lyrics to train Claude to respond to human prompts infringed their copyrights in hundreds of songs by artists including Beyonce, the Rolling Stones and the Beach Boys.
Anthropic has argued that its AI training makes transformative use of song lyrics to “help Claude understand human language and enable progress and productivity in science, business and education”. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

'Sheep in the Box':  A pointless, sweet story of grief, robots - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:17:47 UTC
08:17:47 KST

Hirokazu Koreeda is a director who focuses on stories about people you enjoy spending time with. His characters are usually kind, relatable, and, for lack of a better word, nice.
Even when he tackles subjects like selling babies for adoption, as in Broker, or a family of petty thieves who exploit lonely, vulnerable people in his Palme d’Or-winning movie Shoplifters, most of his characters still have a likable core.
There’s nothing wrong with being nice, but it doesn’t usually mesh well with dystopian AI dramas, and so I was surprised to read that his latest film, Sheep in the Box, which opens in theaters throughout Israel on Thursday, tackles that subject.
It is about how a couple, grieving the loss of their young son who was killed in an accident two years before, decide to adopt an AI robot programmed to mimic their child.
If it sounds like the Steven Spielberg movie A.I. Artificial Intelligence (2001), that’s because it is. The Spielberg film went further than Sheep in the Box in telling the story through the eyes of the robotic child substitute, and it had a different tone.
A different era than Spielberg's AI film
That was at least partly because it was made in a very different era, one in which the robot, played by Haley Joel Osment, could seem cuddly and warm, and in which the idea of such a robot was simply science fiction, instead of something you would expect to become a reality any minute.
Spielberg’s film was a kind of reboot of Pinocchio with a robot who longed to be a real boy.
But Koreeda knows viewers are likely wary of the idea of an artificial child, so we feel stirrings of dread, or at least unease, from the moment the cute robot enters the picture.
Early on, Otone (Ayase Haruka, one of the stars of Koreeda’s most enjoyable films, Our Little Sister), an architect, receives a gift: a heart-shaped object from a company called REbirth that projects a butterfly hologram.
It creates robots of the deceased based on photos, videos, and audio clips. She finds out that her family is entitled to a free robot, as are all those whose loved ones were killed in accidents or were crime victims.
Otone’s husband, Kensuke (Daigo Yamamoto), a down-to-earth contractor, is skeptical that any machine can replace their son, Kakeru (Rimu Kuwaki).
He mentions to his wife that they have been approached by the REbirth corporation several times before and that he isn’t interested. But he finally agrees to attend the company’s presentation.
Once he sees how realistic this robot will be, he gives in. Going over all the old photos and videos to send to the company is a bonding experience for them.
The prospect of the robot is especially cheering for Otone, who is still crippled by her grief. She can’t think of anything but Kakeru and ignores her family's suggestions that she have another child.
Once the robot is created and programmed, they wait anxiously for it to arrive. Otone is instantly soothed when the robot is switched on, but Kensuke tells it to call him “Mister,” not “Dad.”
Otone wants to spend time with robot while Kensuke remains sports-focused
All Otone wants is to spend time with the child-substitute, while Kensuke remains absorbed in sports, which you sense has helped him get through the loss.
Their families and friends, especially Otone’s imperious, self-absorbed mother, are thoroughly creeped out, but Otone doesn’t care. Scenes show her looking beatifically up into the sunlight, the robot boy’s face beside hers.
But there are the stirrings of a subplot about other robot children who were rejected by their owners and sent back. These child-robots have bonded together in the woods to console themselves.
It also seems that their robot child keeps being drawn to the train tracks where their son was killed, which Otone finds alarming.
If you're hoping this will turn into sci-fi horror, you’ve got the wrong director, and the suspense-laden plot fizzles into a story that’s kind of nice. And somewhat pointless.
This will likely be the first time Koreeda fans are disappointed by one of his movies. Most of his films deal with the rupture of a family and the attempt to create a new one.
The lyrical film Our Little Sister, about three sisters who take in the daughter of their father from his second marriage, is a particularly moving example of this.
So is Like Father, Like Son, a drama based on those switched-at-birth cases that periodically make headlines, in which two sets of parents learn they must give up the child they raised for years and welcome their biological offspring, a complete stranger.
The title Sheep in the Box refers to a moment from The Little Prince by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, where the little prince asks the aviator to draw a sheep and isn’t satisfied with his attempts.
Finally, though, the little prince is ecstatic when the aviator draws a box and tells him there is a sheep inside it.
I got the sense that in Sheep in the Box, Koreeda wanted to say something about how technology has started to replace human connection in our lives, but some sweetness in his vision of the world stopped him from scolding us too strongly.
Instead, he tries to help us understand why some people, like Otone, can be soothed by a box alone.

Britain's MI5 spied on NHS founder Bevan, secret documents show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:11:26 UTC
08:11:26 KST

Britain's MI5 spied on NHS founder Bevan, secret documents show
LONDON, Oct 22 - British spies monitored Nye Bevan, the much lauded architect of the National Health Service, for three decades because of his links to the Communist Party and criticism of Britain's government in World War Two, newly released papers show.
Declassified secret documents from MI5 made public by the National Archives on Thursday reveal that Bevan's activities in parliament, and his movements and meetings outside, were closely watched by MI5 from 1933 until his death in 1960.
MI5 had suspected that Bevan, a committed socialist and one of the most prominent parliamentary critics of Winston Churchill and his wartime coalition, was a communist sympathiser.
However, the agency's investigations seem to have determined that there was nothing to worry about.
"What information we have on Bevan's relations with the Communist Party since 1943 show that from time to time both the Communist Party and the Trotskyists have made attempts to get him to work with them without success," a 1955 note said.
Bevan, who died in 1960, became health minister after the war and is credited with founding the state-funded NHS in 1948.
While the one-time Welsh coal miner was heralded for his oratory skills, he was also seen as a highly divisive figure, not just within the Labour Party but the country as whole.
Two years after his death, a review of his MI5 case file stated: "Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame."
The other newly material released also included MI5 files about Wolfgang zu Putlitz, a German diplomat who leaked information about Hitler's plans to Britain, and Soviet agents and suspected operatives such as Frank Bossard who was jailed for 21 years for passing defence material to Russian spies. AI generated
WASHINGTON – A crowdsourced verification system used by Elon Musk’s X failed to flag a vast majority of false claims related to the US midterm elections – including those promoted by the billionaire – a study said on Oct 21.
Community Notes, which allows users to contribute notes that add context or corrections to posts, was introduced by X in late 2022 and the same model is increasingly being adopted by other tech platforms.
But researchers have repeatedly questioned its effectiveness in combating misinformation.
NewsGuard, a US watchdog that rates the credibility of news and information sites, identified dozens of posts on X that advanced false claims related to the elections, including bogus allegations of election fraud.
Only 13 of those posts were tagged with Community Notes.
“X’s crowdsourced fact-checking programme failed to flag 93.1% of false claims related to the US midterm elections,” NewsGuard said.
“The uncorrected X posts have drawn millions of interactions ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.”
The falsehoods included a post by a conservative commentator claiming that New York and California had made it illegal for voters to show – and officials to ask for – their voter ID. No such rule exists in either Democratic stronghold.
Musk has often promoted Community Notes, calling it “awesome” and asserting that all users, including himself, were subject to being corrected by the crowdsourced model.
NewsGuard, however, said that Musk, who has 241.5 million followers on X, has advanced at least four false claims related to the midterm elections, none of which carried Community Notes.
X did not respond to AFP’s request for comment.
Studies have shown Community Notes can work to dispel some falsehoods, like vaccine misinformation, but researchers have long cautioned that it works best for topics where there is broad consensus.
Some researchers have also cautioned that Community Notes users can be motivated to target political opponents by partisan beliefs.
Tech platforms increasingly view the community-driven model as an alternative to professional fact-checking.
In 2025, Meta ended its third-party fact-checking programme in the United States, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg saying it had led to “too much censorship”. Professional fact-checkers vehemently reject the claim.
In September, Meta said it had begun testing its own version of Community Notes in 16 Spanish-speaking countries in Latin America, in a step toward replacing its fact-checking programme.
Meta gave no timeline for when the change will become official.
Meta’s Oversight Board, a quasi-independent body the company funds to review its moderation decisions, said Community Notes was not an adequate replacement for fact-checking.
AFP currently works in 26 languages with Meta’s global fact-checking programme, including in Latin America. AFP

Tunisia sentences 10 anti-pollution activists over protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:04:45 UTC
08:04:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Tunisia sentences 10 anti-pollution activists over protest
A Tunisian court on Wednesday sentenced 10 environmental activists to up to a year in prison over an anti-pollution protest they attended in 2020, a defence lawyer said.
Eight of them were sentenced to six-month suspended sentences, lawyer Hamida Chaieb said.
The activists had taken part in a demonstration against a major phosphate-processing factory in southern Tunisia's coastal city of Gabes, where locals have complained about pollution and health issues they linked to the plant.
The case stemmed from a complaint by the state-run factory, which accused the activists of obstructing its operations, Chaieb said.
The activists were arrested at the time but later released amid pressure from rights groups.
They believed the case against them had been dropped, said Khayreddine Debaya, head of the campaign group, Stop Pollution, which has led several protests against the facility.
But in March this year, the activists discovered they had been sentenced in 2023 to one year in prison in absentia.
The court retried them in their presence this time, handing only two of them one-year jail terms while Debaya was among those who received six-month suspended sentences.
The plant, inaugurated in 1972, processes phosphate to make fertilisers, and some of the gases and waste it discharges into the open air and the Mediterranean are radioactive and can cause cancer, researchers have found.
In February, a court rejected demands to suspend the facility's operations.
Taking advantage of rising prices for fertiliser on global markets, Tunisia now wants its output to increase more than fourfold by 2030.
President Kais Saied has long vowed to revive Tunisia's phosphate sector, hindered by years of underinvestment and unrest, calling it a "pillar of the national economy".

Britain lacks what it needs in the High North, says report
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:01:29 BST
08:01:29 KST

Britain must address serious military capability gaps in the High North, and should consider whether the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force ought to focus more on threats in the region, particularly if it has to plan for uncertainty over American support for NATO, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, published its findings after an inquiry that took evidence between March and July this year and included visits to Norway, Denmark and Greenland.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
He said: “The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North. Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent. Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.”
He added: “And if the UK government means what it says – that Russia could attack NATO as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”
The report warns of serious consequences if the region is left inadequately defended. Failure to deter Russia there, particularly from underwater threats, would put subsea data cables and energy pipelines in and around British waters at particular risk during peacetime. In the event of hostilities, failure to counter Russia in the High North would threaten the British population, military and civilian critical national infrastructure including the nuclear deterrent, and Atlantic resupply routes from the United States.
On the capability gaps themselves, the committee sets out that the Royal Navy has a requirement for eight of its thirteen frigates to carry the Sonar 2087 towed array for anti-submarine work and currently holds five, all of them Type 23s. It records eleven frigates and destroyers in service against a requirement for nineteen, and calls for no further towed array-equipped Type 23 to leave service until replaced one-for-one by a Type 26.
It also finds that Britain has allowed its submarine under-ice capability to lapse just as the region has become strategically more important, leaving it less able to contest Russian freedom of action and at risk of being forced into a more defensive posture.
On the Joint Expeditionary Force, the ten-nation grouping Britain leads alongside the Netherlands and the Baltic and Nordic states, Dhesi said: “Our Defence in the High North inquiry found that the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force has not yet realised its full potential. Although it was originally conceived as capable of operating across the full spectrum of conflict, and of covering both the High North and Baltic regions, its role has become increasingly focused on countering sub-threshold and hybrid threats.”
He said: “Our report calls for the government to reassess the JEF’s role and consider whether it should focus more on countering threats in the High North, particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for NATO. The UK’s presence in the Baltics, particularly in Estonia, may need to be bolstered to offset the effects of any greater JEF focus on the High North.”
Building the British Army force in Estonia up to brigade strength would match what Germany is already undertaking in Lithuania. The committee also asks the government, within a year of assuming leadership of NATO’s Joint Force Command Norfolk, to reassess the added value the force brings to European security, and either strengthen it and align it more closely with NATO or focus its finite resources on NATO instead.
Sir Keir Starmer, then Prime Minister, said in June this year that it was the British intelligence assessment, and that of other NATO countries, that there could be an attack by Russia on NATO as soon as 2030. The Defence Investment Plan published the same month committed £298 billion over four years to 2029-30.
In evidence to the inquiry the Ministry of Defence described anti-submarine warfare as a core strength of Britain’s armed forces, and said capabilities are held at varying levels of readiness, with every platform going through a cycle of deployment, maintenance, training and preparation, and equipment held at different readiness depending on the capability it is required to meet for NATO.
The government is expected to respond to the report within two months.
