Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:01:03 UTC
08:01:03 KST

Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.
The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat.
“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.”
The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating.
The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters in November and January last year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them.
Russia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months.
The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on the Ministry of Defence to draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030.
The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked.
“There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy.
It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy.
The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added.
None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress.
However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer.
Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact.
In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.

Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
23:01:03 UTC
08:01:03 KST

Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public.
Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to the National Archives show. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS.
At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general of MI5 approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him.
However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved.
“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”
Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”
MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”
He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.
Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.
In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.
Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.
The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.
Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937.
While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public.
One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”
Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files.
MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.
The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained.
A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.
However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.

08:00:25 KST

For decades, the distant island of Bougainville has fought for secession from Papua New Guinea, for a future as an independent nation of its own.
This week, that long-running aspiration faces further challenge, with PNG’s parliament slated to debate the ratification of Bougainville’s 2019 UN-sanctioned referendum, in which nearly 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence.
That referendum was a key element of the 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement, which ended a 10-year long civil war estimated to have killed as many as 15,000 people.
Even as violence has reemerged around the controversial Panguna mine – a catalyst for the conflict, but now seen as critical to the island’s independent financial future – Bougainville’s government has insisted it will not be deterred from secession. It has committed to “self-government” from next year, and to breaking away from PNG, as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.
Sources in Port Moresby and Bougainville say they expect the independence referendum result to be rejected on the floor of the PNG parliament, given the threshold for ratification has been raised to three-quarters of all MPs, not the two-thirds usually required for constitutional amendments.
The autonomous island of Bougainville, PNG’s easternmost province and about 1,000km from the capital, is home to about 300,000 people, culturally and ethnically distinct from the rest of the PNG archipelago. It has for decades, sought to break free of rule by Port Moresby.
Divided opinion
Port Moresby has long resisted acting on Bougainville’s post-conflict independence, anxious not to establish a precedent for the break-up of PNG’s vast and culturally diverse archipelago, or to lose a resource-rich and potentially lucrative province.
Bougainville’s attorney-general and vice-president, Ezekiel Masatt, said that the MP vote threshold was “crafted” by the PNG government to defeat the vote.“There is a national government strategy to poison the waters and make it impossible to come close to reach the voting threshold,” he said in a June statement.
Opinions in PNG’s parliament were divided ahead of the referendum vote.
Dr Allan Marat, chair of a bipartisan committee on Bougainville matters, told parliament last month that the island had met all the conditions outlined in the 2001 peace agreement and deserved its independence.
“It seems there is only one humane option for us members of this honourable house to do … to cut the umbilical cord connecting baby ‘Bougainville Independence’ to PNG,” he said.
Others are fiercely opposed. Former deputy prime minister Belden Namah, who served in the PNG army during the Bougainville conflict, said the question went beyond a political debate.
“It is an issue of national sovereignty, it is an issue of constitutional integrity, it is an issue of peace, unity, sacrifice and the future survival of Papua New Guinea as one nation,” he told the same parliamentary sitting.
In June this year, Bougainville’s president Ishmael Toroama presented his government’s “final position” on the island’s political future.
He said Bougainville would enter a stage of “self-government” from 1 September 2027, before declaring itself independent “separate from the state of PNG” in 2030.
Toroama said he did not want a return to violence or conflict with Port Moresby. “Our objective has never been confrontation,” he said. “Our objective has always been reconciliation, partnership and a peaceful transition founded on law and mutual respect.”
The Bougainville government hopes the controversial Panguna gold and copper mine will fund independence. Carved from a mountain in the centre of the island, it was once one of the largest gold and copper mines in the world, and still has an estimated $60bn in unrealised reserves.
“We closed the mine because of oppression,” Toroama told the Guardian in an interview last year. “Today the mine is the key to our economic growth and settling all unresolved issues from the war.”
Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it. The mine and surrounding river deltas remain dangerously polluted. Rio Tinto has signed an MOU with the Bougainville government to address the ongoing environmental and human rights impacts of the dormant mine.
Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as ‘the crisis’ – that ran for a decade.
Violence returned to the mine last month, when up to 30 men carrying high-powered rifles drove into the sprawling Panguna pit site and set fire to nearly 40 heavy haulage trucks, excavators and water tanks owned by the newly appointed contractor, India’s Lloyds Metals and Energy.
Toroama said violence would not intimidate his government from redeveloping the mine.
“We will not cower to terroristic acts of violence designed to cause disunity and distract us from our agenda of creating a socio-politically and economically viable Bougainville,” he said after the incident.
Oliver Nobetau, Pacific islands program director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian thinktank, said it was well known across the island that “not everyone is on-side to reopen the mine”.
He said the incident, while relatively minor, had damaged the independence cause by affirming Port Moresby’s often-overstated concerns that Bougainville was not ready for independence, including that the island had not fully disarmed.
Nobetau said a “no” vote was looking increasingly likely in PNG’s parliament.
“My assessment is that it’s not going to spill over into actual conflict and fighting the way that people fear,” he said. “I think there’s going to be a lot of social tensions, a lot of political tensions, but I think eventually they’ll come back to the table to discuss how to move forward.”
Nobetau said the independence movement on Bougainville would not be deterred by resistance from Port Moresby.
“I think most likely they will try to go at it alone through the self-government model and then rolling out a three-year plan towards independence by 2030.”

Advertising revenue, which accounts for the overwhelming majority of Meta's business, increased to 63.06 billion dollars from 50.08 billion dollars a year earlier.

Meta continued to expand its investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, totaled 34.91 billion dollars during the quarter.
Free cash flow turned negative at 2.12 billion dollars, compared with positive free cash flow of 10.63 billion dollars a year earlier.
Looking ahead, Meta forecast fourth-quarter revenue of between 73 billion and 76 billion dollars. It also narrowed its full-year capital expenditure forecast to between 135 billion and 145 billion dollars, raising the lower end from its previous projection of 130 billion dollars.
Separately, Meta announced plans to establish a new class of publicly listed, non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027. The move is intended to support future investment, acquisitions and employee compensation while preserving the company's existing voting structure. ■

RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Two residents were killed in an attempted drone attack on Saudi energy giant Aramco's field, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Wednesday, while Yemen's Houthi group denied launching any attacks against Saudi territory during the day.
Citing the Saudi Ministry of Energy, the agency said Saudi air defenses intercepted the drone targeting a facility at Aramco's Shaybah field in the Eastern Province, but the incident caused a fire in a contractor's vehicle outside the facility without affecting operations.
The incident killed two residents, one of Filipino and one of Nepali nationality, and injured two others, one of Pakistani and one of Indian nationality, the ministry added.
In a series of statements, the Saudi-led coalition announced it had intercepted and destroyed seven drones launched toward various parts of Saudi Arabia, including four over Medina and the Eastern Province.
No details on casualties or damage were provided.
However, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea denied launching any attacks toward Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, rejecting the coalition's claim that drones had been intercepted over Medina as "false."
Sarea said Saudi warplanes had carried out 62 airstrikes over the previous 24 hours targeting Sanaa and the provinces of Marib, Saada, Lahj and Taiz, claiming civilian casualties, including women and children, without providing figures.
The figures could not be independently verified.
The developments came as the Houthis intensified attacks on the government-held southeastern province of Hadramout in Yemen.
A local security official told Xinhua that Houthi drones and ballistic missiles targeted the vicinity of the Al-Dhabba oil terminal near the coastal city of Al-Shihr and Al-Rayan International Airport in Mukalla, the provincial capital.
The attack on Al-Rayan came hours after four ballistic missiles struck the airport, triggering powerful explosions, according to the official.
There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Sarea claimed responsibility, saying the group targeted military equipment allegedly transported to Al-Rayan aboard Saudi military cargo aircraft, without providing evidence.
Earlier Wednesday, the Houthis said it had also launched a ballistic missile at what it described as a "Saudi military operations room" at Badr military base near Aden International Airport in the southern port city of Aden, where a powerful explosion shook surrounding neighborhoods, with no casualties immediately reported.
The persistent military escalation has drawn heightened diplomatic and security concern from regional and international powers.
The U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia warned Wednesday that ongoing hostilities involving the Houthis could escalate rapidly beyond currently affected areas.
It required U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia to obtain special authorization from the chief of mission to use any airport in the kingdom following recent missile and drone attacks.
Meanwhile, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi said Egypt's military efforts to defend Saudi Arabia would be limited to protecting the kingdom's territory and borders and would not involve attacking Yemen.
On Oct. 17, Sisi called on parliament to authorize possible military support for Saudi Arabia. The vote was postponed to Oct. 26.
Also on Wednesday, French President Emmanuel Macron landed in Riyadh in what the French media called "a surprise solidarity visit." Macron met with Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud to review strategic relations and regional developments.
His visit was part of a Gulf tour that also included Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

The most talked-about documentary of the year is heading to the big screen in Israel.
Following months of intense anticipation, You Can See Everything will premiere in theaters here on November 26, according to Forum Film, the official distributor of Sony Pictures, which recently bought the international rights for the A24 film.
Acclaimed filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and celebrated comedian and creator Nathan Fielder co-direct the intriguing project. The documentary has already generated massive online buzz, with its viral trailer capturing global attention and earning a stellar 98% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes.
At the heart of the film is Elizabeth Holmes, the infamous founder of Theranos, who was convicted of defrauding investors and sentenced to more than 11 years in prison. The documentary offers an unprecedented, intimate look at Holmes and her family, capturing their lives in the final weeks leading up to her imprisonment.
Holmes remains one of the most notorious figures of the modern tech era. She successfully deceived high-profile investors across politics, business, and academia by falsely promising a revolutionary medical technology that would change the world.
Feature promises different perspective than previous Theranos documentary
While the bizarre details of the Theranos affair were previously explored in the 2019 documentary The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, this new feature promises a radically different perspective.
In a characteristically immersive approach, Fielder lived in Holmes’s guesthouse for 34 days. During this time, he and Oppenheim closely documented her day-to-day life. Early glimpses and trailers reveal a painfully close, raw portrait of a woman who managed to fool some of the sharpest minds in Silicon Valley.
After releasing in North America this weekend, the film has already opened to box office numbers not seen in more than 20 years for a narrative documentary.
Film earns $15 million on opening weekend
You Can See Everything earned $15 million on opening weekend, according to Variety.
That’s well short of the $23.9 million record Michael Moore set in 2004 with Fahrenheit 9/11, but very impressive for a documentary that isn’t a concert or tour film.
By comparison, Melania, the Amazon documentary about First Lady Melania Trump, made $7.1 million at opening in January. That film is said to have cost $40 million to make and market. It earned just over $16.6 million in total, according to Box Office Mojo.
Reports estimate that You Can See Everything was made on a budget of around $6 million.
Veteran film writer Peter Travers suggested in his review that You Can See Everything may compete with The Odyssey to win the Academy Award for Best Picture. No documentary has won that Oscar.

‘We’ve lost everything’: Israelis displaced by Iran war fear another round of fighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:58:33 UTC
07:58:33 KST

Seven months after Operation Roaring Lion, as the prime minister and defense minister appear to be seeking to stoke fears of a surprise attack by Iran or Hezbollah, residents whose homes were damaged in the latest round of fighting against the Iranian regime told ynet how they have been coping more than six months after being left without homes to return to. They also addressed the possibility that Israel could be heading into another round of fighting.
Meanwhile, following Netanyahu's statement that Tehran "is once again trying to develop its weapons of death" and a report that U.S. President Donald Trump had thwarted an Israeli strike on Iran, American officials told Reuters that the State Department plans to evacuate some diplomatic staff and their families from Saudi Arabia. According to the officials, the move stems from concerns about an escalation in fighting, particularly involving the Houthis in Yemen.
Regine Shoshan, 55, lost everything when an Iranian missile destroyed her apartment on Yehuda Halevi Street in Tel Aviv on the first night of Operation Roaring Lion. Seven months later, she is still struggling to rebuild her life.
"My home was completely destroyed. I lost everything. Everything. Everything. Nothing was left. I walked out that night with nothing but the clothes I was wearing, and that was it," she said.
"I lived in that apartment for 10 years. Over the past few years, I'd been working on my master's thesis, writing plays and poetry, and preparing lesson plans and workshops I wanted to teach. I had photography equipment and a home I'd made my own, where I could invite people over. I don't do any of those things anymore."
Shoshan now lives in a rented apartment but has been reluctant to replace the possessions she lost.
"I'm homeless, but I've got style," she joked. "I've rented an apartment, but it's an Airbnb-type place because I didn't want to buy anything. I'm still paying rent for my old apartment, which the state is covering, but that won't last forever. Because I was a tenant, I get no compensation for losing my home. The compensation from the Tax Authority is woefully inadequate."
Along with the loss of her home, Shoshan has had to contend with a maze of bureaucracy and a lack of ongoing psychological support.
"I still haven't been officially recognized as someone harmed in an enemy attack, even though that's exactly what happened to me. All the bureaucracy and paperwork are a huge headache. The night the missile hit, I was taken to the hospital. I later received 24 sessions with a psychologist through Amcha, a nonprofit organization. But those sessions have ended, and now I'm left hanging.
"I have no support. Nobody calls to ask how I'm doing or what I need. I'm fighting this battle alone."
Adding to her frustration, companies are still demanding that she return equipment destroyed in the strike.
"My television provider wants its equipment back because I canceled my subscription. I keep trying to explain that there's nothing to return. It's all gone. The same thing happened with my water dispenser. It's absurd and heartless."
For Shoshan, the destruction of her home was the second devastating blow her family suffered in the wars with Iran. During the first confrontation, Operation Rising Lion, an Iranian missile directly hit her parents' home, destroying it completely. Both were hospitalized for three months.
"When I hear people talking about another war with Iran, I almost feel numb. I'm shocked by the very idea," she said.
"I've had to shut down all my anxiety because I started feeling the stress in my heart. My ECG was abnormal, and so was my cardiac CT scan. The damage isn't just financial. It takes a physical toll, too."
She has not been able to return to work since the strike.
"I'm not working right now. I just haven't been able to work since it happened."
'They put us in terrible neighborhoods, without safe rooms'
In Dimona, Ziva Abuaziz, 47, is facing a similarly uncertain future. Her apartment building was hit in the Iranian missile attacks in March and is now slated for demolition.
"Our building is slated for demolition. It was too badly damaged to be repaired," she said. "Other residents were able to renovate their homes and move back in. The municipality tried to help us, but there's only so much it can do."
For the residents of her building, many of whom live in public housing managed by Amidar, a state-owned housing company, the uncertainty has dragged on for months.
"Nothing is clear. They've left the Amidar tenants waiting. Nobody knows what's going to happen to us," she said.
"Time is running out. We were given a year's rental assistance from the day of the strike. We had to set up a residents' committee to get things moving, but in the end, we realized we were just being pushed around. Nobody remembers us. We survived the strike and the trauma, but we've been forgotten."
Abuaziz said the attack also had a devastating effect on her husband, who has a disability.
"The attack undid years of progress my husband had made. Soon a year will have passed, and the rental assistance will end. The Tax Authority has been our lifeline and has helped us, but we have no idea what's going to happen next.
"Who are we supposed to wait for? How much longer are we supposed to wait? I don't have any answers.
"They gave us alternative housing in terrible neighborhoods, without reinforced safe rooms. That means having to run to public shelters again. My husband is disabled. He can't run to a shelter. But nobody seems to care. Unfortunately, no one has managed to help us."
With the possibility of another war looming, Abuaziz said she feels increasingly helpless.
"We're at a loss. This is a city of tens of thousands of people, and even at the cemetery where I work, we still don't have a protected space.
"If, God forbid, there's another round of fighting, and unfortunately it looks like there will be, I won't go to work. I pray it doesn't happen.
"Unfortunately, the wrong people are making the decisions. How many rounds have we already been through? Two. We were hit in the second one."
'We miss the peace and quiet, the greenery and our neighbors'
In Haifa, seven months have passed since an Iranian ballistic missile struck an apartment building on Shimshon Street, causing extensive destruction and ultimately claiming five lives.
The fifth victim, Michael Katz, 82, died in July from injuries he suffered when the missile directly hit his building on April 5.
Katz was pulled from the rubble in critical condition and fought for his life for more than three months. Despite prolonged hospital treatment, he eventually succumbed to his injuries, bringing the death toll from the strike to five.
The evening strike at 57 Shimshon Street was the deadliest attack on Haifa during the war. Four members of the Gershovitz family, who lived on the building's first floor, were killed.
Katz, who turned 82 in May, had worked for decades at Rafael, the Israeli defense technology company, contributing to the country's defense capabilities. He was also a recipient of the Rafael Prize.
He is survived by his wife, Nina, his sons, Itamar and Yoav, and six grandchildren.
All eight families living in the building were forced to move into rental properties in the area, where they are expected to remain until a new building is constructed.
The badly damaged building was demolished several months ago. Residents estimate that the planning and approval process, followed by construction, could take another four or five years.
Among those displaced were Tal Aharonovitch, 44, his wife, Orian, 37, and their son, Ilay, who is about a year old. The family has since moved into a rented apartment on Mount Carmel.
"At first, we stayed with relatives. This week, we finally moved into a rented apartment, with a lot of help from the Home Front Command and Haifa Municipality," Tal said.
"We'd lived there for almost four years when a missile hit our six-story building, destroying everything in seconds.
"And of course, there was the terrible tragedy of the four family members on the first floor who didn't make it to the shelter in time and were killed."
Tal, deputy head of the security department at Rambam Medical Center, remembers every moment of the attack.
"It was evening, and we were giving the baby a bath when the early warnings came through. We didn't hear our phones. Just as we finished bathing him, the siren went off," he recalled.
"The shelter was three floors below us, and we knew we wouldn't make it in time. A few seconds later, there was an enormous explosion.
"We threw ourselves over Ilay to protect him as the apartment filled with shattered glass and smoke. Then we went down to the shelter, where our neighbors helped us."
He knew immediately that the missile had hit nearby.
"The explosion was so powerful that I realized it had to be very close. When the rescue teams arrived, we went outside and saw the scale of the destruction.
"We went to the hospital to get checked out and were discharged, but we knew we had no home to go back to."
The family is now trying to settle into its new surroundings, but Tal said they still miss their former home.
"We've moved to Mount Carmel, but we miss our old place terribly. The Tax Authority is helping us cover the rent for now.
"We miss the peace and quiet, the greenery and our neighbors. They were wonderful people.
"Everything was destroyed in a moment. It was a terrible tragedy. Five people lost their lives in that building."
Although a new building is planned, Tal knows it will be years before the family can return.
"Every so often, we drive by and stop to look at where our building used to stand. We hope construction will start soon, but we know that with all the permits and approvals, it's going to take years."
'Netanyahu is desperately trying to shift the focus to security'
Meanwhile, senior Israeli officials sharply criticized Netanyahu's remarks at an IDF officers' graduation ceremony in southern Israel.
The officials rejected his warnings of an imminent existential threat from Iran.
"There's nothing even close to what Netanyahu described," they said. "We are not facing an existential threat, and Iran is not once again trying to develop 'bombs of death,' as he claimed."
They accused Netanyahu of trying to divert public attention from domestic issues.
"Netanyahu is desperately trying to put security back at the center of the public agenda," the officials said. "Anything to avoid talking about the ultra-Orthodox or the chaos in the government's management."
However, another Israeli source familiar with the intelligence assessments offered a different view, saying Iran had resumed work on its nuclear program and was seeking to improve its readiness.
"The Iranians have indeed restarted their nuclear program, and they want to reach a point where they're ready," the source said.
"That's why I believe another strike is only a matter of time. I don't think it will happen before the elections in Israel and the United States because of various constraints, but it could happen immediately afterward."
The source said the developments had also prompted efforts to accelerate diplomatic negotiations in hopes of reaching an agreement.
"There's a push to speed up the talks and try to reach a deal," the source said. "But as far as the diplomatic track goes, I think the chances of actually reaching an agreement are extremely slim."

Government websites across Europe and around the world are being taken offline en masse due to the threat of large-scale cyberattacks

Government websites are being temporarily taken offline due to two critical PHP vulnerabilities. They could allow malicious code to be executed remotely without authorization.
Government institutions in a number of European countries, as well as in the United Kingdom, Australia and Japan, have begun temporarily taking their websites offline after the discovery of 2 critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language. They could allow hackers to gain unauthorized access to servers. The Moscow Times reports, UNN writes.
Details
In the Netherlands, the websites of the National Cyber Security Centre, the Port of Rotterdam, the government portal Overheid.nl, the football association, the 5 largest political parties and a number of hospitals were taken offline for security reasons.

Experts recommend that website administrators urgently install the updates once they are released. If this is not possible, European cybersecurity authorities advise temporarily taking vulnerable resources offline to prevent possible attacks.

AI-discovered security flaws trigger website shutdowns worldwide
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
01:52:09 EEST
07:52:09 KST

Government websites and online services across Europe and other parts of the world were taken offline on Wednesday, after researchers using artificial intelligence discovered two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language supporting an estimated 70 per cent of websites whose server-side technology is known. Developers released emergency security patches as cybersecurity agencies warned of attacks against systems that remain unprotected.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The disruptions affected Finland, the Netherlands, France, Denmark and other countries, with authorities temporarily suspending public services while preparing software updates. The vulnerabilities received a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10 and allow attackers to execute commands remotely on affected servers without authentication.
Cybersecurity companies Calif and Google-owned Wiz independently identified the flaws using AI-assisted research. Calif reported its discovery to PHP developers in August after using OpenAI technology, while Wiz employed its Atlas research system alongside Google's Gemini and OpenAI models.
The vulnerabilities had existed in PHP's underlying code for years without detection. Researchers said AI tools helped identify and demonstrate weaknesses that would have required extensive manual investigation.
Wiz described the findings as among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP.
PHP developers published corrective updates on Wednesday and urged administrators to install them immediately. Security specialists warned that releasing the patches would also help attackers identify vulnerable systems by examining the changes.
The potential consequences include unauthorised access to servers, theft of information, website manipulation and installation of malicious software.
Internet intelligence company Censys estimated that approximately 1.5 million of 2.6 million identified PHP hosts were running software versions for which no patch was available, Reuters reported.
The vulnerabilities affect systems using PHP, which supports content management platforms including WordPress, Drupal and Joomla. WordPress alone powers approximately 40 per cent of websites worldwide.
In Finland, the Government ICT Centre Valtori began restricting access to government websites earlier on Wednesday.
By Wednesday evening, Valtori confirmed that it had started installing updates across systems under its management. The agency stressed that the shutdowns were precautionary and did not result from a confirmed security breach.
Finnish services affected included the National Land Survey, National Archives, Finnish Defence Forces, Central Finland wellbeing services county and the universities of Jyväskylä and Tampere.
The Helsinki Expo and Convention Center, Finnish Film Foundation and several services operated by public broadcaster Yle also experienced interruptions.
Elsewhere in Europe, the Netherlands took its national cybersecurity agency's website offline, alongside government portals and services operated by the Port of Rotterdam.
France's Interior Ministry placed its websites under preventive maintenance, while Denmark suspended services including a national school communication platform.
In Britain, local authority websites in Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford were temporarily unavailable.
The Wikimedia Foundation also suspended several systems until administrators completed security updates. The Internet Archive reported a temporary interruption.
The US National Security Agency advised organisations unable to install the patches to disconnect affected services. Britain's National Cyber Security Centre issued similar guidance and recommended checking systems for signs of unauthorised access.

The Kremlin subsequently signaled willingness to resume trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
However, Moscow has not abandoned its territorial claims or its opposition to Ukraine joining NATO.
Meanwhile, Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure as winter approaches.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly stressed that any negotiated settlement must include reliable security guarantees to prevent renewed Russian aggression.

Walmart launches tools for AI agents to shop for customers as Anthropic launches its own

Walmart launches tools for AI agents to shop for customers as Anthropic launches its own
- Walmart will let AI agents shop for customers through new “Agent Profiles”, with approval or spending limits, while keeping agent purchases separate from personal orders.
- The move follows growing investment in AI agents from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta, as firms see them as the next phase after ChatGPT.
- Amazon is taking the opposite path by blocking third-party shopping agents, including Meta’s Muse, while pushing its own AI tools such as Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me.
AI generated
US shopping giant Walmart on Oct 21 unveiled tools allowing artificial intelligence agents such as Meta’s Muse to shop on behalf of its customers, taking the opposite approach to rival Amazon, which bars outside AI agents from its platform.
AI agents are programmes that can carry out multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf – such as searching for products, comparing prices and completing a purchase – rather than only answering questions as chatbots do.
Tech companies including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta are investing heavily in agents, which much of the industry sees as the next phase of the AI boom that followed the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.
Anthropic on Oct 21 released a preview of Claude Duet, an agent that works in the background across users’ connected apps and can make online purchases with their approval.
Its archrival OpenAI launched its own always-on agents, called Dots, in September.
Muse, which Meta launched in September and has made available only in the United States and Canada, has been downloaded more than 10 million times, according to an analysis of third-party data by Sensor Tower.
Walmart said it would launch “Agent Profiles” within the next month, letting customers register each AI assistant they use as a separate profile within their Walmart account so that purchases made by the agent appear apart from their own.
Customers will be able to require approval for every purchase or let an agent buy on its own up to a spending limit they set, such as US$50, US$100 or US$200, and delete a profile at any time.
Walmart compared the arrangement to adding an authorised user to a credit card.
Amazon, the largest US online retailer, has taken a harder line, blocking third-party shopping agents while promoting its own AI tools such as Alexa for Shopping and its Buy for Me feature.
In September, Amazon blocked Muse from its site, with users shown a notice saying unauthorized AI agents violate Amazon’s conditions of use.
Amazon sued Perplexity in November 2025, accusing the startup of using its Comet browser agent to covertly make purchases on its marketplace, and has also moved to restrict agents from Google and OpenAI. AFP

Government websites down amid global security flaw scare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:46:37 UTC
07:46:37 KST

Government websites down amid global security flaw scare
Numerous websites worldwide, including government-run pages, temporarily went dark after the AI-assisted discovery of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, which powers around 70% of the web globally.
On Wednesday, the developers of the popular open-source programming language, which helps websites run and display content, issued an urgent security alert over “critical remote code execution vulnerabilities.”
The flaws could allow hackers to take control of affected websites, prompting the release of urgent fixes, with all PHP users “strongly encouraged to update immediately.”
Cybersecurity agencies worldwide, including the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center, the Australian Signals Directorate, and the Canadian Center for Cyber Security, issued their own alerts, advising users to apply the patches immediately and prioritize internet-facing systems.
Organizations that were unable to update immediately or that relied on outdated, unsupported PHP versions were advised to take their systems offline until the fixes could be applied.
The announcement prompted France’s Interior Ministry to temporarily shut down prefecture websites, with local government pages also unavailable. In neighboring Belgium, the Foreign Ministry similarly took its websites offline on Wednesday. In the Netherlands, the National Cyber Security Center, the websites of all major political parties, and at least one port took similar precautionary measures.
In Denmark, the national school communication platform was temporarily shut down; in Finland, the government’s public web services went dark.
Disruptions also affected services operated by the Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia.
The flaws in PHP were identified by two cybersecurity companies, Calif and Wiz, in August. PHP developers have since worked on fixes, while keeping the discovery under wraps to prevent malicious actors from exploiting the vulnerabilities.
The cybersecurity companies said they made extensive use of AI models in the process, including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.
Wiz stated that the “underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve.”
OpenAI described the case as “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” and predicted that more flaws would be discovered in the coming months with the help of AI.

Victorian public schools to be fully funded — but only by 2034
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:44:55 UTC
07:44:55 KST

Victoria strikes deal with Commonwealth to fully fund state schools by 2034
In short:
Victoria currently only pays 70 per cent of the agreed School Resource Standard, recommended by the Gonski review in 2012.
Premier Ben Carroll announced yesterday that the state's contribution would lift to 75 per cent, enabling more federal funds to flow to Victorian public schools.
What's next?
Victorian public schools will not receive 100 per cent of the Schooling Resource Standard until 2034.
The basketball court at Pembroke Primary School has not seen a game in two years.
The court is full of potholes, and parent James Dunn said the school in Melbourne's outer east cannot afford to fix them.
"When you've got 90 kids running around and you've got half your playground fenced off, it's pretty frustrating," said Mr Dunn, who has been treasurer on the school council for three years.
Pembroke students were missing out altogether on school camps and extracurricular activities because the school was "running on a shoestring", Mr Dunn said.
Yesterday Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced his government had finally signed off on a promised deal with the federal government on school funding.
Victoria currently only pays 70 per cent of the agreed School Resource Standard, recommended by the Gonski review in 2012, while the federal government contributes 20 per cent.
Mr Carroll confirmed Victoria will lift its contribution to 75 per cent after a move signed off by state cabinet this week, calling it the "biggest investment in schools ever" by the Victorian government.
However, state schools will not receive 100 per cent of the school resourcing standard until 2034.
Mr Dunn said that the deal had only been made a month out from the state election, after Labor had run Victoria for 12 years, was disappointing.
"It feels like the kids are now a political football," he said, expressing frustration over the prolonged timeline for full funding.
"Things have got to be done now."
Principals, union cautiously welcome deal
The Australian Principals Federation welcomed the deal but said the proposed timeline meant full funding remained years away.
"The challenges facing our schools are immediate," said Victorian branch president Andrew Cock.
"It is essential that meaningful funding increases are delivered progressively, rather than schools having to wait until the end of this period to see the benefits," he said.
"Our message continues to be simple — if we expect Victorian government schools to deliver a world-class education, we must fund them to do so."
Australian Education Union Victorian Branch president Justin Mullaly said while the announcement was welcome and provided greater certainty, there was devil in the detail.
"Victorian public schools will not receive some of the additional funding as soon as other states and territories," he said.
"The delay in signing and the decision to back-end the deal, will short change Victorian public schools by hundreds of millions of dollars over the next few years.
"Funding delays have real consequences, and this needs to be addressed."
Mr Carroll said: "If we can bring forward the timeline and meet the 75 per cent earlier, we will."
Voluntary contributions policy remains a sore point
Prior to yesterday's announcement, tensions had already been growing over parent contributions to keep state schools functioning adequately.
Last month, Victoria's Department of Education instructed schools to tell parents that all curriculum-based instruction and resources, including textbooks, are free and that there was no obligation to pay for school contributions.
Schools can ask for contributions for extra-curricular activities like camps and excursions or learning materials to keep.
Education Minister Gabrielle Williams defended the guidance, telling the ABC it was "updated to make it absolutely clear that school contributions are voluntary".
Kim, a librarian at a Melbourne public high school not given permission to speak publicly, said her school would cover items for lower income students, but could not afford "extras" like school camps.
"Our school is 'free' but it's falling apart, any couches are from hard rubbish and the roof is leaking," she said.
"School is free, but with 12-year-old science textbooks … free with old humanities textbooks with no covers.
"It's not a recipe for a winning education offering."
Australian Catholic University researcher Sarah Langman has analysed how voluntary parent payments were characterised in annual reports from 1500 Victorian public schools in 2024.
She said parent contributions were important for "a wide range of things, everything from school libraries to first aid offices to general programs, excursions and camps".
"The concern is then: what are schools going to be left with if they aren't able to provide these opportunities to their students?"
Ms Langman predicted the new Education Department advice would make budgets tighter.
"We would expect that this problem is probably going to become a lot more widespread as these policy restrictions come into place," she said.
"The real question we want people to consider is whether access to educational opportunities should depend on schools' ability to attract voluntary contributions."
Parents Victoria chief executive Gail McHardy said payments should not feel like a "moral obligation or source of pressure" for families struggling with the cost of living.
"School leaders and school councils should not be made to feel responsible for passing government funding shortfalls on to parents," Ms McHardy said.
Back at Pembroke primary, Mr Dunn was lukewarm on the Gonski funding announcement and whether it would be enough to repair his school's aging facilities.
"We'll see. Politicians aren't at the top of my trust list," he said.

Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:39:50 UTC
07:39:50 KST

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.
During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.
Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.
His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.
Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.
All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”
Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.
But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

US assessments find crime in parts of Latin America comparable to some American cities, despite travel warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:38:44 UTC
07:38:44 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The US State Department has provided asylum officers with internal assessments suggesting that violent crime in Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador is no worse than in some US cities, despite publicly warning Americans about security risks in parts of the same countries, CNN reported Wednesday.
The documents compare crime rates in the four Latin American countries with those in cities including Baltimore, Houston and Memphis.
CNN reported that the documents place less emphasis on human rights abuses, kidnappings and extortion than previous assessments.
Asylum seekers must prove they face persecution at home, with the assessments potentially affecting their eligibility for protection and relocation.
The assessments downplay the dangers posed by criminal groups and weak local institutions, marking a significant shift from previous evaluations despite limited changes on the ground, said Andrew Selee, president of the Migration Policy Institute.
The documents also state that Honduran police are generally willing and able to respond to requests for assistance.
Selee said the assessment overlooked alleged police links to organized crime and the risks of relocating. The State Department said regional experts prepared and reviewed the reports to help US immigration authorities assess asylum claims.
The assessments come as the State Department's annual human rights report has been delayed, leaving officers with alternative information on conditions in applicants' home countries.
Asylum denials reached 94% of cases in June compared with about 50% two years earlier, according to data from Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse cited by CNN.
Trump administration officials have said that travel warnings are intended to inform US citizens about risks abroad and do not necessarily reflect the level of danger faced by people living in those countries.

To intercept Ukrainian drones, Russia is now even scrambling its rare MiG-35 fighter jets; there are only six of them
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is using MiG-35s to intercept Ukrainian long-range drones. It has only six of these fighter jets at its disposal.
The Russian army has begun deploying rare MiG-35 fighter jets to counter long-range Ukrainian Armed Forces drones attacking facilities on the territory of the Russian Federation. Russia’s Aerospace Forces have only 6 such aircraft at their disposal. Defense Express reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to analysts, the Russians are using MiG-35s to intercept Ukrainian strike drones. As confirmation, the community published a photograph of a Russian pilot in the cockpit of a fighter jet who presumably took part in such operations.
Overall, Russian aviation has 86 MiG-29 fighter jets of various modifications and only 6 MiG-35s. At the same time, the actual number of combat-ready MiG-29s remains unknown.
Why Russia has only 6 MiG-35 fighter jets
All 6 MiG-35 aircraft belong to an experimental batch that Russia manufactured over 5 years—from 2018 to 2023. It comprised 4 single-seat and 2 two-seat fighter jets.
The MiG-35 is a modernized version of the MiG-29. According to its stated specifications, it has a 50% longer flight range and can carry up to 6,500 kg of weapons, including air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles.
Russia reported using the MiG-35 in the war against Ukraine as early as 2023. However, serial production of these fighters never reached significant scale, and attempts to sell them to foreign customers did not produce the expected results.

"It's the motivation and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football that you have to bring. We didn't bring that today," he said. "I've got to apologise for the performance."

War-hit Kyiv puts 85 European-funded buses on its streets. Here’s what riders find inside
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:35:52 UTC
07:35:52 KST

Kyiv has put 85 new buses into service. They have been bought under a financing agreement with the European Investment Bank, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, after meeting EIB Group Vice-President Karl Nehammer to mark the project’s completion.
The buses were purchased under the “Ukraine Urban Public Transport” project, backed by an EIB loan of 18.5 million euros, and arrived in several batches. All 85 will carry passengers on the capital’s routes, part of a push to modernize the fleet of the municipal operator Kyivpastrans even as the war grinds on.
“The purchase made it possible to increase the accessibility of public transportation in the capital and improve passenger travel conditions,” Klitschko said, thanking the EIB for its help.
What riders get on the new buses
The vehicles are built for accessibility. The 12-meter low-floor buses carry ramps for people with disabilities and limited mobility, information displays, air conditioning and heating, video surveillance cameras, stop announcements, energy-saving LED lighting, and tinted glass.
Each bus seats 27 passengers and holds another 80 standing. The vehicles are Turkish-built low-floor models that entered Kyiv service in batches between 2025 and 2026, aimed at riders whom older high-floor buses left behind, from wheelchair users to parents with strollers.
A European bank rebuilding the way Kyiv moves
The buses are one piece of a longer partnership. Since Russia’s war began, the EIB has provided more than 2 billion euros for emergency repairs to Ukraine’s infrastructure, the bank reported.
Its urban-transport work for Kyiv has already delivered 20 new low-floor trams, and the bank signed a separate 50-million-euro loan, the first tranche of a 200-million-euro package, to help the Kyiv metro replace coaches that were 80% Russian-made before the war and end its dependence on Russian spare parts, the EIB said. The money is intended to upgrade or replace between 120 and 160 metro coaches.

corten steel tubes lined with spruce plywood ribs form alpine learning burrow by officina 82
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:35:22 UTC
07:35:22 KST

corten steel tubes lined with spruce plywood ribs form alpine learning burrow by officina 82
tana delle marmotte inserts three prefabricated corten steel tubes lined with contoured spruce plywood ribs into the alpine terrain at monte bianco to create a reversible subterranean learning space.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
CORTEN STEEL CONDUITS FRAME REVERSIBLE UNDERGROUND structure
Positioned at an altitude of 2,173 meters at the Pavillon intermediate station of the Skyway Monte Bianco cableway in Aosta Valley, Italy, Tana delle Marmotte (Marmot Den) is a permanent underground educational installation designed by architecture practice Officina 82. Conceived as an experiential learning environment for children and teenagers, the project combines play with environmental education by translating the subterranean habitat of Alpine marmots into a modular architecture integrated directly into the mountain landscape.
SPRUCE RIBS FORM MODULAR TUNNEL INSPIRED BY MARMOT BURROWS
The pavilion’s primary structural shell consists of three prefabricated Corten steel conduits: an 8-meter-long central tube paired with two transverse access pipes measuring 2,200 mm and 1,300 mm in diameter. To preserve the high-altitude ecosystem, the structure by studio Officina 82 rests on a bed of fine gravel without permanent concrete foundations, ensuring complete structural reversibility. The Corten components were manufactured off-site with flanged connections, weight-calibrated for helicopter delivery, and dry-assembled on-site to minimize environmental disruption and eliminate the need for an extended construction footprint at altitude.
Dry assembly reduces construction time and minimizes disruption
Inside, the fit-out is lined with 40 mm thick, three-ply spruce plywood ribs anchored to perimeter timber rings that mirror the circular steel profile. Infilled with tongue-and-groove spruce boarding, these custom-contoured ribs form a continuous, fluid spatial volume inspired by the winter hibernation tunnels dug by marmots. The timber surfaces integrate multiple functions, serving as ergonomic seating, display cases, graphics mounts, and a carved staircase that leads to a transparent acrylic porthole where visitors can look out over the surrounding terrain. Overhead LED strips trace the curved interior profile to guide visitors along the educational route.

French authorities have sought to reassure the public after the country was swept by violent unrest last weekend. The ongoing crisis started with students protesting high prices and demanding education reform, but it soon escalated, with masked rioters looting shops and clashing with police. On Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez admitted the authorities "lost control" and failed to anticipate the scale of the violence.
Large-scale protests are also expected in Paris this weekend. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has already pledged a "massive" security deployment for the event.
Trump blames 'migrants, jihadists, and communists' for unrest
While the European nation has seen two relatively quiet nights in a row, images of burning cars, broken store windows and ransacked buildings have been used by politicians inside and outside of France to increase pressure on the current government, led by President Emmanuel Macron.
Notably, US President Donald Trump attributed the unrest to "migrants, jihadists, and communists," saying they had "conquered, looted, and burned (France) to the ground." While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 22, 2026
Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Russia deal
US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets is unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices, market watchers and analysts said, noting that the promised volumes are too small to ease a global supply squeeze.
Diesel prices have shot to record highs during the US-Israeli war on Iran, creating a political liability for Trump and his Republican party as they campaign to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Critics of Trump’s move said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel could help Moscow fund further attacks on Ukraine, undermining years of efforts to curb Russian energy revenues and raising the risk the Kremlin could profit while consumers get little relief from high fuel prices.
Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Russia frees retired US schoolteacher in goodwill gesture
Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022, from prison on Oct 21 and took him to St Petersburg to fly back to the United States, after talks that Washington said were a step towards ending the war in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin made the announcement at a meeting in St Petersburg with US envoy Steve Witkoff, who later said the talks will continue towards planned technical-level discussions involving the US, Russia and Ukraine.
Witkoff thanked Putin for Hubbard’s release and called the Russian leader a “humanitarian”, in footage of the exchange, a remark that drew sharp rebuke from Republican and Democratic lawmakers given Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Pope Leo will not need further cancer treatment
Pope Leo will not need any further therapy after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said on Oct 21, indicating that his tumour had not spread.
The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on Oct 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
PHP developers issue updates fixing vulnerabilities
Developers of the PHP programming language said a set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was now live, and acknowledged a delay in addressing a previously identified flaw.
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Oct 21 after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in PHP sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet and the vulnerabilities had raised concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack. The developers issued four patches to address two “critical” vulnerabilities that could allow hackers to execute code on vulnerable systems.
‘Mood of defeat’: Como hammer Manchester United
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a “mood of defeat” after conceding early in their 4-1 Champions League loss at Como on Oct 21, a result that increased scrutiny on manager Michael Carrick.
Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.
“We started on the wrong foot, and they scored very early,” Fernandes told TNT Sports. “There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.”

Russian Urals crude oil has plunged to a 1.5-month low — the price fell to $80 per barrel
Kyiv • UNN
Urals fell to around $80 per barrel due to a drop in Brent prices and high freight rates. This reduces Russia’s budget revenues.
The price of Russian Urals crude oil in the ports of the Baltic and Black seas has fallen to its lowest level in approximately 1.5 months. The price declined amid cheaper global oil and high transportation costs. Reuters reports this, citing LSEG data, UNN writes.
Details
This week, the price of Urals for loading in Primorsk, Ust-Luga and Novorossiysk fell to approximately $80 per barrel for the first time since the beginning of September. At the current exchange rate, this is about 6,630 rubles.
The main reason for the decline was a drop in Brent benchmark crude prices. The supply situation on the global market improved, while buyers gained more opportunities to purchase oil with shorter delivery times.
High transportation costs are reducing Russia’s revenues
More expensive transportation is creating additional pressure on Russian exporters. Due to a shortage of available tankers and military risks in the Black and Red seas, freight costs remain high.
Oil jumped by more than $2 amid statements from Iran21.10.26, 17:00 • 5122 views
Back in September, Russian oil prices rose sharply because of supply disruptions amid the conflict in the Middle East. At the time, Urals cost more than $100 per barrel, while on September 16 the price exceeded $110.
At the same time, global supplies of petroleum products partially recovered, in particular due to increased fuel exports from China and agreements between the United States and Russia on diesel fuel.
The decline in the price of Urals directly affects the revenues of the Russian budget, since the price of this grade of oil is used to calculate extraction taxes and determine oil and gas revenues.

Russian ballistic missiles struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, only hours after Washington's special envoy Steve Witkoff visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in in Saint Petersburg.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported these numbers in the morning, saying Russia had struck across Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Svyatoshynskyi and Dnipro dsitricts in Ukraine's capital.

The capital is particularly vulnerable as it is reliant on thermal and cogeneration plants that are exposed to enemy strikes, while substations that connect it to generation sources, including nuclear plants in western Ukraine, are protected against drones but not against ballistic missiles.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported power and Wi-Fi outages in parts of the city after a wave of ballistic missile strikes at around 3:34 a.m.
In the Dniprovskyi District, a car service station and a house were damaged late on Oct. 21 after the two sites were struck, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
"In the same district, debris also hit another house," he said. "There may be people trapped under the rubble."
At around 2 a.m. local time on Oct. 22, Russian attacks on Kyiv continued, filling the sky with the sounds of explosions.
In the Darnitsky District, also on the left bank of the Dnipro River that cuts through the city of 3 million, missiles hit near a transportation infrastructure facility.
"I was at home, in my private house," said Vladyslav, a resident of Kyiv living near one of the strikes. "When the explosion happened, our windows were blown out. Then we saw a terrifying glow outside; we ran out and saw a house on fire, and heard people screaming. 
"Fortunately, we managed to rescue a man and his wife who were inside the burning house. It's a stroke of luck that neighbors were nearby to help save these people."
Ballistic missiles again targeted Kyiv at around 3:00 a.m. local time, with at least 13 explosions rocking the city in less than eight minutes, the Kyiv Independent's Chris York said.
Following a series of explosions, the Kyiv City Military Administration said that a building housing a medical facility was damaged in the city's Pecherskyi District.
"All I see is broken windows on the floor, my neighbors are screaming, going out of their houses, and all they can do is just pray," Heorhii Rezhenko, a 26-year-old resident of Pecherskyi District, told the Kyiv Independent.
"In Europe, in the democratic world, everybody knows what happened here. The people know what happened, ... but they, for now, I think, can do nothing to stop it. Maybe all that I can say is please do something to stop it," Heorhii said.
"I am just very tired, because it was a very difficult day. But we will have more of these days."
Klitschko later confirmed that a paramedic station in the district was damaged, where six ambulances were also wrecked.
"In the Sviatoshynskyi District, a fire broke out inside a restaurant as a result of the enemy attack," the Kyiv City Military Administration added.
The latest attack comes as Russian forces continue to intensify missile and drone campaigns against Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin.
On the city's crucial Southern Bridge, transit infrastructure for the Kyiv Metro was damaged as a result of Russian strikes, Klitschko said.
The Military Administration also said that traffic in the direction from the right bank to the left bank has been restricted on the bridge.

"You, too, are a humanitarian, sir, and I commend you for that. I offer you my respect and thank you once again," he told the Russian leader wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine.
