Meta hit with $25-billion penalty for misleading Facebook users about data privacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:43:21 UTC
06:43:21 KST

Meta hit with $25-billion penalty for misleading Facebook users about data privacy
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Meta, the parent company of Facebook, was ordered by a New Mexico judge on Wednesday to pay $25 billion for misleading users about how it collects and safeguards user data.
The penalty, one of the largest ever levied against Meta or any other company, is the latest legal hit to the social media giant, which has grappled with lawsuits over allegations of social media addiction and child safety.
New Mexico sued the company in 2021 after revelations surfaced that a U.K. political consulting firm had harvested millions of Facebook users’ personal data without their consent. The major data privacy scandal sparked more scrutiny of Facebook and led to lawsuits, congressional hearings and multibillion-dollar fines.
A New Mexico jury dealt a blow to Meta, previously named Facebook, in September, finding that the social media company committed 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws by making false and misleading statements about data privacy protections and efforts to combat misinformation and hate speech.
“Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable,” New Mexico state Atty. Gen. Raúl Torrez said in a statement.
As part of the jury’s ruling, Meta faced up to $5,000 for each willful violation, according to a news release about the verdict.
Meta said in a statement it plans to appeal the ruling.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
Facebook was found to have deceived its users through statements and remarks made on its own platforms, interviews, earnings calls and other channels. The social media platform has privacy settings, but “they do not provide any meaningful control over their data in many ways,” and the company intentionally tried to mislead the public, according to the court’s judgment in the New Mexico case.
The judgment also found that Facebook committed to notifying users when an app misused their data and deliberately didn’t.
Meta made misleading statements about whether it sells people’s data and profits from misinformation or hate speech, along with other practices, the New Mexico jury found.
Meta has long grappled with data privacy lawsuits and complaints. The company has expanded beyond social networking and sells consumer gadgets, including smart glasses, that have also raised privacy concerns after allegations that people are being recorded without their knowledge.
The company has suffered from several high-profile legal blows this year that have resulted in multibillion-dollar penalties. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17 billion to resolve a child safety lawsuit filed by California and other states.
The company lost a child safety case in Los Angeles. New Mexico has also imposed other penalties on Meta this year. A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $942 million and take steps to make the platform safer after the state sued the company over allegations that it violated state consumer protection laws and enabled mental health harms to and sexual exploitation of young people.
In 2025, Meta reported roughly $200 billion in annual revenue and $60 billion in net income.
Meta reported third-quarter revenue of $64 billion on Wednesday, beating Wall Street’s expectations. But legal expenses totaling roughly $10 billion tied to the August agreement to resolve the case over the mental health of young people did affect Meta’s bottom line.
The company’s operating income that quarter was $13 billion, down 37% from the same period last year because of the legal costs.
Meta’s stock was up around 4% in after-hours trading.

New norms for DL: Driving tutorial pass mark may rise to 75%, select licence services to be free
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:43:14 UTC
06:43:14 KST

Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes. (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: Road transport ministry has proposed raising the pass mark for safe-driving tutorial assessment from 60% to 75% and waiving fees for specified driving-licence services availed through online Aadhaar authentication, along with charges for changes to licence particulars such as name and address.The proposed changes to driving licence rules are aimed at tightening assessment requirements and to ensure availing licence-related services without any hassle. The changes proposed in the draft notification to amend sections of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules published late Wednesday night also seek to streamline online driving licence services, specify acceptable identity and residence documents, and introduce time limits for processing applications to change licence particulars.Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes. The higher qualifying score of 70% is aimed at making the assessment more stringent. The draft also proposes a defined procedure for online applications to change driving licence particulars, including name and address. Licencing authorities would have to approve or reject applications for changes within 15 days, giving reasons for rejection.
An application for an address change that remains undecided for 30 days would be deemed approved.The proposed rules also specify documents that can be submitted as proof of identity, age and residence. These include Aadhaar, passport, voter identity card, recognised educational certificates and birth certificates, among other documents. Electricity and household gas bills not older than three months are among the proposed address-proof documents.
LIC policy would no more be accepted as a proof.The draft also provides for a consolidated application form covering services such as licence renewal, issuance of duplicate licences, addition of a vehicle class and changes to personal particulars. Specified applicant details would be retrieved electronically from the SARATHI portal wherever available.In another proposed change, a vehicle class would be deleted from a driving licence within seven days of an application to surrender it. However, applicants permanently surrendering a class would not be eligible to obtain a learner’s or driving licence for that class for one year.The draft notification invites objections and suggestions from stakeholders within 30 days of publication. The proposals will come into force after final notification.

Pope Leo XIV needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:41:19 UTC
06:41:19 KST

Pope Leo XIV needs no further lung cancer treatment, Vatican says
Pope Leo XIV, 71, will require no further treatment for lung cancer after tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said Wednesday. The pontiff underwent surgery last week to remove part of his right lung after being diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. He was discharged Saturday and will gradually resume activities.
Pope Leo XIV got good news from his doctors: The pontiff will need no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said in a statement Wednesday.
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Leo was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Polyclinic on Saturday, four days after surgery, and said he would gradually resume his activities.
The pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the pope's surgery confirmed the diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread.
“A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors said.
The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all the cancer was removed.
Read morePope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
Additional treatment is offered in such cases if follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread, such as through the lymph nodes, or has certain other signs that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumors are caught very early, such as when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot long before it’s large or causing symptoms.
The pope appears to have had one of those “incidental findings", a nodule in his lung spotted during another exam.
In an interview with Vatican News on Saturday, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations, and that the pope had not been experiencing any symptoms.
“The statements suggest that this is a stage I lung cancer for which surgery is highly effective and expected to be curative,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. He said the lack of further treatment suggests a relatively small cancer, and that it had not spread to lymph nodes.
The pope carried on business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St. Peter's Square and Wednesday's longer audience in the square, greeting the faithful from around the world.
“Thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers," Leo said during the audience.
His next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Margaritora told Vatican News that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high altitude stops.
The pope had revealed that a nodule would be surgically removed during the traditional Sunday blessing on October 11, in an unusually transparent disclosure broadcast on live television that broke the tradition of secrecy surrounding papal health issues.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Türkiye plans to invest over $2 billion in space, aviation over next 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:40:46 UTC
06:40:46 KST

Zeynep Duyar
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Ankara is expected to allocate nearly 100 billion Turkish liras ($2.01 billion) to its aviation and space industries over the next three years, according to the 2027 central government budget draft and budget justification.
The budget for the country's space and aviation program stood at $176 million this year and is set to increase by 181.7% to $495.7 million in 2027 to strengthen Türkiye's global competitiveness in the sector.
Funding is projected to increase to $616.9 million in 2028 and $745 million in 2029.
Some $377.3 million will be allocated to the construction, operation and servicing of air transport facilities, while aviation infrastructure investments are projected to reach $581.1 million in 2028 and $596.2 million in 2029 amid growing demand for domestic travel.
Ankara aims to welcome 272 million airport passengers next year, including direct transit passengers, 282 million in 2028 and 291 million in 2029.
The space sector budget will support Türkiye's National Space Program, as well as related research, testing infrastructure and the commercialization of high-value-added homegrown technologies.
Türkiye achieved significant milestones in recent years with its first homegrown communications satellite, Turksat 6A, as well as its sub-meter Earth observation satellite, Imece.
The country also participated in its first crewed science missions in 2024, when space travelers Alper Gezeravci and Tuva Cihangir Atasever completed various experiments in space.
The southwestern city of Antalya hosted the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) on Oct. 5-9, ahead of preparations for Türkiye's first deep-space lunar mission next year.
The lunar mission hinges on a homegrown spacecraft featuring more than 80% local content and a hybrid propulsion system.
The spacecraft has completed assembly and is undergoing further testing.
Meanwhile, the Turkish Space Agency continues its efforts to establish a spaceport in Somalia to ensure Türkiye's independent access to orbit.

U.S. ordering some staff to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes

U.S. ordering some government staff to depart Saudi Arabia, reducing military footprint in Middle East
The U.S. State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia, following an uptick in attacks on the kingdom by Iran-backed Houthi militants.
The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday.
The State Department "issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote in a Wednesday X post, pushing back on a report that orders could apply to other Gulf states.
CBS News has learned several other embassies adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, but have not gone on ordered departure, which involves the mandatory evacuation of designated diplomatic staff and accompanying family due to security risks.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
The decision to draw down personnel in Saudi Arabia comes after U.S. embassies in the kingdom, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries issued warnings over the weekend, urging Americans in the region to exercise caution and prepare for travel disruptions due to Houthi attacks.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said Wednesday.
The Houthis have launched drones and missiles at airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month that killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. One American was among those killed.
The attacks have continued, with a Saudi-led military coalition reporting that it intercepted multiple Houthi drones on Monday and Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Tuesday that air defenses blocked a drone attack on the country's Shaybah oil field. Two people were killed and two were injured by falling debris, according to the agency, which did not specify who launched the drone.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have sought to expand their territorial control in Yemen. The group has controlled a large swath of the country for more than a decade, including the capital of Sanaa.
Some Saudi officials have blamed Iran for the conduct of the Houthis, which are aligned with the Islamic Republic. Iran has denied any role in the escalation.
The conflict could cause problems beyond Saudi Arabia due to the Houthis' proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key maritime chokepoint that a large share of the world's oil flows through. The strait has become more important in recent months due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz wrought by the U.S.-Iran war.
Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the Foreign Minister of Yemen, warned in an interview with CBS News on Tuesday that the Houthis could continue their attacks unless confronted.
"We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," Noman said, adding that the Yemeni government is seeking international assistance.
The United Kingdom has offered support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive air operations.
It's not clear whether the Trump administration is also planning to assist Saudi Arabia. President Trump did not rule out strikes on the Houthis after the group's deadly Oct. 10 attack on the Riyadh airport, telling reporters: "We may."
Mr. Trump said earlier this month: "We have communication with the Houthis, and we'll see what happens. But what they did was very bad."

Russia is preparing to attend the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta, Georgia later this month but sees “concerning trends” in US actions that could prevent its full participation, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Wednesday.

"We have been and are continuing to prepare, and our experts are actively working on this," she stressed.
She described the meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 30-31, as "an important preparatory event" for the G20 Leaders’ Summit on Dec. 14-15 in Doral, Florida, near Miami, where participants were expected to discuss complex issues affecting the global economy, including food supplies, energy security and global supply chains.
"We are observing, to put it mildly, concerning trends that could prevent this scenario from being realized," she said.

"There is no question of us having failed to submit something, complete some paperwork, or provide something to someone," she stressed.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov previously said that no decision had been made on whether Russian President Vladimir Putin would attend the leaders’ summit in Doral in person.
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Putin’s participation.
- Russia seeks clarification from Kazakhstan on new entry rules
Turning to Kazakhstan, Zakharova said Russia expects it to provide additional clarification on its new rules for entry permits, which will also affect citizens of Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states.
"We respect, of course, the republic’s sovereign right to improve its national migration legislation," she said, adding that Moscow expected clarification on how the new provisions would be applied in light of existing international agreements, including those within the EAEU and other Eurasian migration frameworks.
Such clarification would help inform citizens in a timely manner and facilitate travel, employment, business ties and humanitarian contacts between the two countries, she added.
The Kazakh government previously approved rules introducing electronic entry permits for Russian citizens and nationals of other visa-exempt countries from July 1, 2027. The permits will be free of charge and must be obtained electronically at least 72 hours before crossing the border.
From November 2026 until July 1, 2027, the absence of a permit will not constitute grounds for denying entry, although border officials will inform travelers of the requirement. From July 1, 2027 onwards, the permit will become mandatory.
- Zakharova questions Poland and Lithuania’s response to Ukrainian drone incident

With irony, she suggested several possible responses to Kyiv, including closing diplomatic missions, expelling Ukrainian diplomats, summoning Ukrainian ambassadors for a formal protest or preparing a package of sanctions against Ukraine.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk previously called on Ukrainian authorities to explain how a Ukrainian drone had flown over Polish territory before later exploding in Lithuania.

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said the drone, which had taken off from Ukrainian territory, was carrying explosives.
Vilnius and Warsaw have disagreed over the flight path of the drone, which crashed in northern Lithuania. Lithuania maintains that the drone was Ukrainian and had been involved in the attack on St. Petersburg before being diverted by Russian electronic warfare systems and falling in Lithuania. According to the Lithuanian military, it entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland.
Polish media, however, reported that the drone had been launched from Lithuanian territory, approximately 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) from the Polish border.

AIPAC to stop officially endorsing US political candidates following criticism - report

Pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC announced on Wednesday that it will no longer officially endorse candidates in US elections or send direct donations through its political action committee, as first reported by Jewish Insider.
According to the report, the decision comes after several pro-Israel politicians became the target of significant criticism following the group's endorsement of them.
In an official statement, AIPAC explained that "official endorsements of candidates, direct contributions from the political action committee (PAC), and the earmarking of donations for specific candidates will no longer be part of our approach," the report said.
"This will allow us to expand individual contributions and utilize new tools to help our allies win," the statement added.
The statement reportedly says that the decision was reached after a several-month-long strategic process and a review by the AIPAC Board of Directors.
In late 2021, AIPAC launched its first federal action committee (AIPAC PAC) and the United Democracy Project (super PAC). Just five years later, the lobby group has pivoted from official candidate endorsement and direct contributions back to unearmarked donor contributions and continued independent expenditures through its super PAC.
AIPAC support became divisive issue in US midterm elections
In primary elections across the US, AIPAC took center stage as candidates dug up a history of engagement with AIPAC to turn voters against their opponents.
In New York this summer, Brad Lander defeated Dan Goldman in a hotly contested Democratic primary, where their views on Israel, and more specifically on AIPAC, became a focal point.
Lander's campaign emphasized his refusal to take campaign donations from AIPAC, while Goldman came under attack because he had accepted political endorsement from the group.
Similarly, in the Oklahoma Democratic primary election in August, candidate N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas built her platform on anti-AIPAC messaging and defeated the centrist candidate Jim Priest.
Throughout the midterm and primary campaigns, candidates endorsed by AIPAC have increasingly been targeted for that support. AIPAC's decision to cease providing official support to candidates comes amid increasing focus and scrutiny on the actions of Israel by American politicians and voters.

Russia Surrounds Major Shahed Drone Production Hub With 33 Air Defense Positions in Tatarstan
Russia has built 33 air defense positions around the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, a major production hub for Shahed-type attack drones, according to satellite imagery from October 21 analyzed by Radio Liberty.
The images show a substantial expansion of air defense infrastructure around one of Russia's primary facilities for manufacturing Geran-type drones, derived from Iranian Shahed designs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Since spring 2026, Russian forces have constructed several concrete towers for air defense systems and additional elevated platforms designed to accommodate Pantsir or Tor short-range air defense systems.
The Pantsir combines surface-to-air missiles and automatic cannons to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones. The Tor is a mobile short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to engage aerial targets, including precision-guided weapons and unmanned aircraft.
The report also identified towers equipped with heavy anti-aircraft machine guns inside the Alabuga complex. Additional structures have been installed to support anti-drone nets stretched over production buildings, providing another protective layer against aerial attacks.
The extensive fortifications make Alabuga one of Russia's most heavily protected facilities against Ukrainian drone strikes. Radio Liberty noted that Ukrainian drones last reached the site in June 2025, with no comparable attacks recorded there since.
The scale of the protective buildup reflects Alabuga’s growing weight in Russia's drone program. The complex has reportedly reached a capacity of more than 3,000 gasoline-powered Shahed-type drones and more than 3,500 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month.
Chinese suppliers have been linked to that expansion, providing an industrial airframe production line, more than 685,000 engine components valued at about $900,000, and 7,800 lithium-ion batteries in 2024. Chinese technology also contributed to navigation systems designed to withstand electronic warfare, including satellite antennas that were reportedly exported as agricultural products.

The CGT, which took part in the 17 October demonstrations that degenerated into riots and looting in several cities over the weekend, will once again take to the streets on Saturday for the "act II" of the cost-of-living mobilisation announced by a "yellow vest" coordination.
For the unions, the central objective remains the mobilisation launched by almost all of them among private- and public-sector employees for 5 November. "The time has come to move the mobilisation up a gear; from that date strike action must take over", said Sophie Binet.
By then, the secretary-general of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT, the country’s largest union), Marylise Léon, expects "social responses" to workers’ expectations.
According to the president of the French Confederation of Christian Workers (CFTC), Cyril Chabanier, the government has nonetheless "opened the door" to "a discussion" on raising the minimum wage. On this issue, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has called for things to "move quickly".
At Matignon, the unions also regretted that secondary school and student organisations had not been invited to the meeting.
They are expected to be received again on Monday by the education minister. Édouard Geffray has promised initial measures to respond to the demands expressed on the platform set up by the government. On a Middle East tour, Emmanuel Macron calls for "firmness"

The president, however, made no announcements on the many demands voiced by the protesters, including on purchasing power or funding for schools and universities.
Emmanuel Macron, who then travelled on to Saudi Arabia where he was received by crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman, said the French would get a "fair return" from this tour, notably on diesel prices.
On Wednesday, several political figures from across the spectrum again condemned what they see as a failure of those in power. Édouard Philippe, the Horizons presidential candidate, criticised Emmanuel Macron’s decision to maintain his trip to the Gulf. Former head of state François Hollande, for his part, attacked a government he considers weak. Marine Le Pen, the National Rally candidate for the presidential election, targeted what she called the "waning power".
Several curfews renewed
In Paris, the police prefecture has imposed a new curfew in certain areas for the night from Wednesday to Thursday.
The decrees "ban the presence of adults and minors alike in the areas around Place de la République and the Les Halles district from 11 pm today until 6 am tomorrow", the police prefecture said on X.
In Lyon, the Rhône prefecture has decided to renew the curfew and the ban on gatherings, extending the measures that were in force on the previous two nights in Lyon. The curfew runs from 11 pm to 6 am, two hours later than the previous ones, which started at 9 pm.
Around 2,500 people in police custody and 174 jailed
During a visit to Marseille, which saw violent clashes at the weekend and where the town hall was vandalised, justice minister Gérald Darmanin reported 2,500 people taken into police custody following the violence and the looting of numerous shops during the 17 October mobilisation.
Of these, 917 people have been brought before prosecutors with charges to be tried in immediate appearances. The minister, who pledged that justice would be firm, said this figure had doubled, or even tripled.
In Paris, of the 557 people taken into custody after the violence and looting in the capital, 300 appeared before a magistrate by midday on Wednesday. On Tuesday evening, Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said that none had claimed a motive "of whatever political nature", even as the government accuses "the ultra-left" of being largely behind the violence.
The strategy for maintaining public order has also been called into question for several weeks. The Defender of Rights announced on Tuesday that it had received 46 complaints since the start of the secondary school students’ movement, more than ten of which concern incidents from the weekend. At the same time, the IGPN, the police internal affairs body, has been tasked with at least six investigations relating to those two days.

US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as fears of escalating Houthi attacks rise
The State Department is ordering some diplomats and the families of U.S. government employees to leave Saudi Arabia following a series of deadly attacks in the country by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels and rising fears of an escalation in hostilities.
The department said Wednesday it had ordered the departure of non-essential staff at the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the Iran war and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although some diplomats had returned in recent months.
In a new travel alert, the department said, "Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
A series of previous alerts for Saudi Arabia issued over the past several days have used almost identical language and noted that U.S. government personnel need special permission to use any Saudi airport. The Houthis have routinely targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, and it had been closed since Oct. 10 following a severe attack.
But earlier Wednesday, aircraft from a limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the airport, two days after Saudi aviation authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Still, major carriers like Lufthansa and Air France have canceled flights to Riyadh through mid-November. Saudi airlines, including Saudia and FlyNas, were among those operating flights Wednesday.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Although the ordered departure applies only to Saudi Arabia, U.S. embassies in other Gulf countries will see temporary staffing changes, the department said. Those embassies are already under “restricted operations” that limit the number of personnel working there.
Meanwhile, tensions grew as Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said debris from an intercepted drone killed two people and injured two others at an Aramco-operated oil field in the country’s southeast.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said the group had fired five drones toward Saudi Arabia early Wednesday. The coalition said the drones were intercepted and destroyed over the holy city of Madinah and the Eastern Region.
The attempted attack was the latest on Saudi Arabia since the resurgence of fighting with the Houthis in mid-July.

Mexico charges prosecutor with treason over US involvement in drug raid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:25:21 UTC
06:25:21 KST

Mexico charges prosecutor with treason over US involvement in drug raid
The alleged participation of US agents in an April drug operation has raised questions about whether Mexican law was upheld.
Mexico has taken the rare step of charging a former state prosecutor with treason, alleging that he allowed United States agents to take part in a drug raid on the country’s territory.
The case underscores sensitivities about US involvement in Mexico and concerns about the Latin American country’s sovereignty.
On Wednesday, former Chihuahua Attorney General Cesar Jauregui was accused of permitting US agents to take part in an antidrug operation in the northwestern border state.
Under Mexican law, the federal government must approve the activities of foreign forces on the country’s soil.
But questions emerged about whether the law was being adhered to after two US agents and two Mexican law enforcement officials were killed in a car accident on April 19.
News outlets, citing anonymous sources, reported that the US agents had been collaborating with state law enforcement in the destruction of a drug lab.
Matias Gomez Leautaud, an analyst at the Eurasia Group, a US-based risk consultancy firm, told the news service Reuters that the treason charge “seeks to set a precedent and prevent cooperation between [Mexican] states and the US government without the federal government’s coordination and approval”.
While the administration of President Claudia Sheinbaum has collaborated with the US on issues of crime and insecurity, it has opposed any effort by the US to work directly with Mexican states without federal authorisation first.
In the days after the April car crash, Sheinbaum indicated that her government was not aware that US agents had been involved in a drug operation in Chihuahua.
“Evidently, the military didn’t know there were people participating who weren’t Mexican citizens,” Sheinbaum told reporters at the time.
She called for an investigation into whether state officials had respected Mexico’s constitution and its National Security Law, which govern the involvement of foreign forces on Mexican territory.
The constitution, for example, requires Senate approval for the presence of any foreign troops in Mexico. The country has a long history of US intervention, including multiple military invasions continuing into the early 20th century.
But concerns about the US respecting Mexican sovereignty have risen since US President Donald Trump returned to office for a second term.
Trump has suggested that the US could take unilateral military action in Mexico to address cartel drug-trafficking and violence, and he has characterised Mexico’s government as ineffective in addressing the problem.
“We have to eradicate them,” Trump said of the cartels in March. “We have to knock the hell out of them because they’re getting worse. They’re taking over their country. The cartels are running Mexico.”
In the aftermath of the April crash, conflicting reports emerged about why the two US agents were in the country.
Media identified them as members of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), a US foreign intelligence branch with a history of covert operations.
But state officials denied claims that they were involved in a drug bust. In a news release on April 20, Jauregui “ruled out the involvement of foreign personnel” in his state’s drug operations.
Instead, he said that US instructors had been present nearby for a training session about drones. They subsequently requested to join a convoy of Mexican law enforcement personnel to return to the airport, according to Jauregui.
“It is worth explaining what happened, in order to clarify the facts that are causing some confusion,” Jauregui said at the time.
He resigned from his post as state attorney general later that month.
Mexico’s federal Attorney General Ernestina Godoy has since accused Jauregui of permitting foreign agents to participate in operations on Mexican territory without first sharing information with federal officials.
A judge has ordered Jauregui to be held in pretrial detention as the court decides whether there is sufficient evidence to move forward with a criminal case.
Experts say the treason charge he faces is vaguely defined in Mexican law. It broadly covers acts that undermine Mexico’s sovereignty for the benefit of a foreign entity.
Convictions are rare, with the last widely recognised example coming in 1867, when Emperor Maximilian was tried by court-martial and subsequently executed for crimes against Mexico.
Jauregui is a member of the National Action Party, a conservative political movement in Mexico. Sheinbaum, meanwhile, is a leader in the left-wing Morena party.

garnet-red accents and high clerestories punctuate AA Apartments in málaga
crearctive transforms a former commercial space into four residential units using a central service spine, high-level facade glazing, and elevated mezzanines.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
AA Apartments reuse open-plan commercial space in Málaga
Designed by CREARCTIVE, AA Apartments addresses the adaptive reuse of a former open-plan commercial space in Málaga, converting the premises into four independent residential units. To make full use of the building’s four-meter clear height, the interior layout works in section, utilizing a centralized service spine that frees the perimeter and accommodates a mezzanine level above.
CLERESTORIES AND GEOMETRIC OCULUS DISTRIBUTE CROSS-LIGHTING
The central core houses the compact wet and utility functions, including bathrooms, kitchen areas, walk-in closets, storage, and MEP services, enabling unimpeded air circulation and visual continuity across the entire depth of each apartment. Above this service volume, the architects at CREARCTIVE add a flexible mezzanine to serve as a multi-use loft space. A geometric oculus cut into the partition wall establishes a diagonal light connection between the mezzanine and the double-height living area, channeling light toward the rear bedroom zone. Access to the mezzanine is provided via a garnet-red metal ladder mounted onto a built-in bench.
GARNET-RED METALWORK PUNCTUATES RESIDENCES’ NEUTRAL PALETTE
Natural light enters through high-level, atelier-style clerestory windows along the facade, illuminating the interiors while maintaining street-level privacy. The material palette pairs neutral-toned flooring and white walls with a subtle tonal shift along the upper wall boundary to scale the vertical space, punctuated by garnet-red accents across the metalwork and carpentry.

Meta fined $25 billion in New Mexico over Cambridge Analytica scandal
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company deceived users in a case linked to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, media reported Wednesday. The ruling follows an $18 billion settlement with 48 other states over similar claims. Meta called the penalty “a tax on speech".
A New Mexico judge ruled Wednesday that Meta must pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, according to media reports.
The penalty comes a couple of months after Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta slammed the case as "a tax on speech".
"This ruling ... makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Meta said in a statement. "We are confident we will prevail on appeal."
Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting firm found to have improperly harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users for targeted political advertising, notably during the 2016 US presidential election.
Read moreFake AI images of protester go viral after woman punched at Trump's Ohio rally
Revelations at the time showed that the firm had obtained data gathered through a personality quiz app called "thisisyourdigitallife," which was installed by about 270,000 users but also collected information on their friends.
In total, the app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users worldwide.
Facebook learned in December 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had acquired the data but did not disclose it publicly until 2018, after a whistleblower came forward, sparking a major political scandal.
Jurors in the New Mexico trial found that the misconduct affected all of the state's more than 2.1 million residents.
"We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement in September.
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez hailed the ruling as a "historic" win.
This case was "about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexicostood its ground," Torrez said in a statement.
Read more'The harms have come to outweigh the benefits' of social media, researcher says
Penalties pile up
Meta has faced a slew of lawsuits in recent months.
Earlier this year, New Mexico won nearly $1 billion in combined penalties against Metain a separate case over harms to children.
In March, a jury in that case ordered Meta to pay $375 million after finding the company liable for endangering children by making them vulnerable to predators on its platforms, among other harms.
In August, a judge ordered Meta to implement product changes and pay an additional $567 million to the state to fund the treatment and prevention of harms caused by Facebook and Instagram.
That same month, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.7 billion to 52 US states, plus Washington, DC, to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13.
As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to make significant changes to Facebook and Instagram accounts used by teenagers, and portions of the settlement hinge on other major social media companies agreeing to similar changes.
In September, TikTok agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million and enact limits for teen users, avoiding a trial over claims related to child safety on the platform.
TikTok previously settled other cases that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
In a landmark trial that concluded in March, Meta and YouTube were convicted by a Los Angeles jury, which found both companies were responsible for a teenager's social media addiction.
That jury awarded the teenager $6 million.

Palestinian women, girls resume boxing in tent amid Gaza devastation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:21:29 UTC
06:21:29 KST

Hosni Nedim, Muhammed Emin Canik
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Palestinian women and girls have resumed boxing training in a tent in Gaza after their club was destroyed during Israel's attacks on the besieged enclave.
The Gaza Boxing Women club, located in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood west of Gaza City, has restarted activities in a makeshift tent after its gym was destroyed and its equipment was damaged in Israeli attacks.
Although the tent falls far short of the facilities the athletes once used, the club's reopening has provided women and girls with a space to continue training after a lengthy interruption.
Palestinian boxing coach and national referee Nader Yassin is working to revive the club with limited resources. The athletes, aged 7 to 40, are training both to improve their boxing skills and to ease the psychological pressure caused by the conflict.
Yassin told Anadolu that before the attacks, the club had a spacious gym equipped with boxing gloves, punch pads and other necessary equipment.
"We lost all our tools and equipment in the Israeli attacks," Yassin said. "Today, although we do not have a suitable place to practice sports, we are training in a tent with the limited resources available."
He said the training sessions aim to help women and girls cope with the pressure caused by the attacks, improve their physical fitness and temporarily escape the hardships of daily life.
Despite inadequate facilities and growing difficulties, Yassin said he was determined to continue training and hoped to develop athletes capable of competing successfully in matches and tournaments.  
‘We decided to rebuild what was destroyed’
Athlete Vela Abu Neda said returning to training meant more than simply resuming a sport she loved after a three-year break caused by the conflict.
Before the Israeli attacks, Abu Neda trained in better conditions, with a proper gym and adequate equipment. She said the destruction of the club and loss of its facilities prevented her from practicing boxing during the intervening period.
"After three years of Israeli attacks, we decided to start again and rebuild what was destroyed," Abu Neda said. "Today, despite our very limited resources, the lack of a suitable place and insufficient equipment, we did not give up. We continue our training, even in a tent."
Abu Neda said boxing was more than a sport for her, adding that she used training to cope with the stress and psychological pressure accumulated during the attacks.
She said returning to training had helped her release negative energy and partially regain her psychological balance.
"The war prevented me from practicing my sport for three years, but I did not give up. Today, I have returned to start again," she said. 
More than 1,000 athletes, scouts killed
Mustafa Siam, secretary-general of the Palestinian Sports Media Association, previously told Anadolu that Palestinians in Gaza were seeking to revive sporting activities following three years of Israeli attacks.
Siam said more than 1,000 athletes and scouts had been killed during the attacks, while more than 265 sports facilities had been completely or partially destroyed.
He said the return of tournaments to Gaza would mean more than simply resuming sporting competitions, adding that sporting activities could help children and young people affected by war, displacement and loss recover psychologically and socially while preserving their athletic abilities.
Overall, since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, injured 175,000 others and destroyed or damaged about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.

From Oct 2030, all new car models would be required to be equipped with the advanced emergency braking system (AEBS), the most important ADAS feature, TOI has learnt.As for pre-2030 still-in production models, AEBS would mandatory from Oct 2032.The draft notification, with timelines for different ADAS safety features for cars, would be out soon, people aware of the development said, adding that focus would be more on taxis. They said the proposed timelines take into account the lead time that industry and users would need.ADAS is a set of more than 100 electronic technologies that increases safety by detecting potential hazards, warning the driver, and in some cases, automatically controlling brakes or steering to prevent a collision. At present, some cars have ADAS.
Starting Jan 2027, new truck and bus models will have AEBS — it detects an imminent collision with a vehicle or obstacle and automatically applies brakes, if the driver fails to respond adequately, preventing a crash or reducing its severity.
Blind spot information, moving off information and driver drowsiness detection and alert, and lane departure warning systems have been also made mandatory for these commercial vehicles.
It’s learnt that features, including automatic command steering functionalities, emergency lane keeping system, drowsiness and attention warning systems, would be made mandatory for taxis.The introduction of these norms could initially focus on ensuring compliance with Automotive Industry Standards for vehicles already equipped with AEBS or more advanced systems that can intervene in steering and lane-keeping, said Automobile and mobility expert Rama Pandey. “These technologies could prove a boon for commercial drivers who spend hours behind the wheel. By shifting more safety-critical & fatigue-inducing driving decisions to automated systems, ADAS could make driving safer and less strenuous,” he added.

The social effect of MAGA: The American nation breathes

The social effect of MAGA: The American nation breathes
Published 21 Oct, 2026 21:19
Despite the disappointment among voters regarding the state of the economy in the US in recent years, there are observable effects and trends of social improvement.
First and foremost, it’s important to note a significant decrease in the level of violent crime. Of course, after President Donald Trump’s controversial firing of the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Erica McEntarfer, for publishing weak labor market figures, trust in American statistics has been considerably shaken. Thus, reports of achieving the lowest murder rate in history – 4.3 cases per 100,000 population – may be politically motivated and deliberately boastful. Nevertheless, a noticeable decline in the rate of murders and other violent crimes has indeed occurred in recent years. This can be attributed to increased federal funding and strengthening of the police force, as well as intensified efforts against illegal immigration during the Trump administration.
A particularly striking aspect of this is the comparison with Canada, which has been and remains a bastion of liberalism in immigration and domestic policy. Unlike the US, where the level of violent crime is traditionally high, Canada has always been perceived as a safe society. But now, everything is changing before our eyes.
Since 2015, the rate of violent crime per capita in the U.S. has decreased by 15.1%, while in Canada, on the contrary, it has increased by 36.9%. As a result, for the first time in history, the land of the maple leaf has surpassed the U.S. in terms of violent crime per capita.
Another significant trend: Gallup polls show that the perception of homosexual relationships as morally acceptable has stopped increasing and even declined in the US The share of those supporting same-sex marriage fell from 71% in 2023 to 64% in 2026. Support for gender transition practices among Americans decreased from 46% to 38%.
The most radical shift has occurred among Republicans. While Democrats’ acceptance of the morality of homosexual relationships remains at 80%, and independent voters have dropped from 74% in 2021 to 64% in 2026, among Republicans, the acknowledgment of homosexual relations plummeted from 56% in 2022 to 35% today (see chart). Only 5% of Republican voters consider gender transition morally acceptable – compared to 42% of independents and 60% of Democrats.
As we can see, the MAGA effect is concentrated within the Republican electorate and primarily manifests in the consolidation of Republicans based on traditional values. At the same time, there is an intensifying value conflict between conservative Republicans and the Democratic Party electorate.
Perhaps the most vivid manifestation of the MAGA effect is that in the summer of 2024, the trend of decreasing births among white Americans was replaced by steady growth, and by spring 2026, the proportion of newborns from white families reached 51.5%, the first increase in five years.
Let’s see if this trend can be maintained, but the mere fact of the growth in births among white Americans is quite remarkable – it demonstrates a surge of optimism in the WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) community and proves that they still have fight left in them. In an era of victorious globalization, WASPs in the US were already being metaphorically buried with a derogatory epitaph, yet they suddenly breathed life and showed they are ready to fight for their country, which their ancestors built.
It is noteworthy that conservative and religious Americans have twice as many children as their liberal and non-religious counterparts. Thus, the conservative American community reproduces itself (total fertility rate 2.22), while the liberal American environment naturally shrinks by half in each subsequent generation (total fertility rate 1.02), mainly replenishing itself through immigration.
The descendants of pilgrims and pioneers remember that the primary traditional value is the will to live. Everything one needs to know about MAGA can be boiled down to two points. First, it is the rise of the American spirit. Second, it serves as a visual reiteration of a biblical lesson: the salvation of those who are drowning is in the hands of the drowners themselves.

El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele threatened Haitian gangs on Wednesday with a broader military offensive if they fail to release four Salvadoran aviation technicians who are being held hostage in Haiti.
“Today's attack is nothing compared to what is coming if you do not return all four hostages alive,” he wrote on US social media company X.
Bukele said his government launched a military operation to rescue the men, adding that the priority was to bring them home alive and unharmed.
The president said the technicians were part of an international mission in Haiti focused on medical evacuations and saving lives, rather than combat operations.
He accused the gangs of kidnapping the men while they were returning from buying food at a supermarket.
Bukele warned gang leaders that the operation Wednesday was only the beginning if the hostages were not safely returned.
He also invoked his government's crackdown on criminal gangs in El Salvador, warning Haitian groups that his country could take similar action against them.
“We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” said Bukele, adding that the groups still had time to avoid escalation.
The four Salvadorans were deployed as part of the international Gang Suppression Force, which supports Haitian security forces in combating armed criminal groups.
They went missing after an ambush on Sunday, when their armored vehicle came under fire and was hit with explosives near Croix-des-Bouquets, outside the capital, Port-au-Prince.
The vehicle caught fire, and efforts to locate the personnel have been hampered by continued fighting in the area.
The incident underscores the security challenges facing the international mission as gangs maintain a strong presence in parts of Haiti.

Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine and US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:17:09 UTC
06:17:09 KST

Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin says
In short:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
The Russian leader has met with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
What's next?
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he supports the proposal, and is hopeful the three-way talks will take place in early November.
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume three-way negotiations next month with Washington and Kyiv aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
The Russian leader met US envoy Steve Witkoff for talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg.
Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the focus would be on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends".
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Mr Witkoff's talks with Mr Putin about Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took place as US President Donald Trump pushed Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that only a leaders' summit can break the impasse.
Latest proposals have little of value, Kremlin says
The Kremlin said the discussion in St Petersburg lasted about three hours and came a day after Mr Witkoff met Mr Zelenskyy and some European leaders in Norway's capital, Oslo.
Mr Ushakov said the proposals from the Oslo meeting "contained little of real value in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis".
However, he later told Russian state TV that while Moscow was not "fully satisfied" with the Oslo proposals, they were a step in the right direction.
Mr Zelenskyy said he supported the proposal for three-way talks.
"We have received feedback that … Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams," he said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that …The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Mr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Witkoff sees 'some degree of momentum' in peace efforts
Mr Witkoff and Mr Putin met at St Petersburg's Constantine Palace, with Mr Ushakov and Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also at the table.
Mr Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussion via a video link.
Before the meeting, Mr Witkoff said that there was "some degree of momentum" in talks.
In televised opening remarks, Mr Witkoff thanked Mr Putin for agreeing to send diesel to the US after Mr Trump lifted a ban despite anger from some US lawmakers, adding that the fuel would help reduce prices for American farmers and truckers.
Mr Putin said he was ready to consider restoring US-Russia economic ties and was prepared to discuss the US-led conflict with Iran.
He said Moscow stands ready to use its relationship with Tehran to help bring peace.
Mr Ushakov said that "large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant prospects for cooperation" between Russia and the US were discussed in detail with Mr Witkoff.
"Some of these are, in fact, nearing the implementation stage," he said.
Russia resumes attacks on Ukraine
Just as Russia indicated its readiness to join the trilateral peace talks, officials in Ukraine reported the capital Kyiv had been attacked with ballistic missiles on Wednesday evening, local time.
Homes, a petrol station and transport equipment were damaged and six people were injured.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram there were strikes in two districts on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, and posted on social media:
"Explosions in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic attack.
"Stay in shelters!"
The city remained under a drone warning for more than two hours after the initial alert was declared.
Russian authorities also said they downed most of the 630 drones heading towards Moscow overnight.
Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram that two people were injured in the attack outside of the city.

JUBA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan's Political Parties Council (PPC) on Wednesday announced the registration of four pre-election coalitions, comprising 25 political parties, ahead of the country's scheduled general elections on Dec. 22.
James Akol Zakayo, chairperson of the PPC, confirmed that the four coalitions have met the requirements for entry in the council's register.
The approved blocs are the National Agenda Coalition of Political Parties (NAC), the Coalition of National Alliance of Political Parties (CNA), the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), and the National Alliance of Political Parties (NAPP).

The NAC comprises 10 political parties, the CNA includes six, the SSOA holds five, and the NAPP consists of four parties, Zakayo said.
He urged the leaders of the 25 constituent parties to complete outstanding internal documentation, secure the required signatures and make the necessary legal deposits with the council's registry department by Thursday, the Oct. 22 deadline.
The Dec. 22 vote will be South Sudan's first general election since it gained independence in 2011. ■

China is willing to work with Russia to strengthen strategic communication, consolidate political mutual trust, expand all-round mutually beneficial cooperation, and continuously enhance the well-being of the two peoples, he said.
Li noted that China is ready to work with Russia to better leverage their economic complementarity, maintain the sound momentum of bilateral cooperation, strengthen practical cooperation in energy and resources, trade and investment, transportation and other areas, deliver more positive outcomes and promote common prosperity in both countries.

Russia-China relations are built on the basis of equality and mutual respect, mutual benefit and win-win results, and accommodation of each other's concerns, he said, noting that bilateral relations are not affected by changes in the international landscape and not subject to interference from any third party.
China has been and will always be Russia's closest and most reliable partner, Putin noted.

Ebola outbreak rebounds in DR Congo as cross-border spread heightens concerns: WHO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:16:19 CST
06:16:19 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Ebola infections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have rebounded after a brief decline, while the virus's spread to other African countries is complicating efforts to contain an outbreak that has already claimed more than 4,600 lives, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned in its latest situation report Wednesday.
"The most recent seven-day moving average indicates a modest upward trend, suggesting renewed intensification of transmission," the WHO Regional Office for Africa said in the report, highlighting the outbreak's "widening international dimension and the growing complexity."
The DRC recorded 1,466 confirmed cases between Sept. 29 and Oct. 19, up 10.4 percent from the preceding 21-day period, while confirmed deaths rose 7.5 percent to 692, according to the report.
As of Oct. 19, the DRC had recorded 9,637 confirmed cases and 4,646 deaths across eight of its 26 provinces.
Meanwhile, the outbreak's international spread has added a new layer of complexity to containment efforts.
Kenya has reported nine confirmed cases, including one death, with all eight secondary infections linked to an imported case and detected among people already under quarantine, according to the WHO report.
Nigeria confirmed its first case on Tuesday, involving a woman who had travelled from Uganda earlier this month. The WHO warned that the prolonged interval between symptom onset and laboratory confirmation raised concerns about "potentially undetected exposures and secondary transmission".
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warned Tuesday that the outbreak had become the most geographically widespread Ebola epidemic on record, with infections reported across Central, Eastern and Western Africa.
In its latest assessment, the WHO said the outbreak remained "at a critical juncture," warning that escalating insecurity, population displacement and restricted humanitarian access in the DRC were "further challenging response operations and increasing the risk of undetected transmission." ■

Interview: Regular central bank dialogue underpins win-win China-EU economic and financial ties: ECB official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:16:08 CST
06:16:08 KST

SHANGHAI/FRANKFURT, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The European Central Bank (ECB) and the People's Bank of China (PBOC) maintain regular multi-channel exchanges, and deeper mutual understanding yields shared benefits amid extensive trade, technology and financial ties linking China and the euro area, according to a member of the ECB's executive board.
China and Europe are advancing financial connectivity through institutionalized central bank dialogue. The first annual governors' meeting between the PBOC and the ECB, held in Beijing in June 2025, established a high-level communication channel.
"We interact with the People's Bank of China in different venues," Philip R. Lane, member of the ECB's Executive Board, told Xinhua in an interview in Shanghai. "The more we understand one another, the more it benefits everyone."
Together with renewed bilateral currency swap facilities and joint work on green finance standards, this institutional mechanism underpins deeper China-Europe financial ties, while both sides demonstrate leadership in developing sustainable finance frameworks for global markets.
On green finance, Lane said both the ECB and the PBOC recognize the importance of the green transition and have led the Network for Greening the Financial System. "The PBOC and the ECB are leaders in that global effort," he said, describing their joint role as critical in adapting the financial system to the green transition and the risks posed by extreme weather events.
For cross-border payments, Lane said the G20 roadmap is the best way to advance global coordination. As issuers of two of the world's major currencies, China and the euro area stand to gain greatly from steady exchanges under the G20. Regarding China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, he said it is natural for China to develop local-currency settlement facilities given its rising weight in global trade.
Lane, who attended the 2026 Bund Summit in Shanghai, said there is substantial interest in Europe in using China's open-weight AI models. He also expressed appreciation for how China is exploring ways to leverage AI within a regulated framework to manage downside risks.
China's gross domestic product grew 4.5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. Lane said China's economy is an important driver of the world economy. Its strong export performance creates positive spillovers: European consumers enjoy greater product variety with lower prices, and European manufacturers gain access to more intermediate goods. "More domestic consumption would benefit China and the euro area," he added.
Through pragmatic and productive discussions, China and the European Union have shown a willingness to deepen cooperation and work toward a stable, more balanced economic and trade relationship. The two sides agreed to continue discussing the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods under WTO rules and reached an understanding on the trade of hybrid vehicles consistent with WTO rules.
Recent agreements aim to adjust the pace of trade flows, enabling the European automotive sector to adjust "in a more gradual manner," Lane remarked. He voiced optimism over the outlook for China-EU trade and investment ties. "China's growing wealth also allows its savings to finance European investment, representing a financial spillover," he said.
Underpinned by renewable energy expansion that lessens fossil fuel dependence, government fiscal backing, and AI-fuelled investment and manufacturing improvements, the euro area economy has proved more resilient than expected, prompting the ECB to raise its 2026 and 2027 growth forecasts in September.
With energy prices and inflation rising sharply due to the conflict in the Middle East, Lane said policymakers aim to guide inflation back toward the 2-percent target while avoiding derailing economic expansion. He added the ECB has implemented two rate hikes and will not lock in future moves in advance. ■

Energoinvest said its analysis led it to propose a 12 percent increase, rather than passing on the full rise in procurement costs to end users, while maintaining a stable gas supply.
This is the fourth wholesale natural gas price hike in BiH this year. According to local media outlet Avaz, the cumulative increase in natural gas prices in Sarajevo has reached about 31 percent since the beginning of the year. ■

Kenya launches 160-mln-USD initiative to fund wildlife conservation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:15:46 CST
06:15:46 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Kenya on Wednesday launched the Thamani Asili Program, a 160-million-U.S.-dollar initiative to mobilize sustainable financing for wildlife conservation, ecosystem protection, and community development.
Tourism and Wildlife Cabinet Secretary Rebecca Miano said the 10-year program unites the government and conservation partners to safeguard the country's natural heritage while boosting community livelihoods, water security, climate resilience, and sustainable economic growth.
"Under the program agreement, the government has committed 80 million dollars, matched by a similar amount in philanthropic support mobilized through The Nature Conservancy and its alliance partner, Enduring Earth," Miano said at Tsavo West National Park in Taita Taveta County, southeastern Kenya.
Miano noted that by utilizing the Project Finance for Permanence model, Thamani Asili establishes a long-term framework to transition conservation away from short-term funding cycles toward predictable investment, institutional accountability, and measurable results.
She added that the initiative will support conservation across 31 counties, helping advance Kenya's goal of bringing at least 30 percent of its lands, inland waters, and near-shore ecosystems under effective management.
The program includes establishing approximately 2.7 million hectares of new conserved areas, improving the management of 11 million hectares of existing conservation spaces, and empowering communities to manage an additional six million hectares.
According to Miano, the initiative is expected to directly benefit about 1.6 million people, with an estimated 3.9 million more gaining indirect benefits through improved land governance, natural resource management, and nature-based economic opportunities.
She added that the investments will create around 7,800 direct jobs and 15,000 indirect jobs, opening up new prospects in ecotourism, sustainable grazing, carbon initiatives, and other green enterprises.
Kenya Wildlife Service Director General Erustus Kanga emphasized that successful conservation must protect both wildlife and the livelihoods, cultures, and heritage of communities living alongside it.
"In Tsavo, conservation is not just about protecting wildlife; it is about protecting a way of life, honoring the cultures and heritage of our communities, and securing a future where people and wildlife thrive together," Kanga noted.
Thamani Asili is also expected to contribute to avoiding approximately 7.5 million tonnes of carbon emissions by 2035, reinforcing the link between nature conservation, climate action and economic resilience. ■

====================================================================================================

AIPAC changes political strategy after election losses, ends direct donations to candidates, endorsements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:11:51 UTC
06:11:51 KST

Amid a series of political defeats in key races and growing pressure from activists, the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC announced Wednesday evening a sweeping change to its political strategy, saying it would stop formally endorsing congressional candidates and cease making direct contributions from its political action committee.
In an official letter to members, AIPAC's leadership said the decision followed a months-long "strategic review" and would take effect immediately as a permanent, long-term policy change. The move ends three election cycles of direct political involvement through the organization's PAC and marks a shift toward encouraging contributions directly from individual donors, without AIPAC's name appearing on candidates' campaign finance reports.
Despite ending formal endorsements, the organization's leadership emphasized that its independent super PAC, United Democracy Project, would continue operating as usual. The separate entity does not contribute directly to political campaigns and is prohibited from coordinating with candidates, but it can spend unlimited amounts on independent television and digital campaigns supporting pro-Israel candidates and opposing their rivals.
The move is intended to counter the public and political backlash that has developed in recent years over the perceived political cost of an association with AIPAC. The organization's official endorsement has become a target for activists on both the progressive left and the far right, prompting Democratic lawmakers, including Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, to announce that they would refuse contributions from political action committees generally or AIPAC specifically to avoid potential electoral damage.
In the letter, signed by AIPAC President Bernie Kaminetsky, board chair Michael Tuchin, president-elect Yehuda Neuberger and CEO Elliot Brandt, the organization's leadership explained the reasoning behind the shift.
"To win the battle for the future of our country and the U.S.-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, substantial and flexible political operation," the letter said.
The leaders added that "formal endorsements, direct contributions and earmarked donations will no longer be part of our approach, allowing us to expand individual giving and use new tools to help our friends win."
AIPAC's leadership stressed that U.S. elections present "one of the most complex challenges in recent memory" and said it expects those challenges to evolve further ahead of the next election cycle.
Under the system used until now, AIPAC members could donate to candidates through the organization's online portal, with the contributions listed in official campaign finance reports as having been routed through the lobby. Federal law limits direct PAC contributions to approximately $10,000 per candidate per election cycle, a relatively small sum in today's American political landscape.
By contrast, contributions made directly by individual donors were substantially larger. AIPAC spokesperson Darrin Sosa said the organization's members had contributed more than $90 million to candidates during the current election cycle, including earmarked donations made through the portal, compared with approximately $3 million contributed directly by the PAC itself.
"Our measure of success is the strength of the U.S.-Israel relationship," Sosa said. "Our members have always been our greatest strength. We are investing more time and resources in what has proven most effective: direct contributions from AIPAC members to candidates and expanding their influence."
The strategic shift follows a period of political tensions and mounting criticism within the Democratic Party. Earlier this year, AIPAC suspended fundraising activities for 18 Democratic members of the House of Representatives after they voted to reduce U.S. security assistance to Israel. As a result, the organization's portal was left with active fundraising links for just 178 Republicans and 72 Democrats.
Meanwhile, protest organizations and anti-Israel activists, including TrackAIPAC, began identifying individual Jewish and pro-Israel donors and labeling their contributions as AIPAC money, prompting serious accusations of antisemitism. Removing the lobby's official designation is expected to make it harder for such organizations to single out candidates, while allowing politicians who have pledged not to accept lobbying-group money to continue receiving support from individual donors.
Although AIPAC reported playing a prominent role in the victories of 290 candidates and the defeats of 29 candidates it considered hostile to Israel, the organization also suffered several political setbacks in key races.
In Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, the lobby's affiliated super PAC spent tens of millions of dollars supporting Rep. Haley Stevens but failed to prevent her defeat by anti-Zionist candidate Abdul El-Sayed. In New Jersey's 11th Congressional District primary, the organization's advertising attacks weakened former Rep. Tom Malinowski, indirectly paving the way for the victory of progressive candidate Analilia Mejia.
In remarks to the media, Sosa emphasized that the super PAC remains one of the organization's principal tools for defeating candidates it considers hostile to Israel.
"The only tactic we are committed to is the one that is most effective," Sosa said. "We have a determined activist base, and the pro-Israel community is ready to stand with its friends in Congress."

The upcoming selection will determine who will replace the incumbent Antonio Guterres as the 10th UN secretary-general. Guterres will complete his second five-year term on December 31.
Her potential entry comes amid months of intense diplomatic positioning as regional blocs vie for the UN’s top post.
Steep competition for UAE candidate
Six official candidates are currently active, with Nusseibeh as the seventh.
So far, former vice president of Costa Rica Rebeca Grynspan, who currently heads the UN Trade and Development body, has led in straw polls for the next UN secretary-general.
IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi of Argentina is another prominent candidate for UN secretary-general. He advocates for a more practical, streamlined, and results-focused UN, and draws significant backing in informal polling.
Carolyn Rorigues-Brikett, Guyana's permanent representative to the UN, is another serious contender. She has extensive experience as Guyana's foreign affairs minister and in climate advocacy, sustainable development, and developing-states diplomacy.
Customarily, the UN selects the secretary-general on the basis of regional rotation, and it is Latin America's turn for the position. Currently, five of six candidates hail from Latin America or the Caribbean.
Nusseibeh's appointment would run counter to the established norm, but she is not disqualified from the position.
