Trump heads to South Carolina to boost Senator Darline Graham in race
Race between sibling of former Senator Lindsey Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened in deep-red state.
United States President Donald Trump is set to travel to South Carolina to boost the campaign of Darline Graham, the sister of his close ally, the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
The visit on Wednesday, which will include a rally alongside Graham, comes as the Senate race in deep-red South Carolina has grown uncomfortably close for Republicans.
Lindsey Graham, long one of the most hawkish members of the Senate who was an outspoken supporter of the US-Israel war on Iran, had been expected to sail to victory in the November 3 vote. But his unexpected death in July upended the race.
South Carolina’s governor tapped Darline Graham to finish her brother’s term. Trump then made the surprise move of endorsing Graham in a new Republican primary, helping her to claim the party’s nomination. The president said the endorsement was “in honour of her brother”.
In a video message last week, Trump again said Graham had his unconditional support.
“I’m asking everyone in South Carolina to get out and vote for a wonderful person, a great woman … a woman that Lindsey Graham said is the greatest person he’s ever met,” Trump said.
Democratic challenger Annie Andrews, a medical doctor and paediatrician, has seized on Graham’s inexperience and her unorthodox route to the Republican nomination.
Speaking to a local Fox News affiliate before Trump’s rally in Pendleton, South Carolina, Andrews pointed to Graham’s lacklustre debate performance, including one instance where she said she was “not that informed on national security”.
“My opponent needs the highest level of federal government politicians to speak for her. On the debate stage, it was really clear,” Andrews said.
Graham, meanwhile, has called Andrews “the most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina”.
Polls have shown Graham leading by about 2.7 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average. Trump carried the state by 18 percentage points in 2024.
Tensions on Russia
Trump’s visit comes after the president issued an executive order waiving most sanctions and tariffs on Russia, established by a law named after Lindsey Graham and passed with bipartisan support in 2026.
The move prompted a tempered rebuke from Darline Graham.
“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” she told The Associated Press news agency on Saturday.
“I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.
The executive order on sanctions has been part of a wider Trump administration shift in its approach to ending the war with Ukraine, which began with Russia’s invasion in February 2024.
Trump and his allies have heaped pressure on Ukraine, framing its leader, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as the main impediment to peace. In turn, Washington has offered several concessions to Russia, including a deal to buy Russian diesel.
Lindsey Graham had been a staunch supporter of Ukraine. His death came shortly after he returned from his 10th visit to the country since the war began.
Political headwinds
The tightening race in South Carolina underscores the harsh political reality for Republicans heading into the final stretch of the midterms.
Trump has sought to use his political clout to bring party loyalists out to vote, campaigning in strongholds across the country. But the president heads into the vote with the lowest approval ratings of his career, with voters expressing dismay about affordability and the knock-on effects of the US-Israel war with Iran.
Beyond South Carolina, other one-time Republican strongholds have shown signs of shifting towards Democrats.
That includes Kansas, where polls suggest Republican Ashley Hinson is effectively tied with Democrat Joshua Turek. The state, where farmers have been particularly hard hit by rising prices on fuel and equipment, has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1939.
Trump also broke from the Republican establishment to endorse Attorney General Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn in the Texas primary. Polling averages show Paxton, whose career has been marred by a procession of scandals, trailing behind Democratic challenger Talarico by 1.7 percentage points. The race is widely considered a toss-up.
A Republican has not won statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Southwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares.
The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share.
Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expected
- Revenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expected
Southwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year.
"Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release.
The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people.
Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors.
For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion.
Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. Both of those airlines reported top- and bottom-line misses for the third quarter.

Scatterbrained Australian approach opens door to South African victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:05:15 UTC
06:05:15 KST

Among those who fret over the ongoing primacy of Test cricket in the face of the T20 onslaught, Australia's tour of South Africa had long shaped as an enticing proposition: the two best sides in the world squaring off, a clutch of veteran tourists confronting ghosts of controversies past, and Australia commencing a year-long run of battles its aging superstars see as legacy-shaping.
Some of that probably distracted us from what a bittersweet prospect it was, too. For how, as anyone glued to this contest in the past two weeks will have asked themselves at some point or other, can a game so awash with money have conspired to deny us regular helpings of this fun and fascinating South African outfit? Of real cricket that matters?
Twenty-four hours ago, it was centurion Temba Bavuma reminding the world not only of his life-affirming resurgence as a batsman, but of the great shame that in the last two years, he's only had eight other opportunities to strut his stuff at Test level.
Early on day four at Gqeberha, the focus shifted to beanpole all-rounder Marco Jansen, fresh from his swashbuckling 85 with the bat, now tearing through the Australian batting order like the Grim Reaper. Lurking not so much in the shadows as slightly off to the side of the stage, stirring up drama and intrigue, there was also the imposing figure of Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada.
That and a few subtler problems added up to an unmitigated disaster for Australia. Replying to South Africa's declared total of 425, the scatterbrained and frankly embarrassing tourists were skittled for 99 in their first innings and asked to follow on.
By default, Australia fared a little better in the afternoon, finishing the day at 4-156 with Travis Head undefeated on 87. But with its deficit of 170, and a neck injury to Steve Smith — who hasn't appeared to bat yet in the second innings — it will take something truly remarkable for Australia to pull this game out of the fire on the fifth and final day.
The main impression Australia's performance left was of the sheer needlessness of the entire debacle. What was the first innings batting plan, if any? Why were so many batsmen in such a hurry in a scenario from which Australia was never going to win?
Which is not to take the focus of South Africa's unstinting excellence. Another emblematic figure in that sense was off-spinner Simon Harmer, who many thought should have been dropped for this game.
Instead, he's made big runs, caught everything that has come his way, and chipped in with two key wickets. Australia has had no such unassuming star.
Jansen, with 5-33 from 11 overs in the first innings chaos, was the chief destroyer, but there were wheels within wheels. The mere presence of Rabada, who was missing from the first Test, seems to have transformed South Africa's collective energy from a little too amiable in Durban to ruthless and faintly menacing here.
Jansen was the most visible example of this phenomenon. In Durban, he'd bowled with pace and incision to spark Australia's initial collapse. But as his influence waned and Matt Renshaw got going, he silently brooded away in his own world, looking a little like Alain Delon's expressionless assassin in Le Samourai.
Today he was an entirely different man — gregarious, energetic, fired up. To his usual bouncers he added fist-pumps and fiery send-offs. Like Rabada in the memorably testy corresponding game eight years ago, he got up in Australia's grill and wouldn't go away.
A brief catalogue of Australia's worst misdemeanours in the first innings bears mentioning. Marnus Labuschagne again drove with hard hands, slightly off balance, with his bat plane all wrong, therefore couldn't complain about the bad luck of departing to a one-handed screamer by Harmer in the cordon. Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins each either walloped or wafted at deliveries they should have respected, especially given the dire state their team was in at the time.
In the second innings, Nic Maddinson again nudged lamely at Rabada to be caught behind the wicket. As in Durban, Labuschagne again squandered a promising start when a break in sight, heedlessly thrashing Harmer into the deep to hole out for 39 when drinks were about to be brought on. And Webster, again neither looking comfortable nor batting with due caution, was dismissed cheaply at the worst possible time. Renshaw, who had looked relatively comfortable, shouldered arms to be bowled by Rabada.
And for all that, and Australia's loss of 13 wickets for the day, South Africa's attack was a man down for most of the day after lionhearted quick Anrich Nortje suffered a groin injury in his fourth over. Things could actually have been worse.
Only a day ago, one felt the confluence of luck, momentum and a single special innings had changed the game's course without any great culpability on Australia's behalf. The feeling is very different now. South Africa will arrive for the final day with victory in its mind — in this game, foremost, but also perhaps in a series that is now thrillingly alive.

The fierce and bipartisan backlash to gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy's decision to feature his opponent's estranged mother in an ad left Republicans in Ohio and Washington reeling on Wednesday, as both Ramaswamy and Vice President J.D. Vance doubled down on the divisive strategy.
Publicly, Republicans were mounting a defense, led by Vance, who is from Ohio and was campaigning in Cincinnati on Wednesday, treating the ad as a gamechanging October surprise. But privately, old-guard Republicans were baffled that Ramaswamy would dare to deploy Democratic nominee Amy Acton’s own mother, who has not spoken to her daughter since 1978 when she defended Acton’s stepfather who was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Some predicted the ad was likely to draw more empathy and interest in Acton from voters, and turn them away from Ramaswamy.
“We’ve lost the plot,” says one Republican strategist. “We had a real good chance and then we do this two weeks out.”
Adds a second: “We now deserve to lose this race.”
The addition of this ad so close to Election Day roiled races in Ohio up and down the ballot. “I would not have run that ad,” Republican Sen. Jon Husted, running in a tight and expensive race for re-election against Sherrod Brown in Ohio, told The Associated Press on Wednesday. Other players in the state's Republican circles say the ad has all the pieces of a misfire, especially among women.
Recent polls have shown Acton leading but not running away with the race. A Marist University poll released this week showed her up seven points. But Ohio is a state where President Donald Trump won three times, never with fewer than eight points to spare. If elected, Acton would be the first Democrat to become Governor since 2007.
Ramaswamy’s campaign said it was putting $4 million into making sure the ad gets seen, with a goal of targeting persuadable voters still undecided between the billionaire entrepreneur and Acton, the former state health chief who steered Ohio through the pandemic. But the risk of it backfiring is incredibly high with no time to recover.
Ramaswamy’s campaign includes several operatives who previously worked for Vance, who sidestepped questions about the ad’s message on Wednesday as he urged  Republicans to not allow such hard-nosed messaging to distract them from the stakes of the election. “I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” he told reporters. “So I would say to Ohio Republicans: do you actually think that Amy Acton is unfit to serve as Governor of the state of Ohio? I do.”
By Wednesday afternoon, it was clear Vance might be in a decided minority. “I don’t have to agree with Amy Acton’s politics to believe that exploiting someone’s childhood trauma is wrong,” wrote Republican Lydia Mihalik, a member of Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine’s Cabinet.
Mike Murphy, a strategist who was in Sen. John McCain’s inner circle when he ran for President in 2000 and headed Gov. Jeb Bush’s super PAC in 2016, wrote a brutal assessment on social media, saying it “is looking more and more like political suicide.”
And former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy in the 2020 presidential primaries and was a frequent critic of him, was even more direct. “He’s a bad guy,” she said. “It’s a shame he continues to get away with it.”
In an editorial endorsement of Acton published Wednesday, The Columbus Dispatch roundly condemned the video: “It should go without saying that sexual violence against children should not be politicized or taken as lightly as Ramaswamy appears to take it.”
For its part, Acton’s campaign began an ad of its own calling out Ramaswamy’s effort to make her childhood a campaign issue after a half century in the past.

"She was 11- and 12-years-old, and to think that that's somehow a talking point—shame on Vivek,” Stearns continues. “The contempt he has for Amy is the contempt he has for Ohio. He's not fit to lead."

NEW DELHI: The shooters involved in the attack on actor Tiger Shroff received their weapons through a “dead drop” arrangement on Oct 17, just a day before the incident. Couriers Babita and Radha — who have since been arrested — were provided the weapons at New Delhi Railway Station by the main supplier, identified as Kunal.Kunal, who has also been arrested, has emerged as a key character who had been in touch with gangsters Anil Pandit and Randeep Malik for over two months. He had also figured as the source of the weapon used for the murder of a forex-hawala trader in Sonipat last year, sources said.In this case, he was relaying the instructions from Pandit to the two women after dropping them at the station on Oct 15. The women reached Mumbai on Oct 17, got off at Dadar and checked into a hotel. Around 11am, one of the shooters collected the bag with the weapons at an isolated spot near the hotel, an official added.
The dead drop method — borrowed from spycraft — has increasingly surfaced in investigations involving terror modules, drug cartels and organised crime groups of late. Agencies have unearthed non-contact logistics where handlers use encrypted messaging to direct operatives to pre-arranged locations to collect weapons, funds and synthetic drugs.
Some cases in point include IS-linked terror modules, cross-border drone-dropped payloads along the Punjab and J&K frontiers, interstate gang firearm procurements and synthetic drug delivery networks.Investigators reconstruct digital footprints, chat logs and GPS coordinates alongside CCTV footage analysis to establish the timeline. By using technical surveillance, cell tower dumps and financial intelligence tied to encrypted communications, agencies are able to intercept these isolated drop routines to cut off unverified supplier-courier links, sources said.
Raj Shekhar Jha is a journalist for the Times of India with over a decade of experience in reporting on national security, terrorism, crime and prisons.

Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn in fines for Facebook privacy violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:01:32 UTC
06:01:32 KST

Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn in fines for Facebook privacy violations
A jury found Meta guilty of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about access to their data.
A United States judge has ordered Meta to pay $25bn after a jury found the company misled Facebook users about privacy violations, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
New Mexico state District Judge Francis Mathew issued the ruling on Wednesday.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
Last month, a jury found Meta responsible for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez highlighted that the decision was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history.
“This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” Torrez said at a news conference.
Meta lawyer Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40bn would be “shocking to the conscience”, while a lawyer for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want”.
“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” Nicholson argued during a hearing held early this month.
Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all the money awarded would go into a fund for the state’s education system.
The amount awarded in the case far exceeds the $5bn fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
New Mexico accused Meta of misleading users about who could access their personal information and how harmful content was handled on its platforms. Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements made by Meta and its leadership on privacy and content moderation were misleading.
Meta plans to appeal the verdict, potentially reducing the final payment amount.
In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
The lawsuit, filed in 2021, stemmed partly from revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm that is now defunct, had obtained personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent and used it to develop targeted political advertisements. Its clients included President Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
The case, a major setback for the tech giant, marks the second legal defeat for Meta in New Mexico in six months. In March, a jury found the company misled users about the safety of young people on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, ordering it to pay $375m in civil penalties. Meta was later ordered to make an additional $567m payment into a state fund for teen mental health and was required to implement measures to protect young users.

Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:00:01 UTC
06:00:01 KST

Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests.
Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly.
Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning.
“One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.”
Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions.
The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats. They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat.
Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day.
On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl.
The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference.
Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food.
Dr Adriano Lameira, a primatologist and evolutionary psychologist at the University of Warwick, who was not involved in the work, described the results as fascinating.
“Effectively, hearing others clearly having a good time, orangutans placed their food order: ‘I will have what they are having, please!’” he said.
Cartmill added the results suggest it is not only the quantity or frequency of a reward that can be important when learning associations.
“What our work is showing is that it’s also about the state of the animal when they are learning that association,” she said.
“Who you are in that moment – the context, the emotional states, what you’re feeling, what you’re thinking about – can also influence and can carry over in how you remember these things that you’ve learned.”
The findings, she added, could have applications to humans, including in educational environments.
“Students might learn at similar rates if they are in a good mood or not, but our research suggests that they would value information more if they learn it when they are in a good mood,” Cartmill said.
She added that could be useful in helping to understand why some information is more trusted or why students choose to continue studying certain subjects.
“If a student is anxious when they are learning maths for example, it might impact whether they prefer maths versus other subjects when choosing what to pursue in the future,” she said.

‘It's the President's Fault’: The White House Blame Game Starts Early Ahead of the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Trump White House aides have started to cast about for a scapegoat to offer the president in the event of bad midterm election losses, as Republicans stare down brutal predictions in key House and Senate races, sources familiar with the matter say.
Republican political operatives say privately that the real blame lies with Trump for starting the Iran war in an election year, causing higher prices across the board and prompting a nationwide voter backlash, the sources say.
“Clearly it's the president's fault,” one operative tells Inner Loop.
But Trump aides also know, for obvious reasons, they cannot say publicly or tell the president behind closed doors that his own policy decisions are at fault as they contemplate losing not just the House majority, but possibly the Senate.
The result has been an unusually early effort to find a scapegoat, and sources say eyes have fallen on deputy chief of staff and political strategist James Blair, who organized the Trump 2024 campaign's turnout strategy and returned to the role for this midterm cycle.
Blair's efforts included a marquee plan for certain states to redraw congressional maps early, which looked likely—though not certain—to yield favorable House seats for Republicans, so long as the coalition that Trump turned out in 2024 came out to support Republicans in 2026.
Even accounting for the Iran war, the redistricting gambit was supposed to bring roughly 10 to 15 pickups for Republicans in the House. After Virginia's top court blocked Democrats from redrawing maps to keep pace in the redistricting battle, wrote on X: “Lord grant me humility.”
But in a remarkable backfire five months later, election forecasters have found that some of the redistricted seats now favor Democrats.
The redrawn map for Florida's 25th congressional district just south of Fort Lauderdale, for instance, is now characterized as "Lean Democrat," and the outlook is so bad that the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republican–aligned group, has pulled money out of the race.
Maps that were drawn for Republicans in ruby-red Texas are suddenly also vulnerable, even in seats where the party has incumbents. In Texas' 15th congressional district, GOP candidate Monica De La Cruz's race is now rated a "tossup" by the Cook Political Report.
Blair's allies inside and outside the West Wing say the criticism directed at him is grossly unfair because he could not have foreseen the effects of the Iran war and scandals involving Trump officials undoing his planning.
Blair is also viewed as retaining the confidence of Trump and the White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and he traveled on Air Force One to two rallies within the past week, suggesting any blame that ultimately comes his way could be just symbolic.
After all, when Blair left the White House earlier this year to run Trump's midterm strategy from the outside, the president announced the move as only temporary and said that Blair would return after the election.
Responding to the reporting in this story, Blair said in a statement, “the President, our partners in the House and Senate, and I remain focused on winning in November. All Republicans should be spending themselves equally in our worthy cause.”
“The anonymous ‘sources’ peddling this nonsense are self-serving opportunists focused on themselves. We’re focused on the President and the American people,” White House spokesperson Danielle Alvarez added in a statement.
As for Wiles herself, despite reporting that she has been under fire, sources inside Trump's orbit are adamant that if Wiles leaves after the midterms, it will be purely of her own volition.
Trump aides acknowledge that much of the palace intrigue scapegoating is preemptive. Expectations are so low that if Republicans take some wins—like holding on to the Senate—Blair will be “seen as a savior,” one of the sources added.
But they also say that in many ways Blair has perhaps made it too easy for them to single him out. He explicitly owned the House midterm strategy, and now he may be walked to the gallows with that same rope.

Ahead of Midterms, Elena Kagan Says the Supreme Court Is Undermining Voting Rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:59:15 UTC
05:59:15 KST

Liberal Justice Elena Kagan has accused the Supreme Court’s conservative majority of undermining democracy and creating a more polarized electorate through a series of key rulings that have affected the nature of elections ahead of the midterms.
“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effect of their rulings on how the political system works,” Kagan said while speaking to students and faculty at Catholic University’s law school in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday.
She went on to say that the conservative justices have “created a democracy that does not work as well as it should.”
Kagan—who was nominated to the bench in 2010 by President Barack Obama—referenced specific rulings that have had a large impact on electoral maps, campaign finance, and executive authority. Experts tell TIME that these rulings have affected the midterm elections and could, in turn, change the fate of Congress.
“It's no exaggeration to say that the form of our elections and democracy owes a great deal to the decisions of the Supreme Court, sometimes overruling the will of Congress,” says Rick Hasen, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles law school and the director of its Safeguarding Democracy Project.
In fact, he believes Kagan’s remarks do not go far enough in their criticism.
“You're going to hear more voices calling for the Supreme Court to be changed, either by adding more justices, putting in term limits, or doing other things,” he says.
The outcome of the midterm elections might have some influence on these issues going forward, though there are limits to what Congress can accomplish regardless of who controls the majority in the years ahead.
How Supreme Court rulings may affect the 2026 midterms
Kagan’s comments outline how the high court’s rulings have impacted this year’s elections.
She pointed to Louisiana v. Callais, which concerned whether Louisiana had to draw a second congressional district where Black voters made up a majority—giving them a greater chance to elect their preferred candidate. In April, the Supreme Court struck down that map and made it harder to challenge maps that weaken minority voters’ influence. Kagan called the ruling an “evisceration” of the 1965 Voting Rights Act.
Following the decision, many Republican-led states proposed redrawn voting maps that favored their candidates and weakened Black voters’ electoral influence.
Hasen says that Americans are already facing the fallout. He pointed to Louisiana and Alabama, each of which eliminated a district where Black voters could elect their candidates of choice.
“We'll see much more of that in the next few election cycles,” Hasen predicts, calling the decision “the worst election law decision in 100 years at the Supreme Court.”
Kagan also mentioned a 2019 decision in Rucho v. Common Cause that prevents federal courts from blocking electoral maps on the grounds that they unfairly favor one party. States including Texas, North Carolina, Ohio, and Florida have since adopted new congressional maps that could help Republicans win additional House seats in November.
This gerrymandering, Kagan said, strips people of “their rights to voting equality” and has resulted in “driving people away from the center, toward the wings, toward the extremes.” The outcome, she said, is contributing toward what’s already a “too-polarized country.”
She added that these redrawn maps are “very destructive to our democracy.”
How campaign finance rules may come into play ahead of Election Day
In her speech, Kagan also highlighted the role that money increasingly plays in politics.
“The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare, and they’re right,” Kagan said.
A 6-3 ruling split along ideological lines from June in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC removed limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with their candidates, including on television advertisements.
Her comments come amid what is projected to be the most expensive election cycle in history.
Billionaires have poured hundreds of millions into super political action committees (super PACs) for campaign ads—chiefly supporting Republican candidates in tight Senate races.
How the court has expanded presidential powers
Supreme Court rulings have also influenced the scope of presidential power.
Kagan also criticized the court’s decision in Trump v. Slaughter. In June, justices struck down protections against firing Federal Trade Commission commissioners without cause, expanding presidential control over independent agencies.
“The danger is it allows the president to ride roughshod over all the institutions of government,” Kagan said.
Aziz Huq, a professor at the University of Chicago law school and a co-author of How to Save a Constitutional Democracy, tells TIME that “the misuse or the use of prosecutorial discretion at the direction of the president against political foes … flows from the court’s ruling” in Slaughter.
Furthermore, Huq says, it expands “the scope of presidential directive authority over subordinates.”
Huq pointed to the Trump Administration’s investigation into Somali-born Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota as an example of how greater presidential control over executive officials can be used against political opponents.
What Congress can do to check the Supreme Court
Even if Democrats regain control of Congress in November, Trump could veto legislation seeking to counteract the court’s decisions. Overriding him would require two-thirds support in both chambers.
As a result, Hasen says it could take until 2029 “at the earliest,” when a new president enters the White House, for there to be a counteractive response to the high court’s conservative majority.
There are measures Congress and states can take in the meantime, he continues, saying that Congress has the ability to enact a nationwide law that would restrict partisan gerrymandering of House maps.
Chief Justice John Roberts acknowledges that authority in his ruling in Rucho.
“As noted, the Framers gave Congress the power to do something about partisan gerrymandering in the Elections Clause,” Roberts wrote, referring to the 55 delegates who in 1787 met to draft the U.S. Constitution. “That avenue … remains open.”
When it comes to Callais, Hasen says lawmakers could attempt to amend the Voting Rights Act, and restore protections narrowed by the ruling, by forcing the Supreme Court “to decide some of the constitutional questions that they ducked” during the original case.
But any new legislation could face a legal challenge, leaving the Supreme Court to decide whether it can stand.
Those hoping to challenge the highest court’s composition or jurisdiction may go about that in a few ways, such as by petitioning for term limits. Proposals include limiting justices’ active service through legislation—an approach whose constitutionality is disputed—or through a constitutional amendment. Another route is to limit which cases the court can hear.
Complicating matters, Huq says, is that legislative reforms could ultimately come before the Supreme Court, whose methods of interpreting the law leave the justices largely unconstrained in reaching their preferred outcomes.
“Almost all of these proposals are going to fail because the court will strike them down or find ways to undermine them,” Huq says. “We're at a very difficult and perilous point.”

Will Russia’s diesel shipment to the US lower prices before midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:54:27 UTC
05:54:27 KST

Will Russia’s diesel shipment to the US lower prices before midterms?
Moscow dispatches its inaugural diesel shipment to the US, aiming to ease fuel shortages as midterm elections loom.
Russia is set to send its first tanker carrying diesel fuel to the United States on Thursday, as part of an agreement with Washington aimed at easing fuel shortages that have pushed US diesel prices higher before next month’s midterm elections.
Moscow announced on Wednesday that the tanker was headed to an undisclosed US port and was scheduled to depart on Thursday. The shipment is part of a broader effort to send more fuel to the US, even as Russia faces its own supply constraints and US consumers grapple with elevated prices at the pump.
The announcement comes as the White House seeks to contain rising energy costs as cost-of-living concerns weigh on Americans in the run-up to the contentious midterm elections.
Voters increasingly trust Democrats over Republicans on economic issues, according to a recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with 37 percent of voters believing Democrats are more trusted on economics and 28 percent trusting Republicans more, while confidence in President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy has slumped, with 28 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the economy.
The first shipment was announced during a visit to St Petersburg by US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who held talks with Russian officials.
Is this a single shipment or multiple?
The first tanker is part of a broader commitment to increase Russian fuel supplies to the US, rather than a one-off delivery.
Trump had previously said Russia would export 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel. It would be followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.
Russian officials said on Wednesday that the initial shipment would be the first of several.
However, the scale and timing of those shipments remain uncertain. Russia has been dealing with domestic fuel shortages linked to Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries, which have disrupted refining capacity and forced Moscow to introduce restrictions on fuel exports.
The ability to fulfil the promised deliveries will depend on how quickly Russia can restore production while meeting its own domestic demand.
The deal also comes after Trump called off plans for another round of sanctions targeting Russia. Among the proposed measures was a 100 percent tariff on goods from major purchasers of Russian crude oil, including China and India.
Will the shipment lower prices before the midterms?
Analysts say the first shipment is unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections. US retail diesel prices topped $6 a gallon ($1.59 per litre) in September and have remained elevated.
On Wednesday, the national average stood at $6.31 a gallon ($1.67 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), down from $6.51 ($1.72 per litre) a month earlier, marking a 3.1 percent decrease but still significantly higher than this time last year, at $3.62 ($0.96 per litre).
“The volumes Russia can provide are small in comparison to the global shortage and US’s own production. The cargo is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on supply or meaningfully lower the price,” Rachel Ziemba, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
“The reported shipment is equivalent to roughly two hours of US distillate consumption. Even if it arrives as planned, it will make very little difference to national supply,” Aarathi Krishnan, CEO of Raksha Intelligence, told Al Jazeera.
The first tanker may not even reach the US before voters head to the polls, Ziemba said. Departing on Thursday would mark the beginning of its journey, not the date the fuel becomes available to consumers.
Any sustained reduction in prices would depend on a broader improvement in global supply, rather than a single delivery.
“Russia’s ability to supply more diesel depends partly on the condition of its refineries. Ukraine’s attacks affect those facilities. And Washington’s desire for lower fuel prices creates an interest in reducing that disruption,” Krishnan added.
Would a ceasefire impact fuel prices long term?
A long-term ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine could help ease pressure on energy markets by allowing damaged Russian refineries to be rebuilt and production to increase.
“This [the current agreement] is more about political posturing to get the US to further increase pressure on Ukraine and align with Russia,” Ziemba said.
She added that meaningful relief for the global oil market would depend in large part on developments in the Middle East, particularly the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the US-Israel attack on Iran.
The Russian shipment comes as conflict involving Iran and disruptions to energy shipping have intensified pressure on global fuel markets more broadly. There were at least 18 attacks on vessels over the previous two weeks, according to Kpler, a data analytics platform. On Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the Financial Times that Iran was fully prepared to defend itself.
The Russian agreement is unlikely to resolve the underlying supply problem on its own without a chance to rebuild its refineries.
“The agreement may help individual buyers or provide some immediate reassurance to traders. But sustained price relief will depend on actual increases in available diesel, which Russia has not yet demonstrated it can deliver,” Krishnan said.

Reviewing internal documents from Germany's armed forces, Suddeutsche Zeitung reports that this is the military's second-highest threat classification.
"We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for [Germany's armed forces]" said a defense ministry spokesperson, according to Reuters.
According to Suddeutsche Zeitung, the new classification was spurred by the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near the Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony in September, as well as "sabotage incidents involving naval vessels."
Previously, Germany officially accused Moscow of attempting to carry out a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. Whereas the target of the Leipzig sabotage attempt was a Ukrainian plane, the apparent sabotage attempt at the Wunstorf air base marked the first time Germany's military was directly targeted. 
At German armed forces facilities, security measures will be increased under the new threat level, a defense ministry spokesman said.
Germany's reclassification of Russian threats comes as experts warn Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command, experts say.

====================================================================================================

Some KC-135s Damaged by Iran Still in Depot: AFMC Boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:49:16 UTC
05:49:16 KST

At least two KC-135 Stratotankers that were seriously damaged during Operation Epic Fury are still undergoing extensive maintenance depot repairs, the head of Air Force Materiel Command said Oct. 21.
Six of the Air Force’s six-decade-old refueling tankers received varying degrees of damage in the opening weeks of the war against Iran. One KC-135 was involved in a collision with another Stratotanker over western Iraq on March 12 and lost part of its tail. The other tanker in that collision was completely destroyed, killing all six Airmen aboard. Another five KC-135s were hit during an Iranian missile strike on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia.
During an event with the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, AFMC boss Lt. Gen. Linda Hurry said her command sent an aircraft battle damage repair team to the Middle East to make temporary repairs to some KC-135s and “get them back into the fight,” Hurry said. Others were patched up enough to fly back to depots in the U.S., she said. She did not specify how many planes fell into each category.
Photographs emerged online showing one KC-135 flying with a transplanted tail, and others landing in the United Kingdom with patches covering the fragmentation damage that peppered their skins.
At least two Stratotankers “received much more significant damage” and are still in depot, Hurry said. She applauded the work the repair team did on these planes to get them airworthy enough to get back to the U.S.
“One had many, many, many holes in the side,” Hurry said. The repair team was “able to patch it up and get the authority to have it [make] a one-time flight back to the depot. It was just phenomenal that they were able to actually save that aircraft. Now they’re rebuilding it.”
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told lawmakers in June that all of those salvageable KC-135s would eventually return to service, although the most heavily damaged could take a year or two to be completely fixed.
Tinker Air Force Base, Okla., serves as the main KC-135 depot.
Depot Hiring
In addition to Tinker, the Air Force has depots at Warner-Robins Air Force Base, Ga., and Hill Air Force Base, Utah. Officials have called them “national treasures” for their work in repairing critical assets, but there have been concerns about manning and funding for years now.
AFMC as a whole is seeing widespread manpower shortages, Hurry said, with about 8,200 billets—including maintainers, engineers and contracting professionals—currently vacant. The Air Force Sustainment Center, which is part of AFMC and oversees those depots, specifically has a shortage of 2,600 billets, she said.
In response, AFMC is looking to hire depot artisans—the most highly-skilled civilian mechanics, technicians, and engineers—and other maintainers to keep the depots fully staffed, Hurry said.
The command is trying to do more targeted and streamlined hiring to fill the gaps, including by hosting hiring events where they can extend temporary job offers “right there on the spot,” and getting new hires on the job faster, she said.
AFMC is also looking at offering retention benefits and targeted incentives to hold on to vital employees with critical skill sets, “to make sure we’ve got the right artisans to care for some of these airframes that are older than probably most of us on the line,” Hurry said.
But sometimes, Hurry said, the Air Force doesn’t have to wait for a plane to get to one of its three main depots to do some of that necessary work. Airmen have proposed ideas for “a speed line” to push maintainers forward to the field and get the work done on-site, she said.
That would not just help keep planes flying, Hurry said, but also could help with morale and retention.
“They can see what they’re doing would have a direct impact to [U.S. Central Command] operations or operations around the globe,” Hurry said. “It really, really makes a difference. The sense of pride, the sense of purpose, the sense of commitment to our mission has really helped some of our retention.”
When a plane like a KC-135 goes through the depot process, Hurry said, maintainers routinely tear it “down to its ribs to build it back up again, to send it back out to the fight.”
“It is amazing how far we break down the aircraft to build it back up again as part of the routine depot maintenance cycle,” Hurry said.

NMC denotifies medical education rules; annual disclosures risk lacking verification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:49:16 UTC
05:49:16 KST

Any action taken while the regulations were in force would not be affected.
National Medical Commission has denotified the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023. With the denotification, all specific penalties against medical institutions that fail to comply with any of the statutory provisions and regulations or minimum standards are no longer applicable.Any action taken while the regulations were in force would not be affected. However, NMC has not taken any action against many colleges flouting regulations as in the case of non-payment of stipend to MBBS interns and doctors doing PG. Colleges will now have little to fear if they do not pay stipend as the penalty for is not specified in the NMC Act.
Without evaluation, med colleges’ disclosure would just be unverified claims
The Act only states that the Medical Assessment and Rating Board shall take such measures, including issuing warning, imposition of monetary penalty, reducing intake or stoppage of admissions or recommendation for withdrawal of recognition against a medical institution for failure to maintain the minimum essential standards specified.“Notwithstanding such denotification, the requirement of furnishing the annual disclosure report shall continue to operate” in accordance with relevant sections of NMC Act 2019, read the denotification announcement gazetted on Oct 14. NMC Act stipulates that the UnderGraduate Medical Education Board and the Post-Graduate Medical Education Board shall specify norms for compulsory annual disclosures by medical institutions.
The 2019 Act also states that MARB may conduct evaluation of any institute at any time without prior notice. However, with the denotification, the aspects that need to be included in the evaluation report, such as verification of physical infrastructure, availability of the required number of faculty and review of feedback from students, have also been removed.Without evaluation by MARB, the mandated annual disclosure would just be claims by a medical college unverified by an independent assessment.

====================================================================================================

Türkiye submits bill to parliament for approval of joint defense agreement with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:45:47 UTC
05:45:47 KST

Gazi Nogay and Fatma Zehra Solmaz
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
A bill seeking parliamentary approval of a joint defense agreement between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia was submitted to the Turkish parliament Wednesday.
The three-article bill, submitted under the signature of Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, seeks approval of the Mecca Agreement on Joint Defense, signed by the three countries in Mecca on Aug. 7, 2026.
According to the bill's explanatory memorandum, the agreement aims to strengthen strategic dialogue and cooperation based on mutual trust among regional countries.
It also seeks to establish a security framework based on cooperation and collective deterrence in the Middle East and beyond, while developing regional solutions to security challenges.
The memorandum said deterring aggression and establishing lasting regional stability would have positive socioeconomic effects in the medium and long term.
Under the agreement, the three countries undertake to cooperate to protect one another's independence, territorial integrity and sovereignty.
They also pledge mutual support in exercising their right to self-defense under the UN Charter.
Such measures would be subject to each country's constitutional obligations, national legislation and decisions by competent authorities, according to the memorandum.
The memorandum clarified that the collective defense provision would not be triggered automatically.
Instead, any response would depend on decisions reached by mutual agreement following consultations among the parties.
The agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence against threats and attacks that the three countries jointly assess as affecting their security, including terrorism.
It also seeks to improve interoperability, cooperation and coordination among their armed forces and deepen defense industry cooperation.
Agreement does not affect NATO obligations
The memorandum stressed that the agreement is exclusively defensive and does not target any country.
It said the framework is based on regional ownership, cooperative security and inclusivity.
The agreement is open to regional countries seeking to contribute to peace, stability and security while respecting international law, territorial integrity, sovereign equality and noninterference in internal affairs, according to the memorandum.
It emphasized that the agreement would neither cancel nor replace Türkiye's existing bilateral or multilateral obligations.
It said the regional security and stability objectives of the agreement were compatible with NATO's Euro-Atlantic security objectives.
Türkiye's rights and obligations within NATO would remain unaffected, according to the memorandum.
The agreement is expected to deepen Türkiye's bilateral defense and security relations with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia while supporting an inclusive regional security mechanism.
The bill will be considered by parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which has been designated as the lead committee.
If approved by the committee, it will be placed on the agenda of parliament's General Assembly.

Türkiye’s Fergani deploys 6th satellite, advancing indigenous navigation constellation plans
Türkiye’s Fergani Space Technologies has successfully deployed its sixth test satellite, FRG-100D4, into orbit, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Türkiye’s Fergani Space Technologies has successfully deployed its sixth test satellite, FRG-100D4, into orbit.
The 160 kg next-generation indigenous satellite was sent into space from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in the United States at 2:04 p.m. (Türkiye time) on October 20, 2026, as part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission.
The satellite separated from the launch vehicle approximately 63 minutes after launch, at 3:07 p.m. (Türkiye time), and settled into its target orbit at an altitude of 590 km.
Founded by Baykar Chairman and CTO Selçuk Bayraktar, Fergani Space Technologies developed the satellite using domestic engineering capabilities.
The FRG-100D4 marks a significant technological milestone, featuring a range of advanced components developed entirely in-house by Fergani. These include a reaction wheel, magnetorquer, magnetometer, IMU, GNSS receiver, steerable solar panels, battery pack, regenerative modem, and phased-array antenna. The satellite also incorporates an AI-assisted onboard computer designed to support advanced missions.
The launch of the FRG-100D4 also marks a significant step toward the implementation of the Uluğ Bey Satellite Constellation System. Fergani Space aims to complete the constellation, comprising more than 200 satellites, entirely with its own resources within the next five years. Once operational, the system will provide Türkiye with an independent navigation and communications network, while enabling the country to share these critical capabilities with friendly and allied nations.
Earlier, it was reported that Tesla and SpaceX had formed special committees to discuss a potential merger.

Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh enters race for UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:41:25 UTC
05:41:25 KST

Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh enters race for UN chief
DUBAI, Oct 21 - Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh entered the race to become the next United Nations secretary-general on Wednesday, injecting a prominent Middle Eastern candidate into a contest that has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful members.
Nusseibeh, a former UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade, told Reuters she would seek to restore the world body’s role as a diplomatic problem-solver at a time of mounting global crises.
“It's clear that today we need a secretary-general that can recommit to the future of multilateralism and the future of the United Nations as a problem-solver rather than as a spectator to the world's crises,” she said shortly before going public with her candidacy.
Nusseibeh, the UAE minister of state for foreign affairs, is a late entrant to the race. An informal Security Council poll had placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner, sources have said.
Although Grynspan has led the informal "straw polls," last week she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Britain, China, France, Russia and the US.
Council members are negotiating over whether to hold another poll this Friday or at a later stage.
ENTREPRENEURIAL DIPLOMACY
Nusseibeh, 48, said she was approached by multiple countries during the last UN General Assembly to put herself forward. She previously led the UAE's successful campaign for election to the Security Council. Diplomats in New York say she is respected as a competent manager.
"It's recognized today that we need someone who offers generational change for the organization," she said.
Her UN tenure overlapped with the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023 when she secured the adoption of Resolution 2720 paving the way for the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Nusseibeh said she secured support for the resolution by arranging a visit by council members to the Rafah border crossing to see for themselves the situation on the ground, describing the move as part of her "creative entrepreneurial diplomacy" that characterizes her approach.
RELENTLESS DIPLOMACY
As a top UAE diplomat, Nusseibeh has championed Abu Dhabi’s assertive foreign policy and heavy focus on countering political Islam.
The UAE has faced criticism over Sudan after UN sanctions monitors described allegations that it provided military support to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces as credible. The UAE denies the allegations.
Asked how the allegations might affect her candidacy, Nusseibeh said she had taken leave from her UAE post and would focus on Sudan’s humanitarian crisis.
A Nusseibeh victory would make her the second UN chief from the Middle East, after Egypt’s Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
"I come from a country that is younger than the United Nations but our region is one that has been facing severe challenges," she said.
She would also become the first woman to lead the UN, though Nusseibeh said she was not running on her gender.
"I think it would be great if the next secretary-general was a woman but I'm not running because I'm a woman; I'm running because I am stubbornly optimistic about the future of the United Nations and I believe we need someone who is relentless in the pursuit of diplomacy to open doors." REUTERS

Council of Europe urges Ukraine to strengthen protection of Roma and LGBTI people against discrimination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:40:43 UTC
05:40:43 KST

Council of Europe urges Ukraine to strengthen protection of Roma and LGBTI people against discrimination
The findings are set out in ECRI’s new report on Ukraine, published in Strasbourg on October 21, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
“Since the adoption of ECRI’s fifth report on Ukraine on 20 June 2017, progress has been made and good practices have been developed in many areas,” the executive summary states.
Among the positive developments, the experts highlighted increased activity by the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, expanded police training in investigating hate crimes, and the adoption of strategies for Roma inclusion. The report also notes a significant improvement in public attitudes towards LGBTI people.
At the same time, Roma and LGBTI people remain particularly vulnerable to hate speech.
“Many cases of hate crime continue to be misclassified and prosecuted as ordinary offences, including hooliganism,” the report states.
The report contains 15 recommendations for the Ukrainian authorities, two of which have been identified as priorities. The first calls for public awareness campaigns against hate speech, particularly targeting LGBTI people and Roma, to be conducted in cooperation with civil society.
The second calls for the establishment of a working group to identify Roma people who need identity documents and help them obtain them, including by simplifying administrative procedures. ECRI will assess implementation of these two recommendations through an interim follow-up review no later than two years after the report’s publication.
The commission also recommends tackling anti-LGBTI bullying in schools, improving access to healthcare, ensuring quality education for Roma children, and providing the Ombudsman with adequate human and financial resources.
The report covers the period from June 2017 to March 2026 and takes into account the exceptional circumstances caused by Russia’s war of aggression. It does not cover the situation in temporarily occupied territories or that of Ukrainians who have been forced to flee abroad, as ECRI examines the latter as part of its monitoring of other countries.
As reported, Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset presented the main priorities of the organisation’s 2027–2030 Action Plan, “Democratic Security for Ukraine”, which aims to strengthen democratic resilience, the rule of law and judicial independence, and support reforms required for European integration.

Zuckerberg’s company fined a record $25 billion over Facebook data scandal

Zuckerberg’s company fined a record $25 billion over Facebook data scandal
Kyiv • UNN
A New Mexico court found that Meta had misled users about personal data for 11 years. The fine was reduced from $219 billion to $25 billion.
A U.S. court has ordered Meta, the company that owns Facebook, to pay a record fine of $25 billion for misleading users for years about the use of their personal data. BBC reports, UNN writes.
Details
The ruling was issued on October 21 by New Mexico state judge Francis Matthew. He found that over an 11-year period, from 2010 to 2021, the company knowingly concealed the true methods it used to process users’ information.
According to the court’s findings, statements by Meta’s executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were intended to mislead the public. The judge emphasized that the violations concerned not only personal data but also the fundamental principles of the company’s business operations.
The fine could have reached $219 billion
The lawsuit is linked to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, during which Facebook users’ data was used for political consulting, particularly in the context of the 2016 U.S. presidential election.
The New Mexico Attorney General’s Office accused Meta of making false claims that the company had allegedly not shared personal data with third parties.
Initially, the total fines for thousands of violations of state law were estimated at $219 billion. However, the judge reduced the penalty to $25 billion, making it the largest fine in the company’s history.
This year, Meta has also faced other major penalties and legal settlements related to user safety, particularly that of minors.

Russia has signaled support for trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday, Oct 21, confirming that the meeting could take place no later than early November.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The American side proposes to do this [organize the meeting] as soon as possible. We support that,” Zelensky said, adding that ending the war remains in focus.
Kyiv backs ceasefire and prisoner exchanges
Zelensky told reporters that the Ukrainian delegation would support proposals for a ceasefire, an energy truce and humanitarian initiatives, including the return of prisoners of war (POWs).
According to Ukrinform, the president had also expressed hope that Russia would honor its commitments to the trilateral format.
Although Moscow has signaled openness to the discussions, it showed very little willingness for a partial truce. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov earlier said Putin was not considering an energy ceasefire.
“Russia needs peace, not a ceasefire,” he said, rebuking US President Donald Trump’s recent announcement of an energy truce between the Kremlin and Moscow.
‘Capitulating to a Dictator Shows Weakness’ – Republican Senator Slams Trump’s Russia Policy
Following the talks, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said that Putin had told Witkoff Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations around mid-November, with a focus on postwar security arrangements.
The proposed trilateral meeting – including Ukraine – appears to be separate from a possible meeting between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, which Ushakov said Beijing was already preparing.
Speaking ahead of the meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, Zelensky said the three leaders were free to meet. However, any talks about Ukraine’s future could only be discussed with Kyiv present “at the table of negotiations.”
On Tuesday, Oct. 20 Trump said that he was willing to meet Putin and Xi in China next month, possibly without Zelensky. He suggested Ukraine should have someone else negotiate on its behalf.
Sign of a thaw between Kyiv and Washington
The renewed push toward peace talks comes as diplomatic ties between Kyiv and Washington appear to be recovering from more than a week of escalating tensions.
Trump’s rhetoric, however, has continued to cast doubt on that recovery. Speaking in the Oval Office on Oct. 20, as the Oslo talks were underway, he claimed that Russian forces “just keep marching forward” in Ukraine and that the US had given Kyiv $350 billion while getting nothing back, other than grief and high diesel.
Kyiv Post found both claims to be false.
The rift began on Oct. 9, when Trump announced an abrupt, controversial diesel deal with Putin while a Ukrainian delegation was holding peace negotiations with Trump’s administration in Miami.
In the days that followed, Ukraine faced unannounced restrictions on Starlink terminals and a week-long pause in US intelligence sharing.
Trump also called for Ukraine to elect a new president, prompting Zelensky to respond that only Ukrainian citizens could decide on his removal.
For the occasion, Kyiv proposed a 60-day ceasefire, but Moscow rejected the proposal, offering only a one-day truce on the day of the elections itself.
Trump also announced an immediate energy ceasefire on Oct. 11, claiming both sides had agreed to it – although neither formally did. While Ukraine abided by the truce, Peskov claimed Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.
Following discussions in Oslo on Oct. 20, Zelensky confirmed US intelligence sharing with Ukraine has resumed, adding that Kyiv could see results within the next 48 hours on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions.
The latest round of diplomacy builds on Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner’s previous visits to Moscow and Kyiv on Sept. 5-6, where they held three hours of discussions with Putin followed by an informal dinner, before heading to Ukraine for the first time during their tenure.
Although all three sides described the negotiations as substantive and positive, no breakthrough was reached.

Pope's doctors say he requires no further treatment after lung surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:38:22 UTC
05:38:22 KST

Doctors treating Pope Leo XIV have announced that final tissue and molecular tests confirmed that the lung cancer discovered in his body was localized and that he requires no further treatment, the Vatican said Wednesday evening, bringing welcome news to more than a billion Catholics worldwide.
The 71-year-old pontiff, who took office only last year following the death of Pope Francis, underwent surgery last week to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Shortly afterward, the Vatican announced that tests had confirmed suspicions that Leo had lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. At the time, however, the Vatican did not say whether the pope would require additional medical procedures, leaving questions about his condition.
On Wednesday evening, the Vatican said the pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, had confirmed that tests on tissue removed during surgery supported the initial diagnosis that the cancer had not spread.
"Further oncological evaluation confirmed that no additional treatment is necessary," the doctors said.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday and has since been gradually returning to his daily routine. On Wednesday, he returned to St. Peter's Square at the Vatican for his weekly general audience with the faithful, riding among the crowds in his popemobile.
He is scheduled to make an 11-day trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, and Vatican officials expect the visit to proceed as planned.
Leo XIV was elected pope in May 2025 at age 70, relatively young for a leader of the Catholic Church. He is known for his love of sports, including tennis, and was not known to be a smoker or to have experienced recent health problems before the cancer was discovered in his lung.
The pope is the highest earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, and there is no deputy who automatically assumes his duties when he falls ill. When a pope is unable to perform his duties, the Vatican's extensive administrative operations continue, but decisions requiring his direct approval are put on hold.
Pope Leo XIV is the first American pope in history. Born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, he served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pontiff.

Trump Isn’t Even Good at TV Anymore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:38:01 UTC
05:38:01 KST

Once upon a time, Donald Trump’s talents as a TV personality and pitchman were obvious to everyone—most of all himself.
When he launched his 2016 presidential run, millions of Americans knew him best not from his bankrupt casinos or the gossip pages of the New York Post but as the swaggering host of NBC’s The Apprentice, in which aspiring entrepreneurs competed for a full-time job in his real estate empire.
Trump routinely overstated the primetime dominance of The Apprentice, which was a breakout hit in its debut 2003–2004 season but saw its ratings steadily decline over subsequent years. Nonetheless, his rise as a candidate, propelled by his willingness to say anything to stay in the news cycle, seemed to affirm his on-camera star quality (even if it was actually people behind the scenes of The Apprentice who had edited his unscripted and less-than-coherent bluster to make him sound like a straight-talking businessman).
But where is Trump’s TV firepower today? His latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, lasted a mere five days in the job, ousted following a disastrous on-camera performance at her first briefing just weeks before crucial midterm elections. Trump’s own media appearances are unhinged and embarrassing even by his standards; when he’s not falling asleep at events or in meetings, he’s claiming that NATO “gave” Greenland to the US and telling rallygoers about how he checked out Senator Jon Husted’s ass.
During Trump’s second term, his administration has done what it can to circumvent existing media and bring its messaging directly to voters with broadcast content that resembles familiar TV formats. It’s not breaking through at all.
On Tuesday, for example, the US Small Business Administration streamed an hour-long special called the Million Dollar Pitch Competition. The premise was that five business owners would appear before three celebrity judges (property investor Grant Cardone, rapper Nicki Minaj, and Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia, whose credentials as a member of Elon Musk’s DOGE were not mentioned) to vie for the biggest chunk of a $1 million cash prize supplied by Clover Network, a fintech company that provides point-of-sale platforms.
While the show, hosted by actor Dean Cain, was styled as something like a hybrid of Shark Tank and American Idol, it amounted to an extraordinarily dull attempt to prove that the Trump administration is bringing factory jobs back to the US. For some reason, it featured a short video in which Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, talked to an animated strand of DNA, because “America's DNA is small business.” The judges focused more on how animated the presenters were than the economic fundamentals of their pitch. When Marshall Sasse, the owner and CEO of a pressure valve company based in Wyoming, delivered a solid but subdued presentation, Minaj asked if he had access to any “cowgirls” who could’ve added “more punch to the pitch.”
While Trump himself was not on hand for the pitches, the show featured brief segments in which participants met with Trump in the Oval Office. When the judges asked the president for advice on picking a winner, Trump replied, “You know, it's interesting, because with The Apprentice, I had a very good term that I used: ‘You're fired.’”
A day later, the YouTube stream of the SBA’s Million Dollar Pitch Competition had barely cracked 60,000 views. Even on Trump-friendly X, the reaction to the event was hostile, with users suggesting that the White House cared more about game shows than the cost of living and was taking its cues from dystopian fiction such as The Hunger Games.
Other efforts to supplant mainstream programming have also fared poorly. A month after the White House launched a 24/7 Trump TV streaming channel as part of its ongoing war on news outlets, it’s hard to imagine even the most devoted MAGA disciple watching: on Tuesday, unremarkable B-roll footage from border agents driving alongside the US-Mexico wall segued into a series of testimonials from people describing how their loved ones were raped and murdered by migrants. On Wednesday, the channel showed footage from Trump’s February State of the Union address.
As for Robert F. Kennedy’s The Real Food Show on YouTube, a cooking series in which the health secretary enlists chefs to teach viewers affordable and healthy home recipes, audience has declined since a July premiere, with only six episodes released so far. The most recent segment included Cain as well as actor and ex-bodybuilder Lou Ferrigno, as though to underscore that on the celebrity front, some of Trump world’s biggest names are guys known for playing superheroes on TV in the previous century.
If there has been any sort of a ratings win for MAGA media this year, it would be UFC Freedom 250, the mixed martial arts extravaganza held in June at a ring structure controversially erected on the South Lawn of the White House. Though Ultimate Fighting Championship lost some $30 million on the spectacle, it broke the viewership record for a live event airing exclusively on streamer Paramount+, with an average of 7 million viewers tuned in.
That fell well short of the Super Bowl records that Dana White, CEO of UFC, had promised to break. While he was nonetheless able to declare a victory for his sports organization, White has said that he “can’t afford” to return to Trump’s backyard for an encore. Too bad for the administration, which has yet to capture a real TV audience without significant help from a producer who knows what they’re doing.

The comments by Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes come as Republican President Donald Trump has in recent weeks eased economic sanctions on Russia and increased pressure on Ukraine to end its fight against Russian forces.
Warner and Himes told reporters they were limited in revealing what they had learnt in an election security briefing that they had requested from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton because it was classified.
But, they said, Russia was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the US intelligence community had tracked in US elections in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
“And the state of play, I would argue, is that, you know, Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats,” Warner said.
He noted news reports that Democrat James Talarico, who is running for the US Senate in Texas, and Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in Georgia, “in particular are being dinged” by fake advertisements created with artificial intelligence.
The White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Moscow in the past has denied meddling in US elections.
Himes said the pair could not provide details of the misinformation spread by Russia because the material was classified. But he added that Moscow’s conduct has been “the same old, same old”.
“The Russians are kind of throwing everything out there,” said Himes. “Chaos, you know, don’t trust your voting machines.”
He added there was “no reason to believe” that China has not been conducting “extremely targeted” efforts as it has done in the past to influence voters.
The Chinese embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing has previously denied interfering in US elections.
Recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has shown Democrats leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by high single digits to low double digits nationally, bolstering Democratic hopes of regaining control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate.
The lawmakers said they were concerned that Trump could pursue efforts to contest election results, including by claiming foreign hacking of voting infrastructure.
Himes emphasised that there was no evidence that any country could penetrate US election systems and change results.
“Nothing out there suggests that there is even the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment,” said Himes. REUTERS
