Russia signals readiness to resume trilateral talks as Putin meets with US envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:35:31 UTC
05:35:31 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 21. /TASS/. Wednesday’s meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff, which lasted nearly three hours, was detailed and frank, Kremlin Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
According to him, Putin and Witkoff discussed options for resuming talks involving Russia, the United States and Ukraine.
The Russian leader informed the US envoy that Moscow was ready to resume trilateral negotiations in early November, Ushakov added.
TASS has compiled the key details of the meeting.
Ushakov’s statements
Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that the meeting had been arranged several days in advance: "It was a planned meeting, agreed upon several days earlier."
He added that US negotiator Jared Kushner had been unable to travel to St. Petersburg with Witkoff due to illness and had joined the meeting via video link: "As before, Jared Kushner was expected to take part, but he was unable to come due to health issues. He joined via video link and had the opportunity to share his views and assessments on the issues under discussion."
This was the ninth meeting between Putin and Witkoff, which "serves as a useful addition to regular phone calls between the presidents of Russia and the United States."
Ushakov stressed that the meeting was "detailed and frank" and lasted almost three hours.
The Kremlin aide added that Putin highly appreciated US efforts to help resolve the Ukraine conflict: "The Russian president commended the mediation efforts of the US administration, Donald Trump personally and his envoys to find mutually acceptable solutions."
The Kremlin aide also said that "Putin highlighted the effectiveness of efforts being made by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner."
Ushakov noted that the Ukraine issue had been the main focus of the Putin-Witkoff meeting: "The situation surrounding Ukraine was naturally the central topic of the conversation between our president and Steve Witkoff."
Ushakov also told reporters that Witkoff had briefed Putin on new approaches to resolving the conflict put forward by European and Ukrainian officials during talks in Norway: "This time, the Russian president’s meeting with Steve Witkoff was preceded by the US envoy’s negotiations in Oslo with [Vladimir] Zelensky and some officials from European countries, NATO and the European Commission. Clearly, Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the Oslo talks and shared his assessments, highlighting some new approaches - the new aspects of the approaches pursued by the Europeans and Kiev."
According to Ushakov, Putin and Witkoff also exchanged views on ways to achieve lasting peace in Ukraine: "As a follow-up to the October 9 phone call between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, an exchange of views continued on ways to achieve lasting and sustainable peace [in Ukraine]."
The Kremlin aide noted that the meeting included a detailed discussion of potential ways to resume trilateral talks involving representatives of Russia, the US and Ukraine: "It’s important to point out that a framework for a possible resumption of trilateral talks involving representatives of Russia, the US and Ukraine was discussed in detail."
Putin told Witkoff that Russia was ready to resume trilateral negotiations in early November, Ushakov said: "Our president told Steve Witkoff that we were generally ready to resume these talks around November 10 on the main subject, which concerns establishing a security system for Russia and Ukraine."
He added that the Russian leader had briefed the US envoy on the situation in the special military operation zone where the Russian Armed Forces held the strategic initiative: "Vladimir Putin provided the other party with an objective picture of developments along the line of contact where Russian forces completely hold the strategic initiative. It was emphasized that they continued to advance in all key areas."
According to Ushakov, Putin also told Witkoff that the Russian army "is quite effectively eliminating defense industry sites, energy facilities and logistics hubs in Ukraine" in retaliatory strikes.
Putin and Witkoff also addressed ways to implement the diesel supply agreement between Russia and the US, Ushakov said: "Much attention was paid to issues related to the implementation of the agreements on Russian diesel supplies to the United States and global markets, reached by Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump during their October 9 call."
Ushakov stressed that the Russian president and the US presidential envoy agreed that the diesel deal would help stabilize global fuel markets: "Both parties underscored that the deal was both in US and Russian interests and would also help stabilize supply and demand on the global fuel market. With the US administration's waiver in effect for a number of sanctions on Russian diesel, practical work has begun to that end."
According to the Kremlin aide, Putin and Witkoff also considered the prospects for joint economic projects: "They thoroughly discussed other large-scale joint economic projects that offer significant opportunities for cooperation between the two countries. Some of them are nearing their launch."
He noted that "Putin highlighted interest in further joint work between the two countries, particularly at the level of intelligence agencies."
Ushakov said Putin and Witkoff had also addressed the possibility of a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, the United States and China on the sidles of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit: "The possibility of the first-ever meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the US during the APEC summit, set to be held in Shenzhen, China, in November, has attracted much attention around the world and was certainly touched upon today."
According to Ushakov, Putin put forward some practical proposals regarding a potential meeting with Trump and Xi Jinping: "As for the substance of potential trilateral talks, we put forward some practical considerations."
Ushakov noted that China was preparing for a potential meeting between Putin, Xi and Trump: "Our Chinese friends, the hosts of the APEC summit, are already making preparations for it. Under favorable circumstances, our Chinese friends will include the meeting in the program of Shenzhen events."
He stressed that neither Moscow nor Washington, nor Beijing had ruled out the possibility of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting.
Peskov’s statements
Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TV reporter Pavel Zarubin that Vladimir Putin’s meeting with Steve Witkoff had been substantive: "It was substantive. Clearly, they spent three hours together, even a bit more."
According to Peskov, no agreements have been reached so far on the US envoy’s next visit to Russia: "No agreements have been reached on that."
In response to a question, he said that the talks had taken place in a working atmosphere, and that the conversation had been substantive: "This is the way they communicate. There was nothing special, just a substantive conversation."
Peskov added that US entrepreneur Jared Kushner had joined the conversation via video link: "Kushner joined via video conference."
Dmitriev’s comment
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian special presidential envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and director general of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), described Putin’s meeting with Witkoff as "very productive."

David Chau's chart of the day: Fortescue's China problem
Hello there! Every afternoon, I'll give you a sneak peek at what I'll be discussing on my 7pm News finance report.
One thing that caught my eye was Fortescue, which saw its share price drop 4% today — and it's down 34% since the year began!
The mining giant has also wiped out all its gains in the past 15 months.
Earlier today, Fortescue released a trading update saying it might be forced to mine less iron ore, which will hurt its bottom line.
The company has been locked in tense negotiations with China's Mineral Resources Group, a state-owned enterprise that coordinates iron ore purchases for the country's steel mills.
China has been trying to secure a better deal by ordering some of its steelmakers to stop buying Fortescue's iron ore. Basically, it's a high-pressure negotiating tactic that's been going on for almost a year.
In fact, Fortescue said it shipped 46.8 million metric tons of iron ore in the September quarter — but only sold 42.9 million tons during that period!
Fortescue said if these discussions don't finish by the end of this year, it would have to reduce its production guidance (i.e. mine less ore).
It's a particularly severe problem for Fortescue because about 90% of its iron ore gets sold to China.
So it's less diversified (and more vulnerable) compared to BHP and Rio Tinto, which don't have all their eggs in one basket.

Key Event
Government told to overhaul code relating to bids for contracts
After allegations KPMG audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint, Ian Watt has called on KPMG to provide quarterly updates to federal government on its progress in implementing cultural reforms.
To help the Department of Finance in its monitoring role, KPMG needs to provide the department with "regular access".
"Finance should maintain the current pause on KPMG bidding for Commonwealth work for a further short period until KPMG has further demonstrated that the Action Plan and related recommendations are being effectively implemented," Dr Watt said.
The department also needed to ensure that "KPMG is engaging constructively with the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) and the Tax Practitioners Board (TPB) reviews, and is committed to addressing any recommendations that have been made by those organisations".
Dr Watt said finance should consider reinstating the "no bid" arrangement, in full or in part, if in the future:
- KPMG's implementation of the action plan "materially stalls"
- Additional substantive information regarding the KPMG whistleblower matter becomes known
- KPMG is found non-compliant with the Supplier Code of Conduct for matters unrelated to the KPMG whistleblower matter.
Dr Watt also called on Finance to strengthen the Supplier Code of Conduct, which surrounds bids for government contracts.
He said there should be "strengthened sanctions, including the ability to restrict or prohibit suppliers from bidding for Commonwealth government contracts where appropriate" and promote "pathways for individuals and organisations to report concerns about suppliers' potential unethical behaviour".
Dr Watt said there also needed to be clearer guidance for Commonwealth departments and agencies to assist them in assessing disclosures of potential unethical supplier conduct.

Key Event
KPMG needs to rebuild trust: Watt
Ian Watt said in his review the way KPMG had handled the whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings by some senior members of KPMG, significant cultural concerns within KPMG and a lengthy mismanagement of the whistleblower's claims and concerns".
He said his report should not, however, be read as a judgement on every member of KPMG.
"When I met with the whistleblower, they made that distinction directly," Dr Watt said in the review.
"My absolute observation is that 99 per cent of people at KPMG are really good. I know that serving the public interest and serving the Australian government is something they take seriously and passionately.
"Virtually all of KPMG's staff had no involvement in the events that occurred."
He noted the review was instead focused on the leadership and culture of the firm "that had been warned on previous occasions about weaknesses in ethical culture, speak-up confidence and accountability, but did not deal with them with the rigour and urgency required".
Dr Watt said since March, KPMG has undergone significant change, with a new chair and a new CEO, and a number of senior personnel having left the firm.
"KPMG has also commissioned several reviews to understand the root causes of the events and has given assurances that it will implement the recommendations," he said.
"Trust, however, is not restored through assurances alone.
"As was often observed during review interviews, trust takes time to build, and while transparency builds trust, lack of transparency damages it.
"Ultimately, an organisation rebuilds trust when it demonstrates that it has acknowledged and confronted difficult issues honestly, admitted shortcomings where they exist, taken meaningful and sustained action to address their causes, and results publicly confirm essential change."
Dr Watt said in terms of the firm's ongoing engagement with the Commonwealth, it would depend on whether "KPMG can again be fully trusted to provide advice and services that support public outcomes without the current restrictions it faces".
Key Event
Government pausing renewal of KPMG contract
The federal government will put a hold on renewing its contract with KPMG, following allegations its audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it.
Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into the Big Four firm.
The review found that KPMG "failed to respond appropriately to concerns raised by a whistleblower and that this reflected broader weaknesses in the firm's culture, governance and accountability arrangements".
While KPMG had established policies, reporting channels and oversight structures, the review found "these did not operate effectively in practice to provide appropriate support to the whistleblower, identify emerging risks, or ensure timely and coordinated decision-making".
The review concluded that KPMG's response to the matter was "fragmented, lacked clear ownership and did not adequately bring together warning signs that warranted closer scrutiny".
While recognising reform efforts underway within KPMG, the review said restoration of trust will depend on "KPMG's sustained implementation of reforms, independent assurance and demonstrated improvements in practice".
In response to the review, the Department of Finance has agreed with KPMG a further extension to the pause on KPMG bidding for Australian government work until February 28, 2027.
During this period, KPMG will provide the department with an implementation plan and the first of its quarterly progress implementation reports.
ABS releases new monthly regional labour force data
Today, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) released the first issue of its new monthly Regional Labour Force publication, which models labour force estimates for Statistical Area Level 4 (SA4) regions across Australia.
The ABS says this new monthly publication will be released one week after the usual national labour force survey.
It provides a much more granular level of detail about local unemployment rates in our major cities, regions and rural areas.
The national unemployment rate in September was 4.7% (as we reported), but unemployment isn't uniform across the country.
For example, in Sydney, according to today's regional labour force publication, the local unemployment rate was:
- Parramatta: 6.7%.
- Blacktown: 5.8%
- North Sydney and Hornsby: 4%
- Northern beaches: 3.1%
- Eastern suburbs: 2.7%
- etc.
Those numbers give a better indication of the state of the labour market in different parts of the city.
On the ABS website, it shows a map of every state and territory, which you can zoom into to see the local unemployment rates.

The new monthly publication will provide estimates for SA4 regions from January 2012 onwards, with estimates for:
- Employment
- Unemployment
- Not in the labour force (NILF)
- Unemployment rate
- Participation rate
- Employment-to-population ratio.

Here they are, as written in the report.
- KPMG should implement its Action Plan to ensure the necessary measures are put in place as rapidly as is appropriate. KPMG should maintain an implementation focus over the medium term to ensure the desired impact of the Action Plan.

New US law requires dating apps to include warnings on romance scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:33:01 UTC
05:33:01 KST

ROMANCE SCAMS
New US law requires dating apps to include warnings on romance scams
As romance scams incur record losses, the law requires apps to notify users if someone they’ve been talking to is banned for fraud.
A new U.S. law signed by President Donald Trump Tuesday will require online dating services to notify users when someone they’ve been talking to is banned from the platform for fraud.
The bipartisan Romance Scam Prevention Act, backed by senators Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee (R-Ten) and John Hickenlooper of Colorado (D-Colo), was passed unanimously by the Senate in late September and went to the president for signature earlier this month.
Romance fraud schemes accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic when more seniors turned to dating sites for companionship, followed by scammers. Romance scams incurred record-high losses in 2025, with Federal Trade Commission data showing over 70,000 reports and a staggering $1.47 billion lost in the U.S. Losses also reportedly surged in the U.K., South Korea, Australia and across Africa.
Some dating sites already remove fraudsters’ accounts but a victim may continue talking to a scammer off the app long after a scammer’s profile has been deleted. The Romance Scam Prevention Act aims to close that gap by requiring dating platforms to send a fraud ban notification to anyone who has communicated with someone with a fraudulent account.
Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif), who introduced the bill into the House, told the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists that he drafted the consumer protection legislation after hearing firsthand accounts from residents in his California Central Valley district who had fallen victim to online swindlers.
“Millions of Americans use online dating sites to meet significant others, making them the perfect hunting ground for scammers and bad actors to target unsuspecting victims and exploit them for money,” Valadao told ICIJ. “This bipartisan, bicameral legislation is a common sense step toward enhancing online safety and combating financial fraud.”
The law, which will take effect in a year, will be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
The ban notification requirement applies to users who received a message from the banned account through the dating service. The notice, generally required by apps 24 hours after issuing a fraud ban, would need to identify the banned account and tell the recipient when they most recently sent or received a message with that user. It also would need to warn that the person may have used a false identity or attempted to defraud users, advise people not to send cash or financial information and provide fraud-prevention resources and customer-service contact information.
In July, an ICIJ investigation reported that women across four continents alleged they were emotionally manipulated and drained of money on pay-per-interaction dating sites including AmoLatina, Dating.com and DateMyAge.
The sites belong to the Malta-based Social Discovery Group, which is controlled by Russian entrepreneur Dmitry Volkov.
The women paid for every message, photo and video while “dating” attractive, supposedly verified profiles that never agreed to a live video call or an in-person meeting. Many later traced these suitors through reverse image searches to models and influencers, mostly from Brazil and Colombia.
The sites’ own policies set engagement quotas for “free users,” such as replying to most chats within minutes. SDG denies paying models or employing chat operators and says it bans profiles run by third parties.
The new law comes on the heels of a recent report from the Joint Economic Committee minority into scams on Match Group’s dating platforms — including Tinder, Hinge and Match, among others — that found nearly $1.5 billion in reported romance-scam losses last year, up roughly 650% from 2019.
A 2019 Federal Trade Commission lawsuit alleged that Match Group had knowingly exposed Match.com users to accounts previously identified as scammers. Match Group contended that most of the contentious accounts were spammers and bots.
The new report found that while Match Group had significantly expanded its anti-scam efforts, internal company documents show long-standing weaknesses in Tinder’s detection systems, including staff complaints that the AI models had not been updated in years, which degraded their performance and left them blind to common scammer signals, such as location and IP changes.
According to the report, Match Group’s own data showed scammers reaching more and more users. Between May 2024 and December 2025, the median scammer’s profile views before being banned rose from under 70 to over 500, an increase of more than 700%.
Internal documents also indicated that Tinder usually showed scammers to users at higher rates than legitimate accounts
“Scams that began on Match Group platforms have imposed significant human costs,” the report said. “Victims have lost entire savings, incurred lasting debt, and suffered severe psychological distress.”

Moldova Launches Security Review of Russia’s Yandex Go Over Data and Ownership Risks

- Category

Moldova Launches Security Review of Russia’s Yandex Go Over Data and Ownership Risks
Moldova has launched an in-depth assessment of Yandex Go over potential risks involving information security, personal data protection, and the company’s ownership and control structure, the Moldovan government announced on October 16.
The decision was taken on October 15 during a meeting of the Council for the Examination of Investments of Importance for State Security, known as CEIISS.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Yandex has long operated as one of Russia’s largest technology companies, with services extending well beyond the domestic market into neighboring countries, including Moldova. Over time, the company came under increasing Kremlin pressure, including restrictions that reshaped Yandex.News and pushed the platform toward state-approved sources, while its Russian business was ultimately sold in 2024 to investors with ties to the country’s political and business elite.
The council ordered a deeper review of Yandex Go’s investment activities in Moldova, including the wider Yandex group’s involvement in local investment operations.
Yandex Go was given 20 days to provide documents and information required under Moldovan law, including details on its ownership structure and beneficial owners.
The National Center for Personal Data Protection was also instructed to prepare a detailed report on how Yandex Go collects, processes, stores, and transfers user data, and whether those practices comply with Moldovan legislation.
“We must investigate potential risks related to the unauthorized use of personal data, including the collection, storage and processing of, or unjustified access to, significant volumes of personal data belonging to citizens of the Republic of Moldova,” the government stated.
Moldovan authorities noted that CEIISS can impose conditions or restrictions on investments, require divestment of shares or assets, or suspend activities if the assessment identifies risks to state security.
The government also clarified that Yandex Go does not directly provide taxi services in Moldova but licenses use of its platform to local operators.
Operators pay Yandex Go a commission equal to 12% of each fare, while 20% VAT is applied to that commission. In 2025, approximately 12.5 million Moldovan lei ($696.375) in VAT linked to Yandex commissions was paid into the state budget.
Taxi operators, including those using Yandex Go, paid around 216 million lei ($12 million) in taxes and contributions in 2025, up 42% from 2024, according to the government.
Moldova’s State Tax Service is also continuing inspections of taxi operators. During the first months of 2026, authorities identified discrepancies in roughly half of the rides completed by 8,781 drivers.
CEIISS stated that the assessment remains ongoing and that further measures will depend on the risks identified.
Yandex has previously faced scrutiny over the scale of data it provides to Russian authorities. In 2025, the company handed over user information in 93,647 cases, fulfilling 85% of government requests, with most inquiries targeting ride-hailing and transportation services.

Aberfan: King Charles marks Welsh mining disaster that killed a generation of children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:31:16 UTC
05:31:16 KST

Survivors shared their memories with the royal party, six decades after an official verdict, a raid on donations and a fight over the tips that followed.
King Charles III has led tributes to the people of Aberfan on the 60th anniversary of the disaster, in which 116 children and 28 adults died when a colliery spoil tip collapsed onto Pantglas Junior School in Wales in 21 October 1966.
The King, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales met survivors in the Welsh village. The King and Prince William laid wreaths at the memorial garden, and the Queen placed a posy.
"We have heard stories of heartbreak, but also of heroism," the King said. "We have heard of the most agonising grief, but also of the most inspiring grace."
Coal bosses had been warned of the danger beforehand, yet no one was prosecuted or lost their job.
What happened at Aberfan?
Aberfan is a small coal-mining village in the valleys of south Wales, in the United Kingdom. For decades, waste from the local colliery had been dumped in huge heaps, known as tips, on the hillside above the houses.
These tips had moved before - the heap of coal waste had slid in 1944 and again in 1963, but the warning signs were not acted on.
On the morning of Friday 21 October 1966, one of the tips gave way. Shortly after 9.15am, over 100,000 cubic metres of sodden waste poured down the mountain and onto the village school, just as lessons were starting.
The last child to be found alive was pulled out at 11:00 that morning.
The scale of the loss is still hard to grasp. The disaster claimed the lives of 144 people, 116 of them children, and an entire generation of the village was all but wiped out. Within days, the UK Parliament ordered an official inquiry.
What did the inquiry find?
On 26 October 1966, the UK government minister for Wales appointed a tribunal led by senior judge Lord Justice Edmund Davies. It heard evidence first in nearby Merthyr Tydfil and then in the Welsh capital, Cardiff.
Its verdict, published in August 1967, was unequivocal - "Blame for the disaster rests upon the National Coal Board," the state-owned body that ran Britain’s coal industry. As a result of the inquiry, information about every one of the board’s tips was gathered for the first time.
People across Britain and around the world sent money to help the grieving village, and the disaster fund grew to £1.75m (€2.08m).
What happened to the money donated?
In 1968, UK Prime Minister Harold Wilson’s government forced the disaster fund to give up £150,000 (€178,000) to pay for removing the remaining coal waste heaps above Aberfan, even though those tips belonged to the National Coal Board.
The village had to wait almost three decades for the money to be returned. Ron Davies, the UK government’s minister for Wales, repaid it in 1997, and the Welsh Government later gave Aberfan charities a further £2m.
The fund made equal payments to every bereaved family. The UK's Charity Commission tried to block these payments as it wanted the trustees to be satisfied that each parent had been "close" to the child who died. The trustees defied the Commission and paid the families anyway.
The fund was attempting to support families because the National Coal Board was paying them very little. The board raised its compensation offer from £50 to £500 (€596) per bereaved family.
Sixty years later, organisations across Wales were invited to observe a minute’s silence at 9.15am on Wednesday, the moment the tip collapsed.

Underpaid super affects one in four workers, with billions never recovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:30:23 UTC
05:30:23 KST

Workers say ATO not doing enough to recoup unpaid superannuation
In short:
Workers and industry experts are calling on the Australian Taxation Office to be more proactive in responding to unpaid superannuation claims.
Data shows one in four workers are underpaid super, and only 15 per cent of that is recovered by the ATO.
What's next?
The ATO says it is serious about ensuring employers are paying super.
One in four Australian workers are underpaid superannuation by their employers, amounting to about $6 billion each year, with independent reports showing only about 15 per cent is ever recovered by the tax office.
The figures come as no surprise to Pauline Devin and Angela Noack, who were underpaid about $5,000 and $3,000 respectively in super while working at a Brisbane dental clinic two years ago.
Early last year, the oral health therapists filed separate complaints with the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), and the regulator found in their favour in April.
But 18 months later, neither have seen a cent returned to their super fund or received any further information from the ATO.
"All I ever used to get was, 'No, we can't give you any information because it's an invasion of privacy'," Ms Devin said.
"I wasn't asking for financial details or anything like that.
"I just wanted to know when I could maybe, possibly, think about getting that superannuation paid to me."
The long wait and lack of information from the ATO has left Ms Devin and Ms Noack feeling helpless.
"I have come to the conclusion I'm probably not ever going to get my super paid from [my employer] at this point, and the ATO don't seem to be really going in to bat and doing anything about recovering that either," Ms Noack said.
"At the moment we've got no way forward … you just feel like you're in limbo,"
Ms Devin added.
"The ATO is just useless and hopeless."
The ATO declined the ABC's request for an interview, but a spokesperson said in a statement it was "serious about ensuring employers comply with their super obligations and dedicates significant resources to educating employers, undertaking audits and debt recovery actions after liabilities have been raised".
The spokesperson also reiterated the ATO's position that "tax secrecy and privacy laws limit what the ATO can disclose to employees" and said where the tax office collected unpaid super on behalf of employees, it advised them accordingly.
Funds hire private firm to recoup super
Industry Fund Services collects unpaid super on behalf of three super funds, in a role similar to the ATO's regulatory responsibilities.
But the firm's executive manager of super recoveries Natalie Lister said the organisation took a more "proactive approach" to super debt recovery.
"We'll use digital communications, SMS, email … outbound calls and that's where our specialist team really come in … and [get] an understanding of the employer's situation and working with them to actively resolve it," she said.
"If we don't have any success early on, we then have escalation processes, so we'll follow up with … what we call a final demand call and then at that point, we will actually threaten to take legal action."
Loading...
Ms Lister said in most cases, the digital communication and phone calls were enough to successfully engage employers, with only about 10 per cent of cases escalated to the "final call and letter of demand".
She said the firm had for years used data provided by its super fund clients to contact employers who were not paying super, avoiding the need for employees to discover and then flag the discrepancy themselves.
"We'll try and contact the employer as soon as we can to find out if there is any super payments overdue," she said.
"Our experience has largely seen that the ATO, if they are going to intervene, it's much further down the track."
Payday super needs to be 'backed in action'
On July 1, the ATO introduced payday super, meaning employers are now required to pay workers their super at the same time as their wages.
Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said the reform was a game-changer for the industry because it offered workers and the ATO real-time visibility of their super.
However, Ms Schubert said the new laws needed to be backed in action by the tax office taking a more proactive approach.
"It's not OK for people to have to chase and chase and be their own debt collection office. That is the responsibility of the regulator,"
she said.
"[The ATO] now has the tools and the visibility in real time to go and ask those proactive compliance questions of each employer."
The ATO spokesperson told the ABC it used "multiple data sources to help identify non-compliance, including single touch payroll (STP), super fund reporting [and] employee and third-party referrals" to "proactively identify and pursue unpaid superannuation".
The spokesperson also pointed to the regulator's own data, which showed 92 per cent of super contributions by dollar value were paid voluntarily by employers.
However, Ms Schubert and her colleagues said that figure hid the impact on the ground, where one in four workers, who were often in low-paid jobs, were short-changed on their super.
Ms Schubert said on average, only 15 per cent of unpaid superannuation was recovered by the ATO, a figure backed by a 2022 Australian National Audit Office report.
Calls for more transparency, safety net
Ms Devin, who is now retired, and Ms Noack said they felt frustrated by the system and wanted to see the ATO do more for workers.
"I think the ATO needs to be more transparent as to what they're doing to recover unpaid super," Ms Devin said.
"They need to come down harder on employers that don't pay their super, by way of penalties,"
Ms Noack added.
Ms Schubert said the experience the two Brisbane workers had with the ATO was "heartbreaking and completely unacceptable".
"There should be a much clearer, simpler process for keeping workers updated," she said.
"So having a clear contact person, having regular updates provided to those workers and having real visibility on what's been happening in the process."
Ms Schubert said where the ATO could not recover super owed to workers because, for example, an employer was insolvent, the federal government should improve the safety net offered to employees via the Fair Entitlements Guarantee.
"The Fair Entitlements Guarantee scheme covers wages, leave and any redundancy that should have been paid in those circumstances, but it does not yet include super [and] we think it absolutely needs to include any unpaid super," she said.
A spokesperson for the federal government said since July 2024, it had strengthened the scheme's recovery program, which now allowed liquidators funded by the government to "actively pursue unpaid superannuation guarantee charge amounts in eligible insolvencies and improve recovery outcomes".
Ms Devin and Ms Noack said as women who took leave to care for children and aging parents, their experiences had left them feeling even worse off.
"You're already behind the 8-ball as a mother or as a non-working parent … and then to not get what you're entitled to," Ms Noack said.
"Every little bit counts in this economy and retirement is scary. You want to make sure you have enough to live on and you've done the work and you should be paid what you're legally entitled to."
"You can do everything right and if your employer doesn't pay it, then you're the one penalised," Ms Devin added.

Industry Minister Tim Ayres says no government websites have been breached following the discovery of a major vulnerability in programming language.

NACC says corruption ruling threshold is high
TheNational Anti-Corruption Commission says proving corruption requires more than showing a government decision delivered a political benefit.
Appearing before a parliamentary inquiry examining a grant to Marrickville Golf Course in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's electorate, acting commissioner Kylie Kilgour said the watchdog had been following the inquiry closely but could not comment on the specific case, because it could be referred to the commission.
Kilgour says the NACC would need evidence that the predominant purpose of a program was political, noting case law accepts that governments may receive a political benefit as a “side wind” from election commitments.
The comment prompted senators to ask how the commission distinguishes between a side wind that is a “soft breeze” and one that is a "gale".
Kilgour says multiple factors inform that assessment.
AI committee will seek briefing over website vulnerabilities
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam, who is also the deputy chair of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, said the committee would be seeking briefings from the government about the widespread website outage overnight.
Globally, websites, including those of several Australian government agencies, have been pulled offline to patch vulnerabilities identified by AI in a widely-used programming language.
Duniam told News24 the committe, which is hearing submissions today, wanted to know exactly what unfolded and "what processes were put in place to protect data".
He said lessons needed to be learned from the event, and that in this case the vulnerabilities were thankfully detected by a "friendly AI agent".
"God help us in the situation where our adversaries are deploying malevolent AI agents and we are not able to protect ourselves," Duniam said.
First look at the armed Ghost Shark
Earlier this week we got the first insight into how the lethally-armed Ghost Shark autonomous submarine would actually go about…shooting things.
The Navy is acquiring dozens of Ghost Sharks over the next few years, under a $1.7 billion contract with manufacturer Anduril.
Before this week we'd known they were going to be armed, but the details weren't public — then on Monday, it was revealed they will be able to launch aerial explosive drones, and launch sea mines.
If you were wondering how a submarine launches aerial drones (and sea mines) — Anduril has released some new pictures demonstrating just what it looks like.
Labor MP says website outage underlines need for AI safety guardrails
Labor MP Ed Husic says recent website outages to patch potential security flaws reinforce the need for artificial intelligence guardrails.
Several government sites went offline overnight after a vulnerability was discovered in 70 per cent of the world's websites by an OpenAI tool, which detected a flaw in the PHP programming language.
Although the vulnerability was detected by using AI, Husic — a former industry minister — said AI companies liked to push boundaries.
"I also want to make clear, it can't be the case that companies identify these vulnerabilities because they've been doing stuff that they haven't been permitted to do, and they dress it up as a favour," he said.
Husic said he was careful not to suggest that was the case in this instance.
He added when it came to AI: "I don't catastrophise or evangelise, I think we've just got to get the balance right."
On the question of AI and copyright deals for Australian creators, he said people should be paid fairly for their work.
"You shouldn't be ripped off, particularly by firms that will become some of the most powerful commercial and economic firms on the planet," he said.
"Their founders are going from being billionaires to trillionaires … They don't work for free, they shouldn't expect the people producing copyrighted material should work for free either. They need to pay up."
Key Event
Australia signs new defence cooperation agreement with Timor-Leste
Australia has signed a new defence cooperation agreement with Timor-Leste as Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles visits the South-East Asian nation.
Under the new framework, Australia will provide $62 million over five years to strengthen Timor-Leste's cybersecurity, improve digital forensics and disaster preparedness, and enhance the maritime capabilities of its police force, including by providing three police vessels.
The two countries will also expand joint training and exercises.
The reference to cybercrime is noteworthy — Timor-Leste has emerged as a new hub for scam centre operators, with police arresting more than 250 people operating at three separate call centre compounds in the capital Dili in July.
Marles said in Dili yesterday evening that both countries were grappling with a "a very challenging world where the rules-based order is under pressure [and] where we're seeing new developments in relation to cyber capability, artificial intelligence".
"All of these are creating a much more complicated world. Partnerships with friends matter more today than they have," he said.
"This is a time to double down on friendship, to double down on family, and that's certainly how we regard our relationship with Timor‑Leste."

“I didn't think I was going to be so affected,” Kilgour told the hearing.
“I think some of the news that's come through this morning is having an impact.”

Haines's husband, Phil Haines, confirmed on Wednesday night that the independent MP had lost both legs after suffering severe lower-body injuries in the attack outside her electorate office.
Industry minister says Australian govt websites not breached
Industry and Innovation Minister Tim Ayres says there has been no breach of Australian government websites, after multiple pages were pulled offline when a critical security flaw was identified.
Government agencies worldwide, including the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD), are among those affected by a flaw in the widely-used PHP internet programming language.
The flaw was discovered by artificial intelligence researchers with concerns hackers could exploit the vulnerability.
Speaking to News24, Ayres says this is an example of "very good cooperation" with AI researchers to strengthen Australia's cybersecurity.
"This isn't a breach ... this is led by the Australian Signals Directorate on behalf of the Australian government and cybersecurity agencies around the world working with, in this case, OpenAI to identify a weakness in these systems," he said.
"In this case, it does demonstrate how important it is to have that under-the-bonnet cooperation with the artificial intelligence frontier models.
"But it does underline that there is a constant battle on the cybersecurity front and Australian government agencies and private sector firms are constantly engaged in toughening up their cybersecurity."
Analysis: After Helen Haines attack, how do we actually turn down the temperature?
Only two months ago, a group called Compassion in Politics Australia gained the first signatory to its "Civility Pledge".
Helen Haines.
The organisation, based on a similar foundation in the United Kingdom, aims to turn the tide of toxic debate and build a better politics.
As a start, it's asking elected officials to sign a simple pledge. "In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion," is all it states.

National Science Foundation head Brian Stone to retire with no clear replacement in sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:28:18 UTC
05:28:18 KST

The interim head of the National Science Foundation (NSF), Brian Stone, is set to retire as soon as the end of this year, according to reports. There is no clear plan for a successor to steer the agency because President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the NSF, James O'Neill, has yet to have a confirmation hearing in the Senate.
Stone, who has led the agency since the spring of last year, will resign effective December 31, according to a memo that was sent to NSF staff on Tuesday and was obtained by journalist Dan Garisto. In the note, Stone reportedly wrote that he would be “working closely with the White House to identify who will perform the duties of the NSF Director as of January 1, 2027, should Mr. O’Neill’s nomination still be pending at that time.”
In a statement to Scientific American, NSF spokesperson Mike England appeared to confirm Stone’s upcoming retirement but did not confirm whether he would be leaving at the end of 2026.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Stone had “served the U.S. National Science Foundation and the American people with distinction for 26 years, including over the past 18 months while performing the duties of NSF Director,” England said in the statement. “His leadership has been instrumental in advancing NSF's mission, and we thank him for his decades of dedicated public service. Brian will continue to perform the duties of the Director until his retirement and NSF will announce any future leadership updates as they are available.”
The reported memo also indicated that acting NSF chief of staff Rebecca Keiser will depart as well. England did not confirm or deny this reporting.
Stone has led the NSF on an interim basis since April 2025, after the resignation of the agency’s previous director, Sethuraman Panchanathan, who was appointed during the first Trump presidency in 2019. Panchanathan’s departure came amid Elon Musk’s U.S. DOGE Service cuts, which saw mass staff firings, resignations and axes to grant funding. A staff member of the NSF for more than 25 years, Stone had previously spent 10 years as the agency’s chief of staff.
Stone’s imminent departure comes at a moment of turbulence at the top of the NSF. This past April the Trump administration fired all 22 members of the agency’s science advisory board—these positions are appointed by the president and serve staggered six-year terms. The advisers play a critical role in determining how the NSF disperses the roughly $9 billion in funding it doles out annually. The firings were widely criticized by the scientific community, with thousands of researchers signing an open letter that said it constituted an “alarming attack” on U.S. science. No new board members have since been named .

Pope Leo doesn’t need further treatment for lung cancer, doctors say
Follow-up tests show the pontiff’s disease has not spread after he had surgery to remove part of his lung
Pope Leo needs no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said in a statement on Wednesday.
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
He left the hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery and well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.
The pope’s personal doctor, Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the pope’s surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread.

SC said the right to participate in elections by filing nominations is a facet of the free poll process.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Wednesday said instilling confidence in the election process was vital for democracy and the rule of law as it directed Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission (SEC) not to declare the final candidate list for 19 of the 100 local bodies where opposition YSRCP has alleged that its candidates were prevented from filing nominations. However, the court refused to tinker with the Oct 28 polling date.An autumn-break bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and VMohana asked SEC to decide by Thursday if it should, after considering representations from candidates alleging use of force to prevent them from filing nominations, give additional time for filing of nominations or postpone polls. YSRCP importing criminals from Punjab: AP govt in SC

Such philosophy of deference has grown from a doctrine of necessity that the election process be entrusted in the hands of an independent constitutional authority and the process completed within a specified period and not get mired in the quagmire of judicial interference.
“...It also cannot be ignored that the custody of constitutional values lies with constitutional courts and the power of judicial review to ensure fair and impartial elections cannot be wholly muted when the principal opposition political party in a state is before us and has placed on record representations and material expressing serious apprehensions with regard to hindrance in participation in election process through filing of nomination papers.”

Bigger Than a Cessna, Smaller Than a C-130: Air Force Funds Blended-Wing Body Concept
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:18:20 UTC
05:18:20 KST

As the Air Force wrestles to solve the logistics of dispersed operations in the vast Indo-Pacific, it’s investing $3.5 million to help develop a new kind of aircraft: a blended-wing body freighter that’s smaller than a C-130 but larger than a Cessna for “sub-tactical” lift.
The startup firm behind the new aircraft, Natilus, thinks it could answer questions the Air Force faces about fuel, cargo space, and range to make its Agile Combat Employment concept work, an executive told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The Pentagon’s Operational Energy-Innovation Directorate and the office of the Air Force’s assistant secretary for energy, installations, and environment funded the $3.5 million contract with Natilus, which will go toward development of the firm’s KONA aircraft, including “full-scale flight testing” starting in late 2027 or early 2028, Chief Operating Officer Nolan Giblin told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an interview. There is also a demonstration planned during a joint force exercise, likely in the Pacific.
Blended-wing body aircraft are halfway between the traditional tube-and-wing and the flying wing designs, with the wings and fuselage blending together to help create lift. Its shape makes it more aerodynamic and fuel efficient, while increasing the size of the cabin in the fuselage.
“When you couple the aerodynamic efficiency of about 30 percent reduction in fuel with the added volumetric capacity, it really boils down to moving more for less,” said Giblin.
In 2023, the Air Force launched a BWB demonstrator/prototype program with startup JetZero, who is partnering with Northrop Grumman. That aircraft, dubbed Z4, is expected to fly in 2027.
But while the Z4 is a large aircraft on par with a KC-46 or C-17, KONA is far more modest and meant for an entirely different use, Giblin said. JetZero has pitched the Z4 as a potential future aerial refueler for the Air Force, with a wingspan approaching 185 feet and a maximum operating weight of 362,000 pounds; Giblin said KONA is focused on smaller airlift and has a wingspan of 85 feet and a max takeoff weight of 19,000 pounds.
Still, the Air Force’s support for the Z4—the service has invested about $235 million in the project—encouraged Natilus that there are “tailwinds” for BWB aircraft in the Pentagon, Giblin said.
Originally, Natilus developed KONA for “short-haul cargo operations and e-commerce,” according to its website. Companies like FedEx, DHL, and Amazon rely on massive “hub-and-spoke” networks, and a small BWB aircraft could move loads to smaller spokes more efficiently compared to a larger, tube-and-wing airframe. Besides being more fuel efficient, a BWB aircraft’s shape provides more total volume in the cabin, Giblin noted.
“Today’s tube-and-wing aircraft that they’re flying at the spoke-level of the hub and spoke are [maxing] out on volume before they top out on weight, and so they’re literally leaving revenue on the ground every time they take off. And so there’s an interest for a more volume-centric platform” Giblin said of commercial firms.
The Air Force is looking to build its own hub-and-spoke model—agile combat employment calls for dispersing small teams of Airmen and aircraft from large hubs to remote or austere airfields to make it harder for adversaries to target them.
Ensuring those forces can move efficiently and are supplied at their new locations, however, is no small feat. That’s especially true in the Pacific, where the distances are vast and mostly covered by water. The Air Force has about 270 C-130 tactical airlifters, which can haul 40,000 pounds of cargo, but service officials have shown an interest in more flexible solutions.
That’s led industry to develop an onslaught of small cargo drones—some are Cessna 208s modified to fly autonomously, others are clean-sheet designs. They range in payload capacity from 500 pounds to a few thousand.
KONA is at the high end of that range, capable of carrying payloads up to a little more than 8,000 pounds with a range of 800 nautical miles. Its capacity in particular is greater than the modified Cessnas other firms are working on, filling what Giblin described as a “capability gap” between the light utility aircraft and the C-130.
Like the smaller Cessnas, though, KONA will be “optionally manned.” For commercial operations and inside the U.S. under the FAA’s jurisdiction, Giblin said, a human pilot will likely fly. But for the Air Force, autonomy is a key attribute, especially when flying in contested airspace.
“We do have our own homegrown [autonomy] software stack. However, we also have optionality to partner with folks that are already looking at this in a serious way,” Giblin said. “ … And so, we have a couple different paths towards achieving autonomous flight.”
Natilus is already building its demonstrator—the Air Force contract will accelerate that production. Giblin said the “vertical tails, flight control surfaces are already built, the cargo loading system was delivered by Raytheon a couple weeks ago, we just put on order used PT6 engines.” Still to come are the wing shipset and the fuselage.

Resisting uprooting in the West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:17:42 UTC
05:17:42 KST

A fresh breeze makes its way around the porch as my father looks up at the cloudy sky. He zips up his jacket, turning to look at me with his eyebrows raised, and says, “Autumn is here.” In Palestine, especially in the annual calendar of villagers like my father, autumn already started a month ago, in mid-September, with the first rain of the year known as “the rain of the cross.” My father taught me this himself. But on this day, his comment was hinting at something else. “We should already be in the middle of the harvest,” I reply, shrugging my shoulders and looking down.
It is the third year in a row that we can’t harvest our olive groves in Taybeh, my village on the outskirts of Ramallah in the West Bank, due to the threat of Israeli settler attacks. This year, however, the municipality, with the help of local religious leaders, asked the Israeli army for a few days of “coordination”— permission for villagers to access their lands safely. The Israeli army offered “coordination” for three days. It was an indirect admission of their capacity to control settler mobs, if they wanted to. “They start on [October] 16th, but we don’t know if our land will be included or not,” my father says. After three years of waiting, he wishes to see the land he grew up farming. At his age, this disappointment affects him deeply. Although I didn’t grow up farming the land like him, I understand how profoundly personal that famous bond between Palestinians and their land is.
Mine was seeded in many little moments throughout my childhood. One of them was in the summer of 2006. I remember watching the sun set over the hill, while a water tank pulled by a tractor was stationed in the middle of a plain. Little olive trees, planted about a year earlier in rows across the plain, needed to be irrigated until they had grown strong roots. Two teenagers walked back and forth between the trees and the water tank with plastic buckets, dropping a bucket of water at the base of the furthest tree in that row, then the next, and so on, before the tractor pulled the water tank down to the next row of trees.
The man driving the tractor was my uncle. One of those two teenagers was my brother, and the other was me. That land where we had planted those olive trees belonged to my grandfather, and is still collectively owned by all his children and grandchildren. Every year, the extended family reunited in the plain for long days of harvest, gathering beneath the trees for a picnic, and at the end of the season, we celebrated this feat before taking our shares of olive oil home, enough for the rest of the year. That was until October 2023. Last summer, when my uncle risked going to the plain to check on the olive trees, an armed settler told him that our land wasn’t part of Taybeh anymore, and that he shouldn’t return.
My family’s story of the ongoing Israeli settlers’ offensive on the Palestinian olive season is far from being unique, or even one of the most violent. Across the West Bank, Israeli settler groups have been attacking Palestinian villagers harvesting their olives since September of this year. The attacks have been concentrated in the regions of Nablus, Salfit, and Ramallah. In the village of Burqa, near Nablus, one Palestinian was killed, and 16 were injured during a settler raid that erupted into confrontations, before the Israeli army intervened and opened fire. In other Nablus villages like Jaloud, Beita, Beit Umrin, and Ausarin, and in Salfit villages like Zeita and Jamaain, settlers have been violently blocking Palestinians on their way to their groves. In various Ramallah villages, including Turmusayya, Abu Falah, Birzeit, and Aboud, as well as in Burin, near Nablus, settlers have been reportedly stealing the olive either by picking the trees themselves or by assaulting Palestinians carrying their harvest and taking it for themselves.
Friday, October 16 was the first day of harvest in the village of Abu Falah, north east of Ramallah just six kilometers from my village of Taybeh. Since the early morning, villagers were going to the eastern groves of the village to participate in the harvest, whether they own olive groves there or not. It is a centuries-old Palestinian practice called “auneh”, which roughly translates to “group help”. The village sets a date for all residents to help harvest in one part of the village, and then move to another. Those who helped by working in their neighbors’ groves know that they will receive the same help when their turn comes. In the central hills of Palestine, where land ownership was historically based on small family properties, and paid labor was almost absent until the early 20th century, this was how villagers organized the shared labor. Today, Palestinians are bringing this tradition back to life, but for new reasons.
“It has become very risky to go harvest the olives alone, and we have no protection at all, so the best way of doing it is to go in large numbers,” Sameer Shouman, a resident of Abu Falah tells me. Shouman explains that the villagers in Abu Falah decided to go together to each part of the olive groves for mutual support and protection. On Friday, they were in the hundreds, accompanied by journalists covering the harvest.
“Shortly after the harvest had started, Israeli settlers began to arrive in large numbers,” said Shouman. “Dozens of settlers at the same time, armed with clubs, all very aggressive, and they began to threaten us out of the land, but young men from the village confronted them with stones, and clashes erupted.”
According to Shouman, settlers stole several bags of harvested olives from an old man in his own grove. “They injured many people, including two women, and although the Israeli army came supposedly to evacuate the settlers, they were really there to protect them, as they opened fire at the young men who confronted the settlers, but did not treat the settlers who assaulted us in the same manner,” he said.
The Israeli settlers’ assault on Palestinian harvesters in Abu Falah made headlines, as one of its victims was the Washington Post photographer, American journalist Heidi Levine, who was beaten by several settlers while documenting the olive harvest, despite wearing a blue vest clearly marked with “PRESS.”
Levine told the press, from a Palestinian hospital where she was transferred via ambulance, that Israeli settlers stole her passport, her phone, and her gear during the assault. The office of Israel’s Prime Minister was quoted by Israeli media saying that it “unequivocally condemns violence against anyone,” while referring to dubious reports that “some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths” and that they had footage showing violence “from both sides.”
But the violence was, of course, mainly directed at Palestinian harvesters. “Settlers want to terrorize us to force us to leave our land, but we won’t,” Shouman said. “The importance of olives to us is much more than just economic, because these are our lands, our heritage, and our identity.”
None of this is new. Since October 2023, Israeli settlers’ attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest have escalated every year, from attacking farmers to destroying groves. Sameer Shouman himself says that he lost 54 olive trees last year, which he found cut down upon arriving to his groves. Furthermore, this year’s olive harvest is a crucial one, according to Jamal Jumaa, coordinator of the grassroots Stop The Wall campaign.
“The settler groups, emboldened by the current Israeli government, have imposed a status quo of terrorizing Palestinians out of their own spaces, but the olive harvest is about much more than just spaces,” Jumaa said. “It is about economy, culture, social fabric, and eventually what holds Palestinians bound to their land, and this year’s harvest might determine whether there will be olive harvests in the coming years or not.”
Jumaa compares the effect of these settler attacks to the Israeli settlers’ expulsion of Bedouin communities from grazing lands after October 2023. “The expulsion of families who raised livestock severely impacted the market of fresh meat in the West Bank, because 85% of meat consumption in the West Bank depended on local production, much of which came from these communities,” notes Jumaa. “The targeting of the olive harvest will surely have a similar impact on the market of olive oil, a central ingredient for Palestinian families,” he said.
The price of fresh meat did in fact double since October 2023, reaching 120 shekels (~$38) per kilogram. Although many Bedouin families were forced to sell their livestock after losing their grazing lands, it is unclear whether this was the main reason for the rise in fresh meat prices. But olive oil is different. According to Fayad Fayad, the head of the olive press owners union, around 100,000 Palestinian families depend partially or entirely on the olive season for their yearly income. This figure includes 70,000 families who own olive groves and 30,000 families who rely on seasonal jobs in picking, transportation, marketing, and other harvest-related work.
“Olive production has always satisfied the local demand in the West Bank, and we exported olive oil to other countries, but the main factor threatening this entire economy is Israeli settlers’ violence and land grab,” says Fayad. According to his figures, Palestine’s production of olive oil has dropped dramatically in the past three years, from 36,400 tons of olive oil produced in 2022, including 5,000 tons produced in the Gaza Strip, to only 7,300 tons in 2025, from the West Bank alone.
“Olive oil production in Palestine has always depended on small properties, which means that thousands of families are directly affected at their micro-economic level, every time the season is disrupted for whatever reason,” Fayad said. He explained that olive press owners buy directly from farmers, store the pressed oil as a form of payment, before exporting it to companies who package and sell the olive oil abroad. “The macro-economy of Palestine’s agricultural and exporting sector and the micro-economy of farming and other working families are directly connected, and they are being severely shaken by the offensive on olive lands in these recent years,” he said.
This crisis is visible in the northern groves of my village of Taybeh, which haven’t yet been occupied by Israeli settlers and where some families can still harvest their trees. In the groves trapped between the village’s urban area and a valley where Israeli settlers established an outpost, a handful of farmer groups are scattered between olive trees.
Munjid Abu Ali, a Palestinian man in his mid-twenties, is there with his parents and brother, harvesting olive trees that belong to an elderly couple from Taybeh, who can no longer perform the physical labor of the olive harvest themselves. Munjid and his family came from far away to work in Taybeh’s olive groves. “We are from Yatta, in the south of Hebron, and we have been working with the owners of these olive groves for seven years,” Munjid tells me. Every olive season, Munjid and his family stay in a small house in Taybeh’s old town that belongs to the elderly couple who owns the grove.
“The deal is that we take half of the oil after pressing the olives, which usually gives us enough for our yearly consumption, and some extra oil to sell,” Munjid explains. “Before 2023, we harvested all the groves of our employers, but most of them are now controlled by the settlers,” he said. “Our produce has been cut by more than the half, and even now, we don’t feel safe while working.”
Munjid and his family don’t feel safe because the day before, a group of Israeli settlers drove a four-wheel mountain moto-car up the valley and reached the edge of the olive groves. All workers in the area ran away towards the town before the settlers arrived, which is why nobody was hurt.
I walk down to the edge of the valley from where the settlers had come to find a young couple from Taybeh. Mousa Khoury, in his late thirties, and his wife Renad, are also harvesting somebody else’s groves.
“These olive trees here belong to a wealthy man from Ramallah who bought them some years ago, and he gave this year’s harvest to us,” explains Mousa, who works as a blacksmith. Mousa also inherited his father’s olive groves, most of which are in the east of the village, now made inaccessible by settlers’ violence.
“We have the same deal as all other harvesters, where we get to keep half of the pressed oil,” explains Renad. “It helps us secure our oil for the year and make some extra income,” she said.
Not far away, another group of harvesters are also working someone else’s land, when one of them, a young man, hangs up his cell phone and announces loudly: “The settlers’ motorbikes are nearby, they could be here in any moment.” The word spreads, and workers begin to load large sacks of harvested olives into their vehicles. I walk back to Munjid Abu Ali’s family and find them loading their olives to the back of an old Hyundai Getz. “If we have to run, at least we won’t leave the produce behind for settlers to steal,” Munjid said.
Despite the looming threat of settler attacks, the day ended without incident. I went back home to find my father, as always, sitting on the porch, expressionless, looking at his phone screen. That morning, he had gone, once again, to the road leading to our inaccessible olive groves, hoping that the “coordination” given by the Israeli army would allow him to reach them. For the second time, the mayor of Taybeh informed him that the area under the army’s “coordination” didn’t include our groves that day.
I could sense that my father was not up for talking, so I kept my encounters with the other harvesters to myself. I sat beside him and put my arm around his shoulder, sneaking a look at his phone screen. He was watching a video taken days ago by somebody near our unreachable groves, showing the gate that we installed many years ago at the entrance of our plot. It was wide open, and a group of Israeli settlers were inside, between our olive trees, harvesting them.
I tried to say something while choking on my words, but my father was not up for talking. He put his phone in his pocket, gave me a tired smile, and got up from his chair. He stopped at the door to glance at the cloudy sky again, before silently walking into the house, leaving me outside thinking: autumn is here.

Space Force Needs Third Launch Range by 2030, Acquisition Leader Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:16:02 UTC
05:16:02 KST

The head of the Space Force’s largest acquisition organization said the service needs a third spaceport to support medium and heavy launch by 2030—a goal he called “aspirational” even as he stressed the importance of building out the U.S. military’s launch infrastructure.
“We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” Space Systems Command boss Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant said Oct. 21. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities … There are a lot of considerations.”
The Space Force operates ranges at Cape Canaveral Space Force Base, Fla., and Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., but those expect to run out of space in the coming years as demand for government and commercial launch surges. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed in May that the service expects to need a third site.
“We probably need another site that’s capable of heavy and super-heavy launch capability, both from a resiliency perspective and just, even at the Cape, limitations on how much space we’ve got,” Meink said at the time.
The White House signed out an update to its National Space Transportation Policy in August, predicting the U.S. could see its annual launch cadence grow to 1,000 launches by 2030—a fivefold increase over 2025. The document calls on the Defense Department to work with the Department of Homeland Security and NASA to explore options to build additional spaceport infrastructure on federal property.
Garrant, who spoke to reporters during AFCEA’s annual Space Industry Days event, said the Space Force recently formed an operational planning team to “take a hard look” at what building a third spaceport would require.
“That work is pretty nascent, but we’re going to take some ideas to leadership at NASA, the National Reconnaissance Office, and the Space Force, and get some suggestions on how we might actually pursue a third spaceport,” he said. “That’s a recognition that the demand is there, and that we want to make sure that we meet those needs and support our launch service providers.”
The team right now is looking at a range of options for buying or leasing land for the third site, Garrant said—from a public-private partnership to using commercial land to building a new federal installation.
“All have pros and cons,” he said. “We haven’t made that decision yet, but we’re not discounting any of those.”
In the meantime, the Space Force is deepening its partnerships with commercial spaceports like the Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport on Wallops Island, Va., and the Pacific Spaceport Complex in Alaska.
The service is also investing heavily in its existing coastal spaceports and has plans to expand capacity at both ranges over the next five to 10 years. Congress allocated $1.3 billion in 2024 for “Spaceport of the Future” upgrades through 2028, and the Space Force plans to request more funding in the fiscal 2028 budget request to add more pads and launch support facilities, improve roads and bridges, and give launch companies better access to commodities like propellant and water. Both ranges are also looking to expand their harbors to support more providers.

Two polls published Wednesday evening show the bloc led by Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, but short of a parliamentary majority. A Channel 12 poll projects 55 seats for the Eisenkot bloc and 51 for Netanyahu's, while a Channel 13 poll puts the blocs at 52 and 49 seats, respectively.

According to the Channel 12 poll, Yashar remains the largest party despite losing one seat, with 23. The center-left Democrats and the Arab-led Joint List each win nine seats, unchanged from the previous poll.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrichs' Religious Zionism drops to six seats. United Arab List wins five seats, unchanged from last week, while the far-right Amkha Yisrael wins four seats after failing to cross the electoral threshold in the previous poll.
The Reservists and Economic Party falls short of the threshold with 2.8 percent of the vote, as does the Haredi Public Party, with 0.3 percent.
The Channel 13 poll, meanwhile, puts Yashar at 20 seats, unchanged from the previous survey, while Likud gains one to reach 19. Together remains at 14 seats, while the Democrats gain one to reach 10. The Joint List maintains its strength at nine seats.
Religious Zionism and United Torah Judaism each gain one seat, reaching eight. Yisrael Beiteinu remains at eight, while Shas and Otzma Yehudit each win seven, unchanged from the previous poll. United Arab List remains at six seats and the Reservists and Economic Party at four.
Amkha Yisrael, which won five seats in the previous poll, falls below the electoral threshold with 3.2 percent of the vote. The Haredi Public Party also fails to cross the threshold, with 1.2 percent of the vote.
The News 13 poll was conducted Tuesday by the Index, led by Shmuel Rosner and Noah Salfakov, in cooperation with Stat-Net, led by Yosef Maklada; the Sample Project, led by Dr. Ariel Ayalon; and Askaria, led by Dudi Dror. Bose Is Buying Skullcandy. It’s Not as Weird as It Sounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:15:00 UTC
05:15:00 KST

Longtime audio giant Bose announced on Wednesday that it's acquiring Skullcandy, the lifestyle brand known for its bass-heavy headphones. Skullcandy will remain a separate company within Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business and will still be based in Park City, Utah.
The acquisition isn't out of left field. Bose has lent its audio expertise to Skullcandy over the past year under its Sound by Bose licensing program. Skullcandy designs the headphones and then works with Bose on the audio front. The relationship began with the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC earbuds in 2025 and more recently, with the Crusher 1080 ANC headphones in July.
When WIRED spoke with Skullcandy CEO Brian Garofalow in July about the partnership, Garofalow highlighted the 23-year-old company's ability to build community and culture, specifically around the board sports community (the first Skullcandy product was designed on a ski chairlift). But he admitted the company wasn't “the greatest at the engineering part of innovation with products.”
This is hardly Bose's first audio acquisition (though it may be the most mainstream). Bose acquired McIntosh Group, owners of luxury audio brands McIntosh Laboratory and Sonus Faber, back in 2024. But Bose seems to be after Skullcandy's connection to its community.
“What does the brand stand for? Does it have meaning for consumers? Is it relevant to a group of consumers that, frankly, we otherwise aren’t reaching?" Bose CEO Lila Snyder tells WIRED. "If you think about McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Skullcandy, they all fit into that realm. Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we’re largely missing with the Bose brand.”
That's why Bose has no plans to relocate Skullcandy from Park City, Utah, which Snyder says is the epicenter of board sports culture. “We want to make sure we’re right at the heart of it, as they always have been,” she says. Skullcandy products are also affordable, especially compared to other Bose products and Bose-owned brands, which lets Bose compete at both ends of the market.
As WIRED's headphone reviewer, I find Bose and Skullcandy an odd pairing. In consumer audio, Bose pioneered active noise-cancelation (ANC) in headphones, and maintains that legacy with ANC-leading products like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen). Skullcandy, on the other hand, has often been viewed as the butt of the joke when it comes to audio quality. It has had a reputation for middling sound, bass-over-everything headphones, and a loud, bold aesthetic.
Recent collaborations have started to change those perceptions—WIRED rated the Method 360 ANC earbuds an 8/10, noting good sound quality and ANC for the money. Snyder says those buds and the recent Crusher collab are just the tip of the iceberg. “It’s the beginning of what we think we can do together,” she says.
I’m very curious about what comes next from Skullcandy, headphones or otherwise. Either way, we’ll see if Bose's acoustic muscle can give the lifestyle brand the permanent glow-up it’s been chasing.
