This October 27 Israeli election is being billed as a competition between the change bloc and the Netanyahu coalition bloc.
This is the wrong frame for the vote. The fundamental choice is between the tikkun camp – the parties that are committed to repair Israeli society in the aftermath of October 7 – and parties that want to go on with business as usual.
I went to the shiva of Ben Zussman, who died in the Israel-Hamas War. His letter before entering battle drew a lot of attention because he expressed his sense of “the privilege to fulfill my dream and my destiny” in fighting for and defending Israel – even if he lost his life in the process.
His parents said the way to honor his bravery and devotion (and that of the other fallen soldiers) is to make a better Israel.
That is the central issue in this election.
Over 1,200 people died on October 7; 970 soldiers lost their lives in post-October 7 fighting to ensure that Hamas could not inflict such a massacre again. At the cost of these soldiers’ lives (and the wounded), the IDF neutralized the “ring of fire” (Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Iran) threatening Israel.
The calling of the next government is to improve Israel and thus honor the soldiers’ sacrifice.
This is the tikkun bloc’s purpose.
Bringing haredim into the IDF
If elected, it will make Israel a fairer society by ending the haredim’s draft exemption so that every population group of Israel carries an equal share of the burden of defense. Every sector of the Israeli population – this includes the haredi and Arab population as well – will serve in the IDF or in national service.
The unjust phenomenon of reservists serving hundreds of days a year – disrupting their families and professional lives, while tens of thousands are exempt from any service – will be ended.
Gadi Eisenkot has promised legislation to exempt 3% (i.e., the haredi top Torah scholars) to protect high-level Torah study – just as top athletes and musicians are exempted – but everyone else must serve in the IDF or do National Service.
At a time when the IDF reported that it might collapse without more soldiers, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisted on serving his haredi coalition partners by passing a draft exemption bill. This showed the bankruptcy and irresponsibility of a business-as-usual government.
If the tikkun bloc wins, postelection Israel will be a more just society.
Investment in infrastructure and education in the Arab sector will be brought up to the levels of Jewish cities and communities. This would continue a process toward equalization that started in 1955. It was an investment that was promised but not fulfilled by the present government due to its extremists.
Similarly, a comprehensive plan will be developed and a cooperative strategy established with Arab community leaders to fight organized crime and to stem the wave of murders in the Arab sector.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and the current stand-pat government have stood idly by the shedding of Arab blood.
If the tikkun bloc wins, postelection Israel will be more democratic. The assault on the judiciary will be stopped. There is room for greater diversity in judicial appointments, but the current government’s attempt to politicize the judges’ selection process will be ended. Judicial review protects minority rights and provides checks and balances that protect democracy.
Postelection Israel will be more educated. In 2025, Israel recorded one of the OECD’s steepest declines in reading (38 points), math (25), and science (27), leaving the country below average in all three areas. Nearly three out of 10 Israeli students lack basic proficiency in all these areas.
Naftali Bennett of B’Yachad will personally take charge of the Education Ministry, and the new government will supply the funds needed to upgrade the educational system. This includes enforcing the requirement – currently being flouted – to teach English, math, and science in the haredi school system.
Postelection Israel will be more firmly under the rule of law. The present wave of extremist settler violence against Palestinians is criminal and a form of terrorism.
The criminals have not been checked and held accountable because of pressure from Ben-Gvir on the police and from Minister Bezalel Smotrich on the IDF.
This violence undermines the laws of Israel and has greatly damaged Israel’s reputation worldwide. The tikkun government will restore law and order in the West Bank and insist that law-abiding Palestinians have the security and safety they are entitled to.
Post-election Israel will be more informed. A state commission of inquiry will be appointed to objectively and comprehensively gather all the information on October 7. Establishing the facts and the failures will enable us to prevent a repetition and to hold those leaders responsible for the disaster accountable.
The present stand-pat government has blocked any national investigation commission because it wants to escape being held responsible.
The tikkun bloc government will improve Israel’s standing in the world. This coalition government has just about undermined the alliance with America. Netanyahu did get US President Donald Trump to crack down on Iran’s nuclear production program, but this very closeness has evoked alienation from Democrats and independents. Netanyahu basically wrote off the Democratic Party.
Netanyahu is now toxic among Democrats and independents. If he is reelected, this may well break the alliance politically.
This tikkun government will reach out strongly to these groups. Eisenkot will reach out to Trump. While he does not have a close connection to the president, his sincere appreciation of America’s help and his genuine respect for Trump will enable a new connection while the new government rebuilds the bipartisan alliance, which was the firmest foundation for the Israel-American alliance.
The silent majority of the Israeli public must step up and choose tikkun – the repair of society to make it better – and ensure that our heroic soldiers will not have died in vain.

Sisi says Egypt would defend Saudi territory but rules out attack on Yemen
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia would be limited to defending the kingdom's territory and borders and would not include an attack on Yemen, the presidency said on Wednesday, as the Iran-allied Houthis intensify attacks on the kingdom.
Sisi's comments came as Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, Saudi state news agency SPA said. Abdelatty delivered a written message from Sisi to King Salman, and the two sides discussed bilateral ties and regional developments, SPA said.

Egypt would also defend the territory of any other Arab country if asked, Sisi said, but its military effort would not extend beyond Egyptian territory or that of an Arab state whose security and stability Cairo was seeking to protect.
On Monday, Egypt's parliament delayed until October 26 a vote on authorizing the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia if requested, lawmakers said.
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, opening another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Egypt, a regional military power, previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the government against the Houthis, though it played a limited combat role in the civil war.

After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
- Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war 
  - Published9 hours ago
- Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism 
  - Published1 day ago
- US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin 
  - Published10 hours ago
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
All rather vague.
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.

That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
"Of course!"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

War update: 165 clashes on front line over past day, heaviest fighting on Pokrovsk axis
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this in an update on the battlefield situation as of 22:00, Ukrinform reports.
“Since the beginning of the day, there have been 165 combat engagements. The enemy launched 49 airstrikes, dropping 165 guided glide bombs. In addition, it deployed 6,512 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,044 attacks on populated areas and Ukrainian military positions,” the report said.
On the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk axis, Russian forces launched one airstrike, dropped two guided glide bombs and carried out 37 attacks on Ukrainian positions and populated areas, one of them involving multiple-launch rocket systems.
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian positions three times near Starytsia and Vovchanski Khutory, and towards Izbytske.
On the Kupiansk axis, Russian forces made six attempts to improve their positions by launching assaults towards Radkivka.
On the Lyman axis, Ukrainian forces repelled nine Russian attempts to advance near Kolodiazi and Zarichne, and towards Hlushchenkove, Derylove and Lyman.
On the Sloviansk axis, Ukrainian forces stopped one Russian attempt to advance towards Mykolaivka.
On the Kramatorsk axis, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, Ukrainian forces repelled six Russian assaults near Kostiantynivka and towards Novopavlivka.
Russian forces launched 19 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis, seeking to advance near Sofiivka, Dobropillia, Bilytske and Molodetske, and towards Vilne, Kucheriv Yar, Hannivka, Svitle, Krasnopodillia, Serhiivka and Muravka. Two Russian assault operations were still ongoing at the time of the report.
According to preliminary estimates, Russian forces suffered 62 fatalities and 18 wounded in this sector during the day.
Ukrainian forces destroyed five vehicles, four pieces of special equipment, one UAV command post, a fuel and lubricants depot, and 66 shelters. They also damaged two vehicles, one artillery system, one piece of special equipment, four UAV command posts and 136 enemy shelters. A total of 220 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, Russian forces launched one attack towards Ternove.
On the Huliaipole axis, Ukrainian forces repelled nine Russian attacks towards Rizdvianka, Dolynka, Hirke and Yehorivka.
On the Orikhiv axis, Russian forces made one attempt to improve their positions by attacking towards Pavlivka.
On the Dnipro River axis, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
No significant changes were reported on other fronts.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russian sabotage and reconnaissance groups have stepped up their activity along the border areas of Sumy and Chernihiv regions over the past several weeks, according to Ukrainian border guards.

Cuba accuses US of threatening countries ahead of UN embargo vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:51:29 UTC
04:51:29 KST

Cuba accuses US of threatening countries ahead of UN embargo vote
Havana says Washington is threatening countries with retaliation if they refuse to vote against condemning its embargo.
Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions and other retaliatory measures in an effort to get them to change their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running embargo against the island.
Every year, a majority in the UN General Assembly votes in favour of a nonbinding resolution seeking a stop to the US embargo, which began in the early 1960s.
The embargo, considered the longest in modern history, has been credited with exacerbating economic hardship on the island.
But on Wednesday, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said that the administration of US President Donald Trump was seeking to pressure members of the UN General Assembly to vote against the resolution this year.
He explained that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington’s ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz were personally leading the campaign, which he alleged had been going on for months.
“It is a new and dangerous way of conducting multilateral diplomacy,” Rodriguez wrote in a statement on the social media platform X. “It reflects the impotence of those who know they are in the wrong and whose only remaining recourse is force.”
Rodriguez said US officials had threatened to suspend cooperation programmes, deny visas to government officials and their families, and even back opposition parties in upcoming elections if countries refused to change their positions.
He also accused the US of urging some countries to abstain or skip the vote altogether if they were unwilling to vote against Cuba.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the US State Department and the US Mission to the UN for comment, but it did not receive a reply by the time of publication.
Heightening pressure on Cuba
The allegations come amid escalating tensions between the two countries ahead of the vote on the resolution, expected to take place on October 27 or 28.
The Trump administration has long maintained that the Cuban government — not the embargo — is to blame for the country’s struggling economy, and it has called for regime change.
On Monday, Waltz accused Cuban diplomats of harassing and intimidating participants at a US-hosted panel on alleged human rights abuses in Cuba.
Cuba’s UN Ambassador Ernesto Soberon Guzman and other representatives had confronted Waltz as he left the event at UN headquarters in New York City.
Speaking to reporters afterward, Waltz said that, every year, the Cuban government “propagates a lie through its annual resolution”.
“It uses excuse after excuse to justify its oppression, to justify the misery of the Cuban people, and what we are doing here at the US Mission to the UN is exposing those lies,” he said.
In a separate briefing that day, Waltz also acknowledged that Washington had been lobbying European countries to reconsider their support for the resolution. He pointed to allegations from Ukraine that Cuban nationals fighting for Russia weren’t being paid and that the money was instead going to the Cuban government.
“Yes, we’ve asked many of our European colleagues: Given this evidence from the Ukrainian government, how can they continue to vote for this resolution that is a propaganda tool for the Cuban regime and that is directly affecting their national security?” Waltz said.
The UN General Assembly has voted overwhelmingly in support of resolutions calling for an end to the US economic embargo on Cuba almost every year since 1992. The embargo itself has been in place for more than six decades.
Since the start of 2026, the Trump administration has intensified pressure on Cuba by blocking oil supplies and threatening tariffs on countries supplying the country with fuel, leaving Cubans to face more severe shortages of essential supplies and prolonged blackouts.

Netflix loses growth momentum, shares fall - what losses could await the streaming giant

Netflix loses growth momentum, shares fall - what losses could await the streaming giant
Kyiv • UNN
Netflix is forecasting a slowdown in revenue growth for the fourth consecutive quarter, while its advertising business is developing more slowly than expected. Since the beginning of the year, the company's shares have lost about a quarter of their value.
Netflix's downward revision of its advertising revenue forecast is fueling concerns that its "growth engine" is losing momentum. This puts at risk the competitive advantage that once made Netflix a model for the entire media industry, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The company's shares fell nearly 5% on Wednesday afternoon. This came after Netflix forecast slower revenue growth for the fourth consecutive quarter. One of Hollywood's biggest investors in original content is currently struggling to create truly major hits.
Netflix plans major staff cuts amid competition for viewers14.10.26, 21:38 • 17196 views
"Netflix is increasingly being held to standards that match its own exceptionally high benchmarks. This raises the question: has the company lost the focus and flexibility that once set it apart from its competitors?" PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore said in a note to clients. Since the beginning of the year, the company's shares have lost about a quarter of their value. Netflix's unsuccessful attempt to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery only intensified concerns that the company has almost no avenues left for growth other than raising prices and cracking down on password sharing.
Netflix's advertising business, which was long viewed as a key source of future growth, is developing more slowly than expected. At the same time, the company's attempts to establish itself in the gaming industry — including through deals to add games from the Grand Theft Auto series — have so far failed to produce tangible results.
Meanwhile, YouTube and TikTok are competing for viewers' attention by offering a constant stream of relatively inexpensive user-generated content. In addition, competition is expected to intensify further after Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merge under Skydance's leadership.
In response to these challenges, Netflix cut 6% of its workforce and replaced two top executives responsible for content policy.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said on Tuesday that these steps will allow Netflix to focus on its core business — creating series and films — to make the service indispensable to consumers.
Some analysts believe that the new head of content, Peter Rice, will help improve Netflix's selection of films and series. He is expected to place greater emphasis on high-end projects ("prestige content") and draw on his connections with leading creative talent.
"His industry connections could prove useful in attracting and retaining prominent filmmakers — especially after creators such as the Duffer brothers, Shawn Levy and Noah Baumbach left the company," said Citizens analyst Matthew Condon. "Rice's extensive experience managing live sports broadcasts could help implement a more ambitious approach to producing high-end sports content, further enhancing the value proposition of Netflix."
In addition
According to LSEG data, more than 20 brokerage firms revised their share-price targets downward after the results were released.
If the current downward trend continues, the streaming giant could lose about $13 billion in market value.
BofA Global Research analysts said that the management change and staff cuts are a "signal that management is focused on improving content quality and increasing the share of successful, popular projects."
Netflix shares are currently trading at approximately 18.3 times expected earnings for the next 12 months. For comparison, the figure is 14.76 for Walt Disney (DIS.N) and 6.26 for Comcast (CMCSA.O).

The move was due to a possible resumption of hostilities, particularly with Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen, two of the U.S. officials said.
Two of the U.S. officials said the ordered departures would potentially involve the evacuation of all personnel and their families from the U.S. Mission to Saudi Arabia.

How do we actually turn down the temperature in political debate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:47:44 UTC
04:47:44 KST

analysis
After alleged attack on Helen Haines, how do we actually turn down the temperature?
Only two months ago, a group called Compassion in Politics Australia gained the first signatory to its "Civility Pledge".
Helen Haines.
The organisation, based on a similar foundation in the United Kingdom, aims to turn the tide of toxic debate and build a better politics.
As a start, it's asking elected officials to sign a simple pledge. "In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion," is all it states.
This week the independent MP was the victim of an attack widely described as shocking but unsurprising. Sadly predictable was the common reaction amongst MPs who have been at the receiving end of increasing threats and harassment.
Yesterday, security agencies briefed MPs on the risks to their safety. Security will no doubt be improved as much as practicable, without sacrificing MPs' ability to interact in their communities.
The more difficult question is what, if anything, can be done about the increasingly hostile political environment. What can be done to restore the "civility" that Haines, at least, pledged to pursue?
Civility was the word emphasised by the Governor-General late yesterday, who stood alongside the husband of Helen Haines in an effort to calm a worried nation.
"We don't have to all agree, but we can wrestle with the issue not the person," Sam Mostyn said from Melbourne's Alfred Hospital. Her message echoed the call to turn the temperature down.
"Words matter, whether spoken or in written form or increasingly in the virtual world."
This call for civility is something ASIO boss Mike Burgess has been going on about now for years.
"I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint," he said after the attack on Haines.
Burgess draws a line between words and actions: "ASIO has seen direct correlations between inflamed language, inflamed tensions and acts of violence."
The intelligence chief must feel at times he's talking to a brick wall. He warned against "inflamed language" and called for a return to civility after the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel in 2023, again after lifting the terrorism threat level to "probable" in 2024, and again after the Bondi terrorist attack in 2025.
Will anyone listen this time? Will an attack on one of their own force politicians to re-think their part in setting the tone of political discourse?
For some, the answer is clearly yes. There is a degree of self-reflection this week.
"We should all, every single one of us, me included, find ways to minimise the temperature of these debates," said shadow minister Jono Duniam, who will soon depart the Senate.
"We could all do better. I don't exclude myself or any political party," acknowledged the prime minister who, like Burgess, has repeatedly called for a more civil debate.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, by contrast, is worried about limiting robust argument. While condemning anything that intimidates or incites violence, he defended the role of vigorous debate.
"We have, like so few other countries in the world, avoided political violence. This is part of the great Australian achievement, and we've done that by having vigorous and rigorous debate and choice at the ballot box," he said.
"This is what's worked for us. We need to make sure it stays there."
It's certainly true — Australia has long enjoyed robust political debate while largely avoiding political violence.
But this misses the point being made by the ASIO boss. Times have changed.
We're now in an environment, according to Burgess, where "politically motivated violence is more likely than previous years".
Angus Taylor's own colleagues can recognise the deterioration, too.
"It's clear that the political environment has become more heated in recent years," said shadow minister James Paterson.
"In the last few years things have gotten much worse," said independent MP Monique Ryan, adding that "the 2025 election was completely different to 2022", with more aggression and anger. It's a common view, particularly among female politicians.
MPs are worried. For themselves, for their families, and for the fate of Australia's democracy.
So, what does it take to turn the temperature down?
"Gosh, if only I could say what the answer to that is," One Nation's Barnaby Joyce admitted on Radio National yesterday. "I don't know," he said.
It's rare to hear Barnaby Joyce stumped for an answer on anything. He's certainly not accepting any blame on the part of One Nation for raising the temperature.
Many might agree with Joyce that there are no easy solutions to counter the powerful domestic and global forces driving voter frustration, political polarisation, toxic online discourse and hate.
Politicians are certainly limited in what they can control. But they're not entirely powerless.
As Burgess says, language matters: "By all means, disagree. But consider how you disagree."
Signing a "Civility Pledge" might seem like a mere symbolic gesture, but it's something. If it's good enough for Helen Haines, why not others?
Compassion in Politics Australia issued a statement after the horrific attack on Monday, calling it "a stark reminder that compassion and civility in public life are not abstract ideals. They matter profoundly".
The attack on Helen Haines may prove to be just another brief interruption before regular political mud-slinging resumes. Or it could see all sides of politics try to course correct.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or can be streamed anytime on ABC iview.

The announcement came as it was still unclear whether the US-born pope would proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for Nov 6-17.

“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.

The goal of limiting global warming to below 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is largely out of reach. That’s according to the United Nations Environmental Program’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap report released on Wednesday, considered the definitive assessment of global climate action.
“We’ve spent decades postponing cuts to emissions and now we’re facing the consequences,” Anne Olhoff, director of the UNEP-Copenhagen Climate Centre, and one of the report’s authors, said after the report’s publication. “The world can still attain the goals of the Paris Agreement but we must work hard to not only meet but surpass our most ambitious climate targets. The longer we wait, the larger the risk that we jeopardize the temperature goal.”
While the report’s warning is stark, that doesn’t mean that all hope is lost. Coordinated efforts to reduce emissions can still have a meaningful impact on climate change, it says—but action must be taken quickly.
Here are the biggest takeaways from the Emissions Gap report.
The 1.5°C target is mostly out of reach
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world agreed to halt planetary warming at 2°C above pre-industrial temperatures and to pursue efforts to limit warming by 1.5°C. Doing so would provide a greater chance at avoiding the worst impacts of climate change. The window to avoid overshooting the 1.5°C goal, however, is now closed, the report finds.
But that doesn’t mean that there’s no hope for climate action. It is still possible to limit the overshoot and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century. Every fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts, making the goal to limit as much warming beyond 1.5°C all the more important.
The world is on track to reach 2.8°C of warming by 2100
Under the terms of the Paris Agreement, countries must submit updated climate pledges, known as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which outline specific goals to reduce national emissions. Based on the policies currently in place under the NDCs submitted by over 150 nations, the planet is on track to reach 2.8°C of warming by the end of the century.
Based on this, today’s report concludes that global climate pledges are falling short. If countries meet their new NDCs, which set upgraded targets for 2035 and were due last year, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6°C by the end of the century.
Both scenarios would have devastating consequences—dramatically transforming sea levels and ecosystems, and triggering compounding climate extremes such as higher temperatures and drought, increasing the likelihood of wildfires.
We need to cut carbon emissions by 18% in the next four years
The report notes that it is still possible to peak warming at 1.7°C or 1.8°C. Doing so would require major changes. We would need to cut emissions by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. This would require sustained emissions cuts along with carbon dioxide removal.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heat waves, and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year,” said UNEP executive director Inger Andersen. “So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century.”
The U.S. is a major outlier for emissions
While emissions growth has slowed down in most G20 countries, emissions in the United States “far exceeded that of all other countries," the report says. That’s due to the increased electricity demand, in part due to data centers, and new policies that encouraged the use of fossil fuels like coal over clean energy sources.
The report includes a statement from the State Department, noting that the U.S. "does not endorse or agree with its analysis or conclusions, and has not provided comments to this report."
The Trump Administration’s decision to withdraw from the Paris Agreement also worsened the climate projections, as estimates no longer include climate action that would have been taken under the United States’s NDC targets.
The U.S. is the second largest emitter of climate-warming greenhouse gases, behind China, which has quickly become a world leader in renewable energy (while also ramping up coal production.)
Climate policies are reducing emissions
Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement just over a decade ago, global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, while solar PV build-out has increased seven times faster. If these trends were to continue, and coupled with more policies to support clean energy, the world would be on track to reach its renewable energy goals.
The report examined more than 200 climate policies and found that they target emission reductions across a wide range of sectors and countries. That’s an encouraging sign the report notes. All that’s left is for these solutions to be scaled faster.
“We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly,” said Andersen. “It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies.”

Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
Published October 21, 2026last updated October 22, 2026
What you need to know
- One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected
- Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin
- Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect
- Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter
This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.
Thanks for following our blog
We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!
Weidel pitches 'three pillars' of EU reform at European Parliament
Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.
"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."
On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."
"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."
This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.
She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."
Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.
Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."
"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.
She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."
While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.
WATCH — Journalist says Merz 'sounds very much like Trump'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.
That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."

Nvidia CEO Huang dazzles Berlin audience with AI pitch
A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.
The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).
Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.
"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.
Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.
There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.
But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.
Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.
German Bundeswehr sees 'significant' threat of sabotage
The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.
A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.
The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.
"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.
The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."
The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.
He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."
German imports from Russia plunge, but not to zero
German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.
According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.
This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.
Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.
Nvidia CEO urges Europe to build more data centers
Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.
He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.
"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.
He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."
Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.
Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.
Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.
Financial Ministry admits mistake, says tobacco tax coming January 1 as planned
A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."
The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.
The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.
Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.
German youth plans France-style mass protests
"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."
Bundesbank forecasts German growth for Q4
The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.
"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."
The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.
"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.
The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.
Merz: EU doesn't want trade war with China
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.
Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."
The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.
Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."
"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.
That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."
Ifo Institute questions savings target of parental allowance reform
Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.
However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.
The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.
Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.
"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.
The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.
"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.
IDF says it killed Hamas member involved in abduction of German dual national
The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.
The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.
Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.
In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.
The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."
"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.
The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.
Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.
Merz calls on Trump to make sure South Africa is at G20
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.
"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."
Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.
Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.
The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.
Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.
"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."
Russia arrests German national, says he's a 'mercenary' — reports
Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.
"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.
The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.
They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.
Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.
Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:43:42 UTC
04:43:42 KST

Steve Smith doesn't return after reaching a major milestone and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve as Australia is sent barrelling towards a chastening defeat in Gqeberha.
Here are the quick hits from day four of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Fiery Marco tears through the Aussies
Fresh from his swashbuckling 85 on day three, the towering Marco Jansen continued to terrorise the Australians on day four.
The left-arm seamer was at his fiery, probing best, with his aggression and accuracy proving all too much for the tourists in their first innings.
Jansen dismissed both Scott Boland and Travis Head early in the day, before a few tense exchanges with Marnus Labuschagne appeared to light a fuse somewhere deep in the big man.
He proceeded to treat Matt Renshaw to a send-off — seemingly in Afrikaans — upon having the Yorkshire-born Queenslander caught at gully, before sending Alex Carey packing in a double breakthrough in the shadows of lunch.
Unfortunately for the Aussies, Jansen wasn't done there, with the South African having Beau Webster caught in the cordon to claim his fifth wicket and continue Australia's horror day.
2. Sore Smith reaches 11,000 and doesn't return
Amid the carnage up the other end, Steve Smith was just about hanging in there.
Struggling with a neck issue, the Australian received running repairs at multiple points during his innings and never quite looked his usual self.
Even so, Smith was at the crease long enough to become just the 12th batter to score 11,000 Test match runs, joining Ricky Ponting and Allan Border as the only Australians in that rare air.
But the Australia vice-captain was in serious discomfort throughout his innings, and departed promptly after joining that exclusive club.
The stiff-necked Smith was bowled through the gate by Wiaan Mulder for 28 as Australia was asked to follow on after being skittled for just 99, their fourth-lowest Test total against the Proteas.
And in a massive blow for his team, the Australia vice-captain did not recover in time to return to the crease as wickets started falling in the tourists' second dig, remaining in training gear in the dugout as Australia limped towards stumps.
3. Two remarkable grabs, two very different reactions
We have been treated to some seriously sensational slip catching in Gqeberha.
With Australia 3-45 in its first innings and already beginning to teeter, the desperately out-of-touch Labuschagne drove unconvincingly, sending his thick edge flying low and hard towards the cordon.
Harmer dived dramatically to his left, using his sizeable left hand to pluck the quickly dropping ball from the air in front of second slip.
And the off-spinner was absolutely pumped with his effort, throwing his head back and roaring as he got to his feet.
It provided quite some contrast to Renshaw's bewilderment after pouching his similarly excellent catch earlier in the Test.
4. Marnus throws it away after enormous reprieve
With Australia beginning its second innings needing 326 runs to just make South Africa bat again, Labuschagne had a golden opportunity to revive his sputtering Test career and make up for his rash dismissal earlier in the day.
Coming in after the early departure of Nic Maddinson, the signs were good for the Queenslander, who knuckled down with Head to push Australia towards 100.
And it was beginning to feel like Labuschagne might have finally been on for a score when he was the beneficiary of a huge reprieve in the 28th over.
Given out LBW to a Harmer off break, Labuschagne reviewed the decision in a blink and it was high drama as both camps waited for ball tracking to take an unusually long time to build.
Eventually, the technology projected the ball to be missing leg stump by what surely wasn't much more than a coat of paint.
Helmet off and head back, Labuschagne was making no secret of his relief.
But only moments later, he threw it all away, mistiming his slog and holing out to long-on for 39.
It was an ugly, ugly dismissal and one that left Australia once again on the rack with shadows lengthening in St George's.
5. Consecutive night shifts for Boland
With Australia proceeding to lose both Renshaw and Webster late on, Boland once again found himself batting in the dying embers of a day.
It was the second consecutive evening the Victorian had been called on as nightwatchman, and for the second consecutive evening, he made his way through to stumps.
Again, he betrayed no hint of annoyance with his sacrificial role, instead digging in and bravely finding his way through a couple of overs of twilight finger spin.
It was another committed shift from Boland — but boy, it's some reward for taking a five-wicket haul on his return to the team.
He'll begin day five alongside Head (87*) with Australia 4-156 and still 170 runs away from making South Africa bat again.

Talking to Putin: Europe seeks a negotiator-in-chief for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:42:30 UTC
04:42:30 KST

Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with US special envoy in Saint Petersburg on October 21, 2026. | Pool photo by Kristina Solovyova/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — There is a growing realization among European governments that they may soon need to nominate someone to face Russian leader Vladimir Putin in direct talks on a peace deal for Ukraine.
The main problem is deciding who should take on such a hazardous task.
The question gained urgency this week after U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia to offer Putin a three-way summit with Donald Trump and Ukraine’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in an effort to press for a ceasefire.
Advertisement
“President Putin disregards the European Union as an authority,” Czech President Petr Pavel said Tuesday in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters’ Network, of which POLITICO is a part. “He doesn’t want to talk to Ursula von der Leyen, he doesn’t talk to Kaja Kallas. He stopped talking to other European leaders, including Emmanuel Macron.”
He added that the EU should “identify a person or a group of people who would speak for Europe. Not necessarily representatives of the EU or NATO, but simply leaders who would be given a mandate by the others to negotiate.”
Czech President Petr Pavel speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations Headquarters in New York, on September 23, 2026. | Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images
In recent days, Trump has dismayed Ukraine and its European allies by talking over their heads with Putin and appearing increasingly willing to take Russia’s side in the almost five-year war.
That has reignited debate in Brussels and beyond about the need for Europe to have its own direct line to the Kremlin to safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Ukraine’s ability to resist a lopsided deal.
“Much as it sticks in the craw, I do think a channel of some kind to Putin would be a good thing to have,” said David Lidington, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London. “I am not optimistic that it would achieve anything much in the short term, but to have a channel which can then be used as and when an opportunity arises is not a bad thing.”
Diplomats and officials disagree on who would be the best person to represent Europe.
Advertisement
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, has negotiated directly with Trump on trade, while the president of the European Council, António Costa, has previously opened a line of communication with the Kremlin through his office. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas is another potential player who speaks for European interests as a whole.
But the Brussels bubble needs to accept that a deal with Putin and Trump won’t be dictated by EU protocols, in the view of a diplomat from a European Union country who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
“We cannot show up with two or three people all speaking on behalf of the EU,” the diplomat said. “The choice of who ends up representing the EU will be based on what would provide the most value, not personal power struggles or narcissistic preferences.”
Will Stubb step up?
One name outside the EU’s machinery that is gaining attention is Alexander Stubb, the president of Finland. Two key factors count in his favor: He has arguably the best relationship with Trump among EU leaders, and Finland has long experience of dealing with Russia — the two countries share a 1,300 kilometer border and have been at war in the past.
Finland’s President Alexander Stubb delivers a joint press conference after a meeting on the situation in Ukraine on October 20, 2026 in Oslo. | Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images
“Stubb is of interest because of Finnish knowledge of and traditional dialogue with Russia,” the diplomat said. “They know more than anyone on our side [about] what it takes to feel secure in such a situation.”
A second EU diplomat noted that Stubb was “the only person who has come forward so far” to show high-level political leadership, and could serve as a European envoy at a future peace summit. Stubb was in Norway with Zelenskyy and Witkoff on Tuesday for negotiations ahead of the U.S. envoy’s visit to Russia to meet Putin.
Advertisement
Also attending the gathering in Oslo was von der Leyen’s most senior aide, Bjoern Seibert, who has joined meetings of national security advisers as part of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine.
A third European diplomat said it was vital that the EU itself be represented in the talks, instead of a small grouping of powerful countries such as Germany, France and the U.K.
That means both Seibert and Pedro Lourtie, the top aide to Costa, must have seats at the table during preparatory talks, the diplomat said, and that EU member countries must be properly updated on progress.
Calling Costa
According to a fourth EU diplomat, European leaders asked Costa at last week’s summit in Brussels whether it might be time for him to talk to Putin. “Costa said, no, he’s not going to talk to Putin now,” they said. “But Costa should start talking to Putin if we want to play a role in the negotiations. By not speaking, we are playing into the hands of our opponents.”
The fourth diplomat said Costa would be a better choice than von der Leyen or Kallas, who are both seen as too invested in the Ukrainian side to represent the EU effectively at leader level. Kallas in particular has been outspoken in her criticism of Trump. “Costa comes across as more of an honest broker,” they summarized.
The European Commission insists the EU is already present at the peace talks, flagging Seibert’s presence in Oslo on Tuesday. “The main aim [in Oslo] was to explore if the parameters are there for a possible move to trilateral or even multilateral talks with Ukraine and Russia present at the same table,” European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho told reporters on Wednesday.
She said the talks had focused on territory, security and post-war prosperity for Ukraine; Witkoff is expected to debrief Ukraine and the Europeans after his trip to meet Putin. “What is very important is that we are sitting at the table, that we are able to present our position, and that we can engage in what is a shared objective to put an end to this horrific war,” she added.
Gerardo Fortuna and Paul Ronzheimer contributed to this report.

Investors were paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX. But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter.
“With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.”
On a call with SpaceX investors on Tuesday, Musk said it would be a “good idea” to combine the two companies and that “there’s a lot of merit” that would come with it.
Musk said on Tuesday that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders.
On Wednesday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share. Still, the company came in at a slightly lower revenue than last quarter, which was $28.23bn. And its automotive revenue dropped 3% from the year prior.
“We maintained strong momentum on many projects spanning Super Intelligence (SI), robotics and renewable energy that will be critical to building a future of Amazing Abundance,” the company wrote in its report.
Despite the stronger-than-anticipated quarter, Tesla has experienced a rough year with falling stock and increased competition from cheaper Chinese automakers. The company’s share price has fallen by more than 11% this year, although it appears to have rebounded some since last week with the news of the possible SpaceX merger.
Last week, Musk unveiled the company’s electric sports car, the Roadster 2, which he said uses technology from SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. At a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas, a remote-controlled version of the car drove up a steeply curved ramp and then used jet-like thrusters to flip over, hover and land. The vehicle is priced at upwards of $200,000.
“Flying cars are real … It can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics,” Musk said at the event, adding: “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.”
During Tesla’s earnings call on Wednesday, he added that the event was “the coolest demo of any product ever”.
Tesla’s vehicle sales are not as crucial to its market performance as they once were, as the company has pivoted towards robotics, autonomous driving and AI. Tesla’s Optimus robot has faced production hurdles, however; and its driverless taxi service, Robotaxi, has hit road blocks in scaling its fleet and expanding to new cities.
“Tesla’s leaders continue to make big claims about autonomous mobility and physical AI. The company has achieved remarkable things but continues to miss some of its leaders’ bolder bets,” said Paul Miller, a principal analyst for market research firm Forrester. “Tesla robotaxis are undeniably carrying passengers, but not yet at anywhere near the levels the company promised.”
Musk has long declared the Robotaxi will have near-infinite demand and that “probably half the population of the US” would be using the autonomous ride-hailing service by the end of 2025. Similarly, the CEO has forecast the manufacture of as many as 1m Optimus robots each year. As Miller pointed out with Musk’s promises, he has failed to reach those lofty targets and rollout has been slow.
Musk once again touted the robots on Wednesday, saying: “I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on earth and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on earth.” He added that no other company compares to Tesla in developing humanoid robots – this is despite Chinese competitors making vast strides in the technology.

Lithuania seizes major synthetic drugs lab run by Dutch national
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:41:15 UTC
04:41:15 KST

Police recover more than 500kg of methamphetamine and 300kg of amphetamine in a three-day operation targeting a suspected international supply network.
Lithuanian authorities have uncovered one of the largest synthetic drugs laboratories in the Baltics, seizing hundreds of kilograms of drugs and thousands of litres of chemical precursors at a site near Vilnius allegedly run by a Dutch national of Turkish origin.
“[Drugs] were being produced on an almost industrial scale,” Saulius Briginas, Deputy Chief of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told journalists during a press briefing on Wednesday.
Investigators believe the Dutch citizen organised the laboratory's work and coordinated its illegal activities alongside three other members who were all Lithuanian nationals.
Preliminary figures indicate that police recovered more than 3,000 litres of BMK, a chemical precursor used in the production of amphetamines; more than 500kg of methamphetamine; more than 300kg of amphetamine; and around 4.5kg of the synthetic cathinone 3-CMC. This amounts to over 4 million single doses, Briginas said.
“On the wholesale illicit market, the drugs would be worth more than €2 million,” he said. “At street level, the value could be ten times higher.”
Such figures, Lithuanian authorities believe, indicate that the drugs could not have been intended solely for the Lithuanian market.
Instead, the operation was geared towards markets across Europe, with the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and the Czech Republic among the countries to which the drugs may have been destined.
The investigation also uncovered the industrial-scale procurement of chemicals needed to manufacture synthetic drugs. The group sourced laboratory equipment and chemical substances from China, India and several European countries, while also purchasing some uncontrolled substances from specialist suppliers in Lithuania.
Police found 380 cylinders of hydrogen originating from China at the laboratory. Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of synthetic drugs, while sulphuric acid was reportedly purchased in quantities of one tonne per transaction.
The operation extended beyond the laboratory itself. Police intercepted a shipment intended for the Czech Republic after finding 17kg of amphetamine crystals in two plastic containers inside cargo handled by a Lithuanian logistics company.
Under Lithuanian law, offences involving the illegal production, possession and smuggling of particularly large quantities of narcotic or psychotropic substances can carry prison sentences of up to 18 years.

Why are some Israelis paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:39:01 UTC
04:39:01 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel elections 2026
- Israelis living abroad are paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote
Israelis living abroad are paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote
Many Israelis view this election as a sliding doors moment, and are willing to fork out on flight fees and hotel costs to make a difference.
Around 1 million Israelis eligible to vote in the October 27 parliamentary election live outside the country. Yet Israel is one of the few democracies that requires citizens to be physically present to cast a ballot, with no general postal or proxy voting and no voting at embassies except for diplomats and official emissaries.
That has not stopped tens of thousands from making the trip. The AID Coalition’s Fly & Vote initiative estimates that more than 50,000 Israelis living abroad, many of them in the United States, plan to return to Israel to vote, often at a cost of thousands of dollars. For a large proportion of them, this is their first time doing so.
“It’s my duty”
Revital Ganon Baruch moved to California in 2011 with her husband and two children. She had never felt the need to return to vote, but this year she is taking a 14-hour flight because she believes Israel needs change.
“I think the elections are very crucial,” she said. “I felt that if I won’t do it, I would feel bad with myself,”
“It’s an effort of time and money, but if I feel as Israeli as I feel, it’s my duty to do it now.”
She added that she once questioned whether she had the right to vote from abroad. “But the way this government is running Israel is affecting people outside of Israel too.”
Why this election feels different
For many expatriates, the election has become a pivotal moment for Israel’s future, shaped by demographic change, the October 7 massacre, the war in Gaza, the hostage crisis and years of political division.
Ido Kadman, an Israeli living in New York who left the country in 1994, pointed to the growing political influence of ultra-Orthodox communities. “We have generations and decades of Hasidic Jews coming in droves to vote,” he said, arguing that many had “never served in the military, paid taxes, or done anything to actually contribute to this country.”
Others say October 7 was the catalyst. Many are angry at Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over its handling of the attack, the hostages and the war, as well as its judicial overhaul plans and dependence on far-right coalition partners.
Every vote counts
If around 50,000 expatriates vote, their ballots could be worth roughly two Knesset seats. With polls suggesting a close race, organizers believe the number, and the influence that could reach, could be higher.
Nadav Nir, an Israeli living in Berlin, said the tightness of the race made the journey worthwhile. “With the two blocs and everything being so close, I would say every vote counts,” he said.
Nadav, an active climate campaigner, acknowledged the environmental cost of flying, but said he saw it as a necessary trade-off. “Letting go a little of my climate-related worldview, to be a tiny help in this huge crisis that Israel is facing, was obvious for me.”
Who can vote?
Israeli citizens can vote as long as they are in Israel on election day, regardless of how long they have lived outside of the country.
Maya Gur Arieh was born in Israel, moved to Canada as a child and later returned to Israel as a young adult. She moved to London a month ago for her studies, but she and family members in Canada who have not lived in Israel for years are flying back to vote.
“We’re all angry Israelis living abroad,” she said. “It’s still very much our home, and we just want the future of the country to be much brighter.”
Israel’s Law of Return allows any Jew to obtain citizenship, preserving voting rights even for people who have spent most of their lives abroad.
Marco Greenberg, an American-Israeli living in New York, was born in Hollywood and lived in Israel for only three years, between 1993 and 1996. He sees no contradiction in returning to vote.
“I think it’s the right of being a citizen,” he said. “I was granted citizenship. I have every right to take full advantage of that.”
Many believe that it is unfair to that people can vote in elections in countries they were not born in, and have not lived in for a long time.
Marco said reactions within his own family had been mixed. “Some say, all the honor to you, it’s so patriotic. Others don’t say that. They say, WTF.”
He argued, however, that the connection between Israel and its diaspora citizens strengthens the country. “Having a strong relationship between the Jewish people in Israel and Israeli citizens around the globe is only an advantage to the state of Israel.”
Will the laws ever change?
Every expatriate interviewed for this report, both on and off the record, said they planned to vote for parties in the opposition bloc seeking to unseat Netanyahu.
That may explain why the prime minister has shown little interest in changing Israel’s voting rules. Many Israelis left the country in recent years amid dissatisfaction with his government, and making it easier for them to vote from abroad would likely benefit the opposition.
The issue is also legally and politically sensitive. Likud challenged Fly & Vote, an initiative that made it easier for Israelis living in the U.S. to fly to Israel for the October election, arguing that it amounted to improper election interference, before withdrawing its petition under a compromise that bars the group from subsidizing tickets or adding group flights.
And while the opposition may be tempted to loosen the rules if it takes power, the combination of Israel’s Law of Return and overseas voting could open the door to foreign interference. The concern among politicians is that a foreign group or organisation could encourage Jews abroad to obtain Israeli citizenship, remain outside the country, and vote according to that group’s agenda.
For now, Israelis abroad must pay their own way home. But for the tens of thousands making that journey, the cost is an investment in what they see as the future of their homeland.
