====================================================================================================

Could software cloning change the way we use the internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

An AI-cloned free tool is being dubbed 'the end of software'
It is being called "the end of software" and the dawn of a new era of AI-powered piracy.
New AI tools are disrupting the tech industry, making it relatively easy and fast to clone an existing piece of software and replicate its features.
Earlier this month, a small team of developers used AI tools to create near-identical, free versions of two commonly used products: Microsoft Office, with programs such as Word and Excel, and Adobe Creative, which includes Photoshop.
Around the same time, a different tool called Reverse Engineer Anything that helps developers use AI to deconstruct and replicate features in other pieces of software shot to the top of trending projects on software repository GitHub.
For some, this new generation of tools will disrupt software in the same way MP3 file-sharing networks in the late 1990s changed how we listened to music and watched movies, replacing CDs and DVDs with streaming.
But whether this will give more power to users or further concentrate power in the hands of AI companies remains to be seen.
'Set the clock back' to the 1990s internet
Brandon Thomas is one of the developers who recently announced they had used AI tools to copy the Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative suites.
A 15-year veteran of the US tech industry, he sees himself fighting a "war" for the future of the internet.
In the 1990s, "Everything [online] was nerdy, hackable and weird," he told the ABC.
"Everything in this era could be inspected, copied, shared with friends, remixed. It was amazing."
But over time, the internet became more standardised and bland. Spaces for innovation and personalisation, like Geocities or Myspace, were replaced by closed ecosystems that tightly controlled user access.
"Everything became a walled garden fiefdom, extractive and rent seeking,"
he said.
This is "enshittification", a term coined by writer Cory Doctorow in 2022 to describe the perceived decline of online spaces.
Social media platforms like Facebook initially attracted users with clean, chronological feeds and personal connections, then pivoted to intrusive ads and sponsored content.
Search engines became crowded with sponsored ads and affiliate-marketing spam, pushing out organic search results.
Software makers shifted to subscription-only models with automated billing and predatory cancellation fees, in some cases worth 50 per cent of the annual contract.
For some, AI is part of the problem, as "slop" content floods online spaces.
But for Mr Thomas, AI is the solution.
"AI flips the tide of this war in a way legislation never did," he said.
"We can build anything, even triple-A video games and operating systems.
"This is the most excited I've felt for the future in a long time.
"I think we have a great opportunity to take back the internet from the monopolistic platforms that became rent-seekers and behaved badly to us as users and customers."
How AI is making software easier to copy
Think of a piece of software like a cake from a bakery.
To copy the recipe, you could break into the bakery and steal the list of ingredients (the source code), for which you would be quickly prosecuted.
Or you could reverse engineer the cake by tearing it apart, tasting it, and studying it under a microscope. This is known as "decompiling".
You can then bake the cake based on what you learnt. Each time you bake the cake, you tweak the recipe so the result more closely matches your description.
Queensland University of Technology (QUT) digital economy expert Marek Kowalkiewicz said AI dramatically sped up this process.
"[AI-powered reverse engineering] is not very different from having a bunch of human software developers doing the same thing, but it's way faster and cheaper," Professor Kowalkiewicz told the ABC.
"In the past, I could have hired 100 developers to create a copy. Now it's not expensive anymore."
Reverse Engineer Anything, the viral tool on GitHub, dramatically streamlines the reverse-engineering process by allowing a user without coding skills to replicate features from other software at no cost.
The mood is giddy and chaotic in reverse-engineering forums where users share their projects.
These include hacking into the control systems of cars to replace factory dashboards, playing old games that have lost vendor support, or just figuring out ways to remove ads popping up on their smart TVs.
One user wants to make a free version of their therapy practice's management software. Someone else wants their printer to accept less expensive third-party ink cartridges.
One user writes:
"I'm so excited for all the good and bad stuff that will happen onward."
Software could be recreated legally
AI-generated software cloning means some tech companies face similar issues to musicians, authors and artists who have seen big tech steal their work to train AI.
These tech companies have trained the AI models being used to reverse engineer their own software.
"All those big players will be probably now be lobbying for legislative change and more protection of software," Professor Kowalkiewicz said.
"It's an arms race."
But copyright law was not equipped to deal with the emerging scale of the software cloning issue, according to Malcolm Burrows, a lawyer at Dundas Lawyers.
Software in Australia is protected under copyright as a class of literary work.
Reverse-engineered software is illegal where it is a "substantial reproduction" of an original.
But this will be hard to prove where AI tools have been used to copy software without access to the source code.
"It's going to get very grey in terms of source code and reproduction of software," Mr Burrows said.
Tool 'devalues work of developers'
While Mr Thomas and others dream of a retro internet, some fear a dystopian future.
The new AI tools may further entrench the power of AI companies and generate a rash of low-quality "slop" software.
QUT computer scientist Aaron Snoswell said the tools devalued the work of developers and would lead to more cost cutting and worse software.
"I think for the software industry it creates more of the same headaches and exacerbates the existing AI pain points," Dr Snoswell said.
"Companies are probably going to try to automate even more software development labour with AI."
This trend was already apparent among independent game developers.
"I'm seeing all these indie game developers who have spent 14 years developing their dream game … and then someone in one weekend can create a functional copy," Dr Snoswell said.
"What point is there in building with human effort, with human soul, if if can be stolen like that?"

Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:58:29 UTC
03:58:29 KST

Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
Tehran had ‘nothing new’ to tell Washington after latest nuclear proposals reportedly offered by mediators.
Tehran, Iran – There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity in the Middle East in recent days, with hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to end the United States and Israel war on Iran.
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran on Wednesday to discuss the war and recent tensions in Yemen. It comes against the backdrop of fears of a new breakout in conflict in the region.
Despite this, Tehran has held firm to its position that the war will not end, and the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen, until the US accepts its conditions.
Iran maintains an unyielding stance on its contentious nuclear programme, which was a factor in the Trump administration’s decision to launch the war on February 28.
“Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said late Tuesday after meeting Munir.
But he did not rule out downblending the highly enriched uranium inside the country under supervision from monitors, something Iran has offered before.
Iran’s authorities present the decades-old nuclear programme as a sovereign right and an achievement gained despite strikes, sabotage and assassinations. Rezaei described it as “national wealth” on Tuesday.
Iran has also used low-enriched uranium for civilian purposes like manufacturing radiopharmaceuticals and for power generation at the Bushehr plant in cooperation with Russia.
The authorities argue that surrendering the nuclear programme under military pressure would amount to capitulation, if it did not guarantee that Iran would not be left exposed to more attacks.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised since the start of the war that he wanted to dismantle the Iranian nuclear programme. US Vice President JD Vance, however, suggested earlier this month that a “meaningful” reduction in the level of enrichment capacity may satisfy US demands.
Nuclear issue
Before Israeli and US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Tehran possessed 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. A nuclear bomb would need enrichment of more than 90 percent.
The attacks, followed by further US-Israeli strikes on nuclear sites in 2026, severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. With the IAEA unable to inspect key facilities, the current size, condition and whereabouts of much of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile remain unverified.
Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to inspect its nuclear facilities since the war started, accusing the agency of advancing Western interests through adopting resolutions and referring the nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council.
Iranian authorities maintain they are not pursuing a bomb. But senior Iranian officials, like Rezaei, have publicly questioned the validity of being a party to the international nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty if Iran’s nuclear facilities and other infrastructure continue to be attacked.
Still, Iranian officials have hosted numerous foreign diplomats this week. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in Tehran on Monday after attending a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries a day earlier. There were also indications of visits to Tehran by other Arab officials.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also reported to have met Israeli security officials earlier this week. These meetings did not appear to have decreased the prospects of renewed war.
But speaking at a conference for Iranian exporters in Tehran on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi cautioned that the country faces threats of more attacks and expansive economic sanctions.
“The reality is that the country is truly in war conditions and the war continues. We have not reached peace conditions and are away from it, so all decisions must be made within war conditions,” he said.
Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had “nothing new” to tell Washington and expected realisation of conditions offered in New York last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
Mediators did not publicly divulge details of their proposals to Tehran this week, but were told the US needed to build trust by accepting Iran’s conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognising an Iran-Oman deal over temporary transit in the Strait of Hormuz.
In addition to a pledge for immediate talks on a bigger deal regarding Iran’s nuclear issue, the memorandum included removing the US naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, waivers for oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and halting military action in Lebanon and other regional hotspots.
Ellie Geranmayeh, a senior policy fellow and deputy head of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said it was clear that Tehran would be unwilling to give up its enriched uranium without guarantees of sanctions relief.
“The Iranians have made it very clear, and I see no evidence that’s changing, that they are willing to negotiate over the fate of the highly enriched uranium or access for international monitors, but that has to be directly linked with a very clear implementation protocol for US sanctions relief,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are very far from those types of negotiations at this stage.”
US media cited unnamed officials as saying on Tuesday that the Pentagon was sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and a Marine unit to the Middle East. That would present President Trump with a range of strike options after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Over recent weeks, Trump and his officials have further discussed a range of military operations, including hitting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain to diminish nuclear facilities inside, and dropping the “mother of all bombs” on nuclear and energy facilities. They have also previously raised the idea of seizing Iran’s southern islands on the Strait of Hormuz and assassinating more Iranian officials.
Iran’s state-run Press TV cited an unnamed security official as saying on Wednesday that decision-makers in Tehran have chosen to advance “without any limitations or restraint” if there are more US and Israeli attacks or assassinations.
Geranmayeh pointed out that Tehran had also helped its ally, the Houthis in Yemen, with their advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and even considered potential preemptive strikes to rattle the US ahead of the election.
“One thing we should be watching out for is Israel and the US combining forces on military attacks after the Israeli elections and the US midterms,” she said, after Trump backed Netanyahu’s election bid.

Italian authorities are investigating whether Russia or other foreign actors had a role in the violent cost-of-living protests that swept Milan and other European cities over the weekend, as concerns rise across the EU over Moscow’s escalating hybrid warfare.
Italy’s government, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, has reportedly requested a briefing over what role – if any – foreign provocateurs may have played, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Oct. 21, citing people familiar with the matter.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The scale of the violence and the apparent coordination of some attacks led officials to question whether the unrest was entirely spontaneous.
“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other periods,” Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said in Rome on Tuesday.
“They are the product of what I call ‘hybrid warfare,’ which someone is bringing into our countries with unconventional tools that are called TikTok, social media and YouTube, without the West realizing or reacting,” he continued, according to Bloomberg.
Meloni’s spokesperson had declined the request to comment.
Weekend unrest in Milan
According to a report from The New York Times (NYT) on Monday, Oct. 19, thousands of people were brought to the streets by rising food and fuel prices, combined with low wages, high taxes and public spending cuts.
Ukraine Counts on Beijing’s ‘Constructive Role’ as Sybiha Meets Chinese Ambassador
Milan reportedly saw the largest turnout, with about 2,000 demonstrators according to the city’s police, while protests also took place in Bologna, Turin, Brescia and Bergamo.
The initial call to protest came from an anonymous social media account created earlier in October, which urged nationwide anti-government demonstrations to “bring the birth of a new Italy and a new Europe.”
While most participants in Milan marched peacefully, masked groups looted shops, set fires and threw objects at police, who responded with water cannons and tear gas.

The NYT reported that police arrested 32 people, most of them minors, and reported 14 officers injured. A local business association put the damage at more than €1 million (roughly $1.1 million).
“Demonstrating is a right, devastating our cities is not,” Meloni said in a statement on X.
The unrest mirrored similar movements elsewhere in Europe, including student-led riots in France, the country’s worst in decades.
In southern Italy, farmers and truckers have blockaded ports and highways over soaring fuel prices linked to the war in Iran.
Troops deployed to Milan
Crosetto also said that children as young as 11 or 12 who took part appeared to have undergone a form of “counter-education.” He, however, offered no further details on what that would entail.
With more demonstrations expected this weekend, the government announced the deployment of 500 military personnel in Milan until the end of the year.
According to Bloomberg, opposition critics accused Meloni’s conservative coalition of exploiting the unrest ahead of the next year’s elections while neglecting grievances behind it.
Meloni’s firm line on Moscow
Italy’s scrutiny of the protests comes as Meloni has positioned her government among Kyiv’s prominent backers in Europe, which could – in Kremlin’s view – make it a legitimate target for a hybrid operation.
“If Ukraine stopped defending itself tomorrow, as many wish and openly call for, we would not achieve peace,” Meloni said on Oct. 14, speaking ahead of the EU summit in Brussels.
“Instead, we would be discussing the occupation of a European country and the return of Soviet-style imperialism, which Europe endured for half a century,” she continued.
Her support for Kyiv, she said, alongside pressure on Moscow, remained the pillars of Italy’s foreign policy; even at the cost of voter support.
Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign
Italy’s foreign actors probe comes as EU governments report a sharp rise in Russian hybrid operations, ranging from drone incursions into NATO airspace to sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament on Sept. 17 that intelligence assessments showed Moscow planned “hybrid” drone and missile strikes on countries supporting Ukraine, which it could later portray as accidents.
Around the same time, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia could attack another European country directly as Moscow seeks to fracture Western unity and weaken support for Ukraine.
On Oct. 17, Tusk reiterated his earlier warning that Russia may escalate its hybrid warfare before Christmas, pointing to possible attacks on railway lines and energy transit conduits supplying Ukraine.
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) said on Oct. 7 that Russia had begun carrying out sabotage against Danish defense firms supplying Ukraine, often through untrained proxies recruited via Telegram.
Days later, the Financial Times reported that European intelligence agencies had warned arms executives of Russian assassination plots, with Germany’s domestic intelligence agency (BfV) advising them to hire private bodyguards.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in hybrid operations or sabotage in Europe.

Public support for Palestine Action and financial assistance to the group can constitute criminal offenses punishable by up to 14 years in prison under the legislation that designated it a terror organization.
Rooney previously said she would continue donating proceeds from her books to Palestine Action, arguing that the designation equated acts of vandalism, demonstrations and disruptions at military bases with terror crimes.
Earlier this month, Rooney said Faber had determined it could “no longer supply my work within the UK,” and that the decision had been made with her full agreement.
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions,” she said. “And I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

BBC Russian reveals that journalist Darya Shipacheva raised 1.5 million rubles for Ukraine’s military before receiving a 12-year treason sentence

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

BBC Russian reveals that journalist Darya Shipacheva raised 1.5 million rubles for Ukraine’s military before receiving a 12-year treason sentence
The case of medical journalist Darya Shipacheva, sentenced to 12 years in a penal colony for treason in July 2026, drew widespread attention. A photograph of her in handcuffs in the courtroom spread across social media. Her trial was held behind closed doors, and almost nothing was known about the substance of the charges. BBC Russian has learned exactly what led to her conviction. Meduza summarizes its findings.
Shipacheva raised money for Ukraine’s armed forces on behalf of Ukrainian blogger Vasilisa Levchenko, BBC Russian reported. According to investigators, Shipacheva transferred more than 1.5 million rubles to Levchenko.
Darya Shipacheva is 35. Before her arrest, she wrote about medicine, health, and feminism for RBC, Takie Dela, Wonderzine, and Forbes Woman. She also published a book about medicine and health, “Bez paniki” (“Don’t Panic”). As an activist, she organized demonstrations in support of the Khachaturyan sisters and feminist activist Yulia Tsvetkova. She also volunteered at a residential school for children with autism spectrum disorder.
After the war began, Shipacheva chose to stay in Russia. She called Moscow her home and wasn’t considering emigrating. Still, a friend said, she had noticed the security services taking an interest in her. When she traveled abroad, border guards asked why she had been born in Ukraine. Shortly before her arrest, a stranger warned her that people would “soon come” for her.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Vasilisa Levchenko ran a Russian-language psychology blog and had about 60,000 Instagram followers, including some in Russia. After the invasion, she began collecting donations for Ukraine’s armed forces through her Sberbank account. According to the BBC, Russian followers who “felt ashamed” sent her more than a million rubles in the first few days.
In May 2022, Russian propagandists took notice of the fundraising. Sberbank later blocked Levchenko’s card, and Rosfinmonitoring, Russia’s financial monitoring agency, subsequently added her to its list of terrorists and extremists. Shipacheva, who did not know Levchenko personally, then offered to collect donations through her own bank account. According to investigators, Shipacheva raised 1.558 million rubles and transferred the money to Levchenko in cryptocurrency.
In letters to BBC journalists, Shipacheva wrote that concern for her family had driven her decision. She was born in Kharkiv but spent most of her life in Russia. She still has relatives in Ukraine, and her cousin serves in the Ukrainian military.
“I faced an unbearable choice: Supporting one homeland meant betraying the other. I chose to support those who, in my view, are the injured party,” Shipacheva wrote. She emphasized that she had raised money for first-aid kits, jackets, and sleeping bags.
Shipacheva said she realized she would end up in prison as soon as she was detained. There was no point denying it, she said — the officers “had all the evidence.” She pleaded guilty “out of fear and weakness” and signed a pretrial cooperation agreement after being threatened with 18 years in prison.
A transfer “to a Sberbank card belonging to a Ukrainian blogger” may also have been the basis for another criminal prosecution. IT consultant Nina Slobodchikova was sentenced to 12 years for treason over a transfer of 5,000 rubles. Although Slobodchikova declined to tell journalists whom she had sent the money to, her account matches the circumstances of Levchenko’s fundraising, the BBC reported.
Shipacheva hopes to be included in a prisoner exchange and is counting on Levchenko’s help. In letters to her friends, she asks them to let Levchenko know that she has been sentenced to 12 years. “Remind Vasilisa — maybe she’ll put in a word for her somewhere. It would be good if Vasilisa remembered her,” acquaintances of Shipacheva told the BBC.
BBC journalists reached out to Levchenko. She confirmed that Shipacheva had followed her blog but said she had not known her personally. Levchenko declined to answer any other questions. “I don’t see any point in this. I don’t do volunteer work anymore,” she wrote, before blocking the BBC correspondent.

Gulf Oil Exports Climb Above Levels Seen Before the Iran War as Tankers Brave Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

- Category
- World
Gulf Oil Exports Climb Above Levels Seen Before the Iran War as Tankers Brave Attacks
Persian Gulf oil exports have risen above prewar levels despite continued Iranian attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz, as tanker operators accept higher risks in exchange for large profits, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 20.
Middle East oil flows, including shipments through Hormuz and alternative routes, averaged more than 24 million barrels per day in the week through October 18, according to Kpler. That surpassed the prewar level of 23.3 million barrels per day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Oil moving through Hormuz itself, including offshore transfers in the Gulf of Oman, averaged about 14 million barrels per day, or roughly 82% of prewar volumes, The Wall Street Journal reported.
“The big picture is that the system for shipping through a dangerous Strait of Hormuz is now well-established and the risk appetite of those involved in exporting oil has risen,” Hamad Hussain, senior commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the Journal.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have also increased use of pipelines that bypass the strait. In September, about 40% of non-Iranian crude exports from the Gulf avoided Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, according to Kpler.
The recovery in oil flows comes despite escalating attacks on shipping. Around 30 attacks on vessels have been reported in October, accounting for roughly 20% of all ships attacked during the war, according to figures cited by The Wall Street Journal.
“Iran is trying to reassert its blockade of the strait,” Christopher Long, a former British naval officer with Neptune P2P Group, told the outlet.
For traders and shipowners, the profits can outweigh the risks. Kpler estimated that traders can earn around $20 more per barrel reselling Iraqi crude than before the war, amounting to roughly $40 million on a supertanker cargo.
Crew members are also receiving large bonuses for dangerous voyages through the Gulf. Some seafarers have been offered two or three times their normal monthly salary, with one China-based staffing company offering up to $25,000 for a round trip, according to The Wall Street Journal.
“The volumes remain high despite rising attacks, because profits make it worth the risk,” Kpler crude oil analyst Homayoun Falakshahi stated.
Some shipowners have repositioned older vessels previously used to transport sanctioned Venezuelan and Russian oil into the Persian Gulf, where tanker rates have surged.
Many vessels are making short shuttle runs through the highest-risk areas. Tankers load oil inside the Gulf, pass through Hormuz under US air cover along the Omani coast, and often transfer cargo near Oman to ships heading for distant markets.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has continued using drones, missiles, and small-boat tactics against shipping, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The Tanzania-flagged supertanker Loyalty, which previously transported Venezuelan crude to China, entered the Gulf twice since September to load Iraqi oil. On October 16, the tanker was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat while carrying 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude.
The attacks have sharply increased transport costs. Freight for a supertanker carrying Gulf crude to China approached a record $37.37 per barrel, while war-risk insurance rose to as much as 10% of a vessel’s value from less than 3%, according to the report.
“In April, the problem was a shortage of crude. In October, it is the cost of moving it,” JPMorgan commodities strategist Natasha Kaneva stated.
Brent crude remained around $108 per barrel as traders continued to question whether the recovery in Hormuz shipments could be sustained if fighting intensifies again.
The extreme cost of moving oil through the region is also feeding a separate debate over sanctions on Russia-linked shipping. Earlier in October, the Trump administration considered allowing sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers to carry non-sanctioned oil, potentially returning vessels tied to Russia’s sanctions-evasion network to legitimate trade in an effort to bring down freight costs.

Diplomatic efforts to end Sudan war intensify despite continued fighting: UN envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:48:05 UTC
03:48:05 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
- 'We tried these two days to come up with coordinated efforts that will help to establish a peace process that can be inclusive, that involves the people of Sudan, where their voices are heard,' says Swiss ambassador
Diplomatic efforts to end Sudan's civil war are increasing despite continued fighting, the UN secretary-general's personal envoy for Sudan said Wednesday, highlighting new confidence-building initiatives.
"We also are witnessing more diplomatic efforts than earlier around Sudan," Pekka Haavisto told reporters in Geneva following the sixth consultative meeting on Sudan, co-hosted by the UN and Switzerland.
Responding to Anadolu's question about concrete progress compared with previous meetings, Haavisto pointed to growing international engagement with Sudanese political actors.
He highlighted a "successful" visit to Khartoum in September and meetings with political groups, women and youth representatives.
However, Haavisto warned that some parties in Sudan still believed they could achieve a military victory.
"We, the international community, are saying that there is no military solution to the conflict in Sudan," he said, stressing the need for diplomatic negotiations.
Haavisto said the UN had begun exploring two confidence-building measures, including possible exchanges of prisoners of war and detainees, both civilians and soldiers.
The second initiative aims to facilitate students' access to examinations regardless of where they live, he said.
He described the initiatives as "baby steps" compared with the destruction caused by the conflict.
International coordination intensifies
The two-day Geneva meeting brought together representatives of 21 countries and five international institutions to discuss security arrangements, humanitarian truces, possible ceasefires and political solutions.
Haavisto highlighted intensified coordination between the Quad, comprising the US, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates and Egypt, and the Quintet.
The Quintet consists of the African Union, Intergovernmental Authority on Development, League of Arab States, EU and UN.
Haavisto described the increased coordination as "maybe the most important fact."
He said discussions aimed to connect security negotiations with political planning for the period following a possible ceasefire.
Swiss Ambassador Tim Enderlin, head of the Foreign Ministry's peace and human rights division, also stressed the need for coordinated international efforts and an inclusive, Sudanese-led peace process.
"We tried these two days to come up with coordinated efforts that will help to establish a peace process that can be inclusive, that involves the people of Sudan, where their voices are heard," Enderlin said.
He said the aim was to establish a process that "in the end, is Sudan-owned and Sudan-led."
Enderlin warned that the consequences of the conflict extended beyond Sudan to neighboring countries.
He said 34 million people in Sudan depended on humanitarian assistance, describing the country as facing the world's largest humanitarian crisis.

Russia launches round 60 strikes on energy and oil and gas infrastructure in three days
First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal reported this on Facebook following a meeting of the revamped coordination headquarters, Ukrinform reports.
According to Shmyhal, “the focus is on addressing the consequences of emergencies in three key areas”:
Electricity supply. Shmyhal has been appointed by the government to oversee the response.
Heat and water supply, and transport infrastructure. The response will be overseen by Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk.
Electronic communications. The response will be overseen by Minister of Digital Transformation Oksana Ferchuk.
Relevant working groups will be established to coordinate further efforts, Shmyhal said.
Regarding restoration efforts, the first deputy prime minister noted that “emergency repair and restoration work is ongoing wherever the security situation permits. Crews are working at an intensified pace, but the security situation is making the work more difficult.”
Shmyhal thanked energy workers for their resilience and professionalism.

Shmyhal also said that briefings had been held on the state of the Kyiv energy hub. “Russian attacks have caused significant damage to energy infrastructure. Together with NPC Ukrenergo and distribution system operators, we have developed a set of measures to strengthen the resilience of the power system and minimise the impact of Russian strikes,” he said.
The deputy prime minister added: “We also reviewed the situation at the capital’s combined heat and power plants (CHPs). Plant managers reported on the damage caused by Russian strikes and the progress of restoration work. We coordinated equipment requirements.”
Shmyhal instructed officials to ensure that equipment from the Energy Ministry’s hubs is distributed as quickly as possible.

Japan sent a senior diplomat to Moscow this week to discuss the release of a journalist arrested in Russia on spying accusations, Tokyo said Wednesday.
Russia’s FSB security service said last week that a Japanese national had been arrested on the Far Eastern island of Sakhalin.
The individual was later identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, who faces accusations of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory."
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has denied that Japan conducts spying activities in Russia, while the Hokkaido Shimbun has stressed its independence from the government.
On Tuesday, Kimitake Nakamura, Japan's top diplomat for Europe, met Lyudmila Vorobyova, the head of the department at the Russian Foreign Ministry dealing with much of East Asia, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry.
"We lodged a request... that calls for the earliest possible realization of consular access to the Japanese national detained in Russia, as well as the individual's immediate release," Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Wednesday.
Japan also summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a formal protest over the arrest, while its foreign ministry has urged Moscow to provide him "fair and impartial treatment."
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls "unfriendly" countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.
Kihara said the meeting on Tuesday was also held to discuss tense bilateral relations.
"Japan-Russia relations are in a difficult state," he said. "Precisely for that reason, it is necessary for the diplomatic authorities to engage in exchanges on the various issues."
For decades, Russia and Japan have been locked in a territorial dispute over the southern Kuril islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan — which are located northeast of Japan’s Hokkaido prefecture and southwest of Far East Russia’s Sakhalin. The Soviet Union seized control of the islands at the end of World War II.
Japan has also sanctioned Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

'Not Ben-Gvir': Next defense minister should come from Likud, Netanyahu tells ‘Post’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:46:01 UTC
03:46:01 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel’s next defense minister should come from his Likud party, responding to a question about National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s ambition to take the post.
“I think the next defense minister should be from Likud,” Netanyahu told The Jerusalem Post in an interview in the early hours of Wednesday, his 77th birthday.
Netanyahu said he hoped to form another government with his existing coalition partners, while insisting that Likud would determine its policies.
“But it’s going to be our government. We decide what the policy is,” he said.
He did not name a candidate for defense minister. His answer came during an exchange about concerns among regional partners over members of his coalition, including the prospect of Ben-Gvir heading the Defense Ministry.
The full interview will be published in The Jerusalem Post Magazine this Friday.
Ahead of the October 27 election, Netanyahu also outlined conditions for other parties to join a government he would lead, predicted further agreements with Arab countries, and addressed his corruption trial, Qatar, and Israel’s relationship with the United States after President Donald Trump leaves office.
Conditions for a broader coalition
Asked about the possibility of forming a unity government, Netanyahu said he intended first to secure a majority and establish the government’s principles. Other parties could join if they accepted those terms.
“Assuming that I win, and I have 61 seats or more, then I would form a government and define its principles,” he said, referring to a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
“First principle, no Palestinian state, period.”
He also listed Israel’s status as the nation-state of the Jewish people, with minority rights respected; a security doctrine emphasizing initiative; a free-market economy; and an expansion of peace agreements. “If anyone chooses to accept them, yes, they can join the government,” he said.
Former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, separately told 103FM on Wednesday that he would not serve under Netanyahu, even under a rotation agreement for the premiership.
More Arab agreements, without a Palestinian state
Netanyahu said he expected opportunities to expand Israel’s agreements with Arab countries but declined to identify the prospective partners. “Well, we’re definitely talking about more than two,” he said. Later in the interview, he described the potential number as “many more than two.”
Pressed on whether Arab governments objected privately to members of his coalition and its policies toward the Palestinians, Netanyahu disputed that assessment. “Most of them couldn’t care less,” he said of concerns about his partners.
He went further regarding the Palestinian issue: “They said, we have to say it, but we don’t mean it.”
Netanyahu did not identify the officials whose private views he was describing. His account contrasts with the public position of Arab governments including Saudi Arabia, which joined an October 16 statement reaffirming support for a Palestinian state with east Jerusalem as its capital.
Relations with Washington after Trump
Netanyahu said Trump’s decision to endorse him had come as a surprise. Asked about US Vice President JD Vance’s decision not to follow that endorsement, as well as the longer-term prospects for US-Israel relations, he argued that his experience would matter both with a friendly president and under a more difficult administration.
Vance had said his focus was on American candidates and the US midterm elections, rather than endorsing a candidate in Israel’s election.
Netanyahu rejected the description of a possible future administration as merely “less friendly.”
“That’s really laundering words,” he said. “What happens if you have a hostile administration? Who will withstand the pressures? Who will stand up to them? And I think the answer in both cases is the same.”
He was describing a hypothetical future administration, rather than explicitly characterizing a Vance presidency.
Netanyahu said Israel needed to bolster its support in the United States, fight what he called the information war and expand relationships with other countries, citing India as an example.
A demand to end the trial
Asked whether he would consider a unity government with Eisenkot, Netanyahu turned to the criminal proceedings against him and the opposition’s efforts to prevent an indicted politician from serving as prime minister.
“The trial’s collapsed,” he asserted, accusing those involved in the prosecution of criminal wrongdoing. He argued that disqualifying an indicted candidate would effectively allow the attorney-general or state prosecutor to determine who could lead the country: “You cannot do this to any citizen, and I’m a citizen, but also you cannot try to destroy democracy with the abuse of state power.”
“It should be ended right now, and we should start an immediate criminal investigation against those who led it,” he said.
The trial remains ongoing. Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud, and breach of trust; he denies wrongdoing. His demand followed testimony by former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit concerning approvals for the investigations.
Mandelblit maintained that he had authorized Netanyahu’s questioning as a suspect in all three cases, while acknowledging uncertainty over whether he explicitly approved the wording of the bribery warning in Case 4000, the Bezeq-Walla affair.
Qatar and allegations involving his aides
Asked whether Qatar should again act as a mediator on matters involving Israel, Netanyahu said Israel had used Doha’s mediation because the United States had done so.
He accused Qatar of spreading antisemitism and anti-Zionism in American universities and on social media, calling it “one of the engines of our vilification.” He did not give a direct answer on whether it should mediate again.
When challenged about alleged Qatari connections among people in his close circle, Netanyahu dismissed the affair as “a hoax.”
“Except that the judge said there was nothing there,” he said, without identifying a ruling during the interview. He claimed the allegations were intended “to divert attention and to mask what is the real issue in this election.”
The Qatargate investigation concerns alleged work for Qatar by aides associated with the Prime Minister’s Office. Netanyahu’s adviser Jonatan Urich is a central suspect and has denied wrongdoing. Netanyahu has given testimony to police but has not been named as a suspect in that investigation. The affair is separate from his ongoing corruption trial.
Settler violence and the Shin Bet
Questioned about settler violence against Palestinians, including criticism from US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, Netanyahu said the acts were wrong and caused “enormous damage to Israel abroad.”
“I don’t want vigilantism,” he said. Rejecting the expression that perpetrators take the law into their own hands, he added: “They break the law in their own hands.”
He argued that the perpetrators did not represent the wider settlement population and said he had involved Israel’s domestic security agency in confronting them.
“That’s why I put the Shin Bet [Israel Security Agency] into this and continue to do that,” he said.
Asked whether another victory would bring his final term, Netanyahu joked: “Oh no, I’m going to have five more terms.”
He also brushed aside suggestions that he lacked the energy for the job.
“I invite them to come to the gym with me,” he said. “But they’ll have to do the same thing [as I do].”

Thousands march for school funding in Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:45:46 UTC
03:45:46 KST

Thousands march for school funding in Greece
Public sector workers and teachers joined student protesters, amid growing youth-led demonstrations across Europe.
Milan’s youth follow France in violent cost-of-living protests
Thousands of students and teachers have rallied across cities in Greece, demanding more funding for education, including better facilities and smaller class sizes.
The demonstrations echo a wave of youth-led protests across Europe this month, including in France and Albania, where anger over rising costs and alleged corruption has led to clashes with police and major property damage.
Greek police said about 10,000 demonstrators, including school and university students, rallied peacefully in central Athens and the capital’s suburbs on Wednesday.
“From Greece to France, we want public, free education,” protesters chanted as they gathered outside Parliament, where students staged an overnight sit-in nearby before the rally.
Others joined the protests in Thessaloniki, Patras, Larissa and other cities across Greece in solidarity with growing demonstrations in France and elsewhere in Europe, where rallies demanding educational resources have morphed into angry demonstrations over soaring living costs.
Cost-of-living crisis
In Greece, the protests add pressure to Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and his centre-right government as the country prepares to hold elections in mid-2027 amid a weakening economy.
Greece struggled with a serious debt crisis from 2009 to 2018, during which the government agreed to spending cuts in exchange for three European Union and International Monetary Fund bailouts worth about 290 billion euros ($326bn).
But the measures have impacted Greek workers, who are among the poorest in Europe and struggle with stagnant wages, high rents and rising energy costs.
The average monthly salary of 1,500 euros ($1,685) sits at 2009 levels, with many young Greeks having been priced out of housing in cities by skyrocketing rents.
“Surviving here is very difficult; the rent is really high, the houses are really small. Our parents can’t make ends meet to pay for our rent, the electricity, for our life here,” university student Georgia Foukidou, 21, who joined the protest in Athens, told the Reuters news agency.
The protests on Wednesday included strikes by primary and secondary school teachers protesting low pay and staff shortages, while substitute teachers demanded permanent positions and reduced class sizes. Public sector workers and other unions also joined the demonstrations.
Education Minister Sofia Zacharaki said prior to the protests that she was listening to student demands, noting that the government was spending more than 733 million euros ($823m) on new student residences and facilities upgrades.
Mitsotakis’ government has also pledged about one billion euros ($1.12bn) in state subsidies and other benefits to offset increased energy costs for households and businesses due to the Iran war and inflation.

Autogas in Ukraine is getting more expensive: what is the reason and what should drivers expect next
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:42:53 EEST
03:42:53 KST

Autogas in Ukraine is getting more expensive: what is the reason and what should drivers expect next
Kyiv • UNN
Autogas prices are rising due to seasonal demand and Ukraine's dependence on imports. From January 1, an additional increase in prices may be driven by the excise tax.
In Ukraine, the cost of autogas has risen again at some filling stations. At the same time, starting January 1, an additional factor driving up fuel prices may be an increase in the excise tax. Energy expert Hennadiy Ryabtsev told UNN’s journalist more about why autogas is becoming more expensive right now and what affects its price level.
Why autogas is becoming more expensive right now
On Wednesday, October 21, several major filling station networks once again revised fuel prices in Ukraine. In particular, OKKO, WOG and "Ukrnafta" raised the price of autogas by UAH 1, while UPG increased it by 40 kopecks. Diesel and some gasoline grades also became more expensive. An energy expert identifies seasonality as the main reason for the increase in autogas prices. He explains that Ukraine does not have its own production of liquefied petroleum gas in the volumes needed to meet market demand, and therefore depends on imports.
This means that the country currently has no domestic production of liquefied petroleum gas. Therefore, it has to import it. Where is it imported from? From countries where this liquefied petroleum gas is used not only as automotive fuel, but also as fuel for boiler houses
In addition, with the onset of cold weather, demand for heating gas increases, so motorists are forced to compete for the same resource with other consumers, which in turn creates a supply shortage and pushes prices upward. According to the expert, this situation has been repeating for years, as long as Ukraine remains dependent on imported supplies.
If we look at how liquefied gas prices behaved throughout all the years when imports were our main source of supply, we can see that whenever competition between consumers increases—that is, between motorists and those who use this gas as fuel for boilers—we always face a shortage of this resource and its price rises
Is there an autogas shortage in Ukraine
According to the expert, autogas can currently be purchased, although drivers have to pay more.
As far as I know, autogas can be bought at a high price. In other words, it is available at filling stations. But the price is certainly high
At the same time, the current cost of gas is still not high enough compared with gasoline to cause a significant reduction in consumption. According to Hennadiy Ryabtsev, a liter of gasoline usually costs approximately as much as two liters of autogas, while now, he says, the price ratio is around 53–55%; a noticeable decline in demand usually occurs after it exceeds 65%.
When the ratio between gasoline and liquefied petroleum gas exceeds 65%, consumption usually declines significantly because there is then almost no financial benefit from using this resource if the car has a dual-fuel engine
How logistics and the war affect prices
As the expert explains, Ukraine imports autogas mainly by road and rail. After the start of the full-scale war, supplies from Belarus, Russia and Kazakhstan ceased, narrowing the choice of import sources. At the same time, the delivery process itself has not changed significantly, while transportation costs have increased, in particular because of the higher price of diesel fuel used to refuel gas carriers.
Logistics has not changed significantly because it was already like this even before the war. There were problems, of course, after the war began, because much of the supply used to come not from Poland but from Belarus. Belarus was our main supplier of liquefied petroleum gas, followed by Russia, Kazakhstan, and then European countries
As Hennadiy Ryabtsev noted, more expensive transportation also affected the final cost of gas. However, the current price surge should not be explained solely by international events or the situation on the oil market, because the main factor right now is competition for the resource during the heating season.
This has nothing whatsoever to do with Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, or any other countries, because that is not where our liquefied petroleum gas comes from. The increase was driven by growing competition among consumers—motorists and households that use this gas to generate heat. The heating season has arrived, and it has become cold indoors
Could autogas become cheaper in the near future
There is currently no reason to expect a rapid decline in autogas prices, explains Hennadiy Riabtsev. As the weather gets colder, the need for gas for heating in supplier countries may increase, which would limit the availability of the resource for the Ukrainian market. In addition, according to the fuel-market expert, starting January 1, the excise tax on petroleum products, including liquefied petroleum gas, is also set to increase.
There are no objective factors indicating that any decline should be expected. Winter is not ending; on the contrary, more of this same liquefied petroleum gas will be taken for household needs in Poland. And less will remain for us
However, in winter, demand for autogas among drivers may instead decrease, because when temperatures outside are low, starting engines on gas becomes more difficult for drivers.
When the ambient air temperature falls below zero, using liquefied petroleum gas in ordinary cars equipped with the appropriate fuel system is impractical because problems arise when starting the engine. Therefore, demand for this petroleum product decreases in winter, especially at low temperatures. And this limits the price increase

New Mexico sues Jeffrey Epstein's former lawyer and accountant
Oct 21 - New Mexico has filed a civil lawsuit against the former lawyer and accountant of Jeffrey Epstein to block payments by the late sex offender's estate and recover damages for survivors of his alleged sexual abuse, the state's top law enforcement official said on Wednesday.
The suit is the first law enforcement action against Epstein's longtime personal attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn, according to a statement from New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez.
The lawsuit alleges that Indyke and Kahn facilitated, financed, and concealed Epstein's sex trafficking operation, including at Zorro Ranch, 30 miles south of the state capital of Santa Fe. It also names the estate of Jeffrey Epstein and aims to prohibit his private trust -- created days before his death by suicide in a Manhattan jail cell -- from spending any of the more than $100 million it holds. Indyke and Kahn are co-executors of Epstein's estate.
Daniel Weiner, a lawyer representing Indyke and Kahn, rejected allegations the two "knowingly" facilitated Epstein's abuse of women, saying the crimes took place "behind closed doors, in secluded locations" when neither was present.
The suit will test whether authorities are able to pin down allegations that a network of people and financial arrangements helped sustain and conceal Epstein's operations.
“Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible,” Torrez said at a press conference in Albuquerque. He was joined by two survivors of Epstein's alleged abuse, Julia Molchanova and Anouska De Georgiou.
Indyke and Kahn have already been named in civil lawsuits against the Epstein estate, including a complaint last month seeking damages for people pictured in the sex offender's collection of child sexual abuse material.
"Not a single woman has ever accused Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse," Weiner said in a statement, adding that the New Mexico attorney general's office had made no effort to interview the men before filing the lawsuit.
New Mexico's lawsuit comes after the Democratic-run state in February reopened an investigation into activities at Epstein's former New Mexico ranch, where he is accused of abusing women and girls for nearly three decades.
New Mexico has sued the US Department of Justice for access to unredacted files on Epstein, accusing the Trump administration of stonewalling its investigation.
The DOJ said it provided some files but was prevented from handing over most material due to privacy protections. REUTERS

British forces board German warship by air and sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:38:53 BST
03:38:53 KST

Royal Marines boarded the German support ship FGS Berlin by air and by sea during Exercise Strike Warrior, fast-roping from a Merlin helicopter while a second team climbed from a rigid inflatable boat, according to Defence Operations.
The post said the commandos were “making an entrance the commando way” and had boarded the vessel “sharpening their skills alongside NATO allies”, adding: “Training together to defend together.”
⚓ Making an entrance the commando way@RoyalMarines boarded German warship FGS Berlin by air and sea during Exercise Strike Warrior, sharpening their skills alongside @NATO allies.
🛡️Training together to defend together.#ExStrikeWarrior #SW26 pic.twitter.com/F2D1ya5Mhf
— Defence Operations 🇬🇧 (@DefenceOps) October 21, 2026
FGS Berlin is the lead ship of the German Navy’s Berlin class replenishment vessels and was serving as flagship of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s permanent naval force in northern European waters, which is currently under French command.
The boarding was carried out by personnel from K Company, 42 Commando, the Royal Marines unit that specialises in maritime interdiction. One team went up the ship’s side from a rigid inflatable boat using caving ladders, a physically demanding method in strong winds but one that preserves surprise, while another fast-roped onto the deck from a Merlin of 824 Naval Air Squadron, which is quicker but noisier.
Once aboard, the teams cleared the ship compartment by compartment carrying short-barrelled L119A1 rifles, prioritising the bridge and control rooms. A simulated casualty allowed commando and Royal Navy personnel to rehearse evacuating a wounded man from inside a ship.
Exercise Strike Warrior ran from 28 September to 9 October and involved more than two thousand personnel, eight warships and nineteen aircraft across Cape Wrath, the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea. The Royal Navy describes it as the largest test of the United Kingdom Commando Force in fifteen years, and the first time since the war in Afghanistan that all of its specialist elements have trained together.
The exercise rehearses allied crisis-response operations in the High North and the North Atlantic. Alongside Britain it drew in forces from the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, with the Portuguese frigate NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida, the Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s taking part.
Elsewhere in the exercise, soldiers of 148 (Meiktila) Commando Forward Observation Battery were carried to the Scottish coast aboard the German submarine U36, a Type 212A boat, before going ashore near Cape Wrath to direct naval gunfire from Portuguese, Dutch and Canadian warships onto simulated targets.
This publication reported when NATO warships arrived in Glasgow ahead of Strike Warrior and when Merlin helicopters headed to Scotland to protect the submarine force.

More young people are choosing to be child-free. Dita's decision was based on fear of the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:36:40 UTC
03:36:40 KST

The Feed's latest debate brings together a panel of online voices to discuss the question: Why Are More People Choosing a Child-Free Life, and Should Having Kids Still Be a Priority? It can be streamed now on YouTube.
Dita has a husband she loves, financial security and — on paper — the foundations for family life.
But the 37-year-old and her partner have decided not to have children, citing fears about the world their children would inherit as one of the main reasons.
"I'm very pessimistic. I'm surrounded by fear," Dita said during The Feed's debate.
Although Dita believes her husband would make a wonderful father, her concerns about artificial intelligence, climate change and global conflict have reinforced her reluctance to bring a child into a world she cannot control.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The "nail in the coffin" was hearing about a doctor who had been charged with generating AI child sexual abuse material.
"Imagine a world where a man can just walk out, take a picture of your child and then upload it to AI … and be like, 'can you create child pornography of this?'" Dita said.
I'd rather protect my child from that and not give birth at all.
The decision is part of a broader trend — more young people are choosing to go child-free — resulting in Australia’s fertility rate falling to 1.481 births per woman in 2024, according to the ABS. A fertility rate of about 2.1 is generally considered necessary to maintain a population without migration.
A generation rethinking parenthood
The sense of uncertainty was reflected in Monash University's 2024 Australian Youth Barometer where affordable housing, employment and climate change were the three key issues identified as needing immediate action. The barometer, based on 620 young Australians aged 18-24, found that only about half of respondents thought they would have children in the future.
And according to the Growing up in Australia research report from the Australian Institute of Family Studies, 65 per cent of the 4,407 young people surveyed were at least "somewhat concerned" about climate change, with higher environmental concern linked with lower hopes of having children.
Fewer Australians want to become parents, with the number of people reporting that they do not want children rising from 8 per cent in 2005 to 14 per cent in 2023, according to data from the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia survey.
"The cost of raising children and being able to buy a house are all factors becoming increasingly important in people's decision to have a child," Dr Pelin Akyol, a research manager at economic think tank the e61 Institute told The Feed.
A 2026 analysis commissioned for The Parenthood, a non-profit parental advocacy organisation, found that the cost of raising a family with children has increased 134 per cent since 2003 — and the yearly cost of raising two or more kids is about $36,500.
Akyol also said women are increasingly needing to prioritise their careers which is resulting in delaying — or entirely reconsidering — having children.
"Women put more emphasis on having time and energy for their career and they're reporting how important this factor is in their decision to have a child."
"We know that in Australia, the desired number of children is higher than the realised number of children," Akyol said.
Doubts about suitability
But concerns about the world are only part of the decision. Dr Imogene Smith, a clinical psychologist and researcher at Melbourne's Cairnmillar Institute, said some young people were also questioning whether parenthood suited them personally, including whether they felt capable of being a good parent.
"People list something central to their identity … for example, 'I'm not maternal or paternal' as a primary reason [not to have kids]," Smith said.
"Things like fear of overpopulation or the environment often seem to be secondary to that — although it doesn't mean it's any less important."
Smith said changing social expectations had also given young people more freedom to question whether parenthood was right for them. Previous generations often viewed having children as the expected path, whereas today the decision is more openly discussed.
"We have much more social discourse around decision making and this decision in particular ... which means that it's front of people's minds and people know that they have a choice and they're exercising that choice," Smith said.
The pressure to be a good parent
For those who do want to become parents, Smith said social media had made information more accessible, but had also left some prospective parents confused about how to raise children.
"Over the course of the last 50 years, we now have so many different 'expert opinions' about how to raise your child that people are reporting feeling confused now," Smith said.
Akyol said these expectations could affect how people perceive the cost of raising a child.
"Depending on a person's preferences about parenthood, they may also see the cost of having a child differently," she said.
"With the increasing role of social media in our life, people's view about being a better parent might have changed as well. We see parents providing a lot to their kids."
Stephanie Bastiaan, head of advocacy at Women's Forum Australia, a conservative think tank, said modern society was exaggerating the difficulties of parenthood.
"I do think we overthink it, particularly in this day and age where we're so top-heavy with influencers and content online," she said.
I just wonder if we're getting a bit soft as a culture.
Bastiaan, a mother of five with another one on the way, said negative media narratives and concerns about children's wellbeing were overshadowing the positive aspects of raising a family and increasing fear in young people.
"We've got a generation of kids coming out with poor mental health because we are instilling all this fear," she said.
Bastiaan acknowledged the strain on working parents, particularly women, who she said often shoulder much of the emotional and practical burden of raising children.
"If you have both parents in an economy where they have to work, then you've got them coming home after a day of work. They then have two hours where they've got to emotionally give to their kids," Bastiaan said.
We don't ever hear the joy of giving to a child.
"And you can see why there's such a high rate of burnout, particularly for women where that usually falls to them."
But Bastiaan argued that society also needed to talk more about the positive aspects of motherhood and family life.
"I feel sad that you're giving up something that's so beautiful because of that fear," she told Dita during the debate.
'If we don’t have children, we will go extinct'
George Mamalis, from conservative political advocacy group Turning Point Australia, believes negative attitudes towards having kids are having impacts on Australia’s future.
"The youth, they’re obsessed with climate change," Mamalis said on The Feed’s debate.
"I've actually heard in interviews kids saying they're not going to have kids because they're worried about climate change."
Mamalis believes people who opt out of parenthood are "selfish" and "entitled".
"It means that you're relying on those who are willing to have children," he said.
The fact is, if we don't have children, we will go extinct.
Lower fertility will be the main driver of slower population growth and faster ageing over the next four decades, according to the latest Intergenerational Report, however Australia’s population, which hit 28 million in June, is projected to grow to 39.3 million by 2065-66.
Being a 'good enough' parent
Smith said one way to ease the pressure was to reconsider what it means to be a good parent. She pointed to British paediatrician Donald Winnicott's concept of the "good enough parent", which emphasises providing children with the care, safety and love they need without striving for perfection.
"It has a very specific definition, and it means that you do enough to keep that child safe and happy and loved," Smith said.
The concept does not mean neglecting children's needs, Smith said, but recognising that parents cannot do everything perfectly.
She said the constant stream of parenting advice could make people feel they needed to meet unrealistic standards before they were ready to have children.
"The more they hear about how hard parenthood is, the more they're disinclined to participate," she said.
For Dita, the decision is also shaped by her own childhood. Growing up in a single-parent household, she watched her Indian-born mother work multiple jobs to support the family.
"I saw my mum struggle a lot," she said.
Dita said that although they could afford to provide for a child, she worried she and her husband’s demanding working hours would leave them without the time and energy to meet a child's emotional needs.
"We know that we would probably make terrible parents," she said.
Yet Dita has not ruled out motherhood entirely. If the obstacles were removed, she said she might reconsider. For now, she believes the decision should remain a personal one.
"At the end of the day, it's my body, my mind, my feelings, my choice. That's it."

Actors, writers condemn UK anti-terror law targeting Sally Rooney
In an open letter on the cover of the New Statesman, dozens of leading figures term the UK law banning Palestine Action a ‘repressive absurdity’.
Dozens of leading writers, actors and activists have condemned the UK law used to proscribe Palestine Action as a “repressive absurdity” in an open letter backing Irish novelist Sally Rooney, whose books have been withdrawn from sale in the United Kingdom.
The letter comes after Rooney said her books had been pulled from sale in the UK due to her public support for Palestine Action, a group the British government designated as a “terrorist organisation”.
Signatories include actors Paul Mescal – who played in an adaptation of her book Normal People, Susan Sarandon and Tilda Swinton; broadcaster Gary Lineker; and writers Arundhati Roy, Naomi Klein, JM Coetzee, Zadie Smith and William Dalrymple.

“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public,” the letter reads. “Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country.”
The letter appears on the cover of this week’s New Statesman magazine, two weeks before the Supreme Court is set to hear a case on the ban.
“We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity,” the letter concludes.
Rooney’s publisher, Faber & Faber, said on Wednesday that the withdrawal stemmed from “circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work” and to continue sales would be an “unconscionable situation for a publisher”.
Rooney has said that further publication of her work could constitute a “serious criminal offence”.
She said she had made “every effort to be honest” with the public about her beliefs and intentions, adding that she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”.
E-books of Rooney’s work have also been removed from sale in the UK, although some physical copies remain available in bookshops.
She has authored four best-selling novels, selling more than six million books globally.
