====================================================================================================

Israel bans United Airlines pilot over Iran sympathies weeks after flydubai hijacking attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:11:44 UTC
03:11:44 KST

The Transportation Ministry has notified United Airlines on Wednesday that one of its pilots has been barred from entry to Israel as a crew member because of his history of Iranian sympathies.
The Diaspora Affairs and Combatting Antisemitism Ministry forwarded information that the pilot, Sina Amjadian, shared political and pro-Iranian regime posts on his social media accounts.
The case raises new questions regarding the vetting process for foreign airline crews, coming just weeks after an attempted hijacking aboard a flydubai flight en route to Israel.
Amjadian - a pilot of Iranian descent employed by United Airlines - shared images on social media featuring Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, alongside Islamic Republic flags, while criticizing Israeli military strikes in Iran.
Recent reports indicate that the pilot currently resides in Dubai. His LinkedIn profile states that he previously worked for flydubai before joining United.
Vetting process, security protocol
Transportation Ministry officials stated that the information uncovered by the Diaspora Affairs Ministry was initially passed to the Transportation Ministry's Security Department, which then forwarded it to Israeli intelligence and defense agencies. After reviewing the findings, security officials recommended prohibiting Amjadian from entering Israel as flight crew.
A formal notice was then sent to United Airlines, and the pilot's details were submitted to both the Israeli Aviation Security Center and the Population and Immigration Authority to block his air entry.
However, the Transportation Ministry clarified that following inquiries with United, it was determined that Amjadian does not operate international routes. Instead, he flies domestic routes within the United States and Canada. Consequently, the directive does not alter any existing flight assignments to Israel.
Khamenei imagery and criticism of Israeli strikes
Among the content Amjadian shared was a video showing people carrying portraits of Khamenei alongside Iranian flags and a black heart emoji. In an Instagram story dated June 15, 2025, he shared a memorial post for a Mahan Air flight attendant and her family members who were allegedly killed in an Israeli strike on their home in Tehran. Alongside the post, he wrote in English: "Since when did aircrew become military targets?!"
Reports from that period identified the flight attendant as Mahnoosh Haji Soltani, who was killed on the night of June 14 in Tehran's Narmak neighborhood. Citing the Iranian aviation news site Can News, the outlet IranWire reported that her home was destroyed by the blast wave during Israeli strikes.
In another Farsi post, Amjadian accused an unidentified entity of hypocrisy and of disrespecting others' beliefs. In a separate story, he shared an edited image depicting young girls with wings alongside soccer players, captioned in English: "We will never forget Minab." The post was timestamped June 27, without specifying the year.
Minab is a city in southern Iran where the "Shajareh Tayyiba" girls' primary school was struck on February 28, 2026. According to Iranian authorities, 168 children - mostly young girls - were killed in the attack. In March, Reuters cited US officials indicating that preliminary findings pointed to potential American involvement in the strike. However, due to the lack of a year on the story timestamp, it cannot be definitively confirmed whether the post referred to that specific incident.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) researcher Travis Hawley also published a thread attributing expressions of support for the Iranian regime and Hezbollah to Amjadian. Among other claims, Hawley alleged that the pilot shared a video in which he kisses the emblem of the Islamic Republic and salutes. These claims have not been independently verified.
Who is responsible for vetting foreign flight crews?
The incident has reopened debate over who is responsible for screening foreign airline personnel entering Israel. According to Dani Shenar, who headed the Security Department at the Ministry of Transport from 1987 to 2017, a 2003 government decision assigned the department full responsibility for vetting foreign aircrews. Under this agreement, airlines are required to submit personnel data as part of the landing permit authorization process.
However, in this instance, as in previous cases, the Diaspora Affairs Ministry raised the initial red flags about the pilot rather than the Transportation Ministry's Security Department. Only after the information was handed over did authorized agencies initiate a background check, culminating in the directive sent to United.
This oversight issue previously surfaced following an attempted hijacking on a flydubai flight on September 30, when an Omani first officer attacked the captain during a flight from Dubai to Israel. The aircraft entered a steep dive before crew members and passengers managed to subdue the attacker and avert a catastrophe. The flight made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
That incident triggered harsh criticism of the security clearance apparatus for foreign aircrews. At the time, the Transportation Ministry's Security Department argued that intelligence background checks fell outside its scope and noted that it had not been provided with the names of flydubai pilots in advance. A senior department official explained that the ministry relies on background checks conducted by the airlines themselves and by security authorities in the countries of departure.
Police inquiry into senior Transport Ministry officials
Alongside public scrutiny over aviation security procedures, Israel Police have launched an inquiry into two senior officials within the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department: Avri Cohen, head of the Security, Emergency, and Cyber Division, and Dvir Rubinstein, manager of the Aviation Security Operations Center.
Reports indicate that Rubinstein is under investigation for a potential conflict of interest after it emerged that he provided paid training modules to foreign airlines, including flydubai and Emirates, while overseeing their security protocol compliance. Rubinstein works for the ministry as an external contractor, not a state employee.
Cohen is under review for secondary employment in foreign aviation security operations without the required clearance from the Civil Service Commission. Authorities emphasized that these are preliminary inquiries and do not constitute formal charges or findings of wrongdoing. The Transport Ministry previously stated that Rubinstein's side contracts were fully authorized under the law and carried out outside his official working hours.
According to recent reports, Transportation Minister Miri Regev insisted that responsibility for vetting foreign flight crews remain with her ministry's Security Department rather than being transferred to the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). The decision adds to lingering questions about agency jurisdiction and Israel's ability to detect internal crew threats on incoming flights.
Transportation Ministry: 'We acted immediately'
In response to the report, the Transportation Ministry stated that it is not an intelligence agency and is not responsible for monitoring social media networks. It noted that the information regarding Amjadian was flagged by the Diaspora Affairs Ministry and was acted upon immediately once received.
The ministry added that its Security Department passed the information to the relevant Israeli security and intelligence agencies, conducted a direct inquiry with United Airlines management, and reviewed the case details. Following the presentation of findings to defense officials, a recommendation was issued to bar the pilot from flying into Israel as a crew member, and formal notification was sent to the airline accordingly.
While the incident highlights gaps in early warning systems for foreign flight crews, there is no evidence linking Amjadian to the flydubai hijacking attempt, nor do his social media posts directly prove involvement in terror activities.
The flydubai hijacking attempt
The directive regarding Amjadian comes approximately three weeks after the attempted hijacking of the flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel, which ended in an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. On September 30, the first officer assaulted the captain inside the cockpit, causing the aircraft to rapidly lose altitude until crew members regained control.
According to a reconstruction published by Walla, the plane was carrying roughly 170 passengers, almost all of whom were Israeli citizens. During the cockpit struggle, the aircraft plummeted more than 4,000 meters (13,000 feet) in under a minute. Once the crew re-established control, they broadcast emergency squawk code 7500, indicating unlawful interference or a hijacking in progress.
Following the event, Israeli defense officials recommended pausing flydubai flights to Israel pending the conclusion of the investigation. The crisis fueled widespread criticism of foreign aircrew vetting procedures and brought renewed scrutiny to the Transportation Ministry's oversight division.
No information links Amjadian to the flydubai incident, and authorities have not indicated that the ban against him was directly triggered by that event.

What happens next in court case for Helen Haines's accused attacker?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:11:22 UTC
03:11:22 KST

In short:
The man accused of attacking Indi MP Helen Haines made his first court appearance on Wednesday.
Brendan Nugent was brought into the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court dock by security guards, but was not required to speak or enter a plea.
The 43-year-old was remanded in custody and taken to the Melbourne Assessment Prison.
It could be close to four months until the man accused of attacking Indi MP Helen Haines faces court again.
In the meantime, police and lawyers are likely to be very busy.
Brendan Nugent's first court appearance on Wednesday played out in similar fashion to most filing hearings in Victorian magistrates courts.
The 43-year-old was brought into the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court dock by security guards, but was not required to speak or enter a plea.
No details of his alleged offending were aired and the charges were not even read out in open court.
He was remanded in custody and taken to the Melbourne Assessment Prison.
No application for bail was made on Wednesday.
If one was made, Mr Nugent's lawyers would need to prove there were compelling reasons for his release and the risk to the community was not unacceptable.
What do we know about the police brief of evidence?
On Wednesday, Magistrate Allison Vaughan gave police a Christmas Eve deadline to serve the brief of evidence on the defence.
A committal mention hearing was set for February 4, 2027.
Mr Nugent's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told the court his client had a rare neurological condition and orders were made so that Mr Nugent could be seen by a doctor.
Victoria Police's Special Investigation Unit is in charge of the case, and the brief of evidence it submits could be lengthy.
Typically, briefs contain police interviews, witness statements, security footage, downloads of mobile phone and computer data, and extracts of phone cell tower records. In Mr Nugent's case, it is likely police will scour the internet for his online posts.
Police can continue investigating and updating the brief past the December 24 deadline, especially if they need to order reports from specialists or request information from tech companies.
Usually, all relevant material gathered by police should be provided in full to the defence. That includes evidence which may weaken the prosecution case.
Once the defence has the brief, an accused person can decide how to plead to the charges.
What do we know about the charges Brendan Nugent is facing?
After holding Mr Nugent in custody for about a day, Victoria Police charged him with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
He is also facing charges of possessing and cultivating cannabis.
Even though the court process has begun, police are able to add, remove or modify charges.
At a media conference yesterday morning, Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said further serious charges in relation to the alleged attack on Ms Haines were being considered.
Specifically, the Chief Commissioner was asked about a charge of attempted murder.
"That's always a consideration. Of course we have to locate and follow the evidence,"
Chief Commissioner Bush said.
To prove a charge of attempted murder, the prosecution must show beyond reasonable doubt that the accused intended to kill, their actions went beyond mere preparation, and they had no lawful excuse for their actions.
The state charges, dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, are offences under Victoria's Crimes Act 1958.
A person convicted of intentionally causing serious injury faces the potential of a 20-year jail term. The dangerous driving charge carries a maximum penalty of five years' jail.
The causing harm to a Commonwealth public official offence is a federal crime.
Under the federal Criminal Code, the offence can be summarised as an offender intending to harm a Commonwealth official because of their role or something they did in it.
An attack on a politician carries a maximum of 10 years. It is a 13-year maximum if the victim is a federal judge, law enforcement officer or frontline worker.
What happens in a committal mention hearing in Victoria?
Given the nature of the allegations against Mr Nugent, it is highly unlikely the case will be finalised in the Magistrates' Court, which usually deals with less serious charges.
Mr Nugent has a committal mention hearing scheduled for February 4, 2027, at the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court.
However, it is possible the matter could be brought back for mention hearings beforehand, where updates on the legal case could be provided to the court.
At the end of the committal mention, a magistrate must ask Mr Nugent how he pleads to the charges before transferring the case to a higher court.
There is no guarantee that will happen on February 4, though.
Adjournments are common, often because police need more time to gather evidence, legal issues arise or the parties are negotiating.
Once the case has been transferred to the higher court, an accused person formally enters their plea again.
Committal mentions have taken on added significance in Victoria because law changes mean committal hearings rarely occur.
Committals served as "mini trials", with defence lawyers cross-examining witnesses and a magistrate assessing the prosecution evidence, before deciding whether it met the threshold to be sent to a higher court for trial.
Committals often revealed new details of prosecution cases, even though the material was sometimes highly prejudicial and had not been admitted at trial.
The law changes mean the prosecution case may only become clearer to the public once the trial begins or at a pre-sentence hearing.
The charges Mr Nugent is facing would likely be finalised in the County Court.
If he pleads guilty, more administrative court dates would be set before a pre-sentence hearing, where legal arguments are put forward and victim impact statements are read out. Afterwards, a judge would hand down a sentence.
If Mr Nugent pleads not guilty, pre-trial hearings would need to occur in the County Court ahead of a jury trial.
The same process would occur if police charged Mr Nugent with attempted murder, though that would result in the Helen Haines attack-related charges being moved to the Supreme Court.
Mr Nugent's case is well into the sub judice period, given police have laid charges and his first court appearance is complete.
There are limits on what the media can report about the allegations because a jury could one day have to decide the case.

No surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:11:16 UTC
03:11:16 KST

“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.
“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”
Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.
Six years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.
“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”
The inquiry concluded that the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.
The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.
Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.
After that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.
To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”
From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.
“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”
Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.
“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.
Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.
“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”

Ukraine seemed prepared for jet-powered drones, but has yet to find a solution. When will its anti-Geran weapon enter service?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:11:00 EEST
03:11:00 KST

Ukraine seemed prepared for jet-powered drones, but has yet to find a solution. When will its anti-Geran weapon enter service?
The command post of the Ukrainian Posipaky ("Minions") battalion of the 39th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment is a hive of activity. The soldiers are monitoring a large screen showing a map that is constantly updated with markers tracking drones crossing the front line. Their job is to coordinate interceptor-drone crews as they bring down Russian UAVs on the Zaporizhzhia front.
Suddenly, a new blip appears among the dozens already on the screen. It immediately catches the eye, racing along the front line at high speed. It is one of Russia's new jet-powered drones, which began appearing in large numbers in late summer.
Ramses, the battalion commander, orders his team to leave the blip alone. The drone is travelling at 500 km/h – too fast for conventional interceptor drones to bring down.
Within a few months, Russian drones crossing the front line had become a routine occurrence. The flow of UAVs continues unabated, day in, day out. But the tactics are different now: rather than launching large groups of Shaheds, Russia sends jet-powered drones one by one, at intervals of 20-30 minutes. Most get across the front line.
Long-range drones make their way into this sector from a Russian drone base in occupied Donetsk. They fly hundreds of kilometres along the front line towards the Dnipro Reservoir, where the terrain makes interception more difficult.
"They fly undetected across the occupied territories, climbing higher and gaining speed," Ramses said. "Only at the last moment do they appear on our screens, at an altitude of 5,000 to 8,000 m – well beyond the reach of MANPADS and other air defence systems."
Most of the drones are jet-powered Geran-4 loitering munitions derived from Iran's Shahed-136. But Russia is also using the newer Geran-5, which has a radically different design, more akin to a cruise missile.
These drones are piloted by an operator rather than left to fly unguided, making them even more lethal. Since losing access to Starlink, Russian forces have adopted mesh networks that use chains of drones to relay radio signals through the air. Each drone relays the signal to the preceding one, creating a link back to the operator and enabling real-time control.
"In August, Russia used around 2,400 jet-powered Gerans and 2,400 conventional ones in strikes across Ukraine," Ramses said. "Roughly a quarter to a third of those drones passed through our area of responsibility. The proportions are still roughly the same."
The Ukrainian Air Force reports that air defences managed to shoot down only 1,460 Russian jet-powered drones in August. Ukraine's ability to shoot down more jet-powered drones is hampered by a shortage of anti-aircraft missiles and a lack of high-speed interceptor drones.
Ukrainska Pravda explores why jet-powered Gerans are giving Ukraine's air defences such a hard time – and what it could take to stop them.
Russia is putting its faith in jet-powered Gerans
The arrival of jet-powered Gerans has created new opportunities for Russia to launch long-range strikes on Ukraine's rear areas. But scaling up production of the new drones is proving difficult because Russia relies on China for their jet engines.
The high failure rate of Chinese engines poses another challenge. Ukrainska Pravda has obtained a wreckage analysis by a specialist institution, which found that many drones were lost when their engines failed after several hours in the air. Repairing the engines in Russia has helped, but the problem has only been partially resolved.
As of early September, engines supplied by Chinese company Telefly began to be assembled from kits at Russia's drone production centre in Alabuga.
Russia has also begun producing the simplest structural components, suggesting plans to increase output and manufacture more components domestically.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, told Ukrainska Pravda that the new drones still contain Western electronics, including a US-made flight controller. China supplies other critical components, such as the engine, thermal imaging camera and secure communications systems.
"The Chinese side officially receives all the necessary information about the use of these components in Russian weapons," Vlasiuk said. "Yet the only response we get is that a jam-resistant satellite navigation antenna does not fall within the military goods category and is therefore not subject to the relevant export restrictions.
My latest proposal to our Chinese partners was to reclassify certain components as military goods. But I expect that they will reject it."
Trying to develop interceptor drones
Jet-powered drones are proving extremely difficult to intercept, making them one of Ukraine's most pressing air defence challenges alongside ballistic missiles. In response to this new threat, the first prototypes of high-speed interceptor drones are now reaching military units for testing.
Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the state-run Brave1 defence technology cluster, told Ukrainska Pravda that work on a solution had begun a year before the jet-powered Geran loitering munitions started appearing en masse.
"Back in the summer of 2025, once interceptor drones had managed to close the sky to conventional Shaheds, we started looking at where to focus our efforts next," he said. "That's when we began funding teams working on solutions to take down jet-powered drones. We're talking not just about high-speed interceptors, but also anti-aircraft missiles and turrets."
Twenty-two teams have been working on high-speed drones to counter jet-powered Gerans. Twelve have received state funding from Brave1. The projects include drones equipped with miniature turbojet engines and electric-powered models with propellers.
Another promising avenue is drones powered by electric ducted fans, which resemble turbojets in design but run on battery power.
Hrytseniuk said seven interceptor drones have been deployed in combat, where they have successfully brought down jet-powered drones.
One interceptor already in service is an unidentified turbojet-powered drone spotted in use by the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU). Video footage shows it pursuing and striking a Russian Geran-5, which travels at an average speed of 500-600 km/h.
According to Hrytseniuk, the government has ordered well over 1,000 of the new interceptors. However, production is still being ramped up.
"We will definitely catch up with Russia's drone production, but it won't happen overnight," he noted. "Look at what happened with conventional Shaheds: it took us six months to scale up interceptor production. We're doing everything we can to speed things up this time, but we're not talking days or weeks."
One obstacle to scaling up production of the new interceptors is securing a supply of miniature turbojet engines. But Brave1 is confident that the issue can be resolved.
"These engines weren't available in Ukraine before," Hrytseniuk said. "No private company was making them. In 2025, we launched a programme, set up a funding scheme, made this a separate area of work and started working with manufacturers. Now, 11 Ukrainian companies are producing turbojet engines, and six of them have started mass production. It took more than a year and a half to get here."
As of early October, the new developments had not yet noticeably strengthened Ukraine's air defences. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Air Force is still doing the lion's share of the work to counter jet-powered drones, accounting for half of all successful interceptions. With missiles in short supply, pilots are using risky tactics, approaching the drones at close range to destroy them with their aircraft's cannons.
The next most effective system is the previously unknown Bars drone, which intercepted a third of the Gerans shot down in a month. It is not yet clear, however, whether this is a new interceptor or a long-range drone called Bars that has been adapted to shoot down other drones.
Drones alone are not enough
Officials and military personnel who spoke with Ukrainska Pravda warn against pinning hopes on a silver bullet that will solve all the problems. They say only a combination of different weapons, used effectively, can counter the threat posed by jet-powered Shaheds.
Another priority in tackling jet-powered drones is the development of anti-aircraft missiles that are cheaper than long-range drones and can be produced in large quantities.
Ukraine has several projects at different stages of development. Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that Luch, a Ukrainian armaments design office, had presented two missiles at the MSPO-2026 exhibition: one for the Osa air defence system and a smaller one based on the Barrier anti-tank missile system. Another company unveiled a prototype of the Shershen multi-calibre system. President Zelenskyy also mentioned the Nika small missile, which is undergoing testing.
Ukraine is also investing in missile projects led by relatively young companies. The work began within Brave1 in 2024, and developing the first prototypes took two years. Of the ten Ukrainian teams involved, two are already preparing to put their designs into operational use.
"They are cheap and easy to manufacture. One of the requirements was that each missile should cost no more than US$20,000," Hrytseniuk said.
The scale of this ambition becomes clear when compared with the market prices of existing missiles: a single Stinger can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and an AIM-9X missile fired from an F-16 costs around US$500,000.
The idea is that using two or three of these relatively cheap missiles to bring down a Russian long-range drone would still be cost-effective. Various estimates put the cost of a conventional Geran at up to US$70,000, with the jet-powered version potentially costing tens of thousands more.
Ukraine faces a tough battle to protect its strategic infrastructure in the coming months, which Russia is seeking to destroy while it has the chance. And without sufficient weapons supplies, Ukraine's military will have to rely on homegrown technology.
Only a comprehensive approach that combines the latest interceptor drones, autonomous turrets, anti-aircraft guns, aircraft, and air defence missile systems can provide effective protection.
With missiles in short supply, Ukraine has turned to domestically made automated turrets fitted with heavy machine guns. Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara said the military already has hundreds of them in service.
It will take time to work out the best mix of systems to counter the threat.

In Taiwan, a comedian was attacked over a joke about Xi Jinping—the attack was likely ordered from China

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

In Taiwan, a comedian was attacked over a joke about Xi Jinping—the attack was likely ordered from China
Kyiv • UNN
Prosecutors said that the men planned to injure comedian Huang for criticizing the CCP and Xi Jinping. The attacker was allegedly paid from mainland China.
Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men in connection with a conspiracy to run over a comedian with a car after he mocked the Chinese Communist Party and Xi Jinping, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of carrying out transnational repression aimed at silencing critics on the self-governing island. Beijing considers Taiwan its territory and has pledged to seize it by force if necessary.
During one of his performances, Huang Yi-hao mocked the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie the Pooh and sharply criticized his political activities.
On Wednesday, prosecutors in New Taipei City said that a person from mainland China, identified as “K,” paid the five defendants to inflict injuries on Huang that would require hospitalization.
The prosecutors said: “This case concerns a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist Party is suspected of employing tactics of transnational repression. It involves the use of criminal elements in our country to suppress dissent through extreme violence.”
The Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council of the People’s Republic of China did not respond to a request for comment.
According to Taiwan’s Central News Agency, Huang’s scooter was apparently fitted with a GPS tracker several months before the attack in order to monitor his daily routine. Prosecutors said that on September 11, two of the defendants ran into Huang’s scooter as he was riding home, but stopped after hearing him cry out.
The comedian was diagnosed with a pelvic contusion. After the incident, the suspects allegedly offered to “help” process an insurance claim — in reality, they did so to obtain a photograph of Huang’s medical report and send it to the person known as “K.”
According to the statement, “K” refused to pay the full amount of 450,000 new Taiwan dollars (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the perpetrators because Huang’s injuries turned out to be minor.
On Wednesday, Huang posted a video recorded in December 2025. In it, he asked viewers to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.
In his rapid-fire satirical monologue, the comedian, dressed in traditional clothing, referred to “slicked-back hair” and a “full figure,” while also criticizing policies toward Hong Kong, measures related to COVID-19 and the state of the property market. After ending his remark with an expletive, the crowd began chanting Xi’s name, then burst into applause.
In May, two people were prosecuted for scattering excrement and pouring paint at a club in Taipei — several hours before Huang’s performance.
Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that the case described is certainly one of the most extreme, but threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist Party have been occurring here in Taiwan for many years.”
In October, Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council reported that at least 126 people had been affected by transnational repression by the People’s Republic of China.
The Guardian contacted China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment.
In a post published on Wednesday, Huang wrote: “If people can be subjected to such treatment merely for criticizing the Chinese Communist Party — which does not even govern Taiwan — then can we expect the current freedom of speech to be preserved if the CCP were ever to come to power in Taiwan?”
In another Facebook post, Huang said he would not cancel his upcoming performances, although he emphasized that he was “not a hero.”
“I’m writing about this because it’s funny,” he said. “If I ever stop, it will only be because I simply get tired of it.”

British drone downs attack drones with guided rockets
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:09:21 BST
03:09:21 KST

A modified version of the Malloy Aeronautics T-150 uncrewed air system has intercepted multiple one-way attack drones during an American experiment in Florida, firing laser-guided rockets from a three-pod launcher and engaging several targets in succession without landing or reloading, according to BAE Systems.
The trials ran from 21 to 25 September at Eglin Air Force Base during the United States Office of the Under Secretary for Research and Engineering’s Mission Capabilities Joint Readiness Experimentation exercise. BAE Systems conducted them alongside SURVICE Engineering, its Maryland-based partner, using BAE’s own APKWS laser-guided rockets.
Thomas Lancashire, Head of UAS Business Development at BAE Systems’ FalconWorks, said: “Our customers are facing drone threats right now, so we’ve worked at pace with our partners to move from concept to a proven system, which can engage multiple targets in a single mission.
“Military technology is evolving faster than ever and it’s vital that effective capabilities reach those who protect us as quickly as possible. In today’s environment, the speed at which we deliver equipment can be just as important as the system itself.”
Gregory Thompson, President of SURVICE, said: “Supporting the warfighter has been at the core of SURVICE’s mission since its founding over 45 years ago. Bringing the TRV-150 to the US warfighter and now adding APKWS as a proven, precise, and cost-effective capability to our TRV-150 UAS platform is exactly the type of innovation SURVICE was designed to deliver.”
The aircraft is a heavy-lift electric multirotor built by Malloy Aeronautics at Maidenhead in Berkshire, a company BAE Systems took a stake in during 2019 and acquired outright in 2024. The version flown in Florida, designated TRV-150, was adapted to United States Army requirements by SURVICE Engineering, and the APKWS modification kit was developed and integrated by BAE Systems FalconWorks.
APKWS is a laser guidance kit that converts the seventy millimetre Hydra rocket into a precision weapon, built by BAE Systems in New Hampshire. United States Navy and Air Force fighters used it against Houthi drones over the Red Sea in 2024 and 2025, at a unit cost well below that of an air-to-air missile.
BAE Systems said the September trials build on the first firing of a precision munition from an adapted T-150 in July last year, which was a single shot, and that the launcher used in Florida is a production-ready three-pod system.
The T-150 has already served with Britain’s forces in the logistics role. The Royal Navy cleared the Malloy T-150 for front line use and conducted its first drone supply run between warships, and the type carried stores between ships throughout the Prince of Wales carrier strike group’s eight-month Indo-Pacific deployment last year, which this publication covered when drones launched from the British carrier in the Pacific.
Malloy also builds the larger T-650, developed with Royal Navy and Defence Equipment and Support involvement as a heavy-lift aircraft able to carry loads including torpedoes.
BAE Systems said the team will now look to extend the T-150’s use in this role to the maritime environment. The company noted that the imagery released with the announcement comes from an earlier trial.

Pakistan and the Maldives on Wednesday agreed to enhance bilateral cooperation in trade, defense, maritime security and artificial intelligence (AI).
The agreement was reached during a summit between visiting Maldivian President Mohammed Muizzu and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in the capital Islamabad.
The two countries inked 20 Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) in a variety of fields, including defense cooperation, maritime security, information technology, cybersecurity, and AI.
The two sides also inked agreements aimed at fighting against illicit trafficking and narcotics, in addition to bolstering cooperation in agriculture, trade, fisheries, environment, education, tourism, and arts and culture and other sectors.
Muizzu arrived in Islamabad on Tuesday on a three-day state visit at Sharif's invitation .
This marks the first visit by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years, and comes as the two countries celebrate the 60th anniversary of their diplomatic relations in 1966.
Later addressing a joint stakeout with Muizzu, Sharif vowed to strengthen Pakistan’s relations with the Maldives for "all time to come."

Peace in South Asia

He said that "Jammu and Kashmir remains an internationally recognized dispute, whose just resolution must come in line with UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people."

“Pakistan’s position is loud and clear and beyond an array of doubt; legally binding treaties must be respected and shared water resources must never be weaponized or used as an instrument of political pressure or blackmailing,” he said.
Muizzu, for his part, expressed Maldives’ desire to deepen its close relations with Pakistan and explore new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation.
About the latest MoUs, he said they would open new avenues for cooperation among multiple sectors, but agreements are meaningful only when they produce results.
He said he was encouraged by the discussions to establish direct flights between Pakistan and the Maldives, adding that direct flights would help support tourism as well.
Muizzu also emphasized the value of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), and its tremendous tremendous potential for the region to address shared challenges through collective action.
The Maldives remains "firmly committed to playing a constructive and proactive role in revitalizing the SAARC," he said.
The last SAARC summit was held in 2014 in Nepal.
The Maldivian president was later conferred with an honorary doctorate in politics by the International Islamic University.

The attorney general of New Mexico on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime attorney, Darren Indyke, and Epstein’s longtime accountant, Richard Kahn, accusing them of having “facilitated and concealed” Epstein’s crimes, and is seeking to stop them from being paid by Epstein’s estate while the litigation plays out.
The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the district of New Mexico, names Kahn and Indyke as defendants both in their individual capacity, and in their capacity as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. The complaint also names Epstein’s estate, and the 1953 Trust, which holds the estate’s assets.
“Epstein, with the help of his associates, trafficked, isolated, and abused survivors at alluring locations” including at Epstein’s ranch in Stanley, New Mexico, known as Zorro Ranch, the complaint claims. It goes on to allege that “in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project and remaining silent about it, his associates received generous salaries, access to elite social circles, and lavish gifts, including being named beneficiaries of his multimillion-dollar estate”.
In a statement on Wednesday, an attorney for Indyke shared a statement on behalf of both Indyke and Kahn saying that they “emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General’s allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.
“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement added. “The New Mexico Attorney General’s complaint does not allege anything to the contrary.”
The statement goes on to say that “neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General’s investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit”.
Earlier this year, Kahn and Indyke told the US House committee investigating Epstein that they had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes during their employment.
Among the demands the lawsuit seeks is a court order preventing Indyke and Kahn from receiving estate payments while the case proceeds.
The complaint alleges that both men profited personally from their relationships with Epstein. It alleges that from 2011 to 2019, Indyke received more than $16m from Epstein and related entities and that Kahn received more than $10m.
In a statement on Wednesday, Raúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, said that Epstein “did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible”.
“The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico,” he said. “Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences.”
In the complaint, Torrez wrote that “through this action, the State seeks to hold these individuals accountable to the fullest extent possible and to ensure that Epstein’s assets are distributed to the survivors of his horrific crimes”.
Several survivors of Epstein’s abuse signed a letter on Wednesday in support of Torrez’s lawsuit “because it can expose what roles Indyke and Kahn played in Epstein’s operation, examine how they handled survivors’ claims, and prevent Epstein’s trusted loyalists from being rewarded for their roles in Epstein’s organization”.
“Survivors deserve accountability and answers under oath. Epstein’s chosen confidants should not get the last word – or the money,” they added.
At a news conference on Wednesday about the new filing, Epstein survivor Anouska De Georgiou thanked Torrez for “standing with survivors”.
“We have carried this burden for long enough,” she said. “It is time for those responsible to answer for their part in it.”
The announcement on Wednesday comes amid a separate ongoing dispute between New Mexico officials and the Department of Justice over files Torrez is seeking as part of the state’s investigation into Epstein’s possible crimes in the state, including at his ranch outside Santa Fe, where multiple survivors have said they were abused.
Torrez sued the Department of Justice in August, accusing the department and Todd Blanche, the attorney general, of “stonewalling” the state’s investigation, which was reopened in February. Torrez asked the court for access to unredacted Epstein-related files held by the justice department, and said in its filing his prosecutors had requested access to the records but had “faced sustained resistance” from the department.
The case is ongoing and the justice department recently filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that “decisions about law-enforcement information sharing are committed to the agency’s discretion” and that turning over unredacted files would violate victims’ privacy.
Epstein’s Zorro Ranch came under renewed scrutiny after the justice department’s release of roughly 3m files related to Epstein late last year and early this year. The Guardian reported in early February that the newly disclosed Epstein files contained thousands of references to Zorro Ranch, and numerous photos of men and young girls at the property, and that several survivors of Epstein’s abuse had also previously given testimony about abuse they say they were subjected to there.
The Guardian investigation also revealed that, unlike Epstein’s other properties in Palm Beach, in New York and on his private Caribbean island, federal authorities had apparently never searched the New Mexico ranch.
Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges, bought the property in New Mexico 1993. It was later sold by his estate in 2023.
In late February, Torrez announced that New Mexico would reopen its investigation into Epstein’s activities at the ranch, after the state’s initial investigation was put on hold in 2019 at the request of federal prosecutors in New York, who were pursuing the investigation into Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation that led to his arrest. In March, New Mexico authorities launched a search of the ranch.
Torrez has said that he wants to establish what took place at Zorro Ranch. New Mexico lawmakers also established a “truth commission” to examine activities at the ranch.

"This surge in violence in city centres, in Nice, Paris and Lyon, is catastrophic", laments Christelle Cassagne, head of ADN Tourisme, a federation that brings together France's institutional tourism bodies.
"When you book a hotel for a week, it is not to stay shut away in your room", she adds.
Tourists hesitant to go ahead with their stay
In Paris, the closure of the Louvre museum on Monday because of a student gathering at its entrance also frustrated many tourists who had come to discover the famous museum.
In this tense climate, some travellers are reconsidering their stay in the capital.
According to MKG Consulting, the first effects are already visible, with Parisian hotels reporting a slowdown in bookings for the next six weeks.
In the space of just 24 hours, between 19 and 20 October, their lead over the same period in 2025 narrowed significantly, dropping from 1 to 0.2 percentage points for stays scheduled from 20 to 29 October, and from 3.5 to 1.9 points for those from 20 to 25 October.
Fear of fresh riots weighs on tourism
According to Didier Arino, director of the consultancy Protourisme, the scale of the repercussions will depend mainly on whether the unrest continues. A single day of riots in Paris is thought to have triggered the cancellation of around 1% of bookings for the month, still a relatively limited impact.
"The further customers travel, the more sensitive they are to security risks, and the greater the consequences", he points out.
The United States, China and Germany are among the countries that have issued warnings to their nationals planning to travel to France.
These advisories could particularly weigh on arrivals of American and Asian tourists, whose spending is generally higher than that of European visitors.
"If this lasts for two weeks, it is not very serious. But if it continues for several months, it will be catastrophic", warns Laurent Abitbol, chairman of the management board of the Selectour travel agency network.

Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:53 UTC
03:00:53 KST

Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away. Now researchers say they know why.
While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this notion, finding adults outperform preschoolers on creative tasks but generally feel less confident and more anxious doing them.
Dr Mathias Benedek, the senior author of the study at the University of Graz in Austria, said: “Children are so intrinsically motivated and absorbed in play that we often mistake their engagement with greater creative ability.”
Writing in the journal Plos One, the researchers asked 92 preschool children aged four to seven and 70 adults largely in their 20s to complete three tasks.
The first involved coming up with as many creative uses for a tin as possible in three minutes; the second involved drawing anything they liked with no stated time limit; and the third involved drawing an imaginary animal within eight minutes.
The results were then rated by judges on originality, usefulness and overall creativity.
Participants were also asked to rate how much they enjoyed each task, how motivated and confident they felt, and how anxious they were doing it.
The judges deemed the work by adults to be more original, useful and creative than that of children, particularly when clear goals and time limits were set. Conversely, children reported feeling more confident, motivated and less anxious completing tasks.
“Adults outperformed children, demonstrating higher creative potential, but they had far less confidence. We need to look at what makes adults so anxious about their original ideas being rejected,” Benedek said.
He said children approached tasks with greater intrinsic motivation and enjoyed the process of play, “whereas adults place more focus on the goal or objective”, limiting their enjoyment.
As a result, children experimented more freely and treated mistakes as part of the process whereas adults, wary of judgment, often dismissed unusual ideas before trying them.
The study, conducted at the University of Graz in Austria in collaboration with UCLouvain in Belgium and Yale University, has limitations. Among them, the research is based on a snapshot comparison of just two age groups, making it hard to draw conclusions about the impact of ageing on creativity. Children are also more likely to pick extreme answers on rating scales and have obvious differences in cognition.
Nonetheless, Benedek and his colleagues suggest that the idea of creativity fading as we grow into adulthood is a misconception. “Adults don’t lose their creativity, instead they lose the confidence to use it,” Benedek said.

A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

$5,000 per violation
Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading.
They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.
State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico's school system, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez told reporters after the verdict.
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state.

The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.
In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties.
After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico.

====================================================================================================

Intelligence predicts charitable giving and voting in massive Swedish study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:47 UTC
03:00:47 KST

People with higher cognitive abilities are more likely to engage in actions that benefit society, such as donating to charity, voting in elections, and buying environmentally friendly vehicles. These findings suggest that general intelligence plays a direct role in driving cooperative, socially minded actions. The research was published in The Economic Journal.
Humans are uniquely inclined to cooperate with strangers and contribute to public goods. Evolutionary biologists and economists often categorize these actions as prosocial behaviors. Finding a rational explanation for why humans evolved into such cooperative animals has long challenged researchers across multiple disciplines.
One proposed explanation centers on human intelligence. Some theorists suggest that cognitive ability improves logical reasoning and the capacity to understand the perspectives of others. These mental skills naturally foster ethical reasoning, which can ultimately lead to a sense of altruism.
Other researchers propose that intelligent individuals often achieve higher incomes and better social standing. This wealth could lower the personal financial cost of giving away money or time. Up until now, evidence linking intelligence to prosocial behavior has mostly come from brief laboratory games or surveys where people report their own habits.
To find concrete answers, economists Mikael Elinder and Oscar Erixson analyzed a massive set of Swedish administrative records. They wanted to see if objective measures of intelligence predicted documented, real world prosocial behaviors. The researchers focused on three specific actions: charitable giving, voting, and the ownership of environmentally friendly cars.
The researchers first analyzed data from over 1.2 million Swedish men and about 3,000 Swedish women. All of these individuals took a standardized cognitive test during their military enlistment process between 1969 and 1997. This exam evaluated logical, verbal, spatial, and technical abilities on a nine point scale.
The researchers then matched these historical test scores with modern government records. They looked at tax registries from 2012 to 2015 to track charitable donations. Because Swedish charities automatically report donations to the government for tax purposes, the data minimizes biases related to a person’s financial literacy or their willingness to fill out tax forms.
To measure political participation, the researchers examined electoral rolls for the 2009 European Parliament election. By using validated voter turnout data, the team avoided the common problem of people lying about their voting habits in surveys. Finally, they consulted a national vehicle database to identify households that owned cars powered by electricity, ethanol, or natural gas.
Individuals with higher cognitive scores were much more likely to engage in all three prosocial behaviors. Men with the highest cognitive scores were more than five times as likely to donate to charity compared to men with the lowest scores. A one standard deviation increase in intelligence matched a 40 percent relative increase in the likelihood of charitable giving.
The same bump in test scores corresponded to a 31 percent increase in voting. It also matched a 14 percent increase in eco-friendly car ownership. The data from the female participants revealed very similar positive trends for voting and charity, showing that the effect was not limited to men.
When looking at specific types of intelligence, the researchers noticed that logical and verbal reasoning were the strongest predictors of prosocial action. These two traits are widely considered the best indicators of general fluid intelligence. Fluid intelligence is the ability to think abstractly and solve novel problems.
Observing a link in the general population does not prove that intelligence directly causes prosocial behavior. People with high cognitive scores often grow up in wealthy families or specific neighborhoods that might actively encourage civic duties. To account for these shared background variables, Elinder and Erixson conducted a second analysis using a large sample of 5,786 twin pairs.
Because twins typically share the same upbringing, home environment, and a large portion of their genetics, comparing siblings helps account for many confounding factors and better isolate the effect of intelligence. The researchers looked at twin pairs where one sibling scored higher on the enlistment cognitive test than the other. They also controlled for general personality traits evaluated during the military interviews, such as emotional stability and sociality.
The researchers found that the smarter twin was consistently more likely to vote and donate to charity. The associations decreased in size by about half compared to the massive population sample. A one standard deviation increase in cognitive ability among twins matched a 26 percent increase in charitable giving and a 13 percent increase in voting.
The link to eco-friendly car ownership also dropped to a 13 percent increase. This twin based approach indicates that unobserved family factors account for some of the population wide trend. However, those family factors do not entirely explain the connection between cognitive ability and prosocial habits.
Elinder and Erixson then ran a third analysis to test specific lifestyle variables that might bridge the gap between intelligence and behavior. A person’s intelligence influences their life trajectory, which could in turn dictate their civic engagement. The researchers factored in differences in education, total income, marriage status, the presence of children, and the municipality of residence.
Education explained a noticeable portion of the link between cognitive scores and civic habits. This aligns with the idea that schools help transmit prosocial values or develop a person’s ethical awareness. Individuals who spend more years in the educational system often learn to prioritize community well being.
Income did not act as a major mediator. Smarter individuals were not simply donating or buying eco-friendly cars just because they had more money to spare. When accounting for all these lifestyle variables, the direct mathematical link between intelligence and owning an eco-friendly car was not statistically significant.
However, the direct connection to voting and charitable giving held firm even after adjusting for education and income. The researchers interpreted this as evidence of a profound, direct tie between intelligence and certain types of cooperation. General intelligence appears to influence these behaviors independently of a person’s life circumstances.
Finally, the researchers looked at survey responses from a separate sample of about 600 men. These men had previously reported their own feelings of altruism on a numerical scale, along with their patience and risk preferences. The researchers matched these survey answers to the men’s military enlistment cognitive scores.
Individuals with higher cognitive abilities expressed a higher degree of personal altruism, with a one standard deviation increase in cognitive ability associated with a 0.16 standard deviation increase in self-reported altruism. This self reported data is in line with the behavioral records found in the national registries. While the survey results cannot firmly distinguish between different mechanisms, they are consistent with the theory that cognitive ability influences prosocial behavior through ethical reasoning and altruism.
While the twin analysis helps control for many background factors, the findings do not guarantee a strict cause and effect relationship in every scenario. The study relies heavily on data from Swedish men born between 1951 and 1979. The exact percentages might vary across different cultures, age groups, or time periods.
Additionally, the research defines prosocial behavior through three specific financial and political actions. People with lower cognitive scores might be equally cooperative in ways that do not show up in tax or vehicle registries, such as volunteering or helping neighbors physically. Future research will need to explore how other cognitive functions, like empathy and the ability to read emotions, interact with general intelligence to shape human cooperation.
The study, “An inquiry into the relationship between intelligence and prosocial behaviour: Evidence from Swedish population registers,” was authored by Mikael Elinder and Oscar Erixson.

GM Wants Your Car to Do Your Chores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Americans spent about 95 billion hours behind the wheel last year, traveling something like 2.76 trillion miles. On Wednesday, General Motors executives are outlining the future of automotive at the company’s annual GM Forward event in New York City, and they say their goal isn’t to reduce that number. After all, it’s a car company.
But GM does want to make car time better. Or, as Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson put it in an interview with WIRED, “make it more productive, make it more relaxing, make it more engaging. We’d like to make your vehicle a more central, more useful part of your life than it has been historically.” Your future car is sort of a personal assistant, and sort of a spouse, and sort of a tool, and sort of a best friend.
It’s a tall order. But in a raft of announcements this week, GM hopes to demonstrate that, armed with AI-enabled capabilities, the automaker is inching closer to that future.
GM says it will roll out a new in-car AI assistant, called OnStar AI, starting with 2027 Cadillac Lyriqs. (The name borrows from the 30-year-old roadside assistance and security service, which has 12 million subscribers.) Paired with a new app, the system will start by letting drivers, for example, turn on their air conditioning with a voice command without navigating through a menu. Eventually, though, it might coordinate kid pickups and drop-offs depending on which spouse’s car is closer, Anderson says.
GM also says it will use AI to speed up new-vehicle development, eventually cutting its four- to five-year development time in half—the speed at which Chinese carmakers create new vehicles today.
The automaker plans to expand its “eyes-off” highway driving technology to its most popular cars, inching closer to its years-old promise of making a personal self-driving car. It previously said the system was coming to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. Today, the company’s Super Cruise feature lets drivers take their hands off their steering wheels on hundreds of thousands of miles of pre-mapped highways. Reaching true autonomy will take time, but GM isn’t ready to talk about that publicly. “This industry is rife with promises that were not fulfilled. I am not keen on making them,” Anderson says.
But GM is taking a different approach from, say, Tesla. The electric carmaker sells a driver-assistance feature called “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” that can navigate many highways and local roads but requires drivers to stay alert and ready to take over at any moment. That kind of system “presents the illusion of autonomy without its benefits,” Anderson says, who for a time led Tesla’s Autopilot program. If drivers can’t do other things while their car is doing most of the driving, it’s less useful and “comes with the direct expense of the safety of your vehicle and the people around you,” he says. “That would not be a responsible way to operate.”
GM’s method, by contrast, is to slowly expand “eyes-off” capabilities to more sorts of roads, letting drivers text or eat or watch YouTube first on some highways, and then on more highways, and then on local roads, and then maybe everywhere.
That’s when the automaker's vision gets bigger and blurrier. The cabin, the company says in a blog post, can become a space to “relax, work, and unwind. … In time, this will pave the way for a future where your car can take on everyday errands,” the company says. The personal self-driving car will pick up groceries, drop off children, and then maybe even find a parking spot at the end.
Urban planners and infrastructure experts have worried about this vision. If you lower the price of a car trip, in money and time spent driving, won’t everyone send their cars out for every task? Won’t the roads be crowded with pods full of people sleeping, emailing, and YouTubing while their vehicles slowly pilot them onward—or worse, cars with no one in them? Won’t cities become sprawlier?
Anderson says yes. If you have cheap, personal driving robots, “you will very likely incur more of those robots on the roads. And so there's a lot of societal and infrastructural considerations to make here,” he says. But he argues we have time, and that cities take time to sprawl. “I wouldn't call this an imminent thing, but it certainly is something we should be thinking about.”

Supercharged fire seasons now threaten half Australia's homes: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Supercharged fire seasons cost Australia $6b annually as El Niño summer looms
In short:
New modelling reveals bushfires will cost Australia $6 billion a year, with a single major event costing almost $30 billion.
Fire seasons are now 21 per cent longer, with 5.6 million households exposed to bushfire risk.
What's next?
Large parts of Australia are bracing for a hotter and drier summer due to El Niño.
As Australians prepare for a summer influenced by what is likely to become the strongest El Niño on record, a new report reveals billions of dollars are being spent tackling bushfire seasons supercharged by climate change.
The modelling, commissioned by Emergency Leaders for Climate Action (ELCA), found the country's fire seasons have lengthened by 21 per cent since 1979 due to warming global temperatures.
The longer seasons will cost the Australian economy $6 billion each year over the next 30 years, with a majority being spent on harm to health and wellbeing, ahead of damaged businesses and lost homes.
ELCA's Greg Mullins, a former Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner, said the high costs come as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, squeezes fire seasons closer together.
"The fire seasons are longer, they're overlapping between states and we're getting catastrophic fire weather," he said.
"Previous studies only looked at insured costs, which were far less, but costs across the economy are huge; in 30 years that's $180 billion."
Black Summer highlights cost of extreme fires
The ELCA report found half of Australian households are exposed to some bushfire risk, at 5.6 million, while major events, such as the Black Summer fires, cost almost $30 billion. And between 2003 and 2020 more than a million Australians had lived in a home within one kilometre of an active fire front.
The 2019/20 bushfires tore through about 45 per cent of the Snowy Valleys Council (SVC) local government area (LGA), killing one person and destroying almost 200 homes.
There were almost 9,000 livestock fatalities within the LGA and 400,000 hectares of land burnt.
The local council spent more than $50 million on direct recovery, which included road repairs and managing damaged and fallen trees.
SVC's manager of technical services, Glen McGrath, said the region was still recovering from the event more than six years later.
"You look at the softwood industry, they had a very large impact and it takes 20-plus years for softwood or pine tree to grow and be harvested and processed through the local industry processes, so they won't be coming back online until 2040 or thereabouts," he said.
"There's still a number of houses that weren't rebuilt after the fire, so there's widespread impacts and recovery efforts still."
Research has found the Black Summer bushfires cost Australia's tourism industry almost $3b, while the Insurance Council has found the event accounts for about $2b of the $2.58b in bushfire claims since 2019.
Preparation key ahead of high-risk summers
While no two events are the same, El Niño often brings hotter and drier conditions to southern and eastern parts of Australia.
Despite 2026 shaping up to become Australia's wettest El Niño year on record, drier than average conditions are starting to persist across parts of the country's east.
"In the last three months since El Niño has been active, we've seen drier-than-average conditions along much of the eastern seaboard," senior climatologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Felicity Gamble said.
"Extending from central Queensland through to south-east Queensland, down the New South Wales eastern seaboard and across southern Victoria and Tasmania."
There are concerns that unusually hot temperatures, combined with an increase in baseline warming due to climate change, could increase the risk of "flash droughts" this summer.
"When we get heatwaves, vegetation gives up its moisture very quickly … so things can very quickly turn into drought-like conditions and that drives fires," Mr Mullins said.
"All you need then is wind and you can have catastrophic fires."
Given the typical "lag effect" seen during an El Niño, there is speculation next year could become the hottest on record globally, leading to a particularly bad fire season in 2027/28.
But the ELCA report also found that better protecting infrastructure and homes could avoid $600m in bushfire losses and protect more than 5,600 jobs each year.
"The federal government has a Disaster Ready Fund, it's invested hundreds of millions over the last few years, which is great, but it needs to be targeted to help households," Mr Mullins said.
"For example, bringing their homes up to bushfire standards so that they'll withstand fire, making sure that communities still have the electricity on and have communications after a fire."
