Politicians urged to report threats and vary daily habits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Violent threats, intimidation and harassment 'new reality' of Australian politics
In short:
Politicians have revealed harrowing experiences of threats and harassment, including intimidation targeting their children.
The alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines has fuelled concerns about how to keep parliamentarians safe while remaining accessible to the public.
What's next?
The Australian Federal Police has urged MPs to report threats more and advised them to vary their daily routines as a safety precaution.
When a Sydney woman faced court accused of sending death threats to multiple Australian politicians, some of her alleged targets had no idea they were on the list.
They only became aware through media reports on the case, a scenario described by one of the MPs as "surreal".
It was just one example of the increasingly routine nature of threats against elected representatives from across the political spectrum, with police now laying charges almost weekly.
In the wake of the alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines, for which the motive remains unknown, parliamentarians have detailed harrowing accounts of rape threats, intimidation, stalking and harassment.
One senior Labor MP told the ABC the "worst" threat they had received was from a man who sent an "itemised list" of times and places where he had seen the politician's children in public.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has revealed a man previously made a U-Turn and tried to drive at him, while Labor MP Jerome Laxale has told The Guardian he once received a bomb threat.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said someone slipped a note under the door of her home, telling her they hoped her children "die of painful cancers".
Ms Plibersek also said she could not "count" the number of death and rape threats she has received over the years.
Politicians told to vary daily routines
On Wednesday, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) offered safety briefings to parliamentarians who have expressed their horror, but not their surprise, at the alleged attack on Ms Haines.
MPs were encouraged to report more of the threats they received and urged to share their diaries with the AFP to help police keep track of scheduled public events.
They were also advised to frequently change their daily habits, such as the route they took to work or other common destinations.
Parliamentarians have previously been told not to advertise public appearances in advance, and in the briefing were advised to maintain situational awareness of their surroundings, particularly when around their electorate offices.
Police did not advise of any specific or immediate threats but reiterated the importance of vigilance at all times.
Several MPs said they felt the meetings offered an opportunity for them to voice their concerns, which the AFP agreed to take on board.
But others were underwhelmed and told the ABC they did not get the answers they were seeking about baseline security for their homes and electorate offices.
Chalmers says Australia not 'immune' to political violence
The AFP charged 41 people with offences relating to threats against parliamentarians in the past year, while reports of harassing, nuisance, offensive and threatening behaviour have quadrupled since 2020.
In August, a 47-year-old Perth man faced court accused of threatening One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, including in one Facebook post in which he said he would "hunt her down and kill her".
A 19-year-old Western Australian man in March admitted to threatening to kill Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns, though told the court he "didn't mean for it to be a threat".
The man's lawyer told the court her client had made an "error in judgement", adding he had been "reading a lot of political stuff online".
Records show alleged perpetrators often later argued they did not intend to follow through with their threats.
But that excuse was recently rejected by a Queensland magistrate hearing a case in September about a man who left voicemails with violent threats against Mr Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
"That's not relevant to the threat … the people on the receiving end have got no idea what your intentions are," Magistrate Pamela Dowse told the man.
Mr Chalmers told the ABC what had happened to Ms Haines was "shocking, but unfortunately not surprising".
"Helen is the closest thing to a perfect temperament in an imperfect workplace, and it shows even the parliament's most rational person is not safe from random acts of irrational violence," he said.
Mr Chalmers said, more broadly, Australia was not "immune" from the political violence that could be seen around the world.
"Random acts of irrational violence are just as possible in the centre of Paris as the main drag of Wangaratta," he said.
Australia faces 'new reality' amid surge in threats
Labor MP Josh Burns was one of 15 high-profile figures allegedly sent death threats by a 36-year-old woman who in August fronted a Sydney court facing 62 charges, including stalking and intimidation.
He only learned of the incident when the case reached court and said it stood in contrast to the majority of his interactions in the community, which were "overwhelmingly really kind".
Senator Hanson, independent MP Allegra Spender, Labor MP Andrew Charlton and NSW Labor MP Jihad Dib were also allegedly threatened by the accused over a five-year period.
Mr Burns said managing abusive online comments was the "worst bit" of daily life as an MP and he praised how the AFP had responded to serious threats.
"But I do think there is, especially for women online and for what's happened this week, there is a new reality that we have to meet," he said.
"We need to ensure that politics and people who put their hands up for public office can do so safely and good people who have something to contribute to our country are not deterred."
Calls to lift support at state level
In Victoria, Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell has long been a target of abuse and said state politicians were offered considerably less support than federal ones.
"I spent the first few years of my political career reporting voicemails, emails, comments, graffiti on the office and it goes nowhere," she said.
Ms Purcell said having Mr Burns as a partner had given her a "unique" insight into how the AFP tackled threats, and she would like a similar "continuity model" deployed at a state level.
Recently, someone has been "consistently" writing antisemitic graffiti on her office, but Ms Purcell said she has been told to "wipe it off with metho" as it did not meet the threshold of "property damage".
"But it's not the property damage that was my concern, it was the views of the person participating in the behaviour," she said.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced on Wednesday there would be additional resources and arrangements in place for the upcoming state election.
'Don't attack character' in political debate
Speaking at the National Press Club on Tuesday, ACT Senator David Pocock said whatever measures were put in place to protect politicians must be balanced against remaining accessible to voters.
"We have to ensure that we have a democracy where your local politician lives in the community, goes to the local coffee shop, does the groceries," he said.
"That's something Australians love about Australia."
Senator Pocock said the tenor of online discussion was something "we have to grapple with as a society".
"People are saying things online that they would not say to your face," he said.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he had been targeted online and subsequently identified by the AFP for "additional security".
"That's just the nature of our politics at the moment," he said.
Mr Hastie said the Westminster system of government was "adversarial", but there had to be a "line" where opponents were not demonised.
"We don't attack their character, their standing, so that someone might feel justified in using violence against them," he said.

Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:59:14 UTC
02:59:14 KST

The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.
Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.
It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.
Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.
“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.
Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.
“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.
She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.
“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.
“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.
“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”
Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.
“The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.
After the attack, Nathaniel wrote: “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”
He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.
Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.
“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”
The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.
Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.
“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.
On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.
Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.
“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”

The 7 Key Governor Races to Watch in the Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:58:30 UTC
02:58:30 KST

As Election Day looms, much of the national focus is on whether Democrats will win control of Congress. But in several states, the race for governor is among the tightest, and most consequential, races on the ballot.
The party in control of the White House typically fares poorly in midterm elections. While that usually translates most clearly into losing congressional seats, true “wave” elections often lead to similar shifts in state governments as well.
Multiple states could see the party in the governor’s seat flip. Voters in Ohio, Alaska, and Texas might end up electing their first Democratic governors in decades. In Oregon, the reverse could pan out, with a Republican in contention to upend a Democrat’s hold on the office for the first time since 1982.
Here are seven races for governor to watch on Election Day.
Ohio
Ohio's governor's race was thrust into the national spotlight this week after Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign released an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democrat opponent Amy Acton. Acton’s mother lost custody of Acton and her brother after their stepfather was arrested and indicted on a charge of raping Acton when she was a child.
The ad immediately drew widespread outrage, the latest twist in a race that Republicans had thought they were well positioned to win after Trump won the state by 11 points in 2024. Many Republicans had been expected to vie to replace Gov. Mike DeWine, who couldn’t run again because of term limits. But Trump’s endorsement of Ramaswamy essentially cleared the field for him.
Now Ramaswamy is in a very tight race against Acton, who previously led the Ohio Department of Health during the Covid-19 pandemic. While the Cook Political Report previously marked the Ohio gubernatorial race as “Lean Republican,” it later shifted its rating slightly in favor of Democrats, to “Toss Up.”
Many polls show Acton with a narrow lead, but a few suggest that Ramaswamy has a razor-thin lead.
If Acton ultimately wins, it would be the first time in 20 years that Ohio voters had elected a Democrat as governor.
Alaska
The Cook Political Report recently changed its rating for the race in Alaska from a “Toss Up” to “Lean Democrat.” Alaska’s current governor, Republican Mike Dunleavy, is prohibited from running again because of term limits. The open race to replace him includes one Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson, a business owner who has received the backing of President Trump; Dave Bronson, the previous mayor of Anchorage; and Treg Taylor, a former state attorney general.
Kreiss-Tomkins, who was previously a state legislator, finished the state’s open primary race in August in the top spot, with another Democratic candidate, Tom Begich, in second place. In Alaska, the top four candidates in the open primary move on to the general election. But Begich later announced that he was dropping out of the race and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, allowing Taylor to land a spot in the general election ballot.
“The data we’ve seen makes clear that the strongest path to winning in November is not two Democratic candidates competing for the same donors and resources—it’s bringing those people together behind one ticket,” Begich said in a video announcing the suspension of his campaign in August.
Many recent polls show Kreiss-Tomkins leading his three opponents. This month, Trump expressed frustration with all the Republicans still in the race, noting on Truth Social that he had urged Bronson to drop out.
“All Bronson and Taylor will do is take away Votes from the Candidate that has, by far, the best chance of winning,” Trump said in his post. “Now is the time for all Republicans to unite behind Bernadette to ensure she has a tremendous Victory in November!”
Texas
The last time Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ran for re-election in 2022, he won by double digits. He now may be facing his most competitive re-election fight yet; some polls show him holding a slim lead over Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, while others show Hinojosa ahead by a small margin.
“This is an unusual situation in Texas politics,” Joshua Blank, the research director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, previously told TIME. “It’s rather uncommon to see any Democratic candidate leading in anything other than a single outlying poll leading up to the election.”
If Hinojosa were to win, it would be the first time voters chose to put a Democrat in the state’s governor’s mansion in more than three decades. The tightness of the race mirrors that of the state’s Senate race, where Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are locked in an expensive fight.
Still, the Cook Political Report suggests that the odds are in Abbott’s favor, rating the race as “Lean Republican.”
Oregon
Amid talk of a national blue wave, the race for governor in Oregon may prove to be a bright spot for Republicans. Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat, is trying to fend off a challenge by Republican Christine Drazan, a state senator. Some polls show Kotek ahead by a narrow margin, while others show Drazan in the lead by a similarly small measure. The Cook Political Report previously rated the race as “Likely Democrat,” but has since shifted it slightly in Republicans’ favor, to “Lean Democrat.”
The Cook Political Report says the battle “is one of the rare races moving in Republicans’ direction.” If Drazan were to defeat Kotek, it would mark the first time since 1982 that Oregonians have elected a Republican to the governorship.
Georgia
Georgia is shaping up to be one of the tightest gubernatorial races in the country. It’s one of four that the Cook Political Report has marked as a “Toss Up.” Republican Gov. Brian Kemp couldn’t run for re-election because of term limits, leaving the field open for another member of his party, billionaire Rick Jackson, and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the previous mayor of Atlanta. Polls suggest the race is essentially tied, with some indicating Jackson has a razor-thin lead.
A win by Bottoms would mark a significant shift in the southern state’s politics. While both of Georgia’s current Senators are Democrats, it has been led by a Republican governor since 2003. It would also mean the breaking of a national barrier: Georgia would be the first state in the country to have elected a Black woman as governor.
Nevada
A perennial swing state, Republicans are vying to hold on to its leadership of Nevada’s government. Gov. Joe Lombardo is fending off a challenge from Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford. Polls are split over who’s in the lead—some showing Lombardo while others showing Ford, both by slim margins. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a “Toss Up.”.
Wisconsin
The race to lead this swing state became a wide open free-for-all last year, when Democratic Gov. Tony Evers announced he wasn't running for another term. The race was on the verge of becoming a marquee one for democratic socialists, with progressive Francesca Hong leading in the polls ahead of the Democratic primary, before she ultimately lost the nomination to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a moderate.
Crowley is now vying for the job against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in a race where campaign funding has become a prominent issue, as Tiffany’s bid has been largely bankrolled by three billionaires.
While the Cook Political Report rates this a “Toss Up," multiple recent polls show Crowley with a small lead over Tiffany.

Congress pulls up SBI over data breach, seeks accountability; experts call leak 'no ordinary incident'

SBI data leak: Personal details of 3,897 customers were identified on the dark web. Congress's media and publicity department head, Pawan Khera, questioned the bank's ability to detect the breach and its response towards affected customers.
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Wednesday pulled up the State Bank of India (SBI) over the suspected exposure of 3,897 customer records on the dark web, demanding answers from the country's largest bank and accountability for those responsible. Cybersecurity law expert Pawan Duggal called the incident "no ordinary incident", warning that the exposure could have implications for India's national security.The criticism came after SBI said a preliminary analysis of around 3.75 lakh records available on the dark web had identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information. The bank said it was investigating the suspected exposure after receiving alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In).
Congress's media and publicity department head, Pawan Khera, questioned the bank's ability to detect the breach and its response towards affected customers."It is bad enough that the State Bank of India @TheOfficialSBI, the country's largest public sector bank, has suffered a data breach involving 3.75 lakh rows of data, with 3,897 records containing personally identifiable customer information -- including mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and loan-related details."
"What makes this even more alarming is that SBI did not even detect the breach itself. An external agency had to alert the bank that its customers' data had already been published on the dark web," he said on X.Khera alleged that the bank had yet to inform customers whose personal information was exposed." A bank entrusted with the financial security of millions cannot afford such a catastrophic failure of data security, breach detection and customer accountability. SBI owes its customers answers. Those responsible must be held accountable," he asserted.
Pawan Duggal, chairman of the International Commission on Cyber Security Law, said the suspected leak was particularly serious given SBI's size and the volume of sensitive information it holds."The SBI data leak is no ordinary incident. India is the world’s most populous nation. The SBI is the country’s largest bank, holding a volume of accounts unmatched by any other financial institution. A leak here involves far more than just names; it includes numerous government accounts, such as those of public sector employees, meaning a vast amount of sensitive government information is exposed. The intent behind such a leak is clear: state and non-state actors could exploit this data to negatively impact India’s sovereignty, integrity, and security... Section 79 of the IT Act mandates that intermediaries must exercise "due diligence" in the discharge of their functions. The central government has established specific rules, such as the IT Rules, 2021, and the IT Directions, 2022, that define what constitutes due diligence; it remains to be seen whether these requirements were met... It is high time for India to wake up; the country still lacks a dedicated national law on cybersecurity, and the existing Information Technology Act of 2000 does not adequately address these critical aspects..."
The suspected exposure reportedly includes customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses and residential addresses. The records also contain branch and Customer Information File (CIF) identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan and lead records and other related files.
SBI says customer balances are safe
Responding to the incident, SBI said the suspected exposure had affected a very small number of customers and had not materially affected its core business operations, financial performance or business continuity."Customer balances are completely safe, and we are taking all possible steps to protect the interest of our valued customers," the bank said in a post on X.
SBI said it had activated its cyber incident response and containment protocols and engaged an independent cybersecurity agency empanelled by CERT-In to investigate the alleged compromise.The bank said a detailed investigation was needed to establish the authenticity and completeness of the exposed data, determine the potential source and extent of the exposure, and assess the risks to customers and the bank."We reiterate that safety of our customers' financial assets, data and their trust in us remain our highest priorities," it said, adding that remedial and preventive measures were being implemented.
The suspected data exposure comes days after CERT-In issued a 'critical' advisory warning that autonomous artificial intelligence agents had accessed live systems and confidential data belonging to Indian organisations without authorisation.In its advisory, titled 'AI Agents as Attack Vectors', the agency said some AI models and agents undergoing research and evaluation had exceeded the authorised scope of their tasks and accessed live systems. The agents reportedly used credentials and connection settings exposed in application configurations, public code repositories and overly permissive cloud service roles.CERT-In also reported a compromise involving private keys linked to eight intermediate certification authority certificates belonging to India-based certification authority eMudhra Ltd. The affected certificates included six Transport Layer Security certificates and two code-signing certificates.The agency warned that the compromised keys could be used to issue fraudulent certificates, impersonate legitimate websites and potentially intercept or modify encrypted communications.

‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die | Andrew Roth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:57:48 UTC
02:57:48 KST

They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration, the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.
Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.
And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.
As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday, schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.
Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.
“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.
“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”
As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.
Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.
Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.
For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.

Ukraine seemed prepared for jet-powered drones, but has yet to find a solution. When will its anti-Geran weapon enter service?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:56:00 EEST
02:56:00 KST

Ukraine seemed prepared for jet-powered drones, but has yet to find a solution. When will its anti-Geran weapon enter service?
The command post of the Ukrainian Posipaky ("Minions") battalion of the 39th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment is a hive of activity. The soldiers are monitoring a large screen showing a map that is constantly updated with markers tracking drones crossing the front line. Their job is to coordinate interceptor-drone crews as they bring down Russian UAVs on the Zaporizhzhia front.
Suddenly, a new blip appears among the dozens already on the screen. It immediately catches the eye, racing along the front line at high speed. It is one of Russia's new jet-powered drones, which began appearing in large numbers in late summer.
Ramses, the battalion commander, orders his team to leave the blip alone. The drone is travelling at 500 km/h – too fast for conventional interceptor drones to bring down.
Within a few months, Russian drones crossing the front line had become a routine occurrence. The flow of UAVs continues unabated, day in, day out. But the tactics are different now: rather than launching large groups of Shaheds, Russia sends jet-powered drones one by one, at intervals of 20-30 minutes. Most get across the front line.
Long-range drones make their way into this sector from a Russian drone base in occupied Donetsk. They fly hundreds of kilometres along the front line towards the Dnipro Reservoir, where the terrain makes interception more difficult.
"They fly undetected across the occupied territories, climbing higher and gaining speed," Ramses said. "Only at the last moment do they appear on our screens, at an altitude of 5,000 to 8,000 m – well beyond the reach of MANPADS and other air defence systems."
Most of the drones are jet-powered Geran-4 loitering munitions derived from Iran's Shahed-136. But Russia is also using the newer Geran-5, which has a radically different design, more akin to a cruise missile.
These drones are piloted by an operator rather than left to fly unguided, making them even more lethal. Since losing access to Starlink, Russian forces have adopted mesh networks that use chains of drones to relay radio signals through the air. Each drone relays the signal to the preceding one, creating a link back to the operator and enabling real-time control.
"In August, Russia used around 2,400 jet-powered Gerans and 2,400 conventional ones in strikes across Ukraine," Ramses said. "Roughly a quarter to a third of those drones passed through our area of responsibility. The proportions are still roughly the same."
The Ukrainian Air Force reports that air defences managed to shoot down only 1,460 Russian jet-powered drones in August. Ukraine's ability to shoot down more jet-powered drones is hampered by a shortage of anti-aircraft missiles and a lack of high-speed interceptor drones.
Ukrainska Pravda explores why jet-powered Gerans are giving Ukraine's air defences such a hard time – and what it could take to stop them.
Russia is putting its faith in jet-powered Gerans
The arrival of jet-powered Gerans has created new opportunities for Russia to launch long-range strikes on Ukraine's rear areas. But scaling up production of the new drones is proving difficult because Russia relies on China for their jet engines.
The high failure rate of Chinese engines poses another challenge. Ukrainska Pravda has obtained a wreckage analysis by a specialist institution, which found that many drones were lost when their engines failed after several hours in the air. Repairing the engines in Russia has helped, but the problem has only been partially resolved.
As of early September, engines supplied by Chinese company Telefly began to be assembled from kits at Russia's drone production centre in Alabuga.
Russia has also begun producing the simplest structural components, suggesting plans to increase output and manufacture more components domestically.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, told Ukrainska Pravda that the new drones still contain Western electronics, including a US-made flight controller. China supplies other critical components, such as the engine, thermal imaging camera and secure communications systems.
"The Chinese side officially receives all the necessary information about the use of these components in Russian weapons," Vlasiuk said. "Yet the only response we get is that a jam-resistant satellite navigation antenna does not fall within the military goods category and is therefore not subject to the relevant export restrictions.
My latest proposal to our Chinese partners was to reclassify certain components as military goods. But I expect that they will reject it."
Trying to develop interceptor drones
Jet-powered drones are proving extremely difficult to intercept, making them one of Ukraine's most pressing air defence challenges alongside ballistic missiles. In response to this new threat, the first prototypes of high-speed interceptor drones are now reaching military units for testing.
Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the state-run Brave1 defence technology cluster, told Ukrainska Pravda that work on a solution had begun a year before the jet-powered Geran loitering munitions started appearing en masse.
"Back in the summer of 2025, once interceptor drones had managed to close the sky to conventional Shaheds, we started looking at where to focus our efforts next," he said. "That's when we began funding teams working on solutions to take down jet-powered drones. We're talking not just about high-speed interceptors, but also anti-aircraft missiles and turrets."
Twenty-two teams have been working on high-speed drones to counter jet-powered Gerans. Twelve have received state funding from Brave1. The projects include drones equipped with miniature turbojet engines and electric-powered models with propellers.
Another promising avenue is drones powered by electric ducted fans, which resemble turbojets in design but run on battery power.
Hrytseniuk said seven interceptor drones have been deployed in combat, where they have successfully brought down jet-powered drones.
One interceptor already in service is an unidentified turbojet-powered drone spotted in use by the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU). Video footage shows it pursuing and striking a Russian Geran-5, which travels at an average speed of 500-600 km/h.
According to Hrytseniuk, the government has ordered well over 1,000 of the new interceptors. However, production is still being ramped up.
"We will definitely catch up with Russia's drone production, but it won't happen overnight," he noted. "Look at what happened with conventional Shaheds: it took us six months to scale up interceptor production. We're doing everything we can to speed things up this time, but we're not talking days or weeks."
One obstacle to scaling up production of the new interceptors is securing a supply of miniature turbojet engines. But Brave1 is confident that the issue can be resolved.
"These engines weren't available in Ukraine before," Hrytseniuk said. "No private company was making them. In 2025, we launched a programme, set up a funding scheme, made this a separate area of work and started working with manufacturers. Now, 11 Ukrainian companies are producing turbojet engines, and six of them have started mass production. It took more than a year and a half to get here."
As of early October, the new developments had not yet noticeably strengthened Ukraine's air defences. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Air Force is still doing the lion's share of the work to counter jet-powered drones, accounting for half of all successful interceptions. With missiles in short supply, pilots are using risky tactics, approaching the drones at close range to destroy them with their aircraft's cannons.
The next most effective system is the previously unknown Bars drone, which intercepted a third of the Gerans shot down in a month. It is not yet clear, however, whether this is a new interceptor or a long-range drone called Bars that has been adapted to shoot down other drones.
Drones alone are not enough
Officials and military personnel who spoke with Ukrainska Pravda warn against pinning hopes on a silver bullet that will solve all the problems. They say only a combination of different weapons, used effectively, can counter the threat posed by jet-powered Shaheds.
Another priority in tackling jet-powered drones is the development of anti-aircraft missiles that are cheaper than long-range drones and can be produced in large quantities.
Ukraine has several projects at different stages of development. Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that Luch, a Ukrainian armaments design office, had presented two missiles at the MSPO-2026 exhibition: one for the Osa air defence system and a smaller one based on the Barrier anti-tank missile system. Another company unveiled a prototype of the Shershen multi-calibre system. President Zelenskyy also mentioned the Nika small missile, which is undergoing testing.
Ukraine is also investing in missile projects led by relatively young companies. The work began within Brave1 in 2024, and developing the first prototypes took two years. Of the ten Ukrainian teams involved, two are already preparing to put their designs into operational use.
"They are cheap and easy to manufacture. One of the requirements was that each missile should cost no more than US$20,000," Hrytseniuk said.
The scale of this ambition becomes clear when compared with the market prices of existing missiles: a single Stinger can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and an AIM-9X missile fired from an F-16 costs around US$500,000.
The idea is that using two or three of these relatively cheap missiles to bring down a Russian long-range drone would still be cost-effective. Various estimates put the cost of a conventional Geran at up to US$70,000, with the jet-powered version potentially costing tens of thousands more.
Ukraine faces a tough battle to protect its strategic infrastructure in the coming months, which Russia is seeking to destroy while it has the chance. And without sufficient weapons supplies, Ukraine's military will have to rely on homegrown technology.
Only a comprehensive approach that combines the latest interceptor drones, autonomous turrets, anti-aircraft guns, aircraft, and air defence missile systems can provide effective protection.
With missiles in short supply, Ukraine has turned to domestically made automated turrets fitted with heavy machine guns. Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara said the military already has hundreds of them in service.
It will take time to work out the best mix of systems to counter the threat.

steel spheres moving across curved glass frame leonardo garza’s sensory installation for BYREDO
rather than interpreting scent through conventional visual representations, garza approaches five fragrances as individual memories, translating their character into physical materials and spatial experiences.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
GARZA TRANSLATES BYREDO FRAGRANCES INTO SPATIAL INSTALLATION
Designed by Mexican creator Leonardo Garza for BYREDO’s official launch in Mexico, Matter / Memory is an interactive spatial installation that translates five of the brand’s signature fragrances into physical materials, tactile movement, reflection, and acoustic soundscapes. Moving away from conventional visual representations of scent, the design approaches each fragrance as a distinct memory, reinterpreting its sensory notes through raw, tactile mediums and structured spatial experiences.
movable STEEL SPHERES float ACROSS CURVED GLASS FRAGMENTS
The installation by GARZA Studio consists of five curved fragments, each containing a different material composition beneath a transparent surface. Thousands of stainless steel spheres form a movable curtain across the installation, inviting visitors to interact by shifting the spheres to gradually reveal the materials beneath. As the spheres move, their interaction generates a subtle metallic soundscape, introducing an additional sensory dimension to the experience. Through movement and interaction, Matter / Memory invites visitors to discover the installation gradually, exploring the relationship between what is concealed and what is revealed.
RAW MATERIALS AND ATMOSPHERIC FOG ENCLOSE FIVE COMPOSITIONS
Each fragment interprets a different BYREDO fragrance through material: Gypsy Water through charcoal and ash, Rose of No Man’s Land through fractured glass, Mojave Ghost through mineral dust, Bal d’Afrique through red ochre earth, and Blanche through folded white textile. A low veil of fog surrounds the installation, creating an atmospheric landscape in which light, reflection, and material continuously shift. The project reflects GARZA’s ongoing interest in creating encounters between art and design, exploring new forms of expression across objects, furniture, and spatial installations.

The Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transition | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:54:23 UTC
02:54:23 KST

This week a report from the UN Environment Programme concluded that holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece commitment of the Paris climate agreement – is no longer achievable. If the disastrous consequences of a significant overshoot are to be mitigated, it argued, governments must start delivering the short-term actions to meet long-term targets on reducing fossil fuel consumption.
Disappointingly, Andy Burnham and his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, took a different view of short-term priorities on Wednesday. Before the November Cop summit, where regaining lost momentum on climate action will be crucial, their decision to approve new drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield sent a dismal signal. The prime minister justified it as a pragmatic move “at a time when people are really struggling”. But the pragmatic arguments don’t stack up.
Going ahead with Jackdaw will have no impact on bills this winter and little in the longer run. It will deliver only a small number of jobs for a very limited period. Tax revenues from new drilling will be substantially negated by the various concessions and breaks enjoyed by the oil and gas industry. Claims that Jackdaw will enhance the UK’s national energy security are hugely overblown, given that it will satisfy a mere 2% of national demand. The country’s heavy reliance on natural gas imports will remain unaltered.
So why? Mr Burnham would doubtless have preferred not to be landed with the judgment call on either Jackdaw or the much larger Rosebank oil and gas field (on which an announcement has yet to be made). Both were already in the licensing system, having been approved by Rishi Sunak as he sought a dividing line with Labour. A successful legal challenge meant the final decision fell in the present prime minister’s lap.
On Jackdaw at least, Mr Burnham appears to have judged that political expediency, particularly in Scotland, was best served by waving it through. A failure by governments to invest gamechanging sums in the green transition has made the politics of net zero more fraught. The recent Tory byelection victory in Aberdeen South followed a campaign focused on reviving oil and gas production in the North Sea. One of the first acts of Scottish Labour’s new leader, Michael Marra, has been to back both the Rosebank and Jackdaw developments.
Mr Burnham inherited this complicated set of circumstances. But rather than rubber-stamping a regressive rearguard action by the fossil fuel industry, he should be using his rhetorical gifts to make the pragmatic case for Britain’s green energy future. As research by the E3G thinktank has laid out, the dubious benefits of drilling for disappearing oil and gas reserves are dwarfed by the potential economic impact of insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps. The government’s warm homes plan, it estimated, would significantly reduce household energy bills and generate 50,000 new jobs. Yet Ms Fahnbulleh is reportedly under pressure to find cuts so spending can be diverted to defence.
The best way to achieve energy security, back British workers and bring down bills – the three imperatives identified by Mr Burnham in his statement on Wednesday – is to invest ambitiously in the country’s climate goals. Proceeding with Jackdaw does not, in itself, signify a prime ministerial reluctance to do that. But this decision suggests there are grounds for concern about which way the wind is blowing in Downing Street.

US Treasury targets Iran's shadow fleet with sweeping new sanctions on a variety of Greek legal and shipping front firms

- i24NEWS

- US Treasury targets Iran's shadow fleet with sweeping new sanctions
US Treasury targets Iran's shadow fleet with sweeping new sanctions
US Treasury Department sanctions multiple firms involved in supporting Iran's shadow fleet network
The US Treasury Department on Wednesday announced a raft of sanctions against firms involved in supporting Iran's shadow fleet network, which it uses to circumvent existing sanctions.
The major sanctions are focused on Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis, which the Department accuses of supporting "illicit Iranian shipping activity for years, indirectly aiding Tehran’s ability to generate revenue to fund its military, weapons, and nuclear programs."
In particular, the sanctions list several phony Greek shipping companies that are used to disguise Iranian assets.
The sanctions also targeted several members of the Karnakis-Kosmas and Ortega-Jones families, who are listed as employees and directors of the firm.
A Syrian cement company was also listed as a front for the IRGC's Quds Force.
The US also sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents that it says directly aid Iranian shadow fleet operations.
Both of these shipping agents are accused of supplying the shadow fleet with food and fuel during operations.
“Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Iran’s facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you’re doing, and we will continue to take action.”

The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:54:16 UTC
02:54:16 KST

It is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. He raked in $2.2bn in 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. Yet this week’s poll finding that 34% of Republicans (and 66% of all American voters) think that he is using his position to make himself rich merits attention. Separately, voters in a Fox News poll last week put government corruption at the top of their list of concerns – just ahead of inflation and high prices.
Mr Trump pledged that people would be better off if they voted for him. Billionaires are; not the rest. He promised to lower grocery costs (they have risen) and to cut the price of gasoline to below $2 a gallon. It’s more than double that, thanks to his illegal war on Iran. Tariffs haven’t helped. Incumbents struggle when life feels unaffordable, and polling for the Guardian has shown the disenchantment of key voting groups. The gulf between his own prosperity and the lives of his base now looks less like an inspiration and more like an insult. Cash offers seem unlikely to help much.
The president’s popularity rating sank to a record low of 36% in a poll on Wednesday. Mr Trump, of course, is not on the ballot. But he is touring red states as he seeks to shore up the vote in places where the idea of a Democratic victory looked laughable two years ago. Democrats are rightly cautious about their midterms prospects, having been burned too many times. But less than a fortnight from 3 November, with many votes already cast, polls suggest that they will take the House and could well claim the Senate too.
The party is still unpopular, though impressive candidates are performing far better than anyone expected in surprising places – notably Texas and Kansas. But they are now more trusted on economic issues. Independents are turning away from Mr Trump and his party, and many Republicans seem unenthused, for multiple reasons. The “Maga-sympathetic” pollster Rich Baris argues that “Donald Trump did this to himself”. His base believed Mr Trump was their champion. Now they suspect that he is “just another politician”.
There is merited concern about how the president has already used his power to tilt the midterms, and more about what he may do if his party fares as badly as forecast. Republicans still hope to reclaim ground through traditional if unsavoury means, massively outspending Democrats.
Yet while some polls are tightening, culture war attacks and salacious lies about opponents such as James Talarico in Texas do not seem, at least so far, to be as powerful as Republicans hoped. That’s not just because Democratic candidates are repositioning themselves. The toxic messaging of the presidential race – that Kamala Harris “is for they/them, President Trump is for you” – doesn’t land if voters believe that he’s actually for himself and his friends.
Republicans now point to France’s unrest and claim that a Democrat-dominated Congress would bring chaos and destruction to America. Their fearmongering has often motivated core voters. But while Democrats stick to the economic attack, Republicans are trying to change the subject instead of offering answers. Mr Trump’s bread-and-circuses politics is floundering, cage fights on the South Lawn of the White House notwithstanding, as voters ask what happened to the bread.

Witkoff's visit to St. Petersburg follows his Oct. 20 meeting with Zelensky and European allies in Oslo to discuss peace proposals to pass along to the Kremlin. Witkoff described both the Oslo and St. Petersburg meetings as "constructive," but said "there is still important work left to do."
Zelensky confirmed that Kyiv received briefings of the Kremlin's readiness to meet.

'Everything was in ruins' — At least 2 killed, 2 injured in Russian drone attack on Kyiv
A Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least two people and injured two others on the morning of Oct. 21, local authorities said.
An air raid alert sounded in Kyiv at around 5:20 a.m. local time as drones approached the capital, which has faced an unrelenting barrage of Russian drone attacks this fall.
In the Sviatoshynskyi District, a Russian drone struck a 24-story residential building, sparking a fire on the 20th floor. At least two people were killed, and two others were hospitalized with injuries, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Nataliia, a 63-year-old resident who requested anonymity beyond her first name for security reasons, said she heard drones flying over her neighborhood throughout the night until she heard an "incredibly powerful explosion."
The whole building shook, Nataliia recalled. She only realized that her building had been hit when she checked the group chat with her neighbors, in which she was instructed to go outside because part of it had caught on fire.
"When I finally got outside, I saw the whole horror of it — everything was in ruins," Nataliia said.
In the Desnianskyi District, drone debris fell on a car, while in the Solomianskyi District, debris landed in an open area, Klitschko said.

Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Kaliningrad Oblast during training exercises, Moscow says
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed during a scheduled training flight in Kaliningrad Oblast, a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea bordering Poland and Lithuania, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21.
Moscow has not elaborated on the reason for the plane crash. The Russian Defense Ministry said the crew ejected and evacuated by a ground search-and-rescue team, without disclosing whether they were injured.
The jet crashed near the town of Chernyakhovsk, about 90 kilometers (about 56 miles) east of Kaliningrad, according to the pro-Kremlin Mash Telegram channel. It said that both pilots were injured and were taken to a military hospital.
The Su-30 is a two-seat, multirole fighter for air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Moscow said that the jet was not carrying any weapons at the time of the crash.

Lockheed Martin delegation meets Ukraine's defense chiefs in Kyiv amid severe Patriot shortage
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi met with a delegation from the U.S. defense company Lockheed Martin, the Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21, as Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles.
The meeting came as Russia intensifies its ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and elsewhere across Ukraine, posing an immense challenge to Ukrainian air defenses. Lockheed Martin manufactures PAC-3 interceptors used by the Patriot air-defense system, which can engage Russian ballistic missiles, and has supported the U.S. move to grant Ukraine a Patriot production license.
The Defense Ministry said in its statement that Khmara and Drapatyi discussed "the importance of stable arms deliveries and further cooperation" with the Lockheed Martin delegation, led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The meeting also included discussions to scale up the supply of PAC-3 interceptors in response to the Russian ballistic missile threat, according to the Defense Ministry.

Denmark guarantees $113 million loan for Ukrainian defense company Fire Point
Denmark will guarantee a 750 million Danish kroner ($113 million) loan to the Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, the Danish government announced on Oct. 21.
The guarantee highlights Denmark's role in helping Ukraine expand defense production beyond its borders as Russian attacks threaten domestic manufacturing and supply chains.
The loan is backed by the Danish state as Russia's war against Ukraine prevents the company from borrowing on ordinary terms in Denmark. The funding will be channeled through Denmark’s Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
"Denmark strongly supports the Ukrainians' fight for freedom," Business and Industry Minister Martin Lidegaard said. He added that hosting a Ukrainian defense company in Denmark would bring "knowledge and production, as well as partnerships" that could strengthen Ukraine, Denmark’s defense industry and a more independent Europe.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said locating Ukrainian defense production outside Ukraine would make it more resilient to Russian attacks.

Unknown Publisher

EU leaders will discuss funding for Ukraine for 2027 and the European Union’s next budget on November 26–27
Kyiv • UNN
At the November 26–27 summit, EU leaders will discuss funding for Ukraine for 2027. The deficit is estimated at €70 billion.
At the special summit to be held on November 26–27, European leaders will try to agree on a mechanism to finance Ukraine’s needs for 2027 amounting to €70 billion, which currently has no funding sources secured. This was reported by an EU representative involved in preparations for the event. The summit will also discuss the European Union’s next long-term budget, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The article states that Ukraine, which has been resisting Russia’s invasion since 2022, needs certainty about how to cover its funding shortfall for the coming year.
Meanwhile, EU governments must agree on the bloc’s budget for 2028–2034 by the end of the current year — before election campaigns unfolding next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland, and Slovakia politicize the issue.
Ukraine’s financing for 2026 has already been secured: around €31 billion from the EU is expected to be disbursed this year — as soon as Kyiv adopts the agreed reforms. These funds are part of the total €45 billion earmarked by the EU for Ukraine for the current year (€14 billion of which has already been disbursed).
For 2027, the EU has also earmarked €45 billion ($50 billion) for Ukraine; however, Ukraine’s needs will be significantly higher as the war with Russia drags on. EU countries had expected non-EU countries — including Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan, and the United Kingdom — to provide an additional €45 billion, distributed across 2026 and 2027.
However, according to EU officials, not all of these funds have been secured. As Ukraine’s funding shortfall for 2027 is currently estimated at approximately €70 billion (even taking the EU’s planned contribution into account), EU countries will have to agree on a new form of financing — possibly another loan.

Russia’s Supreme Court allows father to keep daughter taken to Russia without permission, citing France’s ‘unfriendly’ status and NATO membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:50:06 UTC
02:50:06 KST

Russia’s Supreme Court allows father to keep daughter taken to Russia without permission, citing France’s ‘unfriendly’ status and NATO membership
Russia’s Supreme Court has ruled that a Russian man does not have to return his daughter to her mother in France, even though he took the child to Russia without permission, Kommersant reported.
The case concerns Veronika Tishkova, a Ukrainian citizen who married Russian citizen Alexey Yermakov in 2018. They lived in Kyiv, where their daughter was born. The couple divorced in 2021, and the child stayed with her mother. Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, Tishkova moved to France with her 3-year-old daughter, while Yermakov remained in Ukraine.
In June 2023, he asked a Kyiv court to order his former wife to bring their daughter to Ukraine every six weeks. The court denied his request.
Yermakov also took legal action against his former wife in France. In April 2024, he consented to the child’s living permanently in France. The following March, he asked for permission to take his daughter on vacation to Turkey and Slovakia, promising the court he would return her in two weeks. He did not. It soon emerged that he had taken the child to Russia.
In July 2025, Tishkova asked a court in Novosibirsk to order her daughter’s return. During the proceedings, the girl was granted Russian citizenship at her father’s request. The court nevertheless sided with Tishkova and ordered Yermakov to return the child to France under the Hague Convention. Higher courts rejected Yermakov’s appeals.
He then appealed to Russia’s Supreme Court, which ruled in his favor in July 2026. The court found that the girl had adjusted to life in Russia and that moving to France could therefore adversely affect her. It cited an article of the Hague Convention that allows courts to refuse to return a child “if there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm.” The court also said the girl has Russian citizenship and that France is an “unfriendly” country and a member of NATO and the European Union.
Tishkova challenged the ruling, which is now under review by the Supreme Court’s Presidium. Her lawyer, Dmitry Litvinsky, said the Supreme Court had “put its own political interpretation of the situation above the applicable law.” Andrey Targashov, Yermakov’s lawyer, said the court’s position was “in line with international practice.”

Russia hits gas production facility in Kharkiv Oblast, critical infrastructure in Dnipro, leaving 30,000 consumers without power

Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure in the regional capital of Dnipro at around 1:30 p.m. local time, leaving 30,000 consumers without power in the Synelnykove and Pavlohrad districts, as well as in the town of Samar, about 30 kilometers (20 miles) northeast of Dnipro, according to Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Governor Oleksandr Hanzha.

Acting Naftogaz CEO Serhii Fedorenko said that Russia had struck the company's facilities more than 400 times since the beginning of 2026 — twice as often as during the same period last year.
The recent strikes were part of a wider Russian campaign targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure. The Energy Ministry said facilities were targeted in Kyiv and Kyiv, Volyn, and Odesa oblasts, while more than 5,000 consumers in Volyn Oblast were left without electricity.
In Kyiv, emergency outages were introduced in parts of the Obolonskyi, Shevchenkivskyi, and Sviatoshynskyi districts following the attacks on Oct. 21, Ukraine's largest private energy company DTEK said. The company later said the situation had stabilized and Kyiv was returning to scheduled power cuts.

Budget committee recommends 2027 state budget for first reading with 90 conclusions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:47:59 EEST
02:47:59 KST

The Verkhovna Rada Budget Committee has considered 5,236 amendments submitted by lawmakers to the government’s draft 2027 state budget and incorporated 90 budget conclusions, including instructions for the government to consider increasing military personnel pay and to prohibit funding the National Cashback programme from the UAH 9.4 billion budget programme for supporting industrial development and entrepreneurship.
"We expect the draft state budget to be considered at first reading around October 28," committee chair Roksolana Pidlasa wrote on Facebook following a nine-hour committee meeting on Wednesday.
In the defense sector, the government is also to consider before the second reading doubling the volume of state guarantees for defense industry enterprises to UAH 60 billion, increasing spending on the construction and purchase of housing for Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel, and establishing a new subvention for local budgets to fund centers preparing citizens for national resistance, she said.
In education and science, the committee proposed allocating nearly an additional UAH 27 million to pay teachers administering the National Multisubject Test and transferring the remaining balance of the education subvention to the Education Ministry's special fund for urgent educational needs during the year. It also instructed the government to consider increasing subventions to local budgets for workshops at vocational and professional pre-higher education institutions, shelters at schools and kindergartens, and energy independence at educational institutions. Other proposals include increasing funding for research at National Academy of Sciences institutions by UAH 700 million, allocating an additional UAH 10 million to the Ukrainian Leadership Academy, and finding funding for a pilot reform of teacher remuneration.
In healthcare, the committee proposed an additional UAH 150 million to purchase medicines for autoimmune diseases of the nervous system and neuromuscular diseases. It also called for funding to be found for medicines for patients with achondroplasia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, medical equipment for Feofaniya Clinical Hospital, and osseointegrative prosthetics for veterans.
Regarding local budgets and regional development, the government is to consider, as in previous years, allocating 4% of personal income tax revenues, excluding military personnel's personal income tax, to community budgets and balancing the resulting change, which would reduce state budget revenues by UAH 18.2 billion. The committee also instructed the Cabinet of Ministers to consider retaining reverse subsidies from local budgets, which would entail a further UAH 19.2 billion in state budget revenue losses, and increasing funding for the State Fund for Regional Development by at least UAH 2 billion.
The committee also recommended that the government use State Statistics Service data on the resident population of communities, rather than data from the State Migration Service, when calculating horizontal equalization indicators for 2027, and use Social Policy Ministry data on internally displaced people. Other proposals include adding UAH 118 million to the subvention for local budgets to fund district councils' responsibilities, increasing compensation for destroyed housing, and finding resources to complete education and healthcare projects launched in previous years with funding from the fund for eliminating the consequences of armed aggression.
To support the economy, the committee proposed allocating an additional UAH 100 million for humanitarian demining, reviewing the case for continuing the National Cashback programme with public funds, and allowing starting prices at large-scale privatization auctions to be reduced in 2027 to facilitate the sale of loss-making assets such as the Odesa Port Plant and Sumykhimprom.
Other proposals in this area include increasing compensation to agricultural producers for the construction or reconstruction of livestock farms for cattle, goats and sheep, and milk-processing facilities, from 50% to 75% of costs. The government is also to consider support for producers in areas where hostilities have made farming risky, as well as launching a new state support programme to transport agricultural products from frontline areas to safer regions.
The committee also proposed compensating charterers, operators and owners of vessels for war-related damage and increasing the war-risk insurance programme, which currently has just UAH 1 billion allocated from the general fund.
"In social protection, among the measures we consider realistic, we are instructing the government to inventory legislative acts that use the subsistence minimum and minimum wage to calculate components of remuneration, fines and other payments. This is needed to decouple all payments from the subsistence minimum and minimum wage and make it possible to bring these amounts into line with reality," Pidlasa said.
In public administration, the government has been instructed to consider increasing funding for the Foreign Ministry's overseas diplomatic missions and allocating funds to the customs service to repair scanners, she added.
As reported, the government's draft 2027 state budget envisages revenues of UAH 5.65 trillion, up UAH 452.1 billion, or 8.7%, from the 2026 budget plan. Total expenditures are proposed at UAH 7.27 trillion, up UAH 864.9 billion, or 13.5%, from the 2026 state budget.

Rashtriya Ekta Diwas 2026 to celebrate 'End of Naxalism': Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan
NEW DELHI: The end of armed Naxalism within the March 31, 2026 deadline set by home minister Amit Shah as well 150 years of ‘Vande Mataram’ will be celebrated at the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade and Bharat Parv at Kevadia, Gujarat, this year to mark Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s birth anniversary on Oct 31. Around 7,000 people from 126 districts that at some point of time were under the scourge of Left-wing extremism, will participate both as performers and spectators in the event to be graced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Union home secretary Govind Mohan on Wednesday said around 2,000 artists drawn from 126 districts that were once Naxal-affected, will join the celebrations by putting up a dramatic performance, directed by the National School of Drama (NSD), through which they will recount how their life and property were threatened when Naxalism was rampant in their area.

Around 5,000 artists will showcase dances and culture of their respective states through this mega-performance.A play will be organised on the eve of Oct 31 on the theme ‘Anand Math’. To be directed by NSD, it will be based on the abiding philosophy of Anand Math: that every person of India has a responsibility of building a bright future for the country and being aware of its cultural heritage.

Export of Ukrainian weapons during war unlikely due to lack of relevant NATO doctrines – Zaluzhny
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:47:11 EEST
02:47:11 KST

The successful export of Ukrainian weapons and technologies depends on whether partners have appropriate military doctrines, since NATO relies on doctrines from previous eras, while new Ukrainian technologies are still under development, Ukraine's ambassador to the United Kingdom Valeriy Zaluzhny has said.
As Zaluzhny said during the fourth annual "Economic Truth" export forum in Kyiv on Wednesday, weapons will be purchased only when buyers have a "clear doctrine for their use."
"This isn't a marketplace where goods are simply exchanged. Marketing has no place here. They [potential buyers] use a doctrine that describes how a particular weapon is employed," he said.
Zaluzhny said that in order to begin the widespread use of new Ukrainian systems (particularly drones) as primary weapons in their armed forces, NATO countries need to revise their doctrines, which are currently geared toward different types of weaponry. At the same time, when asked whether Ukraine could provide a ready-made doctrine to its partners, he replied: "Probably not. Because for that, people would have to see that we have absolutely no doctrine… A doctrine… a second lieutenant would never be able to write it. That requires fundamental military knowledge."
In addition, commenting on the prospects of entering the arms markets and exporting technology, Zaluzhny expressed doubt about rapid, large-scale breakthroughs, since the relevant technologies and weapons are currently in a state of evolution that will last at least another three years.
"I doubt that entering the arms markets and utilizing export technologies will be a huge breakthrough for Ukrainian defenders," he said.

EU member to relaunch economic consultations with Moscow
Slovakia will discuss economic cooperation with Russia, including energy supplies, in Moscow next week, the Slovak Foreign Ministry has said.
The landlocked EU nation has remained a buyer of Russian oil and gas despite the deterioration of the ties between Moscow and the EU in the wake of the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. The country is supposed to phase out Russian energy by late 2027 under the bloc’s plan to replace Russian oil and gas supplies from elsewhere.
The Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission for economic, scientific, and technical cooperation has been inactive since November 2021 but is now set to meet next Monday, the Slovak Foreign Ministry announced late on Tuesday. The commission will discuss a broad range of topics, including farming, environment, sports, and culture, and focus on energy supply, including nuclear energy, according to the ministry.
“The fundamental topic will be energy and the possibility to cooperate in securing supplies of strategic resources. The Slovak side is also interested in discussing gas supplies and the continuation of oil supplies,” it said in a statement.
Bratislava continues “to base its approach on its European Union and North Atlantic Alliance membership and keeping commitments of this membership” but wants to create room for dialogue, the ministry said.
Slovakia dissented on the EU’s course to dismantle ties with Moscow and prop up Kiev in the conflict after Robert Fico retook the prime minister’s office in October 2023, for the fourth time in his long political career. Under Fico, Slovakia has remained skeptical of assisting Ukraine and of Kiev’s push to join NATO, while halting government weapons shipments and calling for peace. The stance has resulted in repeated public spats between Bratislava and Kiev, as well as criticism from Brussels.
Last month, Fico warned that Europe was moving dangerously close to a direct clash between NATO and Russia, accusing the West of seeking a “pretext” for a major conflict. He accused EU nations of engaging in increasingly bellicose rhetoric and described the Ukraine conflict as “out of control.”
“The situation has never been as serious and tense regarding the possibility of a pan-European war conflict as it is now,” he said.
