Stay or flee? Kyiv mothers torn on how to keep children safe as Russian attacks step up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:46:08 UTC
02:46:08 KST

Stay or flee? Kyiv mothers torn on how to keep children safe as Russian attacks step up
Nina Shkurba, a writer and mother, with her son Veniamin in the Osokorky neighborhood of Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 4, 2026. (Khrystyna Kulakovska / The Kyiv Independent)
Anna Lodyhina, a mother of a 5-year-old, spent many nights on the cold floor of Kyiv's metro, driven there — like many others — by relentless Russian attacks. As her child slept, she watched over him, exhausted by the constant threat and lack of sleep.
This is just a glimpse of what Ukrainian mothers have been facing daily as Russia intensified its drone and missile campaign against Kyiv over the summer and early autumn.
Mothers are now confronted with the same question they faced almost five years ago — to stay or to leave.
Many left for abroad at the onset of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, but returned to give their children the possibility of a childhood in their native Ukraine. But now, as Kyiv increasingly resembles cities closer to the front line, relocation has become a necessity for some.
read also
'I never dreamed of emigration'
Lodyhina, a journalist and art researcher who moved to Warsaw in March 2022 with her then-1-year-old son, said she never imagined leaving Kyiv before Russia's full-scale invasion.
"I never dreamed of emigration," she said. After two years, they returned to Kyiv.
But as Russian attacks intensified earlier this year, Lodyhina once again faced the question of whether to leave Kyiv. Living in a building without a shelter, she and her son were often forced to take refuge in the metro and sleep on its cold concrete floor amid mass strikes.
"The child slept, but I stayed awake the entire night in the metro," adds Lodyhina. With a constant lack of sleep, her health started to deteriorate, affecting her ability to focus.
She told the Kyiv Independent that she had been actively involved in volunteer work to support Ukraine's Armed Forces, but lamented that much of it stopped once the attacks intensified.
By the start of September, she had had enough. Lodyhina and her son moved to Lviv in western Ukraine to escape the never-ending terror.
"For the past three weeks, we have slept calmly. We can't get enough of it."
"For the past three weeks, we have slept calmly. We can't get enough of it; we go to bed early and still wake up late the next morning."
Despite a relative sense of tranquility in the weeks of September, reminders of war pierce any illusion of peace. While picking up her son from kindergarten, Lodyhina overheard him say he had never known life without war. His friend agreed with childlike excitement.
read also
Her son knows the daily moment of silence — the nationwide pause at 9 a.m. to commemorate the fallen — and how to greet soldiers, she says.
As Russia continues changing its tactics, it is uncertain how long families will have to stay away from their homes in Kyiv. With winter approaching, many are also afraid of attacks on critical infrastructure that can leave the capital without heat, electricity, and water for days on end.
Lodyhina's winter preparations have been ongoing for a while now. In her new Lviv apartment, she made sure to check all the radiators and gas systems and bought a portable generator.
"I feel privileged to have a chance to relocate within the country," Lodyhina added. However, she told the Kyiv Independent that she never rules out the possibility of having to move abroad again if security and living conditions worsen in western Ukraine as well.
By October, this question is no longer theoretical, as drone attacks and air raid alerts grow more frequent in Lviv as well. Even western Ukraine is becoming less of a refuge from Russian aggression.
Children first
The turning point for Anna Ablitsova, 33, was a strike just a street away from her home. She recalls being in the kitchen while her 4-year-old son, Mykyta, was playing in the other room.
"He got really scared, started crying, ran, and put his arms around me. I got very nervous," Ablitsova told the Kyiv Independent. She notes that previous strikes, even nightly mass attacks, never affected her son this much.
When Mykyta started kindergarten, Ablitsova realized he was spending almost the entire day in an underground shelter.
"All these stories he tells me are about how (the children) were in shelters, and the teacher says, 'air raid alert, let's go to shelter,' and what kind of missile is flying their way," she says while wondering what sort of long-term repercussions such conditions will have on her son's mental health.
In August, Ablitsova and her husband began considering relocating from Kyiv amid increasingly frequent air raid alerts and drone attacks. The couple settled on Lutsk, a western city they had temporarily stayed in at the onset of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Lutsk is a five-hour drive from Kyiv, where Ablitsova and her husband work, where their family resides, and where a big part of their life remains. However, after experiencing just over a week of relative peace in Lutsk, it may prove hard to return to Kyiv.
"Now I'm a little afraid when we need to go to Kyiv. We promised to come for a birthday, but I haven't been there for a week and a half. Everything changes so quickly, and just a week ago, I lived there."
Despite having to move everything to Lutsk, at least for the next six months, Ablitsova is happy to see Mykyta no longer spending hours in the kindergarten shelter, speaking Ukrainian, and not sleeping in the hallway.
"Everyone here speaks Ukrainian. I have my child in the environment that I want him to be in, where he doesn't bring home some stupid Russian words from the kindergarten," adds Ablitsova, whose family was Russian-speaking but switched to Ukrainian on the very first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
But as in Lviv, the security situation in Lutsk is changing too. Weeks after the Kyiv Independent talked with Ablitsova, a Russian drone attack struck the city on Oct. 14, killing six civilians.
read also
Adjusting to Kyiv's new reality
Leaving Kyiv amid relentless Russian attacks is not something every mother wants — or can — do.
Although many have decided to move to a safer place in Ukraine or abroad, some remain hopeful that the current difficulties will end.
"Safety is not the absence of a threat," Nina Shkurba, a 38-year-old writer, summarizes an idea developed by American psychotherapist Peter Levine.
Shkurba, along with her 9-year-old son and 16-year-old daughter, knows what it's like to be forced to leave Kyiv due to Russian aggression. Just two days after the start of the full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she left Ukraine for the Spanish coastal city of Santander, but returned two and a half years later.
For now, she is determined to stay in Kyiv to keep the family united in their native home.
"I don't have that feeling that I need to run."
During her time in Spain, Shkurba wrote a book on the sense of belonging, which was then published in Ukraine. However, almost the entire printed supply was destroyed in August when a Russian attack struck her publisher. All that is left are the few copies in bookstores, she told the Kyiv Independent.
"I don't have that feeling that I need to run," she said, adding that going to their "dacha" — a seasonal home on the city's outskirts — helps the family recharge and find some peace.
But life in Kyiv is not the same as it was a mere few months ago. "September (was) very difficult in terms of anxiety. This is a new reality that we still have to get used to — that Kyiv feels like a front-line city," says Shkurba.
"My son has been wanting to celebrate at the Blockbuster (shopping mall in Kyiv) all year; he was looking forward to it. But we canceled both our children's celebrations in the shopping centers because of the drone threat."
Shkurba adds that children, especially her teenage daughter, are aware of the worsening security situation.
As a precaution, Shkurba renews her and her children's Spanish documents in case they have to leave Ukraine again. It is not something she is considering now, but being prepared offers a sense of control in what seems like never-ending uncertainty about tomorrow.
No end in sight
No one can say for certain how long Russia's daily drone and missile campaign against Kyiv will continue. For over a month now, the air raid alert has been on for most of the day, with the city recording over 20 hours of alert on Sep. 30.
The city and its families endure, adjusting to the new alert system and avoiding places like shopping malls and train stations. Mothers who stayed in Kyiv or relocated elsewhere are victims of the same Russian terror that aims to paralyze daily life.
Despite feeling a sense of peace in Lviv, Lodyhina refuses to accept what is happening in Ukraine as the new norm.
"This is not our life," she says.

====================================================================================================

Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis' deadly attacks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom, with missiles hitting energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing at least 20 people.
The Iranian proxy group has struck the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, and is fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of Yemen's coastline on the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global energy supplies. The fighting has put further upward pressure on oil and gas prices as Iran and the U.S. fight over the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels. The kingdom's opaque government releases regular statements about Houthi ballistic missiles and drones being intercepted, including five it said were destroyed Wednesday.
But many have got through, including an Oct. 10 strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid Airport, including a U.S. citizen.
"No country can ever have a 100% interception rating, that just doesn't really exist," Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told CBS News, but that "was a hell of a one to miss."
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East, including Israel.
So why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage?
Geography
Saudi Arabia is vast and, analysts say, geographically vulnerable.
Its east, home to the kingdom's oil fields, is bordered by the Persian Gulf — all that separates Saudi Arabia from longtime foe Iran. Early in the war, Iran launched strikes targeting bases used by the U.S. in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for U.S. attacks.
To the north, across Saudi Arabia's long border with Iraq, are Iran-backed militia groups that the Saudis — along with the U.S. — struck in July in response to dozens of attempted drone attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure and on U.S. installations in the region.
To the south, Saudi Arabia shares a more-than-800-mile border with Yemen. A vast portion of the war-wracked nation is controlled by the Houthis. To Saudi Arabia's west, the Houthis have also been battling for control of the Red Sea's vital shipping lanes.
"Over the last eight months, they have been facing threats from every direction," said Dent.
"There is a lot of critical infrastructure: multiple airports, many pipelines, as well as extensive oil production and export infrastructure, military bases, government buildings, royal palaces, and so on," said Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program. "It is simply extremely difficult to provide air defenses for all these sites over such a large area."
"If the Houthis are able to hit Saudi infrastructure with only a minority of their attempted drone or missile attacks, it counts as a success for them and an embarrassment and a loss for Saudi Arabia," Juneau told CBS News.
Neither Saudi nor Houthi authorities responded to CBS News' request for comment on this story.
The interceptor shortage
The ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused a global supply shortage of the interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles and other weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot system used by Saudi Arabia and other American allies.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about Ukraine's longstanding request for Patriot interceptors, said Tuesday that "every other country in the world" also wants them.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling it "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."
"Demand coming from the international [market] is stronger than ever," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, the world's biggest weapons manufacturer and maker of the Patriot interceptors, told CBS News last week when asked about the short supply.
Saudi Arabia is secretive about its weapons systems and stockpiles, but CBS News reported in March that Gulf countries were seeking emergency resupplies of interceptors, while the Wall Street Journal and Associated Press have reported that the kingdom has sought air defense systems from Japan, South Korea, France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.
Patriot interceptors are expensive, costing as much as $4 million per unit.
"If there's fear over utilizing or drawing down your resources," said Dent, "are you more reticent to pull the trigger?"
Evolving Houthi tactics
Saudi Arabia has purchased 730 Patriot interceptors from Washington since 2020, according to U.S. military data, but even if it does have enough, the pricey missiles aren't ideal for combating everything in the Houthi arsenal.
Patriots were designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and the Houthis have launched those at Saudi Arabia. But the rebels also have an array of relatively cheap drones, including weapons supplied by Iran, and locally made copies of Iranian attack drones.
These inexpensive weapons have been a key element in the Houthis' tactics, analysts say.
They can be launched in swarms, Allison Minor, a senior fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CBS News.
The Houthis "combine an overwhelming number of relatively cheap systems, namely drones, to distract and disrupt and exhaust, and then amid that, also weave in these more catastrophic missile attacks," she said.
The Saudis' multi-layered air defense system is sophisticated, but Houthi drones and cruise missiles can change their trajectory, making them harder to track, said Dent, "so if one aspect of that layered defense system breaks down, it can create a gap in coverage, like what may have occurred for the airport attack."
"This is a whole new ballgame," said Dent. "It's a tactic that requires some adjustments."
One possible solution could be Ukrainian-developed drone interceptors, which cost in the thousands of dollars to manufacture and are produced in the tens of thousands annually, unlike Patriots, which are produced in the hundreds.
Saudi Arabia and some of its neighbors have already made deals with Ukraine to acquire such systems, but Dent said they won't be a quick fix as "a lot of what the Ukrainians have been implementing is very hands-on."
The systems require skilled operators, in other words, and they require training.
A military with a narrow focus
Another issue is the Saudi personnel available to receive that training. Analysts do not rate the kingdom's military among the world's best, despite its huge defense budget.
Saudi Arabia's armed forces have a reputation for being "structured and run according to the interests of its royal leadership, with an emphasis on regime security," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean.
"You can spend all the money you want on your military and your missile defenses, but you also have to have a culture of readiness and excellence among the troops responsible," he said.
"If that's lacking, again, the problem is inherently a hard one: fighting intelligent people who really are trying to kill you and are willing to be quite creative in their pursuit of that goal," he said. "Some shots are going to get through."
When patchwork support "is too patchy"
Faced with Houthi successes and dwindling Patriots, the Saudis have been "aggressively seeking out air defense support from a variety of partners," said Minor, at CSIS.
The kingdom has invoked a mutual defense pact signed last year with Pakistan and Turkey, under which an attack on one country is considered an attack on all three, much like the NATO alliance's Article 5. Pakistan has already confirmed a troop deployment to the kingdom, and Turkey is also working toward sending forces.
France recently agreed to send "military means" to help protect the crucial Yanbu oil terminal on the Red Sea, and announced a separate agreement to help protect other Saudi oil facilities, without offering details.
The U.K. government said Tuesday that it would "fly defensive counter air missions" to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from Houthi attacks, but that the aircraft would not take part in strikes against the group in Yemen.
Egypt announced Sunday that it was prepared to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia.
Greece has operated a Patriot battery in Yanbu since 2021 and Italy, which has troops in Saudi Arabia and provided the Saudis with radar and anti-missile batteries before the war broke out in February, said in October that it could be willing to bolster the European Union mission protecting Red Sea shipping if other EU nations also step up.
There have also been reports of Saudi Arabia attempting to recruit foreign fighters, and using less reliable Chinese interceptors.
But this many-pronged approach to national defense could be problematic.
"Do you eventually get to a point where that patchwork is too patchy?" asked Minor. "The interoperability of different troops and aircraft and radar and interception systems — does that become too much to manage at some point?"
The key question, she said, is the extent of the Houthis' own weapons stockpiles.
"The Houthis have maintained a very steady pace of attacks over the past few weeks," she said. "It's not clear to me if the Houthis are able to sustain that for the long term — if they're gearing up for another years-long confrontation, or if this is an intense shorter-term salvo to try to get back to the negotiating table on better terms."

Neither Washington nor Beijing has publicly confirmed this account, and Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning previously said on Oct. 19 that China has no information on the rumored trilateral meeting.
Meanwhile, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned against excluding Ukraine on Tuesday, Oct. 20, insisting Kyiv must participate in any talks concerning its sovereignty and the war’s outcome.
According to the Wall Street Journal on Oct. 19, Putin first proposed the format during an Oct. 9 telephone call with US President Donald Trump, hoping to settle the war with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on terms favorable to Moscow.

Moscow open to talks with Kyiv

Beijing – Moscow’s longstanding partner
Although China presented itself as neutral in Russia’s war, its military and economic ties with Russia have continued to deepen since the full-scale invasion was launched in 2022.
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) told Kyiv Post in July that more than 550 Chinese service members have trained at Russian military institutions, while over 180 Russian troops completed similar internships in China in November 2025 alone.
China was also the largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in August, at €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion), according to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Cut off from Western technology by the European sanctions, Russia has increasingly turned to Chinese suppliers.
Chinese components, including turbo-jet engines, have helped Moscow build faster Shahed-type drones that are significantly harder for Ukraine to intercept due to their speed, able to reach 400-600 kilometers per hour (250-370 miles per hour).

Days prior, Zelensky warned that Beijing is assisting Russia’s efforts in building their own domestic Starlink rival, “Rassvet.” The system, still under development, could strengthen military communications, reconnaissance capabilities, and long-range drone operations.
“It is a pity that China is not on our side in this war – politically. It is not even about weapons,” Zelensky said on Sept. 17, noting that Beijing has enough influence to push Putin to the negotiating table, but chooses not to.

Ambassador Giuseppe Buccino Grimaldi participated last night in the event titled “The Italian and Spanish Innovation Ecosystems,” hosted by the Consulate General of Italy in Madrid and promoted by the Italian Embassy in Spain and the ICE Madrid Investment Promotion Office, in collaboration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation and the Italian Tech Alliance. The discussion focused on the life sciences sector, a field that, despite the challenges, is experiencing strong momentum and rapid growth in both Italy and Spain. 
    The meeting, which featured a presentation by Carme Artigas, co-chair of the United Nations Global Advisory Board on Artificial Intelligence, was attended by representatives from venture capital funds, startups, researchers, and companies in the pharmaceutical sector. 
   Four emerging Italian startups had the opportunity to present their projects, offering a genuine and representative demonstration of the potential and dynamism of the Italian innovation ecosystem.
                                    
In his remarks to those present, the ambassador highlighted how Italy and Spain maintain deep and well-established economic ties, given that bilateral trade exceeds 70 billion euros annually, with pharmaceutical and chemical products accounting for a significant share, with the pharmaceutical sector alone accounting for 10.8% of exports. Buccino Grimaldi also noted that the two countries share important distinctive features in their respective life sciences ecosystems, including robust university research, specialized healthcare institutions, and centers of scientific and industrial excellence—elements that provide an ideal foundation for close bilateral cooperation. 
   However, Italian and Spanish companies in the sector face a common challenge: although they emerge from world-class research, they often require more substantial capital injections for the growth and scaling phases—something that national funds cannot always guarantee. It is for this reason, the ambassador also emphasized, that joint efforts between the two countries’ systems can lead to a shared perspective in the European debate, starting with the implementation of the European Biotech Act—an extraordinary plan to make the development of new medicines and medical technologies in Europe faster, more cost-effective, and safer.

Denmark announced that it has provided a state guarantee for a loan of DKK 750 million, or $112.6 million, to a Danish subsidiary of Fire Point, a Ukrainian defense technology manufacturer.
"This loan is backed by a Danish state guarantee, as the war in Ukraine makes it difficult for Fire Point to obtain a loan in Denmark on standard commercial terms," according to a statement from the Danish Ministry of Entrepreneurship, Business, and Finance.
The Danish ministry said in the statement, financing for Fire Point's Danish subsidiary will be provided through the country's Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
According to Minister of Industry, Business, and Finance Martin Lidegaard, establishing Ukrainian production facilities on Danish territory to meet Ukraine's defense needs allows the two countries to build partnerships in this area.
"Denmark remains steadfast in its support for the Ukrainians' struggle for freedom. Therefore, Denmark is providing support – both now and in the future – that makes both Ukraine and Europe more resilient," the Danish Minister of Industry, Business, and Finance said.
In turn, Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Brøus said his country became the first nation to allow the establishment of a Ukrainian defense enterprise.
He also added that Fire Point's presence opens up broader opportunities for cooperation with the Danish Armed Forces and companies, which could also provide the country with access to technologies and expertise gained during a full-scale invasion.
"It is crucial for Ukraine's defense to gain broader access to critical defense materials and technologies through reliable supply chains; locating Ukrainian defense production outside of Ukraine provides better protection for facilities against Russian attacks," the Danish defense minister said.
Among other things, EIFO CEO Peder Lundquist said the fund is currently involved in nearly 40 projects aimed at assisting Ukraine and fostering deeper cooperation between Ukrainian and Danish partners.
"Funding for the Fire Point project is a concrete example of how these efforts are being implemented," Lundquist said.
As previously reported, Fire Point is working with Denmark to develop plans for building a solid-fuel production facility in that country. It was noted at the time that the plant is being built in South Jutland.
The defense company Fire Point specializes in the development and production of unmanned systems, long-range strike drones, and cruise and ballistic missiles.

Finnish government drops plans for tourist tax
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:36:48 EEST
02:36:48 KST

The Finnish government has abandoned plans to introduce a tourist tax after coalition parties failed to agree on a proposed levy of 2–5 per cent on accommodation costs. The decision ends preparations for a tax intended to help municipalities, particularly in Lapland, cover expenses linked to growing visitor numbers.
Finance Minister Riikka Purra of the Finns Party announced on Tuesday that the proposal would not reach parliament during the current government's term.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
"The government did not reach an agreement on the proposal," Purra wrote on X, expressing disappointment that a measure requested by tourism destinations such as Rovaniemi had failed.
The Finance Ministry began preparing the legislation following a government decision in spring 2025. Under the draft circulated for consultation in June, municipalities would have decided whether to introduce a tax ranging from 2 to 5 per cent of accommodation prices excluding VAT.
Accommodation providers would have collected the tax and transferred the proceeds through the Finnish Tax Administration. Revenue would have remained with participating municipalities.
Government estimates suggested annual nationwide revenue of several million euros, potentially reaching €20 million. Rovaniemi alone was projected to collect between €3.1 million and €7.9 million, depending on the rate.
The proposal faced opposition from the National Coalition Party, whose representatives argued that the Finance Ministry had departed from the original plan for a small, fixed accommodation charge.
National Coalition MP Heikki Autto, who represents Rovaniemi, told Helsingin Sanomat that the initial proposal involved a regional trial allowing municipalities to charge visitors a few euros per night.
He argued that replacing the fixed charge with a percentage-based tax would increase costs for hotels and other registered accommodation businesses.
Autto also questioned whether the system would treat accommodation providers equally, pointing to differences in registration requirements between hotels and short-term rental operators such as Airbnb hosts.
Purra defended the percentage-based model, arguing that accommodation costing thousands of euros should not face the same charge as an inexpensive holiday cottage. She said officials had considered introducing a maximum payment to address concerns about higher-priced accommodation.
The proposed legislation had been scheduled to enter into force in March 2027, with the tax taking effect from January 2028.

Putin agrees to resume three-way peace talks with Ukraine, US, after meeting with Witkoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:35:20 UTC
02:35:20 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two.
The negotiations in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia - the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher held in Russia whom US President Trump had asked the Kremlin chief to release.
Wednesday's encounter unfolded amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.
The latest talks also came more than two years after Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
The Kremlin said the new three-way peace talks, which would be at a technical level, could take place in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. They could begin sometime on or after November 10, it said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran.
The Kremlin was less upbeat, however, about the outcome of talks Witkoff had held a day earlier in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. Witkoff told Putin the talks had been characterized by "some degree of momentum" and a US official said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals.
"These nuances, so to speak, do not entirely satisfy us," Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the St Petersburg meeting - which lasted nearly three hours.
Possible meeting between Trump, Putin, Xi
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, though Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."
Putin also used Wednesday's talks to offer to help Trump deal with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear program. Putin told Witkoff it was possible and necessary to get a deal with Tehran, the Kremlin said.
Russia could also supply vast quantities of fertilizer to the United States to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first meeting of its kind in history.
New peace ideas for peace shared during meeting
Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, no NATO membership for Kyiv, and an overall peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy, was also present at the talks with Witkoff, and the Kremlin said that major joint economic projects had been discussed, including some that were close to being realized.
Witkoff said he had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin. Kushner later joined the meeting remotely by phone.
Zelensky said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelensky meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile.
US-Ukraine ties fray after Russian diesel export deal
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelensky said that Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

Washington must urge Beirut to repeal Lebanon’s 1955 Boycott Law, which criminalizes social and business ties with Israel, and ensure that Hezbollah does not regain the explosives seized from the group several weeks ago, the American Mideast Coalition for Democracy said in an open letter to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday.
Lebanese Americans Tom Harb and John Hajjar, AMCD co-chairs, argued that the 1955 law was being overextended beyond its original intentions and is now being used to criminalize basic conversations with Israelis and prevent religious pilgrimages to the Land of Israel, which holds religious sites for Abrahamic faiths.
AMCD calls for dialogue between Lebanon and Israel's militaries

Beyond calling for contact between Israeli and Lebanese citizens to be legalized, particularly ahead of the Christmas season, the signatories said channels of communication should be established between the two countries’ militaries to prevent the loss of innocent lives due to miscalculations during military operations. They also called for diplomatic channels to be opened to advance peace.
To advance this goal, AMCD said that the US should condition financial and military assistance to Lebanon on the repeal of the 1955 law and on Beirut implementing concrete steps to facilitate military, diplomatic, and civilian communication with Israel, and impose sanctions against any Lebanese government body, institution, or individual that prosecutes or penalizes people for peaceful contact with Israelis or for visiting the holy sites.
“American taxpayers should not underwrite a government that criminalizes the pursuit of peace,” the letter said. “We respectfully urge you to continue pressing [Lebanese] President Aoun on these issues and to support these measures in Congress.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for the end of what he called genocide and occupation at the hands of the Israeli government, along with the release of several activists affiliated with Rabbis for Human Rights.
“Today, Brad Lander, rabbis, and other New Yorkers accompanied Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest. For that, they were detained by the Israeli government,” he wrote, specifically noting that Lander was released by Israel Police.
“Harvesting olives is not illegal. The occupation is. The same Israeli government detaining them has committed a horrific genocide against Palestinians, killing more than 74,000 people over the last few years alone.
“The detention of these New Yorkers must end. The occupation must end. The genocide must end.”
Mamdani’s comments come after several other Jewish organizations and world leaders decried the IDF’s decision to detain around 90 volunteers who went to help Palestinian farmers with the olive harvest in the West Bank town of Nahalin.
Israel's Consul-General in New York, Ofir Akunis, denounced Mamdani's comments, saying, "Mind your business. The land of Israel is the homeland of the Jewish people, including Judea and Samaria."
"Clean New York City before you talk about the State of Israel," he added.
'Harvesting olives isn't a crime under any law I know'
The IDF claimed that it detained the activists and declared the olive grove a closed military area because the Palestinian person who owned the private land did not coordinate any security measures with the IDF.
However, activists with Rabbis for Human Rights told The Jerusalem Post that they wrote letters to several IDF personnel who command the area, and that they never received a response.
The activists noted that they mostly coordinated with the Palestinian landowner because the grove was on his private property.
Notably, KAN News reported that the area that volunteers were helping harvest in does not require IDF coordination.
For his part, Lander wrote in an initial statement after his detainment that he was "simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim in the West Bank."
"The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know," he added.
Former attorney-general and former deputy attorney-general Yehoshua Schoffman called the incident a “complete hallucination.”
Rabbis say Israel's actions are causing 'terrible damage' to Jewish world
In response to reports that Israeli authorities are inclined to deport the foreign activists, The Democrats MK and Rabbi Gilad Kariv called for Jewish organizations in Israel and the Diaspora to intervene.
"According to the information we have, the police and military are seeking to deport the dozens of Jewish volunteers from North America who came today to assist with the olive harvest in Gush Etzion. Among this group are prominent and influential rabbis, community leaders, and public figures," he wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
"They did not break any laws or violate any lawful orders, nor did they confront anyone. Their deportation, if carried out, would cause enormous damage to Israel's standing among Jewish and general public opinion in the US.
"I call on the leaders of the Jewish Agency, the heads of Jewish organizations in the US, and AIPAC leadership to intervene in this madness. I have no expectations of Ben-Gvir, Katz, or Netanyahu, but it is time for us to stand up against the terrible damage they are causing to the Jewish world and Israel's standing internationally.
Rabbi Jacobs says incident demonstrates 'state-backed campaign of ethnic cleansing'
T'ruah CEO Rabbi Jill Jacobs was among those detained. In a statement, she criticized the IDF, stating that "rather than protecting Palestinian farmers and ensuring their right to work their own land, the Israeli military forcibly removed those who came to provide a protective presence."
"This is an outrageous abuse of power, and part of a systematic, state-backed campaign of ethnic cleansing aimed at driving Palestinians from their land," she added.
“The Israeli government is actively advancing the forced displacement of Palestinian communities across the West Bank, using its military to deny Palestinians access to their land and intimidate those who stand alongside them. As rabbis, we have a moral obligation to confront these injustices, especially when they are carried out in our name.”
In a joint statement, the Reform, Conservative and Reconstructionist movement slammed the incident.
“That farmers need to have others serve as a protective presence from violent settlers is itself a betrayal of Jewish values. Yet recent settler attacks on Palestinian harvesters and those working alongside them and authorities’ failure or refusal to stop such attacks have made that protective presence necessary,” the joint statement said.
“Our global memberships span the political and ideological spectrum. Yet we are united in opposing all forms of terrorism across the region and in our conviction that detaining rabbis working for justice undermines Israel’s democratic values,” the groups add.
“We call on the Israeli government to release the detainees immediately, enable the productive harvesting of land, and turn its law enforcement efforts toward the violent settlers who have long been attacking Palestinian farmers and, more recently, journalists and diplomats,” the statement says.
In a joint statement, the Reform Movement in Israel and the Council of Reform Rabbis in Israel called the incident appalling.
"It is inconceivable that, instead of arresting and prosecuting the Jewish extremists who engage in theft and violence, security forces are arresting rabbi activists who are acting in accordance with Jewish values of love for humanity and the pursuit of justice," said Executive Director of the Israel Movement for Progressive and Reform Judaism Anna Kislanski.

“The fact that Israeli and American rabbis are compelled to stand alongside Palestinian farmers to help them harvest their olives and protect them from settler violence is a damning indictment of the Israeli government. The fact that these same rabbis are detained by security forces, rather than the authorities protecting the farmers and taking action against those perpetrating the violence, is nothing short of a disgrace," said Dr. Yizhar Hess, Vice Chairman of the World Zionist Organization.
"But today’s events are not merely a moral failure; they are also a devastating blow to Israel–Diaspora relations. As a Zionist and as a Jew, I want to remind us all: a Jewish and democratic state is judged not only by its ability to protect its citizens, but also by how it treats those living under its control. These values are not at odds with Zionism; they are the very values without which Zionism loses its soul," Hess added.

Netanyahu is destroying Israel’s bipartisan support in the US - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:34:29 UTC
02:34:29 KST

Tip O’Neil, the legendary speaker of the House, famously said “All politics is local.” The Gershwins said, “It ain’t necessarily so.”
The elections taking place throughout Israel next Tuesday and in the United States a week later will reverberate in distant corners of the earth.
The whole world is watching to see what direction voters will send a pair of authoritarian-leaning governments in the coming year.
The future course of the US-Israel alliance is very much on the line. One thing is certain: change is coming. We may not know where it is heading, but the days when Israel enjoyed broad bipartisan support in America, when lawmakers competed to see who loved Israel more, and billions in virtually unrestricted military assistance passed as if on autopilot are gone, never to return.
After weeks of waiting to see which way the polls were going, US President Donald Trump gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a seemingly reluctant endorsement just nine days before the election.
“Anyone” else would be “the wrong leader,” he said. Maybe that’s because, as he has said, he is confident Netanyahu “will do whatever I tell him to do.”
Trump’s rock-bottom approval ratings are largely traced to the Iran war, both for rising inflation and for breaking promises to avoid forever wars. Many of his America First and MAGA cult followers blame Netanyahu for pushing him into that costly conflict, which is endangering Trump’s agenda and Republican majorities in Congress.
Change is coming. The devastating and ongoing Israeli attacks on Gaza and the deaths of tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians have unfortunately overshadowed for many the tragedy of the Hamas massacre of Israelis on October 7, 2023. That translates to calls to restrict or even halt weapons sales as well as technology and intelligence sharing with Israel.
Democrats more outspoken against Israel
Democrats, who are considered likely to control at least one chamber in the next Congress, have been more outspoken but are not alone in their criticism of Netanyahu and his actions.
Increasing numbers have demanded restrictions, including many Jewish lawmakers and legislators with large Jewish constituencies. Expect bipartisan support in the next Congress for restrictions on aid levels and weapons sales.
The Senate is too close to call. If the Democrats win, Sen. Chuck Schumer is likely to again be majority leader.
The highest-ranking elected Jew ever in American politics, he once called himself Bibi’s best friend on Capitol Hill. That ended more than two years ago when Schumer said his friend had “lost his way” by pressing antidemocratic changes at home and the Gaza war and by being an “obstacle to peace.”
Netanyahu is a strident foe of Palestinian statehood, and all his election opponents in all directions have declared their opposition as well. But the two-state solution retains considerable support on Capitol Hill, in the Jewish community, and among Americans generally, who are now, for the first time, telling pollsters they are more sympathetic toward the Palestinian cause than toward Israel.
A further wedge is the spreading violence of Jewish settler terrorism against West Bank Palestinians. Netanyahu dismisses the violence as the work of a few dozen “juvenile delinquents.” He publicly condemns their actions but does nothing.
He dismissed attacks on an American photojournalist and several European diplomats in recent days as “alleged,” suggesting the well-documented reports were part of a “coordinated campaign to smear Israel.”
He’s right about Israel being the victim of a smear, but the perpetrators are Bibi and the violent settlers he is protecting.
There were a few arrests of last week’s alleged attackers, but experience suggests they will soon be released.
A West Bank settler interviewed on CBS’s 60 Minutes said if America is “turning on us... Israel will find other allies.”
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has instructed his diplomats to scour the planet for other allies if the United States cuts back.
Under Netanyahu’s leadership, Israel has plunged from popular to pariah among many nations, notably major Western democracies and those with the advanced economies, technology, and intelligence that his country needs.
ISRAEL DOESN’T need new allies as much as it needs to shore up old alliances, and for that it needs a new government.
If Israel’s longest-serving prime minister returns for a seventh term, particularly with much the same cast of religious and nationalist extremists, relationships will continue to implode, particularly if Jewish terrorism spreads, the Iran war heats up again, fighting intensifies in Gaza and Lebanon, and the flow of oil remains clogged.
Challenges facing a new centrist government, if there is one, include rolling back Netanyahu’s antidemocratic judicial “reforms,” establishing an independent October 7 commission of inquiry, cracking down on Jewish terrorists, and repairing relations with allies and the Diaspora.
Longtime supporters who want to see even modest change are dangerously being targeted in this year’s US elections by groups like AIPAC, which demand unquestioning loyalty to Netanyahu’s version of Israel.
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told The Wall Street Journal that he is having trouble hiring staff because many young conservatives object to his support for Israel.
“I’ve seen more antisemitism on the Right in the last two years than at any point in my lifetime,” he said, singling out people like Nick Fuentes and his growing white supremacy movement “Groyperism.”
The foundation of the US-Israel alliance is not, as Netanyahu has preached, white Christian Evangelists and the Republican Party. It is the principle of democracy, shared values, and a committed Jewish community. If the Jews don’t care about Israel, why should anyone else?
And Israel is losing the Jews. Generations of Americans grew up believing Israel is a democracy that wants to live in peace with its neighbors who just want to destroy it. Now they see many Arabs making peace, but they’re not so sure Israel wants to. They see an increasingly authoritarian Israeli government moving to dismantle democracy, waging war on all fronts, and losing friends at warp speed. In this election, no one is talking about making peace.
The golden age of wall-to-wall bipartisan support for Israel is ancient history, and Netanyahu deserves much of the credit. One former Israeli ambassador and Washington veteran told me he “will do anything to stay in power” and “he knows the damage and simply doesn’t care.”
The choice facing Israeli voters is whether they want more of the same deterioration or a leader who can repair damaged bridges and build new ones – with their fellow Israelis, with the Palestinians, with the Diaspora, with America, and around the world.
I’ve heard too many Israelis tell me, “You need us as much as we need you. We can get along very well without you.” I wish it were true, but it ain’t necessarily so.
The writer is a Washington-based journalist, consultant, lobbyist, and former legislative director at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

Some of Ukraine’s artillery soldiers were TikTokers yesterday, ComBat Vision says. Their new plugin teaches them to aim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:32:44 UTC
02:32:44 KST

Ukraine receives Western weapons, but the code that teaches soldiers to aim them is increasingly its own. Developers of the Ukrainian battlefield reconnaissance and coordination system ComBat Vision have released a new plugin that turns the abstract math of artillery fire into a visual tool, letting crews simulate firing and learn to adjust it, the team says.
The developers built the tool around a problem they name plainly: the quality of specialists entering the military is falling rapidly.
“Artillery soldiers are sometimes yesterday’s TikTokers or "tanks" players,” the team explain, so the plugin makes firing and aiming as visual as possible to teach indirect fire quickly.
On screen, it draws a round’s flight path from the weapon’s firing tables and the dispersion ellipse for that gun and munition, warns of obstacles on the calculated trajectory, and simulates the shell after the shot with a training error added. It then shows real or simulated bursts, averages the correction across a series of hits, and lets the user enter corrections, including by voice, and watch the result.
The plugin draws its ballistics from MyGun, an app by Yaroslav Sherstiuk that automates ballistic and fire calculations for artillery. ComBat Vision itself coordinates troops and shares object data, integrating with optical sensors such as drones, ground robots and security cameras to fix targets in space.
From a single app to a platform with a plugin store
ComBat Vision’s bigger move is becoming a platform rather than a single app. The developers say they will open a plugin store within a week, where units can download the new artillery feature and others, such as repeater-coverage calculations and remote control of minefields.
The team has announced plans to open it, not results from using it, so its payoff, letting one platform add new tools without building a separate system each time, is a claim to watch rather than a proven gain.

Quantum Systems Gets Interceptor Drone Up to 777 km/h
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:32:22 UTC
02:32:22 KST

German company Quantum Systems has developed the Apex Recordhunter technology demonstrator, which reached a speed of 777 km/h.
Quantum Systems representatives told Militarnyi details about the project and shared a post on social media.
The company’s N3XT research and development division is responsible for developing the aircraft.
The need for such systems arose from Russia’s use of jet-powered strike drones capable of reaching speeds of 600 km/h, creating demand for faster interceptors.
“Russia is using jet-powered strike drones, such as the Geran-5, with speeds of up to 600 km/h. This creates a need for faster interceptors capable of keeping pace with the evolving threat,” Quantum Systems said.
To achieve high speeds, the developers combined a revised aerodynamic design, a powerful electric motor and a cooling system in a compact airframe.
The drone accelerated from 0 to 777 km/h in 27 seconds.
It reached this speed for a fraction of a second, after which the pilot began slowing down and landed the aircraft.
During the flight, the engineers’ main challenge was ensuring the aircraft’s stability, as even minor deviations create additional drag and consume energy.
The project’s findings are already being applied to the development of new counter-UAV systems.
Militarnyi previously reported that Germany will fund the production in Ukraine of tens of thousands of Quantum Systems interceptor drones to strengthen defenses against Russian strike UAVs.
The funding will be part of Germany’s military aid package for Ukraine for the winter of 2026-2027.

Louise Haigh riles up lobbyists with war on UK ‘consultation culture’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:30:55 UTC
02:30:55 KST

LONDON — Andy Burnham’s top lieutenant is in a hurry to get things done — but lobbyists fear her plans to cut red tape will make law-making in Whitehall more exclusive.
The British prime minister’s de facto deputy Louise Haigh launched an attack on the British state’s “consultation culture” last month. She claimed that Whitehall's established method of seeking input on policy plans has morphed from a “sensible mechanism” for gathering views into an “industry of dither and delay.”
Haigh, the first secretary of state, has pledged to overhaul the process by running consultations on government plans only when there is a statutory requirement to do so — or where it would be “conspicuously unfair” not to do so.
Advertisement
She has urged colleagues to ditch the “comfort blanket” of a consultation and evaluate if thousands of requirements can be chopped.
But the announcement has left public affairs outfits in Westminster bristling. Multiple industry figures now say Haigh’s plans could shut small players out of the decision-making process and entrench civil service thinking.
Leena El-Refaey, a partner at the London-based agency Portland, said that while there is “clearly a case for reform,” there is “very little detail on what might replace the current system or how it will be robust, transparent and inclusive.”
“Without some form of formal process, there’s a real risk that engagement becomes exclusionary,” she adds.
The Cabinet Office did not respond to a request for comment.
Closing the door
Senior lobbyists — some of whom have made a cottage industry out of managing consultation responses for clients — insist they are sympathetic to the view that the policy process needs streamlining.
Advertisement
But they warn that a lack of detail about the next steps has triggered significant unease.
Haigh has only hinted at some form of "participatory policymaking" as a potential replacement for the status quo. She has promised that more clarity will come this fall.
The partial nature of last month's announcement has left industry figures concerned that rather than addressing fundamental problems with the policymaking approach, ministers are using the formal consultation process as a scapegoat for more deep-rooted flaws in government delivery.
Commuters cross a road beside Westminster on Oct. 13, 2026. | Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images
Daniel Wild, director of communications and strategy firm St. Michael Advisory, told POLITICO ministers could instead tackle Whitehall's culture of shifting responsibility between departments by rewarding bodies that can demonstrate delivery. "Without that, cutting consultations in the name of speed will shut out sound, reputable private sector voices and hand even more sway to those with the ear of the government of the day," he argued.
Amy Gray, a veteran freelance public affairs consultant, argued that ministers need to accept that swathes of consultations have failed due to the government's lack of expertise — rather than any fundamental flaw with the process.
After writing a response on behalf of a major supermarket to the government's consultation on banning tobacco displays, Gray said it was immediately obvious it had been drafted by someone with "absolutely no idea how you actually put cigarettes on the shelf, and had never spoken to anyone who worked in a shop."
Advertisement
Gray said most experienced lobbyists can provide examples of the government drafting an "incredibly stupid" consultation that clearly wouldn't "survive contact with reality."
"If government wants to peel back the number of consultations then they've got to do a much better job of engaging with businesses and affected organizations when civil servants are still developing the policy," she added.
Lobbyists' fear that Haigh's alternative approach will shut out those with the most expertise has been amplified by recent experiences of ad hoc and unofficial consultations by officials.
Portland's El-Refaey said this had included a "disappointing" trend of officials seeking feedback from businesses on a policy, only to reveal the following day it was already being sent to ministers for approval.
"There is a risk that will just get worse, with officials and special advisers turning to the organisations they already have relationships with, rather than seeking a broad range of views," she added.

Türkiye vows joint production under Badr defence pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:30:07 UTC
02:30:07 KST

Türkiye aims to turn its defence industry cooperation with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia into joint production and technology development projects, the country's defence industry chief said in a statement.
Haluk Gorgun, the head of Türkiye's Secretariat of Defence Industries, said on Wednesday that the Badr Memorandum of Understanding signed by the four countries in Doha provides a strategic framework for combining their capabilities.
"We believe the Badr Memorandum of Understanding will help translate the complementary capabilities of Qatar, Pakistan, Indonesia and Türkiye into concrete projects," Gorgun said in a statement issued by the secretariat.
The agreement aims to support joint military production projects and strengthen cooperation in technical training, research and development, according to the statement.
International partnerships
Gorgun said Türkiye's engineering, design, manufacturing and systems integration capabilities offer opportunities for international partnerships.
He stressed that Ankara's approach extends beyond supplying defence equipment to sharing technical knowledge and experience with partner countries.
"Our approach in the defence industry is to produce together, develop together and grow stronger together by sharing our knowledge, engineering capabilities and experience," he said.
Gorgun said sustainable defence partnerships depend on technology sharing, joint development and stronger local manufacturing capabilities.
"As Türkiye, we value partnerships that go beyond off-the-shelf procurement models and develop countries' own human resources and industrial infrastructure," he said.
He identified technological independence and sustainable production infrastructure as key priorities, saying Türkiye seeks mutual benefits and stronger strategic capabilities through international partnerships.
"Today's security environment requires countries to have strong, sustainable and technology-focused industrial ecosystems capable of meeting their defence needs," Gorgun said.
Defence and deterrence
Türkiye views the technologies it develops as tools to strengthen defence and deterrence while contributing to regional peace and stability, he added.
Gorgun said Ankara wants cooperation with friendly and allied countries to create lasting capabilities in line with that approach.
Gorgun also highlighted the contribution of defence industry diplomacy to export growth, saying multilateral partnerships such as Badr would help expand technological capabilities and overseas sales.
Türkiye's defence industry generated more than $30 billion in exports during the four years from 2023 to 2026, accounting for over 55% of the sector's total exports over the past 14 years, he said.
"In 2025, we increased our exports by 48 percent, taking them above $10 billion. Over the past 12 months, we exceeded the $11 billion mark for the first time," Gorgun added.

NSA, FBI urge fixes for security flaws in widely used website software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:26:56 UTC
02:26:56 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Developers of the widely used PHP programming language urged users to install security updates immediately on Wednesday after two critical vulnerabilities were found that could allow remote code execution, raising concerns about the security of websites and servers worldwide.
The developers released patched versions of the program and warned that attackers could exploit the flaws without authentication.
In a security advisory, the PHP team said all installations handling web requests were potentially at risk.
The developers identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The flaws involve memory-handling errors and outdated internal state that can persist between requests, potentially allowing attackers to execute malicious code on affected servers.
The US National Security Agency (NSA) also asked organizations using PHP to prepare for an immediate update, warning that the vulnerabilities could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems or databases.
“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database. If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” according to the agency, adding that more detailed guidance would follow.
The FBI Cyber Division urged organizations to immediately update affected PHP installations and inventory systems running PHP, prioritizing internet-facing servers and third-party products that include the programming language
The bureau also called for monitoring web servers for suspicious activity, including PHP processes unexpectedly launching command shells or downloading files, to help identify potential exploitation.
OpenAI said in a statement that its models helped researchers discover the flaws through its Patch the Planet initiative, which brought together software maintainers, researchers and security providers to develop fixes before public disclosure.
The company said the preparation process took two months because addressing the vulnerabilities required a complex change to the PHP engine.
PHP is used in a substantial share of the internet, with OpenAI estimating that it powers around 70% of websites. Its scale means unpatched systems could create significant opportunities for attackers.

New Mexico sues Epstein's lawyer, accountant over trafficking cover-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:26:00 UTC
02:26:00 KST

New Mexico's attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein's lawyer and accountant Wednesday, accusing them of helping conceal the disgraced financier's sex trafficking operation at his sprawling ranch in the state.
The lawsuit seeks to stop attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn from accepting any payments from Epstein's estate, estimated at more than $100 million.
Indyke worked as Epstein’s attorney for roughly two decades. Both he and Kahn have testified in Congress that they did not know about Epstein’s abuse, though New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez has a different view.
He said Indyke and Kahn "stand to benefit substantially” from Epstein's estate unless a court intervenes.
"Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors,” Torrez said, referring to victims of Epstein’s abuse.
Epstein killed himself in August 2019 in a federal jail in New York City, where he was awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.
Epstein’s former girlfriend and close associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence after her 2021 conviction on sex trafficking charges in New York. Witness testimony at Maxwell’s trial alleged she and Epstein had sexually abused women at the New Mexico ranch.
Epstein purchased the ranch in Stanley, New Mexico, a sparsely populated ranching community about 30 miles (48 kilometers) south of Santa Fe, in 1993. He built a 26,700-square-foot mansion with a sprawling courtyard, a living room roughly the size of the average American home, and a private airstrip and helipad.
Epstein never faced charges in New Mexico, though the state attorney general's office in 2019 confirmed that it was investigating and planned to forward its findings to federal authorities in New York. Hector Balderas, who was attorney general at the time, said the state’s outdated laws failed to protect children from abuse.
Torrez reopened the state’s investigation this year. In August, he sued the Department of Justice, accusing it of blocking the state from investigating alleged sex crimes at the ranch. The lawsuit said state prosecutors faced "sustained resistance” to the kind of information-sharing common between state and federal investigators. The Justice Department said it was not releasing some information the state requested to avoid disclosing victim-identifying information.
Also in August, a commission established by state lawmakers to investigate the allegations and whether local authorities looked the other way released a 119-page report that found that authorities repeatedly deferred to investigations in New York, Palm Beach, Florida, and the Virgin Islands, while leaving Epstein’s offenses in New Mexico unexamined and unpunished.
The ranch was sold by Epstein’s estate in 2023 - with proceeds going toward creditors - to the family of Don Huffines, a Republican recently appointed Texas’ state comptroller.

Vigilance coupled with avoidance of provocative actions

Vigilance coupled with avoidance of provocative actions
Sazandegi examined the distinction between a preemptive strike during an active military confrontation and military action undertaken during a relative pause in hostilities. Quoting Mohammad Atrianfar, a member of the central council of the Servants of Construction Party (Sazandegi), the article stated that a preemptive attack may be considered within the logic of military operations during an active conflict.
However, this differs fundamentally from situations in which both sides are observing a temporary ceasefire or experiencing a relative suspension of hostilities. In such circumstances, launching a preemptive attack would not necessarily resolve existing issues and could instead intensify tensions and broaden the scope of conflict. The path out of the current situation lies in a combination of defensive vigilance, restraint from provocative actions, and preserving diplomatic channels. The primary goal should be preventing the crisis from escalating and creating conditions for a lasting reduction in tensions.
Etemad: The West at an impasse
Etemad analyzed the visit of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to Tehran. His trip has fueled renewed speculation regarding Iran-US negotiations aimed at reviving the Islamabad understanding, a topic frequently discussed in Iran s political sphere. According to Mashaallah Shamsolvaezin, the United States bears the greatest responsibility for undermining the agreement because it approached the issue with the expectation of Iran s surrender. At the same time, Iran has succeeded in establishing a new balance against Washington and its allies through both military and diplomatic means. This balance has increased Western concerns about extending the conflict and opening new fronts, particularly in areas such as Bab al-Mandab. Shamsolvaezin believes that three major challenges, namely the Strait of Hormuz, the nuclear issue, and Bab al-Mandab, have pushed Washington toward negotiations that may accommodate some Iranian demands. However, he contends that the United States is attempting to downplay Iran s strategic advantages, even though those advantages have grown significantly stronger than they were before the war.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Diplomatic players in Tehran
From Sergey Lavrov s visit to the arrival of Asim Munir, the simultaneous diplomatic activity involving Pakistan, Oman, Qatar, and Russia, along with indirect Chinese support, signals an intensive effort to break the deadlock in Iran-US negotiations ahead of two crucial elections involving the Knesset and the US Congress. While this sequence of events does not by itself prove the existence of a coordinated agreement between Moscow and Islamabad, it carries considerable political significance at a time when talks between Tehran and Washington face deep mistrust and disagreements over the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions, and the nuclear file. The common message of these diplomatic exchanges is clear: the channel for diplomacy remains open, and various actors are seeking a way to halt the cycle of escalating tensions before it develops into another round of military confrontation.
Arman-e-Melli: Iran-US tensions at an unprecedented level
In an article, Arman-e-Melli highlighted the complexity of the Iran-US dispute, arguing that the confrontation, shaped by joint US and Israeli attacks on Iran, possesses a level of complexity unlike previous crises. A review of conflicts involving Afghanistan, Libya, Iraq, Syria, and even border disputes over the past decade reveals that none had as many dimensions and layers as the current tensions between Iran and the United States. Part of this complexity stems from Iran s strategic geography and Tehran s geopolitical leverage against Washington and its allies. Another factor is the central role of energy, combined with the connection of these issues to broader regional developments, including the wars in Yemen and Lebanon. Given these circumstances, it is natural that new mediators, including actors from outside the region, continue to become involved. The result is a deeply interconnected conflict environment in which not only Pakistan, Qatar, Oman, Turkey, and China have become active, but Russia has also intensified its engagement.
Kayhan: Hormuz, where the oil price is still decided
Kayhan explained how Iran has used the Strait of Hormuz as leverage to increase economic pressure on the United States. The Strait of Hormuz remains at the center of the regional crisis, providing Iran with a significant geopolitical and economic advantage. In addition to possessing vast oil and gas reserves, Iran is situated alongside one of the world s most critical energy corridors. With oil prices remaining above $100 per barrel and strategic reserves under unprecedented strain, the United States is experiencing the costs of its confrontational policies through historically high interest rates and persistent inflation. Under these conditions, markets are closely monitoring not only military and diplomatic developments but also statements by Iranian officials regarding the security of the Strait of Hormuz, oil exports, and future tensions. Reassuring messages can reduce part of the oil market s risk premium, whereas signs of growing uncertainty can have the opposite effect. The newspaper argued that Iranian officials should carefully consider the market impact of their economic and diplomatic statements.

Supreme court blocks Trump’s bid to restrict gender care for trans prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:25:02 UTC
02:25:02 KST

The US supreme court went against Donald Trump’s administration on Wednesday, refusing to allow the immediate enforcement of sweeping restrictions on gender-affirming care for transgender individuals held in prisons and federal facilities.
The decision marks an unusual victory for transgender rights before the nation’s highest court, which has largely sided with the administration and other opponents of transgender rights in several major cases.
In its latest action, the supreme court turned away an emergency appeal from the justice department seeking to overturn a federal judge’s order that prevents the Federal Bureau of Prisons from putting the controversial restrictions into effect while a lawsuit challenging them moves forward.
Two conservative members of the court, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, publicly opposed the decision.
At the center of the legal battle is a policy introduced earlier this year that would sharply limit medical care and other accommodations available to transgender people in federal custody.
Under the measure, medical and surgical treatments related to gender transition would be prohibited. The restrictions would also extend to “social accommodations”, including access to clothing and hair-removal devices intended to help prisoners present themselves in a way that matches their gender identity. Psychiatric care would remain available under the policy.
The restrictions prompted three transgender people incarcerated at federal correctional facilities in New Jersey, Florida and Minnesota to bring a class-action lawsuit challenging the government’s actions.
The proposed changes represent a big departure from longstanding federal prison practices. According to the plaintiffs, the federal prison system has provided hormone treatment to prisoners experiencing gender dysphoria since at least 1992.
The dispute comes amid Trump’s broader campaign to roll back transgender rights since beginning his second presidential term.
On his first day back in the White House, Trump signed an executive order declaring that the federal government would recognize only two genders, male and female, while portraying transgender identity as false.
The order directed multiple federal agencies to revise their practices, including requirements ensuring that “males are not detained in women’s prisons” and ending government funding for medical procedures provided “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex”.
In defending the prison restrictions in court, government lawyers have characterized gender-transition medical treatment as “unproven sex-rejecting interventions”.
But the plaintiffs challenging the policy have warned that allowing the restrictions to take effect could have devastating consequences. In their legal filing, the plaintiffs argued that a decision favoring the administration would result in “immediate and catastrophic” harm.
They pointed to serious mental health concerns, warning: “Patients who are denied hormone therapy can suffer from increased depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm.”
Wednesday’s decision stands in contrast to several recent supreme court actions involving transgender rights. The court, which holds a 6-3 conservative majority, has issued multiple decisions since last year that have favored restrictions affecting transgender Americans.
Among those decisions, the justices supported state laws preventing transgender athletes from competing on female sports teams at public schools, including colleges and universities.
The court also permitted the Trump administration to enforce its ban on transgender people in the military. In another decision, the justices allowed the administration to prevent passport applicants from selecting gender designations reflecting their gender identities.
The legal fight carries potential consequences for thousands of people within the federal correctional system. More than 2,000 transgender prisoners were housed in federal prisons and halfway houses in 2025, according to reporting from NPR.

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro leads Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by one percentage point in voting intentions ahead of a presidential runoff, according to a Quaest poll published Wednesday by Brazilian news portal UOL.
The survey showed Bolsonaro with 45% of voter preferences, compared with 44% for Lula, placing the candidates in a technical tie within the poll's margin of error of two percentage points.
The survey was conducted nationwide with 2,154 voters aged 16 and older from Oct. 17 to 20. It was commissioned by TV Globo and registered with Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
The results show a slight narrowing of Bolsonaro's lead from the previous Quaest survey on Oct. 14, when he received 46% of voting intentions, with 44% for Lula.
UOL said 9% of respondents said they would cast blank or invalid ballots, or would not vote, while 2% remained undecided.
In a spontaneous voting survey, Lula and Bolsonaro received 40% of responses. An additional 14% of respondents were undecided, while 6% said they would cast blank or invalid ballots or abstain.
The runoff is scheduled for Oct. 25, following the first round on Oct. 4, when Bolsonaro received 47.3% of valid votes, according to official results. Lula secured 45.2%.
Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, is challenging Lula in Sunday's runoff as both candidates seek the presidency.
The region is watching the election closely, given Brazil's economic weight and diplomatic role in Latin America.
The next president will face challenges including economic growth, public security and Brazil’s position on international issues.
Lula is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term, while Bolsonaro is trying to secure the presidency for his political family after his father's 2022 defeat.
