Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:14:42 UTC
02:14:42 KST

When the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?
There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.
It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.
The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.
Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensus that the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail”, while this week’s emissions-gap report could not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short time and won’t on its own reduce energy bills, which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.
The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of the collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whether that is even possible. We talk about heat deaths across 854 European cities over the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously. We look at the social unrest across Europe – which is the fastest-warming continent – and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.
Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy prices won’t be reduced, the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.
We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs, research recently found, and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.
Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.
Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.
One depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means the most depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking by Labour, trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.
- Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say preparing to unveil ‘father of all bombs’

17:12:06 UTC
02:12:06 KST

Iran is preparing to unveil a new weapon described as the “father of all bombs,” a spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday, Anadolu reports.
“We are in the stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs.’ This is something new for the enemy,” Hossein Mohebi said in statements carried by Iran’s Young Journalists Club news agency.
He did not provide further details about the weapon.
On Friday, US President Donald Trump hinted at the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the “mother of all bombs,” to target Iranian nuclear facilities.
Weighing around 9,800 kilograms (21,600 pounds), the GBU-43/B is one of the largest non-nuclear conventional bombs in the US arsenal.
It was first used in April 2017, during Trump’s first presidential term, against a tunnel complex belonging to the ISIS (Daesh) terrorist organization in Afghanistan.
Mohebi also said Iran’s missile stockpile has increased by 1.5 times following the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, without providing specific figures.
“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” he added.
The IRGC spokesman said Iran is shifting its defense doctrine toward establishing permanent and absolute deterrence.
“Previously, Iran’s defense doctrine was purely defensive. We used to say that if a country attacked us, we would respond,” Mohebi said.
“Now, we say that if a country attacks us, we will not only respond but also launch an offensive,” he added.
Mohebi said Iran would respond to any assault with similar measures, stressing that the country’s military doctrine would increasingly rely on asymmetric warfare.
“Our doctrine will no longer be merely offensive; it will be asymmetric. We will attack the enemy in a way that makes them feel the intensity of our response,” he said.
Israel and the US launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, while Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, then began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements concerning freedom of navigation and security in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for energy and goods supplies.

The Sargan-3000 naval drone has destroyed a Russian Geran strike drone using an interceptor drone.
The Ukrainian Navy published footage of the engagement on its social media.
The interception was carried out using a Ukrainian Sting interceptor manufactured by Wild Hornets. It was launched from a container-based platform on the surface vessel.
The Sargan-3000 was officially commissioned into the Ukrainian Navy in April 2026.
It is designed to carry out combat missions at considerable distances from Ukraine’s coast.
The naval drone has an operational radius of up to 1,600 km. It can reach speeds of 40 to 55 knots and carry a payload of up to 450 kg.
In September, the vessel destroyed a Russian unmanned surface vessel with machine-gun fire during the first engagement between unmanned surface platforms.
In early October, the Sargan-3000 also successfully shot down a Russian Geran drone using its machine gun.
To engage the aerial target, it used a remotely operated Protector remote weapon station (RWS) equipped with a 12.7 mm machine gun.
The Ukrainian Defense Ministry has also authorized Wild Hornets to conduct air defense operations.
The ministry’s order allows the company to form its own air defense groups for its Night Hornets counter-drone unit.
The new network will include remote-control centers, field positions and a remote drone-launch system based on Hornet Vision Ctrl technology.

Defense Without Limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:10:54 UTC
02:10:54 KST

Defense Without Limits
Iranian officials say Tehran will place no limits on hitting aggressors and their regional backers in case of a renewed US-Israeli attack
TEHRAN – The tone of the enemy toward Iran has sharply escalated again, with senior American and Israeli officials openly speaking of finishing the job and some analysts warning a new round of war is near, while Iranian political and military officials say the country is fully ready for a severe and unrestricted response.
An informed Iranian source told Press TV that Iran has prepared for an all-out, multi-layered and comprehensive war. According to the source, Tehran has made a firm decision that in reaction to any aggression, assassination and terror, it will respond without any limitation or restraint and will crush with full force the accessible interests and targets of the aggressors and their supporters in the region.
From Tehran's point of view, the source said, the US will not launch an attack without Israel, nor Israel without the US, and talk of their independence from each other in a war against Iran resembles a bitter joke. The explicit threats by American officials and the Zionist regime to attack Iran, the source added, have provided the legal and moral license for Iran to adopt necessary defensive measures.
"We will soon finish the job"
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had been "systematically destroyed, both militarily and financially, and unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job."
In the same post, Trump gave his "complete and total endorsement" to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 parliamentary election, suggesting Washington could take on the fight itself if Netanyahu failed to stay in power: with the "wrong Leader" in Israel, "America will have to do this work ourselves."
Trump did not specify what action he had in mind. Earlier this month he had said the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 US midterm elections and had spoken of "productive discussions." His latest comments came after he and Netanyahu discussed a possible new military operation, according to Axios, which reported last week that Netanyahu raised intelligence suggesting Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear program. Trump has also raised the possibility of striking the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near Natanz.
At a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, Trump said the US was in a position to walk away from the war now, describing Iran as devastated and adding: "They're not going to have a nuclear weapon."
Netanyahu matched the tone. In a briefing with Israeli journalists on Sunday, he declared that bringing down the Islamic Republic remained a key objective and that he had directed all security agencies to pursue it: "We must bring this regime down once and for all."
Presenting an updated security doctrine, he said, as reported by Israel Hayom: "The objectives I set do not depend on American approval. To the extent necessary, we will also act independently. We have done so before, and if necessary, we will do so again. We are prepared to take the initiative. We must prevent the enemy from delivering the first blow."
He described confronting Iran as his "life's mission," claimed "90% of the job is done" by pointing to economic pressure and protests, and responded to Trump's endorsement with: "Together we will complete the mission!" In a video of a phone call released Monday, he told Trump: "Donald, we have a job to finish, you said it, and we'll finish it together."
In an interview with Fox News on October 18, Netanyahu warned Iran is developing intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching US cities and seeking nuclear warheads, saying: "You are the real target." He listed as his first priority if reelected: "First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world."
Unannounced visit and election countdown
The rhetoric moved with military signals. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth paid an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, October 19, meeting Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz at Ovda Air Base in the Negev. Spokesman Doron Spielman said they discussed "the threats in the region" and offensive-defensive cooperation. The Pentagon gave no details.
On Tuesday, Hegseth told US troops in the Central Command area: "I got to see some of our warfighters — they're preparing and ready to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon," adding they were "ready to go."
Israel canceled soldiers' leave from Thursday ahead of the vote. Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said forces were on "a high level of alertness and readiness" against "external interference." Netanyahu told i24NEWS on Tuesday that Iran and its proxies could try to disrupt the October 27 election.
"Either a deal or an attack"
The Financial Times reported on Wednesday, October 21, citing a person familiar with Israeli planning, that renewed US-Israeli strikes in the coming weeks are "not an unreasonable scenario." Three sources said Netanyahu urged the military earlier this month to prepare a multi-day offensive including nuclear sites, planned for the weekend of October 10, which did not proceed after Trump opposed action before the US midterms. One source said: "There will either be a deal or an attack."
White House deputy spokesperson Anna Kelly told the FT the US "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections." The New York Times quoted Raz Zimmt of Tel Aviv's INSS as saying: "The baseline expectation in Iran, and in Israel, is that it's a matter of when the war restarts, not if." He added a strike alone would likely not achieve Washington's goals but might give Trump "an image of victory and a way out."
Ready for war, ready for diplomacy
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iraq's Al-Ekhbariya chanel that Iran entered three rounds of talks and all three led to war. "We were in the midst of negotiations and in the end it was proven that the Americans cannot be trusted. In the third round, we reached an understanding with Trump, but Trump himself violated it and adhered to it for only two weeks."
After more than eight months, Washington has achieved none of its objectives, he said, calling that a strategic failure for the US and a strategic success for Iran. America is now in a deep quagmire, resorting to military threats, sanctions and pressure on neighbors not to cooperate with Tehran, without result. "Iran will never surrender, neither to sanctions nor to military threats. The only solution is diplomacy and a negotiated solution."
"Every possibility exists, including that the Americans and the Zionist regime will start another war. But we are in full readiness. We are fully prepared to defend ourselves and will stand until the last moment," Araghchi said. "When I say we are ready for war, it does not mean we want war. It is a message to do calculations and not enter that war again. We are as ready for diplomacy as we are for war."
The main deterrent, he argued, is that readiness: Americans know war cannot deliver their goals. In the two wars, they "fell into Israel's trap, more precisely Netanyahu's trap. Netanyahu will do anything for his personal goal, not for America, Israel or anyone else."
In a Financial Times essay titled "The false assumptions about us are dangerous," Araghchi wrote that a way forward requires Washington to accept it has "no military options." Trump entered the war on "fundamentally erroneous assumptions," being wrongly told Iranian forces are unprepared, despite lessons learned since 2025. "In June 2025 and February 2026, they bombed us while we were negotiating. And in June this year, shortly after an agreement was signed by Presidents Pezeshkian and Trump, we were attacked a third time. How can we trust a US president again?"
He recalled presenting a Seven-Day Plan via mediators at the UN General Assembly under which the US would do nothing it had not already agreed to: the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on Day 6, talks for a final deal on Day 7. He cited Moody's that the war has cost US consumers $265 billion this year, about $2,000 per household, half from energy prices, plus damaged bases and equipment losses. Further escalation, he warned, would put civilian lives, regional states and the world economy at great risk and bring "even greater strategic failure."
Defense without restraint
Armed Forces General Staff spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi replied to Trump and Netanyahu: "We tell the child-killing twins, Trump and Netanyahu: you are on the slope of decline, and with boasting you will not save yourselves from the swamp of death."
New Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, approved Sunday with 237 votes, wrote he devoted his first working hour to the IRGC Aerospace Force and Army air defense: "For us, responding to threats is not a rhetorical contest; it is turning threats into greater readiness. We are focused on our targets with new technologies; we eat dust but we will not give away soil."
National Security Commission Chairman Ebrahim Azizi wrote on X: "Regardless of your election results, we have no doubt about your hostility. We are ready, in response to any operational mistake, to wipe you off the map."
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei wrote Wednesday on X, reacting to the US Secretary of State's call to condemn Iran over Persian Gulf insecurity: "In less than nine months, they attacked Iran twice in the middle of negotiations; they slaughtered our children in Minab, killed our daughters in Lamard, assassinated our leaders, and intensified sanctions; and now, after blatantly violating the understanding they signed, while claiming victory, they ask the world to condemn Iran." The world, he said, is paying for US-Israeli law-breaking, from regional turmoil to energy insecurity. "You cannot set fires, throw the region into chaos, then stand as plaintiff and ask others to condemn the victim."
Ball in Washington's court
Tehran sees a deadlock not easily broken. The gap over the balance of conflict, US pressure to force submission before the midterms, Iran's tighter control of Hormuz and action against violating vessels, oil above $110 after two tankers carrying 4 million barrels hit mines — one burning, one halted — the criticized diesel deal with Russia, and Hegseth's secret talks with Netanyahu alongside UAE officials all point to continued tension.
 
While unofficial sources speak of a Pakistan-Qatar proposal, Tehran believes Trump seeks to pass the midterms, not end a costly war whose declared goals keep changing. Iran does not doubt Islamabad's sincerity, but the ball, officials say, is in Washington's court. Until the US abandons the illusion of forcing surrender and imposing unilateral terms, by negotiation or aggression, the conflict will not end.

Russian Su-30SM Fighter Jet Falls From Sky and Crashes Near Cemetery in Kaliningrad
A Russian Su-30SM fighter jet fell from the sky and crashed near a cemetery in Russia’s Kaliningrad region on October 21 during a training flight. Both pilots managed to eject before the aircraft hit the ground but reportedly sustained injuries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russian media outlet REN TV on October 21, the crash occurred at approximately 12:53 p.m. local time in the Chernyakhovsk district, between the villages of Timofeyevka and Zelyony Bor. Both crew members reportedly sustained injuries and were transported to a military hospital.
Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed the crash, stating that the Su-30SM had been conducting a scheduled training flight without ammunition. The ministry claimed the aircraft fell in an unpopulated area and that neither pilot’s injuries were life-threatening.
The Ukrainian OSINT Telegram channel Exilenova+ released footage purportedly capturing the moment the Russian fighter descended toward the ground and crashed near a cemetery.
The cause of the crash remains unknown, with Russian authorities investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Kaliningrad is a strategically important Russian exclave situated between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. The region hosts the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and several military aviation facilities, including an air base near Chernyakhovsk that operates Su-30SM fighters.
The Su-30SM is a twin-engine, two-seat multirole fighter designed for air superiority missions, interception, and strikes against ground and maritime targets. The aircraft is operated by both the Russian Aerospace Forces and Russian Naval Aviation.
Earlier, on September 7, two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collided mid-air over Russia’s Kursk region, killing one pilot while the other survived. The cause of the collision remains unknown.

Macron visits Riyadh to show solidarity amid Houthi attacks, ease tensions at home via fuel deal
French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday paid an unannounced visit to Riyadh in a bid to underscore French support for the kingdom amid intensified attacks by Houthi rebels and an attempt to ease tensions at home by securing oil and diesel imports.

French President Emmanuel Macron visited Riyadh on Wednesday for a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in the kingdom since Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis intensified their attacks this month.
The unannounced trip sent a strong signal to his oil-rich Saudi ally as Riyadh comes under near-daily attack.
Read moreSaudi reports fresh Houthi attacks as France pledges to defend key oil port
It was part of a Gulf tour to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France, following a weekend of violent protests over soaring living costs.
Faced with criticism of his Gulf tour in France, Macron told reporters he was just “doing his job” in a bid to “ease tensions” over gas prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France.
“There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.”
Read more'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence
Macron met de facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the Élysée Palace said. An AFP journalist on the scene said the French president spent less than three hours on the ground.
The pair agreed that Saudi Arabia would supply additional diesel to France “for as many months as necessary”, and to consult on expanded security cooperation and infrastructure projects to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, the palace added.
Earlier the presidency said the visit would “demonstrate France’s solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory”.
In recent weeks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing Riyadh to shut its main airport and postpone a major investment conference.
A Houthi maritime blockade is also threatening oil exports from the kingdom.
Macron’s visit comes as Saudi Arabia seeks to rally Western support in the face of Houthi attacks.
Watch moreWar escalates between Houthis and Riyadh: How did we get here?
‘Personnel deployed’
Earlier on Wednesday, Macron said France had sent troops to help shield the key Saudi oil terminal of Yanbu on the Red Sea from Houthi attacks, while insisting it was important that “discussions resume” with the group.
“For the past eight days, we’ve had personnel and capabilities deployed (in Yanbu); we’re working with Saudi Arabia in this direction, and so we have a defensive role to play,” he told reporters in the Qatari capital.
The world’s biggest crude exporter had been relying on Yanbu to export its oil, after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war.
Last month, Macron said in a televised interview that France would send “military means” to help shield the Yanbu terminal from Houthi attacks.
On Tuesday, the UK government announced it would deploy British fighter jets to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against increasing attacks.
As part of his tour, Macron secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, as well as two terawatt-hours per month of LNG from Qatar.
In July, a truce in Yemen dating back to 2022 fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh’s control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.
In response, the Saudi air force has frequently targeted the group in support of pro-government forces.

Mexico revives rare treason charge against former state prosecutor
Unknown

02:06:43 KST

Mexico levies rare treason charge against ex-official over US drug operation
MEXICO CITY, Oct 21 - Mexican federal prosecutors charged a former state prosecutor with treason on Wednesday after accusing him of allowing US personnel to take part in a drug operation in northern Mexico without the federal government's approval.
Authorities dusted off one of the country's gravest and least-used criminal charges against former Chihuahua Attorney General Cesar Jauregui, in a case that could reshape how Mexican officials work with US security forces.
Prosecutors allege Jauregui allowed US agents to participate in an April raid on a suspected drug lab in Chihuahua, a border state that has long been central to Mexico's fight against organized crime.
The raid only came to light after two of the US agents were killed in a car crash returning from the scene, drawing scrutiny from President Claudia Sheinbaum and pitting her against opposition Governor Maru Campos.
A judge ordered Jauregui be held in pretrial detention while the court decides whether there is enough evidence to formally proceed with a criminal case. A follow-up hearing is scheduled for Saturday, according to a statement from the Attorney General's Office.
Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said Jauregui allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and failed to share information with federal officials as required.
FEDERAL CONTROL OVER US TIES
Analysts said the case could have consequences beyond Chihuahua, as the federal government moves to tighten control over security cooperation with the United States.
"The treason charge... seeks to set a precedent and prevent cooperation between (Mexican) states and the US government without the federal government's coordination and approval," said Matias Gomez Leautaud, an analyst at Eurasia Group.
He said the case fits a broader push by the federal Security Ministry to centralize information-sharing with the United States, curb unilateral actions by US agencies and bring state-level initiatives under federal control.
Gomez Leautaud said there was also a clear political dimension, given Chihuahua is governed by the opposition and could become a key battleground ahead of Mexico's 2027 midterm elections.
TREASON LAW RARELY TESTED
Treason cases are extremely rare in Mexico. No widely recognized conviction has been recorded since 1867, when Emperor Maximilian was executed after the government of Benito Juarez found that his French-backed rule violated Mexico's sovereignty.
Mexican law does not spell out treason in a single definition, but it broadly covers acts against the country's sovereignty, independence or territorial integrity carried out for the benefit of a foreign power.
In 2024, prosecutors also sought to bring treason charges against Joaquin Guzman Lopez, one of the sons of jailed drug lord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. That case has not led to a conviction, with Guzman Lopez currently detained in the US. REUTERS

As Miatta ignites the speaker’s gas-fuelled inferno, Reform show up as snowflakes | John Crace
Unknown

2026-10-21
17:06:41 UTC

When is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.
There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.
Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current one.
Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.
Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.
The speaker was less than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.
For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.
PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.
Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.
By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water.
For the rest of PMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.
It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?
That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.
As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.
How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.

OpenAI has revealed that two of its artificial intelligence agents disabled or weakened systems built to catch them misbehaving, with one later denying it had done so.
The cases are the latest in a string of safety scares at the world's top AI developers involving agents, AI programs that carry out tasks without human involvement.

Three days later, a GPT-6 Astra agent stripped out its own monitor while copying code from another project, then told the human programmer it had done no such thing.
The company said it had also seen several cases of agents launching software with monitoring switched off, exposing a gap in its oversight.
OpenAI said it is still trying to determine whether the models were simply overzealous in following instructions or have a particular tendency to evade monitoring.
"We don't yet have a satisfying explanation for this behaviour,"
it said.
The disclosure adds to mounting unease over how well leading labs can control increasingly autonomous systems.

Super Typhoon Champi sets the record for strongest storm of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:01:31 UTC
02:01:31 KST

A cyclone in the Philippine Sea reached wind speeds of about 185 miles per hour (around 290 kilometers per hour) on Tuesday afternoon EST. Those wind speeds are the strongest of any storm this year, forecasters say.
As of Wednesday morning EST, Super Typhoon Champi had winds of 175 miles per hour; it is expected to weaken in the next day or so, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The storm is currently about 430 nautical miles south of Kadena Air Base in Japan and is heading northwest, according to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.
You’re more likely to see strong storms in the western Pacific than anywhere else on the planet. But the typhoon underscores how tumultuous Pacific storm activity has been in comparison with activity in the Atlantic. In the North Atlantic, 2026’s strongest storm so far was Hurricane Isaias, which had maximum winds of about 120 mph (193 kph), according to Colorado State University’s (CSU’s) cyclone database. By contrast, in the northeastern Pacific, September’s Hurricane Polo hit wind speeds of about 178 mph (286 kph), while in the northwestern Pacific, April’s Typhoon Sinlaku and July’s Typhoon Bavi also reached around the same strength. Champi is the 25th northwestern Pacific storm this year, according to CSU’s tracker.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To be considered a typhoon or a hurricane, a cyclone must achieve wind speeds of at least 74 mph (119 kph). The designation of hurricane or typhoon depends on where the cyclone occurs. In the Northern Hemisphere, Pacific cyclones that occur west of the international date line are considered typhoons, while those occurring east of that border are categorized as hurricanes.
It’s been a historic year for cyclones. As Scientific American previously reported, the Atlantic has been unusually quiet: Hurricane Isaias was the first storm of its kind for the season, setting a record for the latest-forming first Atlantic hurricane since reliable record-keeping began. Meanwhile the Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific Ocean have seen an unusually high number of hurricanes this season.
Those trends are driven in part by El Niño, a climate pattern that influences weather across the globe. During El Niño years, hurricanes activity tends to slow in the Atlantic and pick up in parts of the Pacific.

Johnston Marklee unveils designs for Bass Museum expansion

Johnston Marklee unveils designs for Bass Museum expansion
California architecture studio Johnston Marklee has unveiled designs to expand the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach, USA, including elevated galleries and courtyard spaces.
The project will extend the Museum of Art (the Bass) into the 22,000-square-foot area at the southwest corner of the museum’s campus with indoor and outdoor space.
Renderings show two rectangular pavilion structures that sit on a thin concrete plane, elevated off the ground to meet “resiliency guidelines”, likely in reference to Miami-Dade County’s stated floodwater risks due to sea-level rise. Courtyards will pass underneath the structure.
This elevated structure also keeps the corner of the property open and increases public access, according to Johnston Marklee founding partner Sharon Johnston, who called the project “transformative”.
“Through careful analysis of light and shadow, space and volume, and the surrounding park and urban context, we are planning a transformative project that will increase public access to the museum’s programs and artworks,” said Johnston.
Formally, the expansion will feature sheer white walls for the upper structures, with more texture on the walls at ground level, underneath the elevated structures.
At the centre of the project, a backlit oculus will illuminate the passage under the structure at night.
The passages will also lead to landscape garden areas, with the blank face of one of the pavilions providing a screen for screenings.
This space will connect to the trees that are part of Collins Park, which extends from the east face of the museum.
Facade perforations will be placed at the top of the rectangular pavilions and on the walls separating the covered courtyards from the street.
The expansion builds upon the original art deco building designed by Russell Pancoast as a library in the 1930s before the Bass opened in 1964 and the Arata Isozaki expansion.
Primary exhibition space will be held in the rectangular pavilion structures, with renderings showing white-wall galleries, rectangular windows and a skylight placed on top of the one nearest to the Isozaki building.
“We are thrilled to reimagine the southwest corner of Collins Park for The Bass,” said Johnston Marklee founding partner Mark Lee.
“This project continues the storied architectural heritage of the museum, preserving Russell Pancoast’s 1942 Art Deco design while honoring Arata Isozaki’s vision of a porous campus.”
Other recent projects by Johnston Marklee include a green-metal skyscraper in Phoenix and a minimalist pavilion for Danish furniture brand Vipp in Upstate New York.

AI could turn scientific papers into research assistants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

AI could turn scientific papers into research assistants
One method for doing this works faster and more accurately than general-purpose AI
Scientific papers may be getting a 21st century update.
A system called Paper2Agent lets scientists do more than read a new scientific study. When a paper comes with code, methods and data, the system packages these into a tool set that an AI assistant can use to work with new data, researchers report September 16 in Nature.
The system is essentially “a virtual author of the paper,” available around the clock, says James Zou, a computer scientist at Stanford University.
In tests, Zou and colleagues tried to convert 100 computational biology papers into working tool sets and succeeded with 74. The others had obstacles such as missing code or data, or software that wouldn’t run. With the papers that were converted, the Paper2Agent tool set could run analyses of the published work and answer questions about the results. It did so more accurately and also more than twice as fast as the same agent working from the original papers and accompanying code.
Making another scientist’s code usable can take substantial work, says Peter Clark, a senior research director at the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in Seattle who was not involved in developing Paper2Agent. Researchers already share code on platforms such as GitHub. But Clark says he often has to “grub around” for half a day to figure out how to get it running.
A general-purpose AI assistant such as Claude can help, he says, but it typically generates new code on the fly. Paper2Agent instead packages code associated with a paper into reusable tools, tests them against reference outputs and writes step-by-step instructions guiding an AI assistant on which tools to use and in what order. This streamlines and standardizes the process of using AI to interact with scientific research, Clark says. It’s “an exciting step” toward papers that actively help scientists.
To Zou, transforming scientific papers into agents seem like a natural next step for transmitting knowledge. We’ve already moved from stone tablets and papyrus to paper and then to digital formats, he says, and now it’s time to move from passive to active formats for human knowledge. A paper-agent can help one human scientist quickly use another’s code and methods. The tool can also search for paper-agents about similar topics with the aim of alerting their human authors about potential collaborations.
Zou says his team has already created “over 100 different paper-agents” from their own work and that these have already helped him find other scientists to collaborate with.
Clark notes that Paper2Agent specializes in helping scientists reuse methods and code, and not in answering general questions, like a true virtual author should be able to do. Also, he worries about what could happen if millions of low-quality papers get turned into agents capable of pestering scientists. That could make things “worse rather than better,” he says, recalling the days of Clippy, the much-maligned Microsoft Office assistant. But he’d love for a “non-annoying agent” to pop up and tell him about work that he should be paying attention to.
For more open-ended questions about a paper, Clark says he would still want to talk to the people who did the research. “The reason I would write to a corresponding author is for precisely the things they didn’t put in the paper.”

From learning to leading: How students can pass on Jewish tradition - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

I know when I am being influenced.
I’ve spent a good portion of my career involved in marketing. I am familiar with the mechanics behind influencer marketing, the commercial relationships, and the carefully constructed campaigns. Despite this knowledge, when I trust the person speaking, something changes. I become curious about the product and, despite knowing exactly what is happening, I find myself paying closer attention.
The world’s largest brands have been paying close attention to this phenomenon. Earlier this year, Unilever CEO Fernando Fernandez announced plans to significantly increase the company’s investment in influencers and creators, identifying social media as a primary driver of consumer engagement and brand growth.
This decision reflects a broader evolution in marketing strategy, in which companies increasingly recognize that individuals can carry a brand’s message into networks of existing relationships, where trust has already been established.
Where influence becomes education
Influence itself is hardly a new phenomenon. Long before social media made it possible to accumulate millions of followers, people learned from one another. Parents shape the way children see the world; teachers offer guidance to their students; friends introduce one another to ideas, products, and experiences; and religious and communal leaders shape the values and behaviors of the people around them.
While technology evolves, human nature doesn’t. People connect with people. Consumers respond to individuals they find credible, which is why brands now route their messages through them. Students behave the same way. A message lands differently when it comes from someone in their own orbit who speaks with conviction.
Education sits squarely within this dynamic. Schools are environments of influence, where ideas, values, and ways of understanding the world move continually between teachers, students, and peers.
Over the past two years, I have personally visited more than 50 schools in 15 countries. Through the Yael Foundation, we have a bird’s-eye view of 150 schools across 49 countries. Seeing such a wide range of educational environments has made me increasingly attentive to what happens when students themselves become part of that process of influence.
Some schools are creating deliberate opportunities for students to explain, represent, teach, advocate, and lead. In doing so, they give young people the experience of owning an idea and carrying it to someone else.
That raises a question for Jewish education: how deliberately are we preparing students to carry forward to their peers what they have learned?
Influencer marketing works on the creator, too. To speak convincingly about a topic, a creator has to study it, internalize it, and make it their own. Over time, an idea presented again and again becomes part of the person presenting it. When students hear about Jewish culture and identity from a peer, the message arrives with that peer’s conviction attached. They see an identity someone their own age has chosen to adopt.
Jewish continuity depends upon the transmission of knowledge, values, and traditions. A teacher who has earned the respect of his or her students will be far more successful at teaching them about the power of prayer. A parent who understands what excites their child will do a better job of making Jewish holidays positive experiences. A camp counselor to whom campers relate can model joyful and proud Jewish identity so that young people can picture it for themselves.
If influence is one of the primary ways human beings learn from one another, then learning how to influence responsibly is itself an educational opportunity.
We were all influencers once
Show-and-tell is a child’s first masterclass in influencer marketing. The child has to decide what matters, figure out how to advocate for its value, and make their peers care about it. The exercise teaches ownership and communication, beginning with the child’s own judgment about what is worth sharing.
This is where the concept of “influencer education” becomes useful.
The phrase “influencer education” may raise eyebrows in a Jewish school. However, it is a principle the practice of show-and-tell already offers: choosing an idea, understanding it well enough to advocate for it, and bringing others along. Schools can build that practice into students’ experience purposefully and intentionally.
What influence looks like in a school
I have seen this happen in schools in ways that are easy to overlook because they often sit outside the formal curriculum. At one school, high school students conduct campus tours for visitors without the head of school or principal accompanying them. They explain the school’s ethos and traditions, answer questions, and describe their experience of the community in their own words. The adults have entrusted the students with the institution’s story, giving them an opportunity to discover what it means to represent something larger than themselves.
The educational value extends well past public speaking. A student responsible for explaining a community to an outsider must understand that community well enough to articulate its character, make judgments about what matters, and respond thoughtfully to a question they did not anticipate.
Another school has entrusted nine-year-olds with responsibility for a tzedakah (charity) committee. The students research local charities and present their recommendations to their peers, while photographs of the committee members are displayed prominently on the school wall. The visual reminder reinforces the seriousness of their role, and the process itself requires them to move from learning about a Jewish value to deciding how to express it.
The same principle appears in school-wide events and assemblies, where students take responsibility for the content and execution, with adults deliberately stepping out of the visible role. It appears when older students mentor younger children and introduce them to traditions, ideas, and practices that would otherwise reach them only through adults.
Each experience gives students something to carry and someone to carry it to. That is the essence of influencer education.
Cultivating influence intentionally
Influence is often treated as a personality trait. We describe certain children as natural leaders or gifted communicators, as though their ability to bring others along were something they simply possessed.
Psychologist Albert Bandura’s work on self-efficacy identified “mastery experiences” as the most reliable source of confidence-building. Confidence develops when individuals take action, assume responsibility, and experience the results of their efforts firsthand. The experience of leading a discussion, mentoring a younger student, organizing an event, or representing a community shapes how young people understand their own capabilities.
If influence develops through practice, schools can offer these opportunities to every child, including students who would never volunteer. Each child who leads a discussion or explains a tradition to a younger student gains evidence that their perspective has value.
From traditional instruction to influencer education
Conventional pedagogy is built to deliver knowledge. Educators present material, and students learn it, demonstrate mastery, and move forward. Jewish learning has an added responsibility, because every child receives a heritage that existed before they were born and must last beyond them.
Pirkei Avot opens with that heritage passing from person to person: Moshe received the Torah at Sinai and passed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. It has moved the same way ever since, through stories told at Shabbat tables and through teachers, parents, and counselors we trusted, respected, and loved. We remember what they taught us and how they made us feel.
The world’s largest brands have spent billions arriving at the same insight: people follow the example of those they trust and feel connected to.
A student who explains a holiday to a younger sibling, rallies classmates around a tzedakah cause, or welcomes a new family into the community has joined that chain. They have become the trusted person in someone else’s Jewish life.
Educators have already asked, “What does a student need to learn at this stage?” Influencer education adds a second question: “Where will they practice passing it on?” A campus tour, a tzedakah committee, or a younger student to mentor gives them somewhere to teach, something to represent, and a chance to speak in their own words. At the end of each school day, that leaves one final question: “Who did our students inspire today?”
The writer is the COO of the Yael Foundation, which nurtures and expands accessible, high-quality educational opportunities for Jewish children globally.

Macron makes surprise Saudi visit as France secures extra diesel supplies
French president meets Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh to discuss energy, security, and infrastructure as cost-of-living protests rage at home.
French President Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Riyadh on a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s Houthis intensified their attacks this month.
Macron met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Saudi capital, and the two discussed regional and international developments, as well as coordinating efforts to strengthen security and stability, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported on Wednesday.
The unannounced trip comes as Saudi Arabia agreed to supply extra diesel to France “for as many months as necessary”, the Elysee Palace told the AFP news agency.
The visit aims to “demonstrate France’s solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies”, the French presidency said earlier.
The diplomatic push follows days of rioting in France, fuelled by the cost of living, especially as the US-Iran war and Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy prices high.
Faced with criticism of his Gulf tour at home, Macron told reporters earlier in Doha that he was just “doing his job” in a bid to “ease tensions” over petrol prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France.
“There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.”
Macron’s Gulf tour
The deal follows pledges secured earlier in Macron’s Gulf tour. The presidency said on Tuesday that the United Arab Emirates had committed to about 100,000 tonnes a month, with a further 100,000 tonnes monthly to be secured in Bahrain.
Together with Saudi deliveries, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just more than 10 percent of its consumption, it said.
Meanwhile, France is also sending military assets to Saudi Arabia, under an earlier agreement, to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
The United Kingdom also announced on Tuesday that it would deploy fighter jets to help shield the kingdom. Both countries say their support is purely defensive.
Analysts say the moves protect Saudi oil exports that matter to Europe’s energy markets and bolster the Gulf alliance as the US shows reluctance to offer direct military help. They also carry risks, analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

Russian scientist convicted of treason refuses food and water over alleged abuse in detention
Valery Kachin, a geodesist from Birobidzhan who was sentenced in January 2025 to 14 years in a penal colony for treason, has begun a dry hunger strike at Pretrial Detention Center No. 1 in Izhevsk, the human rights group Department One (Pervy Otdel) reported.
In a letter from the detention center, Kachin, 39, said he had stopped eating and drinking after staff tormented and physically assaulted him. He said he has been held continuously in a punishment cell: After an initial seven days, he was given another 10 days, followed by two consecutive 15-day terms. He said staff force him to raise and lower a heavy bed by himself, even though he is not required to do so. He said staff also conduct nighttime inspections and confiscate personal belongings from his cell.
“This morning, after we traded insults, they forced me to the floor. I bruised my face on the floor, and my elbows and knees are scraped. I started a hunger strike this morning — no water or food. Tell everyone,” he wrote, according to Pervy Otdel.
Kachin is 182 centimeters (about 6 feet) tall and weighs just 60 kilograms (132 pounds), the group said.
Kachin previously began a dry hunger strike in September 2025 at Penal Colony No. 8, known as Khokhryaki, in Udmurtia. He went on that strike after spending 60 days in a punishment cell. He said that while there, he was unable to keep to the vegan diet he has followed for 14 years. He had received food assistance from Vegan Peredachki (Vegan Care Packages), an initiative whose volunteers arrange vegan meals for political prisoners, but prisoners in punishment cells cannot receive care packages.
Kachin’s case became public in December 2022. On January 27, 2025, the Birobidzhan City Court sentenced him to 14 years in a high-security prison. He was then transferred to a penal colony in Udmurtia.
Kachin last worked as a junior researcher at the Bastak Nature Reserve in Birobidzhan. The news outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti reported that he had used social media to voice support for Alexei Navalny and the protests in Belarus and to speak out against the war in Ukraine.

Developers say key patches ready after websites go dark
October 21, 2026
The updates patching the recently leaked PHP security issues are now online, developers of the open-source programming language said on Wednesday afternoon.
"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the team said in an online statement.
Millions of websites worldwide, including critical infrastructure and government portals, as well as news sites and online shops, rely on PHP. The software is free.
The new patches aim to fix two "critical vulnerabilities" hackers could exploit to remotely take control of websites and servers, bypassing usual obstacles such as password-protected accounts. The gaps were labeled CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.
By exploiting them, malicious actors could gain access to government databases and customer data, deface websites, or compromise entire businesses or other online services.
"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation said in a blog post.
Cloudflare reports 'early attacks'
The weaknesses were flagged by two separate security companies, Calif and Wiz, this August. Both of the firms used AI tools to detect the PHP issues.
PHP developers kept the flaws confidential while working on the fix. News of the security issues, however, leaked on Tuesday, a day before the scheduled update.
Hours before the PHP update, Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of security firm Cloudflare, said hackers were already trying to exploit these weaknesses.
"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," he said in an online post.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
NSA urges taking websites offline if update not feasible
Authorities in multiple countries, including Australia, Japan, and several European nations, issued warnings and took down government websites in an effort to preempt potential attacks.
In France, the website of the Paris Police Prefecture was taken offline due to "detection of a critical security vulnerability," along with local government pages. Germany's government IT service took down some sites that used PHP. Belgium's Foreign Ministry temporarily blocked its own online presence, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency took itself online as a precaution.
The US National Security Agency (NSA) warned that vulnerabilities "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database."
"If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," they said on X.
Meanwhile, the White House said it was informed of the issue last week and that US federal agencies were assessing the potential impact to government systems and infrastructure.

Macron calls Trump's France riot claims ‘stupid’ as Mélenchon accuses Netanyahu of meddling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:55:31 UTC
01:55:31 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday sharply criticized U.S. President Donald Trump and other foreign leaders for exploiting France's recent riots for political gain, accusing them of amplifying misinformation and promoting false claims that Muslim immigrants were attempting to take over the country.
The diplomatic confrontation came as France faced growing political tensions ahead of its 2027 presidential election, with far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon separately accusing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of influencing French elections.
Speaking to reporters in Doha, Qatar, during a tour of Gulf states, Macron said the looting and violence that swept Paris and other French cities over the weekend had been followed by foreign manipulation of information, producing statements he described as unacceptable and foolish.
Asked directly whether his criticism was aimed at Trump, Macron replied: "Among others."
The French president said AI-generated images depicting events that had never occurred in France were being circulated alongside misleading narratives about the unrest. He rejected claims that the violence amounted to an Islamist or immigrant uprising.
Macron argued that politicians facing elections, both in the Middle East and across the Atlantic, were using France's domestic crisis to advance their own political agendas.
Trump claims Islam is trying to take over France
Trump first intervened in the French unrest early last week, when demonstrations initially centered on deteriorating conditions in the country's schools. The U.S. president rejected the explanation that education-related grievances were driving the protests, instead blaming immigration and Islam.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump described the situation as uncontrolled mass migration and claimed that Islam was seeking to take over what he called a once-great country.
Following Saturday's violent disturbances, during which more than 2,000 people were arrested and approximately 3,000 businesses were reportedly looted or damaged, Trump again attacked France's immigration policies.
"France is burning!" he declared, blaming immigration from societies he described as fundamentally different and urging French authorities to close the country's borders before it was too late.
The protests, however, began over school funding, deteriorating educational facilities and rising living costs. Hundreds of thousands of people participated in largely peaceful demonstrations, although widespread looting, vandalism and confrontations with police erupted on their margins. French authorities have not established that Muslim immigrants were chiefly responsible for the violence.
Macron pointed to the circulation of fabricated images as evidence of how the unrest was being misrepresented internationally. One widely shared AI-generated image purported to show an elderly couple who had been robbed and stripped to their underwear during the riots. Fact-checkers established that the picture was fabricated, while French prosecutors said they had no evidence confirming the alleged attack.
The president did not specify precisely which AI-generated images he was referring to in his remarks Wednesday or identify the foreign actors responsible for the alleged manipulation.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said his ministry was prepared to provide explanations to foreign governments to help them avoid spreading misinformation or amplifying baseless allegations on social media.
Macron's criticism also appeared to extend beyond Trump. Netanyahu, who faces an Israeli election on October 27, said Tuesday that France was experiencing what he described as an invasion of extremist Islam. Macron did not mention the Israeli prime minister by name, although he referred to foreign leaders campaigning both in the region and across the Atlantic.
Mélenchon accuses Netanyahu of influencing French elections
The accusations of foreign involvement have also become part of France's increasingly heated domestic political debate.
Last week, Foreign Minister Barrot warned of attempts by foreign actors to interfere in France's presidential election, scheduled for April and May 2027. He cited billionaire Elon Musk and an Israeli company among those raising concerns about outside influence on French political discourse.
According to Barrot, foreign actors have sought to exploit existing divisions over immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, using those contentious issues to deepen hostility and social tensions.
The minister referred specifically to an Israeli company accused of creating fake French social media accounts to manufacture confrontations over the Palestinian issue. The company was apparently BlackCore, which French authorities linked to an online influence operation targeting candidates from Mélenchon's La France Insoumise party, or LFI, during the municipal elections in March.
In June, Viginum, France's government agency responsible for detecting foreign digital interference, reported evidence linking the operation to Israeli actors, including BlackCore. The campaign sought to discredit LFI candidates and amplify divisive political messages. The agency also noted that the operation had achieved very limited visibility online.
French authorities requested Israeli assistance in investigating the allegations. However, the findings did not establish that Netanyahu personally directed the campaign or that the Israeli government had ordered it.
Mélenchon nevertheless invoked Netanyahu on Tuesday evening while responding to plans by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to convene political and civic representatives for discussions about the unrest and possible threats surrounding next year's presidential election.
The far-left leader rejected accusations that his political camp posed the principal danger to the electoral process. Instead, he singled out Netanyahu, claiming that the Israeli prime minister was influencing elections in Marseille, Toulouse, Roubaix and Paris.
Mélenchon's remarks came amid mounting criticism of his party over the unrest. LFI played a prominent role in the demonstrations that preceded Saturday's violence, and politicians from other parties have accused the movement of contributing to the confrontational atmosphere.
Mélenchon, a longstanding critic of Israeli government policy and an outspoken supporter of the Palestinian cause, has repeatedly faced accusations from political opponents that his rhetoric fuels antisemitism and hostility toward Israel. He has disputed accusations of antisemitism.
The dispute over alleged foreign influence now forms another front in France's political confrontation, as the government and opposition exchange accusations about the origins of the unrest and the risks facing the presidential election.
Macron heads to Saudi Arabia as France braces for more protests
Meanwhile, Macron has faced criticism at home for continuing his Gulf tour while French security forces prepare for another major day of demonstrations on Saturday.
On Wednesday evening, the French president made an unannounced visit to Saudi Arabia, becoming the first Western leader to visit the kingdom since the latest escalation of Houthi attacks earlier this month.
He met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman after earlier stops in Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar. The Saudi visit had not been announced in advance, apparently because of security considerations.
Macron has defended his decision to travel, arguing that securing additional energy supplies is essential to addressing the soaring fuel prices that have contributed to public anger in France.
During the tour, France secured commitments for an additional 200,000 metric tons of diesel each month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, with each country expected to supply approximately 100,000 tons.
Saudi Arabia had already committed to providing another 95,000 tons per month for October and November. During his visit to Riyadh, Macron secured a commitment to extend those additional supplies for as long as necessary.
Together, the agreements amount to approximately 295,000 tons of diesel per month, equivalent to more than 10% of France's monthly consumption.
The French government hopes the additional supplies will help contain fuel prices and ease some of the economic pressure driving the demonstrations.
But with another major protest planned for Saturday, Macron faces two immediate challenges: preventing a repeat of the violence that devastated parts of French cities and responding to the economic grievances underlying the unrest.
At the same time, the confrontation with Trump and Mélenchon's accusations against Netanyahu underscore how France's domestic crisis has become entangled with international politics and a growing battle over disinformation ahead of the presidential election.

India sees a drop in GHG emissions in 2025, even as UNEP flags huge gap in global reduction efforts

16:54:53 UTC
01:54:53 KST

NEW DELHI: Rise in global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions may continue to pose a serious threat of global warming but India reported a decrease in its level of emission in 2025 over the previous year and its trend broke from a longer period of rapid growth, in part due to weather effects, but also due to the country’s “structural shifts towards renewables”, the UN Environment Programme has observed in its annual ‘Emission Gap Report’ released on Wednesday.The report shows that India is currently the third-largest emitter in terms of total GHG emissions but the country’s per capita emission is not only less than half of the global average but also substantially lower than the top two emitters - China and the US - where total emissions increased last year.
.Total GHG emission of the six largest emitters in 2025 in gigaton of CO2 equivalent (GtCO2e) per year.
Besides India, the EU (27 nations collectively) and Russia too reported decreases in their levels of emissions in 2025 when the total global emissions were similar to the 2024 levels.In terms of magnitude, the increase in the US far exceeded those of all other countries. The next largest estimated increases were in Türkiye (the host of the upcoming UN climate conference, COP31), Iran and Indonesia.Though the efforts are being made in most of the countries to reduce their carbon footprints, the report underlines that the temperature projections are still “far too higher” and the chance to keep global warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius with no overshoot is gone.
Per capita GHG emission of the six largest emitters in 2025 in tonnes of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e) per person per year.
It notes that if the current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius within this century over the pre-industrial levels (1850-1900) and increase thereafter.Flagging the huge gap in the emission reduction requirement, the report observed that the world is required to reduce the GHG emissions by 18% by 2030 and by 45% by 2035 from the 2025 levels to remain within the less devastating warming limit, but the full implementation of the current climate action pledges by all nations, put together, would only reduce emissions by 5-8% by 2030 and 11-15% by 2035, relative to 2025 levels, leaving the countries more vulnerable to the disastrous consequences of climate change.“These outcomes are worse than last year’s projections due to the withdrawal of the USA from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. New nationally determined contributions (NDCs) submitted since last year’s report have made a negligible difference for these projections,” it said.The report, while pitching for urgent emissions cuts to come back from an overshoot of 1.5 degrees C, notes that keeping peak warming below 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C (by mid-century) will quickly become impossible without urgent action. “Every five years of CO2 emissions at current levels pushes peak warming up by around 0.1 degree C,” it said.“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5 degree C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year. So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 degree C by the end of the century,” said Inger Andersen, executive director of UNEP.The report looks at a ‘lowest possible’ 1.5 degree C overshoot scenario, in which peak warming is limited to 1.7-1.8 degree C. To get onto this pathway, global GHG emissions would have to be cut by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels."Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible – and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a message on the report.Collectively, G20 members increased their emissions by 0.7% in 2025. Under current policies, only six G20 members (China, India, Indonesia, Russian Federation, South Africa and Türkiye) are assessed as likely to achieve their unconditional 2030 targets, while the assessment of the European Union is inconclusive.
“India also appears likely to achieve its 2035 target based on policies already in place. However, this should be interpreted differently, because India’s NDC is formulated as an emissions-intensity target,” says the report.
The report notes that though the global GHG emissions in 2025 were similar to 2024 levels, CO2 emissions from fossil fuel combustion of oil, coal and gas, and nitrous oxide (N2O) and fluorinated gases (F-gases) emissions continued to increase last year while methane (CH4) emissions remained almost the same as in 2024."These increases were offset by a decrease in CO2 emissions from the land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) sector of about 0.5 gigatons of CO2 equivalent (GtCO2e). The decrease in LULUCF CO2 emissions was partially driven by a decline in biomass-burning emissions, including a decline in global wildfire carbon emissions in 2025, compared with the exceptionally active 2024 season," it said.
