In a Vienna Bakery, Fresh Pastries and a Backdoor for Serbian Votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:51:00 UTC
01:51:00 KST

At a desk covered with voter lists and photocopied identity documents, two people were busy processing applicants. The association is a non-governmental organization registered under Austrian law. Legally, it has no authority to collect voter registration materials on behalf of Serbian authorities. 
Yet behind these closed doors, that is exactly what it has been doing — specifically for those who support the ruling party, an investigation by the Serbian investigative outlet KRIK found. Journalists obtained three recordings made by applicants that captured the process, as well as WhatsApp messages and flyers shared by the association with voters.
The parliamentary elections scheduled for Sunday in Serbia could be pivotal, with Vučić’s long-dominant party facing a significant challenge from a student-led movement fed up with corruption and state capture. 
Yet Serbian elections have long been marred by irregularities and a voting landscape warped in favor of the SNS, according to international and local observers.
Following the last parliamentary poll in December 2023, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) concluded that the vote was technically well-administered but fundamentally skewed by the president and the ruling party’s systemic advantages. The mission warned of an unlevel playing field in the form of pervasive media bias, pressure on public-sector employees to vote for the ruling party, and the routine misuse of state resources for partisan campaigning.
The association in Vienna’s 16th District reveals how those imbalances can also reach across international borders.
Under Serbian election law, overseas voter registrations must be handled exclusively by Serbia’s diplomatic missions. But multiple Serbians living in Austria say registering through the embassy or consulate is almost impossible for some: phones ring unanswered, appointments are nearly impossible to get, and applicants are routinely turned away for missing paperwork. 
Jelena Živanović Valtner, a quality coordinator in the pharmaceutical industry who has lived in Vienna with her daughter since 2009, told KRIK that she tried to register through the official consular channel, but was stonewalled.
“As required, I sent the consular department a completed and hand-signed application,” she said. 
She later received a blunt email from the embassy written in all caps: “YOUR APPLICATION IS INCOMPLETE.”
Živanović Valtner followed up over email and eventually filed formal appeals with both the Republic Electoral Commission and the embassy in Vienna. She says she received a phone call assuring her that her application was under review, but that it was ultimately rejected again, without any explanation.
Now, she can only vote if she travels back to Serbia on election day.
“If my job allows me to travel to Serbia to vote, I’ll go,” she said. “If not, well, that’s that.”
Inside the association next to the bakery, meanwhile, the process appears to be entirely frictionless — for those bearing the right political stripes. 
According to the undercover recordings made by applicants and obtained by KRIK, staff members processed registrations in less than five minutes. They copied identity papers, filled out forms, and took phone numbers so they could send confirmation once the registration was cleared through the Serbian embassy.
Applicants were also asked to leave the contact numbers of family and friends living in Austria who were likely to support the ruling party.
“We don’t register those road-blockers and fools,” a male voice can be heard telling an applicant in one recording, referring to the student protesters who have shut down highways and bridges during anti-government demonstrations. “We only communicate with our people who support Vučić.”

Why the China-US Naval Encounter at Sabina Shoal Is Different
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:49:00 UTC
01:49:00 KST

On October 20, China accused a U.S. naval vessel of “undermining regional stability” by entering waters near Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands. According to a spokesperson for the People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theater Command Navy, the U.S. Littoral Combat Ship USS Charleston (LCS-18) “illegally intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal “without approval from the Chinese government.” By contrast, a U.S. Navy 7th Fleet spokesperson maintained that the Charleston conducted “routine operations in international waters” consistent with international law.
This latest naval encounter reflects the long-standing legal dispute between China and the U.S. over the freedom of navigation of warships in the South China Sea. What makes it distinct is the location of the incident: unlike all previous U.S. Freedom of Navigation Operations (FONOPs) targeted at China in the South China Sea, the encounter occurred near Sabina Shoal, a maritime feature not occupied by China. Thus, this is also the first time that the PLA Navy (PLA) officially admitted that it “dispatched forces to track and monitor the U.S. vessel” near a feature China doesn’t occupy.
This new kind of close encounter may reveal that the Chinese government is upgrading its strategy to respond to perceived U.S. naval intrusions in the South China Sea. At the same time, the incident may also serve as a warning to the Philippines, which considers Sabina Shoal to be a part of its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). These interpretations remain tentative, and non-exclusive, but they make the encounter worth examining beyond the immediate exchange of official statements.
Disputes Between China and the U.S. over “Freedom of Navigation” of Warships
The United States holds that the right to sail and operate its military vessels “wherever customary international law allows” is “a long-standing national interest.” The U.S. military uses FONOPs to challenge maritime claims and restrictions that it considers excessive.
China, by contrast, argues that freedom of navigation cannot be invoked to justify activities that it views as threatening its territorial integrity or security, including foreign warships’ operations near maritime features over which China asserts sovereignty. Beijing considers the intentional “intrusion” of warships into its claimed territorial sea to be “hegemonic freedom of navigation.” China argues U.S. FONOPs have no place in contemporary international law.
A semi-official research report published by the China Institute for Marine Affairs under the Ministry of Natural Resources in August 2025 highlighted this issue. The report concluded that the “U.S. Freedom of Navigation lacks a basis in international law and seriously distorts the interpretation and development of international law.” These competing positions have underpinned repeated Chinese protests against U.S. naval operations in the South China Sea.
Notably, news reports of the Charleston’s October 20 operation did not officially describe it as a FONOP. The U.S. spokesperson’s statement instead emphasized that “all nations enjoy freedom of navigation and other lawful uses of the sea in this area.” That language is consistent with Washington’s broader position on maritime access, but it does not establish that the operation was a formally designated FONOP or identify the specific legal claim, if any, that the vessel intended to challenge.
The distinction matters: a naval transit, a routine operation, and a FONOP may overlap in practice, but they are not necessarily interchangeable descriptions of an operation’s purpose.
Why Sabina Shoal Is Distinct
U.S. FONOPs generally identify a particular maritime claim or restriction they seek to challenge. For instance, the United States explicitly labeled a previous operation that took place on August 13, 2025, near Scarborough Shoal as a FONOP intended to challenge Chinese domestic legislation requiring prior authorization for foreign warships to enter China’s territorial sea. In such cases, the stated legal objective provides a relatively clear basis for interpreting the operation and anticipating a Chinese response. In the August 2025 case, the PLA said it had “organized forces to lawfully track, monitor, issue warnings, and expel the U.S. warship.”
Sabina Shoal presents a different situation for a number of reasons. First of all, unlike Scarborough Shoal, Sabina Shoal was not among the contested maritime features in the 2016 South China Sea Arbitration Award.
At the same time, there is no mutual understanding between China and the Philippines on the legal status of the shoal and its surrounding waters. The United States and the Philippines regard Sabina Shoal as a low-tide elevation that cannot, in its own right, generate a territorial sea. They thus regard the surrounding waters as part of the Philippines’ EEZ.
By contrast, the Chinese government disputes that Sabina Shoal (known in Chinese as Xianbin Jiao) is a low-tide elevation. In fact, a “Survey Report on the Coral Reef Ecosystem of Xianbin Jiao” published by the Ministry of Natural Resources of China in August 2024, said that there are at least three naturally formed cays above water at high tide. Accordingly, China considers Sabina Shoal to be a rock that can claim a territorial sea. This may explain why China accused the Charleston of an “illegal intrusion” into the “adjacent waters” of Sabina Shoal.
Nevertheless, the most peculiar scenario at Sabina Shoal is that this maritime feature has never been formally occupied by China, thanks to the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC), which prohibits “inhabitation” on previously unoccupied maritime features.
Yet in Beijing’s view, Sabina Shoal is part of the “Nansha Qundao” (Spratly Islands), which as a whole belongs to China. That might be the reason that China never formally claimed any territorial sea around its occupied maritime features such as Johnson Reef (Chigua Jiao), Fiery Cross Reef (Yongshu Jiao), or Cuarteron Reef (Huayang Jiao). Instead, Beijing claims “indisputable territorial sovereignty, sovereign rights and interests” within the whole of the Spratly Islands group.
The ambiguity surrounding the nature of the Charleston’s operation makes it difficult to interpret. It’s unclear if the United States intended to challenge a Chinese claim to maritime entitlements around Sabina Shoal or a requirement for prior authorization of transiting its territorial sea. If, however, the operation was instead intended to demonstrate support for the Philippines, the significance would lie less in a specific legal challenge than in the strategic signal conveyed by a U.S. naval presence near a flashpoint in the China-Philippines dispute.
A Possible Warning to the Philippines
The encounter occurred amid heightened tensions between China and the Philippines. On October 14, Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan reportedly remarked that China could “easily win a conflict” against the Philippines if it chose to use force. The remark followed a serious confrontation between a Chinese Coast Guard vessel and a Philippine government vessel at Sabina Shoal on September 18.
In fact, since the beginning of October, at least eight close encounters between China and the Philippines have occurred across the South China Sea and Luzon Strait, according to Reuters. This wider context helps explain why the Philippines might view the Charleston’s presence at Sabina Shoal as a sign of U.S. support, even if the operation was not formally identified as a FONOP against Chinese maritime claims.
China’s response, on the other hand, could be interpreted as a fresh warning to the Philippines. By dispatching naval forces to track and monitor the U.S. warship at an unoccupied maritime feature for the first time, China showcased its determination to protect its claimed rights and interests at Sabina Shoal.
This upgraded response also sends a straightforward warning to the Philippines that any further provocation at Sabina Shoal, with or without support from the U.S., will predictably receive an escalated Chinese response.
The Outlook of China-U.S. Naval Encounters in the South China Sea
While international law provides a common framework for maritime conduct, its interpretation and application remain deeply contested by major powers. The United States advocates its naval operations as a defense of freedom of navigation, whereas China views U.S. naval operations near South China Sea maritime features as challenges to its territorial sovereignty and security. Without a shared understanding of the legal and strategic implications of such operations, similar encounters are likely to recur.
The outlook is therefore one of persistent competition accompanied by risks of unintended escalation. As both navies maintain a significant presence in the South China Sea, close encounters – including, as in this case – China-U.S. naval encounters at maritime features not occupied by China, may become increasingly frequent, particularly amid intensifying Philippine-U.S. security cooperation. Even when neither side seeks confrontation, miscalculation, communication failures, or domestic political pressure could turn a “routine operation” into a serious crisis.
Yet confrontation is not inevitable. Both China and the United States have strong incentives to prevent tactical incidents from escalating into broader military conflict. Maintaining effective military communication channels, strengthening incident-management mechanisms, and clarifying operational protocols should therefore remain priorities. Equally important is a willingness to address maritime disagreements through diplomacy and international law rather than relying exclusively on military assertions such as the FONOPs.
Ultimately, the significance of the Sabina Shoal naval encounter lies not simply in the actions of the two navies, but in what it reveals about the future of maritime order in the South China Sea. Whether such encounters become catalysts for escalation or opportunities for improved crisis management will depend on the strategic choices made in Beijing and Washington.

Millions gather in Tanta to celebrate Egypt's Sufi warrior-saint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:47:44 UTC
01:47:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Millions of Egyptians gather to celebrate life of blind Sufi warrior-saint who 'killed Crusaders'
Millions of Egyptians are expected to take part in celebrations honouring the 13th-century Sufi saint Sayyid Ahmad al-Badawi in the Nile Delta city of Tanta, as one of the country's largest religious festivals approaches its climax on Thursday.
The week-long festival, known as the Mawlid al-Sayyid al-Badawi, an annual celebration commemorating the birth of the revered Sufi saint, began on 16 October and is expected to attract more than two million visitors, according to Egyptian media reports.
Worshippers and pilgrims have travelled from across Egypt, including the Nile Delta and Upper Egypt, to visit al-Badawi's shrine and participate in collective prayers, devotional chanting and dhikr, the Sufi practice of remembering God through the repetition of sacred phrases.
The celebrations centre on the Sayyid al-Badawi Mosque in Tanta, where the saint is buried, while surrounding streets host religious gatherings, food stalls and traditional festivities.
Egypt's General Sheikhdom of Sufi Orders announced that the celebrations would culminate on 22 October, with a major Sufi conference scheduled for Wednesday in Tanta's Sigar district.
Who was Sayyid Ahmad al-Badawi?
Ahmad al-Badawi was a Muslim mystic who travelled through the Islamic world before settling in Tanta in the 13th century.
He became renowned for his asceticism, religious devotion and spiritual teachings, eventually becoming one of the most revered figures in Egyptian Sufism.
Al-Badawi also occupies a prominent place in Egyptian popular traditions surrounding the struggle against the Crusaders.
According to accounts passed down through Sufi traditions and folklore, he helped fight the Crusaders while blind during the Seventh Crusade, launched by King Louis IX of France in 1249, and was associated with the Egyptian resistance that culminated in the Crusaders' defeat and Louis IX's capture in 1250.
Although his personal participation in the fighting is not firmly established by contemporary historical evidence, the tradition helped establish his reputation as a spiritual protector of Egypt as well as a religious teacher.
Al-Badawi, who died in 1276, is associated with the founding of the Badawiyya, also known as the Ahmadiyya, one of Egypt's historic Sufi orders.
His followers regard him as a "wali", or friend of God, a designation used in Sufi traditions for individuals believed to have attained exceptional spiritual closeness to the divine.
For generations, his shrine has been a major destination for religious pilgrimage, and his annual mawlid has developed into one of the most prominent expressions of Egypt's popular Islamic culture.
For Egyptian Sufis, the occasion is both an act of religious remembrance and a celebration of spiritual continuity, connecting contemporary worshippers with centuries-old traditions of devotion, hospitality and communal solidarity.
The festival also attracts many Egyptians who do not belong to any particular Sufi order, reflecting the enduring place of saints, shrines and religious festivals in the country's social and cultural life.
The celebrations come ahead of another major Sufi festival honouring Ibrahim al-Desouki, which is scheduled to begin on Friday in the Nile Delta city of Desouk.

The US has imposed a trade embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years.
The administration of US President Donald Trump, however, has ramped up pressure on Cuba since January, imposing a fuel blockade on the island and stiff sanctions against a swath of Cuban officials and state entities.

From UAH 120,000 to nearly UAH 200,000: where and when Ukrainians will be able to buy the iPhone Duo
Kyiv • UNN
The new foldable iPhone Duo will be sold in Ukraine starting October 30. Prices for the different storage versions reach UAH 199,999.
In Ukraine, Apple’s new product — the iPhone Duo — will be available for purchase in the stores and on the websites of several major household-appliance retailers as early as October 30. This was reported by UNN.
The long-awaited smartphone will be available to order from the ALLO online store. The retailer offers models in white (Star White) and dark blue (Night Sky), with RAM capacities ranging from 256 and 512 GB to 1–2 TB.
In addition, the chain offers a trade-in service and a discount on the purchase of a new device when exchanging an old one.
This will be possible as early as October 30.
In response to UNN’s inquiry about the possibility of purchasing Apple’s new phone, the MOYO online store said:
"The iPhone Duo will appear in Ukraine as early as October 30. On that day, it will already be possible to collect devices ordered in advance."
Citrus has not yet decided on the start of iPhone Duo sales. They explained that everything depends on the supplier, which has not yet determined a specific delivery date.
"At present, the delivery date for this product has not been specified by the manufacturer or supplier companies. We, together with you, are also waiting for this product to be delivered," replied a manager of the electronics store chain.
She also clarified that the product can be pre-ordered on the website.
"As soon as the smartphone becomes available for sale, the online store’s managers will begin calling customers who left pre-orders," the manager said.
In addition, a representative of Citrus emphasized that the price of the iPhone Duo will become known only after the store receives the smartphone for sale.
"The product’s price depends on a large number of factors, including the device’s cost at the time of delivery. If the final price does not suit you, you will be able to refuse to proceed with placing the order," she explained.
It should be noted that even those chains that are ready to begin selling the new iPhone as early as October 30 have not yet set a price for the new product. It is listed only on the website of the eStore.ua chain of stores. There, the 256 GB smartphone is offered for UAH 119,999, the 512 GB phone costs UAH 132,999, and the 1 TB iPhone can be purchased for UAH 159,999. The most expensive is the 2 TB iPhone Duo: it will cost UAH 198,999.
Apple warns of an iPhone Duo shortage at launch: smartphones sold out within minutes
The American company Apple announced that its first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, will be available in limited quantities at its branded stores during the official sales launch on October 23. Advance online orders for the new product sold out within minutes, meaning some buyers will have to wait for delivery until January 2027.
The company said that on Friday, October 23, customers will be able to visit Apple Stores in person to see the new smartphone model. At the same time, the number of devices available for purchase without a pre-order will be limited. Apple representatives emphasized that the company is making efforts to provide customers with the new smartphones as quickly as possible.
However, the availability of the iPhone Duo will depend on the country. In particular, customers in the United States, Canada, Australia, Mexico, the United Kingdom, and most European countries will be able to purchase the device without a pre-order. However, even in these markets, the number of smartphones available for open sale will be small. At the same time, in mainland China, France, India, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and the United Arab Emirates, stores will serve only customers who placed orders online. The exception will be Macau, where smartphones can be purchased without a pre-order, although supplies there will also be limited.
Why there is an iPhone Duo shortage
Apple unveiled its first foldable smartphone in September 2026. The new product marked the American company’s entry into a market where premium devices from Samsung and Huawei have already been available for several years. According to analysts, one of the reasons for the limited supplies may be the complexity of manufacturing the iPhone Duo.
Unlike traditional smartphones, the new model is equipped with a special hinge mechanism that enables the device to be folded and unfolded. Manufacturing it on an industrial scale requires more complex technological processes. Experts suggest that Apple will need additional time to ramp up production volumes.
At the same time, the company has not yet disclosed exact figures for the number of smartphones manufactured or the total volume of pre-orders.
What is known about the new smartphone
The iPhone Duo became the first foldable smartphone in Apple's history. The device features an external display with a 5.4-inch diagonal and an internal screen with a 7.6-inch diagonal.
The starting price of the new product in the U.S. market is $1,999 for the version with 256 GB of storage.
Pre-orders for the smartphone opened on October 16, but due to strong demand, delivery times for certain configurations have already been pushed back to the end of January 2027.

Mada Masr editor-in-chief questioned by Egyptian prosecutors

The summons came after Mada Masr published a report detailing complaints by detainees who said they had been subjected to violations inside Egyptian prisons.
"Prosecutors have been investigating Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah for three hours at the headquarters of the Supreme State Security Prosecution in New Cairo. Her defence team has been present with her throughout the questioning. The investigation session is ongoing," Mada Masr wrote on X on Wednesday.

The most recent was in August 2025, when the State Security Prosecution ordered Attalah's release on bail of 30,000 Egyptian pounds after charging her with "publishing false news" and "using a website without a licence".
Egyptian authorities arrested Attalah in May 2020 while she was interviewing Laila Soueif, the mother of political activist Alaa Abdel Fattah, outside Tora Prison, where he was being held at the time. Attalah was detained for seven hours before being released on bail.
The latest summons comes amid mounting pressure and a continued crackdown on press freedom in Egypt. In September, authorities arrested six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsad2sh (Don't Believe It).
After five days in secret detention under the country's anti-terrorism law, the six journalists appeared before the Supreme State Security Prosecution.
Some said they had been subjected to torture and ill-treatment, including blindfolding, being handcuffed behind their backs, being stripped of their clothes, beatings and electric shocks.
On 13 October, the prosecution ordered the journalists' detention to be extended by a further 15 days pending investigation by the Supreme State Security Prosecution. They face charges of joining and financing a "terrorist group" and "publishing false news".
Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders' 2026 World Press Freedom Index. The organisation says 18 Egyptian journalists are currently behind bars.

Why Rubio is seeking India’s help after coercion over Russian oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:43:06 UTC
01:43:06 KST

Why Rubio is seeking India’s help after coercion over Russian oil
After spending years pressuring New Delhi to cut back its Russian oil purchases, and isolate Moscow, Washington has now changed tack and is seeking India’s help to bring down elevated domestic fuel prices that are largely of its own making.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who skipped New Delhi entirely on his second visit to India this year, made clear what had brought him to the country – the massive refining capacity of Reliance Industries, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani.
“I’m also here in my capacity as the National Security Adviser,” Rubio said in Mumbai. “Energy is related to national security … we’re going to go see a company that has a tremendous amount of refining capability.”
President Donald Trump’s administration is showing a new urgency to bring down the high fuel prices that threaten Republicans’ prospects in November’s midterm elections. US retail diesel prices reached a record average of about $6.32 a gallon on Tuesday.
American refineries are already operating at close to capacity, and Washington is working with India to increase refining output and bring more petroleum products to global markets, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in Houston the same day.
“Energy politics is inseparable from American geopolitics,” Jindal School of International Affairs adjunct professor and former Jawaharlal Nehru University professor Anuradha Mitra Chenoy told RT. “The US is using energy as a geopolitical instrument, and that is central to understanding Rubio’s visit.”
From Russian oil tariffs to Venezuelan crude
Washington has regularly used energy sanctions to achieve its geopolitical aims. First it took Iranian, and then Venezuelan, crude off the market with the threat of sanctions. Since the Ukraine conflict began, Washington also pressured India to stop buying Russian crude. The argument was that choking off Moscow’s oil revenues would help end the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.
At the same time, the US continued to supply Ukraine with weapons and funds, and started a war with Iran that disrupted energy supplies from the Middle East.
New Delhi has maintained that providing affordable energy to its 1.4 billion people is central to its oil-purchasing decisions. India imports about 85% of its energy requirements, and Russia remains one of its biggest sources of oil.
But the pressure reached a breaking point when the US Congress passed a law last month that threatened “bone-crushing sanctions” on major buyers of Russian energy. New Delhi warned that the proposed measures could affect bilateral relations and global energy markets.
However, as the affordability crisis in America got worse, and Trump’s rhetoric failed to bring down domestic fuel prices in a connected global market, the administration swiftly changed course.
Trump announced a deal with Russia to buy diesel for the domestic market. And cleared the deck for Rubio’s visit by waiving off sanctions on Moscow’s top oil buyers – which includes China and India, allowing Russian oil to flow more freely into global markets.
“None of these tariffs are meant to punish or harm India,” Rubio said in Mumbai, adopting a more conciliatory tone than has come out of Washington until recently.
Why Reliance, and Jamnagar, matter to Washington
Washington’s top diplomat held talks with Mukesh Ambani at Jamnagar in India’s Gujarat state on the second day of his visit. The Reliance refinery in Jamnagar is the largest single-site refining complex in the world, and can process around 1.4 million barrels of crude a day.
It is also one of the few facilities capable of processing large volumes of Venezuela’s extra-heavy crude, which is good for producing diesel – showing its importance to a US administration worried about domestic fuel prices.
Jamnagar already plays a major part in keeping global fuel prices in check – by selling fuel refined from Russian crude to markets including Europe, which sanctions the same crude.
And it is buying more Venezuelan oil, accounting for more than 74% of the nearly $3.6 billion worth of Venezuelan crude imported by India between April and August, according to figures shared by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank.
Rubio wants Reliance to buy, and process, more of the Venezuelan crude, which the US now controls after kidnapping the country’s President Nicolas Maduro.
“The refining capability exists,” GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava told RT. “The question is whether expanding purchases makes commercial sense.”
Venezuelan crude is cheaper but it also costs more to refine, he pointed out. He also questioned the wisdom of India buying more of the South American country’s oil, which was once subjected to US sanctions.
“It would be very unwise for India to stop using Russian oil,” Chenoy said, pointing out that there are only a limited number of major sources available internationally, and Russia remains one of the most important.
Reliance is also involved in a proposed refinery project in Brownsville, Texas, under a long-term agreement to purchase its output. The facility, which Trump called a $300 billion project in March, is designed to process lighter American shale crude.
The Indian conglomerate “helps utilize and unleash the energy that is being developed in the Western Hemisphere,” Rubio told the Indian Express, describing his visit as an opportunity to identify ways of diversifying energy supplies.
Rubio dodges a Musk-ignited controversy
Ahead of his meeting with Ambani, Rubio had to sidestep the controversy ignited by trillionaire Elon Musk.
The world’s richest man, a prominent donor to the Republican party, had accused Ambani earlier this month of obstructing the launch of his Starlink satellite internet service in India.
Musk targeted Ambani, sarcastically addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and questioning whether his company would allow Starlink to compete in the country.
Starlink, Ambani’s Jio Satellite Communications, and Bharti Group-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are all at broadly the same stage of regulatory approval for satellite internet connectivity in the country, with security assessments underway, according to India’s Communications Ministry.
Reliance also dismissed suggestions that it was blocking competition.
“Elon Musk is a private citizen,” Rubio told the Indian Express, adding that Musk had the right to express his views.
Rubio also sought to assuage concerns about the India-US trade deal, which has been holding fire despite months of tortuous negotiations. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as deadlocked earlier this month, saying both sides were finding it “very difficult” to make further concessions.
“We are weeks, not months, away from, I think, finalizing it,” Rubio said. “I would say we are about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement.”
India has been holding off on finalizing the deal as it wants to lock in a competitive advantage in the US market relative to rival exporter nations.
Pragmatism back on the table
The US administration turning on the charm, so to speak, suggests that Washington’s energy and political interests are taking precedence over its geopolitical considerations and moral grandstanding.
With pragmatism back on the table, Rubio’s visit could mark a step toward easing bilateral tensions and strengthening cooperation beyond the immediate fuel crisis driving the change.
Still India must “carefully examine what it is being asked to commit to, what commercial benefits it can expect, and the risks of future changes in US policy,” Srivastava said.

Moody’s upgrades TSMC credit rating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

Moody’s Ratings yesterday upgraded Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC, 台積電) credit rating to “Aa2” from “Aa3,” citing its technological leadership in advanced chipmaking, exceptionally strong financial position and strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips.
The agency also revised its outlook for TSMC from “positive” to “stable,” reflecting expectations that the world’s largest contract chipmaker would maintain its dominant foundry position and robust financial profile over the next two to three years.
The upgrade applies to senior unsecured debt issued by TSMC’s wholly owned subsidiaries, TSMC Arizona Corp and TSMC Global Ltd, and guaranteed by TSMC, Moody’s said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
With the company’s technological edge, manufacturing excellence, diversified customer base and sustained AI demand, TSMC’s revenue is forecast to grow 30 to 45 percent annually over the next 12 to 18 months, the agency said.
TSMC reported 51 percent year-on-year revenue growth in the third quarter, with advanced technologies of 7 nanometers and below accounting for 79 percent of revenue, company data showed.
The company’s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) margin are projected to rise to about 75 percent over the next 12 to 18 months, up from 72 percent last year, Moody’s said, citing higher capacity utilization and productivity gains that offset costs associated with new technologies and overseas facilities.
Despite rising investment needs, TSMC is expected to maintain positive free cash flow and a strong net cash position, it said.
The company’s adjusted debt-to-EBITDA ratio is projected to remain at about 0.3 times, reflecting low leverage, it said.
As of Sept. 30, TSMC held about NT$4 trillion (US$123.1 billion) in cash and marketable securities, enough to cover short-term debt, projected capital spending and dividends over the next 12 months, Moody’s said.
However, as semiconductor manufacturing is capital-intensive and cyclical, it requires continued heavy investment in technology and production capacity in the US, Japan and Germany, the agency said.
A further upgrade in TSMC’s credit rating is unlikely in the near term given the company’s substantial investment needs and the geographic concentration of its manufacturing operations. Its rating is also closely linked to Taiwan’s sovereign rating, because most of its production facilities remain in Taiwan, Moody’s said.
However, a downgrade could follow if the company faces a material loss of technological leadership or market share, sustained deterioration in profitability and cash flow, or investment and shareholder payouts that significantly weaken its net cash position, the agency said.

Book review: A Tibetan Buddhist in the world of finance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

The Taipei that Tsering Namgyal Khortsa gives us in his new novella, A Season of Retreat, takes us back to the 1990s and 2000s. In that not so distant past, Taipei was a city on the cusp of affluence, though its blossoms were only starting to sprout through its grubby exterior. At the same time, the city was also a moody milieu for postmodern alienation, where even the rain was “quieter, gentler, somehow lonelier.”
It is in this Taipei that a young Tibetan exile, Tashi, finds himself living between two worlds. One of those worlds is his professional life as a business reporter and financial editor, with weekends spent in cruisy expat bars and funky student cafes. The other is that of Tibetan Buddhist centers, where he does duty assisting newly arrived lamas and translating religious teachings for Taiwanese devotees.
The novella, at only 192 pages, offers a taut yet endearing parable of a young Tibetan adrift in a sea of globalization. Its central irony is that Tashi, a financial reporter, sits in the beating heart of neoliberal capitalism — a system which he cannot help but look upon as the apogee of Buddhist “impermanence.”
For Khortsa, the novella is also a reckoning with his own younger self. Though he now lives in India, its story mirrors, though does not exactly describe, his formative years in Taipei. I worked with him in the early 2000s at the Taipei Times. Dapper and fastidious, he was a reporter on the business desk, while I sat in an adjoining island of cubicles in the Features Section. In those days, he used only his first two names for his byline, Tsering Namgyal.
Though the novella’s setting is the 1990s, the Taipei it describes is that of the 2000s. Most of its references are to real places I remember well. Tashi’s apartment is near Grandma Nitti’s, which served American-style brunch and was Taipei’s answer to a backpacker cafe. His favorite bar is Watersheds, a trendy dive off Anhe Road where I drank with Khortsa on occasion. There is also a brief mention of Eslite’s legendary 24-hour bookstore on Dunhua South Road, where lonely nerds once roamed through the wee hours. These places are all gone now.
The novel begins with Tashi, who has come from India to attend university in Taipei, landing his first job as a business reporter at the Taiwan News. (This, too, was and is a real media platform.) The job marks not only the start of his adulthood, but also his own personal crisis of being.
Skilled at his work, Tashi rapidly climbs the career ladder. It does not take him long to make a lateral move to an investment house, where he edits financial reports. Then after passing a test to obtain a brokerage license, he is offered a high-paying position as a full analyst.
On weekends, Tashi retreats to an artsy student cafe, Norwegian Wood — another real place. It was a literary-minded haunt near National Taiwan University that took its name from a novel by Haruki Murakami, not the Beatles’ song. There he dreams of Sikkim and taps out stories of the Himalayas on his laptop computer.
In the cafe, he manages to spark a romance with an American art critic, a fellow freefloating “exile.” But as the relationship goes forward, he is cavalier, flirting with other girls in other bars. After a time, the love affair goes as easily as it had come.
Though Tashi is doing everything right career-wise, he stills feels unmoored and spiritually restless. He experiences Taipei’s version of globalism as an absurdity — a Tibetan dating an American in Japanese-themed cafes and Thai restaurants, and where everybody speaks Chinese! Such dislocations fortify his sense of alienation and exile. At one point he compares his existence to that of the bardo, which for Tibetans is where souls are left to wander between the stages of death and rebirth.
It is only in Taipei’s community of Tibetan Buddhists that Tashi finds a sense of grounding. In previous writings, Khortsa has noted somewhat ironically that Buddhism is Tibet’s greatest export and the cornerstone of its identity. In the Taiwan of this novella, he finds further irony when he describes how the Taiwanese, amusingly, often treat the visiting lamas like fortune tellers.
But assisting newly arrived monks also gives Tashi a tangible sense of purpose, and this is reinforced by letters from his father, who has just been elected as a parliamentarian in Tibet’s exiled government. Though Buddhism for Tashi is a kind of life in the background, he nevertheless finds realness there. His most meaningful friendship is with a Buddhist nun who is dying of cancer.
As Tashi advances up the corporate ladder, he is increasingly torn between these two worlds. As a financial editor, he has a nagging sense that he is unfulfilled, that he is letting his authentic self down. At this point, he comes to see his weekend writing sessions as “a way of paying a sacred debt — to his motherland, Tibet — now fading from the world’s memory like a prayer half-whispered and lost to wind.”
The novella’s moment of truth comes with the arrival of the Asian financial crisis of 1997. Debts threaten to collapse Tashi’s firm. But while those around him scramble, he sees only impermanence. It is at this fork in the road that he knows he must choose his direction.
A Season of Retreat is Khortsa’s third book, all written since leaving Taipei in the mid-2000s. His second effort, The Tibetan Suitcase (2013) was a critically successful novel whose title still stands as a grand metaphor for the identity crisis of more than 100,000 exiled Tibetans worldwide. Reprising this theme in this latest work, he writes, “What you lose becomes part of the suitcase you must carry.”
In this newest work, Khortsa writes with lucid and disarmingly simple prose — almost like Murakami’s “invisible prose.” It is however hard for me, having known him, to disentangle his own life from this fiction. And in places I feel he, as a writer, did not solve the problem fully. But all told, it is an engaging and subtly complex read. I was quickly swept up in this tale of a young man facing down his own personal paradox, that of being a Tibetan Buddhist, and also a business reporter in Taipei.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: TSMC’s  record-breaking investments are transforming Arizona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) was in Arizona on Oct. 5, to launch the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Phoenix, the 14th such de facto Taiwanese consulate in the US.
In response, Liu Chang (劉暢), a spokesperson for China’s embassy in the US, said in a statement the same day: “China firmly opposes official interactions of any form between China’s Taiwan region and the US, including its federal and state governments.”
After the office plans were announced in July, Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles asking her to object to the proposal. The AP reported the following: “In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called on the governor to ‘refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the state of Arizona.’” Whether AP had intentionally been echoing Chinese state media’s use of “Taiwan authorities” by using “Chinese authority” or not, it was still amusing.
Photo: Reuters
Not so long ago, such missives would have given many state governors pause. In Arizona today, the chances are zero.
“Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said while attending the TECO office launch with Lin. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.”
Advanced chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) recently pledged an additional US$100 billion to expand its operation in northern Phoenix, bringing its total investment in the Phoenix area to US$265 billion (NT$8.6 trillion).
LARGEST IN HISTORY
That quarter of a trillion US dollars is the largest foreign direct investment in American history.
It does not stop there; the region is attracting companies in TSMC’s supply chain from Taiwan and around the world. These investments bring high-paying jobs to locals, career opportunities for students in Arizona universities and a higher tax base.
A whole ecosystem of local businesses are necessary to support and maintain this investment, from construction firms to shoe shops.
Governor Hobbs was a guest of President William Lai (賴清德) in March last year on a visit to Taiwan. He made some interesting remarks.
“Due to our close industrial engagement, we now have more than 30,000 Taiwanese living in Arizona. I would like to thank Governor Hobbs for taking care of Taiwanese businesses and people. I believe that through our joint efforts, Arizona will become a shining example for Taiwan-US high-tech collaboration and the creation of non-red supply chains,” Lai said.
That 30,000 number likely includes spouses and dependents, which local employment numbers would not catch, but Taiwan’s de facto Washington embassy Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in the United States (TECRO) would be more attuned to.
With the announced increased investments from TSMC and as more supply chain partners set up camp, that number is likely to grow fast — even accounting for some positions currently filled by Taiwanese eventually being replaced by fully trained replacements.
Arizona is also working to bring in a more diversified portfolio of Taiwanese investment. At a July conference in Taipei, Steve Hsu (徐竹先), head of the Arizona Commerce Authority’s Taiwan office, told the audience: “The investment opportunity in Arizona is not just available for tech companies — it’s an opportunity for everyone, including investors in hospitality, family offices and other industries.” His office has signed several MOUs with Taiwanese institutions to further expand connections.
Describing talking to attendees at that conference, a reporter from Rest of the World noted: “Several venture capital and family office representatives seemed excited and told me they plan to join investment delegation trips to Arizona soon.”
How effective Arizona is in further attracting Taiwanese remains to be seen, but the ground is fertile as investment continues to flow in from major players, spreading capital like fertilizer.
A further draw for Taiwanese is the phenomenon where expatriate communities lay the groundwork, build the connections and develop the infrastructure that makes it easier for compatriots to follow.
In other words, the Taiwanese community is likely to grow fast beyond what the massive influx of TSMC and supplier investment alone requires.
UNPRECEDENTED EXPERIMENT
Assuming the president’s 30,000 figure is correct, according a 2025 Pew Research report that would make the Phoenix metropolitan area the second-largest Taiwanese community, ahead of the New York City metro area population of around 25,000.
With the investment boom ongoing and showing no signs of tapering off, it is not inconceivable that the Phoenix area Taiwanese community could rival that of the Los Angeles metro area’s estimated 60,000.
This is unprecedented as the Phoenix community arose almost entirely in just the last few years. Communities in New York, Los Angeles and other areas arose organically over generations.
What is unfolding is an unprecedented social experiment fueled by the largest foreign direct investment in American history, making it groundbreaking both financially and in terms of immigration.
Even in a city of 1.7 million, adding a large town-sized population of highly educated, high-income people from the other side of the planet is going to have major impacts that will ripple throughout the region. The reverse is also true, as the community establishes itself and is influenced by American Southwestern culture, ripples of this cultural mixing will reach Taiwan’s shores. Rapid expansion of American-style Mexican food in Taiwan in the 2030s would not be surprising.
Also attending the TECO office launch was Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego, who said the city is seeing a sort of “baby boom” in its Taiwanese communities, with several labor and delivery rooms even launching Mandarin-language programs. As a Sept. 1 Phoenix magazine report titled “Taipei of the Desert” notes: “Earlier this year, Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego announced that more than 300 ‘TSMC babies’ had been born in Arizona since the company established its Phoenix campus.”
That same report describes hundreds of students enrolling in local schools and stated: “Now, hearing Mandarin at school pickup and seeing Taiwanese products at Costco have become commonplace — echoes of a larger cultural transformation taking shape across the Valley.”
Unsurprisingly, there are “TSMC villages,” new Taiwanese civic associations and of course plenty of new Taiwanese restaurants and food options.
For those following American politics, no doubt the recent tightening of regulations and raising the costs of H-1B visas comes to mind. This is indeed creating headaches for American high tech firms.
However, many of TSMC and other investors are not impacted by that, as their employees are receiving L-1A and L-1B visas, which allow multinational companies to transfer executives, managers and employees with specialized knowledge to a US office. The Trump administration has been loudly touting their success in attracting TSMC’s investment, so these visas will likely continue to be available.
Those visas also allow Taiwanese to apply for a green card and eventually become naturalized citizens.
How this unprecedented, fast-moving social experiment will play out remains to be seen. No doubt there will be many positives for the people involved as well as the wider Phoenix community — but also incidents of conflict. An interesting cultural marker will be if Taiwanese elements such as food and some cultural practices work their way into the identity of the city.
This experiment is now set to be replicated elsewhere, if on a smaller scale. On Monday, Oct. 12 Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) told Bloomberg that Taiwan plans to establish industrial parks in the US to help smaller domestic suppliers set up local operations and strengthen semiconductor and AI supply chains, starting with a park in Texas expected to cost up to US$4 billion.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

Semiconductor industry’s electricity use hits record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:48 UTC

Electricity consumption by Taiwan’s semiconductor industry topped 4.5 terawatt-hours (TWh) for the first time last month, a record driven by stronger-than-expected demand for artificial intelligence (AI), the Taiwan Research Institute (TRI, 台綜院) said yesterday.
As AI technologies develop rapidly and the demand for computing power grows, global demand for cutting-edge chips, advanced packaging and high-performance chips continues to rise, pushing up the industry’s electricity consumption, the institute said in a statement.
Nationwide, electricity consumption by high-voltage and extra-high-voltage industrial users rose 1.76 percent year-on-year last month, while consumption by manufacturers rose 1.96 percent and that by the semiconductor industry rose 11.55 percent — returning to double-digit growth, it said.
Photo: CNA
The economic monitoring indicator for the power industry remained at “red,” marking robust activity for the 18th consecutive month, the institute said.
Strong production in the high-tech sector has gradually spurred investment demand in other industries, boosting exports, production and corporate investment, and supporting rapid economic growth, which the institute estimates grew 12.6 percent last month.
The TRI forecast that the semiconductor industry’s annual electricity consumption would exceed 50TWh this year, as AI-related business opportunities expand from high-end chips to servers, equipment, materials and key components, benefiting investment and production across the supply chain.
The chemical materials and textile industries continued to show “blue” monitoring readings, signaling contraction, although for different reasons.
The chemical materials industry remained under pressure from global petrochemical overcapacity and a slow recovery in demand, while the textile industry faced weak international end-market demand and price competition, which continued to weigh on orders and production, the institute said.

China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:45 UTC
01:42:45 KST

When Leon Lu was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.
“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”
She traveled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fueled flooding scenario.
Photo: Reuters
Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation.
“One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”
Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer,” or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism.”
Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.
At a 200,000 square meter facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.
“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. “They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”
It plans to open five more centers across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.
The offerings are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theater, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-story center to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.
Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. China last year recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.
In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centers, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.
NEW GENERATION OF TRAVELERS
“The new generation of Chinese travelers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.
But some travelers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are traveling to real sites of death and destruction.
A magnitude 8.0 earthquake in May 2008 devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.
In Yingxue close to the epicenter, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.
“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.
In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine.”
Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.
“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.
Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.

TASA launches two more satellites in CubeSat program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

The Taiwan Space Agency’s (TASA) Startup CubeSat Program has launched two more satellites to test technologies for a future low-Earth orbit communications network. Both spacecraft established preliminary contact with ground stations after liftoff aboard a SpaceX rideshare mission.
The two 8U CubeSats, T.MicroSat-3 and T.MicroSat-4, developed by Tron Future Tech Inc, were launched at 7:04pm on Tuesday aboard SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 mission, which deployed satellites into a mid-inclination orbit, TASA said yesterday.
The satellites established preliminary communications with ground stations in Chile and Azerbaijan before 3am yesterday, and were in good condition with sufficient power reserves, the agency said.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Space Agency
The launch marked the third batch of satellites under the Startup CubeSat Program, which follows a constellation-development strategy. By launching multiple satellites in stages, domestic companies can refine their designs based on the in-orbit performance of earlier spacecraft while progressively testing more advanced technologies, TASA said.
The two satellites would test beam-hopping technology, which allows them to adjust beam service times and coverage areas according to communications demand, improving the efficiency of satellite resources.
They would also test an intersatellite link to verify their ability to establish two-way communications and exchange data directly.
The team would further assess end-to-end data relay between the spacecraft to determine whether multiple satellites can work together to provide communications services, TASA said.
The tests aim to advance key technologies for low-Earth orbit broadband communications and coordinated satellite operations, the agency said, adding that other teams in the program are preparing additional launches.
Two more satellites in the Black Kite series, developed by Radiant Tech, and two in Fang Hsing Technology’s Albatross series are scheduled to launch in the first quarter of next year.
Those missions would continue testing satellite Internet of Things and ocean remote-sensing technologies, expanding opportunities for Taiwan’s space industry, TASA said.

The match was poised at 2-2 when the Portuguese playmaker, who came third in last year’s Ballon d’Or ranking, controlled on his chest and fired in from just outside the box in the 81st minute at the Parc des Princes.
Photo: AFP
Fabian Ruiz then sealed PSG’s third victory in as many outings in this season’s competition, as they aim to win the Champions League for the third season running.
It had briefly looked as though Barcelona would leave with a point when Lamine Yamal, who is hoping to win this year’s Ballon d’Or, stabbed in Barcelona’s second equalizer on the night.
Desire Doue had earlier opened the scoring for PSG, and Lucas Hernandez got their second goal after teenager Xavi Espart netted for the Catalans.
The defeat is a setback for Barcelona, albeit not one that is likely to seriously hurt their prospects of advancing further in Europe.
They had traveled to France on a run of 11 consecutive wins this season. That sequence is over, but the goals keep coming, and Yamal’s strike was Barcelona’s 50th of the campaign.
“I think it was a fantastic game from both teams, but we made too many mistakes,” Barcelona coach Hansi Flick said. “But I also saw a lot of good things. It was a great test for us, and we have to learn from this game. Today, in October, you cannot win titles. You win the Champions League in June.”
PSG have now won seven games in a row altogether, but they lost Ousmane Dembele — last year’s Ballon d’Or winner — and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to injury.
It remains to be seen how seriously hurt they are, but Luis Enrique’s team are well set to comfortably reach the knockout phase anyway.
“It is just the start of the season and there will be a lot more big matches, but the hunger is there, and we will keep our focus,” Doue told broadcaster Canal Plus.

That helps explain why Rodri, the 2024 Ballon d’Or winner, was on the bench at kick-off, although Raphinha was back in the lineup after a spell out.
Fresh from winning 4-2 at Manchester City last week, PSG almost scored inside 90 seconds as Kvaratskhelia hit the post, but they were dealt a blow as Dembele came off after just 20 minutes with a hamstring injury.
Ferran Torres replaced him, coming on against his former club, who themselves then lost Dani Olmo to injury.
Paris opened the scoring in the 38th minute following an error by Yamal — he gave away possession in his own half, and the ball came to Doue who showed superb footwork before firing into the bottom corner from just outside the area.
The home side were worthy of their lead at the interval, yet Barcelona drew level soon after halftime as Fermin Lopez released Espart who drove into the box and fired in his second senior goal.
Rodri soon entered the fray for Barca, but the game became increasingly unbridled, and Torres hit the post for the hosts just before Hernandez headed them back in front from a corner.
The defender was called into the side to mark Yamal in the absence of usual starting left-back Nuno Mendes. The goal was just his third for PSG, and a first since February 2024.
That crowned a fine performance for Hernandez, but he was substituted moments later by coach Luis Enrique, and replacement Warren Zaire-Emery was at fault for Barcelona’s second equalizer.

Stuck shark in Busan finally returns to sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

A shark that became a sensation after spending more than a month in a canal in the South Korean port city of Busan was yesterday guided back into the open sea, following two failed rescue attempts, the South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said.
The shark, affectionately nicknamed “Bukhangi,” was first spotted in a narrow waterway at North Port on Sept. 18.
More than 1.6 million people visited the waterfront park through Tuesday to catch a glimpse of the animal, the Busan Infrastructure Corp said.
Photo: Reuters
The South Korean National Institute of Fisheries Science confirmed that Bukhangi is a female dusky shark measuring about 3m in length.
The species, which inhabits tropical, subtropical and temperate waters, is classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
The shark’s prolonged stay drew particular attention because of the unusual location. The narrow canal is close to high-rise buildings and a major high-speed rail station in the heart of Busan.
Authorities on Sept. 29 first attempted to guide the shark toward the sea using vessels equipped with water jets, but the shark swam away and remained in the canal.
A second attempt on Oct. 2 involved a 50m-long and 6.8m-high net, but rescuers had to end the operation after the net was caught on rocks on the canal floor.
For yesterday’s attempt, authorities used a net attached to floating platforms, along with divers, to overcome difficulties posed by the canal’s underwater terrain and varying depths.
Workers moved the net toward the open sea while preventing the shark from swimming back into the canal. Drones were also mobilized to track its movements.
Busan livestreamed the operation as curious onlookers gathered along the canal for another glimpse of the shark.
The shark has been celebrated for its unexpected boost to the local economy, with Busan Mayor Chun Jae-soo thanking it for generating publicity he said would otherwise have cost “trillions.”
However, environmental groups said the shark’s appearance should be seen as a warning of the climate crisis, rather than a spectacle or economic boost.
They linked its arrival to warming seas, saying rising temperatures are pushing warm-water fish northward — and subtropical sharks in pursuit.
Additional reporting by AFP

Mapping beaches for mine plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:39 UTC
01:42:39 KST

The navy IS planning to hire fishers (“Military to enlist civilians to map coast,” Oct. 18, page 1). The Ministry of National Defense’s Defense Innovation Division is to contract private survey firms to fit civilian fishing boats with multibeam echo sounders to map the seabed to depths of up to 3m off “red beaches” where the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would be most likely to land in a hypothetical invasion. Chartered aircraft carrying Lidar would map the sand above and below the waterline.
A senior official called the effort a first-of-its-kind initiative and said the data could show where to lay mines and place obstacles.
The move is overdue. The navy’s 192nd and 151st fleets have gathered hydrographic data on their own during exercises, but that method cannot keep up with near-shore topography reshaped every season and by every typhoon.
The ministry, US think tanks and the Institute for National Defense and Security Research have identified four to 20 potential landing sites, among them Jhuwei (竹圍) in Taoyuan, Wazihwei (挖子尾) in New Taipei City and Sishu (喜樹) in Tainan. Knowing the lay of those beaches is a precondition for denying access.
A survey is not a defense. It answers where to put mines, but it does not answer with what, by whom or on whose order, and the reports give no budget, no schedule and no list of which beaches come first.
Taiwan should treat the survey as the first line item in a funded mining plan for its red beaches. Otherwise it will end up with nothing more than an excellent set of maps.
The mine-warfare force Taiwan has was not built for the surf zone. The navy’s four Min Jiang-class minelayers, with six more due by the end of this year, carry 32 to 64 mines each. They draw about 1.6m, which lets them work up to the edge of the 0m to 3m band the survey boats will map, but not its inner reaches. Public reporting describes no surf-zone mine, and no public inventory of any kind exists.
“Delay, Disrupt, Degrade: Mine Warfare in Taiwan’s Porcupine Defense — an assessment by Jonathan Dorsey, Kelly Grieco and Jennifer Kavanagh published online by War on the Rocks on March 21, 2024 — said that Taiwan’s mine stock was relatively small and old.
The army has a partial answer on land. Taiwan News on Oct. 7 reported that the military is to take delivery of 14 Volcano systems, each able to carry 960 anti-tank mines, next year under a revised delivery schedule. The vehicles can seed beaches above the waterline, but nothing comparable has been described for near-shore waters.
The picture is bleaker when it comes to the issue of mine clearance. The navy’s six minehunters are four Yung Feng-class ships built in Germany in 1991 and two secondhand Yung Jin-class ships from the US. They can conduct limited clearance in calm seas against known minefields.
The NT$35.85 billion (US$1.1 billion) Ching Fu program meant to replace them collapsed in a corruption scandal in 2017, as I have written (“Mine strategy needs an exit plan,” Aug. 12, page 8), and no successor has been announced.
The Taiwan Security Monitor has described this gap between concept and capability in detail.
None of this makes the survey program a mistake, but it does make it a forcing function. The navy has to decide how it would use bathymetry at that resolution: bottom mines in deep channels and moored mines at varied depths to build the layered curtain that War on the Rocks describes, and decoys among the real mines to multiply clearance time.
Each choice implies a purchase and the survey sets the clock for making the decisions.
The case for mining beaches is strong. Geography helps: Taiwan has a limited number of landing beaches, and many are narrow and steep, which lets the defender concentrate its mining in a few places.
Timing helps too. During operations focused on Wonsan in 1950 during the Korean War, mines cost a US-led amphibious force eight days and four ships. China’s roughly 40 operational mine countermeasure ships might clear 32 to 80 mines a day between them, so cutting a passage through even a field containing 600 mines might take 0.75 to 1.8 days or longer.
Simple moored contact mines can cost as little as US$2,000 each. They target landing craft and hovercraft that are worth far more.
Mining can also tell the defender where an attack is coming. The War on the Rocks assessment said that clearing efforts are easy to detect and that China likely lacks the capacity for multiple feints, so the location of Chinese sweeping would be one of the most reliable indicators of intent.
Taiwan could reinforce the one or two beaches being swept instead of spreading thin across 20.
Officials say the data from the Defense Innovation Division program would identify deep channels for mines and reefs for obstacles, blocking routes that Chinese craft would use.
However, Taiwan is also not the only party mapping its seafloor. On Oct. 18, National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said that there were six survey vessels among 16 Chinese ships detected near Taiwan.
The implications of the program to collect the data raises several issues:
The first issue is authority. Would Taiwan’s leaders authorize mining before the first shots are fired?
Pre-conflict mining is far more effective than mining under fire, but it risks escalation, and the question has not been tested in a public drill.
A plan has to name who makes the decision to act, when and on what warning. The Han Kuang exercises should rehearse that decision with real survey data on the table.
The second issue is mine clearance. A beach barrier that buys time should not become a self-imposed blockade of nearby ports.
Taiwan needs funding and a timeline to replace its minehunters, because mines that cannot be cleared constrain Taiwan’s own navy and shipping.
The third issue is civilian risk. Surf zones are fishing areas. The crews who survey them will know where mines might be and will not want to work the same water afterward.
A plan needs notice procedures, charts and a clearance commitment, or Taiwan will have mined its own fishers.
The fourth issue is data security. Defense officials say that civilian boats and aircraft collect only raw data, and that noise reduction, integration and the military’s tactical linkage would be conducted by the Naval Meteorological and Oceanographic Office.
That is a sound design on paper. It becomes a policy only when the contracts spell it out, particularly when Chinese survey ships, and by Wu’s count four suspected maritime militia vessels, are already working the waters around Taiwan.
The last issue is that the PLA might not land on beaches at all.
Planners already speak of “composite red beaches” that combine port facilities with terrain suited to airborne operations. That is an argument for extending the survey to port approaches, not for skipping the beaches.
The ministry should prepare the outline of a mine-warfare plan: how many mines, which types, laid at what depths, and from which platforms.
It should fund a replacement minehunting fleet and give the legislature a deadline for completion.
It should test the authorization chain in the Han Kuang exercises, assessing every facet of the process from collecting survey data to issuing orders to lay mines.
Mapping a beach is the easy part. The navy has shown it can pay fishers to do it. The harder test is whether it would pay for what goes in the water.
Ethan Connell is an assistant director at Taiwan Security Monitor and a graduate student at George Mason University’s Schar School of Policy and Government. His research focuses on maritime security and cross-Strait military affairs.

Brewers’ ‘Timeless Ticket’ deal upsets some fans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:37 UTC
01:42:37 KST

The Milwaukee Brewers ran a promotion over a decade ago offering fans a “Timeless Ticket” granting them admission to any game in the future if they paid US$1,000.
Now that the Brewers are in the MLB World Series for the first time since 1982, fans who took that deal are eager to redeem those tickets they bought in 2015. That has led to some complications.
Brewers president of business operations Rick Schlesinger said on Tuesday that several hundred fans had indicated they wanted to redeem their Timeless Tickets for a World Series game.
Photo: Getty Images, AFP
Schlesinger said that “we subsequently erred in our internal communications on the logistics of fulfilling the requests.”
“While we were able to accommodate all with seats, we received feedback from some that they were unhappy with their seat locations,” he said. “Clearly, even with extraordinary limitations on available seats, we did not live up to the spirit of the program, and we have been working through a resolution.”
Danny Fochesato of Milwaukee bought a Timeless Ticket on his 27th birthday, planning all along to redeem it whenever the Brewers reached the World Series.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
The promotion enabled a Timeless Ticket holder to redeem that ticket and become eligible to buy three additional tickets to that game for the full retail price. The offer said the tickets “may be redeemed for the best available seat locations, subject to ticket availability at the time of redemption.”
“Back in 2015, that was a big selling point from the sales people about this,” Fochesato said. “They really touted: ‘Hey, this is going to be the best available seats. You’re getting the priority just behind season ticket holders. Anything the season ticket holders don’t have, you’ll have dibs at it for the World Series.’ That’s kind of the story they sold.”
That would have worked out fine when Fochesato tried redeeming his Timeless Ticket for a potential World Series game in 2018, when the Brewers reached the National League Championship Series.
Fochesato said he got four tickets in the 100 level behind home plate that he could have used if the Brewers had made the World Series that year, when they ended up losing to the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 7 of the NLCS.
This time, he was not as fortunate.
“We had a form, and it only had 400-level or standing-room options,” Fochesato said. “We couldn’t even know what game we had. We just had to put a preference of which ones we wanted, and then we had to submit the form, and just sit and wait for them what we got. I immediately was like: ‘No, that’s bogus.’”
Fochesato said he bargained his way to three 400-level seats for Saturday’s Game 2 with the Tampa Bay Rays and one lower-level seat in the right-field corner for tomorrow’s Game 1.
He said he was in line for the public sale of tickets and saw better seats were available than those that were offered to him under the Timeless Ticket program.
The Brewers are trying to make amends.
Schlesinger said any Timeless Ticket holder who applied for World Series tickets before the deadline will now get to keep those World Series tickets while also being able to retain their Timeless Ticket to redeem for another game in any future season.
“We regret our mistake and look forward to welcoming them to American Family Field for their World Series experience,” Schlesinger said.

Earlier yesterday, the TAO slammed the Taiwanese government, saying that Taiwan should “cease its political maneuverings and unreasonable restrictions” aimed at impeding cross-strait cultural exchanges.
Photo: Chen Yu-fu, Taipei Times
The MAC said Taiwan welcomes visits by all Chinese entertainers who are not complicit in Beijing’s campaign to undermine Taiwan’s national sovereignty.
Zhang has posted multiple comments on social media denigrating Taiwan’s sovereignty and was a guest speaker at the Straits Forum, a platform for Beijing’s united front work targeting the nation, it said.

Meanwhile, a national security expert warned that Beijing’s celebrations for Retrocession Day on Sunday and the anniversary of Sun Yat-sen’s (孫逸仙) birth next month are a bid to rewrite history to legitimize Chinese claims on Taiwan.
China over the past few years has repeatedly attempted to establish legal justifications for its claims over Taiwan through reframing World War II history, the Central News Agency cited the expert as saying in a government brief.
Beijing had commemorated Retrocession Day no more than once every five years until last year, when the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress declared it an annual holiday, they said.
Similarly, China’s move to celebrate the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth with fanfare next month is an effort to rewrite history with the narrative that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the Republic of China’s legal successor and therefore Taiwan’s rightful owner, the expert said.
Beijing is inserting the PRC into historical events that predated the communist state’s founding in 1949, they said.
China is uninterested in history, save for the advantages that come with being its author: the ability to control perceptions, dominate the narrative and provide legal cover for its ambitions to annex Taiwan, they added.
