The China-US Quantum Computing Contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Matt Kinsella – the CEO of Infleqtion, a leading U.S. quantum technology company – is the 531st in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Briefly describe U.S. advancements in quantum computing technology.
The United States is moving from experimental quantum systems toward logical, fault-tolerant computing. The key measure is no longer the number of physical qubits, but whether those qubits can be organized into reliable logical qubits and used for meaningful applications.
Infleqtion is at the forefront of that shift. Our neutral-atom platform has demonstrated 12 logical qubits with error detection and loss correction, a 99.73 percent two-qubit gate fidelity, and arrays of up to 1,600 neutral-atom sites. With Nvidia, we published a materials-science demonstration in which logical encoding reduced error approximately sixfold compared with physical-qubit execution.
Our roadmap achieves 30 logical qubits later this year, 100 by 2028, and 1,000 by 2030. We see approximately 100 high-quality logical qubits as the threshold for outperforming classical systems on selected valuable problems.
Hardware alone will not get us there. As our CTO, Pranav Gokhale, has emphasized, hardware-aware software can force-multiply quantum performance. Infleqtion is developing the complete stack – from atoms, photonics, and control systems to error correction, Superstaq compilation, resource estimation, and integration with GPU-accelerated computing. That full-system approach is how quantum computing becomes useful.
In what ways is the U.S. collaborating with partners in the Asia Pacific in developing quantum computing technology?
The United States is building a trusted quantum ecosystem with Asia-Pacific partners through joint research, technology development, workforce training, and access to advanced systems.
Japan provides a strong example. Japan’s Science and Technology Agency selected Infleqtion as the first foreign company – and the only foreign quantum-computing partner – to participate in its Quantum Moonshot program. In a consortium led by Professor Kenji Ohmori of the Institute for Molecular Science, we are contributing neutral-atom technology, photonics expertise, and systems engineering to the development of a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer based on atomic qubits.
This is more than a research exchange. It combines an American commercial platform with Japanese leadership in ultrafast atomic control and aligns both countries around a shared technical objective. To this end, Infleqtion has delivered neutral-atom systems, helping researchers build the practical experience required to operate and develop applications for advanced quantum machines.
In Australia, Infleqtion has established an Asia-Pacific presence at Swinburne University of Technology and worked with the Australian Army and Australian industry on trustworthy quantum computation. One collaboration with Australian quantum company Diraq explored quantum physically unclonable functions intended to help verify the identity and integrity of remotely accessed quantum computers.
We are also engaging Australian leaders on the future use of quantum computing in energy and infrastructure. This application-led approach is essential: allied programs should begin with consequential problems and jointly determine the hardware, software, and classical resources required to address them.
These partnerships expand the talent, facilities, test environments, and applications available to the United States. Our alliances are not simply diplomatic relationships; they are a practical technology advantage.
Analyze the scope and scale of the U.S.-China quantum computing competition.
The U.S.-China quantum competition is not a single race. It spans computing architecture, logical reliability, software, photonics, manufacturing, talent, supply chains, data-center integration, and applications.
China can concentrate substantial state resources behind selected national programs. The United States operates through a more distributed system of companies, universities, federal laboratories, private capital, and international partners. That diversity supports several technical pathways while creating strong pressure to demonstrate practical results.
Infleqtion represents the strength of the American model. We are advancing a vertically integrated neutral-atom platform while expanding from research milestones into deployed systems and application centers. Our technology is operational in national institutions, and our teams are working with government and industry on energy, materials, AI, and scientific discovery.
We have delivered a 100-physical-qubit system to the U.K. National Quantum Computing Centre, announced a fault-tolerant system for Illinois, opened a Chicago Quantum Innovation Center, and expanded our U.K. engineering and manufacturing presence. These are signs of an industry developing the infrastructure to scale – not merely producing individual experiments.
The competition will be decided by sustained execution: who can build dependable logical systems, reduce resource overhead, manufacture them, connect them to classical supercomputers, and solve consequential problems. The United States has a powerful innovation network, and Infleqtion is rapidly converting that advantage into operating capability.
Examine China’s quantum computing technology developments.
China has demonstrated credible progress in superconducting and photonic quantum computing, supported by centralized programs that coordinate across universities, national laboratories, and state-linked companies. In particular, the University of Science and Technology of China’s Zuchongzhi 3.0 superconducting processor and Jiuzhang 4.0 photonic system have now achieved world-leading results.
These are technically impressive demonstrations, but more consequential questions concern logical error rates, programmable circuit depth, application performance, system availability, and the resources required to outperform the best classical alternative. Of note, China’s leading results in neutral atom quantum computing have lagged developments here in the U.S., though there have been recent accelerations in China’s efforts over the past year.
China is also building domestic control electronics, cloud platforms, software, and industrial capacity. Its 2026-2030 planning framework treats quantum technology as a strategic emerging field, so the United States should expect continued progress.
The appropriate response is disciplined acceleration. We should measure China’s achievements accurately while investing in the capabilities that determine practical advantage: logical qubits, efficient error correction, hardware-aware software, advanced manufacturing, and application deployment. Those are the areas where Infleqtion is concentrating its computing roadmap.
Assess how quantum computing technology is integrated into U.S. national security and defense systems and its implications for the U.S.-China tech race.
Large-scale quantum computers are not yet embedded in operational defense systems. Current integration is occurring through research programs, independent technical validation, hybrid computing infrastructure, and development of mission-relevant applications.
An exemplar is DARPA’s HARQ program exploring heterogeneous systems that combine different quantum processors with classical resources. To meet that demand, Infleqtion is developing Multistaq, a software layer designed to compile and coordinate workloads across multiple qubit technologies.
Infleqtion is also supporting three Department of Energy Genesis Mission projects involving AI-optimized quantum circuits for nuclear applications, fusion research, and deployable atomic sensing. Our planned Illinois system will connect a neutral-atom QPU with Nvidia GPU infrastructure, providing a test environment for quantum-classical workflows and real-time error correction. The associated Chicago center is initially focused on energy-grid and nuclear optimization problems with direct implications for national resilience.
Quantum sensing and timing are closer to field deployment than fault-tolerant computing. Infleqtion’s work in GPS-independent navigation, spectrum awareness, precision timing, gravity sensing, and space systems gives the company operating experience with government missions while strengthening the shared photonics, controls, software, and manufacturing base behind our computers.
For the U.S.-China competition, the objective should be clear: move quantum computing from scientific potential to trusted national infrastructure. Infleqtion is helping the United States do that by combining technical progress, deployed systems, application development, and allied partnerships on one scalable neutral-atom platform.

He listed his titles and achievements — Ronaldo secured a reduction in his punishment following the scandal in the Portugal national team

He listed his titles and achievements — Ronaldo secured a reduction in his punishment following the scandal in the Portugal national team
Kyiv • UNN
The Disciplinary Committee reduced Ronaldo’s punishment for leaving the national team camp, taking into account his achievements and admission of guilt.
Cristiano Ronaldo succeeded in having his punishment for leaving the Portugal national team’s training camp reduced, despite having previously stated publicly that sanctions should be imposed on him "without taking mitigating circumstances into account," reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
In an extensive statement on social media, published after he left the camp in Denmark last month, Ronaldo said that the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) should punish him at its own discretion, adding that his status as captain was an "aggravating circumstance."
However, during the disciplinary committee’s consideration of the case, the 41-year-old footballer put forward several arguments in favor of reducing the punishment, including the absence of disciplinary violations in previous seasons and his merits in football.
Ronaldo received a 30-day suspension and a €255 fine. According to the documents accompanying the decision, he presented three arguments for mitigating the punishment: the absence of disciplinary violations in the current and three previous seasons; his merits in football, including recognition of his sporting achievements; and his assistance in establishing the facts of the case.
To support his claims, Ronaldo listed the club titles and achievements he had earned with the national team: victory at the 2016 European Championship and two UEFA Nations League titles. His individual awards were also mentioned, including the fact that the "Al-Nassr" forward had won the "Ballon d’Or" five times. In addition to his sporting achievements, he referred to state awards received from the country’s highest-ranking officials.
The members of the disciplinary body took Ronaldo’s arguments regarding his achievements and merits to the country into account, which allowed the suspension and the fine to be reduced by half. The punishment was subsequently reduced by half again because Ronaldo acknowledged responsibility for his actions.
Ronaldo’s suspension falls during a period when no international matches are being played. It is currently unknown whether he plans to return to the national team and whether head coach Jorge Jesus will call him up again.
The description of events provides a clearer picture of the circumstances in which Ronaldo left the training camp. After head coach Jorge Jesus held a press conference in which he stressed that he was in charge of the team and that no player would influence his squad-selection decisions, Ronaldo asked the FPF for a car and headed to Copenhagen airport. During the journey, he called Portuguese Football Federation president Pedro Proença and said that he was "not in the right psychological state" to remain with the team.
"The respondent (Ronaldo) did not inform the federation or representatives of the men’s national team of his intention to leave the stadium and training camp, nor did he provide any prior explanation," the decision states. The document notes that between September 30 and October 4, Ronaldo missed more than 30 team activities, including transfers, training sessions, and communal meals.
Ronaldo revealed the reason for leaving Portugal's training camp07.10.26, 04:53 • 26070 views
The federation states that Ronaldo’s promise, made on social media after he had already left the training camp, to tell fans "the whole truth" drew additional negative attention to the incident. "Given his status as a public figure of global stature, the respondent could not have failed to realize that his behavior in such circumstances would attract intense media scrutiny, which is precisely what happened."
Therefore, Ronaldo was "expected to exercise particular caution in choosing the timing and manner of expressing dissatisfaction with the head coach’s decisions and actions." Instead, the player "only fueled rumors and public curiosity by posting on Instagram — on the very day he left Copenhagen — a message stating that he would, "later," tell "all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to his departure from the men’s national team," the investigation’s findings conclude.
Portugal's next match — again against Denmark — is scheduled for November 14 in the city of Braga.

End of an era? How the Hermes Birkin bag is losing its scarcity appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:39:00 UTC
23:39:00 KST

End of an era? How the Hermes Birkin bag is losing its scarcity appeal
- Hermes Birkin bags are losing resale value as more bags appear online, reducing the profit for resellers like Cai Baochun and Antoinette Hunter.
- The Birkin’s scarcity has driven Hermes’ success, but rising supply, wider resale platforms and softer demand are now putting pressure on its premium image.
- Analysts warn the changing market may weaken Hermes’ business model, even as the company says production depends on trained artisans and quality leather.
AI generated
PARIS/LONDON - London-based Cai Baochun used to make a hefty profit reselling Hermes’ famed Birkin bags for more than double their US$10,000 (S$12,778) retail price. Now he has stopped stockpiling them as second-hand prices fall.
“I don’t want to lose money,” said Cai, who started selling the bags on online platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and on social media in 2020 and rode a Covid-19-pandemic-era luxury spending boom.
The resale value of unworn Birkins sold as second-hand online has dropped by more than US$6,000 from its 2022 peak, he said.
The decline reflects a broader shift in the market for one of luxury’s most exclusive products whose appeal and success have been driven by scarcity.
Increasing supply of Birkin bags in the second-hand market is depressing resale premiums, according to resellers, industry consultants and analysts interviewed by Reuters, raising questions about a strategy that helped propel Hermes to become one of the world’s most profitable luxury companies.
Named after the late British-French actor Jane Birkin, the handbag has been central to Hermes’ performance.
Between 2015 and 2025, group annual sales tripled to €16 billion (S$22.95 billion) while its market value surged.
In 2025, Hermes posted an operating margin of 41%, above that of rivals including Chanel, Kering-owned Gucci and LVMH’s leather and fashion division, which includes Louis Vuitton and Dior.
Resale market under pressure
All of that was underpinned by an aura of exclusivity.
Six resellers who source bags directly from Hermes shoppers said access to a Birkin is generally linked to spending on Hermes scarves, clothes and shoes, although the exact policy differs between regions and stores.
Two estimated customers typically spend US$10,000 to US$20,000 before being offered the Birkin or the Kelly, the brand’s other popular bag.
Hermes, which says a Birkin takes 15 hours to craft, does not disclose its selling policies or how many bags it makes. It declined to comment for this story.
Of the nine Birkin resellers Reuters interviewed in the US, Europe and Asia, six said resale prices had fallen over the past year as more handbags became available, while five reported softer demand.
Antoinette Hunter, who founded luxury handbag reseller Lilac Blue in 2007, said when she got the first request for a Birkin, few people knew the bag.
She eventually sourced one from a member of Japan’s royal family.
Acquiring Birkins is no longer a challenge, Hunter said, but it’s harder to make money from resales.
She said the price for an unworn black Birkin 25 bag, one of the most sought-after models, has fallen by around £4,000 (S$6,842) since 2022, to around £24,000.
Cai, who sells via Vestiaire Collective and Instagram, says his price for the bag is around £20,000.
Hermes sells the same model for £9,390 in Britain, a Hermes sales assistant in London said.
Although Hunter still sees plenty of demand for Hermes bags, particularly the most high-end ones, she said the decline in resale prices might dissuade some from buying directly from Hermes.
“If Hermes continues to raise the prices, and the prices on the resale market continue to drop, that margin gets squeezed, and perhaps it will become less appealing,” she said.
Brokerage Bernstein, which tracks individual auction results, said in a September note the resale price on Birkin 25 bags averaged about 1.7 times the retail tag in the third quarter, down from about 2.6 times at their 2022 peak.
Business model under scrutiny
Hermes’ leather goods division, which includes other handbag models, generates 44% of annual group revenue.
For more than a decade, limited supply and strong demand allowed Birkins to command hefty resale premiums, benefiting both Hermes and resellers as the prospects of making a profit via the secondary market encouraged Hermes clients to buy more from the brand.
“It was a win-win,” said Sarah Davis, founder of California-based Fashionphile.
The company said its Birkin listings have grown 32-fold in 15 years. The company’s website currently lists 212 Birkins on sale.
Hermes has gradually expanded the production of its handcrafted items, opening one workshop per year on average.
Meanwhile, the rise of resale platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and The RealReal, alongside vintage boutiques with online shops and social media channels, has made it easier than ever to resell.
The bags and other Hermes items remain highly sought after, resellers said, but the brand is showing some strain.
Hermes’ shares have lost nearly 40% of their market value in 2026, making the brand one of the worst performers among listed luxury companies.
Earlier in October, UBS analysts downgraded Hermes shares to “sell”, saying that growing secondary-market supply of Birkins and Kellys could weaken the brand’s scarcity-driven business model.
“We believe the nature of the business is changing,” they said in a note, estimating that the number of the handbags listed for sale worldwide is now six to seven times higher than before the Covid-19 pandemic.
The company is expected to report quarterly sales growth of 5.2% on Oct 22, which would mark its weakest quarterly growth in six years, according to Visible Alpha estimates.
While leather goods revenue is still expected to grow by 10%, demand for clothing, silk scarves and perfumes is cooling, a sign fewer customers are making the purchases traditionally required to buy a Birkin at a later stage, two equities analysts and two industry consultants said.
Asked in July whether Hermes should slow production to protect the brand, Hermes CEO Axel Dumas told reporters that some people feared making too many bags would hurt its exclusivity, while others questioned why it was not making more.
He added that output depended largely on the number of fully trained artisans and available high-quality leather.
Not all resellers see weakness.
Davis said prices for the bag on the Fashionphile platform have remained firm and even risen slightly in 2026, pointing to renewed attention generated by Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland’s handbag collection. REUTERS

Türkiye’s first lady urges global action to protect children in conflict zones
Unknown

2026-10-21

Irem Demir and Fatma Zehra Solmaz
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
- 'Some 700,000 students have been deprived of their right to education in Gaza. ... A world where no one is left behind is possible only when the sirens of war fall silent'
Türkiye’s first lady Emine Erdogan on Wednesday called for global efforts to protect children, particularly those living in conflict zones, saying their needs must remain at the center of the international agenda.
“As representatives of more than 100 countries, we are gathered here to provide fair and equal opportunities for all children around the world and to give voice to their needs,” Erdogan said at the World Summit on Investing in the Well-being of Children: A Path to Sustainable and Equitable Development for Future Generations in Samarkand.
“Let us raise this voice to address the problems of children living in war zones, who cannot even dream of a future,” she added.
Erdogan said investment in child well-being was directly linked to a society’s sustainable development and future, stressing that traditional indicators should be reassessed to reflect the challenges children face today.
She said access to food, shelter, security, education, and health care remained essential, while climate change, armed conflicts, forced displacement, and emerging digital threats must also be taken into account.
She cited climate anxiety, artificial intelligence, digital violence, and the exploitation of attention as emerging challenges requiring a broader understanding of child well-being.
 
700,000 students in Gaza deprived of their right to education
Erdogan urged participants to pay particular attention to children living through war, highlighting the stark contrast between children attending school in some parts of the world and those fleeing air raid sirens elsewhere.
She said 60% of deaths from childhood cancer occurred in areas affected by armed conflict.
More than 21,000 children have been killed in Gaza over the past three years, Erdogan said, adding that more than 10,000 had suffered permanent disabilities or lost limbs.
"Children in Gaza deprived of their childhood," she added.
She said 197 ambulances, 38 hospitals, and 96 health centers had been bombed and rendered inoperable.
"Some 700,000 students have been deprived of their right to education. Today, more than 1 million children in Gaza live with the hope of being able to enjoy the rights and conditions of child well-being," she added. “A world where no one is left behind is possible only when the sirens of war fall silent."
Erdogan thanked Ziroat Mirziyoyeva, wife of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, for hosting the summit and expressed hope that the gathering would benefit children and humanity.
The summit brought together representatives from more than 100 countries. Türkiye’s Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas and Dr. Esra Albayrak, chair of the board of the NUN Education and Culture Foundation, also attended.
 
Türkiye one of first countries to take action to protect children from digital world risks
Erdogan said Türkiye was developing social policies that address children’s physical, mental, emotional and moral needs.
She noted that 2025 was declared the Year of the Family and that Türkiye had designated 2026-2035 as the “Decade of Family and Population.”
She also highlighted Türkiye’s Digital Children’s Rights Convention, saying the country was among the first to take action to protect children from risks in the digital world.
Erdogan said Türkiye had restricted social media access for children under 15 years old and introduced obligations for platforms, including age verification and parental controls.
The first lady also cited the country’s Foster Family Project, which she said provides care for more than 11,000 children, including children displaced by war.
“Children are the heart of humanity. Issues concerning them must always remain at the center of the global agenda,” she said.

CyberWell sends social media companies recommendations to improve antisemitism moderation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:37:41 UTC
23:37:41 KST

CyberWell released new guidance for social media companies earlier this month on improving artificial intelligence content moderation to better target antisemitism, while protecting free expression.
The guidance was submitted as a public comment this month in response to a call for input from Meta’s Oversight Board on the use of large language models (LLMs) in content moderation, addressing both the potential efficiencies of automated review and the persistent challenges of interpreting nuanced content at scale.
“AI gives platforms an unprecedented opportunity to improve the enforcement of their own rules at scale, moving beyond slur lists toward context-based decisions that can help reduce human error. However, expert input is crucial to ensuring these systems can effectively address specific forms of online hate,” CyberWell founder and CEO Tal-Or Cohen Montemayor said.
“Antisemitism constantly evolves through coded language, symbols, cultural references, and forms of ‘algospeak’ designed to evade automated detection. AI moderation systems must draw on contextual, linguistic, and subject-matter expertise to recognize the antisemitic message, not just the words, while protecting legitimate expression. Social media platforms have also struggled to draw the line between anti-Jewish scapegoating – a classic form of antisemitism– and misinformation and disinformation campaigns that receive different moderation treatment,” Cohen Montemayor added.
In its submission, Cyberwell detailed several technical challenges that automated systems frequently fail to catch.
AI safety filters miss posts with hidden antisemitism
The report noted that online bad actors use modern AI tools to create tricky new versions of hate speech, meaning computer programs have to understand hidden meanings instead of just searching for banned words.
For example, automated safety filters often miss posts that combine harmless-looking images with hidden insults, such as an AI-generated video showing Adolf Hitler dancing in front of the Auschwitz concentration camp alongside text celebrating the mass murder of Jewish people.
Posts like these also frequently slip past automated checks by using innocent symbols in place of words, such as using a juice box emoji because it sounds similar to the word Jews when spoken.
The research revealed that internet users often try to hide hateful content by pretending they are just jokes, memes, or educational material.
For instance, automated filters often struggle to catch posts that mock the Holocaust by wrapping denialist ideas in absurd scenarios, such as a video calculating how difficult it would be to bake six million pizzas in five years.
Similarly, users frequently attach misleading labels, such as comedy or humor, or educational disclaimers to posts containing explicitly anti-Jewish stereotypes and hate speech, tricking basic computer filters into thinking the content is harmless.
The report also documented non-English hurdles, pointing to Arabic-language content that employs subtle letter modifications and punctuation dots between words to evade automated moderation while amplifying violent messaging and praising attackers.
Content moderation struggles to review hate spread in comment sections
Furthermore, harmful content frequently hides in comment sections where automated filters struggle because they evaluate text in isolation rather than looking at the original post.
For example, under a news post reporting on Israeli embassy workers murdered in Washington, DC, users bypassed filters and praised Hitler by referring to him as “the half moustache guy,” while other commenters used the phrase “promised 3,000 years ago” to mock and attempt to delegitimize the Jewish historical connection to the Land of Israel.
While social media platforms might not consider that specific phrase a policy violation when used in standalone posts, its appearance in comments responding to reports of antisemitic violence constitutes a violation used to mock victims and justify violence against them.
The core problem enabling this is that automated moderation tools fail to analyze how comments relate to the original post, missing how harmless-sounding phrases become toxic when used to target victims.
The report also noted that harmful content slips past automated tools by hiding inside account usernames and display handles and by circulating within audio clips that utilize non-English lyrics or varying lengths to escape detection.
The submission underscored severe inconsistencies in enforcement for high-reach accounts, demonstrating that identical policy-violating posts shared by influencers with large followings remain active even after repeated appeals, whereas ordinary user reposts are instantly removed.
CyberWell's five core recommendations for tech companies
To resolve these vulnerabilities, CyberWell issued five core recommendations for tech companies deploying LLMs for safety enforcement.
Platforms should collaborate with independent subject-matter experts to refine model training and evaluation using real-world annotated datasets.
Companies must ensure consistent moderation across platform surfaces and multi-modal formats, including comments, usernames, images, GIFs, videos, and audio.
Platforms need to improve multilingual and cultural accuracy by testing models against slang, dialects, irony, and coded language.
Tech firms should establish clear escalation pathways for human review during rapidly evolving global events.
Companies must increase public and user transparency through regular reporting on model performance, error rates, enforcement outcomes, and content-specific removal explanations.
“The future of effective trust and safety will depend on combining advanced technology with reliable data and real-world expertise,” Cohen Montemayor said.
“Our working relationship with Meta and other major social media platforms demonstrates what that can look like in practice. The potential to scale effective moderation through AI makes it even more important to deepen relationships with trusted experts and partners who understand technology and digital policy,” she explained.
“CyberWell is turning its expertise in how antisemitism and online hate evolve into practical datasets, evaluation tools, and technological solutions that can scale, helping platforms optimize their moderation systems to identify policy violations, including nuanced and coded forms of hate, and enforce their rules more accurately and consistently,” Cohen Montemayor said.

Government websites go dark as vulnerabilities in programming language send shudder across internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:37:40 UTC
23:37:40 KST

Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had quietly been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying that all users were "encouraged to update immediately."
With tech firms warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.
Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of fixes.
AI was powering a "race to exploit," said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet."
PHP - a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page" - underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning that any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences.
"All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable," said Tiffany Farriss, the interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. "This issue impacts the majority of the Internet."
Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied.
The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched.
Even some world leaders, who don't typically get involved with software updates, weighed in. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a post on X said website owners should "check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix."
PHP bug found with AI, Wiz says
The flaw in PHP was discovered using artificial intelligence, Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post.
The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to have taken advantage of, the post said.
"Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale," it said. "With AI this is no longer a barrier."
Wiz said its research relied on Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz said it coordinated with the PHP team, OpenAI, and the cybersecurity company Calif on the discovery of the vulnerability and patch verification.
The company said it also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Amazon's AWS, Microsoft, WordPress.com operator Automattic, and other companies such as Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, and Vercel to protect customers and prepare mitigations.
In a statement, the White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday.
"This discovery demonstrates exactly why American leadership in SI is so critical," the White House said, referring to President Donald Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence. "This is American innovation strengthening our national security.”
Significant number of websites vulnerable to attack
PHP is a programming language used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers.
Because of its ubiquity - PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs - and because the vulnerabilities are considered so dangerous, experts are anxious about a potentially vast pool of sitting ducks. AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have proliferated in recent weeks, would only make things worse, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London.
"The scale is huge, and with AI exploitation may happen instantly, on a large scale," Olejnik said.
The risk is particularly acute for small websites run by individuals or organizations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly manage the underlying servers. Security experts said such sites could take longer to patch and remain exposed well after fixes become available.
Mass outages as governments take websites offline
In the Netherlands, several organizations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national soccer association KNVB, the websites for the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites.
Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform.
Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure."
France's Interior Ministry said it had placed all of its websites into preventive maintenance. Japanese cloud service provider Sakura Internet said on Wednesday it had suspended a database appliance function.

Iran's Baloch minority want Israeli strikes to continue until regime falls, activist tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:37:32 UTC
23:37:32 KST

The Islamic regime in Iran is paying and blackmailing people to manufacture displays of support for Tehran in Sistan and Baluchestan province. It is pursuing the same policy among minority communities across Iran, a Baloch human rights activist in hiding told The Jerusalem Post late Tuesday night.
Identified only as “B” for security reasons, the activist has spent a decade in an Iranian prison over his ties to the Jebhe-ye Mobarezin-e Mardomi (People’s Fighters Front), an armed coalition of Sunni Baloch nationalists that has long fought the Islamic regime. The group has come under renewed attack in recent weeks following successful operations targeting the regime’s security apparatus, as the Post reported last week.
Through translation, B described the dire conditions facing the Baloch community since the revolution, from the psychological toll of repeated executions to extreme poverty in a region rich in oil and minerals. He claimed that across Sistan and Baluchestan, a vast province accounting for approximately 10% of Iran’s landmass, not a single Baloch family had been spared the loss of at least one of its members to the regime, either through shootings or executions.
According to Iran Human Rights, a nongovernmental organization that monitors executions, at least 108 Baloch individuals were executed in Iran in 2024, accounting for 11% of all recorded executions, despite the minority making up an estimated 2% to 6% of the country’s population. A report submitted to the UN Universal Periodic Review by several human rights organizations also found that Baloch people accounted for 29% of the 154 individuals executed in Iran between 2010 and 2023.
Although almost all Baloch are Muslim, the majority belong to Sunni or Zikri communities, which the regime views as heretical, B explained. He added that Tehran brands the Baloch and other minority groups as collaborators with Israel because they focus on human rights abuses committed in front of them rather than on a Jewish state more than 1,500 miles away.
'Israelis should be able to live a simple life'
“They tell members of the armed groups that the Baloch are enemies of the government, asking them, ‘Why are you not fighting Israel? Why do you have no problem with Israel? Why do you fight us?’ But Baloch people do not want to fight Israel or harbor hostility toward Israelis,” he said. “Most Baloch are religious Sunnis, and unlike the IRGC, which spreads hatred of Israel every day, they do not promote that kind of hatred. They believe Israelis should be able to live a simple life alongside Palestinians.”
Discrimination also limits the Baloch community’s economic opportunities. B noted that Iran’s Selection Law and other forms of discrimination prevent many Baloch from advancing in society, leaving some with few options but to smuggle subsidized fuel across borders to earn a living. Many have been burned to death by regime security forces, he said, adding that the forces knowingly opened fire on vehicles carrying the fuel.
Using the case of Ya’qub Mehrnahad as an example, a young blogger hanged in 2008 after a closed-door trial widely condemned as unfair, B said the Baloch people were denied justice at even the most basic level.
“He was just having a small protest about the regime, and he got executed,” B said. “They punish and torture people, forcing them to say on television whatever the regime wants them to say. The person is being punished or tortured, and they film them making statements they are being forced to make, then broadcast the footage on television. There is no court or proper judgment. They just arrest people, and this is still happening today.”
Reflecting on his own years in prison, B said he had seen multiple minors and individuals being held without charge.
Describing a reality in which people cannot afford food, and children must attend schools without shoes, classrooms, chairs or tables, he said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had not worsened conditions for his community. B said the supplies imported to Iran had never been meant for his people and that it was better to continue the blockade than risk supplying the regime.
Love and respect for all Abrahamic religions
“Every penny that comes through this Strait of Hormuz goes to the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC. Even when it comes to medicine and other supplies, they go to the Houthis and the Lebanese people. Not even one person benefits from the Strait of Hormuz, so it should be closed. It is better anyway because if it gets closed and the regime comes under pressure, maybe we can get this regime to go. Any benefit it gets from the Strait of Hormuz or anywhere else allows it to rebuild from within and grow stronger to beat the people, stop them from protesting, and prevent the regime from falling. It will do anything for that.”
After signaling his own curiosity about how Israelis view the Baloch people, B said he and his community were happy when Israel began striking the regime and hoped the attacks would continue.
“People were incredibly happy about this war. I could hear how happy they were. They were saying the war should not stop and expressing their love for Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump for carrying it out,” he said. “They were sending Trump messages of support for waging this war against the regime… I think Iranians love Netanyahu. They strongly support this war, and some have even been praying for it to continue, saying it should not stop until the regime falls and is replaced.”
B noted that he was an observant Muslim, but he had love and respect for all Abrahamic people, insisting that once the regime was gone, they would be able to live in peace together.
“We understand you. You are people who deserve to live in peace. We don’t think you are bad people or that you should die. That is how the regime thinks, not us. We share the same enemy, and we understand each other’s situation,” he said. “We have the right to life and peace. You and I are human beings, and even other living creatures have the right to life. We believe in one God, who created us all, and we are no different from anyone else. We deserve to live in peace. No one has the right to tell us that we do not deserve to live.”

Norway bars deals with 33 more Russian financial institutions—and 22 more from India to Nigeria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:37:05 UTC
23:37:05 KST

Norway has put into force a new round of sanctions against Russia that hits banks, listed oil refineries, ports, airports, and suppliers of Russia’s military industry, the Norwegian Foreign Ministry announced. The rules mirror the EU’s 21st sanctions package, which Brussels adopted in July.
The EU’s 22nd package, adopted on 12 October, is principally a list of names, while the 21st brought significant new measures, lawyers noted. Among them are new tools against the shadow fleet, the tankers with murky ownership that Russia uses to move oil around sanctions. That fleet also sails along Norway’s coast, and a new Norwegian Coastal Administration report found that it poses a growing threat to security and the environment there.
Banks, refineries, and Sheremetyevo
Norway is not an EU member, but it has joined every EU sanctions package against Russia, with a few exceptions and national adjustments. Oslo backed this one politically on 11 August, and the rules took effect on 21 October. Part of the package was already in force. It placed travel restrictions and asset freezes on 48 people and asset freezes on 168 entities, and it listed 41 shadow fleet vessels on 14 August.
Norway’s transaction ban now covers 33 more Russian credit and financial institutions. A separate ban covers 22 more abroad, including in India, Mongolia, Nigeria, and the UAE.
Another transaction ban reaches listed refineries in Russia and third countries that process Russian oil or help dodge sanctions. A Georgian refinery joins that list on 25 January 2027. The same ban adds two Russian ports and four Russian airports, including Moscow’s Sheremetyevo.
Drone gear and the shadow fleet
Export curbs on dual-use goods now cover 51 new entities that back Russia’s military industry. Some are in China, including Hong Kong, and others are in India, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Türkiye, and the UAE. The banned-exports list adds nickel and beryllium powder, along with drone gear such as jamming and interception systems, launchers, and servo motors.
Oslo can now also list ships that service sanctioned shadow fleet tankers or swap cargo with them at sea. Elsewhere in Europe, France’s navy and UK forces have boarded sanctioned shadow fleet tankers this year.

“Vladimir Putin emphasized that diplomatic opportunities are far from exhausted. And that it is possible and necessary to reach an agreement with Tehran, our strategic partner,” Ushakov went on to say.
He also said Witkoff, for his part, briefed Putin on the substance of talks he took part in Tuesday in the Norwegian capital Oslo, which included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and said Moscow’s decision to release US citizen Stephen Hubbard would be appreciated by Trump and the American public.
He added that Hubbard was handed over to Witkoff at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg for his return to the US following his release.

Missile strike in Aden
Separately, state-run Saba reported that the Houthi militia had targeted Aden International Airport with a ballistic missile, without providing further details.
Residents told Anadolu they heard a loud explosion near the airport.
The militia claimed a ballistic missile strike on Aden but identified its target as “the Saudi operations room at the Badr camp”.
The claim was made in a Telegram statement by the group’s spokesperson, Yahya Saree.
Yemen TV also reported air strikes on Houthi militia positions east of the coastal city of Mokha, without providing details of the targets or casualties.
Meanwhile, Al-Jumhuriya TV reported renewed heavy clashes between Yemeni armed forces and Houthi militia at the old airport and around Mount Han, west of Taiz.
Government offensive
The developments come amid an ongoing offensive by Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthi militia in the country’s southwest.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni army said it had carried out 744 attacks against the militia over 24 hours, claiming to have “neutralised” around 200 of its members and destroyed or damaged 90 vehicles and other military assets.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthi militia seized Sanaa and several other provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The militia controls much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:36:23 UTC
23:36:23 KST

Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.
Months away from key elections in Spain, France and Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.
Those in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-right National Rally (RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.
The party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader, Marine Le Pen, said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.
Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.
In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.
Weidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”
In Portugal, populists have used peaceful protests to blame immigration for the country’s housing crisis, which André Ventura of the far-right Chega party said was chiefly a consequence of an “uncontrolled influx of people from abroad”.
In Spain, where the housing crisis has led to huge protests and a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap election next month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”
Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked the mammoth protests would have had a home had she been an immigrant from north Africa.
In Belgium, where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.
“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”
Meloni has previously enacted sweeping security measures aimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.
This week she passed emergency decrees creating an offence of violent participation in a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.
Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.
Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”
The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.
Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.
JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.
Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reporting

​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:33:28 UTC
23:33:28 KST

Europe woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran.
The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”.
The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker, Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn.
While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees.
Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion.
First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied.
Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine.
Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany.
The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs.
Top donors to Ukraine by percentage of GDP
Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said.
France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£), Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention.
Putin’s ‘strategic patience’ rewarded?
“European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said.
That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.”
 
To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum.
Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.”
To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months.
But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.”

Spaceplane Without a Spaceport: Czech Company Introduces NEBESA Suborbital Flight Platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:33:21 UTC
23:33:21 KST

Czech company Nebesa Aerospace has presented its first development, the NEBESA suborbital flight platform, designed for testing, research, and defense missions.
Nebesa Aerospace representative Vojtěch Kubuš spoke to Militarnyi about the platform at the Future Forces Forum in Prague.
The platform features a tailless aerodynamic configuration with an elongated delta wing. Two vertical fins are mounted on the wing panels, and a rocket engine exhaust nozzle is located at the rear.
The platform can reach an altitude of 110 km and a speed of Mach 3.5 (3,700–4,300 km/h). Its maximum modular payload capacity is 25 kg.
The company is also developing a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle with a range of 1,000 km, a speed of 800 km/h and a payload capacity of 80 kg.
Potential applications for the suborbital platform include microgravity research; testing materials, aerodynamics and avionics; reconnaissance and surveillance; and serving as a target for testing air defense, detection, and tracking systems.
The platform is powered by a liquid-propellant rocket engine with a maximum thrust of 9 kN. Its development involves metal 3D printing, computer modeling and AI algorithms.
The NEBESA can take off and land at conventional airfields or on road sections, eliminating the need for a spaceport.
“We wanted to stand out among other drone manufacturers and present our vision of independent access to space. The main advantage of this platform is that you don’t need a spaceport,” Kubuš emphasized.
The company is currently seeking international partners and its first customers to launch serial production and testing of its spacecraft.

Rome Takes Center Stage During Italian Language Week in Bosnia
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:31:59 CEST
23:31:59 KST

The 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World was a huge success with the public in Sarajevo, celebrated last night with a cultural event organized by the Italian Embassy in collaboration with the Sarajevo Committee of the Dante Alighieri Society. The event, hosted at the city’s Music High School and dedicated to the theme “A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian,” was organized once again this year in collaboration with Zetema, Rome’s in-house agency for culture and tourism. The star of the evening was writer and translator Elvira Mujčić. Originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina and a well-established figure in the Italian literary scene for many years, Mujčić presented one of her unpublished short stories, introduced by Simona Cives, Director of the Rome Capital Library System. Mujčić, who arrived in Italy during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, chose Italian as the language of her literary work, using her novels and short stories to give voice to experiences and memories that transcend geographical and cultural boundaries.
                                    
In her introductory remarks, the Italian Ambassador, Sarah Eti Castellani, emphasized the value of the Italian language as a tool for creativity, innovation, and intercultural dialogue. Particular attention was given to the relations between Rome and Sarajevo. In the words of Rome’s Councilor for Culture, Massimiliano Smeriglio, who was present at the event, “Rome and Sarajevo share a relationship that we want to continue strengthening. We view cultural cooperation as a concrete way to bring people together, create opportunities, and build lasting bonds,” recalling the memorandum of understanding signed in 2024 between the two cities and the cultural initiatives carried out in recent years.
                                    
The President of the Sarajevo Committee of the Dante Alighieri Society, Renato Scuzzarello, highlighted the role of Italian Language Week in promoting Italy’s linguistic and cultural heritage around the world, emphasizing that “language is also a way to bring people together, learn about other cultures, and build bonds that transcend borders.”
The event brought together representatives from various Italian institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, teachers, students, and numerous enthusiasts of the Italian language and culture. The evening featured musical and theatrical performances by the students, as well as a musical interlude by soprano Hana Andrle, accompanied on the piano by Bakir Samardžić, and concluded with a roundtable discussion dedicated to the many forms of expression in the Italian language.
                                    
Councilor Smeriglio’s visit also provided an opportunity for a meeting today at Sarajevo City Hall with Mayor Samir Avdic and Deputy Mayor Pedrag Puharic, during which ongoing and future collaborative activities were discussed. Among upcoming activities is the planned visit to Rome in November by the directors of Sarajevo’s museums. The possibility of collaboration in the library sector, as well as in the field of archaeological conservation, was also raised. Rome’s museum experience was also highlighted in support of the Ars Aevi Museum of Contemporary Art currently under construction in Sarajevo—designed by architect Renzo Piano—as an example of the role of art in building bridges between cities and countries.

Russia releases American Stephen Hubbard after four years in prison
Hubbard was jailed after Russia said he fought alongside Ukrainian forces against Russia.
American Stephen Hubbard has been freed from a Russian prison and is on his way home after United States President Donald Trump said his administration had secured his release.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote in a social media post on Wednesday, adding that the US was not required to give anything in return for the release of the 74-year-old former teacher from Michigan.
The deal came during a visit to Russia by a top US envoy, and just days after Trump took a series of actions seen as beneficial to Moscow.
Hubbard, whose family says had been living in Ukraine since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, was tried and convicted in a closed-door trial, with Russian prosecutors saying he had signed a contract with the Ukrainian military and had fought alongside its forces before being captured. He was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2024.
The US had declared Hubbard a wrongfully detained American.
Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is in Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin on the Ukraine war, told him that “our whole nation sends their thanks” and that Putin was a “humanitarian” for allowing Hubbard to walk free. Witkoff briefly met with Hubbard in St. Petersburg after his release, telling him, “from today is a new life for you”.
The release came at a dynamic moment in relations between the US, Ukraine and Russia, with the Washington-Kyiv relationship under strain at the same time that the Trump administration has pursued policies which Ukraine says have rewarded Putin.
Those include Trump’s decision last week to waive sanctions on Russia imposed by a bill that the US Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine.
Named after the late South Carolina Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fuelling Moscow’s war on Ukraine.
That reversal followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in an effort to curb high gas prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

Pro-Palestine protests sweep Latin America as Brazil&#8217;s presidential race intensifies

Thousands of demonstrators have taken to the streets across Latin America in solidarity with Palestine, as Brazil approaches a closely contested presidential runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known for his pro-Palestinian stance, and pro-Israel Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.
The demonstrations formed part of a global campaign involving more than 200 organisations in over 60 countries, calling for an end to arms transfers to Israel and stronger international measures to hold it accountable for violations of international law.
Organised by the Global Alliance for Palestine, the international mobilisation brought together trade unions, student movements, human rights organisations and grassroots solidarity groups. Demonstrations and solidarity activities took place in Brazil, Mexico, Chile, Uruguay and Peru, as activists called for increased political, economic and diplomatic pressure on Israel.
In São Paulo, Brazil’s Unified Workers’ Central (CUT) joined the mobilisation, announcing the participation of healthcare workers demanding the release of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza, and other detained Palestinian medical personnel. The union also called for the protection of Palestinian hospitals and healthcare workers.
Soraya Misleh, a Palestinian-Brazilian activist, member of the Brazilian Press Union and the Coordination Committee of the Front for the Defence of the Palestinian People, and an activist in Brazil’s Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, warned that the presidential election could have consequences for Brazil’s position on Palestine and its relations with Israel.
Misleh warned that the growing influence of far-right governments across Latin America could lead to stronger economic, military and diplomatic relations with Israel, potentially undermining international efforts to hold it accountable.
She said Brazil’s political direction was particularly significant given the country’s regional influence, warning that developments elsewhere in Latin America should raise concerns among Brazilians ahead of the vote.
“This should raise even greater alarm among Brazilians at this moment of elections in Brazil, whose role is crucial in Latin America,” she said.
Misleh also criticised the limited international measures taken against Israel, arguing that too few governments had severed relations or implemented concrete steps to hold it accountable over the war in Gaza. “There is still a long road ahead in the struggle to isolate the State of Israel internationally, with very few countries having broken relations with Israel and adopted concrete measures,” she said.
She called for stronger solidarity with Palestinians and continued pressure on governments to pursue accountability, linking these demands to wider political developments across Latin America. “This makes it even more necessary to strengthen mobilisation and solidarity with the Palestinian people in order to continue demanding accountability,” she said.
Misleh added that efforts to hold Israel accountable should be accompanied by opposition to far-right political movements in the region. “The struggle for accountability must be combined with the struggle against the far right throughout Latin America, including in Brazil,” she said.
View this post on Instagram
Mohamad El Kadri, a founding member of the Front for the Defence of the Palestinian People in São Paulo, told MEMO that demonstrations across Brazil and Latin America were helping transform solidarity with Palestine into a sustained awareness campaign.
“The importance of these demonstrations lies in turning solidarity with Palestine from a reaction to immediate events into a continuous process of raising awareness about Palestinian society, its history and developments in the Palestinian territories,” he said.
El Kadri noted that similar activities had been organised in several Brazilian cities and states, reaching wider sections of society and raising awareness of the Palestinian cause.

He also highlighted the participation of trade unions and healthcare workers, particularly in the campaign demanding the release of Palestinian doctor Hussam Abu Safiya.
“The involvement of doctors and healthcare workers draws particular attention to the conditions facing Palestinian medical personnel and facilities,” he said.

View this post on Instagram
In Colombia, the government’s recent rapprochement with Israel has raised concerns among pro-Palestinian activists over the future of international efforts to hold Israel accountable.
Misleh pointed to recent developments in Colombia as an example of how changes in political leadership can reshape a country’s approach to Israel. “Unfortunately, with the far-right Abelardo de la Espriella assuming Colombia’s presidency in August 2026, he decided to reverse the measures adopted by Gustavo Petro regarding recognition of the genocide and intervention in the case brought by South Africa against Israel,” Misleh said.
She argued that Colombia’s policy reversal reflected a wider regional trend among far-right governments seeking closer relations with Israel. “All far-right governments in Latin America are committed to this alignment and to deepening economic, military and diplomatic relations with Israel,” she said.
For Misleh, the developments in Colombia carry particular significance as Brazil approaches its presidential runoff. “This should raise even greater alarm among Brazilians at this moment of elections in Brazil, whose role is crucial in Latin America,” she added.
Her remarks come amid growing concerns among Palestine solidarity activists about the potential implications of political changes in major Latin American countries for international efforts to hold Israel accountable.
She warned that international efforts to isolate Israel remained limited, noting that relatively few countries had severed diplomatic relations or adopted concrete measures. “There is still a long road ahead in the struggle to isolate the State of Israel internationally, with very few countries having broken relations with Israel and adopted concrete measures,” she said.
Misleh called for continued mobilisation in solidarity with Palestinians, arguing that such efforts were increasingly important amid the changing political landscape in Latin America. “This is certainly a step backwards, which makes it even more necessary to strengthen mobilisation and solidarity with the Palestinian people in order to continue demanding accountability,” she said.
“The struggle for accountability must be combined with the struggle against the far right throughout Latin America, including in Brazil,” she added.
View this post on Instagram
In Chile, thousands of people took to the streets of Santiago in a show of solidarity with Palestine. Organised by student groups, trade unions and human rights organisations, the march began near the Universidad Católica metro station and continued along Alameda Avenue towards Los Héroes. Demonstrators carried Palestinian flags and banners condemning Israel’s war on Gaza.
In neighbouring Uruguay, thousands marched through Montevideo under the slogan “Free Palestine or Barbarism”, calling on the government to take stronger action against Israel.
In Peru, student groups and human rights organisations joined the wave of solidarity, including representatives from the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, Free Palestine–Peru and the National University of San Marcos. The groups called for demonstrations in Lima, urging the government to take a stronger position on the war in Gaza and reconsider its relations with Israel.

Macron calls for extreme caution in Gulf, secures critical gas deal in Qatar state visit
