From one house to whole villages: Settlers have Palestinians surrounded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:20:27 UTC
22:20:27 KST

From one house to villages: Israeli settlers have Palestinians surrounded
A family in the South Hebron Hills has spent more than two weeks cut off by settlers camped outside. Israeli siege tactics are spreading across hamlets and villages in the occupied West Bank.
Yousef Shanaran, 52, built a well beside his house, which he can no longer reach. Since October 5, Israeli settlers have besieged his family home in Wadi Rakhim around the clock, a once-quiet corner of the South Hebron Hills among limestone rocks and thorny brush. They are unable to go outside on their own, even to fetch a little water from the well.
It took five days for the army to coordinate the family’s access to the well. After running out of water three days earlier, the Israeli army on Tuesday allowed them to retrieve some from the well.
“Food, there’s none,” Shanaran, who built the sturdy two-storey house in 2016 on land between the Palestinian town of as-Samu and the village of Susiya, planting about 70 grapevines and 30 to 40 olive trees, told Al Jazeera by phone.
“My well, full of water; I built it and lost money on it,” he said. “They keep me from it because they want to get me out of my house.”
More than half a year ago, settlers pitched a tent 300 metres (about 1,000 feet) from the Shanaran residence, restricting the family’s movement and exposing them to attacks and intimidation. On October 5, the tent was moved just 30 metres from their home. That day, about 50 settlers attacked the family with sticks and pepper spray. This marked the beginning of the full siege on Shanaran’s home.
A siege the army ‘doesn’t recognise’
Nasser Nawajeh, a longtime B’Tselem field researcher who now heads the Susiya village council in Masafer Yatta, has tried to deliver supplies to the Shanaran family during the siege, but most attempts have failed. “Once I tried to bring aid to the people, and right away there was an attack from the settlers,” he told Al Jazeera. “I mean they’re there 24 hours to attack.”
Nothing can move in or out of Shanaran’s home without the army’s permission. “This is a displacement policy,” he said. “If they want to take the kids out to school, we have to wait for the army to take them. If you want to bring in food or water, we have to do coordination.”
Since October 15, he has kept asking the army for coordination to deliver supplies to the family — and given excuses each day: “‘The army’s busy, can’t come, there aren’t any forces’ — they tell us ‘tomorrow and tomorrow’,” he said.
There are now two armies to contend with, Nawajeh said: the settlers’ regional units, the Kitat Konenut, meaning rapid response squads in Hebrew; and the regular army, which “comes, demolishes [the settlers’ tent] and leaves”. When the soldiers leave, the settlers simply pitch up their tent again.
Shanaran said the soldiers stationed outside his house do nothing. “They stand and sit, eating and drinking, relaxed, at the door of the house,” he said.
Nawajeh said the soldiers’ presence essentially amounts to a green light for the siege to continue.
“Sometimes the soldiers don’t even stop the settlers coming close; they hit people and sit with the soldiers at the door,” he said. As the house is in Area B, an area technically under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, the army could arrest all the settlers as there is a closure order against them. “But there’s no enforcement of these laws,” he added.
The soldiers posted outside the family home see their ostensible job as shielding the family from a beating, not ending the blockade. “In practice, the Palestinians are living in a prison inside. The siege is basically a prison,” he added.
Shanaran said his family, trapped in their home, is living a life worse than prison.
“Prison ends. Here, you’re sitting in your own house, and they’ve locked you up in it — and you’re afraid,” he said.
‘If they drive out the first house, they drive out the second’
The Shanaran home is the closest Palestinian one to the outposts encroaching on it, Nawajeh said. Settlers see no difference between Area A, intended to be administered by Palestinians, Area B under mixed Israeli-Palestinian authority, and Area C, which is fully under Israeli military and civil control.
“They start with the house on the edge, in the corner. If they drive out the first house, they drive out the second,” he added.
This tactic is now being applied in Masafer Yatta, an area south of the occupied West Bank which has come under repeated Israeli settler and military attacks.
Following similar sieges further north in Jalud, where the Tubasi family was forced from their home in July and attacked in September when they tried to return under a court order, and in Qusra, where settlers besieged three homes, one owned by an American citizen, before the army set up barracks beside the besieged homes.
B’Tselem’s Yair Dvir believes that the fact that the Qusra siege drew wide coverage was because one of the Palestinians involved held US citizenship.
“In reality, attacks like these occur continually across the West Bank,” Dvir said.
Settlers have now built more than 400 outposts across the West Bank, isolating Palestinian homes and communities through their control of nearby hilltops and pathways.
Dror Etkes, cofounder of the settlement-monitoring group Kerem Navot, said, with Palestinians surrounded, these doorstep sieges reflect “an advanced stage of the complete collapse of any rule of law, any attempt to enforce law in the West Bank”.
Violence that once kept Palestinians off open grazing and farmland is gradually moving into built-up areas, Etkes said. Driving whole farming communities off their land in one fell swoop is still beyond settlers’ reach, he said, but “what they’re trying to do right now is to expel certain families … who are residing outside of the big cluster of a built-up area”.
At the eastern end of the farming village of Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, stands the home of Muhammad al-Abayat. The family has lived there since 1973, before the nearby illegal settlement of Ateret was established, according to the village mayor, Marwan Sabah. It now sits between Ateret and one of the six outposts surrounding the village.
Late in September, Israeli settlers pitched a tent at the family’s door, then fixed a gate blocking the path to their home, where 15 people live. The children cannot get to school, and al-Abayat’s wife is ill and needs an operation.
“Even his kids are banned; the family can barely get the basic supplies to him,” Sabah said. Anyone who tries to reach the family is attacked or pepper-sprayed. The village won a court ruling and a police decision to open the gate, but “the settlers lock the gate themselves most of the time”, he said.
The mayor says the village as a whole faces a “suffocating siege”, with illegal outposts surrounding it and military support buttressing them. “Right now all of Umm Safa’s land is under the settlers’ control, including the village cemetery,” he said. Now that the harvest is under way, “all the olives are in their hands”.
Even basic services are becoming impossible, “all the rubbish — we can’t get it out”, he added.
Amid the settler siege on October 20, the Israeli Civil Administration issued a demolition notice for the Abayat family home.
When the army carries out the siege
In Madama, south of Nablus, settler outposts in Area B to the north and west, along with an illegal settlement and bypass road to the south, have surrounded the village. On October 12, the army sealed all three main entrances to the village with earth mounds. On the same day, a weeklong siege of neighbouring Burin was lifted.
This forced villagers, including teachers, women and children, to quickly cross the mounds on foot while two cars waited on either side, said Wail Qut, a Madama resident and lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), which is challenging a new Area B outpost near the village before Israel’s High Court. A teacher was beaten by settlers while trying to cross, he said, and two dialysis patients now face a far longer route to the hospital where they need regular treatment.
On October 18, a bulldozer that villagers say came from the Yitzhar illegal settlement shut the last road in use – a backroad towards Asira al-Qibliya, uprooting nearby olive trees. According to Qut, the army’s District Coordination Office told the mayor the barriers would stay until “the farmers don’t go to their land [during the olive harvest], especially in the north”, where the settler outpost in question lies.
“I’ve lived here all my life, and this is unprecedented for Madama village,” Qut said after the backroad was sealed. “The settlers are seizing a golden opportunity. No deterrence from the Israeli government … they are just trying to do their best before the Israeli election.”
On Tuesday, the northern entrance was finally reopened. But villagers reported that settlers from the Area B outpost attacked olive harvesters near the approach to the village that evening. The next day, the military sealed the entrance again, with many olive trees filmed being destroyed in the process. The siege continues, residents say.
Different stages of the same squeeze
Last week, settlers east of Jerusalem strung barbed wire around the Bedouin communities of al-Tabna and al-Muhtawish, near Khan al-Ahmar. Suleiman Ali Salem al-Arab, known as Abu Ra’id, said their livestock are penned in and have nowhere to graze, and the five-minute trip to a nearby road now takes an hour. Settlers are driving posts for a fence to enclose the communities completely. “They put it between the houses and shut people in so they can drive people out,” said Abu Raid.
In Ras al-Ahmar, in the northern Jordan Valley, the siege is closer to dispossessing its inhabitants altogether. Israeli forces have sealed other access points and confiscated tractors and water tanks as the “Crimson Thread” barrier is built through the area.
According to the Israeli group Jordan Valley Activists, another 11 families have left in the past two weeks, leaving about 20 of the 59 families that originally lived there. “More than half the families have been displaced because of thirst,” says Thaer Bisharat, a local herder. “We fast like it’s Ramadan, and the sheep become like camels.”
As settler sieges intensify — enabled and eventually replaced by the military itself — Nawajeh fears another wave of Palestinian displacement is under way. “It’s becoming something normal,” he said. “Every day dozens of settlers could take a Palestinian house and besiege it.”
“Imagine someone set an unjust enemy upon you, pitched a tent under your window, holding a grudge against you,” said Shanaran, from his besieged home. “Every time you go out, he comes, beats you, or stops you. How would your life be?”

Republicans bet Musk’s millions can rescue Texas’ Ken Paxton in US Senate race
- Elon Musk and other donors have poured hundreds of millions into Ken Paxton’s Texas Senate bid, but it is unclear if late spending can change a race with few undecided voters.
- Republicans have spent more than US$500 million overall, with heavy use of culture-war ads to boost turnout, while Democrats say voters care more about living costs and the economy.
- James Talarico has raised US$64 million from July to September and leads narrowly, while Paxton faces renewed scrutiny over past impeachment and fraud cases, which he denies.
AI generated
HOUSTON, Texas - Texas Democrats’ best chance at a statewide win in more than three decades is facing a wall of Republican money, with Elon Musk and other donors pouring hundreds of millions into a late effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
With two weeks until the Nov 3 election and early voting under way, however, it is unclear how much impact the spending can still have.
Polls show few undecided voters remain, and Republicans say their biggest challenge is turning out their own voters, many of whom are frustrated by the cost of living and the war with Iran launched by US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Paxton.
“The money being spent now isn’t for persuasion. It’s for mobilisation,” said pollster James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas. “In most of the statewide polling we’ve seen, Republicans are suffering from an enthusiasm gap.”
Republican strategists say internal polling shows that gap has narrowed considerably.
“We’ve seen it collapse, thank God. It was one of our concerns,” said Dave Carney, a longtime Republican strategist and chief adviser to Texas Governor Greg Abbott.
That turnout challenge helps explain the tone of Republican advertising.
Rather than focusing on inflation and the economy, which polls consistently show are among voters’ top concerns, Republicans in Texas and other battleground states have leaned heavily on culture-war themes to energise their base.
Republican groups have spent more than US$100 million (S$127.73 million) nationally since Aug 1 on more than 200 ads accusing Democrats of backing “sex change” procedures for children, according to an analysis of AdImpact data by FactCheck.org.
Texas-sized spending
Combined advertising spending in the race between Paxton, the state’s Republican attorney-general, and Democrat James Talarico has topped US$500 million, according to ad-tracking data, putting it on pace to become the most expensive US Senate contest ever.
Talarico has held a small but consistent lead over Paxton, though generally within the margin of error, making it Texas’ most competitive statewide race since 1994, Henson said.
Outside groups backing Paxton have spent about US$239 million, more than five times the roughly US$45 million spent by the largest Democratic-aligned groups. Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC, alone has accounted for nearly US$149 million.
The group was launched by the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC.
Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed US$158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, which subsequently transferred matching sums to Texas PAC, according to federal filings.
Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising.
His campaign says it raised US$64 million from July through September, more than triple Paxton’s total, with 97% of donations under US$100.
He spent US$61 million on ads through September, according to AdImpact, while the biggest Democratic outside group, Lone Star Rising PAC, has spent US$19.3 million.
The influx of Republican money arrived relatively late in the campaign, with Trump’s MAGA Inc super PAC not beginning major spending until early September.
“I think the cavalry arrived just in the nick of time for Paxton,” said Republican donor and oil businessman Dan Eberhart.
Going negative
Much of that spending has funded attacks portraying Talarico as out of step with Texas voters on culture-war issues.
Independent fact checkers say the ads distort Talarico’s record, and Henson said their goal is “arousing negative sentiment among Republican voters” to boost turnout.
Texas PAC ads tell voters that Talarico is “for they/them, not you” and accuse him of supporting taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries for minors.
PolitiFact rated that claim false, noting that while Talarico opposed a 2023 ban on gender-transition care for minors, he has said he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for children.
A Paxton campaign ad featured an AI-generated Talarico reading from a fictional “King James (Talarico) Bible” that combined excerpts of his past remarks, including one describing God as “non-binary.”
FactCheck.org said the ad lacked key context.
Talarico has responded by casting Paxton as “the most corrupt politician in Texas.”
Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on abuse-of-office allegations but was acquitted by the state Senate.
Separate state securities-fraud charges dating to 2015 were dropped in 2024 under an agreement requiring community service, ethics training and restitution.
Paxton denied wrongdoing.
The Paxton campaign did not respond to requests for comment. It has previously said Talarico raises the allegations to distract from his own record.
Some voters say the Republican attacks are unconvincing.
Sal Anthony Rodriguez, a 32-year-old Houston operations manager who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said he now supports Talarico, partly because of what he views as misleading attacks.
“I’ve seen a lot of ads saying that he is in 100% support for transgender surgeries on kids, and a quick Google search showed that that was not accurate,” Rodriguez said.
Democrats argue the focus on cultural issues reflects Republican difficulty addressing voters’ economic concerns.
“Voters are really pissed off about the state of their lives right now, and you can only run so many trans ads at people who are sick of paying US$6 for diesel,” said Chuck Rocha, a senior adviser to the Talarico campaign. REUTERS

Is China Getting Involved in the Japan-Russia Territorial Dispute?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

According to information released by the government of Russia’s Sakhalin Oblast on October 13, a delegation from China’s Heilongjiang Province, including government officials and entrepreneurs, recently visited Iturup Island (Etorofu in Japanese). The island is part of the Southern Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan, which are currently under Russian de facto control, though Japan claims sovereignty over them.
The Chinese group’s visit led to an immediate expression of dissatisfaction from Tokyo, with Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu declaring it “absolutely unacceptable.” In response, Beijing stated that it “consistently advocates for respecting and upholding the outcomes of the victory [of World War II].” A Japanese media outlet suggested that this reflects “a coordinated stance between China and Russia regarding the Northern Territories issue and a joint approach in dealing with Japan.”
The islands in question were under Japanese control until they were occupied by the Soviet Union at the end of World War II. The Japanese government has maintained its claim ever since. Tokyo has made repeated attempts to advance negotiations on the territorial issue with Russia by leveraging economic cooperation and investment. Ultimately, however, these efforts have not yielded satisfactory results.
Despite possessing abundant fishery and mineral resources, the economic potential of these islands remains largely untapped due to the lagging economic development of the Russian Far East, inadequate infrastructure, and high transportation costs. In 2022, Russia announced the establishment of a special economic zone on the islands to foster economic growth. If Chinese enterprises become more involved in the economic development of the Southern Kuril Islands in the future, it would not only exert political pressure on Japan but could also strengthen Russia’s de facto control over these islands.
Although maps currently published in China label these islands as Japanese territory under Russian occupation, Beijing generally avoids taking an explicit stance on their sovereignty. In August 2026, following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup Island, the Chinese and Russian ambassadors to Japan co-authored an article stating: “The preservation of historical memory of World War II and its outcomes is particularly important for our countries.” This appeared to imply China’s acknowledgment of the status quo without an overt declaration. Some Japanese media outlets perceive Beijing as shifting away from the position it held during the later Mao era and moving toward the Russian side.
It remains unclear whether this delegation’s visit was intentionally orchestrated by Beijing. However, given that the delegation included officials from the Heilongjiang provincial government, the visit clearly had at least the tacit approval of the authorities.
Over the past few months, Japanese lawmakers from various political parties have visited Taiwan, and most notably, a group of 27 Japanese parliamentarians arrived in Taiwan around the same time as this delegation’s visit. Beijing typically views such actions as an infringement upon China’s territorial sovereignty. Consequently, this visit by the Chinese delegation may well be a countermeasure by Beijing against Japan.
One disadvantage for Japan is that it is involved in territorial or maritime disputes with nearly all of its neighbors. These disputes currently remain largely a matter of bilateral relations between Japan and the respective countries involved. However, the Chinese delegation’s visit to the Southern Kuril Islands against the backdrop of deteriorating China-Japan relations may signal that Beijing has deployed a diplomatic card against Japan that had previously received little attention.
The deepening of China-Russia relations has further complicated this issue. In recent years, the frequent joint patrols conducted by Chinese and Russian military aircraft and naval vessels in the vicinity of Japan have drawn concern from Tokyo.
Concurrently, China and Russia have aligned their historical narratives. In May 2025, the two nations issued a joint statement commemorating their respective victories in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Great Patriotic War, while also pledging to strengthen bilateral cooperation and uphold the authority of international law. The statement characterized both China and Russia as “pivotal forces in the fight against militarism and fascism” and asserts their commitment to “defending the outcomes of the Second World War” and resisting any “resurgence of militarism.” This aligns with Beijing’s accusations that Japan is pursuing a “new-type militarism.”
Given these shared historical perceptions, China and Russia can be expected to coordinate more closely on historical and security-related issues in their diplomatic approaches toward Japan.
However, it remains highly likely that Beijing will continue to avoid formally recognizing Russian sovereignty over the islands. This is not only because China needs to maintain diplomatic maneuvering room vis-à-vis Japan, but also because it seeks to avoid becoming entirely tethered to Russia’s interests.
Japan’s response, meanwhile, is constrained by both its own policy toward Russia and the state of its relations with China. Japan’s continued imposition of sanctions against Russia makes any substantive improvement in its relations with Moscow in the near term highly unlikely. At the same time, there are no signs of any meaningful improvement in Tokyo’s relations with China. Against this backdrop, it is difficult for Japan to effectively counter the activities of China and Russia in the region.
More significantly, should China begin to actively engage in economic activities or even pursue military cooperation with Russia on the islands, the issue could gradually evolve from a bilateral dispute between Japan and Russia into a new variable affecting China-Japan relations and, by extension, the security landscape of Northeast Asia.

Merz Urges Trump to Invite South Africa to G-20 Summit in Miami

French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:17:32 UTC
22:17:32 KST

France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.
With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.
The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks.
Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.
Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges.
No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.
International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.
Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.
“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

German economy stalls as inflation hits highest level since late 2023: Bundesbank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:16:37 UTC
22:16:37 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Germany's economy likely stagnated in the third quarter as rising energy costs weighed on households, while September inflation reached its highest level since late 2023, the Bundesbank said Wednesday.
In its October report, the central bank attributed the pause in recovery partly to temporary factors, including low Rhine water levels and effects linked to fuel-tax relief.
High energy prices dampened household purchasing power, while weakness in the automotive sector weighed on industrial production in August. Factory holidays concentrated in that month also contributed.
Low water levels disrupted shipping and raised transport costs for energy-intensive industries, including oil refining and chemicals, weighing on foreign trade.
Construction output increased in August, although rising mortgage rates were expected to constrain activity.
Annual harmonized inflation climbed to 3.3% in September from 2.9% in August as the Middle East conflict drove energy prices higher.
The bank expects inflation to remain elevated, with energy costs increasingly feeding into industrial goods, food and services.
The expiration of fuel-tax relief and a health reform raising patient payments for medicines and hospital services in early 2027 are expected to add further inflationary pressure.

Witkoff’s proposals, possibility of trilateral meeting: Kremlin's statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:16:08 UTC
22:16:08 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin will consider and assess all the developments and proposals that special envoy of the US leader Steve Witkoff brought to the talks, Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in a comment to Vesti.
He also said that a meeting between Putin, American leader Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is possible, although there is no clear agenda yet.
TASS has compiled the key statements of the Kremlin representative.
The Ukrainian settlement
Trump is open and consistent in his desire to bring the Ukrainian conflict to a peaceful settlement: "We see that President Trump is quite sincere and consistent in his wish to facilitate a peaceful resolution and to set everything on the path toward a peace settlement."
American negotiators Witkoff and Jared Kushner are following Trump's general line aimed at resolving the Ukrainian conflict: "The negotiators pursue this general line."
Putin will study and evaluate all the developments and proposals that Witkoff brought to the talks: "Witkoff brought some ideas -- especially in light of the meetings he held in Oslo with Zelensky and representatives of European countries. Naturally, all these proposals will be reviewed and evaluated by the president. We will see what happens next."
A lot depends on Ukrainians in the peaceful settlement of the conflict, but their situation, including on the ground, is getting worse every day: "A lot, of course, depends on the Ukrainians, including whether they are ready for a peace [settlement]. Trump made it very clear that if they had agreed to a peace settlement a year or two years ago, they could have reached a deal on conditions that would have been more advantageous for them," Peskov noted. "Their position has deteriorated. And the situation on the ground has also worsened, with conditions getting worse by the day."
It is "theoretically possible" to take a significant step forward in the settlement: "It is theoretically possible to make an important step forward."
"Putin is open to seeking ways of achieving a peace settlement."
The possibility of a Putin-Trump-Xi meeting
A meeting between Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is possible, but there is no clear agenda yet: "All three sides understand that it would be a good idea to meet. All three sides are hypothetically ready for such a meeting. However, there is no clear agenda right now, so this is something that needs to be worked on."
A meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping would attract the attention of the whole world: " It is incorrect to use words like ‘new Yalta’ (the 1945 Yalta Conference -- TASS) and so on, but, of course, if the leaders of the US, China and Russia get together, it will be a meeting that attracts the attention of the whole world."
The United States wants to discuss strategic stability and nuclear disarmament at the meeting, but China does not want this, while Russia is ready for both: "You know that the Americans are seeking to discuss nuclear disarmament, something that the Chinese are opposed to. We are ready for either scenario."
There are many questions that could be considered at the meeting: "There are lots of issues apart from that."
Hubbard's release
The United States has raised the issue of the release of its citizen Stephen Hubbard, convicted of participating in hostilities on the Ukrainian side for a while: "This issue has indeed been raised by the US side for quite some time."
Putin released Hubbard based on humanitarian considerations: "As regards that decision, the president made it for humanitarian reasons."
Contacts on prisoner exchanges continue all the time through the special services: "In general, contacts on exchanges, etc., continue on an ongoing basis through the special services."

Fact-Checked: Trump’s Latest Ukraine Claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:15:55 UTC
22:15:55 KST

US President Donald J. Trump on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 during an Oval Office presentation of new whistleblower law fielded reporter questions on among other subjects Ukraine, its past history, and his administration’s policies towards that country.
Kyiv Post fact-checked what Trump said. The transcript of the exchanges is here:https://trump-archive.com/item/7c941fa6-26b0-4278-9d62-a0a1d5f78a83
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump answered reporter questions during some 30 minutes of the 1:05 hour public appearance. Of that time, about ten minutes covered Ukraine.
1. Russia is advancing in Ukraine, its forces cannot be stopped.
Trump said: “I think that – and, you know, Russia’s a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that’s what they’ve done. They’ve taken a very large piece of land. And, you know, you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week. It’s just a march forward. They just keep marching forward.”
This is false. The reality is that the front is generally at stalemate and that Ukrainian forces, not Russian, are gaining ground at the moment.
On-the-ground reporting by independent media, including Kyiv Post, confirms that Russia’s advances slowed to a crawl in early 2026, largely due to Ukraine’s expanding use of drone swarms and improved defensive tactics. Assessments by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and other think tanks indicate that Russia’s net territorial gains across the entire front in 2026 amount to roughly 100 square kilometers (39 square miles), an area comparable to the British island of Jersey or New York City’s Bronx borough.
Trump Envoy Witkoff Calls Putin a ‘Humanist’ Amid Deadly Russian Attacks on Ukraine
In September and October 2026, according to Ukrainian military announcements generally confirmed by OSINT trackers and internal unit information feeds monitored by Kyiv Post, Ukrainian counteroffensives in the Lyman and Oleksandrivka sectors resulted in modest net territorial gains for Ukraine and major losses for Russia.
2. Russia is continuously advancing because it has bottomless reserves of manpower.
Trump said: “They (Russia) have an unlimited supply of people...They can lose a lot of people in a war, and they have lost a lot of people. They lost 50 million people in the Second World War. They lose a lot of people, but they’re very big.”
Aside from Trump’s point that Russia is a large country, this statement is false.
Russian manpower shortages are longstanding and widely-reported – undermining Russia’s ability to prosecute combat operations.
Russia mobilized reserves in 2022, began mass recruitment of prison felons in 2023, and since then has mobilized law enforcement and offered signing bonuses equivalent to a year’s salary of a professional worker in order to convince men to join their armed forces.
Ukrainian army intelligence, in an estimate supported by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), estimates that Russia is currently recruiting about 30,000 contract soldiers per month. That figure is significantly below reported monthly losses of 40,000-50,000 personnel killed and wounded, according to estimates by Ukraine’s General Staff and NATO.
Ukrainian combat units report that Russian forces attack almost exclusively with small groups of foot soldiers unsupported by tanks or other fighting vehicles. Those infantries are, per those accounts, effectively defenseless against drones and suffer severe casualties executing orders to advance. Near-total absence of Russian tactical medical evacuation exacerbates casualty rates and prevents many otherwise savable injured soldiers from dying.
Currently, the best example of Russian casualty-intensive tactics gaining little or no ground is in the eastern Dobropillya sector, where Ukrainian 1st Corps ground units, backed by Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) drone squadrons, have reported breaking their record for the number of Russian soldiers killed or wounded in a single day three times during October.
Therefore, Trump’s claim about Soviet World War II deaths is exaggerated.
3. The US has given Ukraine $350 billion in assistance.
Trump said: “We gave $350 billion to Ukraine...Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve gotten nothing back, other than high diesel. We have – we have given probably – possibly more money to Ukraine than almost anybody over the years, hundreds of billions of dollars.”
This is absolutely false, nevertheless, Trump has repeated this statement for years.
No credible source supports a $350 billion figure for US aid to Ukraine. Official US and independent tallies put total US bilateral aid commitments to Ukraine at roughly $130-136 billion in direct military, financial, and humanitarian aid since 2022.
Trump’s administration in Feb. 2025 cut off all financial assistance and practically all military assistance to Ukraine. On Trump’s orders, since that time, US weaponry can be sold to Europe in limited quantities for donation to Ukraine, but for that service the US charges a 10 percent markup. The total value of quantifiable US-donated aid to Ukraine since Trump took office is less than $1 billion.
Compared to the US, Europe has donated about twice as much to Ukraine, and since early 2025, has been overwhelmingly Ukraine’s main source of foreign support.
Regarding Trump’s claim that the US “got nothing back,” Ukraine, at the insistence of the Trump administration, signed a “mineral deal” in April 2025 granting selected US corporations monopoly access to major Ukrainian rare-earth reserves. More generally, thanks to Ukraine’s sacrifice in blood and treasure, the cost to the US of deterring Russia in Europe and worldwide has been reduced.
4. Ukraine would have been defeated by Russia on the first day of the war, but an incompetent Russian general lost 1,000 tanks in a swamp.
Trump said: “When the stupid general for Russia, very stupid gentleman, they had 1,000 tanks riding up a concrete highway, they would have been in Ukraine in four hours, going maximum tank speed, which is 48 miles an hour to be exact. Nothing to stop them, the war would have been over in one day. And this very stupid general, I have no idea who he is. I doubt he’s still with us, I doubt he’s still living. He decided to hang a right onto the farmland and then take a left and go up to Kyiv. And rather than staying on the highway, the concrete highway, perfectly good highway where they were doing very nicely, would have been there in three and a half or four hours and the whole war would have ended. He ended up getting stuck in the mud. It was like quicksand. They had -- the night before they had the heaviest rainfall they’ve had in 10 years, and the land was soaking wet; it was like quicksand. Most people don’t remember, but I do, because it’s called war, you never know what happens. But he made a terrible decision, legendarily bad decision and the tanks got stuck. They couldn’t go forward, they couldn’t go back, they were dead stuck.”
This narrative is false and effectively fiction. The Battle of Kyiv was one of the most decisive and large-scale battles of the Russo-Ukraine War with tens of thousands of participants and even more civilian eyewitnesses. Their accounts and experiences differ dramatically from Trump’s narrative.
In early 2022, Russia attempted to capture Kyiv by launching paratrooper and air assault infantry attacks to capture a key airfield north of the city, following up with a massive ground force offensive invading Ukraine from the territory of Belarus – at the time a neutral state. The airborne operation went awry when Ukrainian air defenses shot down Russian helicopters and paratrooper planes approaching the airport, and failed after Ukrainian ground forces and artillery surrounded and destroyed lightly-armed Russian paratroopers on the ground.
Simultaneously, Ukrainian commanders opened sluices in dams containing water from drained wetlands north of Kyiv. That inundation and difficult forested terrain, part of it including the irradiated Chernobyl exclusion zone, forced Russian tank columns driving to reinforce the paratroopers to stay on roads leading south. Those advancing Russian forces met fierce resistance by Ukrainian regular forces, national guard, and volunteer civilian militia. This created Russian armored vehicle traffic jams 50 km (31 miles) long and even visible from space.
Over the following month, Russian armored units suffered heavy losses in ambushes, typically set by Ukrainian anti-armor teams in villages or along forested stretches of road. Ukrainian strike drones armed with anti-tank missiles added to Russian casualties. Russian attempts to bypass roads and move cross-country resulted in some vehicles becoming bogged down and subsequently destroyed by Ukrainian forces. However, according to most historians, the main causes of Russia’s failure to take Kyiv were due to widespread Ukrainian resistance, combined with a Russian invasion plan that assumed Ukrainian military forces would surrender and civilians would welcome the invading troops. A standard historical treatment of the battle is available here:
https://www.amazon.co.uk/Battle-Kyiv-Fight-Ukraines-Capital/dp/1399048481/?tag=5812456021-20
5. Ukraine’s survival was the result of Trump’s agreement to transfer Javelin missiles
Trump said: “And they [Ukrainian forces] used the Javelins – that’s the anti-tank weapon that I gave them. So, you know, the statement is Obama gave them sheets, I gave them Javelins. So, I’ve helped Ukraine a lot.”
This statement is also very misleading.
Limited use of Javelin anti-tank missiles against Russian armor north of Kyiv in February and March 2022 is well documented, but only in isolated incidents. Almost all of those engagements were against tanks on roads or in open fields, and not against tanks mired in swamps.
Besides Javelins, among other weapons, Ukrainian forces used British NLAW missiles, Swedish AT-4, and Carl Gustav anti-tank rockets, Swedish- and Turkish-made Bayraktar drones, domestically produced Stugna missiles, regular Ukrainian army T-64, T-72, and T-80 tanks, anti-tank mines, and anti-armor grenades to blunt the Russian armored attack. Compared to the mass of anti-armor weaponry operated by Ukrainian forces, Javelins were rare and usually reserved for use by commando teams specially trained in their use.During his first term as US President, Trump did green-light the first US delivery of lethal weaponry to Ukraine, including 210 Javelin missiles delivered in 2018. A second batch of 150 missiles was sent in 2019. Besides Trump, Estonia and the Biden administration also supplied Ukraine with Javelins in early 2022.
By far the most significant foreign anti-tank weapon delivery to Ukraine prior to Russia’s second invasion was the shipment of more than 2,000 NLAW missiles, a weapon similar to the Javelin, in late 2021 and early 2022. Those deliveries had increased to more than 5,000 by April 2022.
Given the scale of those anti-armor deliveries and the wide range of anti-armor weaponry available to Ukraine’s armed forces, Trump’s claim that the 360 Javelin missiles his administration sent to Ukraine in 2018-19 won the Battle of Kyiv is not credible.
Relevant to any discussion of US arms deliveries to Ukraine between 2016-22 is a 2019 phone call between Presidents Zelensky and Trump, during which the release of $391 million in US military aid to Ukraine was made contingent on Kyiv launching a criminal investigation into Ukrainian businesses linked to Hunter Biden, the son of then-US Vice President Joe Biden. Biden was Trump’s principal political rival at the time and would go on to defeat him in the 2020 US presidential election.
Prior to leaving office, Trump was impeached by the House of Representatives for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress over allegations that he attempted to leverage US military aid to Ukraine for personal political gain and pressure a foreign government to investigate the child of a political opponent. Arguably, that impeachment undermines Trump’s October 2026 contention that he has been a significant and effective supporter of US arms transfers to Ukraine.

Germany news: Nvidia CEO optimistic about EU's AI economy

Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
Published October 21, 2026last updated October 22, 2026
What you need to know
- One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected
- Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin
- Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect
- Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter
This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.
Thanks for following our blog
We'll be back with the latest headlines out of the country on Thursday. Tschüss!
Weidel pitches 'three pillars' of EU reform at European Parliament
Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.
"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."
On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."
"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."
This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.
She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."
Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.
Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."
"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.
She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."
While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

Nvidia CEO Huang dazzles Berlin audience with AI pitch
A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.
The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).
Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.
"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.
Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.
There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.
But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.
Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.

The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.

The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.
"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."

Ifo Institute questions savings target of parental allowance reform
Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.
However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.
The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.
Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.
"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.
The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.
"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.

Mortgage rates drop for the first time in 2 months, but demand still falls further
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:13:48 UTC
22:13:48 KST

Mortgage demand took another leg lower, despite a brief respite from rising interest rates.
Total mortgage application volume fell 5.3% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, dropped last week to 7.41% from 7.50%, with points falling to 0.75 from 0.83 including the origination fee for loans with a 20% down payment.
"Mortgage rates decreased for the first time in over two months," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "However, lower rates were not enough to boost application activity, as both purchase and refinance applications continued to decline."
Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly moves, fell just 2% week to week, a smaller drop than some previous weeks when rates were moving higher. Refinance demand was still 59% lower than the same week one year ago. With rates now over a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago, there is a very small pool of borrowers who can benefit from a refinance.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home declined a steeper 7% for the week and were 18% lower from the year before. Buyers are reacting less to the weekly move in rates but more to the overall higher level. A report from the National Association of Realtors on Tuesday showed a sharp drop in September pending home sales. These are measured by signed contracts, so it showed the real-time impact of rising rates during the month. Rates remained at that higher level in October.
For those buyers in the market, a continued high share are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages, or ARMs, which offer lower rates but are considered riskier because they will eventually reset to whatever the market rate is at the end of their term.
"The ARM share held steady at 10.5 percent, as ARM rates remained almost a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed rate, giving qualified borrowers a lower rate option to purchase a home," Kan added.
Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. Last week was a particularly volatile week for rates, due to multiple monthly inflation reports. This week the moves have seemed to follow oil prices.
"But we'd caution against placing too much emphasis on the oil price correlation," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "It's been highly unreliable for more than a month."
Correction: The National Association of Realtors on Tuesday reported September pending home sales. An earlier version misstated the day.

Why the US Needs Ukraine as Much as Ukraine Needs the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:12:57 UTC
22:12:57 KST

The US appears to have picked a side over Ukraine, and it’s not Kyiv.
As President Volodymyr Zelensky not so subtly called on US President Donald Trump to “stay in the middle,” Trump has pursued deals with Moscow and has ostensibly chosen Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s side – that of a man who, according to Ukraine, has been responsible for 228,992 war crimes committed by the Russian army as of Oct. 12, 2026.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, a total of 17,605 civilians have been killed and more than 55,000 injured as a result of the war. Among them, 760 children have been killed and 2,950 injured.
And that is on top of more than 114,000 Ukrainian civilians, including over 2,000 children, who are considered missing due to Russia’s war in Ukraine. The largest group, estimated at between 20,000 and 40,000 people, consists primarily of those killed in Russian bombardments of Mariupol, a city leveled in the initial days of the 2022 invasion.
One of the latest victims was a one-year-old girl killed while sitting in her stroller, when Russia struck a park in eastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv region on Monday, killing six locals.
The attack coincided with Trump’s statement about the war, which, perhaps unsurprisingly, was not taken kindly by Ukrainians:
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.”
‘He Just Doesn’t Like Him’: Trump’s Personal Animosity Toward Zelensky May Be Shaping US Policy on Ukraine
That, on top of his administration’s recent plan to exempt Russian shadow fleets from sanctions and its decision to throttle Starlink access for Kyiv, which crippled Ukraine’s ability to conduct deep strikes and intercept incoming drones, raises one simple question.
Why?
The most logical and straightforward explanation is that the US wants to end the war as early as possible, and it’s easier to pressure a non-nuclear nation than a nuclear power. And business deals, of course.
But for a country working hard to rebuild its democracy from the ashes of the USSR, establish anti-corruption institutions and an independent judiciary, and align itself with the best examples of democracy, these developments are nothing short of a betrayal.
Moral questions aside, foresight is also a good thing to have for any government, and here’s why aiding Russia can backfire on Washington long after Trump is gone.
Russia is not a friend
The central issue behind Trump’s seemingly misguided shift toward Russia is that Russia has never been an ally of the United States – and never will be.
In Russia’s national mindset, the US is an adversary and its principal global competitor, even during Trump’s presidency and despite the fact that the US has come to Russia’s aid numerous times.
The Lend-Lease program during World War II is just one example. More recently, Dmitry Medvedev, Russia’s former president and close Putin ally who sits on Russia’s Security Council, put it plainly.
“We have been, are, and will remain systemic adversaries,” he wrote on Tuesday.
Second, Russians themselves believe that the United States should become Russia’s next target after Ukraine. In 2014, Kremlin mouthpiece Vladimir Solovyov threatened to turn “Washington into radioactive ash,” and the latest polls on the street indicate that Russians view the US as an enemy and NATO countries as US proxies.
Moscow’s values are also far removed from those of the US. Democracy, freedom, an independent judiciary and parliament are not considered core values in Russia – just look at how Putin’s term limit was removed in 2021 and how anti-war parties were simply barred from running in this year’s elections.
Unlike democratic countries, autocrats do not remember acts of goodwill. They exploit them.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has spent 35 years steadily building democratic institutions and working with the US on a range of issues, particularly reforms and improvements to its legislation. There are hiccups, of course, but big changes come in small steps, and the Ukrainian people have kept marching in the streets, rallying against corruption, war or not.
Relations with Kyiv have always been a two-way street
Speaking to journalists on Monday, Trump claimed, among other things, that Ukraine had received a great deal from the US but had contributed little during the war.
Neither claim is true.
Ukraine received not simply cash from the US, but weapons and equipment, not “$350 billion,” as Trump claimed and debunked by Kyiv Post; it received only $66 billion, much of it drawn from old Cold War-era stockpiles that would otherwise have needed to be disposed of.
It’s also worth noting that restocking US arms means jobs at the factories making those weapons.
Beyond that, Ukraine has given the US two of the most valuable things in this war: real-world combat data on US weapons and air defense systems against a world power, and time to rearm and prepare for a major conflict that is now looming among the world’s powers.
The US can use these lessons, and it has gained this experience without losing a single soldier.
The Ukrainian military, with its invaluable combat experience in modern warfare, could also become a genuine pillar of European security and NATO’s eastern flank should the day come.
Ukraine today, US and Europe tomorrow
Russia’s ambitions extend beyond eastern Ukraine.
By Putin’s 2022 decree, Russia incorporated four Ukrainian regions into its constitution, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, which Russian forces do not fully control. If Russia were to achieve its objectives, it would become the dominant power in the Black Sea.
Russia has also openly called for a government change in Ukraine, with its advance on Kyiv in the spring of 2022 showing that it does not just seek to subjugate a part of Ukraine, but the entire country, either as part of Russia or as a puppet state.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has considerable industrial potential, a strong base of educated engineers, and a population with combat experience. If defeated and then used by Russia as a battering ram against its Western neighbors, Ukraine could become a threat to NATO.
Russia has also long portrayed NATO as an ideological enemy, calling not only for Ukraine’s membership ban but the alliance’s withdrawal from the entire eastern flank in its pre-2022 invasion ultimatum.
Without an eastern flank, the problem is no longer a Ukraine problem; it becomes a NATO problem, and, under the Article 5 mutual defense clause, also a US problem after Trump leaves office.
Ukraine is preventing that with the lives of its people, and NATO’s cost for helping Ukraine is nothing more than financial contributions and weapons drawn from its stockpiles.
With power comes responsibility
Turning its back on Ukraine – a victim of aggression – does not bode well for global trust in Washington.
Just as Americans once fought for independence from British rule, Ukraine is fighting to break free of Moscow’s sphere of influence, which plagued the country throughout the Russian Empire and the USSR.
These are not merely lofty words – the US is long seen as a bastion of democracy, and the success of US companies around the world stems not only from Washington’s economic and military power, but primarily from the perception of the US as a reliable partner.
Eroded trust is not easily restored, as recent examples show when the US, whether the White House or billionaire Elon Musk, flipped the switch on Ukrainian access to Starlink and Starshield during the latest row, with Europe now seeking alternatives worth billions in government contracts.
Betraying allies, refusing them support promised under previous commitments, and siding with autocrats and dictators undermines the most valuable form of capital the US possessed until recently: trust, and the expectation that its words are backed by the principles of freedom and solidarity with everyone fighting for that freedom.
It’s also worth noting the commitments made when Ukraine gained independence.
On Dec. 8, 1994, Ukraine, the US, the UK and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, under which Ukraine voluntarily gave up the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal at the time in exchange for security assurances and guarantees respecting its borders from Britain, the US and Russia.
Ukraine was still invaded.

UN warns climate pledges leave world far off track for 1.5°C goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:10:37 UTC
22:10:37 KST

Current climate pledges would cut global greenhouse gas emissions by only 11 percent to 15 percent by 2035, far short of the 45 percent reduction needed to help bring warming back below 1.5°C by the end of the century, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) warned Wednesday.
In its Emissions Gap Report 2026, UNEP said emissions must fall 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040 from 2025 levels to limit peak warming to around 1.7°C-1.8°C before potentially returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100.
However, fully implementing countries' existing climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5 percent to 8 percent by 2030 and 11 percent to 15 percent by 2035.
The report found that current climate policies could lead to 2.8°C of global warming this century, while fulfilling all national climate commitments would limit warming to 2.6°C.
Even meeting additional net-zero targets alongside national climate commitments would limit warming to only 2.1°C, according to UNEP.
"Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year," UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen said in the report.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stressed that exceeding the 1.5°C threshold does not mean abandoning efforts to reverse warming.
"Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.°C degrees by the end of the century," he said.
The report also found that returning to 1.5°C would require removing and permanently storing approximately 320 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere this century, a task facing significant technological and economic challenges.
Despite the warnings, UNEP noted that renewable energy expansion and climate policies have already reduced emissions in several countries.
"It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies," Andersen said.
The report warned that without urgent action, keeping peak warming below 1.7-1.8°C "will quickly become impossible."

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action, UN chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:09:58 UTC
22:09:58 KST

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action, UN chief warns
- UN report says current climate pledges are far too weak, putting the world on track for 2.6 deg C warming by 2100 and missing the Paris goals.
- UN chief Antonio Guterres warned that 1.5 deg C is already out of reach, with record emissions causing floods, heatwaves, wildfires and rising inequality.
- The report says 2025 emissions stayed near record highs, with the US the biggest driver of increases, and calls for urgent cuts and 5,000 gigawatts more renewables.
AI generated
PARIS – Global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals and put the world on course for 2.6 deg C warming this century, the UN warned on Oct 21.
The report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November’s COP31 climate summit.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 deg C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, said the annual Emissions Gap Report.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed in 2015 in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 deg C while striving for a safer 1.5 deg C. Any chance of keeping to 1.5 deg C has been “lost” due to decades of insufficient action, the report said.
“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 degree limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres in a statement to launch the closely watched report.
“Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst,” he said.
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on a par with record levels in 2024, with the difference between the two years too small to call, the report said.
Carbon emissions just from burning coal, oil and gas – the main driver of climate change – rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep and immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts, but instead “emissions remain at record levels, and national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short”.
Sticking just with current policies would see warming hit 2.8 deg C by the end of the century, the report said.
No country immune
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree above 1.5 deg C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 deg C relative to pre-industrial times, and crossing 1.5 deg C is expected in a matter of years.
This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than in 2025 because of the formal withdrawal of the United States from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, said report co-author Anne Olhoff.
Emissions growth slowed among the G-20, but the US was a “major exception”, it added.
The Group of 20 major economies (G-20) accounts for three-quarters of global emissions.
Among the world’s top six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the US, Indonesia and China, and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
But the US increase of 133 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent “far exceeded” that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.
The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit in Antalya from Nov 9 to 20.
The US is the world’s second-largest polluter, behind China.
US President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP executive secretary Inger Andersen said she would not put the blame “squarely on one nation”, saying every country, especially those in the G-20, has “a specific duty to find a way to phase down their carbon emissions”.
To limit the overshoot beyond 1.5 deg C, Andersen said the world has an “urgent to-do item”: adding another 5,000 gigawatts of renewable energy over the next five years.
‘Historic failure’
The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5 deg C by 2100.
To get there, warming must peak around 1.8 deg C by 2050, and vast amounts of carbon dioxide would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.
But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% per year, every year, until 2035, nowhere near current projections.
Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals, and a showdown over the 1.5 deg C target is expected at COP31.
“This is a historic failure of political leadership,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
“The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action,” Adow said. “The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming.” AFP

Latvia ranks among top five importers of Russian grain this season as Moscow’s exports pivot toward Baltic ports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:09:02 UTC
22:09:02 KST

Latvia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has become one of the five largest importers of Russian grain in the current agricultural season despite strained political relations with Moscow, according to a Reuters report citing an agricultural consultancy firm.
The shift comes as Russia redirects grain exports from the Azov-Black Sea basin to ports in the Baltic Sea.
According to agricultural consultancy ProZerno, Latvia imported 431,700 metric tons of Russian grain from July through October.
Iran remained the largest buyer, importing 1.7 million metric tons, driven largely by major purchases of barley and corn. Egypt, once the biggest buyer of Russian wheat, remains one of the main destinations for Black Sea shipments, importing 1.35 million metric tons.
Azerbaijan, with 545,000 metric tons, and Nigeria, with 420,900 metric tons, also ranked among the five largest importers.
Russia has been restructuring its grain export routes since shipments through the Azov-Black Sea basin — its main export corridor — nearly came to a halt in mid-August.
Deepwater Baltic ports have since become the main route, particularly for wheat exports. According to calculations by rail freight operator Rusagrotrans, the Baltic accounted for 65% of Russian grain exports in September.
Cargo is being shipped both through Russian Baltic ports and through ports in the Baltic states, especially Latvia.
Shipments across the Caspian Sea have also risen sharply, with most of that grain bound for Iran.
Estonia, meanwhile, has banned the transit of Russian grain through its territory. In early October, the Baltic states proposed introducing a similar ban across the entire European Union.
At the same time, Latvia has been tightening its policies toward Russian citizens.
On Oct. 1, the Latvian parliament referred proposed amendments to its Legal Affairs Committee. The changes to Latvia’s citizenship law would impose a complete ban on holding Russian citizenship as a second nationality.
Dual Latvian-Russian citizenship is already effectively prohibited, but exceptions remain — with billionaire former Alfa-Bank head Petr Aven being the most notable among them. The amendments were drafted after Latvia’s Interior Ministry was unable to find a legal way to strip Aven of his Latvian citizenship.
