Monsoon's gone, El Niño isn't: Why India's weather worries are far from over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:23:26 UTC
20:23:26 KST

El Niño is putting the world on alert, and India could be among the countries facing its next major weather test. After a monsoon marked by a 13 per cent rainfall deficit, attention is shifting to whether the climate phenomenon will bring a warmer winter, disrupt rainfall patterns and add to the pressure on agriculture.From Indonesia’s raging wildfires to an unusually active Pacific hurricane season, its effects are already emerging across the globe. Now, the question is what a strengthening El Niño could mean for India in the months ahead.According to the BBC, El Niño has been strengthening for several months and is already influencing weather patterns worldwide, with Indonesia experiencing its worst wildfire season since 2015, heightened hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific and reduced monsoon rainfall in India.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has warned that the phenomenon could intensify further towards the end of 2026 and persist into 2027, raising concerns over its potential impact on temperatures, rainfall and extreme weather events across different regions.For India, the immediate concern is whether the strengthening El Niño will compound the effects of the deficient monsoon and influence winter temperatures, rainfall and agricultural conditions in the coming months.
What is El Niño and how does it affect India's weather?El Niño is a climate phenomenon characterised by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate pattern that influences atmospheric circulation, wind systems and rainfall distribution across the world.For India, El Niño is closely watched because it is generally associated with a higher risk of below-normal southwest monsoon rainfall.The warming of Pacific waters alters atmospheric circulation and can weaken conditions that support the Indian monsoon, increasing the possibility of prolonged dry spells and rainfall shortages.While central India received near-normal rainfall, eastern and northeastern India recorded a 26 per cent deficit, classified as an exceptional drought, while southern states received 24 per cent less rainfall than average, according to the BBC.A strengthening El Niño could contribute to warmer-than-normal conditions in parts of India, potentially increasing pressure on water resources and agriculture.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), citing the South Asian Climate Outlook Forum, projected normal to above-normal maximum and minimum temperatures across much of South Asia during October–December 2026.Higher temperatures later in the winter could also threaten wheat yields if heat coincides with the grain-filling stage, although the impact will depend on actual weather conditions.However, conditions in January and February will depend on evolving climate patterns, including western disturbances.
Global impact of El NiñoEl Niño is expected to push temperatures higher across much of the world while shifting rainfall patterns, increasing the risks of drought, wildfires and flooding in different regions.
In Southeast Asia, including Indonesia, hotter and drier conditions are raising wildfire and drought risks. In contrast, parts of East Africa could experience heavier rainfall and flooding, while drought risks remain a concern in other areas.El Niño is also influencing tropical storms. The eastern Pacific has experienced heightened hurricane activity, while stronger upper-level winds over the Atlantic have suppressed hurricane development.In South America, its effects vary, with drier conditions possible in parts of the Amazon and increased rainfall and flooding in some southern areas.
Aryan Singh is a journalist with The Times of India, covering breaking news, defence and global conflicts. An alumnus of the IIMC, he tracks the people, weapons and geopolitics behind the headlines, with a focus on India’s national security, military affairs and conflicts shaping the world.

The agency, seen as a Western-backed beach-head for tackling rampant corruption in Ukraine, neither confirmed nor denied media reports that Pyshny was involved.
Pyshny was identified by several opposition MPs and law enforcement sources cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda and the US-funded Ukrainian branch of RFE/RL. Both outlets have a track record of obtaining insider information from NABU.

The anti-corruption agency accused Irina Mudraya, then-deputy head of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s office, of improperly influencing state-owned Sense Bank to conceal the origins of millions of dollars in cash. She was subsequently dismissed.
Vadim Vesyoly, a former adviser to the bank’s supervisory board, has been described by Ukrainian media as an informal overseer influencing its decisions on behalf of Zelensky’s inner circle. Pyshny has denied allegations that he arranged Vesyoly’s appointment in 2023, shortly after the bank was nationalized. Vesyoly’s formal advisory role ended last year, although some Ukrainian outlets claim he continued to wield influence.
Vesyoly’s name surfaced in surveillance recordings linked to Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of Zelensky. Last November, Mindich was accused of masterminding a $100 million kickback scheme involving the state-owned nuclear power company Energoatom.
After Mindich fled Ukraine, Sense Bank and Vesyoly reportedly began dealing directly with Zelensky’s office, allegedly enabling Mudraya to carry out the money-laundering operation. Galushchenko, the former minister whose bail was allegedly financed with dirty money, is also a suspect in the Mindich case.
In surveillance recordings leaked to Ukrainskaya Pravda, Vesyoly and one of Mindich’s alleged accomplices can be heard discussing appointments to Sense Bank’s supervisory board and a potential takeover of Karpatneftekhim, a major petrochemical complex in western Ukraine.
MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak, one of the lawmakers who first publicized Wednesday’s searches, claimed NABU detectives were pursuing leads concerning Vesyoly’s involvement with Sense Bank and Karpatneftekhim at the central bank.

Ukraine expands defence procurement to include aircraft and tactical missiles
The Ukrainian Defence Procurement Agency (DPA) has begun procuring tactical missiles and aircraft in 2026.
Source: RBK-Ukraine, citing Artem Romaniukov, director of the DPA

Poland says social media firms are ‘silent ally’ of Russia, threatens fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:16:23 UTC
20:16:23 KST

Poland says social media firms are ‘silent ally’ of Russia, threatens fines
WARSAW - Social media platforms are a “silent ally” of Russia in a “digital war” and are doing nothing to curb disinformation, Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on Oct 21, threatening fines for firms that ignore state requests.
Poland and other Western countries have on many occasions accused Russia of spreading disinformation to sow division and destabilise their societies.
Moscow denies such accusations and says Western leaders are intentionally exaggerating the threat from Russia for their own political ends.
Data from Poland’s NASK National Research Institute showed platforms acted on fewer than a quarter of the more than 65,000 reports of fake accounts and disinformation it sent them in the first half of 2026.
Discord, Google, Meta, X, Telegram and TikTok did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
“A digital war with Russia is underway, and within this digital war lies a front of disinformation. On this disinformation front, there is a silent ally to the Russian bots and the Kremlin’s GRU: social media platforms,” Gawkowski said.
“Social media platforms are doing nothing about this,” he added during a press conference.
Poland’s NASK data showed that, of all cases of disinformation and fake accounts reported, social media platforms deleted 7% and moderated over 17%.
“The data points not merely to a failure, but to deliberate action by the platforms – which profit from disinformation, use it, and treat it as a source of their revenue,” Gawkowski said.
He added that he issued a demand to the platforms to establish effective Polish-speaking content moderation teams, which would maintain a direct, real-time link to the relevant entities reporting such content.
He also demanded the elimination of what he called sham appeals processes, the immediate removal of any identified bot networks and a reduction in response times for all such reports.
“Furthermore, I have made it clear that any state request left unfulfilled by these platforms will trigger proceedings to impose financial penalties upon them,” Gawkowski also said. REUTERS

Israel's occupation, Hezbollah's arms: A looming war in Lebanon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:16:04 UTC
20:16:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's occupation, Hezbollah's arms: The road to a new war in Lebanon?
On 5 October, Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces stopped a van with two people on board at the Dahr al-Baydar checkpoint.
When searched, authorities discovered and then seized about 780 kg of explosives, including TNT and Composition C-4 plastic.
The two people arrested were reportedly linked to Hezbollah. They were tasked with transporting the cargo from the Bekaa region to Beirut.
The reported involvement of Hezbollah members in the explosives seizure prompted a wave of accusations from the group’s political rivals, with some suggesting they could be used for internal political assassinations.
Lebanese Forces leader Samir Geagea called the seizure “the most dangerous incident in years”, saying the weapons were probably meant for use inside Lebanon.
Kataeb leader Samy Gemayel wrote they were probably intended for a new wave of assassinations like those between 2004 and 2008, including that of former prime minister Rafic Hariri in 2005.
Lebanon’s prime minister, Nawaf Salam, also noted that C-4 had been used in previous assassinations and promised a full investigation.
However, on 15 October, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah acknowledged that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the group. He denied allegations of an assassination plot and stated that the explosives are part of the capabilities Hezbollah uses against Israel, demanding the return of the shipment.
On the same day, US Secretary of State Marc Rubio reportedly called Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun, urging him not to return confiscated explosives to Hezbollah.
Hezbollah’s demand for the return of the explosives has further strained its relationship with a government that has banned the group’s military activity and is pushing to disarm it.
Israel's occupation creates openings for Hezbollah to rebuild
The discovery of explosive materials comes as Israel continues to occupy swathes of southern Lebanon and launch near-daily strikes despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed in June.
Hezbollah has halted its attacks since then, but the seizure of explosives points to efforts to rebuild its military capabilities as the risk of renewed US-Iran conflict threatens to reignite the Lebanese front.
It is not uncommon for Hezbollah to use ceasefire windows to rebuild its capabilities following a conflict with Israel.
Between the November 2024 ceasefire that ended the Israel-Hezbollah war linked to Gaza and March 2026, reports indicate that the group has rebuilt its command structure and rearmed with assistance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
David Wood, senior Lebanon analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG), said that Israel’s continued occupation and attacks in Lebanon also contribute to the conditions that enable the group’s rebuilding.
“While it might be true that Hezbollah continues to operate militarily, despite the Lebanese government wanting to have a state monopoly over arms, it would be much harder for Hezbollah to do that if Israel were more willing to grant actual concessions as part of its negotiations with Lebanon and to create a viable and fair security arrangement between the two countries,” he told The New Arab.
The US-brokered framework signed in June between Lebanon and Israel has yielded limited results. Lebanon demands an end to Israeli attacks and occupation, the release of detainees, and the return of the displaced. Israel ties these conditions to Hezbollah’s disarmament, which the group rejects.
Israel has continued its military operations in southern Lebanon, occupying more than 600 square kilometres of Lebanese territory while conducting near-daily airstrikes, artillery fire, and home demolitions.
It has mostly levelled 48 of about 60 occupied southern Lebanese towns and villages. In September, Israeli forces took control of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh. They previously captured Beaufort Castle and crossed the Litani River.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry says more than 4,300 people have been killed since 2 March, following Hezbollah’s entry into the wider US-Iran war. Nearly 9,000 have been killed since 2023. Almost 330,000 people remain internally displaced.
Nicholas Blandford, a non-resident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Middle East Programmes, told The New Arab that daily shelling and drone surveillance are ongoing, along with efforts to prevent reconstruction south of the Litani River, even outside the occupied zone.
“So in effect, the Israeli occupation extends far beyond where they are physically deployed. It's been quite intense over the last month,” he said.
Israel is also escalating threats to expand its southern Lebanon occupation. Last week, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz warned that Lebanon would lose Nabatieh and the Litani area to permanent Israeli control if Hezbollah joins Iran in attacking Israel.
A renewed Iran war could draw Lebanon back into conflict
In fact, US President Donald Trump is weighing fresh strikes against Iran, with Israel reportedly pushing for renewed hostilities. Iran is likewise preparing for war, and the conflict in Yemen further fuels regional escalation.
RANE’s lead MENA and defence analyst Freddy Khoueiry explained that repeated interceptions of weapons transfers in Syria and recent seizures of Hezbollah-linked material inside Lebanon show that the group is "clearly attempting to reconstitute parts of its military capability" to rebuild supply lines and replenish stock.
“Hezbollah is likely attempting to restore enough capability to at some point defend against a potential Israeli preemptive campaign and at the same time preserve the option to participate in another regional conflict involving Iran,” he told The New Arab.
For example, Khoueiry explained that seized TNT and C-4 could be used in explosive-drone payloads, rocket and missile warheads, and roadside bombs, mines and demolition charges against Israeli forces in southern Lebanon if conflict resumes.
Dual-use items like fibre-optic cables for drones could enter Lebanon through standard commercial channels, providing Hezbollah with an alternative route to Syria.
Hezbollah may be prioritising experimenting with and expanding the use of low-cost, fibre-optic-guided FPV drones, heavily deployed against Israeli troops in southern Lebanon before the June ceasefire, as they offer a cheap, effective, and hard-to-intercept option.
On the ground, the presence of Israeli troops in southern Lebanon may give Hezbollah an opening to use guerrilla tactics, such as small units staging hit-and-run attacks from familiar terrain. Its drone operations there could also expand the pool of trained drone operators.
Wood said that while Israel has vast military superiority, Hezbollah, this year, “has still managed to make a nuisance of itself”, demonstrating that “while it can't win a military victory over Israel, it can still inflict casualties”. Hezbollah drone attacks have reportedly killed at least 12 Israeli soldiers.
However, what Hezbollah’s role would be if the US and Israel resume strikes on Iran remains to be seen.
Blandford said that Hezbollah’s involvement would depend on Iran’s ability to absorb renewed US and Israeli attacks.
“The Iranians may conclude that if they can absorb fresh Israeli and US strikes, they don’t need to involve Hezbollah,” he said. However, if Iran deems additional pressure necessary, it may activate Hezbollah to engage Israel along the border, stretching and diverting Israel's resources.
Khoueiry further explained that Hezbollah’s weakened capabilities and fragile domestic position may limit its initial involvement, though opening a Lebanese front could pressure Israel and strengthen Hezbollah’s and Iran’s negotiating leverage.
“Hezbollah could specifically seek to link pressure on Israeli military presence inside of Lebanon and potentially northern Israel again to demand an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, while Tehran could again attempt to incorporate the Lebanese front into a broader regional ceasefire or negotiating framework,” he said.
However, other kinds of pressures are also likely to shape Hezbollah’s calculations. The Shia community, estimated at 32% of Lebanon’s population, has borne much of the war’s human cost during the war. Last week, Hezbollah announced plans to financially help families in Lebanon whose homes were destroyed or rendered uninhabitable.
Polls diverge on Shia support for Hezbollah’s weapons, with a May poll finding that most respondents opposed disarmament and a September survey finding that most favoured placing their weapons under state control, reflecting the complexity of the group’s relationship with its constituency.
Wood said that Hezbollah weighs the suffering of its constituency but, at the same time, also weighs its deep alliance with Iran.
The group also argues that disarmament would leave the Shia community and Lebanon “wide open to Israeli abuses,” and at times, it “has used those factors to justify its decision to enter conflict in Lebanon, in the knowledge that the Shia will first and foremost pay the price”.
Blandford also argued that if Hezbollah loses Shia support, “then the game is over.”
“It doesn't matter how many weapons or how much money the Iranians give Hezbollah; if they haven't got the support of the Shia community, it's finished.”

Germany's Merz: Ukraine's capitulation would mean the capitulation of all its allies
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Ukraine's capitulation in the war with Russia is not an option, as it would mean the capitulation of all its allies.
Source: Deutsche Welle, a German international broadcaster and media outlet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Merz stressed that Germany and other European countries remain willing to negotiate at any time.
"We are supporting Ukraine not to prolong this war. But capitulation – or even Ukraine's unconditional capitulation – is out of the question. Because that would mean the capitulation of all of us," he said at an economic forum in Berlin on Wednesday.
Merz noted that Russian disinformation and hybrid attacks pose the greatest threat to Germany's security.
He accused Moscow of launching "a fundamental attack on the political order established after the end of the Cold War".
"My greatest concern at this moment is not our economy, not the US or China, but Russia's influence on our society," Merz said.
The chancellor said he is referring to acts of sabotage, hybrid attacks on telecommunication systems and attempts to destabilise Germany.
Merz stressed that such attacks take place every day and that their significance is still being underestimated in Germany.
Background:
- Recently, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that US negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender on Russian leader Vladimir Putin's terms for a year and a half, but Ukraine has not surrendered thanks to Europe's support.
- Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of trying to pressure Kyiv into capitulating to Russia.

Who are major candidates in Israel's election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Israeli voters go to the polls Oct. 27 to decide whether to grant Benjamin Netanyahu another term or usher in a new political era.
Polling shows a tight race between Netanyahu’s nationalist Likud party and his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar! party.
Israelis vote for parties, which then form alliances to create a majority coalition. No single party has ever won a majority in the 120-member parliament, or Knesset.
Netanyahu, 77, is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and the most dominant force in Israeli politics, having persevered through wars, crises and scandals. He is the longtime leader of the Likud party, and supporters point to his record on security and the economy, as well as his close ties with U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's opponents say he's responsible for the policy and security failures that preceded the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion and accuse him of mismanaging the wars that followed. In 2024, the International Criminal Court issued a warrant for Netanyahu's arrest over allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity. He is also embroiled in a yearslong legal scandal at home, having been charged with fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. Netanyahu denies any wrongdoing.
Eisenkot, 66, comes from a working-class family of Jewish Moroccan immigrants. He spent four decades rising through the ranks of Israel's military, eventually becoming the chief of staff. The general currently leads the largest opposition party – the centrist Yashar! – after entering politics in 2022. His son and two nephews were all killed in combat in Gaza following the Oct. 7 incursion.
Eisenkot also served as an observer in Netanyahu's war Cabinet, but resigned after eight months, when he accused the prime minister of lacking a clear strategy. He has since positioned himself as a moderate alternative to Netanyahu, but remains hawkish on security. Eisenkot is credited with formulating Israel’s so‑called "Dahiyeh Doctrine,” a military strategy calling for the use of disproportionate power in areas where attacks are launched.
If he succeeds in forming a coalition, Eisenkot could become the first Israeli prime minister of Mizrahi descent. Israel's Mizrahim, who come from North Africa and the Middle East, have historically faced discrimination from the country's European-descended elite.
Naftali Bennett, 54, is the right-wing and religiously observant leader of Beyachad (Together), a joint ticket with centrist politician Yair Lapid. He opposes Palestinian independence and supports settlement-building in the occupied West Bank.
Before entering the Knesset in 2013, Bennett served as Netanyahu's chief of staff and also was head of the Yesha Council, an umbrella organization of local authorities inside Israeli settlements. His conservative Yamina party won seven seats, which helped him cobble together a coalition of both left-wing and Arab parties. He then briefly served as prime minister in 2021, the result of a power-sharing agreement, also with Lapid.
While Bennett, like Netanyahu, takes a hard line toward the Palestinians, the two men have deep disagreements over Netanyahu's handling of security issues and his battle against the Israeli legal system.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, is Israel's national security minister and a far-right provocateur with multiple convictions, including for supporting a terrorist organization. He leads Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), an ultra-nationalist party whose strong showing in the last election secured him his Cabinet post and helped push Netanyahu's coalition further to the right.
He is a trained lawyer who gained recognition by successfully defending right-wing Jewish extremists accused of violence against Palestinians. When Ben-Gvir was a teenager, the military refused to draft him because of his extreme views. He was also a follower of Meir Kahane, the violently racist rabbi who advocated for expelling Palestinians from Israel, Gaza and the West Bank.
Ben-Gvir has also laid out plans for what he says would be the "voluntary" emigration of roughly 2 million Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, where he has advocated for re-building Jewish settlements.
Mansour Abbas, 52, is a Palestinian Arab politician and dentist from northern Israel. He leads Ra'am, the first Arab-led party to join a governing coalition in 2021.
His strategy has been to focus on more local issues, such as crime in Arab communities, rather than the larger Israeli-Palestinian conflict, in the hopes it will win Ra'am more seats in the Knesset and court potential coalition partners.
As part of this push, Abbas named former police commander and centrist Jewish politician Yoav Segalovitz as the number two candidate on Ra'am's electoral list. Abbas has served in the Knesset since 2019.

WHO delivers 10,000 cholera rapid diagnostic tests to Iran with CERF support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:14:52 UTC
20:14:52 KST

WHO delivers 10,000 cholera rapid diagnostic tests to Iran with CERF support
TEHRAN – The World Health Organization (WHO), with support from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), has delivered 10,000 cholera rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) to Iran’s Ministry of Health and Medical Education to strengthen early detection and help prevent potential outbreaks.
The tests will be distributed to the high-risk provinces of Hormozgan, Kerman, Sistan-Baluchestan, and Khuzestan to enable the rapid identification of cases and support timely public health responses.
“Early detection is our most critical tool in preventing infectious disease outbreaks. By equipping local health systems with these tests, we are empowering frontline workers to respond swiftly and protect vulnerable communities,” said Dr. Jean Jabbour, WHO Representative to Iran.
The broader project aims to benefit more than 112,000 people. Despite logistical challenges affecting air and sea transport, WHO is also working to deliver essential supplies for malaria and dengue fever.
In response to the growing crises affecting public health infrastructures in Iran, the World Health Organization, in cooperation with the Health Ministry, kicked off in May a two-million-dollar project to support urgent health responses in the country.
Supported by the United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the project, titled ‘preventing the spread of diseases and maintaining essential health services during emergencies’, aims to minimize the outbreaks of diseases, stabilize the process of providing health services, and safeguard health system from declining performance across the country, the health ministry’s website reported.
Since the beginning of the imposed US-Israeli war against Iran, on February 28, airstrikes have lowered the country’s capacity to provide vital health services.
The aggressors destroyed 229 health centers, 49 hospitals, 78 pharmaceutical facilities, laboratories, and warehouses.
Moreover, 56 emergency bases were targeted, nine hospitals were evacuated, 47 ambulances and 10 emergency vehicles were severely damaged.
Attacks on pharmaceutical and diagnostic equipment manufacturing facilities and their surrounding areas have disrupted the domestic supply chain of medical equipment and challenged the process of providing critical care to those in need.
Climatic shocks in southern provinces of the country have exacerbated the situation. Irregular, above-normal rainfall, following prolonged periods of drought in 2025-2026, has led to localized flooding and the accumulation of stagnant water.
High-risk provinces, including Sistan-Baluchestan, Hormozgan, Kerman, and Khuzestan, are at greater risk of exposure to contaminated water sources. The situation, coupled with conflicts in water and sanitation infrastructure and disease surveillance, has increased the risks of infectious disease outbreaks and waterborne diseases, particularly cholera, and acute water diarrhea.
According to John Jabbour, WHO Representative, “The ongoing conflicts and severe climatic shocks have placed an unprecedented burden on Iran’s health infrastructure, exposing vulnerable communities to serious hazards.
The allocated funds for emergency response will play a critical role in managing health system challenges. It allows us to take immediate measures to protect essential supply chains and ensure that life-saving care is available to those most affected by crises.
Without urgent action, local transmission of diseases could quickly result in widespread outbreaks and increase the cases and deaths from preventable diseases.”
To accelerate immediate action, the WHO is deploying a set of high-impact interventions. The strategy prioritizes strengthening surveillance and early warning systems, as well as deployment of essential equipment to respond to disease outbreaks, including rapid diagnostic tests for malaria, dengue fever, and cholera, the official noted.
The intervention also includes the distribution of insecticide-treated mosquito nets, insect repellents, larvicide, along with rapid technical assistance to strengthen integrated vector management in high-risk provinces.
Over the next six months, the WHO project will directly serve an estimated 112,500 people by scaling up epidemic management and restoring access to health services. Some 272,550 people will be protected indirectly by strengthening rapid response capacities and reducing the risks of disease outbreaks.
Ultimately, the goal of this comprehensive effort is to manage the outbreak of preventable diseases and maintain essential health services at a time when they are needed more than ever.

Erdoğan vows tangible action to avoid repeat of fund crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:14:42 UTC
20:14:42 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan spoke to his Justice and Development Party’s (AKP) lawmakers on Oct. 21, 2026. (AA Photo)
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has reaffirmed that his government is implementing concrete measures to avoid a future fund crisis, informing that compensation for victims of the Ponzi scheme will commence immediately following parliamentary ratification of an upcoming bill.
“I would like to express this openly once more. We take this issue very seriously and are handling it with great sensitivity,” Erdoğan told his Justice and Development Party’s (AKP) lawmakers on Oct. 21.
Erdoğan noted that the 455,000 investors affected by the fund crisis, along with their families, make up a big segment of the population.
“We are addressing this matter with surgical precision, prioritizing the welfare of our nation above any political or personal calculations,” he said.
Türkiye has been dealing with a major financial crisis since mid-September after an investment bubble burst, forcing market regulators to shut down and cash out 131 manipulated investment funds. This led to the resignation of senior bureaucrats as well as AKP deputy leader Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya.
The opposition claims the cost of fund crisis to the Turkish economy has exceeded $100 billion.
Erdoğan outlined three government priorities to tackle the issue, making it clear that covering investor losses tops the list.
“Our coordination committee to tackle the fund crisis and our economy officials are meeting regularly and announce the decisions to the public opinion transparently. Once the bill currently on Parliament’s agenda takes effect, the payment process will speed up a bit more,” he stated.
The government’s second priority focuses on accelerating legal action against those behind the Ponzi scheme, Erdoğan said. “Our chief prosecutors are taking essential judicial moves in line with the evidence and testimonies,” he recalled.
“The third stage includes the measures needed to ensure we never face a similar problem again. Based on the comprehensive report to be prepared by our State Supervisory Council, as well as other studies conducted under our directives, every necessary step will be taken across institutional, individual and regulatory frameworks,” the president added.

The agreement determines “how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” he said.
Rubio said he was not aware that the administration knew about the decision beforehand. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
WSJ says Musk ordered the restrictions
The remarks followed a Wall Street Journal report published on Tuesday, Oct. 20, which said Musk ordered restrictions on the military-grade satellite service used by Ukraine, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
The newspaper said the decision disrupted Ukrainian offensive and interceptor drones and caused confusion inside the Trump administration.
Accounts differed over the timing of discussions with Trump. One source said Musk, Trump, and White House officials discussed the matter before the restrictions, while two said Musk and the president discussed it afterward.
Reuters has separately cited two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter as saying the decision ultimately came from the White House. The administration has denied that account.
Kyiv Mayor Klitschko Accuses Government of Staging Anti-Mayor Protest
Conflicting accounts from Washington and Musk
Trump previously denied ordering the restrictions and said he did not think Musk was responsible either.
His comments came despite Ukrainian reports that satellite connections were failing during military operations. Kyiv has repeatedly sought an explanation and the restoration of full service.
Musk, meanwhile, said on Oct. 14 that limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals were determined by the US military and ultimately the president.
The distinction between Starlink and Starshield has also become a point of contention. Rubio has said Ukraine never had access to Starshield, while President Volodymyr Zelensky has described disruptions affecting both services.
Why speed limits matter for Ukraine
The restrictions concern the speed at which a terminal can move while remaining connected, a separate issue from how quickly it transfers internet data.
Zelensky said on Oct. 17 that terminals in Ukraine disconnected above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), causing Ukrainian forces to lose control of interceptor drones.
He said Ukrainian specialists tested terminals traveling at 180 kilometers per hour (112 miles per hour) in EU territory without experiencing the same disconnections. He argued that the comparison showed the limits were specific to Ukraine.
The effects are concentrated on faster aircraft relying on satellite links, including drones used to intercept Russian jet-powered Shaheds and conduct strikes beyond conventional radio range.
Stationary ground terminals and most short-range first-person-view drones, which normally use direct radio links, have been largely unaffected by the movement-speed restriction.
Starlink also carries military communications, targeting information, and logistics data, making the network important well beyond individual drone missions.
Kyiv seeks answers as Europe weighs alternatives
During a virtual meeting with US lawmakers on Monday, Oct. 19, Zelensky said Washington had still not explained the satellite restrictions or failures to provide advance warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks.
He raised the issues with a bipartisan group from the Senate and House as Ukraine sought to restore communications needed for its defenses.
European governments have also been examining alternatives, but EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned on Oct. 16 that Europe could not replace Starlink’s capabilities in the short term.
The European Commission has been discussing Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM, a program pooling satellite resources for secure government communications. Brussels has not confirmed that it could meet the same battlefield requirements as Starlink.

Government websites taken offline over hacking vulnerabilities

11:13:24 UTC

Some important websites remain down after emergency shutdowns
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Websites in the Netherlands are coming back online following emergency shutdowns. This follows the discovery of vulnerabilities in the programming language on which many government, hospital and news sites are built, including Dutch News.
The organisation behind PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages, said on Tuesday it would patch two flaws in its code.
The announcement prompted hackers to search for the holes and begin trying to attack sites, which US cyber security firm Cloudflare said on Wednesday it was noticing and defending against.
Sites were then swiftly taken down, including the government’s digital ID system DigiD and its online services portal MijnOverheid, the website of parliament, the umbrella organisation for the water boards, and a tool used by local councils for storing documents and scheduling meetings.
Some important sites, like anonymous crime reporting site Meld Misdaad Anoniem and domestic safety reporting network Veilig Thuis, were still offline on Thursday morning.
Disruptions 
Dutch media companies were hit – RTL’s news website and app went down, and broadcaster NPO shut down the system used to upload content to its streaming services.
Several hospitals also took their websites down, as well as charities such as KWF cancer fund and the Dutch Heart Foundation.
Schiphol airport’s app stopped showing live flight information, and benefits agency UWV took a tool people use to report sick or recovered offline.
The problem was not limited to the Netherlands – the Flemish, German, French and Finnish governments all took websites offline.
What happened
Two critical flaws in PHP’s programming language were discovered in August using AI models from OpenAI and Google.
Google-owned cybersecurity firm Wiz, one of the firms that reported the flaws to PHP, said that the vulnerabilities in PHP had existed for over a decade, and said they ranked “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.
PHP built fixes for the vulnerabilities into an update and said all companies using its code should install the update immediately. Prime minister Rob Jetten reiterated this call on social media.
Justice minister David van Weel said the fact that so many websites had been taken offline as a precaution “has an impact on our digital society”.
“Fortunately, there are currently no indications that the vulnerabilities are being actively exploited,” Van Weel stated through his spokesperson.
The National Cyber Security Centre said it had not seen any active hacks, and the PHP Foundation told news agency ANP it also had no indication of breaches.

Bereaved civil service families could face ‘unjust’ tax bills due to pension scheme delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:12:49 UTC
20:12:49 KST

Bereaved families could face “unconscionable” tax bills because of “chaos” in the civil service pension scheme, the government has been warned.
Some lump sum pension payments to families are only tax-free if made within two years of a scheme being told of the member’s death.
MPs are now voicing fears that severe delays in the administration of the civil service pension scheme, which is run by the outsourcing company Capita, could push some families over that threshold. They would then be hit with a tax bill calculated at the recipient’s personal rate.
The families of more than 1,600 deceased civil servants have been waiting for more than 100 days for their “death in benefit” claim to be processed, according to the latest figures. Some of those have reported struggling to pay bills because of the delay.
The Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Commons public accounts committee (PAC), said: “The chaos currently engulfing the civil service pensions scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim.”
He added: “It is unconscionable that the families of loyal and dedicated civil servants, who are continuing to suffer through this serious government failing, could potentially face such an unjust financial penalty.”
The Cabinet Office, which is responsible for the pension scheme, said it was unable to prevent HM Revenue and Customs from taxing delayed claims, and that affected members would have to claw back the money by taking their case to the Pensions Ombudsman.
The ombudsman estimates an 18-month wait to resolve cases because of the volume of complaints from those affected.
The PAC has called for a change in legislation to prevent relatives paying the price for administrative delays.
The government has already been accused of letting down civil servants and their families by repeatedly outsourcing the 1.7-million-member pension scheme to private companies that failed to deliver.
The PAC last year urged ministers to take the scheme in-house after a previous contractor, MyCSP, was blamed for plummeting service levels. However, the £239m contract passed to Capita last December, despite concerns voiced by some that the company was inadequately prepared.
The Cabinet Office said it was confident that Capita would offer an improved service. It has since acknowledged that service levels were “unacceptable”. MyCSP and Capita were contacted for a comment.
In February, a dedicated email address was set up for unions to escalate cases of severe hardship caused by the delays. The cases referred included claimants at risk of suicide or of losing their homes.
Clare Norris has been waiting 11 months for the death benefit and pension payments she is due after her husband died last November.
“I was petrified – I am 52 and early death was not part of our financial plan,” she said. “Losing your partner is one of the most difficult experiences anyone can go through. The lack of clarity, communication and basic administrative handling from Civil Service Pensions has made it considerably worse.”
Capita said her case would be progressed under a new process. “It remains a high priority and the member can expect to hear on next steps as soon as possible.”
Under HMRC rules, in cases in which someone dies under the age of 75, tax-free lump sum payments must be made within two years, otherwise they will be taxed at the recipient’s marginal rate of tax.
The Cabinet Office said it was committed to ensuring scheme members were not left out of pocket. “We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure individuals do not experience delays,” said a spokesperson.
“If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses.”

Japan Fighter Scrambles Jump 67% Amid Increased Chinese and Russian Military Presence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:11:26 UTC
20:11:26 KST

- Category
- World
Japan Fighter Scrambles Jump 67% Amid Increased Chinese and Russian Military Presence
Japan scrambled fighter jets 442 times in response to Chinese and Russian aircraft during the first half of fiscal year 2026, up sharply from 265 scrambles during the same period last year, USNI News reported on October 20.
From April 1 through September 30, 285 scrambles, or 65% of the total, were triggered by Chinese aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles. Russian aircraft accounted for 152 scrambles, or 34%, while five were classified as other incidents.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
USNI News noted that no violations of Japanese sovereign airspace were recorded during the period. Most of the activity took place inside Japan’s Air Defense Identification Zone, which extends beyond the country’s 12-nautical-mile territorial airspace.
The documented activity included Russian Il-20 electronic intelligence aircraft operating over the Sea of Japan and Pacific Ocean, Chinese Y-9 intelligence aircraft over the East China Sea, and joint long-range flights by Chinese H-6 and Russian Tu-95 bombers.
The largest share of Chinese activity occurred over the East China Sea near southwestern Japan, while most Russian flights were recorded over the Sea of Japan and Pacific Ocean near Hokkaido and northern Honshu, USNI News wrote.
Japan’s Southwestern Air Defense Command carried out 201 scrambles during the six months, compared with 189 a year earlier. The Northern Air Defense Command, which frequently responds to Russian military aviation near Hokkaido, recorded 112 scrambles, more than double the 53 reported during the same period in 2025.
The Western Air Defense Command recorded one of the sharpest increases, conducting 102 scrambles compared with just 14 a year earlier. USNI News attributed the rise to increased Chinese activity in the East China Sea and Russian aircraft flying south to join Chinese forces for coordinated operations.
Japan’s Joint Staff Office also recorded 25 instances of what it classified as unusual flight activity, involving Russian Il-20 aircraft, Chinese Y-9 intelligence planes, TB-001 drones, and bomber formations.
Between September 3 and 7, Japanese fighters scrambled on five consecutive days in response to a Chinese Y-9 electronic intelligence aircraft operating over the East China Sea.
One of the largest coordinated missions occurred on June 27, when two Chinese H-6 bombers and two J-16 fighters flew from the East China Sea toward the Sea of Japan and joined Russian Tu-95 bombers, Tu-142 maritime patrol aircraft, and a Su-35 fighter.
The combined force later continued through the area between Okinawa and Miyako Island before operating over the Philippine Sea and Pacific Ocean, USNI News reported.
“In the vicinity of Japan, China and Russia conducted joint flights of bombers and joint navigations of vessels,” Japan’s Ministry of Defense stated in its 2026 defense white paper. “Such repeated joint activities are obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan and pose a grave concern for Japan’s security.”
The increased Russian air activity comes amid heightened tensions between Moscow and Tokyo over the disputed Kuril Islands. In August, Russia’s State Duma speaker Vyacheslav Volodin invoked Russia’s nuclear arsenal while warning Japan over its territorial claims, after the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, visited the disputed island chain and triggered a formal protest from Tokyo.

Claude and Mistral Echo Kremlin-Aligned Claims in Over 70% of Tested Answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:10:53 UTC
20:10:53 KST

- Category
- Investigations
Claude and Mistral Echo Kremlin-Aligned Claims in Over 70% of Tested Answers
Claude and Mistral, AI models developed by US-based Anthropic and French company Mistral AI, respectively, repeated contested or false claims from Kremlin-aligned sites in roughly 70% of answers on topics with little mainstream coverage.
This was reported by the Global Disinformation Index (GDI) in a study published on October 12, titled “Russia benefitting from Data Voids to influence LLMs.” The analysis, commissioned by GDI and conducted with the AI analytics firm Sy.nexus, tested Claude Sonnet 5 and Mistral Large.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Researchers used 85 plain-language questions, repeated some prompts to assess consistency, and collected 280 answers from each model. According to the report, Claude repeated such claims in 70% of those answers and Mistral in 71%.
Neither model consistently rebutted the claims, GDI found. Among answers that repeated a claim, Mistral presented it as true in 48% and Claude in 28%. Claude flagged or contradicted the claim in 60% of such answers, compared with about 20% for Mistral.
GDI stressed that the tests ran through the models’ APIs, not consumer chatbot interfaces. The report noted that some companies add guardrails to their user-facing chatbots, but a growing number of corporate customers rely on APIs. It made no claims about what people using the chat interfaces might see.
The questions were built from data voids, meaning topics that Kremlin-aligned sites promote but that mainstream outlets rarely cover. In one example, GDI examined a fabricated Russian claim that its forces had captured Volnoye (Ukrainian: Vilne), a real village in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region. The report emphasized that the alleged Russian capture had never happened.
In the responses highlighted by GDI, neither model cited Ukrainian news outlets to substantiate the alleged capture. Mistral presented the Russian Ministry of Defense's claim as fact without caveats. Claude attributed the claim to Russian state media but acknowledged that it could not find independent confirmation from Ukrainian officials, the Ukrainian monitoring group DeepState, or the Institute for the Study of War.
Mistral's answers to that question varied widely, the report added. Asked eight times, it produced four distinct kinds of responses, ranging from rejecting the claim to presenting it as settled fact. GDI described this inconsistency as a known challenge requiring further research.
The two models also searched differently, according to GDI. Claude ran 3.6 searches per answer, compared with 1.2 for Mistral, and its searches returned a Russian- or Chinese-state-linked source in 88.2% of answers, compared with 32.1% for Mistral. TASS appeared in searches behind 140 of Claude’s answers and the Pravda network in 130, while neither appeared for Mistral.
GDI reported encountering the problem firsthand on July 1, 2026, when it asked an LLM about GDI itself. Claude cited the Strategic Culture Foundation, a Kremlin-aligned think tank added to a US Treasury sanctions list in 2021. The report stressed that the risk came from drawing on a sanctioned site without caveats, not from the content itself.
GDI linked the findings to the rise of zero-click searches, which it put at around 60%, where users accept an AI summary without visiting the original source. “Whoever controls the AI answer summary will control the narrative,” GDI concluded.
As a possible safeguard, GDI tested an exclusion list on Claude. A list of 191 blocked sites cut state-linked results from 30 of 34 matched answers to one, the report stated. It did not change whether answers agreed with the claim: 10 of 34 agreed with the list and 13 of 34 without it, too few to show a difference.
The report noted that the tool accepts lists of up to 250 sites, while lists of 500 or more were rejected, and that Mistral’s API offers no such option. GDI cautioned that any exclusion list would need to be continuously updated as new sites emerge and called for further research.
Russian exploitation of Claude has not been limited to the information space. In September, a Russian state-linked hacking group was found to have used the models to automate cyberespionage against more than 20 organizations, primarily in Ukraine and Europe.
Targets included government ministries, diplomatic missions, defense companies and drone technology suppliers, with AI-driven workflows handling reconnaissance, phishing, malware evasion and the processing of hundreds of gigabytes of stolen data. The hackers also stole a proprietary software development kit for a military drone vision system and spent several days reverse-engineering it.

Europe weighs energy-saving measures as Middle East crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:10:31 UTC
20:10:31 KST

EU Energy Ministers will consider demand cuts if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed in the months ahead, according to a document seen by Euronews.
EU governments could ask households and businesses to cut their energy use as the war in the Middle East drives up prices and threatens oil and gas supplies, according to a document seen by Euronews.
Energy ministers will discuss possible EU-wide measures to reduce consumption when they meet on 29 October, amid growing fears that disruption to supplies through the Strait of Hormuz could persist for months.
The proposal to consider demand cuts comes from Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU and is chairing negotiations between member states.
Gas prices have surged by 140% since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, while Brent crude was trading at $110 a barrel on Wednesday. Even if the conflict ends, its impact on oil markets could last for months, while the consequences for gas supplies could be felt for years, the Irish presidency warns.
EU officials have so far identified energy prices as the biggest ripple effect coming from the Middle East, even if Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen has urged EU capitals in September, for the second time, to consider energy demand cuts.
The EU's gas transmission operators recently warned that the bloc could face a gas shortfall of 12% to 15% of demand if a severe cold snap hits this winter. Storage levels are at 74% as of 20 October, according to data from the industry body Gas Infrastructure Europe, their lowest since 2011.
Nearly eight months after military attacks led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint accounting for 20% of the world's oil and gas transit, diesel and jet fuel are particularly exposed to price and potential supply disruptions.
EU weighs demand cuts
With the European Commission running out of options to cushion the impact of the crisis, ministers will consider whether reducing consumption should become part of the EU's response, alongside emergency stock releases and financial support.
"What are the lessons learned from EU coordination in responding to energy impacts as a result of the Middle East Conflict, and how should the EU prepare for a scenario in which the Strait of Hormuz remains partially or fully closed in the months ahead? What, if any, demand reduction measures should be considered at EU level?," reads the Council document.
The Council document does not propose specific energy cuts or establish that ministers have agreed to them. But it sets the stage to assess how far EU capitals are willing to go in managing consumption if supply disruptions persist.
The debate signals a growing recognition that the EU can't guarantee energy security through imports and emergency stock releases alone if a major supply route remains blocked.
French President Emmanuel Macron secured diesel from Gulf countries on Tuesday after Saudi Arabia offered additional spot crude cargoes for delivery to Europe from late October to mid-November. The move followed the G7 agreement to release more emergency oil stocks, under pressure from Washington.
Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said it is ready to coordinate more emergency oil releases by member countries if they wish to do so in order to counter rising prices.
Spain confirmed it would release 4.4 million barrels of strategic oil stocks during October, as part of its existing emergency commitment.
More car-free Sundays?
Shortly after the US-Israeli military attacks against Iran, the Paris-based IEA also announced a 10-point plan for countries to cut oil use, including "Car-free Sundays", a practice widely used during the energy crisis in the 1970s.
Other measures could range from voluntary appeals to households and businesses to save energy to targeted restrictions on consumption by particular sectors, depending on the severity of the crisis.
However, any EU-wide initiative would raise questions over who should bear the burden, whether industry should face restrictions and how to protect vulnerable households without further damaging the bloc's competitiveness.
The central question for ministers is whether demand reduction should be coordinated at EU level or left to national governments.
A common approach could help prevent countries from competing for scarce supplies, but EU governments face different levels of exposure to gas shortages, different electricity prices and different industrial needs.
A proposal from the Commission tabled at the 15-16 October Council summit to aggregate energy demand at the EU level is also currently on the table for capitals to assess. The goal is for Brussels to coordinate energy demand and distribute it to EU countries based on their needs.

Germany's far-right AfD rocked by major cyberattack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:10:14 UTC
20:10:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Germany's far-right AfD rocked by major cyberattack
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party announced on Tuesday that it was investigating the online publication of emails allegedly stolen in a major cyberattack targeting an email service provider used by the party.
More than 421,000 emails were reportedly stolen during the attack last month, including messages sent by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel and co-founder Alexander Gauland, according to German newspaper Bild.
The leak comes as the AfD, which has topped national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections, faces calls from some politicians and civil society groups to be banned over concerns that it threatens Germany's democratic constitutional order.
The New Arab breaks down what we know about the alleged breach and its implications.
What do we know about the AfD email leak?
According to an official statement from the AfD, hackers targeted a hosting service provider used by the party and apparently copied data from a small number of email accounts, most of which had not been used for years.
"The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," a party spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded."
The far-right party did not disclose how much data had been stolen, while a website published what it described as summaries of some of the emails rather than the original messages.
The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon, but archived versions showed a trove of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited".
Meanwhile, Bild reported that the published material included photographs of identity cards belonging to some party members, alongside bank statements, membership applications and membership lists from several local AfD branches.
The leaked material also allegedly contained discriminatory messages, with online summaries reportedly referencing Adolf Hitler, Nazi slogans, swastikas, racism and antisemitism.
These included an email concerning a so-called "Hitler pilgrimage" and a separate incident involving a Christmas card bearing a swastika.
One summary reportedly described party figures discussing having a photographer forcibly removed from an event, while other messages allegedly contained aggressive rhetoric directed at former German chancellor Angela Merkel.
The archive also reportedly included correspondence about disciplinary proceedings and the possible expulsion of party members.
However, the authenticity, context and extent of these claims have yet to be independently verified.
Cybersecurity experts have noted that the reported breach appeared to involve a third-party hosting provider rather than a direct attack on the party's own systems.
The potential exposure of sensitive information could nevertheless have significant implications for the AfD and Germany's wider political landscape.
The developments come as the anti-immigration party tops national opinion polls, having finished first in two state elections last month, comfortably ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
Several AfD state branches have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional offices of Germany's domestic intelligence agency.
The party secured its strongest result in Saxony-Anhalt, where it hopes to form Germany's first far-right state government since the Second World War.
On Monday, several migrant rights groups urged Merz and state premiers to establish legal, administrative and financial safeguards to protect migrants and asylum seekers from potential threats under a possible AfD-led administration in Saxony-Anhalt.
"In the coming weeks, a party whose state branch has been classified as confirmed right-wing extremist by the domestic intelligence agency could join government for the first time," the organisations warned.
"They would then have a say in key areas such as policing, education and security. Yet there is still no plan to protect the people who would be threatened by such a government."

Germany renews its hard stance on EU budget demanding hundreds of billions in cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:08:56 UTC
20:08:56 KST

Germany is demanding deep cuts to the European Commission’s proposed EU budget and ruling out new common borrowing, setting up a bruising battle over how Europe funds Ukraine, defence and competitiveness.
Germany wants the EU’s next long-term budget cut by “at least several hundreds of billions of euros”, German Ambassador to the EU Thomas Ossowski said in an interview with Euronews, signalling that member states remain far from a deal despite last week’s summit.
“The Commission proposal was far too high,” Ossowski said.
The Irish EU presidency has already reduced the proposal by around €140 billion in its latest negotiating framework. But Berlin says that is not enough.
“We are not there yet,” Ossowski said. “More cuts will definitely be necessary.”
The next key step will be a new negotiating proposal from European Council President António Costa ahead of an informal EU summit at the end of November. The goal is to reach a deal before Christmas.
“It is an ambitious plan,” Ossowski acknowledged.
No new common debt
Germany is also drawing a red line over how the EU should finance its ambitions.
Asked whether Berlin would accept another round of common EU borrowing if member states refuse to increase their contributions, Ossowski was unequivocal: “No, definitely not new common borrowing.”
Germany believes further joint debt would undermine national sovereignty. Berlin is willing to discuss new EU “own resources”, but rejects the idea of an EU-level tax on European companies.
The argument is part of a broader German push for a smaller but more strategically focused EU budget.
Ossowski said spending should prioritise competitiveness, innovation, research, defence, security and Ukraine.
Agriculture and cohesion funding would remain, but Germany supports cutting their combined share of the EU budget from roughly 66% today to 50%. “We think that is a sustainable approach,” he said.
Ukraine adds to the pressure
The budget fight comes as EU leaders face growing demands to finance Ukraine’s war effort.
Ossowski rejected the idea that additional support for Kyiv would necessarily come at the expense of farmers, families or cohesion funding. The €90 billion in loans already arranged for Ukraine, he said, was financed outside the regular EU budget using the bloc’s existing “headroom”.
But further support will be needed to get Ukraine through the winter and into next year.
“Germany stands with Ukraine and the European Union stands with Ukraine,” Ossowski said, while stressing that Berlin also expects the G7 and other international partners to contribute.
Berlin sees no Russian readiness for talks
Ossowski was meanwhile sceptical about the latest US-led diplomatic push to end the war.
“We don't see any readiness by Russia to engage in any kind of negotiations,” he said, pointing to continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilians.
Until that changes, European support for Kyiv will continue, he said.
For Germany, the stakes extend beyond Ukraine. Ossowski cast the conflict as a test of Europe’s ability to defend the rules-based international order and its own security architecture.
“The European Union is now the actor who defends the rule-based international order,” he said.
The message from Berlin is therefore clear: a smaller EU budget, no new common debt — but more spending on the geopolitical priorities Germany believes Europe can no longer afford to ignore.

Excalibur Army Unveils Self-Propelled Mortar On PATRIOT 4×4 Chassis With Alakran System Used in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:08:55 UTC
20:08:55 KST

Excalibur Army, part of the Czech Czechoslovak Group (CSG) holding, has unveiled a self-propelled mortar based on the PATRIOT 4×4 chassis and equipped with the Alakran system, which supports 81 mm and 120 mm mortars.
Militarnyi correspondent reported this from the FUTURE FORCES FORUM, a military forum taking place in Prague from October 21 to 23, 2026.
The system was developed in 2015 by Spanish companies Everis Aeroespacial y Defensa SLU and New Technologies Global Systems SL. It is used by the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Such systems are known to be in service with the 210th Separate Assault Regiment, mounted on VAMTAC chassis.
The PATRIOT is a modular armored tactical vehicle built on a TATRA chassis. Before today’s presentation, the vehicle had been produced in command-and-staff, reconnaissance, medevac, and other configurations. Previously, the self-propelled mortar version had only been shown in renderings.
The PATRIOT served as the basis for the Polish Waran armored vehicle, manufactured by Huta Stalowa Wola, particularly for the Gladius reconnaissance and strike system.
The PATRIOT’s design allows it to be equipped with a remotely operated weapon station armed with a gun of up to 30 mm, a remotely operated missile system, 7.62 mm, 12.7 mm, or 14.5 mm machine guns, and automatic grenade launchers.
The PATRIOT’s ballistic protection is rated at Levels 2–4 under STANAG 4569, while its mine protection is at Levels 2a/2b–3a/3b.
The Alakran mortar system can be produced in 81/82 mm and 120 mm calibers. It weighs approximately one tonne and can be mounted on various chassis with sufficient load capacity. In Ukraine, for example, the system is mounted on the Spanish VAMTAC S3 armored vehicle.
The system can also be mounted on a number of other chassis, including the Toyota Land Cruiser, Land Rover Defender, Jeep J8, and Agrale Marrua.
The manufacturer of the PATRIOT 4×4 with the ALAKRAN mortar system says the solution offers greater operational flexibility through 81 mm and 120 mm mortar configurations tailored to meet the requirements of different missions.
The stated rate of fire is 25 rounds per minute for the 81 mm mortar and 19 rounds per minute for the 120 mm mortar when using the maximum charge.
The maximum firing range is 6,900 m for the 81 mm mortar and 8,250 m for the 120 mm mortar, raising questions about the suitability of these systems in this configuration for the modern battlefield in Ukraine.

UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:08:04 UTC
20:08:04 KST

Breadcrumb
UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher
Inflation in the UK rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month.
The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That's the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month.
The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England's target rate of 2%.
Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August.
Fuel costs have been soaring because of the US-Israeli war on Iran and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families "some breathing space" from the upward march in the cost of living.
Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on 5 November. Last month, rate-setters held the bank's main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon.
“With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW.
Most economists expect an increase in the bank's main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, have raised rates recently.
Interest rates in the UK had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

From brain science to quantum computing: a look at the Peres Center presenting Israeli groundbreaking technologies to the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:07:29 UTC
20:07:29 KST

- i24NEWS
- INNOV'NATION
- From brain science to quantum computing: Israeli entrepreneurs take the stage at the Peres Center
From brain science to quantum computing: Israeli entrepreneurs take the stage at the Peres Center
Three Israeli tech entrepreneurs are turning breakthroughs in mental health, quantum computing and sustainable materials into real-world solutions
What does the future look like? It could mean finding the right antidepressant before treatment begins, unlocking the potential of quantum computers, or turning household garbage into new materials.
These are the challenges being tackled by three entrepreneurs who joined i24NEWS for a special panel at the Innovation Expo at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Tel Aviv-Jaffa.
Dr. Talia Cohen Solal of NeuroKaire, Simon Fried of Classiq and Jack 'Tato' Bigio of UBQ Materials are developing technologies across very different fields, united by a common ambition: translating scientific breakthroughs into solutions that can make a tangible difference.
NeuroKaire is working to transform mental health treatment through precision neuroscience. Its technology uses a patient’s blood cells to create neurons in the laboratory, then combines biological measurements and artificial intelligence to help predict how a person may respond to antidepressants. The goal is to reduce the trial-and-error process that can leave patients waiting months to find an effective treatment.
Dr. Cohen Solal says the growing excitement around AI should not overshadow the underlying science that makes these advances possible.
“People think we can use AI to replace everything, but people are forgetting to pay attention to the real core technologies that you need,” she told i24NEWS, emphasizing the importance of biological research and medical technologies in building a healthier healthcare system.
At Classiq, Fried is helping prepare for another technological turning point: quantum computing. The Israeli company develops software that allows users to design and optimize quantum algorithms without having to manage every complex technical detail themselves.
While quantum computing has yet to deliver its full commercial promise, Fried believes the industry is approaching a crucial phase. He estimates that the next two to three years could bring significant progress toward the stability and computing power needed to deliver results that businesses and researchers are waiting for.
Meanwhile, Bigio’s UBQ Materials is tackling one of the world’s most persistent environmental problems: waste. The company has developed a process that converts unsorted household waste, including food scraps, cardboard and mixed plastics, into a thermoplastic material that can replace conventional oil-based plastics in manufacturing.
For Bigio, the challenge is not simply inventing a greener alternative, but changing how industries use resources. By giving discarded materials a second life, UBQ aims to support a more circular economy.
The entrepreneurs presented their work at the Innovation Expo, part of the Peres Center’s Israeli Innovation Center, which showcases Israeli startups and technological developments to visitors from Israel and around the world. The event offers an opportunity for the public to discover emerging technologies and meet the people behind them.
All three entrepreneurs are also part of the Peres Center’s Innovation Dream Team, a community that connects innovators with new audiences, potential investors and collaborators. Through exhibitions, events and international delegations, the initiative helps entrepreneurs expand their reach and build relationships that can support their work.
For Dr. Cohen Solal, that exposure is particularly important for a small country with global ambitions. Fried describes the experience as an opportunity to meet collaborators and investors who can help bring future technologies to life.
Bigio, whose company has been involved with the center for several years, says the platform has provided significant exposure. He also received the Peres Center’s Outstanding Entrepreneur Award, which he sees as a meaningful connection between the late Shimon Peres’s vision and the work of entrepreneurs today.
Ultimately, the Innovation Expo is about more than showcasing new technologies. It is about connecting ideas with people — and helping innovations move beyond the laboratory and into the world.

European Commission outlines main issues of Ukraine talks in Oslo

European Commission outlines main issues of Ukraine talks in Oslo
Territorial issues, security and Ukraine's post-war prosperity were the main topics discussed by Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Steve Witkoff and European representatives during their talks in Oslo on 20 October.
Source: European Pravda's Brussels correspondent, citing Paula Pinho, spokesperson for the European Commission
Details: The 20 October talks in Oslo covered three main issues related to securing peace in Ukraine: territory, security and post-war recovery.
Quote: "The core topics of the discussion yesterday were territory, security, and post-war prosperity."
Details: Pinho said the talks were a follow-up to the meeting in Miami two weeks earlier.
She added that it is extremely important that "we are sitting at the table, that we are able to present our position, and that we can engage in what is a shared objective to put an end to this horrific war, which has lasted for far too long".
Background:
- On 20 October, talks were held in Oslo between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and US President Donald Trump's representatives, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The European Union was represented by Björn Seibert, Head of Cabinet for the President of the European Commission.
- On 21 October, Witkoff arrived in St Petersburg for talks with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.
- Following the 20 October Oslo talks, Stubb noted that the discussions had focused on issues related to security, energy and the economy in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine.
- Zelenskyy later said that the US side had assured Ukraine during the talks in Oslo that it would receive "strong" security guarantees.

Water rationing, rubbish pile-up raise disease fears in Yemen's besieged Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:06:30 UTC
20:06:30 KST

Water rationing, rubbish pile-up raise disease fears in Yemen's besieged Taiz
GENEVA/TAIZ, Yemen Oct 21 - Families have started rationing water in and around Yemen's Taiz city, where renewed fighting has disrupted fuel supplies and access to water systems serving 3 million people, aid groups and UN agencies said.
Meanwhile, mounting piles of rubbish along major roads are raising fears of disease outbreaks in the city, Yemen's third-largest.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-allied Houthi group since September has cut key supply routes, including the Taiz-Aden corridor, worsening shortages of water, food and fuel in and around the city.
The lack of fuel is hampering the operation of water pumps and hospitals, while disruption to waste collection has left rubbish piled along roads of the city, a stronghold of anti-Houthi forces which is now under siege by the armed movement.
The Taiz governorate hosts nearly half of the 250,000 people displaced by the latest escalation, aid groups said.
"The state of the rubbish in the city is very wretched, and the build-up is terrible, like nothing before,” Taiz resident Abdelbari al-Qadi told Reuters.
Sanitation worker Ali Ahmed said authorities could no longer go to the main dumping site because of clashes, and they were forced to burn it in the streets.
'EXTREMELY DANGEROUS SITUATION' FOR CHILDREN, SAYS RELIEF OFFICIAL
Families are rationing drinking water as diesel shortages hobble pumping stations and sanitation systems, said Akhil Iyer, UNICEF's representative in Yemen.
"I get the water with difficulty. We wait in queues from the morning until our turn comes,” Alaa Khalil told Reuters while people queued to fill jerry cans in Taiz, where most residents depend on trucked water.
Access to the Al-Dhubab aquifer, a major source of trucked water for Taiz, has been restricted, while fuel disruptions have affected pumps, creating a severe water crisis, said Wathiq Aghbari, director general of the Local Water and Sanitation Authority in the governorate.
Water production in Taiz has fallen by about 50%, according to Save the Children.
“We find children in an extremely dangerous situation where they are not able to have their basic needs satisfied. They are not able to access sufficient food and water and healthcare,” said Rishana Haniffa, Save the Children's country director for Yemen.
Aid groups are exploring other sources, including a shallow aquifer west of the city. The cost of a water truck has tripled from about 23,000 Yemeni rials ($14.80) before the latest escalation to about 70,000 rials ($45), according to UNICEF.
CARE International says cash assistance is buying less food and water as prices rise.
“We feel the situation is really getting out of hand unless we able to negotiate access to have water tankers come in to the city,” said Iman Abdullahi, CARE Yemen country director.
RUBBISH BUILD-UP 'WILL CAUSE DISEASES', SAYS HEALTH OFFICIAL
"The build-up of rubbish is very harmful and will cause diseases, whether respiratory or otherwise," said Abdulrahman al-Sabri, director of Taiz Governorate's Health Office, adding that dengue fever and cholera cases were spreading.
Cholera cases have tripled since early September from 221 to 683 this month, while hospitals face medicine shortages and 12 facilities have fuel supplies sufficient for only about four days, the World Health Organization said.
A doctor who asked not to be named for security reasons said some families could not reach healthcare facilities because of fighting around the city.
The Danish Refugee Council said the impact of deteriorating water and sanitation conditions could spread beyond Taiz city. It pointed to overstretched resources in crowded displacement sites across the governorates of Taiz, Lahj, Abyan and Aden.
The spread of disease could also worsen hunger in Taiz governorate, UNICEF said. It has identified 52,000 acutely malnourished children in Taiz so far this year. Road closures have halted UNICEF's deliveries of a therapeutic food for severely malnourished children in Taiz. REUTERS
