Russia Releases Imprisoned American Man as Trump Envoy Meets With Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:05:51 UTC
20:05:51 KST

Russia has released a retired American teacher who had been imprisoned for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff confirmed the release Wednesday, during a meeting in St. Petersburg.
Witkoff referred to Putin as a "humanitarian" and thanked him on behalf of U.S. President Donald Trump. "You talk so much about my President, President Trump, being a humanitarian—you are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that," he said.
Stephen Hubbard, 74, was sentenced to nearly seven years in a penal colony in 2024, after being detained in April 2022. Russian authorities accused the Michigan man of signing a contract with Ukraine’s military in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022. The U.S. State Department under the Biden Administration declared that Hubbard, who was sentenced in a closed trial, had been wrongfully detained.
Trump said the release was secured at his request, "made directly" to Putin in a telephone conversation last week and was not part of a swap.
"Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family," Trump said, noting that the U.S. "was not required to give anything in return."
Trump had hinted to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday that Hubbard’s release was pending. "Just stick with me," he replied, when asked about the American man’s case. "I don't want to talk about it, but everybody has been after Hubbard for a long time, long before I got here. And just remember that question for a couple of days from now, okay? Because I do things that nobody else can do."
Yet experts advise against viewing Putin's decision to release a prisoner as a sign of progress in the broader context of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
"The release of Hubbard was a gesture to Trump, nothing more, and does not imply a larger willingness on Putin’s part to make concessions or end the war," argues Brian Taylor, a professor of political science at Syracuse University who specializes in Russian politics.
Hubbard is the second American to be freed by Russia within the past three months. Marine veteran Robert Gilman was released on Aug. 11, having spent more than four years imprisoned on disputed charges of assaulting a police officer. Referencing Gilman's reported poor health, Trump at the time said Russia had agreed to release him "on a humanitarian basis."
Hubbard was the last American on the State Department’s list of “wrongfully detained” U.S. citizens in Russia. His release comes in the wake of Trump waiving sanctions on Russia in a bid to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin as he attempts to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran.
The deal has earned bipartisan condemnation, with several Republican lawmakers joining calls for Trump to reverse course, insisting the action will only serve to bolster Putin’s war efforts as Ukraine braces for a fifth winter under attack.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
Relations between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have deteriorated, with the latter voicing grave concern over the U.S.-Russia diesel deal. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, calling on the two countries to stop targeting each other’s assets. Zelensky accused Moscow of breaking the apparent agreement and, in turn, resumed strikes against Russian oil facilities, defying pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes a "disgrace" and said Zelensky is "more difficult to deal with than Putin."
Russia agrees to resume U.S.-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, Kremlin says
During their meeting at the grand imperial palace, Witkoff asked Putin to reconsider participating in peace talks with Ukraine, with the U.S. serving as an intermediary.
"Even if we don't have a resolution today, if we just talk about and sort of consider what that next step might be, I think that would be important and the world is waiting to hear that," Witkoff said as he pitched the idea.
The Kremlin later announced that Putin had agreed "in principle" to resume trilateral talks as soon as next month, anytime after Nov. 10. Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters the technical talks would likely focus on security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia once the war comes to an end. Ushakov suggested the sit-down could take place in Abu Dhabi.
"These talks happened before and did not lead to any meaningful progress on reaching a settlement," Taylor says, again advising a cautionary approach. Reflecting on the Kremlin's strategy, he adds that Putin likely "wants to show Trump he’s willing to play ball, without actually changing his behavior."
Senior Ukrainian and Russian officials last convened in Switzerland in February for U.S.-brokered peace talks, just ahead of the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The discussions, which Zelensky suggested had been "difficult," ended without a breakthrough.
In August 2025, Trump met Putin for a high-stakes summit in Anchorage, Alaska, marking the first in-person encounter between the two leaders since 2019. The sit-down was aimed at exploring a path toward a cease-fire in the war in Ukraine, yet it ended earlier than expected and yielded no tangible results.
Witkoff, meanwhile, met with Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday ahead of his trip to Russia. Zelensky said the meeting was productive and expressed his openness to a "potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do." However, he emphasized that any meetings to negotiate an end to the war must include Ukrainian officials, insisting there should be “nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine."
Zelensky's remarks came after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin had floated the idea of a summit with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss a potential Ukraine deal. Trump on Monday said he was open to a trilateral summit with those attendees to discuss matters related to “denuclearization.”
U.S.-Ukraine tensions escalate
Ukraine and U.S. officials remain at odds as to why Kyiv has experienced limited access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart of SpaceX’s Starlink commercial service. The program, which offers remote Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit, has become a lifeline for Ukraine on the battlefield, allowing it to execute long-reach drone strike missions and counter attacks.
On Oct. 14, Ukraine said its access to Starshield was abruptly limited. Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky, said speed restrictions had been imposed, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. Beskrestnov claimed the restrictions, which he said applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were “related to the current political situation.” During an Oct. 18 appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelensky said he believed the limited Starshield speed was a “message” from the U.S. government. He also said that Washington had briefly stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, drawing a denial from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Zelensky’s remarks came after Reuters reported, citing two U.S. officials, that an order to limit Starshield services in Ukraine had come from inside the White House. When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.” Some Republican lawmakers, including Representative Mike Turner of Ohio and Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, have joined bipartisan calls for an investigation to determine the cause.
Addressing the matter, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.”

House committee says Webull messages point to China access to U.S. customer data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:05:18 UTC
20:05:18 KST

Internal messages between employees of online investing platform Webull suggest a company employee in China had access to information about a U.S. customer, despite the company having said it bars such sharing, according to an analysis of the messages by the House Select Committee on China.
The analysis comes nearly two weeks after CNBC first detailed the bipartisan select committee's report that concluded that Webull, which counts 28 million users, is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to American finance.
Webull shares slid more than 19% on the heels of that Oct. 7 report.
At the time of the report, Webull told CNBC in a statement that "U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S."
But the newly released internal messages by the House Select Committee on China, which CNBC exclusively obtained, raise questions about whether that has always been the case.
The committee has focused on threats posed by China and protecting U.S. industry from Chinese competition.
One message thread suggests a Webull employee was in China during a discussion about a U.S. customer account.
The thread also indicates the account was previously approved by a China Webull team member and an American counterpart.
The messages, dating to 2021, were sent on Microsoft Teams between Brendan Fuller, a manager at Webull's U.S. brokerage, and an employee named Zhenghan Wang, whose nickname is "Rock."
The select committee says Wang was likely in China at the time.
In one message, Fuller messaged Wang about concerns involving a particular trading account.
"We saw these problems ... and approve account," Fuller wrote.
Wang replied: "Yes,CIP."
CIP is an acronym for Customer Identification Program, a U.S. regulatory requirement that financial institutions verify the identities of individuals and entities opening accounts.
"I thought so," Fuller responded.
Wang asked Fuller: "Who approve the account?"
Fuller responded: "One China team member and one US team."
Wang then asked: "I want to know in what situation (CIP), can we approve the account open?"
Fuller responded: "I think we just approve them all no matter what ..."
"And then we pay for vendors. And create report and work," Fuller added.
Wang then replied that "CIP=" followed by Mandarin Chinese characters forming a common phrase that translates as "Exists in name only," or "Useless."
A spokesperson for the select committee, in a statement to CNBC, said, "All the evidence in these text messages points to Zhenghan Wang, a Webull employee, being located in China with access to U.S. customer data at the time he worked for the company."
An analysis by the committee concluded that Wang was in China at the time of the exchange because the messages' time stamps indicated that Wang was working daytime hours in Beijing, and because he set his software to translate the messages into simplified Chinese.
A Webull spokesperson did not directly respond to CNBC's questions about Wang's access to U.S. customer data in 2021 and whether that disproved the company's assertion that its U.S. data does not go to China.
The Webull spokesperson said, "Protecting customer data is central to Webull's operations."
"Webull's U.S. customer data is stored only in the U.S. on AWS servers in Virginia and Oregon, with access to sensitive data restricted to U.S.-based employees," the spokesperson said.
"U.S. broker-dealer operations are directed exclusively by U.S.-based personnel, and no individuals based outside the U.S. have ever exercised operational or decision-making authority over Webull's U.S. broker-dealer business."
The company spokesperson also criticized the select committee's release of the messages.
"The Teams messages now being referenced date back to a 2021 routine FINRA matter, which was concluded," the spokesperson said. FINRA, or the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, is the self-regulatory organization for member broker-dealers.
The messages' "recent disclosure, alongside the Select Committee's report relying on preliminary and outdated information, raises legitimate questions about the timing and circumstances surrounding their release," Webull's spokesperson said.
"Webull rejects irresponsible speculation and stands on our well-documented record: Webull's data protection practices are robust, continuously enhanced, and independently verified."
The select committee's Oct. 7 report argued that Webull's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. Those Chinese laws can compel firms to cooperate with the government in various ways, including mandating data transfers.
The select committee on Tuesday issued a press release titled, "The Facts on Webull's Ties to China."
The release said that since the committee issued its report, Webull "has ... responded with numerous false statements about its business and its interactions with the Select Committee."
The committee listed five claims by Webull, followed by what the committee labeled "The Truth."
One section, titled "Webull Claim: 'U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S.,'" was followed by a rebuttal that said, "The Truth: The Select Committee's report does not dispute where the data is stored.
"Its finding is about who can reach the data and the systems that process it," the committee continued. "The report found that Webull affiliate Webull Technologies Limited previously used Tencent Cloud, a China-based provider, to host certain user data ... Webull has not said what data Tencent hosted or when that ended."
Webull said Tuesday that it was partnering with Kalshi, the prediction market platform, to offer so-called perpetual futures to U.S. customers.
The first set of perpetual futures, which do not have an expiration date, as traditional futures do, would be for cryptocurrencies, Webull said.

Iran joins countries with advanced quantum training laboratories

Unknown Publisher

Iran joins countries with advanced quantum training laboratories
TEHRAN – Iran has joined countries with advanced laboratories for hands-on training in quantum technologies with the inauguration of three specialized facilities in quantum optics and quantum information, established with support from the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-Based Economy.
Quantum technologies are considered one of the strategic fields of science and technology, globally. The development of quantum technologies requires advancement in fundamental research, specialized training, and advanced laboratories, IRNA reported.
The three advanced laboratories inaugurated in Isfahan University of technology (on October 14), Shahid Beheshti University (on October 17), and Sharif University of Technology (on October 20) with the aim of strengthening the scientific capacities of the universities, developing national quantum technology ecosystem, providing practical training, expanding students’ experiences, and developing human resources required to advance quantum research and technologies.
Now, Iranian students have gained access to infrastructure for directly conducting advanced experiments, including entangled photon generation, single-photon detection and generation, experimental tests of Bell’s inequality, two-photon interference, quantum tomography, quantum key distribution, and the investigation of diamond-based quantum systems.
In July 2025, President Masoud Pezeshkian declared the implementation of the ‘national document on quantum science and technology’.
The document is a comprehensive set of main objectives, assessment indicators, national strategies, implementing and monitoring mechanisms, IRNA quoted Abdolhassan Bahrami, an official with the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology, and Knowledge-based Economy, as saying.
It has been developed as a roadmap for the progress of research, expansion of technology, and commercialization of quantum technologies, the official added.
In this line, quantum science and technology headquarters will be established to enhance coordination among relevant organizations, develop an implementation roadmap, pursue the development of regulations, observe national and global advancements, as well as propose amendments to revise the document.
To implement the document, the vice-presidency, in cooperation with other relevant institutions, will initially provide a national plan for division of labor in the quantum science and technology sector. It will be followed by providing support for the development of applications, commercialization, and participation of knowledge-based companies to make the best use of domestic innovative capacities.
Iran ranks first in key scientific output among Islamic countries
Iran ranks first among Islamic nations in key fields of scientific output such as quantum science, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced materials, the head of the Presidential Affairs Office at the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) announced in August.
The country is in close competition with Turkey and Saudi Arabia in these fields, IRNA quoted Saeed Bakhtiari as saying.
He made the remarks in a press briefing on August 17, noting that the development of science in these fields has also been emphasized in national development plans.
Based on the reputable Web of Science database, Iran ranks first among Islamic countries in scientific output in some of these fields, while placing second or third in others. Overall, however, Iran holds the top position, he said.
Bakhtiari noted that in advanced materials—a multidisciplinary field spanning physics, chemistry, mechanics and materials science—Iran ranks second among Islamic countries and ninth worldwide.
He added that Iran ranks third in artificial intelligence, behind Saudi Arabia and Turkey, while in quantum science it ranks second, after Saudi Arabia.
The ISC official further said that Iran holds the top position among Islamic countries in scientific output in cognitive sciences and ranks first overall.
According to Web of Science (WoS) data, over a five-year period (from 2021 to 2025), Iran (with 32 documents) ranks first in cognitive sciences among Islamic countries.
Turkey, with 23 documents, and Saudi Arabia, with 22 documents, are placed second and third, respectively, IRNA reported.
From 2014 to 2023, Iran ranked either first or second in most fields of cognitive sciences among Islamic countries. Over the course of the decade, the country ranked first in cognitive neuroscience, cognitive rehabilitation, and cognitive linguistics with 387, 156, and 30 documents, respectively.
It ranked second in cognitive psychology (124 documents), cognitive education (561 documents), philosophy of mind (34 documents), and cognitive evaluation (898 documents). The country’s best ranking globally was in cognitive neuroscience; it ranked 15.
Tehran University of Medical Sciences, with 73 documents, University of Tehran, with 39 documents, and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, with 32 documents, ranked first to third in cognitive neuroscience. In cognitive psychology, University of Tehran(10 documents ), Ferdowsi University of Mashhad (7 documents), and Allameh Tabatabai University (6 documents) were the top three universities.
In cognitive linguistics, University of Tehran (with 3 documents), Al-Zahra University (3 documents), and Allameh Tabatabei University (2 documents ) ranked first to third. In cognitive education, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences were placed first to third, respectively.
In cognitive rehabilitation, Tehran University of Medical Sciences (21 documents), University of Tehran (16 documents), and Iran University of Medical Sciences (12 documents) ranked first to third. The best three universities in philosophy of mind were University of Tehran, Isfahan University, and Amirkabir University of Technology.
In cognitive evaluation, Tehran University of Medical Sciences ranked first with 196 documents. Iran University of Medical Sciences (105 documents) and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (91 documents) ranked second and third.
The country is placed second in quantum (with 216 documents) and advanced materials (with 5975 documents), after Saudi Arabia, with 283 and 6160 documents in quantum and advanced materials. Malaysia (with 154 documents) and Egypt (with 3151 documents) are placed third in quantum and advanced materials, respectively.
Despite illegal sanctions, Iran secures first place in cognitive sciences among Islamic nations and ranks ninth globally in advanced materials. Numerous prestigious Iranian universities and institutions are included in international rankings. These accomplishments underscore the country’s scientific capabilities, IRIB quoted Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf as saying, addressing the 7th Turkey Educational Technologies Summit (known as TETZ 2026), held in Istanbul from June 26 to 28.
Iran serves as a great opportunity to invest in higher education and modern technologies. The country has one of the largest higher education systems in the region, with more than three million students and over seventy thousand faculty members and researchers.
Highlighting that the rapid development of emerging technologies, including AI, is fundamentally transforming human relationships and higher education systems around the world at an unprecedented pace, Simaei-Sarraf said that effective use of smart technologies requires the establishment of a system based on algorithmic transparency, educational justice, accountability, protection of learners’ rights, and responsible data governance.

Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:03:52 UTC
20:03:52 KST

Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bonn
- Summary:
- Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.
- Share:
Scientists in Germany have found a way to dramatically reverse the molecular age of human cells, transforming blood cells from an 80-year-old person into stem cells with an age signature of less than 20 years.
Researchers at the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn achieved this remarkable transformation by reprogramming immature red blood cells into neural stem cells, which can eventually develop into brain cells. During the process, molecular markers associated with aging were effectively reset, making the cells more than 60 years younger at the molecular level.
Unlike earlier approaches, the rejuvenation happened gradually, allowing scientists to follow the changes over an extended period. This slower process could provide important clues about how cellular aging can be reversed and potentially help researchers investigate treatments for diseases associated with aging.
The findings were published in the journal Aging Cell.
How Scientists Turn Blood Cells Into Brain Stem Cells
The human body contains hundreds of specialized cell types, all of which originate from a single fertilized egg and carry essentially the same genetic instructions. As cells develop, however, they take on specific roles. Under normal circumstances, a skin cell cannot transform into a liver cell, and a blood cell cannot become a nerve cell.
Modern laboratory techniques have made it possible to overcome these biological restrictions. Scientists can now reprogram certain mature cells to adopt entirely different identities. For example, skin cells can be converted into cells capable of producing nerve tissue, an approach that could eventually contribute to treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
The process relies on a combination of proteins called transcription factors, which regulate how genes are activated. By changing which genetic instructions a cell follows, these proteins can redirect its development and give it a new cellular identity.
"Using this method, we have directly converted red blood cell precursors into neural stem cells," explains Prof. Dr. Oliver Brüstle, director of the Institute of Reconstructive Neurobiology at the University Hospital of Bonn.
Earlier experiments by the Bonn team had already demonstrated that nerve cells generated through this approach could successfully connect with existing neurons after being transplanted into the brains of mice.
Scientists Reverse More Than 60 Years of Cellular Aging
The latest investigation focused on an especially intriguing consequence of cellular reprogramming: the dramatic reversal of molecular aging.
"In our current study, however, we focused on a different phenomenon: namely, the observation that cells become significantly rejuvenated during reprogramming," emphasizes Brüstle, who is also a member of the Transdisciplinary Research Area (TRA) Life & Health at the University of Bonn.
To determine how much the cells had rejuvenated, the researchers examined their molecular clocks, particularly biological markers known as epigenetic clocks. These clocks estimate a cell's biological age by analyzing chemical modifications to DNA that tend to accumulate or change as organisms grow older.
Importantly, these modifications do not alter the DNA sequence itself. Instead, they affect how frequently certain genetic instructions are used (epigenetics). Because these patterns change predictably with age, scientists can use them to estimate how old a cell appears at the molecular level.
The results were striking. After reprogramming, cells taken from an 80-year-old individual displayed molecular age signatures corresponding to someone younger than 20. In other words, the process had reversed more than six decades of cellular aging.
"We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells," says the scientist.
A Slower Rejuvenation Process Reveals New Clues
Scientists have previously observed that reprogramming cells can reset their biological age. However, earlier demonstrations of this effect involved a more complicated process requiring two distinct stages.
First, researchers would convert an existing cell, such as a blood cell, into a pluripotent stem cell. These versatile cells have nearly unlimited developmental "career paths" because they can give rise to many different cell types throughout the body.
The pluripotent stem cell would then be guided into becoming a neural stem cell, which is more specialized and can produce cells found in the nervous system.
This conventional approach produces rejuvenation relatively quickly, making it difficult to examine all the changes taking place.
The Bonn researchers instead bypassed the pluripotent stage entirely.
"In contrast, we converted blood cells directly into neural stem cells -- that is, without first passing through the pluripotent cell stage," said Brüstle. "In our approach, rejuvenation occurred gradually and could be tracked for over 100 days."
The researchers observed a dramatic reduction in molecular age, with the study highlighting rejuvenation of approximately 60 years after 50 days. Because the process continued over a much longer period, scientists could examine the biological changes as they unfolded rather than observing only the final result.
What Cellular Rejuvenation Could Mean for Alzheimer's Research
The ability to watch cells gradually become younger could be particularly valuable for scientists trying to understand the mechanisms that control biological aging.
By studying this extended transformation, researchers can investigate which molecular pathways are involved and test whether particular substances can speed up or slow down the rejuvenation process.
"Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model: Since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process."
The findings could be especially relevant to neuroscience, where aging is closely connected to the development of serious neurological conditions. Although the work does not establish a treatment capable of reversing aging in people, it offers a laboratory model for investigating how cells regain youthful characteristics.
This could eventually help scientists better understand the cellular changes associated with conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
"After all, age is the most important risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's!"
The research involved teams from the University Hospital of Bonn, the University of Bonn, and RWTH Aachen University. Funding was provided by the EU's Horizon 2020 program, the German Research Foundation (DFG), and the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFRT).

Members of the French navy stand on the deck of the Dixmude amphibious helicopter carrier in Toulon, France on Feb. 17, 2026. | Thibaud Moritz/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Suspicious drones flew over military facilities in southeastern France earlier this month, the French navy said on Wednesday.
During a large-scale armed forces exercise that lasted from Oct. 5 to Oct. 16, "unauthorized drones were detected in the no-fly zone, near and above military sites," the navy said in a press statement.
"In each instance, the planned security measures were activated by the deployment of anti-drone devices, in coordination with domestic security forces," it continued, adding that a judicial investigation was opened.
Advertisement
Suspicious drones are increasingly spotted in several European countries including Denmark, Germany and France, close to military sites and defense industry facilities. In July, a Moldovan man was arrested on suspicion of espionage after flying an unmanned aerial vehicle over a KNDS factory in Munich. Some of these drone incursions are attributed to Russia, as Moscow intensifies its hybrid attacks against European countries.
The French navy's statement confirms local media reporting about drone sightings around Toulon. The southeastern town is home to one of France's largest naval bases, which hosts the country's aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle as well as attack submarines.
According to local broadcaster Ici Provence, the drones flew at night above the naval base, the General Directorate of Armaments facility in Toulon, and the 54th Artillery Regiment in Hyères. The military exercise, dubbed Typhon, was precisely aimed at training against drone sightings.
The navy said that no sensitive infrastructure was threatened. "The Ministry of the Armed Forces and Veterans Affairs reminds the public that unauthorized drone flights near or over military facilities are strictly prohibited," the statement concluded.

Dezeen launches "richer and more versatile" new website
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Dezeen has updated its website for the first time in 10 years. Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li explain the changes.
You might have noticed that things look a little different around here. Yes, after many years, we have redesigned our website!
It has been 10 years, in fact – the last major revamp of Dezeen was in 2016. And as with our previous redesign, evolution, not revolution, has been the aim.
Dezeen was launched by Marcus Fairs from his spare room as a basic WordPress blog in 2006. When it started to take off, he brought designer and typographer Micha Weidmann on board to design a logo and layout for it, and this has been the foundation upon which Dezeen has been built ever since.
We really like it, and millions of readers around the world seem to like it too.
So our ambition for this redesign was to bring the site up to date while staying true to the core identity that has helped Dezeen become what it is today.
Underneath the bonnet, there’s been a complete overhaul
We have worked with creative technology studio Made by On to refresh the look and feel of the site and improve the user interface to make it more useful and enjoyable to use.
Underneath the bonnet, there’s been a complete overhaul.
Our previous site was built on ageing technology that had grown clunky over time. Things broke too often and, as regular readers will know, fixing them was a slow and often painful process.
So we tasked Made by On with rebuilding both the front- and back-ends of the site from the ground up to make Dezeen much more stable and responsive.
Reducing the carbon impact of the website was also a key priority, so Made by On focused on performance and efficiency throughout the build, doing a lot of work on image optimisation in particular.
We also used the opportunity of the rebuild to move our hosting to The Positive Internet Company, whose server infrastructure runs on 100-per-cent-renewable energy, and moved our search and recommendation engines, which were previously run by external services, onto our own infrastructure.
Dezeen has expanded far beyond a daily news publishing platform
The new website is faster, richer and, we hope, more enjoyable to use. It also better reflects what Dezeen is today.
Over the past two decades, Dezeen has expanded far beyond a daily news publishing platform to become a suite of services for the global architecture and design community: Dezeen Awards, Dezeen Events Guide and Dezeen Showroom, to name a few.
These were added in a fairly ad hoc way over time, so the overall experience could feel fragmented.
To bring everything together, we returned to Micha Weidmann, who refreshed our brand guidelines, introducing updated colour schemes and logos across all our sub-brands to create a coherent family.
Made By On then used these guidelines to create a cohesive web experience, carefully engineered to meet the latest web accessibility standards, ensuring Dezeen can be enjoyed comfortably by all our readers.
Every service across dezeen.com has undergone a major redesign to ensure it offers real value to our readers. Our jobs website dezeenjobs.com will be updated in the coming weeks.
Navigating the site should now be easier thanks to a fresh menu, search and filtering system
So, what has changed? (And what has not?)
Visually, we have retained the classic typographic treatments that go back to Micha’s first design nearly 20 years ago. However, we have introduced new styling formats to bring greater hierarchy and visual interest to the pages, as well as splashes of colour to better identify content relating to our different services.
We love how eclectic Dezeen is – every story starts at the top and works its way down the homepage, regardless of subject matter – and this will continue. At the same time, our content offering has expanded significantly over the years, and it was too easy for some of our best content to get lost.
So the core, reverse-chronological feed of news stories remains, as do our signature square images. However, we have introduced varied image sizes alongside new horizontal scrolling sections to break up the vertical feed and spotlight specific content types.
Navigating the site should now be much easier thanks to a fresh menu, search and filtering system, which is unified across all of our services. We have also decluttered the right sidebar and added parallax scrolling to create what we hope readers will find to be an intuitive, easily navigable and enjoyable experience.
Video and audio have also been improved: we can now integrate vertical video much more seamlessly, and our podcast Dezeen Weekly, which we launched earlier this year, has been given greater prominence.
We have also built significantly more flexible and visual article layouts.
We will continue publishing amazing buildings, interiors and products from around the world, and we can now include larger images, as well as photo galleries and slideshows, in our articles and across our services to ensure these projects really shine.
In an era increasingly dominated by AI, we believe human-created journalism is more important than ever
Since starting as a basic blog, our editorial range has expanded into long-form features, interviews and opinion pieces, and the new layouts will create a far richer environment for these stories too.
In an era increasingly dominated by AI-generated content and algorithmic feeds, we believe human-created journalism, curation and critical opinion are more important than ever.
While we are using smarter technology to power our new search, filtering and content-recommendation systems, the stories you read on Dezeen continue to be sourced, written and edited by our team. This takes a lot of time and effort, and with this redesign we want to ensure this content has the high-quality platform it deserves.
We know readers generally do not love advertisements, but Dezeen would not exist without them (and if you use an ad blocker, we’d like to use this as an opportunity to kindly ask you to turn it off for Dezeen so we can continue bringing you our content for free).
We have updated our ad formats to deliver better performance for our partners while respecting our readers’ experience. We have also introduced clearer and more consistent badging of partnership content.
Our aim has been to create an ad experience not dissimilar to a high-end glossy magazine: integrated thoughtfully with appropriate partners so that it enhances the page rather than detracts from it.
The aim has been to retain the spirit of Dezeen
Overall, the ambition has been to create a richer and more versatile site that retains the spirit of the Dezeen that you know and love.
Marcus’s vision when he started Dezeen almost 20 years ago was to set the global architecture and design agenda, and Dezeen has since grown to become one of the most influential architecture and design media brands in the world.
The new website will enable us to continue that mission for the years ahead. We hope you enjoy exploring it.
Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li are co-CEOs of Dezeen.

Bozhidar Bozhanov (DB) and Asen Vassilev (PP) accused the ruling coalition of blocking parliamentary scrutiny of pardons granted to convicted drug traffickers by Iliana Yotova, after an extraordinary session of the National Assembly failed to convene.
Bozhanov, an MP from the Democratic Bulgaria parliamentary group and co-chair of Yes, Bulgaria, said the coalition had covered up a scandal by preventing the session on the case of the so-called “Petrich Escobar” from taking place.
He revealed that another individual, convicted three times of drug-related offenses, had continued criminal activities after being released on medical grounds, raising questions about the criteria used to grant pardons.
“These are individuals from the criminal underworld, repeat offenders. Yotova has repeatedly granted pardons to such people. This is absolutely irresponsible and completely inadequate. Given these actions and judgments, Iliana Yotova is unfit to serve as Vice President of Bulgaria, and the Bulgarian citizens clearly see this,” Bozhanov said.
He also pointed to an incident in which the “Escobar of Petrich” was involved in a physical altercation in prison that was never reported to the Presidency. Maria Pavlova, then deputy justice minister responsible for the prison system, was a person close to both President Radev and Vice President Yotova, Bozhanov said.
“The truth regarding Yotova’s controversial pardons is further illuminated by another interesting fact. Following a physical altercation in prison involving the 'Escobar of Petrich,' the incident was never reported to the Presidency. Do you know which Deputy Minister of Justice was responsible for the prison system at that time? It was Maria Pavlova - an individual very close to both President Radev and Vice President Yotova. This all points to a likely well-orchestrated scheme, which is precisely why the security services are now keeping things under wraps,” Bozhanov said.
He demanded that the authorities provide explanations rather than conceal information from the public.
Bozhanov also called for an audit of the Pardons Commission's membership and work, arguing that it did not have enough specialists with the necessary expertise and that its decisions raised questions about whether consistent criteria were being applied. He contrasted the pardons granted to some convicts with the refusal to release a prisoner suffering from metastatic cancer.
“Clearly, it is not merely a question of who is suffering from what medical condition,” Bozhanov said, calling for the reasons behind the decisions to be made public.
He further announced that lawmakers were collecting signatures to convene another extraordinary parliamentary session over the arson attack on antennas belonging to the Starlink satellite internet system. Bozhanov said the authorities needed to explain why the suspects had been allowed to leave the country and why the process of issuing a European Arrest Warrant had been delayed.
“The government, through its downplaying of the situation and refusal to acknowledge the risks to Bulgaria, is jeopardizing national security,” he said.

Addressing protests by young medical professionals, he said the caretaker government had prepared amendments to a regulation that the current administration should have adopted. He described demonstrations by young doctors and citizens protesting rising prices as a natural response to widespread dissatisfaction, arguing that the authorities could not keep blaming the opposition.
“When you have 131 MPs, you cannot just say, 'It’s the opposition’s fault,'” Bozhanov said.
Asen Vassilev, leader of We Continue the Change and an MP from its parliamentary group, separately accused Progressive Bulgaria of causing a lack of quorum for the second consecutive week by failing to attend parliamentary proceedings. Speaking at a briefing at the National Assembly, he said the absence had again prevented lawmakers from examining what Yotova knew when she pardoned convicted drug traffickers.
Vassilev described the second case, involving a man known as “Dinko the Madman” (Dinko Ludiya), as even more scandalous than the case of the “Petrich Escobar .”
“If the claims made by his ex-wife are true, that he continues to sell drugs in Sliven and that the Ministry of Interior is doing absolutely nothing, it means that Ms. Yotova’s actions have, for a second time, released a drug dealer who, following his pardon, has been able to continue distributing drugs to Bulgarian children and citizens,” Vassilev said.
He challenged Progressive Bulgaria's MPs to explain whose interests they were serving, reminding them that all members of Parliament had sworn to act solely in the interests of the Bulgarian people.
Vassilev asked whether they would accept drug dealers selling drugs to their own children and grandchildren, or to the families of voters who had elected them. He also questioned whether lawmakers considered it acceptable to skip parliamentary work to keep information from the public and continue supporting a presidential candidate whom he accused of showing compassion for drug dealers rather than concern for Bulgarian children and citizens.
Vassilev announced that the National Assembly would hold another session on the matter next Wednesday.

Among the main events are music workshops organized by the “Quanto Basta” association of Bologna with students from four elementary schools in Belgrade, the exhibition “The Image of Italy Through Design” in Novi Sad, creative writing workshops with author Antonio Cucciniello in Subotica, Kragujevac, and Belgrade; the play “Alice Anfitrua” by students from the Third High School in Belgrade; and initiatives dedicated to linguistic and musical creativity organized by the “Piazza Italia” Italian Cultural Center in Subotica, including a special project focused on the figure of Dante Alighieri. Finally, worth noting in Belgrade on October 23 was a roundtable discussion titled “Eco and the Brilliant Language: Words, Signs, Worlds,” dedicated to the intellectual and linguistic legacy of Umberto Eco.
                                    
The celebrations coincide with the events of the 69th Belgrade International Book Fair, scheduled for October 23–31, during which the Italian Cultural Institute’s booth will host numerous events dedicated to Italian literature, featuring authors such as Antonio Cucciniello, Diego Marani, Stefano Redaelli, Snežana Milinković, Mila Mihajlović, Luigi Guarnieri, and Melania Mazzucco.
                                    
“Through the events linked to the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, we aim to reaffirm that the Italian language is one of the most precious assets of our identity and an extraordinary tool for creativity,” stated Luca Gori, the Italian Ambassador to Serbia. “In Serbia,” he added, “thanks to the commitment of the Italian Cultural Institute, the teachers, the passion of the students, and collaboration with local institutions, the Italian language continues to be an important tool for dialogue and friendship between our two countries.”

Iran unveils advanced quantum labs. at 3 academic centers

20:01:35 KST

The facilities were inaugurated on October 14, 17, and 20, respectively, in ceremonies attended by Hossein Afshin, Iran’s vice president for science, technology, and knowledge-based economy.
Quantum technologies are considered a strategic field of science and technology worldwide. Their development depends not only on advances in fundamental research but also on the training of specialized personnel and access to advanced laboratory facilities.
Specialized quantum training laboratories enable students and researchers to connect theoretical knowledge with practical experience by directly observing, measuring, and examining quantum phenomena.
The three new facilities are intended to expand students’ opportunities for hands-on training, increase their access to specialized equipment, and strengthen universities’ capacity to train the workforce needed to advance quantum research and technology.
A key feature of the laboratories is the opportunity to conduct advanced experiments directly rather than relying solely on theoretical instruction or computer simulations. Students can work with laboratory equipment, measure quantum phenomena, and examine and analyze the results, Press TV reported.
The experiments available at the facilities include the generation and detection of single photons and photon pairs, the study of quantum entanglement, tests of Bell inequalities, and two-photon interference.

====================================================================================================

One in three teen boys follows Andrew Tate at least a little, and those who do hold more rigid views of manhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

Teenage boys who follow prominent online personalities associated with the “manosphere” are more likely to support traditional beliefs about manhood, such as the idea that men should hide their emotions, remain dominant, and reject anything considered feminine. For the two best-known figures, Andrew Tate and Jordan Peterson, this pattern held even after accounting for the gender messages boys hear at home and how masculine they already perceive themselves to be, according to research published in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.
The term “manosphere” describes a loose network of websites, podcasts, and social media accounts focused on male interests, often while framing women or modern feminism as threats to men’s status. Content creators in this digital space, frequently referred to as “manfluencers,” often promote hegemonic masculinity. This concept refers to a culturally idealized form of manhood characterized by power, physical toughness, emotional detachment, and the subordination of femininity.
Earlier research had begun tracking the reach of these online ideas. For instance, a 2024 study that included focus groups with 13- and 14-year-old boys in London found that some were drawn to Andrew Tate, who paired anti-feminist commentary with advice about dating and making money, and some saw him as funny or authentic. Around the same time, a 2024 study of young men in Sweden found that those who followed more manfluencers were more likely to hold dehumanizing views of women. A 2025 Common Sense Media report, which was not peer reviewed, found that boys who saw more masculinity-focused content online tended to hold more traditional views, but it did not ask about specific figures or parental messages.
Despite these insights, little quantitative evidence existed about what leads younger adolescent boys to engage with these figures in the first place, or how this media consumption interacts with the guidance they receive from their families. The new research was led by Erica Scharrer, a professor of communication at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and author of Children, Media, and Technology: Access, Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion and co-author of Quantitative Research Methods in Communication: The Power of Numbers for Social Justice. She worked with University of Michigan psychologists L. Monique Ward and Brenda L. Volling to understand the real-world dynamics driving boys toward these online figures.
“Andrew Tate and ‘the manosphere’ had been in the headlines for quite a while,” Scharrer told PsyPost. “I noticed that even though some of the concern expressed in news and popular discourse was about the potential of the manosphere or ‘manfluencers’ to influence adolescent boys, there were no quantitative studies on the topic.”
“I approached L. Monique Ward–who is one of the premier scholars of adolescents, masculinities, and media–to see if she wanted to study the phenomenon with me, and she introduced me to another stellar scholar, Brenda L. Volling, who has deep expertise in gendered dynamics in family contexts,” Scharrer explained. “Together, our team designed and carried out this study. While we were writing our paper (but well after we collected our data), the Netflix show, Adolescence, put the issue of the manosphere and adolescent boys further into the spotlight.”
The 2025 Netflix drama depicts a teenage boy, immersed in manosphere content, who is accused of murdering a female classmate. To explore how real-world adolescents interact with these online communities, the scientists surveyed a diverse group of 601 adolescent boys aged 13 to 17 living across the United States. Participants were recruited through online panels managed by Qualtrics, with parent consent and youth assent obtained before the teens completed the questions privately on their own mobile devices. The sample was balanced across different age groups, racial backgrounds, and geographic regions to roughly match national population proportions.
To measure engagement with the manosphere, the authors took two distinct approaches. First, they directly asked boys how often they followed two prominent online commentators: former kickboxer Andrew Tate, who has been banned from several social media platforms for hate speech, and clinical psychologist Jordan Peterson. Second, the authors asked participants to write in their favorite celebrity and top three favorite social media stars, later cross-referencing those names against a list of 31 manosphere-linked figures the researchers compiled from news and scholarly sources.
The boys also completed established psychological questionnaires. These included scales assessing traditional masculinity beliefs, which measure the degree to which an individual believes men should avoid showing vulnerability, remain emotionally detached, use physical toughness, and avoid feminine behaviors. Participants also reported the kinds of gender lessons they received from their caregivers, answered how masculine they perceived themselves to be on a 1-to-5 scale, and completed assessments of social support, depressive symptoms, and hostility.
The survey revealed that about 33.2 percent of the boys reported following Andrew Tate at least a little, while 11.6 percent reported following Jordan Peterson. In contrast, when asked open-ended questions about their absolute favorite personalities, only about 9 percent wrote in a figure associated with the manosphere, most commonly naming mainstream creators, musicians, or athletes instead. The authors described it as encouraging that only a small share of participants named a manosphere figure among their favorites.
Boys who expressed an affinity for manosphere personalities reported receiving more messages from their parents encouraging traditional gender expectations and physical toughness. They also rated their own personal masculinity higher compared to their peers. However, they were not statistically different in terms of age, racial background, total weekly time spent watching YouTube, or reported feelings of hostility, depression, or perceived support from family and friends. The authors note that this runs counter to the idea that isolated or distressed boys are the ones who turn to the manosphere.
Before any statistical controls, all three measures of manosphere engagement were linked to stronger traditional masculinity beliefs on every scale. For example, boys who named a manosphere figure as a favorite averaged 4.12 on a 7-point measure of traditional masculinity beliefs, compared with 3.39 for other boys.
When running statistical models that controlled for age, self-perceived masculinity, and parental messages, the authors found that following Andrew Tate remained a positive predictor across every measure of traditional masculinity ideology. Following Jordan Peterson also predicted higher support for male toughness, dominance, and relationship-specific masculinity norms, though it did not predict anti-femininity beliefs. The authors suggest this may reflect Peterson’s emphasis on self-improvement rather than overtly anti-women messaging. Having an affinity for manosphere figures on the open-ended list predicted beliefs favoring physical toughness, but was not related to emotional detachment or anti-femininity after accounting for the other variables.
Parental messages about being big and tough were the strongest predictor in every model, carrying roughly two to three times the weight of following Tate, and following Peterson was a weaker predictor than following Tate. Younger boys also tended to hold more traditional beliefs than older boys. Taken together, the predictors in these models explained roughly 37 to 44 percent of the variation in the boys’ overall traditional masculinity scores.
“Our study cannot show causality, but our data do show that in our sample of teen boys, following manosphere influencers online goes hand in hand with having narrow, stereotypical conceptions of masculinity,” Scharrer noted.
The findings echo that Swedish study, which PsyPost covered in 2025, although it measured misogyny and dehumanization of women among young adult men rather than traditional masculinity beliefs among American teenage boys.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relies on survey responses gathered at a single point in time, meaning the scientists cannot determine whether watching these creators causes boys to adopt traditional beliefs, or if boys who already favor traditional roles simply seek out compatible media. It is plausible that both processes occur together, reinforcing one another over time.
Additionally, the authors noted that endorsing masculine traits like emotional stoicism and strength is not the same as expressing outright hostility toward women, an outcome this particular project did not directly evaluate. The researchers also pointed out that online creators within the manosphere vary widely in tone and focus, ranging from financial self-help to overt anti-feminism, meaning adolescent viewers may be reacting to very different messages depending on whom they watch. The survey also recorded whether boys followed these figures but not why, so some may have been watching out of curiosity or skepticism rather than agreement, and the 33 percent figure includes boys who said they followed Tate only “a little.”
Recruiting participants through online survey panels can also introduce selection biases, as families who join these panels may not reflect the entire adolescent population. Looking ahead, the authors recommend long-term studies that track the same boys over time, incorporate direct measures of misogynistic attitudes, and explore the specific reasons why teens choose to follow these online figures.
The study, “Following Manosphere Influencers and Endorsement of Traditional Masculinity Beliefs Among Adolescent Boys,” was authored by Erica Scharrer, L. Monique Ward, and Brenda L. Volling.

Samarkand summit calls for greater investment in children’s well-being
SAMARKAND, Uzbekistan - Hundreds of policymakers, international officials and child welfare advocates gathered in the historic Uzbek city of Samarkand on Wednesday for a global summit aimed at making children’s health, education and protection a greater priority for governments.
The two-day World Summit on Investing in Children’s Well-being brought together more than 600 participants from over 100 countries, including senior United Nations officials, government representatives, first ladies and experts in children’s rights and development.
The meeting comes at a time when many countries are struggling to tackle child poverty, improve access to healthcare and education, and protect millions of children from violence, exploitation, malnutrition and social exclusion.
A key message running through the discussions was that investing in children is not only a social responsibility but also an investment in the future. Without proper healthcare, education and protection, children face greater risks of long-term hardship, with consequences that can affect entire communities and national economies.
The opening ceremony featured a message from Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, whose government has introduced reforms aimed at expanding social services and providing greater support for vulnerable families.
Uzbekistan’s First Lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva also addressed the gathering, alongside senior UN officials and representatives of participating countries.
Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman, who is also serving as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, was among the prominent speakers.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres sent a message that was delivered by the organization’s resident coordinator in Uzbekistan, while Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed addressed the summit through a video message.
Najat Maalla M’jid, the UN special representative on violence against children, also spoke at the opening, stressing the need to protect children from abuse, exploitation and neglect.
Several first ladies took part in the high-level discussions, including Emine Erdoğan of Türkiye, Aigul Japarova of Kyrgyzstan, Tamara Vučić of Serbia, Nehmat Aoun of Lebanon and Auxillia Mnangagwa of Zimbabwe.
Their presence highlighted the international attention being given to children’s welfare. But the main challenge remains turning political statements into practical measures that improve the lives of children and their families.
Participants also discussed the needs of children with disabilities, those without adequate family support and those whose education and development are affected by poverty, discrimination or social exclusion.
A separate international congress on childhood cancer is being held alongside the summit, drawing attention to the wide gap in access to diagnosis and treatment around the world.
According to the World Health Organization, about 400,000 children and adolescents develop cancer each year.
Survival rates vary considerably between countries. More than 80% of children with cancer survive in high-income countries, while the rate remains below 30% in many low- and middle-income countries.
This gap reflects differences in access to early diagnosis, essential medicines, specialized treatment and long-term medical care.
For many families, a child’s chances of survival depend not only on the type of cancer but also on where they live and whether they can afford and access the treatment they need.
Improving outcomes requires investment in hospitals, trained medical staff, reliable supplies of medicines and healthcare systems that allow children to receive treatment without placing an overwhelming financial burden on their families.
The childhood cancer congress brings these inequalities into the broader discussion on children’s well-being, underlining the need to ensure that every child has access to quality healthcare, regardless of their family’s financial circumstances or country of residence.
Mental health, childhood obesity and preventable illnesses are also among the issues being discussed in Samarkand.
For millions of children facing poverty, illness, inadequate education or a lack of protection, the significance of the Samarkand summit will ultimately depend not on the number of countries represented, but on whether the commitments made here lead to meaningful changes in their everyday lives.

Building digital resilience: Qatar, Iraq and the new Gulf–Europe fibre corridor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:00:08 UTC
20:00:08 KST

Qatar’s Ooredoo is working to establish a new data route from the Persian Gulf to Turkiye and Europe through Iraq. On 7th October 2026, its international connectivity arm, OFN, signed an agreement with Iraq’s iQ Networks to acquire several pairs of dark fibre across the country. The route is intended to connect with Ooredoo’s planned Fibre in Gulf (FIG) subsea cable system.
The agreement is part of Ooredoo’s wider commitment of more than $500 million to international cable and connectivity projects. That figure covers the broader programme; it is not the stated cost of the Iraq agreement alone.
FIG is planned as a subsea loop connecting Qatar, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq. Ooredoo says it will have a design capacity of up to 720 terabits per second across 24 fibre pairs, making it the largest subsea cable system planned for the Gulf Cooperation Council. Data landing in southern Iraq would travel north over iQ Networks’ fibre infrastructure, toward the Turkish border near Rabia, and then onward to Turkiye and Europe. The plan still requires regulatory and other approvals.
The deal involves dark fibre: installed cables that have not yet been equipped to transmit data. Customers add and manage their own transmission equipment, giving them flexibility to expand capacity and configure the network to their needs. That can appeal to cloud and data-centre operators, telecom companies and other large users of bandwidth. Ooredoo and iQ Networks are targeting demand from cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data centres.
A new route, and a more resilient network
The project’s main strategic value is the additional route it could offer between the Gulf and Europe.
Much of the world’s digital traffic travels through subsea cables, and dependence on a limited number of routes leaves networks exposed to accidents, technical failures and geopolitical disruption.
A land route through Iraq could give operators another way to carry data between the Gulf, Turkiye and Europe.
That would add flexibility, but it would not remove risk. Traffic entering or leaving the Gulf would still depend on the FIG cable and its landing points. The route would also rely on working connections across Iraq, Turkiye and Europe. Its value lies in giving operators another option when a particular link is disrupted.
Recent threats to regional digital infrastructure have brought these vulnerabilities into sharper focus. Al Jazeera has reported on concerns about possible attacks on Gulf data centres and internet infrastructure.
Such warnings reinforce the case for alternative routes, while making clear that cables and related facilities may themselves become targets.
For Ooredoo, the agreement is part of a broader effort to expand its international connectivity business. For customers, the route could provide additional capacity and a backup path for data. Whether companies use it at scale will depend on its cost, speed and reliability, as well as how easily it connects with networks in Turkiye and Europe.
READ: Iraq seeks to host talks between Iran and Gulf States in Baghdad
Iraq’s chance to become a digital bridge
Iraq sits between the Gulf, the Levant and Turkiye, giving it a natural advantage as a potential land route for data. The agreement links the planned subsea cable in the south with terrestrial fibre running north through the country. iQ Networks brings existing fibre assets and data-centre capabilities to the project. Its infrastructure includes networks developed through initiatives such as the Silk Route Transit Project.
Iraqi officials see the corridor as a way to attract international operators and earn revenue from data transit. Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad has said Iraq was chosen over alternative routes because it is shorter and offers competitive government pricing. He has also said that some connected segments could be completed within months once the necessary links are in place. Those are the government’s projections; the route’s commercial value will depend on whether the infrastructure is delivered on time and performs as promised.
If the corridor proves reliable, it could bring investment in fibre networks, data centres and related services, while helping Iraq develop its digital economy. But its location alone will not make Iraq a regional digital hub. Operators need dependable service, competitive prices and smooth connections with neighbouring networks. They also need confidence that data can cross the country without lengthy interruptions.
What could hold the project back
The October agreement is a significant step, but it does not mean the complete route is already operational. Regulatory and government approvals are still needed, and the project requires coordination among OFN, iQ Networks, the state-owned Iraqi Telecommunications and Post Company, and relevant authorities.
The full path from the cable landing in southern Iraq to the Turkish border and beyond must be connected, tested and integrated. Public announcements have not yet set out a ready-for-service date or all the operational arrangements.
Security will matter throughout. Long-distance fibre can be damaged accidentally or targeted, and disruption to a single section can affect service across the route. Keeping the network available will require monitoring, fast repairs and close coordination among the companies responsible for different sections. Regional conflict could also threaten the subsea cable, landing stations or neighbouring networks. Adding a route reduces dependence on existing links; it cannot protect the entire system from attack or failure.
The route will also have to prove its technical and commercial value. Customers will compare its speed, reliability and price with other options. Dark fibre gives them flexibility over the equipment they use, but dependable service still depends on the quality and maintenance of the underlying network and its connections. Other regional routes will compete for the same customers.
The OFN–iQ Networks agreement is best understood as a building block for a Gulf–Europe data corridor. Ooredoo’s wider investment programme gives the effort scale, and Iraq could provide a useful land route between the Gulf and Turkiye. Turning that promise into a dependable commercial service will require approvals, secure infrastructure, working cross-border connections and customers willing to use the route. If those pieces come together, the project could give operators more options for carrying data and help Iraq establish itself as an international transit point.
