Stratford International on track to get cross-Channel trains in budget boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:57:12 UTC
19:57:12 KST

Stratford International train station in east London will receive funding in next week’s budget, according to reports, putting it on track to live up to its name and become a hub for cross-Channel services.
London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has been making a case to ministers for funding to upgrade the station to allow it to start running international rail services.
Until now only domestic routes running to and from central London and Kent have stopped at the station, although Eurostar services pass through on the way to and from St Pancras.
Khan said: “We’ve been working closely with the government to make Stratford International truly ‘international’ for the first time – opening up new opportunities for jobs, investment and tourism, while connecting one of the UK’s fastest-growing economic centres directly to Europe.
“It’s time to unlock the full potential of this station and help write the next chapter in Stratford’s remarkable success story.”
Khan recently argued that growth in international rail travel and environmental concerns meant it would be better to improve Stratford International than expand Heathrow airport by building a third runway.
Stratford International would require a significant upgrade from its current two platforms to allow it to welcome international services, including adding a border post and security checks as well as a check-in zone, waiting area and facilities for passengers.
The work opening up the station and the mothballed international section of the station, including platforms and a waiting area, would cost an estimated £20m, according to the Standard. It reported Khan’s plan was for one in three trains to and from France to stop at the station, while it could also become a hub for rail services from the continent to the Midlands and the north of England.
The station, located close to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, opened in late 2009 and was originally designed and built with the intention of handling Eurostar trains, but this was not fully developed.
The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly planning to greenlight the mayor’s proposal to create a business rate retention zone, according to the Financial Times, to help fund the station’s redevelopment. Such zones allow local authorities to keep all of the businesses rates growth collected in their area – rather than half of the rates collected, as is standard – to fund local regeneration directly.
In recent months, Virgin and other rail companies have been in talks with City Hall about operating future international rail services from Stratford.
Virgin is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, bringing direct competition to Eurostar on the cross-Channel route for the first time since the opening of the tunnel. The operator has been granted access by the rail regulator to the track and to Eurostar’s nearby Temple Mills depot.
A spokesperson for the Virgin Group said the operator was “looking forward to exploring additional stops, including Stratford International”. They added that the company had been “actively engaging with stakeholders to explore future expansion” beyond its initial launch plans.
Gemini Trains, chaired by the Labour peer Tony Berkeley, is hoping to run trains to France, Belgium and Germany and has said it wanted to use Stratford as its London hub. However, it has not yet been granted depot and track access.

First diesel shipment to US and timeline for restoring export volumes: statements by Novak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:56:49 UTC
19:56:49 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 21. /TASS/. The first tanker loaded with 40,000 tons of Russian diesel fuel is set to leave the port on October 22, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
Russia could fully restore its diesel export volumes by the end of this year, which would make supplies available not only to the US, but also to other countries, he added.
TASS has gathered the main statements by Novak.
Diesel for US
The first tanker carrying Russian diesel fuel will leave for the United States on Thursday, October 22: "The first tanker is scheduled to leave the port tomorrow, on [October] 22, for the United States."
The tanker can carry 40,000 tons.
"Further shipments will follow, of course. As agreed upon by the two leaders, we will satisfy the needs of the United States to the extent of our capabilities."
The contract-signing process between Russia and the US on diesel supplies is "nearing completion."
Export
Russia could fully restore its diesel export volumes by the end of this year: "I would like to emphasize that we are not fully restoring exports at this stage, but operating within the limits of our refineries’ capabilities. Therefore, if we can only return to full [export] volumes by the end of the year according to the schedule, other countries will also receive the volumes they were getting previously at that point."
Other countries, not only the US, will also be able to receive Russian diesel toward year-end: "It will depend on the volumes we can supply beyond the needs of the United States. I think other countries will also receive diesel."
Supplies to other countries will depend on Russia’s plant capacity: "Therefore, if we can only reach full volumes by the end of the year in line with the schedule, other countries will also get the volumes they previously received."
Nord Stream pipelines
The damaged lines of the Nord Stream gas pipeline system can technically be repaired: "Three lines, as previously stated, can technically be repaired, should there be a need, justification, or necessity."
Supplies through the intact pipeline could resume shortly: "One of the four lines is in working order. If European consumers, or European countries and politicians, wish, gas could certainly be supplied via this line. It depends on the Europeans, primarily Germany, as the pipeline runs to Germany."
Power of Baikal
Russian and Chinese companies may reach commercial agreements on the Power of Baikal gas pipeline by the end of 2026: "We are waiting for our companies to conduct commercial negotiations. We hope that they will reach relevant agreements by the end of the year."
The Power of Siberia 2 pipeline has been renamed Power of Baikal "to distinguish between the names of Power of Siberia and Power of Baikal": "It is probably important to highlight the region through which the route will pass as well. The route will run along the southern shore of Lake Baikal."

The lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the mandate would be sent to parliament once a bill ratifying the accord has been approved.

The AKP lawmaker said that no Turkish troops deployed to other countries under the pact would take part in offensive operations, adding that technical personnel and experts would be sent initially to help with air defences, electronic warfare technologies, and other defensive support.

Turkey, which has condemned the Houthi attacks, has also agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. REUTERS

Digital financial services are also growing, with gross transaction value expected to reach 1.65 trillion dollars, up 16 percent, while digital lending balances are projected to rise 22 percent to 116 billion dollars.
Singapore's digital economy GMV is forecast to grow 8 percent to 31 billion dollars in 2026, with the country strengthening its position as a regional AI hub. Its digital economy is projected to reach 59 billion dollars by 2035.
Singapore's growth is "strongly supported by AI-driven semiconductor demand and innovations in digital mobility, such as autonomous shuttles and licensed cross-border ride-hailing," said the report. ■

Africa CDC urges greater global solidarity to contain Ebola as Nigeria confirms 1st case
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:56:02 CST
19:56:02 KST

A medical worker checks an infected patient at an Ebola treatment center in Bunia, capital of Ituri Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), on Oct. 18, 2026. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for greater global solidarity and international support to contain the rapidly expanding Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak. (Xinhua)
ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for greater global solidarity and international support to contain the rapidly expanding Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak.
The urgent call came as the Nigerian government on Tuesday confirmed the first Ebola case in the country's capital, Abuja, following laboratory tests. According to Ali Pate, coordinating minister of health and social welfare, a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda is now in isolation and receiving medical care, amid efforts to prevent community transmission of the hemorrhagic fever.
The West African nation became the fourth on the continent to record a confirmed case, as the deadly virus has now affected three African countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo in Central Africa, and Uganda and Kenya.
"We cannot allow this outbreak to spread to more countries or continue for another year," warned Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya in a statement issued late Tuesday. He noted that the outbreak has become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history.
He said that the African Union's specialized continental public health agency has already begun mobilizing support for Nigeria, while intensifying its response in the DRC and Kenya, and maintaining heightened vigilance in Uganda.
"Every day of delay costs lives. Africa's health security is global health security. Stopping Ebola in Africa today means protecting the world. Nigeria has our full solidarity. Together, we must defeat this outbreak," Kaseya added.
Noting that the Africa CDC warned of the outbreak's regional dimension and implications when it was declared a public health emergency of continental security in May this year, he stressed that "with mortality approaching 50 percent in DRC, we face an extremely serious threat."
"My appeal to the international community is urgent: act now. We need immediate, flexible financing, medical supplies, diagnostics, trained responders and stronger community-based surveillance," Kaseya said. ■

Power use surges in China's EV charging, data service sectors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:55:54 CST
19:55:54 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Electricity consumption by China's electric vehicle charging and internet data service sectors soared in September, highlighting robust demand from the country's fast-growing new-energy vehicle and digital industries, official data showed on Wednesday.
Power consumption by charging and battery-swapping services reached 16.8 billion kilowatt-hours in September, surging 57 percent year on year, while that of internet data services jumped 35.4 percent to 9.8 billion kilowatt-hours, according to the National Energy Administration.
In September, new energy vehicles (NEVs) accounted for a record 61.6 percent of China's monthly new car sales, marking the third consecutive month above the 60 percent threshold, while the cumulative share for the first three quarters rose to 53.6 percent.
By the end of September, China's smart computing power had reached 2,592 EFLOPS, up 146 percent year on year. EFLOPS refers to a unit measuring computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
China's total electricity consumption for September stood at 899.7 billion kilowatt-hours, an increase of 1.2 percent year on year.
A closer look reveals that electricity consumption by the primary industry stood at 13.5 billion kilowatt-hours in September, up 4.1 percent year on year. Power use by the secondary industry rose 1.7 percent to 580 billion kilowatt-hours, while electricity consumption by the tertiary industry increased 4.9 percent to 185.2 billion kilowatt-hours last month.
Notably, power consumption by high-tech and equipment manufacturing industries climbed 4.6 percent year on year to 116.7 billion kilowatt-hours in September.
Electricity consumption is widely seen as a barometer of economic activity, with shifts in power demand offering clues to changes in industrial structure and growth drivers.
Wednesday's data revealed that while overall power consumption grew at a moderate pace, electricity use in high-tech and equipment manufacturing expanded significantly faster, pointing to the growing role of advanced manufacturing in China's economy.
The sharp increases in power use by EV charging and data services also underscored the emergence of new sources of demand associated with the green and digital transitions.
In the first three quarters of 2026, China's total electricity consumption rose 3.9 percent year on year to 8.07 trillion kilowatt-hours. Electricity use by charging and battery-swapping services surged 55.4 percent in this period, while that of internet data services increased by 41.6 percent.
According to an annual development report on China's electric power industry released by the China Electricity Council in July, total electricity consumption nationwide in 2026 is expected to increase by 5 percent to 6 percent year on year. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government is backing a major heat battery project at Rio Tinto's Yarwun alumina refinery in Gladstone, the state of Queensland, to help industry cut emissions by replacing fossil fuels with electricity.
The demonstration is expected to cut on-site emissions by around 67,000 tonnes a year. Once operational, it will be one of the world's largest industrial heat battery demonstrations, according to a government statement on Wednesday.
"We're backing practical projects that help Australian industry cut emissions and compete in a global market that is increasingly demanding cleaner products," Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen was quoted as saying.
The project will integrate a 360-megawatt-hour thermal energy storage system, known as a heat battery, into the refinery's existing steam system, using cheaper electricity to charge the battery, then release the stored heat to produce high-pressure steam, the statement said.
The project includes an initial 3.6 million Australian dollars (about 2.53 million U.S. dollars) for front-end engineering and design, followed by up to 38 million Australian dollars for construction and commissioning, plus up to 33.3 million Australian dollars in conditional contingency support, it said.
The demonstration, supported by funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency, will help assess the technology's potential for wider use across Australian heavy industry, with lessons shared to support future projects, according to the government. ■

Nuclear safety risk grows: Russian-occupied nuclear plant’s cooling pond keeps sinking, Russia runs short of diesel and staff, Ukraine says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is short of cooling water, diesel, and qualified staff, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) said on 20 October, warning of rising risks to nuclear safety. The water level in the plant’s cooling pond fell to 12.27 meters on 12 October, down from 12.86 meters in July, while the plant needs at least 15 meters to fully meet its needs, according to HUR. Russian managers are also considering cutting the number of backup generators kept on automatic standby, which would inevitably raise the risk of emergencies, the intelligence agency said.
Europe’s largest nuclear plant has been under Russian control since March 2022. Its six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, but they and their spent fuel still need constant cooling, which depends on water, on a single remaining external power line, and on diesel generators as the last resort. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned on 16 October that depleted diesel reserves increase the risk that nuclear safety is challenged if the plant loses power again, and that the situation may become acute in winter.
A pond with no source to refill it
The cooling pond has been sinking since Russia destroyed the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, cutting off the reservoir that fed it. Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear operator, recorded 15.70 meters in October 2023. By June 2025, the level had fallen below 14 meters against a norm of above 16, Oleh Korikov, head of Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate, said.
HUR’s figures show the decline continuing this year, from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 in early August, 12.55 at the end of August, and 12.34 at the start of October. In 2025, the IAEA said groundwater wells on site were supplying cooling water for the safety systems. Its team had not been allowed to inspect a new dam in the cooling channel, access IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called essential to assess the cooling water situation.
Diesel for a blackout that Russia cannot supply
If the plant loses external power, its diesel generators would burn about 150 metric tons of fuel a day in a prolonged blackout, HUR said. The occupation administration cannot deliver enough, so reserves stay minimal. Russian managers are also looking for covert fuel supplies, including low-quality fuel, without informing the IAEA mission, according to HUR.
The IAEA has already reported fewer generators on automatic standby. Since late September, only four of the plant’s 20 emergency generators would start automatically in a blackout, with the rest needing manual connection, which Grossi said deviates from normal practice. No diesel deliveries have reached the plant since March, the agency said on 16 October.
The plant spent nearly three weeks on generators after losing its last external line on 20 August, EP reported, until the Ferosplavna-1 line was restored under an IAEA-brokered ceasefire. The main 750 kV Dniprovska line remains out. HUR said the Kremlin rejected Ukraine’s proposal to supply power through it, which raises the nuclear safety risks.
Russia blacked out Europe’s largest nuclear plant 15 times since occupying it in 2022
A plant short of the people who know it
About 5,000 people now work at the plant, against roughly 11,000 before the full-scale invasion, and only 1,450 were on site, HUR said. The plant lacks specialists who know its equipment, as well as the experts needed for repairs and for reconnecting it to external power. Russian managers plan training courses for applicants from Russian regions to replace Ukrainian staff, according to HUR.
In Enerhodar, the city where the plant’s staff live, mobile, internet, electricity, and water supplies keep failing, HUR said.

Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava seeks new ways to reach the public
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:53:02 UTC
19:53:02 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
News
Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava seeks new ways to reach the public
An interview with Denica Sekoulitchka-Ruseva, Director of the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava
Wednesday 21 October 2026 12:31
Wednesday, 21 October 2026, 12:31
Bratislava’s Old Town square
PHOTO BNR
Font size
Being recognised within your own community is one thing, but reaching the wider public in the country where you promote Bulgarian culture is an entirely different challenge. This is the goal behind the new approach of the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava.
Since May 15 this year, the institute has been headed by Denica Sekoulitchka-Ruseva, who, after ten years leading the Bulgarian Cultural Union in Slovakia, sees her new role as a natural continuation of her previous work, but also as a greater responsibility.
In an interview with Radio Bulgaria, conducted during celebrations marking 100 years of Bulgarian Studies at Comenius University in Bratislava, Denica Sekoulitchka said her main goal is to expand the presence of Bulgarian culture in the Slovak capital.
Denica Sekoulitchka in front of one of the exhibitions marking 100 years of Bulgarian Studies in Slovakia
PHOTO BNR
''My vision was to turn the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava into a vibrant place-not just a space where we open an exhibition and close it a month later, but a place that draws people in, where everyone can find their own kind of art'', the director explains.
One of the key priorities of the new director of the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava is to reach a wider local audience.That is why she aims to take a significant part of the institute’s programme beyond its own walls, through partnerships with Slovak cultural organisations and participation in major city events.
''My priority is to be where the public is, rather than simply expecting people to come to us. I plan to make the institute part of the city’s major festivals. One example is the large carnival held as part of the Bratislava Cultural Summer festival. We have never participated in it before, but we aim to change that next year. I also want the institute to play an active role in the city’s Christmas programme.''
The Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava also relies on close cooperation with the Embassy of the Republic of Bulgaria in Slovakia to bring its future plans to fruition. The new ambassador, Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova, who also has professional ties to the cultural sector, is a natural partner for the institute in implementing larger-scale initiatives, says Denica Sekoulitchka.
The institute’s busy schedule over the past six months suggests that this strategy is working. “Bulgarian cultural events are held in Bratislava two or three times a week”, the institute’s director says.
Denica Sekoulitchka and Ambassador Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova
PHOTO facebook.com/BKISBA
We ask what Slovaks associate Bulgaria with and how their perception of the country could be broadened.
“Slovaks really like Bulgaria and our Black Sea coast. They know about the Bulgarian gardeners who were among the first to settle in these lands. They are already familiar with much of Bulgarian culture, but I hope we can reach further into their cultural space. I believe we can achieve this through partnerships with local cultural institutions and venues, as well as joint events involving Slovakia and Bulgaria.
For me, it is extremely important not to focus solely on tradition and history, but to show that Bulgaria is a modern European country with achievements in contemporary art, performance art and other fields—areas that have rarely featured in the institute’s programme until now.”
The Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava
PHOTO BNR
In November, the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava marks the 55th anniversary of its founding. The anniversary is an opportunity not only to reflect on the past but also to look ahead to the future. According to Denica Sekoulitchka, the institute’s history reflects both the changes within the Bulgarian community in Slovakia and the development of Bulgaria’s cultural presence in the country.
“I want the anniversary to be a reflection on the past, while also considering what the institute’s vision for the future should be”, Denica Sekoulitchka says in conclusion.

Two Taiwan CubeSats launch aboard SpaceX mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:52:49 UTC
19:52:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Hsinchu-based Taiwan Space Agency announced Wednesday that two satellites from its Start-up Starchasing program had launched into space, according to a press release.
TASA said the program’s third batch included T.MicroSat-3 and T.MicroSat-4, two CubeSats developed by Tron Future. They launched aboard SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 mission at 7:04 p.m. Taiwan time on Oct. 20 and established contact with ground stations in Chile and Azerbaijan before 3 a.m. Wednesday.
The mission will test beam hopping, inter-satellite links, and end-to-end satellite transmission to validate low Earth orbit broadband communications and coordination between satellites.
The program launches groups of satellites to test technologies in stages, allowing domestic manufacturers to refine designs and expand testing. Operating multiple satellites also allows companies to test communication and data transmission between them, TASA said.
Tron Future’s earlier T.MicroSat-1 and T.MicroSat-2 satellites have completed basic function and payload tests. The company completed initial in-orbit operations for T.MicroSat-2 within a week.
T.MicroSat-3 and T.MicroSat-4 will test coordination between satellites. Beam hopping allows flexible adjustments to when and where communications capacity is provided, while inter-satellite links enable satellites to communicate and exchange data.
These links allow data transmission between satellites in space, complementing connections with ground stations. Together, beam hopping and inter-satellite communications could make low Earth orbit networks more flexible, TASA said.
CubeSats’ smaller size, shorter development time, and lower costs attracted Tron Future to the field, the agency said. The program encourages domestic participation in satellite manufacturing and orbital operations, with repeated launch tests supporting the development of commercial products and services.
Other participating companies have launches planned for early 2027, including two satellites each from Rapidtek’s Black Kite and Pyras Technology’s Toro series. These will test satellite Internet of Things services, ocean remote sensing, and other applications, TASA said.

19:52:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Micron Taiwan and its Taichung union said Wednesday they have signed a labor-management agreement and will both withdraw from the mediation session scheduled for Thursday.
The terms of the deal were not disclosed. In a joint statement, the two sides said they would brief team members on the details in the coming days.
Micron said it had engaged in “constructive dialogue” with the union in good faith and hoped other ongoing labor matters could be resolved “in the same spirit of mutual support and cooperation.”
The company employs about 15,000 people in Taichung and Taoyuan. Unions representing workers in both cities have demanded a permanent profit-sharing plan that would allocate 15% of Micron’s profits to quarterly bonuses.
The agreement came a day before the Taoyuan union’s planned one-day strike, which was timed to coincide with the Thursday mediation session.
The Taoyuan union said it remains open to talks and urged the company to present a reasonable plan. The union did not respond to a request for comment on whether the strike will go ahead given Micron’s agreement with the Taichung union.

EU probes Booking.com over online fraud risks
- The EU opened its first Digital Services Act probe into Booking.com over fake listings, phishing scams and weak protection of user data.
- Brussels said the firm may have failed to label paid ads clearly and may have underestimated fraud linked to unlicensed or non-existent accommodation.
- Booking.com said it is “cooperating fully”, while the EU warned it could face fines of up to 6% of global turnover for serious breaches.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - The European Union opened an investigation into online travel agent Booking.com on Oct 21 over alleged failures to tackle fake listings and phishing scams.
The EU fears Booking.com has underestimated the impact of fraud and unlicensed accommodation, and is not sufficiently protecting users’ data from being misused for scams.
The probe is the first into Booking.com under the Digital Services Act (DSA), a mammoth online content law that covers a wide array of platforms including social media and digital marketplaces.
“Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
The EU said it was also looking into whether the Netherlands-based firm breached rules “because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users”.
The DSA “sets clear responsibilities” and “we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously”, Virkkunen added.
Booking.com said that it was “cooperating fully” and that “security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities”.
“We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners,” it added.
Booking.com is among over 20 very large online platforms that must comply with the DSA’s stricter rules or risk fines that could go as high as 6% of their global turnover, or even a ban for serious and repeated breaches.
There is no legal deadline for the completion of the probe but the targeted company can offer commitments to address the European Commission’s concerns.
Suspicions over data
A senior EU official was critical of Booking.com and its risk assessment efforts since 2023.
“We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” the official said on condition of anonymity.
The commission – the EU’s digital watchdog – said it would assess whether the online platform “properly identified” risks linked to the spread of illegal content such as non-existent properties and fraudsters portraying themselves as the owner of a property and putting it up for rent.
In some cases, customers discover on arrival that the property they thought they had booked does not exist, or more often, photographs or property descriptions do not accurately reflect reality.
The EU will also investigate whether Booking.com is doing enough to address the risks that phishing scams pose to European consumers.
Phishing is broadly defined as the practice of tricking people into sharing sensitive information through deceptive messages.
The EU said it would look at how reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and whether Booking.com has put in place “sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused”.
“We suspect that Booking is not sufficiently protecting the data of... private users and business users, and (this) makes the system vulnerable for this kind of phishing,” the senior official said.
Meta is also under investigation over potentially fraudulent advertising on its platforms in a probe that began in 2024. AFP

Fair Trade Commission blocks Grab-Foodpanda deal over 4 concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:51:52 UTC
19:51:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Fair Trade Commission blocked Grab's proposed acquisition of Foodpanda on Wednesday over concerns that Uber's investment in Grab could weaken competition in the food delivery market.
CNA reported that three commissioners voted to reject the deal, while one supported approval with conditions and another recused themselves. The commission cited four concerns about competition between Grab and Uber Eats, Uber's food delivery arm.
Foodpanda and Uber Eats currently dominate the domestic food delivery market. Under the proposed deal, Singapore-based Grab would have taken over Foodpanda's operations and become Uber Eats' main competitor.
However, Uber owns about 13.1% of Grab's shares and holds 3.9% of its voting rights. The commission said the financial ties could discourage both companies from competing aggressively, even though Uber cannot directly control Grab's business decisions.
First, the commission said Uber Eats might become less willing to cut prices or offer discounts to attract customers. Such measures could reduce Grab's profits and lower the value of Uber's investment.
Second, Grab might also have less incentive to compete with Uber Eats because of their financial ties. The commission said their shared interests could encourage both companies to avoid actions that might hurt each other's profits.
Third, the commission raised concerns about the companies' history of cooperation, including Grab's 2018 takeover of Uber's Southeast Asian operations. It said their longstanding relationship could make it easier to predict each other's business decisions and reduce competition.
Fourth, the commission said high costs make it difficult for new companies to enter Taiwan's food delivery market. New operators must attract enough restaurants, delivery workers, and customers to compete with established platforms.
The commission said restaurants and consumers also have little power to challenge major delivery platforms. Without stronger competition, the companies could face less pressure to keep prices low or offer discounts.
The commission reviewed proposals to reduce Uber's stake in Grab, restrict shared board memberships, and limit exchanges of sensitive business information. However, it found the measures difficult to enforce and insufficient to protect competition.
The commission concluded that the deal's potential harm to competition outweighed its economic benefits. It rejected the acquisition under Article 13 of the Fair Trade Act.

Iran says Saudi, Houthis have not responded to mediation offer

Breadcrumb
Iran says Saudi Arabia, Houthis have not responded to mediation offer
Iran has yet to receive a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's Houthi rebels to its offer to mediate between the two sides, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday, as the war in Yemen continues to fuel regional tensions.
Speaking to Iraq's Al-Ikhbariya television channel, Araghchi said Tehran remained willing to help bridge differences between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthis, who have launched repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia.
He claimed that the Houthis' failure to respond to Iran's mediation offer demonstrated the group's independence in making its own decisions, despite longstanding accusations that Tehran provides it with military support.
"Ansar Allah certainly has conditions for ending the conflict with the Saudi side, and Saudi Arabia also has its own conditions that Ansar Allah does not accept," Araghchi said, referring to the Houthis by their official name.
"We must provide assistance and cooperation to bring the two sides' positions closer together," he added.
The Iranian foreign minister also accused Saudi Arabia of imposing an economic blockade on Yemen for more than a decade, claiming the Houthis were now using the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait to exert pressure on Riyadh.
"The Yemeni people now believe they have found an opportunity to break this blockade. They have imposed a blockade on the Saudi side using Bab al-Mandeb," he said.
"What does this have to do with us as Iran?" he asked.
Earlier this month, Yemen's internationally recognised government rejected Tehran's mediation offer, accusing Iran of arming, training and providing military and technical expertise to the Houthis.
Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba questioned Iran's credibility as a potential mediator, arguing that its alleged military support for the Houthis undermined its stated commitment to ending the conflict.
Iran says US talks continue despite Hormuz dispute
In the same interview, Araghchi addressed ongoing diplomatic efforts between Tehran and Washington, insisting that negotiations through intermediaries, including Pakistan and Qatar, were continuing.
According to details of the interview carried by Iran's official IRNA news agency, Araghchi said Tehran had previously submitted a proposal known as the "seven-day plan", setting out its conditions for reaching an agreement with the United States.
Under the proposal, the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route for global energy supplies, would be fully reopened on the sixth day.
Araghchi claimed Washington had accepted Iran's initial conditions but subsequently sought to introduce additional provisions.
"The Americans informed us of their agreement to these conditions, but they want to add some other clauses," he said.
He insisted that Washington must first honour the terms of a memorandum of understanding previously signed in Islamabad before negotiations could move on to other outstanding issues.
"After they comply with these provisions, we can enter into negotiations on other files," he said, adding that further disputes could be addressed during the final stages of talks.
The Iranian foreign minister also accused the United States of repeatedly undermining diplomacy through military action.
"We entered into three rounds of negotiations with the American side, and each of the previous three rounds ended with war being declared against us," he said.
"We were in the middle of negotiations, and in the end it became clear to us that the Americans cannot be trusted in negotiations."
Despite his criticism, Araghchi insisted that Tehran remained open to a negotiated settlement, provided Washington respected previous understandings.
"The negotiating table remains open," he said, accusing the United States rather than Iran of obstructing diplomatic progress.
He reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until an agreement or understanding was reached on the conditions for reopening it to shipping.
"We have also said that the American side must accept our conditions for opening the strait to vessels," he said.
"Before such an understanding or agreement is reached, the strait will naturally remain closed, and shipping traffic through it and the existing maritime routes will face difficulties."
Araghchi blamed the disruption in the strategic waterway on US and Israeli military attacks against Iran, warning that the situation would continue unless Washington changed its approach.
The Iranian minister maintained that diplomacy remained the best route to resolving the crisis, but insisted that any agreement must begin with the United States honouring its previous commitments.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

Representatives of Ukraine, NATO and partner countries discussed in Vilnius the modernization of military rehabilitation centers, provision of modern equipment and training of Ukrainian specialists, the NATO Representation in Ukraine said.
A meeting of representatives of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, NATO and partner countries on developing the system of physical and psychological rehabilitation for wounded Ukrainian servicemen under the RENOVATOR project was held in Vilnius on October 14, the representation said. Participants from Ukraine, Lithuania, Britain, Norway, Sweden and Latvia discussed the priority needs of Ukrainian rehabilitation centers, supplying them with modern medical equipment, raising specialists' qualifications and continuity of medical care during the full-scale war.
RENOVATOR is aimed at strengthening the capacity of Ukraine's military rehabilitation system, it said. It provides for modernizing rehabilitation infrastructure, supplying the necessary equipment and professional development of medical workers who help Ukrainian defenders recover from injuries.
"The main measure of our cooperation is not the number of events held but a tangible result for the serviceman. Every wounded defender should receive proper help on time, reach the fullest possible functional recovery and have a clear and understandable further rehabilitation route. RENOVATOR can become a practical basis for this through common standards, capacity development and scaling up proven best practices," Medical Forces Commander Colonel Kostiantyn Humeniuk said.
The team of NATO's Comprehensive Assistance Package for Ukraine (CAP) stressed the importance of coordinating the efforts of Ukraine, Lithuania and other lead countries of the project, the representation said. This cooperation makes it possible to align support with the current needs of Ukrainian troops, develop rehabilitation infrastructure and strengthen the professional capacity of Ukrainian specialists.
CAP team head Iryna Novakova said the aim is to provide infrastructure, equipment and training to strengthen rehabilitation capacity for Ukrainian defenders and for NATO allies.
"We work together, learn and improve, supporting Ukraine and at the same time building our own collective defense capabilities," she said.
RENOVATOR is one of the key projects under the Comprehensive Assistance Package for Ukraine. Its implementation involves coordinating the efforts of NATO, Ukrainian defense institutions and partner countries to create a sustainable rehabilitation system that can meet the needs of Ukrainian defenders both during the war and in the long term. The NATO Representation in Ukraine works with Ukrainian partners at all stages of the project, from identifying needs to delivering equipment. NATO continues

Reform Party leader: 20 seats in parliament enough to be a political player
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:47:00 UTC
19:47:00 KST

Reform Party leader: 20 seats in parliament enough to be a political player
The Reform Party is aiming for 20 seats after the March elections for a strong team with which to defend the liberal worldview, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said.
The Reform Party held a party council meeting over the weekend, setting a goal of winning 20 seats in parliament in next spring's Riigikogu elections. Host Arp Müller noted in his question that 20 seats would not be enough to win an election.
"You can get a strong team into parliament. I remember speaking with Siim Kallas a little while ago and his message was that even when times are difficult, populism is on the rise and the media often criticizes those in power rather indiscriminately, you still have to hold your head high and make sure there is a strong team in the next parliament. And a strong team means that our goal is to win 20 seats, which would give us a foundation to work from, remain a force in Estonian politics and defend what we believe in," Michal replied.
"Because the thing is, Social Democrats are not liberals, conservatives are neither Social Democrats nor liberals and liberals are neither Social Democrats nor conservatives. We are clearly a strong liberal party that stands for individual freedoms, economic freedoms and many other things and you can't get that anywhere else," he added.
'Scope for lowering income tax'
Asked whether the Reform Party plans to cut income tax during the next parliamentary term, Michal said there was scope to do so.
"We have already reduced the tax burden. Last year it was 36.2 percent and next year it will be 35.2 percent, so the tax burden is declining. We have cut income tax and we are cutting it this year. And I think it will be possible to do so in the next term as well, if we review how we do things. We will need to find ways to pay for it because my recommendation is to prioritize several things. First, defense spending must remain at 5 percent. Second, when it comes to the budget, we need to continue what we have been doing — reducing the deficit by half a percentage point a year. That will bring borrowing under control and should eventually start reducing it. At the same time, we can review public services or find other ways for the state to generate revenue, including through new technologies, whether by cutting costs or generating revenue from them. That would also create room to cut income tax," Michal said.
The prime minister declined to specify how large an income tax cut would realistically be possible.
"You'll have to wait a little longer and enjoy the suspense. It will take some time before the election platforms are unveiled, but perhaps I'll talk about it on the next show or the one after that," he said.
'Possibility to cancel next year's fuel excise hike'
Regarding a possible increase in fuel excise duty next May, Michal said it was important to consider developments in the global market more broadly.
"We don't know what fuel excise duties or fuel prices will be next spring. I've said this several times at government press conferences, but we're monitoring the situation quite regularly. At our last couple of Cabinet meetings, we've met with representatives of the Bank of Estonia, the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and the Ministry of Finance. Market participants, including Neste and Alexela, have also attended and shared their assessments of the situation. We're keeping a very close eye on the fuel market," Michal said.
"There are several factors we're monitoring. The first, and the state's main concern and responsibility, is ensuring that reserves are sufficient and security of supply is guaranteed. That means making sure there is enough fuel of every type, which is the responsibility of the Estonian Stockpiling Agency. Based on assurances from the agency's head, Ando Leppiman, I would say that our current reserves are sufficient to see us through," he noted.
"Why is this important? Because if we look at the current risks, the rise in fuel prices originated in the Strait of Hormuz, but now, according to market participants and experts, the bottleneck has shifted to refineries, which are unable to supply enough fuel to the market. We certainly need to ensure that any new disruptions do not lead to shortages of physical fuel supplies. Fortunately, at the moment, there appear to be no such shortages in any fuel category. The second thing we're monitoring is, of course, prices. When it comes to prices, we're looking at the potential risk of losing tax revenue to Latvia, for example. Latvia has repeatedly taken various measures concerning fuel and if we look at average pump prices, we're at virtually the same level. Generally, prices are higher in Latvia on one day, while occasionally it's the other way around and so on. We're fairly evenly matched. But if Latvia takes further steps next year, we'll certainly have to monitor the situation and make decisions about our own fuel excise duty rates accordingly. That's something we're assessing on an ongoing basis," Michal said.
Michal acknowledged that if the government planned to cancel next year's excise duty increase, it would have to take that into account when preparing the budget.
"But we certainly won't make that decision before next year because we don't currently know what fuel prices will be next year. How will the U.S. midterm elections turn out? What will happen next in the Strait of Hormuz? There is an enormous amount of uncertainty. What happens after that? Will fuel supplies recover? Will refineries be able to meet demand? Which direction will things go? We simply don't know yet. So we'll make our decisions accordingly. And I would remind you that this year when it became necessary and we in the government considered it appropriate to cancel the excise duty increases, we made that decision. We can do the same next year," Michal said.
Estonia's Rail Baltica cost sharing component could go up
Michal has previously said that delaying the Rail Baltica construction deadline would make the project cheaper for Estonia.
"When the infrastructure construction market isn't so overheated and overstretched, the cost per unit doesn't rise as much. If you inject a very large amount of money into a single market very quickly, each unit becomes more expensive. That's the first point. Second, from the Estonian state's financial perspective, if you can use more EU funding and other external financing for the project from the next budget period, which you otherwise wouldn't be able to use, you don't have to borrow money on behalf of taxpayers and pay interest on it later. So it's cheaper financially and cheaper in terms of construction costs — cheaper in both respects," Michal said.
However, Estonia's share of the project's costs could rise to 25 percent, with European Union funding covering the remaining 75 percent.
"Yes, the original plan, or the original approach, was an 85-15 split. The idea is that the European Union covers most of Rail Baltica's construction costs. I think the current split for Estonia is probably closer to 80-20, roughly speaking. And the European Commission's new proposal has been to reduce the EU co-financing rate to 75 percent. That would mean a ratio of about 75-25. That's what the debate is about," Michal said.
According to Michal, Estonia would still come out ahead even if it received less funding from the European Union.
"The benefit for us becomes clear when you compare it with completing construction by 2030. During the gap years in EU funding, we would have to contribute more of our own money. That would mean a substantial increase in Estonia's share of the costs, requiring us to borrow money and repay it with interest. On top of that, because we would be pouring so much money into the infrastructure construction market all at once, the cost per unit would also be higher. So spreading construction over a longer period means we can make greater use of EU funds, regardless of whether the co-financing rate is 75 or 80 percent at the time," Michal said.
"Even if it's 75 percent, that still brings money into Estonia's budget in any case," he added.
Passport functionality more important than color
Speaking about the Ministry of the Interior's plan to change the color of Estonian passports back to blue, Michal said he would discuss the matter with Taro on Thursday.
"That's a good question. We can certainly give it plenty of thought. There's a certain nostalgic appeal to blue and we've had blue passports before. But when you travel elsewhere in the world, border guards recognize the burgundy color as indicating an EU passport. In my view, what's far more important than either color is that, regardless of the color of the passport cover, it allows you to pass through all checkpoints electronically as quickly as possible. But to add a little good-natured discussion to the debate, why should it be blue? It might as well be blue, black and white, like the Estonian flag," Michal said.

Britain’s cargo drone becomes a low-cost drone interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:46:59 UTC
19:46:59 KST

- A BAE Systems TRV-150 drone armed with a three-pod APKWS launcher intercepted several attack drones during a Pentagon experiment at Eglin Air Force Base.
- The adapted Malloy T-150 fired laser-guided rockets at multiple targets in one flight without landing to reload.
A heavy-lift cargo drone built by BAE Systems subsidiary Malloy Aeronautics has shot down several one-way attack drones with laser-guided rockets during a Pentagon experiment in Florida, firing one rocket after another without having to land and reload.
The modified aircraft, known as the TRV-150, carried a three-pod launcher loaded with BAE Systems’ APKWS rockets during the Joint Readiness Experimentation exercise run by the Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering at Eglin Air Force Base from Sept. 21 to 25, BAE Systems said in a statement on Oct. 21.
The TRV-150 is a version of Malloy’s T-150 quadcopter, a British-built electric drone designed to carry cargo, which Maryland-based SURVICE Engineering adapted to meet U.S. Army requirements while BAE Systems’ FalconWorks division developed the APKWS kit and integrated it on the aircraft. BAE Systems says the trials show that low-cost precision weapons can be fitted to uncrewed platforms to counter drone threats on the battlefield, and the company now wants to take the same setup to sea to protect ships from similar attacks.
“Our customers are facing drone threats right now, so we’ve worked at pace with our partners to move from concept to a proven system, which can engage multiple targets in a single mission,” said Thomas Lancashire, head of UAS business development at BAE Systems FalconWorks.
APKWS, short for Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, turns an ordinary unguided 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rocket into a precision weapon by fitting a laser-guidance section between the warhead and the motor, which makes it far cheaper than the air-to-air missiles traditionally used to shoot down drones. The rocket has become one of the U.S. military’s main low-cost answers to cheap attack drones, and in May the U.S. Navy awarded L3Harris a contract worth up to $98.4 million for proximity fuzes that make APKWS more effective against drones, while BAE Systems test-fired the rocket from a Royal Air Force Typhoon in March as it adds counter-drone rockets to the fighter.
The Eglin trials build on the first firing of a precision munition from an adapted T-150 in July 2025, when the drone launched a single APKWS rocket, and this time the team used a production-ready three-pod launcher to engage targets in the air. The ability to fire several shots in one sortie matters against attack drones, which often arrive in groups and leave little time for a launcher to land, reload and take off again.
“Supporting the warfighter has been at the core of SURVICE’s mission since its founding over 45 years ago. Bringing the TRV-150 to the US warfighter and now adding APKWS as a proven, precise, and cost-effective capability to our TRV-150 UAS platform is exactly the type of innovation SURVICE was designed to deliver,” said Gregory Thompson, president of SURVICE Engineering.
BAE Systems bought Malloy Aeronautics in 2024, and the T-150 is already in service with British forces as a logistics drone. During the Royal Navy Carrier Strike Group’s eight-month deployment to the Indo-Pacific last year, the drone carried supplies between ships throughout the voyage, and SURVICE is one of several partners BAE Systems is working with around the world to turn the aircraft into a multi-role counter-drone system.
BAE Systems has not said when an armed TRV-150 could enter service, but the company’s next step is to adapt the rocket-armed version for maritime use, where it would help defend ships against the kind of drone attacks that have hit vessels in the Red Sea and the Black Sea.

FAO to strengthen pest management, protect production in Kerman date palm groves
TEHRAN – A delegation from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) has visited date palm groves in Kerman Province to strengthen the management of pests and diseases through technical cooperation, field-based interventions and engagement with national and provincial stakeholders.
From 11 to 14 October, the delegation led by FAO Representative to Iran Farrukh Toirov visited project sites in Jiroft, Anbarabad, Bam and Narmashir to review progress on integrated Pest Management (IPM) in date palm groves.
The mission assessed the application of project-supported interventions, examined the use of equipment provided to pilot sites and engaged with farmers, researchers, plant protection specialists, agricultural authorities and private-sector stakeholders across the date value chain.
The project addresses key threats to date production, including the red palm weevil, palm borers, Dubas bug and Date Palm Fruit Bunch Wilting Disorder. During field visits, the team observed pest management interventions in both modern, large-scale orchards using drip irrigation and traditional orchards employing flood irrigation.
The delegation also examined orchards affected by pest infestations and visited date sorting, packaging and processing facilities serving domestic and export markets.
The mission also provided an opportunity to discuss current pest control practices and explore potential approaches to improving the effectiveness and sustainability of interventions.
Discussions with stakeholders highlighted the red palm weevil as one of the most significant challenges facing date production in the province. Meetings held at the South Kerman Agricultural Jihad Organization and the Bam County Governor’s Office brought together local governors, agricultural authorities, researchers, farmers and private-sector representatives to discuss pest management, production challenges and constraints affecting the date value chain, including the control measures and access to export markets.
The FAO Representative welcomed the strong engagement and shared commitment demonstrated by stakeholders in Kerman, noting that their collaboration provides a favourable foundation for expanding technical cooperation.
Through this project, FAO continues to work with national and provincial counterparts to strengthen technical capacities and promote more effective management of date palm pests and diseases. The project’s field-based approach supports the assessment of practical interventions under local production conditions and helps identify opportunities to protect date palm groves, reduce pest-related losses and strengthen the sustainability of date production in Iran.

Bud Light Boycotters Are Still Waiting for Their ‘Woke-Free’ Beer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

“Go woke, go broke” was a culture war rallying cry of the Biden years, with American conservatives waging battles against any corporate entity that dared to pay lip service to diversity or LGBTQ rights.
But customers of one successful anti-woke alternative brand later found their own wallets a bit lighter—with nothing to show for it.
In April 2023, at the height of a right-wing freakout over a sponsored Instagram post in which transgender actress and singer Dylan Mulvaney showed off a can of Bud Light with her face on it, a Georgia man named Seth Weathers smelled an opportunity to cash in. Conservatives were vowing to ditch the Budweiser brand and take their business elsewhere. (A tearful Kid Rock even filmed himself shooting up a few cases with a semiautomatic rifle.) It was an angry political demographic in need of a new low-ABV lager.
Weathers, a political consultant who briefly served as Georgia state director for Donald Trump’s presidential campaign in 2015 and went on to work with a county commissioner known for racist Facebook posts, swooped in to pitch a replacement beverage. Under his social brand “Conservative Dad,” he marketed a brew called Ultra Right Beer to the MAGA voters making a stink about trans inclusivity.
“America’s been drinking beer from a company that doesn’t even know what restroom to use,” Weathers said in a YouTube ad that included a clip of Mulvaney sipping Bud Light. “That’s why I created Conservative Dad’s Ultra Right 100 percent woke-free beer.” The commercial shows Weathers teeing up a can of Bud Light and walloping it with a baseball bat. “Stop giving money to woke corporations that hate our values,” he said, warning such companies to “stay the fuck away from our kids.”
The concept made a splash in right-wing media, which sent droves of readers and viewers to the Ultra Right Beer website to place orders—even though Weathers had yet to find a brewery to make the stuff. (He was also facing logistical hurdles to shipping the hypothetical beer, a process subject to heavy regulations that vary from one state to the next.) Within two weeks, Weathers had partnered with Big Kettle Brewing in Lawrenceville, Georgia, to produce the beer, and claimed he was closing in on $1 million in sales of six-packs priced at $19.99 apiece.
But while Fox News and similar outlets continued to tout Ultra Right as a stunning victory over Budweiser’s brewer, Anheuser-Busch, deliveries were slow to materialize. Weathers’ company, Ultra Right Beer LLC, would eventually receive an “F” rating from the Better Business Bureau, which notes that it has failed to respond to nearly 200 complaints over missing six-packs and virtually nonexistent customer service. The author of a one-star review of Ultra Right on the BBB website griped that its special edition “Revenge” cans of beer with Trump’s mugshot on them took a year and a half to arrive, while a “Fight”-themed six-pack (styled with the image of Trump raising his fist after surviving an assassination attempt at a July 2024 campaign rally) never arrived at all.
Weathers claimed in August 2024 that sales of the special edition Fight beer had reached the $1 million mark. It’s not clear how many orders of Fight beer ultimately shipped. On eBay, resellers have listed empty six-packs for as much as $115.
Two years later, around 400 people are members of a Facebook group called “People Still Waiting for Ultra Right Fight Beer,” with many claiming that they have received neither the limited-edition beer nor a refund after placing orders in 2024. “I no longer want the beer … just my money back!” reads a recent post on the page.
Enough of these customers have contacted Georgia attorney general Chris Carr to report on Ultra Right Beer LLC that the office has opened an investigation into the company, which has been unresponsive to compliance orders, according to court filings. Ironshield Brewing, the company that operated Big Kettle Brewing as a contract brewer, announced that it was shutting down in December 2023. Weathers did not respond to a request for comment and hasn’t posted to his Facebook or Instagram pages since late last year.
Many of the comments on Weathers’ dormant social media pages are from people demanding refunds or updates on beer orders. In response to a Facebook commenter who wrote that Weathers’ announcement of an Ultra Right restock in November was “plain bullshit” and called him a “thief,” Weathers wrote, “We do not want you as a customer,” adding that he had refunded the person’s order. “I cannot imagine how miserable someone must be to reach your age in life, to spend your time harassing small businesses who have made mistakes but is [sic] out here fighting for the causes you supposedly believe in,” he wrote.
Rich Alan, a police officer in New Jersey who spent more than $60 on two sixers of Fight beer that he says he never got, claims Weathers is a “fraud” and “scammer” who took advantage of Trump supporters. As his Conservative Dad character, Alan says, Weathers was “ stealing the hearts of these patriots and making you think that you're like you're one of them, basically. Like, ‘Hey, I'm just like you, I'm standing up to woke Bud Light.’ And then just taking their money and running with it.”
Paul Roberts, an employee of the Oregon department of transportation who shared a September 2024 receipt for three six-packs of Ultra Right Fight beer totaling $91.36, says he has tried in vain to get an update on the order. “Sent many emails, replies to texts, and on their Facebook page,” he says, and called a listed number as well. “No response.”
Both Roberts and Alan tell WIRED they only purchased the beers as collectible items and had no plans to actually drink them. They also say that their orders were not motivated by the Bud Light boycott. “I don't care what people drink,” Alan says. “You drink Bud Light, you drink Bud Light.” Roberts had previously bought the Revenge beer with Trump’s mugshot on it, which did arrive, although he says delivery was slow. “The mugshot had been used in a negative light, so I thought it was cool and collectible that they placed it on a beer can.”
Alan notes that as Weathers began running into difficulties with catching up on orders, he blamed these on legal wrangling with Anheuser-Busch. The company filed trademark opposition against Ultra Right Beer LLC in 2024, citing similarities to its own Michelob Ultra beer. Weathers called it an attempt at “corporate intimidation.” That litigation remains ongoing.
While Alan and Roberts have given up hope of getting their money back, they’d like to see justice served in some way or another. “I would like the state to enforce whatever laws apply to a business that takes your money and doesn't provide the product or service,” Roberts says. Alan adds that in his experience as a law enforcement officer, he’s used to seeing people get away with petty scams. “Accountability would be nice, whether it's seizing assets or seizing everything he has, some jail time,” he says.
“I'd like to cross paths with him one day,” Alan says of Weathers. “I'm sure a lot of people would.”

Families in Gaza fear return to hunger as WFP slashes food aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:44:10 UTC
19:44:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Families in Gaza fear return to hunger as WFP slashes food assistance
Safiya Abu Sabha, a displaced Palestinian woman from Gaza City, questions how she will be able to feed her four children if the food aid her family depends on vanishes.
Since the Israeli army killed her husband in an attack and she fled the Shuja'iyya neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City, the 40-year-old has been raising her children alone, struggling to cope with soaring living costs without an income.
Her concerns have deepened following the World Food Programme's (WFP) announcement of cuts to its assistance in Gaza amid funding shortages.
On Monday, the WFP announced a one-third reduction in its food assistance in Gaza due to funding shortages, affecting approximately 500,000 people.
Around 1.1 million vulnerable Palestinians will receive food or cash assistance, down from approximately 1.6 million the previous month, the WFP said in a press statement.
Food rations will be halved, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, while wheat flour distributions will also be reduced, it added.
The number of hot meals provided daily will fall from 250,000 to 150,000, and cash assistance for 75,000 households will be reduced, it explained. In hard-to-reach areas, including those near the so-called "Yellow Line", hot meals will be distributed every other day instead of daily.
For Safiya, who lives in a worn-out tent at a shelter in western Gaza City, the prospect of receiving less assistance threatens the limited support she relies on to feed her children.
"What scares me most today is that the aid might be cut back even further. I have no income with which to buy food for my children. I don't know how I will manage to feed them if we lose this support," she told The New Arab.
"The aid we receive isn't enough to cover everything my children need, and I can't always provide the most suitable food for them, but at least it helps me ensure they have something to eat. Something is better than nothing," she said.
Although the assistance does not meet all her family's nutritional needs, it helps Safiya put food on the table when buying groceries is beyond her means.
Losing a lifeline
Safiya's concerns are shared by Samir Abu Hasira, who lives with his wife and three children in a tent near Gaza's beach.
The Israeli army destroyed his house during the genocidal war, leaving his family without shelter or a livelihood.
His situation worsened when Israeli forces shot him as he tried to reach food aid trucks during the famine, costing him a leg and leaving him unable to work. He has since become increasingly dependent on humanitarian assistance to feed his wife and three children.
"I used to regularly receive a sack of flour and a carton of canned goods, which helped me provide food for my wife and children," he told TNA.
The supplies helped cover part of the family's needs, but further reductions could leave Samir struggling to compensate for the shortfall. With no income and no alternative means of support, buying food from local markets is difficult.
"The war has turned our lives upside down. I lost my home, and after losing my leg, I lost my ability to work. My family now depends on aid to survive," he said. "I never imagined reaching a point where I couldn't provide food for my own children. What frightens me most is not knowing what tomorrow will bring for them."
His experience highlights the vulnerability of families that have lost their livelihoods, particularly those caring for people whose injuries or disabilities prevent them from working.
For such households, reduced assistance means more than smaller food rations; it threatens their ability to meet basic needs.
Despite the cuts, the WFP intends to continue supporting bakeries that meet around one-third of Gaza's bread requirements, providing food assistance to approximately 300,000 women and children and nutritious snacks to 200,000 schoolchildren.
However, the funding crisis threatens the programme's ability to maintain assistance at a time when many families have few alternatives. For households such as Safiya and Samir's, the prospect of receiving less food aid adds to the uncertainty of living without stable shelter or income.
Hunger, with psychological and social pressures
The WFP estimates that approximately 1.4 million people, or 67 per cent of Gaza's population, face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. Only one in five children has access to a sufficiently diverse diet.
According to the programme, with unemployment exceeding 80 per cent, many families cannot afford fresh produce and protein-rich foods, even when these are available in local markets. Food assistance has served as a lifeline for up to 90 per cent of households in Gaza over the past three years.
Since the ceasefire began in October 2025, the WFP has reached approximately 1.6 million people each month through food parcels, flour, bread, hot meals, nutrition programmes and cash assistance.
However, funding received for its operations in Palestine in 2026 amounted to no more than half of what it had received in previous years. The programme urgently needs US$450 million to sustain its operations in Gaza and the West Bank from October 2026 through March 2027.
Beyond its physical consequences, food insecurity is taking a psychological toll on families, particularly mothers struggling to provide for their children amid displacement, poverty and the loss of their homes.
Mustafa Ayesh, a social expert from Gaza City, told TNA that food shortages affect mental health and family relationships.
"When a mother cannot provide food for her children or fears she will not be able to feed them the next day, she faces intense psychological pressure and a sense of helplessness," Ayesh said.
He added that cuts to aid increase families' anxiety about the future, while children may feel more fearful and insecure as tensions rise at home.
Ayesh warned that continued shortages could force families to eat whatever food they can find, increasing the risk of malnutrition, particularly among children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers.
"For many families, food assistance is a basic safeguard against hunger when they have no income or other support. Any reduction adds to the pressure on people already struggling to survive," he said.
For Safiya, food aid cannot restore her home or bring back her husband, but it helps her feed her children.
For her and Samir, the assistance they receive remains essential despite falling short of their needs. As funding shortages threaten further cuts, both families face growing uncertainty about how they will secure their next meal.

Reform UK claims undercover racism exposé has left some of its members 'psychologically damaged' as it reports ITV to police
Reform UK says it has reported “multiple” ITV journalists, and the company’s board of directors, to the police on the grounds that their undercover reporters working on the exposé of racism in the party broke the law. The party says it will also be suing them for damages.
Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, posted this on social media summarising his party’s allegations.
Reform UK has reported ITV, its board, and its undercover reporters to the police.
Some of the crimes carry up to 10 years in prison.
They forged a passport.
They directly interfered in elections and almost certainly altered the results. Being paid to “canvass” for Reform in crucial wards we lost by a few dozen votes.
They lied to a veteran about their service and left him “violated”.
This is unprecedented.
The police are now involved.
Scrutiny of political parties is one thing.
But anyone breaking the law to try and ruin the lives of Reform’s staff, members or volunteers will be reported to the police and pursued relentlessly in the courts.
In a video setting out his case against ITV at greater length, Yusuf claimed ITV “psychologically damaged innocent and decent Reform staff and members who were not featured in any documentary”.
As an example of this, Yusuf said that one of the undercover reporters met a Reform UK member in Portsmouth who had served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He said:
One of the undercover reporters told him that they shared the same military background. That was a lie. The marine, believing him, took him for a drink. They spent hours talking about their service, and the marine shared deeply personal stories from the front line because he believed he was talking to a friend and a fellow soldier. He has told us he feels violated.
Yusuf also explained why he was alleging electoral interference. In Portsmouth two undercover reporters were tasked with delivering leaflets in one ward where Reform UK lost in the local elections by 24 votes, and in another ward where Reform UK lost by just 85 votes. Yusuf said these margins were smaller than the number of leaflets the undercover reporters were supposed to deliver.
But he did not assert in the video that they failed to deliver the leaflets, and he offered no evidence that they had done anything to suppress the Reform UK vote at the time.
Asked about the legal threats, an ITV spokesperson said:
ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch we would fully cooperate.
People tend to assume that a public interest defence will protect journalists from allegations of minor law-breaking if they are investigating wrongdoing. In fact, the law is more complicated than that, a public interest defence applies in some instances and not in others, and there are probably enough allegations in the Yusuf video to keep a media lawyer busy for days assessing the evidence.
But, in practice, it is rare for the criminal law to be used successfully against legitimate journalists. When the Crown Prosecution Service prosecuted police officers who had taken bribes, and the journalists who had paid them, under Operation Elveden, the officers were largely convicted but the journalists were largely acquitted. Juries seemed to accept they were operating in the public interest.
In the ITV case, the public interest case for the programme is particularly strong. Reform UK has accepted that some of the people exposed making racist comments should not be in the party – although it has also claimed they were not representative of the membership as a whole.
Reform UK says it has reported ITV to the police over its undercover racism exposé about the party, which it claims left some members “pyschologically damaged”. (See 3.50pm.)

This decision is salted with the tears of every Nepalese person who saw someone they loved swept away in a river tsunami and it’s stained with the blood of everyone in Valencia who died as cars afloat in mud, sewage and enough rainwater for a year collided into their bodies in streets that had become rivers.
Although we cannot right now hear people in Australia, LA and Portugal crying in fear as their homes and worlds burn, these are the knock-on consequences of corporations that continue to drill fossil fuels and the governments that permit it, knowing the damage caused.
Our government must not double down on madness now. They must not lap-up industry propaganda again for the next North Sea project in their in-tray. If they believe in a future that protects people’s homes and safety, not endangers them, they must stop Rosebank.
