US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
- Published
Russia has released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.
Stephen Hubbard had been taken to the city's Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday.
President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary". Following the release, Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian".
Hubbard, who was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, was accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine when he was captured in 2022, shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion.
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.
Witkoff praised Putin for releasing Hubbard, saying: "You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian - you are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you."
His comments sparked a backlash from lawmakers in the Republican Party, with Representative Don Bacon posting on social media that it was "another embarrassment". Senator John Cornyn said Putin "is a stone cold killer".
In response to a question from the BBC about the backlash, Vice-President JD Vance said Witkoff's "job is to go over there and get a job done".
"I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family," he said during a press conference in Ohio on Wednesday.
In the past, detained Americans have primarily been released from Russia through prisoner swaps.
Hubbard was later seen thanking Witkoff as they met separately. Putin's financial adviser Kirill Dmitriev was also present.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
"I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine," Trump later told reporters.
"I mentioned, could you let Steven Hubbard out, please? And, he agreed to do it," he continued.
Trump called Hubbard "a very high quality, innocent man", and said that his family was travelling with him on his return to the US.
"They didn't think he'd come out for 20, 25 years. So we appreciate that fact that we were able to get them," Trump said, adding that he had spoken to Hubbard on Wednesday morning, and that "he is the happiest man around".
Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing online that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".
The US state department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and Trump on Tuesday suggested his release might be imminent.
"Watch what happens," he told reporters. "We have been focused on Hubbard".
The state department said in a statement that the release was "a welcome step that we hope leads to the release of all Americans unjustly held in Russia". It also said that "there are currently no Americans determined to be wrongfully detained in Russia".
Russian prosecutors had accused Hubbard of joining a Ukrainian military unit and receiving training and weapons. But his sister, Patricia Fox Hubbard, previously told Reuters that this was unlikely because of his older age and his disinterest in the military.
Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, who is a Greek Orthodox priest, said in a statement that he had prayed for many years for his father's release.
"As I await the blessing of embracing him again, I receive his freedom not as a political victory, but as a gift of mercy," Coleman said.
A lawyer for Hubbard, Martin De Luca, posted on social media on Wednesday: "The road to peace is difficult, but its human dividends need not wait for a final agreement."
A spokesman for Putin, Dmitry Peskov, told Russian media that American officials had been seeking Hubbard's for some time, and Putin decided to do it for humanitarian reasons.
- Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war 
  - Published9 hours ago
- Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia 
  - Published22 hours ago
Witkoff also thanked Putin for the deal struck with Washington earlier this month to import Russian diesel, saying Trump was "deeply grateful" for it. Ahead of the US midterm elections in November, where affordability is top issue for many voters, Trump has sought to bring down fuel costs.
The first shipment under the agreement will leave Russia "in two to three days", Putin said during the meeting, as quoted by state news agency TASS.
The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky and triggered a tumultuous few weeks of deteriorating relations during which Trump suspended a number of sanctions and said it was time for Ukraine to elect a new leader.
Kyiv meanwhile accused Washington of halting intelligence sharing on deadly Russian strikes, and claimed a sudden restriction to the Starshield internet service in its war effort had been deliberate. Zelensky said on Tuesday that intelligence sharing had resumed.
As talks were under way in St Petersburg, Zelensky posted on social media that "much depends on whether the American side can hear something new from Russia today – about peace, and not about continuing the war".

Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states held an extraordinary meeting in Riyadh on Wednesday to discuss strengthening cooperation and coordination among their armed forces amid continued attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on Saudi Arabia.
The meeting was held by the GCC Armed Forces Operations and Training Committee, according to a statement from the UAE Defense Ministry.
The GCC comprises Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman.
The ministry said the extraordinary meeting took place at the headquarters of the GCC General Secretariat but did not disclose the names of the participants.
It said the meeting discussed “several issues aimed at strengthening joint military cooperation in operations and training,” as well as “developing coordination and integration mechanisms” among Gulf armed forces.
The discussions also sought to “support joint Gulf defense efforts and enhance military readiness and efficiency in the fields of operations and training,” the ministry said.
The statement did not detail any decisions made at the meeting or directly mention discussions on Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.
The meeting comes amid escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group on Saudi Arabia and Gulf and international efforts to halt them.
The GCC has not issued a statement on the meeting so far. However, its Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi called Sunday for “effective” international action against the Houthi group at the conclusion of a ministerial meeting in Manama.
Yemen has seen a military escalation since July between government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis, following a period of relative calm associated with a truce that began in April 2022.
The conflict in Yemen began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014.

UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in limbo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:21:00 UTC
18:21:00 KST

UK approves controversial Jackdaw gas project after years of delays
October 21, 2026
The UK government gave its approval for drilling to begin in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Wednesday following years of legal and political problems that had blocked the controversial fossil fuel venture.
The Labour government justified the move saying it would strengthen the UK's energy security amid rising energy costs due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.
The gas field had previously been approved by the previous Conservative government, but wes held up by a Scottish court that said the approval had failed to consider carbon emissions.
The field lies about 150 miles (240 kilometres) east of Aberdeen in Scotland.
What did the UK government say about the Jackdaw approval?
Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to increase drilling in the North Sea, said the new gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter."
"At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," he said.
"We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea," Burnham added.
Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas could start flowing to British houses and businesses by the end of the month. It is expected that Jackdaw will increase domestic gas production by 6% and run for 11 years.
What has been the reaction to the UK's new gas project?
Shell, which is part of the Adura joint venture along with Norway's Equinor, welcomed the decision.
"Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions," Shell said.
However, the move has also been met with strong criticism. The Green Party called it "climate vandalism," while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy."
"True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said the environmental group's Ami McCarthy.
Critics have also questioned whether the new project would indeed have an impact on British gas bills since prices are determined by global energy markets.
In an attempt to show the government's commitment to its climate targets, alongside the Jackdaw approval, it announced the set up of a new Energy Wealth Fund, with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion), aimed at channeling oil and gas revenues into funding the transition to cleaner energy.
The UK is targeting net zero emissions by 2050, although this target must be examined under the realities already facing the planet, with a new UN report saying the world is heading for 2.8 degrees of warming, way beyond the 1.5 degrees target set in the Paris Climate Agreement.
It also comes after the UK experienced its hottest ever summer on record, with temperatures hitting previously unheard of 38 degrees in some areas in June, according to the Met Office.

Belgian police face complaints over alleged violence against young protesters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:19:33 UTC
18:19:33 KST

Belgium’s police oversight body, Committee P, has received 26 complaints over alleged police misconduct during youth protests in Brussels, following two weeks of unrest that resulted in more than 250 arrests, news portal Bruzz reported on Wednesday.
The complaints concern police conduct during demonstrations on October 9 and 17, according to Committee P.
The unrest erupted amid protests against federal government austerity measures and cuts to French-speaking education.
On October 9, trade unions ACV and ABVV organised a nationwide day of action, joined by student movements.
Police estimated that around 1,000 people were involved in the unrest, during which public transport buses, shared vehicles and street furniture were damaged. Protesters also threw bricks and pyrotechnic devices at police officers.
Police arrested 110 people, including 30 in judicial arrests. Of those, 21 were brought before the public prosecutor’s office over alleged offences including weapons possession, violence and vandalism.
Further clashes erupted during another youth demonstration on October 17, resulting in widespread property damage and 152 arrests, including 19 in judicial arrests.
Rights groups raise concerns
Rights groups have reported allegations of disproportionate police force during the demonstrations, including violence against minors.
Pierre-Yves Rosset, director of the Service Droit des Jeunes (SDJ), said his organisation had received testimonies alleging that police officers injured young protesters.
“One minor was hit on the head with a baton. Another had to be hospitalised with a broken collarbone after being struck with a baton,” Rosset said.
The SDJ has received several testimonies concerning the events of October 9 and 12, while reports relating to the October 17 demonstration are still coming in.
The SDJ and the French-speaking human rights organisation Ligue des Droits Humains (LDH) have also questioned police tactics, particularly the frequent use of tear gas at demonstrations attended by minors and children.

====================================================================================================

Censoring Palestine: Who gets to tell its story and how?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:15:27 UTC
18:15:27 KST

Who will tell Palestine’s story? It is a million-dollar question begging an answer.
From editorial disputes over Palestinian history to the legal consequences of supporting Palestine, the struggle extends beyond what can be said and who gets to decide how it is heard.
A people can lose their homes, their land and the security of their future. But another struggle follows: telling the world what happened, why it happened, and who bears responsibility.
For Palestinians, this struggle increasingly extends into publishing houses, literary events and the institutions that determine which stories reach the public.
Their suffering may be acknowledged, but the historical context that explains it can become contested. Their writers may find opportunities to publish, but disputes over language and framing can determine how much of their intended message survives.
Two recent controversies in the literary world illustrate different dimensions of this problem: the withdrawal of a Palestinian children's book from Penguin Random House following an editorial dispute, and the decision by Irish novelist Sally Rooney and her publisher to withdraw her books from the British market amid the legal consequences of her support for Palestine Action.
The cases are not identical. One concerns editorial disagreements over historical representation; the other concerns how Britain's terrorism legislation affects a writer's earnings and the distribution of her work.
But both raise a question that deserves greater scrutiny: who gets to determine the boundaries of acceptable expression about Palestine?
When history becomes contested
In October, Palestinian-American writers Alana Hadid and Jenan Matari withdrew their forthcoming children's book, ‘Displacement and the Palestinian American Story’, from Penguin Random House after months of disagreement over editorial changes.
The book was intended for readers aged 10 to 13 and would have introduced them to Palestinian history, the 1948 Nakba, Israeli occupation, resistance, and diaspora experiences.
The authors argued that proposed changes would distort their account, including passages concerning the Hamas-led blitz of October 7, 2023, and descriptions of Zionist militias involved in the displacement of Palestinians in 1948.
According to The Guardian, the publisher added language describing the October 7 blitz as violations of international law, while the authors objected to changes they believed contradicted their narrative.
Penguin Random House defended its editorial process as standard practice. The authors ultimately withdrew the manuscript, which is now expected to be published by Interlink Books in 2027.
Publishers have a responsibility to ensure accuracy and provide age-appropriate context. But whose history receives that context, and whose suffering is subjected to endless qualifications?
If children are expected to learn about October 7, they must also be taught about the Nakba, the mass displacement of Palestinians in 1948, and the decades of occupation, dispossession and violence that followed.
Palestinian history cannot be understood through isolated events stripped of their historical context, nor should political sensitivities shape the telling of that history by determining which truths can be expressed and which must be softened or left out.
The question is not whether editors can challenge an author's interpretation. They can, and sometimes should. It is whether editorial intervention improves an account or fundamentally changes what its author is trying to say.
The authors' withdrawal of the book demonstrates the stakes of that disagreement. They concluded that the manuscript being prepared for publication was no longer the book they had written.
This is where the politics of publishing becomes a question of narrative control. A story can remain technically publishable while its historical interpretation is progressively altered.
Suffering can be acknowledged while responsibility becomes less explicit. Displacement can be described without adequately explaining the events that produced it.
Such sanitisation does not necessarily involve a formal ban. It can occur through omissions, selective framing and decisions about which words require qualification and which historical claims are allowed to stand without challenge.
The cost of expressing solidarity
Rooney’s case is distinct from the dispute over Hadid and Matari's manuscript.
Nevertheless, the outcome raises questions about the boundaries of political expression and the consequences of Britain's approach to Palestine-related activism.
The distinction matters. It would be inaccurate to describe every consequence of a legal restriction as equivalent to a conventional book ban.
But it would be equally inadequate to ignore the implications for cultural expression when a writer's political commitments affect whether her work can continue to circulate.
The broader question is how far restrictions intended to address security concerns can affect artistic freedom, political solidarity and the willingness of other writers to express controversial views.
When cultural participation carries significant legal or professional risks, the consequences can extend beyond the individuals directly affected.
Others may become more cautious about the causes they support, the language they use and the subjects they address.
These controversies point towards a broader problem: narrative control does not always require a single authority to prohibit a story outright.
It can emerge through the cumulative decisions of publishers, institutions and legal systems that shape which accounts reach audiences and under what conditions.
Each decision may have its own justification, and each case must be examined on its own evidence. But their combined effects on public discourse deserve scrutiny.
For Palestinians, representation is inseparable from history.
The Nakba was not simply a humanitarian tragedy; it involved the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians and the destruction or depopulation of hundreds of Palestinian localities.
The subsequent history of occupation, illegal settlement expansion and recurring violence cannot be understood without examining the political and military structures through which these realities developed.
Yet public discussions of Palestine can become detached from that historical continuum.
Particular acts of Palestinian violence may be examined in isolation, while the conditions surrounding them receive less attention.
Palestinian suffering may be presented as a regrettable consequence of conflict rather than an experience that requires sustained examination of power, responsibility, and historical continuity.
Beyond the visible act of censorship
The problem is not simply that Palestinian suffering is denied, but that it is also detached from the history that gives it meaning.
The Nakba becomes a tragedy without perpetrators, displacement becomes a condition without a cause, and resistance becomes an isolated act stripped of the historical realities against which it emerged.
The language of neutrality can itself become a means of obscuring these relationships, particularly when the demands for qualification and restraint fall disproportionately upon those attempting to document Palestinian dispossession.
This is how narrative control operates: not always through the outright denial of history, but through the gradual narrowing of what can be said about it.
A story may be permitted to circulate so long as its political implications remain muted, its account of responsibility softened and its challenge to established power sufficiently diluted.
The result is a version of Palestine that can be mourned but not fully understood, acknowledged but not allowed to disrupt the narratives through which its dispossession is justified or normalised.
Children's literature makes these questions especially important.
Books help shape how young readers understand history, responsibility and the experiences of people beyond their own communities.
If Palestinian history reaches children only after its most contested dimensions have been softened, their understanding of the conflict will inevitably be incomplete.
The issue, therefore, is not merely whether Palestine can be mentioned in a book. It is whether Palestinians can participate in defining how their own history is told.
The withdrawal of a manuscript and the withdrawal of an author's books from a national market reveal different pressures operating on cultural expression. Neither case alone establishes a universal policy of suppressing Palestinian narratives.
Together, however, they invite a serious examination of the institutions and rules that shape what readers can access and what writers can say.
The struggle over Palestine is fought over land, sovereignty and political freedom.
It is also fought over memory, language and representation. A people whose history is contested must be able to challenge not only the denial of their suffering, but also the selective telling of it.
The answer is not to replace one sanitised narrative with another. It is to defend the conditions in which historical accounts can be examined, challenged and debated without the removal of essential context or the unnecessary restriction of political expression.
Palestine should not have to become a more comfortable story to become a publishable one. Its history, with all its complexities and uncomfortable truths, deserves to be told in full.

Red tourism thrives in Liupan Mountain, China's Ningxia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:14:09 CST
18:14:09 KST

A drone photo taken on Sept. 18, 2026 shows a park commemorating the history of the Long March in Xiji County of Guyuan City, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region.
The Liupan Mountain runs through Guyuan City in Ningxia. In October 1935, Red Army soldiers crossed Liupan Mountain during the Long March, a historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history. It marks a key turning point in the history of the Long March.
Now, the Liupan Mountain serves as a crucial ecological barrier and water resource conservation area, and local revolution-themed tourism is booming. Former revolutionary base areas in the region have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about China's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. Japan's Takaichi gov't faces growing criticism over military buildup, security policy shift
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:13:59 CST
18:13:59 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- As Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi marks one year in office, criticism is growing over her push to expand the country's military capabilities, revise its pacifist Constitution and consider introducing nuclear-powered submarines, with politicians, protesters and nuclear experts warning that the moves could heighten regional tensions and undermine Japan's postwar pacifist principles.
Former Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba recently expressed concern over Takaichi's political course in a television program, criticizing her government and right-wing forces for a lack of honesty in addressing Japan's wartime history.
In the program aired by BS-TBS on Monday, Ishiba said that Japan launched wars that resulted in tens of millions of deaths, questioning whether a country that failed to fully acknowledge these historical facts could establish solid diplomatic relations.
Ishiba also questioned Takaichi's pledge to make Japan "strong and prosperous," noting that the country's gross domestic product could fall to sixth place globally next year; in other words, the so-called "Sanae-nomics" has failed to bring prosperity to the country, adding that Takaichi's political course "will not make people happy."
On Monday evening, Japanese citizens gathered in front of the National Diet in Tokyo to protest against the government's military buildup and moves to revise the Constitution, calling for the preservation of peace.
Taku Yamazoe, policy chief of the Japanese Communist Party, said the government's continued deployment of missiles and pursuit of increasingly advanced weapons had not brought peace, warning that Japanese politics is now showing signs of a dangerous, full-scale revival of militarism.
Mizuho Fukushima, leader of the Social Democratic Party, called for efforts to prevent the House of Representatives from beginning work on drafting proposed constitutional amendments. She also criticized attempts by the Takaichi government to pave the way for constitutional revision by reducing the number of seats allocated through proportional representation.
Pointing to the large-scale Japan-U.S. joint military exercises that began Monday, Fukushima said they demonstrated the continued advance of Japan's militarization, stressing that what the country truly needed was peace.
Concerns have also mounted over the Takaichi government's consideration of introducing nuclear-powered submarines, as it prepares to revise Japan's three key security documents by the end of this year. Nuclear experts and peace advocates warn that the move could undermine Japan's longstanding exclusively defense-oriented policy and weaken the international nuclear nonproliferation regime.
At a seminar held in Tokyo on Monday, participants highlighted policy, financial and nuclear safety challenges associated with introducing such submarines, warning that the move could aggravate regional tensions and increase the risk of nuclear conflict.
Tatsujiro Suzuki, a visiting professor at Nagasaki University, said Japan's move could encourage other countries to follow suit, undermining international nuclear nonproliferation efforts, warning that such a trend could intensify regional tensions and ultimately increase the risk of nuclear war.
Sumiko Hatakeyama, co-representative of the Japanese nongovernmental organization Peace Boat, said Japan must not abandon its postwar principles of exclusively defense-oriented policy and the peaceful use of nuclear energy, stressing that the government should not introduce nuclear-powered submarines.
Hajime Matsukubo, secretary-general of the Citizens' Nuclear Information Center and a member of the Nuclear Energy Subcommittee under the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said that nuclear-powered submarines could enable Japan to operate for extended periods across wider maritime areas, significantly affecting the regional security environment.
Matsukubo also noted that previous Japanese governments had explicitly stated that using nuclear energy to power military submarines did not qualify as the peaceful use of nuclear energy when nuclear-powered vessels had yet to become widespread.
The Takaichi cabinet's discussions on introducing nuclear-powered submarines therefore represented a clear contradiction with the government's previous position, he said, calling it a serious issue. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China's Long March legacy endures from trek to tech
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:13:57 CST
18:13:57 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- One of the most visible legacies of the Red Army's Long March, a roughly 12,500-km military odyssey that ended 90 years ago, may well be an active rocket family that bears the same name.
Among the world's busiest launch vehicles, China's Long March rockets have for more than half a century carried satellites, crewed spacecraft and scientific probes into orbit and beyond, helping open the country's path to space.
This name for the rocket was suggested by several pioneers of China's aerospace industry. "It meant that the development of the rockets would overcome all difficulties and achieve victory, just as the Red Army had done during the Long March," said Han Houjian, a general designer of the Long March-1 rocket, which made its maiden flight in 1970.
On April 24, 1970, the Long March-1 lifted off carrying Dongfanghong-1, China's first satellite, into orbit. Since then, this rocket family has grown into a diverse fleet of launch vehicles with increasing payload capabilities. As of October 10, 2026, it had completed 671 orbital launches.
The journey behind these Chinese rockets echoes that of the Red Army: both were marked by immense hardships, determined perseverance, and the resolve to press ahead against the odds.
In October 1934, the Communist Party of China (CPC) was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi Province and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party. The CPC-led Red Army broke through enemy blockades, crossed rugged terrain, and endured fierce battles and immense hardship. Tens of thousands of soldiers lost their lives along the way.
Few people represent the connection between these two journeys better than Sun Jixian. During the Long March, Sun, as a Red Army officer, led his men across a major river under enemy fire, helping the Red Army break through a dangerous bottleneck in 1935. More than a decade later, after the founding of the People's Republic of China, he took on a different mission -- building the country's first missile and satellite launch site in the remote Gobi Desert. His team battled sandstorms, drank alkaline water, lived in tents and caves, and transferred equipment by hand across the barren landscape.
"I remember once when my father returned from the desert, he reached into his coat pocket to look for candies for me, but what he touched was a handful of rough, cold sand," recalled Sun Dongning, his 75-year-old son.
In the 1960s, when China began developing its first rocket, the country had a weak industrial base and was cut off from access to many key foreign technologies. Scientists performed calculations using hand-cranked computing machines and worked day and night in poor workshops.
China's first nuclear-powered submarine emerged from similarly difficult conditions and relied on technological self-reliance to overcome obstacles. Commissioned on Aug. 1, 1974, it was also named Long March-1. Subsequent generations of Chinese nuclear submarines have continued to carry the Long March name.
The epic trek's legacy has since spread across military and technology sectors. Naval vessels such as Zunyi and Chishui bear the names of places associated with the historic march. Loongson, a major Chinese chipmaker, also gave two generations of its chips the project codes CZ70 and CZ80 in 2006 and 2016, respectively. CZ stands for Changzheng, the Chinese name for the Long March.
For Chinese scientists and engineers, the legacy is not simply a name but a determination to persevere in facing daunting challenges, maintain faith in eventual success, and grow more resilient with every setback.
Long Lehao, a leading Chinese rocket designer, cited the launch failure of Long March-3B as an example. As the rocket's first chief designer and chief commander, Long recalled that his hair "turned white overnight."
"There was no time to think about personal honor or disgrace. I threw myself into the new battle of tracing faults," Long recalled at a recent press conference.
After 30 days and nights of continuous work, his team identified the cause of the failure. Some 551 days later, the Long March-3B successfully delivered its payloads into orbit.
The Long March-5, designed to carry lunar and Mars probes, suffered a rare setback when its second flight failed in 2017. The failure marked the darkest chapter in this rocket's development. The research team carried out painstaking reviews and repeated trials to resolve the technical problem. On Dec. 27, 2019, the rocket completed a successful third flight and subsequently launched several spacecraft, including the Chang'e-6 probe for a far-side lunar sample-return mission.
And the journey continues. In July 2026, the Long March-10B completed China's first controlled recovery of a rocket's first stage, marking a step forward in reusable launch technology. Meanwhile, development of rockets with greater capability is being accelerated.
China aims to land astronauts on the moon before 2030 and launch a Mars sample-return mission around 2028. Additionally, it is pursuing the broader goal of becoming an innovative nation and a world-class science and technology power.
For generations of Chinese researchers, the Long March is a journey that never ends. From rugged trails to the frontiers of technology, its legacy is continuing to inspire further exploration and innovation. ■

KAMPALA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Uganda has reported no confirmed active Ebola cases following reports that a Nigerian woman who tested positive for the disease had transited through the country earlier this month, the Ministry of Health said in a statement issued late Tuesday.
The Nigerian woman had traveled to the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for business before passing through Uganda in early October, according to the statement. She reportedly showed no symptoms while in Uganda but developed them after arriving in Nigeria.

The ministry said Nigerian authorities had yet to provide detailed information about the woman's travel itinerary and clinical history to support further investigations and any necessary contact tracing.
According to Nigerian authorities, the woman, who had recently arrived in the country on an international flight from Uganda, was admitted to a private hospital, receiving care for several days. ■

Citadel air defense system AI components ensure 99% target engagement rate — Rostec
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:13:00 UTC
18:13:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Artificial intelligence in the Citadel air defense missile system achieves a 99% target engagement rate, the state corporation Rostec said.
"The system is equipped with an AI-based fire control system. Machine learning algorithms enable a 99% target engagement rate," Rostec stressed.
The corporation noted that the system is already deployed to safeguard critical facilities and can engage both small FPV drones and heavy unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as cruise missiles.
The state corporation said that Citadel learns in real combat conditions. "If the first round misses the target, the system assesses the error and adjusts its next shot. Target recognition and trajectory calculation take only seconds. There is no need to fire in bursts. A projectile with a programmable fuse detonates at the required location, covering the drone in a cloud of shrapnel. As a result, several times fewer projectiles are needed to destroy a target," Rostec said.
It added that military personnel confirm that it takes no more than four shots to neutralize a single target.
Citadel can operate independently or as part of a layered air defense system. By intercepting drones, the system reduces the workload of heavy anti-aircraft missile systems, allowing them to concentrate on priority targets.

====================================================================================================

Poland’s 360-degree Patriot radars move closer to fielding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:11:53 UTC
18:11:53 KST

- The Defense Logistics Agency asked Raytheon to price production of support hardware for Poland’s LTAMDS radars, with proposals due Dec. 18, 2026.
- The work will be ordered under a new LTAMDS contract vehicle, and DLA did not disclose its estimated value or quantities.
The Defense Logistics Agency has asked Raytheon to price the production of support equipment for Poland’s new LTAMDS radars, the 360-degree sensors that will replace the old Patriot radar in Warsaw’s air and missile defense network, under a sole-source request for proposal posted on U.S. government’s contracting website on Oct. 20.
The agency wants the hardware added to a new LTAMDS contract vehicle that is still being set up, with the Polish production and hardware work to be awarded as a standalone delivery order once that umbrella contract is in place, and it has given Raytheon until Dec. 18 to submit its offer.
The request, issued by DLA Aviation in Huntsville, Alabama, on behalf of the U.S. Army’s STARE (Search Track Acquire Radiate Eliminate) project office, covers several items listed only by their abbreviations, including a BMC and an SRPT, along with frequency converters and non-recurring engineering work. The frequency converters will need both design and development, paid on a cost-plus basis, and production under a fixed price, while the other hardware is also planned as fixed-price work, and DLA asked Raytheon to propose its own line-item structure for the deal.
DLA did not disclose an estimated value for the work or the number of equipment sets involved, and the draft statement of work attached to the request also covers engineering services that are not part of this proposal. The agency said it posted the notice publicly so that, if another company shows interest after reading it, a formal competitive solicitation can be issued to give that supplier a chance to bid.
Poland became the first foreign buyer of the Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor when it signed for 12 of the radars in 2023 as part of the second phase of its Wisła air defense program, a package that also includes 48 more Patriot launchers and a large stock of PAC-3 missiles in deals worth more than $15.5 billion. The radars are meant to give Poland’s Patriot batteries full coverage against aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles, with the first Wisła Phase 2 batteries scheduled for delivery in 2026 and 2027 and the program planned for completion in 2029.
LTAMDS uses three active electronically scanned array faces built with gallium nitride, a main forward array and two smaller rear arrays, to watch the full circle around a battery, while the legacy AN/MPQ-65 radar it replaces can only look in one direction at a time. The U.S. Army moved the radar into low-rate initial production in April 2025, and in September that year Raytheon won a $1.7 billion contract for nine radars for the U.S. Army and Poland.
Production has kept growing since then, and in April the U.S. Army awarded Raytheon a $904.6 million modification for five more radars and six spare systems, pushing the program’s total contract value past $5.35 billion, as we reported at the time. Polish industry is also part of the supply chain, with state-owned Military Electronic Works (WZE) in Warsaw building energy storage modules for the radar under a subcontract that made it the first foreign supplier on the program.

Construction output in Bulgaria rose by 4.2% year-on-year in August 2026 and by 0.7% from July, according to preliminary Eurostat estimates.
The annual increase marked a slowdown from the 4.7% growth recorded in July and 5.6% in June. Construction output had expanded by 4.0% year-on-year in May, 6.8% in April and 6.4% in March.
On a monthly basis, Bulgaria's construction sector recovered in August after contracting by 0.6% in July. Output had increased by 1.7% in June, while declines of 2.0% in May, 0.1% in April and 0.2% in March were recorded.
Across the European Union, construction output increased by 2.0% in August compared with July, while the euro area registered growth of 1.8%. In July, output had risen by 0.2% in the eurozone but fallen by 0.1% across the EU.
Compared with August 2025, construction output grew by 2.6% in the EU and 1.4% in the euro area. The previous month had seen annual declines of 1.6% across the EU and 1.7% in the eurozone.
Among EU member states with available data, Hungary posted the strongest monthly growth in August at 14.0%, followed by Germany at 9.3% and Romania at 7.2%. The largest monthly contractions occurred in Slovenia, where output fell by 5.1%, Slovakia, down 4.9%, and Italy, down 2.9%.
Romania led annual growth with a 39.0% increase, followed by Hungary at 22.0% and Finland at 12.7%. The steepest year-on-year declines were recorded in France, at 7.8%, Slovakia, at 4.9%, and Spain, at 4.3%.
A breakdown by construction activity showed different trends across the EU and euro area. Between July and August, building construction fell by 1.0% in the EU and 0.4% in the eurozone. Civil engineering output declined by 0.2% in the EU and 2.1% in the euro area.
Specialized construction activities moved in the opposite direction, increasing by 2.3% across the EU and 2.5% in the eurozone over the same period.
Compared with August 2025, building construction decreased by 4.1% in the EU and 3.7% in the euro area. Civil engineering output rose by 2.8% across the EU but remained unchanged in the eurozone. Specialized construction activities recorded annual growth of 2.9% in the EU and 3.1% in the euro area.

U.S. Army awards $308M for digital investigation software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:06:54 UTC
18:06:54 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Authentic8 a $307.7 million modification to set up a department-wide contract for its Silo digital investigation software.
- The Army solicited a single bid for the sole-source deal, which covers secure browsing tools used for open-source intelligence and dark web research.
The Pentagon is spending up to $307.7 million on software that lets its analysts browse the darkest corners of the internet without leaving a trace, after the U.S. Army awarded California-based Authentic8 a department-wide deal for its Silo platform on Oct. 20.
Silo is designed for the kind of online detective work that military intelligence now depends on, from monitoring Telegram channels and extremist forums to tracking weapons sales on dark web marketplaces, while hiding the fact that the person on the other end works for the U.S. government.
The problem Silo tries to solve is simple: every time an analyst opens a website from an official network, that site can log the visit, fingerprint the browser and, in the worst case, push malicious code onto a military computer. Silo moves the whole browsing session onto Authentic8’s own cloud servers, so nothing from the website ever reaches the user’s machine, and it lets investigators choose where they appear to be connecting from, so a visit from an Army analyst in Virginia can look like an ordinary user in another country.
That capability has become more valuable as open-source intelligence has grown into a core part of modern warfare, with Russia’s war against Ukraine showing how much can be learned from soldiers’ social media posts, geolocated videos and commercial satellite images. Analysts who dig through that material regularly visit sites run by hostile governments, militant groups and criminal networks, where a careless click from a government address can tip off the target or expose the analyst’s own network to hackers.
The Army ran the purchase as a sole-source deal and received a single bid, after telling industry in August that its requirement was specific to Authentic8’s product and that it planned to buy directly from the company unless another firm could show it offered the same capability. The award gives commands across the Department of War one place to order Silo licenses, add-on tools and support, with the amount and location of the work decided order by order rather than fixed up front.
Authentic8 is already a familiar name in federal law enforcement and financial investigations, with the Department of the Treasury, the Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Secret Service among the agencies that have bought Silo for secure browsing and dark web research. The new contract expands an initial award made in September into a much larger vehicle that the whole department can use, which puts the Redwood City company’s tools on track to become a standard part of the military’s online investigation kit.

====================================================================================================

Trump's push for Israel-Saudi relations faces obstacles amid elections, Houthi attacks - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:05:20 UTC
18:05:20 KST

US President Donald Trump’s renewed call for Saudi Arabia to accept Israeli assistance against Yemen’s Houthis has revived questions about whether shared security threats could bring Riyadh and Jerusalem closer to normalization. But mounting attacks on Saudi infrastructure, Israel’s approaching election, and unresolved disagreements over Palestinian statehood continue to complicate the prospect of formal relations.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Asked on October 16 whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli help, Trump replied: “I do, I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” He also suggested that Saudi-Israeli normalization could be back on the table, “maybe more than ever.”
His comments did not establish whether Riyadh had requested Israeli military assistance or agreed to any overt security partnership.
Saudi Arabia is confronting an intensified campaign by the Iran-backed Houthis, whose missiles and drones have targeted airports, oil facilities, and shipping. An attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people, while repeated strikes have disrupted aviation and raised concerns about the kingdom’s ability to protect infrastructure central to its economic development plans.
For Riyadh, however, accepting Israeli military assistance would carry political consequences at home and throughout an Arab region deeply affected by the wars since October 7, 2023.
“Since the Yemen war, there have been contacts with Israel. Israel wanted to assist with the Houthis, but the Saudis, because of public opinion, did not guarantee any open contact,” Dr. Yoel Guzansky, senior researcher and head of the Gulf Program at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Media Line.
A September 30 incident illustrated the limits of cooperation. Following the emergency landing in Saudi Arabia of a flydubai aircraft bound for Israel after an attack in its cockpit, Riyadh refused an Israeli request to allow military aircraft to retrieve the Israeli passengers, according to Reuters. The passengers instead returned on another flydubai plane.
“Saudi Arabia did the minimum and didn’t want any normalization,” Guzansky said, referring to the refusal to permit Israeli aircraft to land.
Before the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, Saudi Arabia and Israel had been moving toward a possible US-brokered normalization agreement. The subsequent wars and destruction in Gaza have made formal recognition considerably more contentious.
Riyadh has maintained that any agreement must include a credible pathway toward an independent Palestinian state, a condition Israel’s current government has resisted.
“Since October 7, the Arab world is very much against Israel. The Palestinian issue is formally at the center because it helps maintain a form of stability for Arab governments,” Guzansky said.
He argued that public opposition to Israel would remain a substantial obstacle even if the two governments identified additional areas of cooperation.
“There is no common ground between Israel and Saudi Arabia in terms of societies. Public opinion is against Israel in Saudi Arabia, and it will be hard to shift that.”
Saudi crown prince politically challenged by ongoing security crisis
For Dr. Cyril Widdershoven, senior advisor at Blue Water Strategy, the security crisis also presents an economic and political challenge for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 development program depends heavily on foreign investment, infrastructure expansion, and the kingdom’s reputation as a stable destination for international business. Continued attacks on airports, ports, and energy facilities threaten those ambitions while increasing defense and reconstruction costs.
Widdershoven warned that mounting expenses and persistent insecurity could fuel domestic criticism of the crown prince, making an openly acknowledged relationship with Israel even more politically sensitive.
The economic consequences of the conflict are already apparent. On October 19, organizers announced that Saudi Arabia’s flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, originally scheduled for October 26–29, would be postponed until 2027. The decision followed deadly Houthi attacks and growing security concerns, although organizers did not explicitly cite the attacks as the reason.
Military considerations present another obstacle. Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis for more than a decade, yet repeated air campaigns have failed to eliminate the group’s ability to strike across the border or threaten shipping through the Red Sea.
“I don’t think that Saudi is militarily able to crush the Houthis. Hurt them, yes. But to go inside Yemen is something else,” Widdershoven said. “I would say it’s like a potential Afghanistan or Vietnam scenario.”
He also warned that direct Israeli military involvement could expand the confrontation by provoking responses from Iran and allied armed groups elsewhere in the region.
“I would say to the Israelis, I would offer my help, but I would keep my soldiers out. Let’s have the Arabs deal with the Arabs.”
Saudi Arabia is meanwhile seeking assistance from regional partners whose involvement may be more politically acceptable.
On October 18, Egypt’s National Defense Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, agreed to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself against Houthi attacks. The Saudi defense minister also met the president of the United Arab Emirates as the two governments sought closer coordination despite longstanding differences over Yemen.
Turkey submitted the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to its parliament for ratification on October 20.
Signed in August, the three-country pact provides for mutual defense if a signatory comes under armed attack. Turkish officials have indicated that assistance to Riyadh could include military equipment and intelligence sharing, while any Turkish troop deployment abroad would require parliamentary approval.
Britain also announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would conduct defensive patrols over Saudi territory, expanding British military support against Houthi missile and drone attacks.
“The Saudis need the Emiratis now in terms of Yemen. It is temporary, not fixing their competition,” Guzansky said, distinguishing immediate security needs from the continuing rivalry between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi.
Widdershoven similarly identified Egypt and the Emirates as potential partners while questioning how far arrangements involving Turkey and Pakistan would translate into operational commitments.
He also distinguished official diplomatic relations from informal contacts, suggesting that Saudi and Israeli representatives might continue discussions without public acknowledgment.
“So to expect that officially there will be a discussion between Riyadh and Jerusalem, I think that will not happen officially,” he said.
Change in Israel leadership could improve potential Saudi relations
Israel’s October 27 election adds another layer of uncertainty.
The vote, the first national election since the October 7 attacks, will determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu can assemble another governing coalition or whether opposition parties can form an alternative government.
Guzansky believes a leadership change could improve prospects for renewed contact with Riyadh.
“The elections are crucial in this situation, since a new government, the current opposition, would help a lot in terms of rapprochement,” he said.
Netanyahu, Guzansky added, “is not well seen in the Arab world.”
Widdershoven offered a similar assessment, suggesting that Saudi opposition to closer relations with Israel is tied partly to Netanyahu personally.
“I don’t expect that as long as Bibi Netanyahu is in power, that this will happen,” he said. “The current feeling in Saudi is not that they are anti-Israeli. I think that they are anti-Bibi Netanyahu.”
Yet a change of government would not necessarily remove Riyadh’s principal diplomatic condition.
Gadi Eisenkot, a prominent opposition contender, has avoided endorsing a two-state formula, while other parties seeking to replace Netanyahu hold substantially different positions on Palestinian statehood, settlements, and negotiations.
An opposition coalition united around replacing the prime minister would therefore not automatically agree on a policy capable of satisfying Saudi demands.
Washington faces its own political pressures ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 20 placed Trump’s approval rating at 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, as Americans expressed growing frustration over high gasoline prices and the economic consequences of the war with Iran.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu’s reelection campaign on October 18, even as both experts interviewed by The Media Line suggested that a different Israeli government might be better positioned to improve relations with Saudi Arabia.
The endorsement highlights a potential conflict between Washington’s immediate political alliances and its longer-term ambition to expand the Abraham Accords.
“Trump may keep pushing rhetorically for normalization with Saudi, but in practice it is very different,” Guzansky said.
Iran extending US negotiations to deny Trump pre-midterm success
The approaching US elections are also influencing calculations in Tehran. Senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Iran had deliberately prolonged negotiations with Washington partly to deny Trump a political success before the midterms.
Widdershoven argued that Iran could continue pressuring its adversaries through threats to shipping, rising insurance premiums, and regional instability without necessarily launching another major military offensive.
“They are playing the long game,” he said. “Iran can play this for another two, three, five years. We cannot.”
For Saudi Arabia, continued instability increases the incentive to strengthen regional security arrangements. But neither common threats nor a possible change in Israeli leadership would necessarily overcome the diplomatic barriers to normalization.
“A new government in Israel may push new talks with Saudi Arabia, but still the opposition won’t guarantee a Palestinian state,” Guzansky said.

Taiwan reports 18 mpox cases in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:02:38 UTC
18:02:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has reported 18 confirmed mpox cases so far in October, the highest monthly total in two years, the Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday.
Sixteen patients had clade Ib infections, according to a CDC press release. They were in their 20s to 40s and had engaged in higher-risk sexual behavior, while only two had previously received an mpox vaccine.
Taiwan recorded 52 confirmed cases this year as of Oct. 19, including 41 locally acquired and 11 imported infections.
The CDC urged eligible people to complete the two-dose vaccination series. As of the end of September, 31,927 people, or 28% of those who had received at least one dose, had yet to receive their second shot.
Two doses provide about 90% protection, compared with 40% to 80% for one dose, the agency said. Vaccination can also reduce the severity of symptoms if infection occurs.
Free vaccination is available at 327 medical institutions nationwide. Eligible recipients include people who have engaged in higher-risk sexual behavior in the past year, those with a history of sexually transmitted infections, and people whose sexual partners meet either criterion.
Mpox has an incubation period of up to 21 days, and some infected people can transmit the virus one to four days before symptoms appear, the CDC said. Symptoms include fever, swollen lymph nodes, rashes, blisters, and pustules.
Young children, pregnant women, and people with chronic diseases or weakened immune systems may face a greater risk of severe illness.
Further information is available on the Taiwan CDC website or through the toll-free epidemic prevention hotline at 1922 or 0800-001922.

There was no immediate comment on the claim from the Yemeni government or the Saudi-led coalition.
The attack was the third on Aden in a week. On Friday, two missiles landed within the perimeter of the city’s airport, with the Houthis claiming the attack.
A day earlier, the group launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, hitting command centres located inside the compound, which is used by government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.
Elsewhere in Yemen, government forces said that they had repelled a Houthi attack on western Taiz city, while clashes were ongoing since Wednesday morning in the area of the Old Airport and Madrat, also in western Taiz city.
The Saudi-led coalition separately said that pro-government forces were engaged in heavy fighting with the Houthis in Kahboub in southwest Yemen.
A coalition spokesperson said they were trying to repel a large-scale attack and were experiencing intense Houthi bombardment, describing the situation as “very dangerous”.
Clashes are ongoing under “intensive air cover” by coalition and Yemeni forces, the spokesperson said.
In a separate statement, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted five drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.
“Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern province as well as Medina.
Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said another drone had been intercepted in the Eastern province.
The Houthis denied having targeted the kingdom, with Saree saying their forces had not carried out any “deep” operations in Saudi territory.
Fighting in Yemen escalated sharply last month when the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, have been responding with a counteroffensive and have started Operation Dawn of Yemen, which aims to seize and recapture territory from the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa, which has been under the group’s control since 2014.

Lin Restaurant transforms childhood nostalgia into fine dining
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:02:07 UTC
18:02:07 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chef Kai-lin Tsai (蔡凱霖) of Lin Restaurant is drawing on childhood memories and family traditions for an autumn menu that reinterprets home cooking and street snacks through contemporary French techniques.
Following the pressure of the Michelin evaluation season, Tsai is taking a more playful, reflective approach. At the heart of the menu is his grandmother’s chicken soup, a source of comfort during difficult times.
The season’s centerpiece is Shanghai-style braised beef with fermented baby Chinese cabbage and chicken jus.
Tsai considers the dish his most complex creation. He spent months refining its braised flavors before finding inspiration at a Shanghai street stall, where he encountered the balance of soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, and savory aromas he sought.
Tsai selected Australian boneless M3 wagyu short rib for its fat content. He omitted Sichuan peppercorns and chilies, instead simmering French chicken jus with Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, and rock sugar.
The accompanying fermented baby Chinese cabbage presented another challenge. To avoid overwhelming acidity, Tsai halted fermentation after one hour, producing a crisp, mildly tart contrast to the beef.
The signature soup, “Hung Chin Hsiu-pao (洪金秀寶),” honors Tsai’s grandmother.
Recalling the comfort of her cooking, Tsai simmers chicken stock with two varieties of ginseng, flower mushrooms, and South African abalone.
Elsewhere on the menu, Taiwanese street snacks and coastal memories inform the dishes.
Inspired by after-school snacks, Tsai uses French pastry techniques to turn scallion pancakes into thin, crisp bases topped with seared beef tartare.
Growing up near Changhua with an uncle who owned a fishing boat, Tsai ate cured mullet roe as a childhood snack. On the autumn menu, it is seared tableside and served with taro cake and garlic potato.
King crab is paired with a French butter sauce flavored with Shaoxing wine and shiso.
Other dishes include a poached egg with traditional dried radish and Comte cheese, and threadfin fish served with a savory broth thickened with sago pearls.
A citrus palate cleanser and chestnut souffle precede a petit four inspired by mian fen jian, a traditional pan-fried batter cake Tsai loved at Changhua markets as a child. Made with peanut butter and toasted buckwheat, it closes the meal with another childhood flavor.

Hong Kong sees last-minute IPO cancellations amid increased regulatory checks, weak market

Hong Kong’s tougher oversight and weak investor demand have put many mainland China issuers in a dilemma, forcing many small-cap non-technology firms to delay their fundraising plans or even cancel them at the last minute, according to industry players.
On Tuesday Jiangsu Slender West Lake Culture and Tourism (SWL Tour) became the latest such case, when the state-owned aquatic tourism service provider postponed a HK$227 million (US$28.93 million) listing. The company attributed the decision to “several factors, including the prevailing market conditions,” it said just hours after closing its order books.
“Institutional investors are now more cautious about small-cap stocks with limited fundamentals and growth prospects,” said Roy Lo Wa-kei, managing partner at the accounting and consulting firm SW Hong Kong.
The SWL Tour deal did not bring in any cornerstone investor, according to its prospectus, and with the firm opting for the city’s so-called Mechanism B, which caps a public tranche at just 10 per cent, leaving allocation and pricing power more dependent on institutional buyers.

Type 31 support deal being rethought
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:00:53 BST
18:00:53 KST

The Type 31 Through Life Support procurement has been discontinued after a review concluded that the assumptions behind it no longer reflected the right route for supporting the class, and the department is now considering fresh arrangements to meet a requirement it says is unchanged, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked by when the Secretary of State will make a decision on the replacement for Type 31 Through Life Support, and was referred to an answer given on 6 October to his earlier question about the corrigendum to the tender published on 22 July.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said in that answer: “The Type 31 Through Life Support procurement was discontinued following a review of the proposed approach. The Department concluded that the assumptions underpinning that procurement no longer reflected the most appropriate route for delivering support to the Type 31 class. Those assumptions included the delivery context for the programme and the way in which future support arrangements should be structured. The requirement to provide effective through-life support for the Type 31 fleet remains unchanged.”
“The Department is now considering the most appropriate arrangements to meet that requirement. Any future procurement activity will be taken forward in accordance with Defence requirements, value for money considerations and established commercial procedures.”
Through life support covers the maintenance, spares, training, documentation and engineering authority that keep a warship class running across thirty years, and it is usually worth more over a ship’s life than the ship cost to build.
Five Type 31 frigates are being built by Babcock at Rosyth under a contract signed in 2019, with HMS Venturer the first of class, and this publication has tracked the programme’s progress towards launch and the build work on Venturer.

Takero Shimazaki upgrades makeshift theatre into permanent "church-like" London venue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Takero Shimazaki upgrades makeshift theatre into permanent “church-like” London venue
A crane tower becomes a soaring beacon at The Yard Theatre in London‘s Hackney Wick, which local studio Takero Shimazaki Architects has revamped and extended using reclaimed materials.
Originally established in 2011 in a converted warehouse and designed by Practice Architecture to last as a three-month project, Takero Shimazaki Architects‘ redesign transforms the theatre from a makeshift space to a permanent performance venue with a bar, backstage facilities and community space.
Aiming to maintain the character of the site, Takero Shimazaki Architects used reclaimed materials to overhaul the existing 110-seat theatre space and extend the venue into the adjacent studios and former brewery with brick walls.
“The core discussion had been about The Yard Theatre ‘growing up’ and for it to have a more permanent presence in the new architecture,” Takero Shimazaki Architects founder Takero Shimazaki told Dezeen.
“The building’s form emerged from the playful idea of creating a civic cultural space by referring to a church-like form made from industrial light-weight materials, as well as the facade brickwork,” he continued.
“The overall architectural form also created stacked boxes on top of the existing warehouse, breaking up the horizontal industrial language and creating a more monumental presence using readily available and sustainable materials.”
Takero Shimazaki Architects retained the brick walls of the former brewery, which now contains a new 224-capacity theatre space with curved amphitheatre seating.
The theatre’s pitched structural frame was made from laminated veneer lumber atop reclaimed tubular steel.
A crane tower was refashioned as a ventilation chimney that rises 23 metres tall, clad in translucent polycarbonate boards to form an eye-catching beacon from outside.
A bar and public foyer occupy the former theatre building, where Takero Shimazaki Architects added a new roof and retained as much of the walls, floors and windows as possible.
The theatre’s backstage facilities are located under the auditorium’s tiered seating, and lifts and stairs were added to connect the bar to the theatre’s upper-level seating.
Materials that were demolished in the construction of the transformation were reused, including exterior bricks used for the stage wall and external infills.
The extended exterior of The Yard Theatre was finished in fibre-cement sheeting, polycarbonate panels and colourful low-carbon named K-Briq, which are made from more than 95 per cent recycled materials.
Atop the roof of the boxy volumes stands a human-shaped sculpture designed by British sculptor Antony Gormley.
Other projects by Takero Shimazaki Architects include a Japan-influenced overhaul of a flat in the Barbican estate and a renovated 1960s house with black-painted brickwork outside of London.

Serbia announced a deal to sell Russia’s stake in NIS to Hungary’s MOL - what it means
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:59:24 EEST
17:59:24 KST

Serbia announced a deal to sell Russia’s stake in NIS to Hungary’s MOL - what it means
Kyiv • UNN
MOL has agreed to purchase Russia’s stake in Serbia’s NIS. The deal is awaiting approval from antitrust authorities, while Serbia’s stake\r\nwill increase to 35%.
The agreement on the sale of the Russian stake in Serbian oil company NIS to Hungarian company MOL has been signed, but still requires approval from antitrust authorities. Serbia's Finance Minister Siniša Mali said this, UNN reports, citing HVG.
Details
In an interview with Bloomberg Adria, Siniša Mali said that the Russian owners and MOL had reached an agreement, and that the Serbian state had concluded a shareholders' agreement with the Hungarian side. The Hungarian minister expects applications for licenses to be submitted to the Serbian and, to his knowledge, Bosnian and Herzegovinian antitrust authorities in the near future, and that the change of ownership could be completed shortly thereafter.
Siniša Mali confirmed that the agreement would increase Serbia's stake in the company. According to him, a written agreement was reached to increase the Serbian state's stake from approximately 30 to 35 percent. He added that Belgrade's goal is to exceed one third.
In early October, Serbian Forbes reported that the negotiations had failed. According to the publication, Russian "Gazprom" clearly does not want to sell its stake in the Serbian state-owned oil company and is merely keeping silent about it to buy time in case the United States lifts its sanctions, which would primarily force it to sell NIS.
Shortly thereafter, information began circulating that American companies might seek to purchase NIS.
What the decision means
By acquiring more than half of NIS, Mol, as the publication writes, could obtain Serbia's only operating oil refinery, as well as the unit in Pančevo, through which the company led by Chairman and CEO Zsolt Hernádi would gain additional oil-processing capacity of 4.8 million tonnes per year, in addition to the combined capacity of its refineries in Százhalombatta in Hungary, Bratislava (owned by Slovnaft) in Slovakia, and Rijeka (owned by INA) in Croatia, amounting to nearly 19 million tonnes per year.
"What makes this deal a real bombshell is that Pančevo covers 80 percent of the country's market demand, and in addition to supplies to its own filling stations and stations bearing the \"Gazprom\" logo, other major consumers also buy from it," the publication states.
If an agreement is reached, Mol could also reportedly become the owner of petrochemical company HIP-Petrohemija, 90% of whose shares have been owned by NIS since 2021.
NIS also has interests outside Serbia. The company explores for oil and gas in Romania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Angola, and also has retail outlets in Bosnia and Romania, as well as in Bulgaria. This means more than 400 filling stations in the region, including household outlets. The company is also involved in electricity trading and is active in the Serbian market, as well as in the markets of Bosnia, Montenegro, Romania, Slovenia, and Hungary.

Turkey says troops will remain in Syria and Iraq until border security is guaranteed

17:58:39 KST

Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Guler said Tuesday that Turkish forces would remain deployed in Syria and Iraq until border security is fully guaranteed and threats to the country’s security have been eliminated.
In written responses to journalists, Guler reaffirmed Ankara’s intention to maintain its military presence in both neighbouring countries, saying any decision to reconsider troop deployments would depend on security developments.
“We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria,” Guler said.
“Once we are certain that the necessary conditions regarding regional and border security have been met, the status of our deployment sites and our presence in the region will be reviewed.”
Turkey has maintained military forces in northern Syria and Iraq for years, primarily to counter threats from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and ISIS.
However, the regional security landscape has changed significantly following the overthrow of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad and the establishment of a new government in Damascus with close ties to Ankara.
The developments have coincided with Turkish efforts to end its decades-long conflict with the PKK.
READ: Turkiye strongly condemns Israel’s activities in Syria’s Quneitra province
Guler said any reassessment of Turkey’s military presence in Syria would require the complete elimination of security threats, guarantees for border security and the restoration of unified state authority throughout Syrian territory.
“Once the terrorist threat in the region has been completely eliminated, border security is guaranteed, and the authority of the state is fully and uniformly established across all parts of Syria—without exception—the status of our forces will be re-evaluated,” he said.
At the time of Assad’s overthrow, Turkey had an estimated 16,000 to 18,000 troops stationed in northern Syria, according to a Turkish official.
However, updated figures on Turkish troop deployments have not been made available.
A Turkish official said last month that discussions were underway to determine the legal status of Turkish forces operating in Syria.
Guler declined to provide details about possible future military deployments or bases, saying it would be premature to discuss plans that had not been formally announced.
He emphasised that decisions concerning the future of Turkish forces in Syria would be made through consultations with Damascus, taking into account Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The process would also consider security conditions on the ground and developments in the threat posed by armed groups, he added.
