At least 226 reported killed in Sudan drone strike on crowded market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:56:43 UTC
17:56:43 KST

At least 226 people have reportedly been killed in a devastating drone strike on a crowded market in Abyei, a disputed territory between Sudan and South Sudan, according to local authorities. The attack, which took place Monday, October 19, triggered powerful explosions and a massive fire after a fuel depot inside the market was hit, leaving charred buildings, destroyed vehicles and bodies trapped beneath the wreckage. Thousands of residents fled the area as rescue workers struggled to recover the dead, with flames continuing to burn into the following day.
The updated death toll was reported by South Sudan's Eye Radio, citing Yohana Akol Ngor, Abyei's caretaker information minister. According to Ngor, 153 victims were buried in one mass grave and another 73 in a second, bringing the reported total to 226. The figure has not been independently verified. Earlier reports by Reuters and the Associated Press placed the death toll at 153. Ngor said an initial strike also hit a tractor-trailer carrying approximately 26 people, while an estimated 8,000 residents were displaced, some seeking shelter beneath trees and in open spaces.
An eyewitness who spoke to Reuters described hearing five powerful explosions before flames engulfed a fuel storage facility inside the market. As people rushed to evacuate the wounded, many were found suffering from shrapnel injuries to their stomachs and legs. The witness, who requested anonymity for security reasons, said he had seen 28 burned bodies in one location. Images from the aftermath showed scorched vehicles, destroyed buildings and twisted metal scattered across the marketplace, while satellite imagery revealed extensive fire damage.
Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, reported that more than 20 wounded people were taken to nearby Ameth Bek Hospital, including patients with severe burns and other critical injuries. Dr. Christian Lindauer, the organization's medical activities manager at the hospital, said medical teams were providing emergency treatment, wound care and surgical assistance. Photographs released by the organization showed bandaged patients receiving treatment while lying on the hospital floor. Local officials warned that some bodies had been burned beyond recognition, complicating efforts to identify victims and recover their remains.
Abyei's local authorities and South Sudan's government accused the Sudanese Armed Forces of carrying out the attack. A senior Sudanese military officer subsequently acknowledged to the Associated Press, on condition of anonymity, that the army had conducted a drone strike in the area. However, he claimed the intended targets were fuel tankers arriving from South Sudan and believed to be transporting supplies to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, which has been fighting Sudan's army since April 2023. The officer maintained that those killed were RSF members or people involved in fuel smuggling, insisting: "We do not target civilians."
That account was disputed by the Reuters eyewitness, who said he had not seen RSF fighters or other uniformed armed personnel in the market. He described the site as a busy commercial center selling basic goods, including sugar, flour and biscuits, some of which are transported onward into Sudan. Three diplomatic sources told Reuters that the fuel depot struck in the attack had previously been used by the RSF to supply its forces. However, it could not be independently established whether the facility was serving a military purpose at the time of the strike.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest the attack, condemning the civilian casualties and extensive destruction. The ministry urged Sudan to refrain from military actions that endanger civilians and called for disputes involving Abyei to be resolved through diplomatic channels. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the drone attacks in the region, while the UN said women and children were among the victims. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei, or UNISFA, deployed medical personnel, firefighting teams and rapid-response units to help evacuate casualties and prevent the flames from spreading.
Deadly escalation in Sudan's civil war
The Abyei attack came amid a wider wave of deadly drone strikes across Sudan. According to the BBC, the Sudan War Observatory reported that approximately 150 people were killed in two drone strikes Sunday near Al-Dabab in West Kordofan state. One strike reportedly hit a truck carrying about 200 people traveling to a funeral, killing 145, while another five people were killed when a drone struck a tent where mourners had gathered. The organization also reported 150 wounded and assessed that the drones were launched from Kadugli, a city in South Kordofan controlled by the Sudanese army. The figures and attribution have not been independently verified.
The attacks highlight the growing role of unmanned aerial vehicles in Sudan's civil war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between army chief Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. The conflict has devastated large parts of Sudan and created one of the world's worst humanitarian emergencies. According to UN figures cited in the reports, approximately 13 million people have been displaced and more than 33 million require humanitarian assistance. Around 20 million people face severe food insecurity, with aid organizations warning of worsening famine risks in parts of Darfur and Kordofan.
Drone attacks have increasingly targeted strategic infrastructure, supply routes and populated areas. Despite a partial international arms embargo, foreign suppliers have reportedly continued providing unmanned aircraft and other military equipment to both sides. Kordofan, a region rich in oil and gold, has become a crucial battlefield linking RSF strongholds in Darfur with central Sudan and the army-held capital, Khartoum. Control of the region's roads, fuel supplies and trading centers carries significant military and economic importance.
Abyei itself has long been a flashpoint between Sudan and South Sudan. The oil-rich territory's status was left unresolved under the 2005 peace agreement that ended Sudan's previous north-south civil war. The dispute persisted after South Sudan gained independence in 2011, with a referendum intended to determine Abyei's future never taking place because of disagreements over who would be eligible to vote. The Ngok Dinka community generally supports joining South Sudan, while the nomadic Misseriya community favors remaining part of Sudan.
The territory has experienced repeated violence over land, grazing rights and access to resources. Since Sudan's current civil war began, Abyei has also become an important transit corridor for supplies moving toward areas controlled by the RSF. The United Nations warned in May that the presence of RSF members in the region was increasing instability and endangering residents and international peacekeepers. UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric has warned that repeated drone attacks and the destruction of essential infrastructure are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling to survive more than three years of war.

Pope Leo takes to popemobile for first time since cancer surgery
VATICAN CITY, Oct 21 - Pope Leo returned to St. Peter's Square on Wednesday, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from his open-air popemobile as he held his first general audience at the Vatican since undergoing lung cancer surgery eight days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff, who pledged on Sunday he would slowly resume his duties as leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, stood in the back of the vehicle as it drove through the square, waving, smiling and stopping to talk to pilgrims.
Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on October 13 and has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy.
Wednesday's audience, the first held by the pope since October 7, followed a normal format. Crowds began gathering hours ahead of the 9:45 a.m. (0745 GMT) starting time, holding umbrellas under drizzling grey skies.
"The first thing I want to say to you is thank you for the support and prayers," Leo told the crowds in his opening remarks for the 50-minute event, without specifically mentioning his health.
"Thanks be to God for his generosity," said the pope, speaking in a clear voice as cheers broke out in the Square. "Let's renew our trust in the goodness and mercy of God."
PAPAL CALENDAR STILL IN FLUX
After touring the Square on Wednesday, Leo offered a sermon in Italian. In the only major change from previous occasions, he gave brief greetings afterwards in seven instead of nine other languages.
Leo's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
The Vatican has provided no indication of Leo's schedule beyond Wednesday.
The pope is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades, but it remains unclear if that trip will go ahead as planned.
Leo's lead surgeon has said the pope could be fully recovered in time for the trip, but the Vatican's secretary of state has indicated the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid in recovery. REUTERS

Probe exposes UAH 2.6 mln eRecovery scheme in Mykolaiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:48:14 EEST
17:48:14 KST

The State Bureau of Investigation, with the help of National Police leadership, has exposed a scheme of illegally obtaining state compensation under the eRecovery program in Mykolaiv region, the bureau said.
"To obtain a housing certificate, community officials in Mykolaiv region changed the status of a renovated service apartment and registered it as destroyed by Russian shelling," the bureau said on its website on Wednesday.
In March 2022 the Shevchenkivska community in Mykolaiv region came under shelling, and the service apartment of the community's police officer suffered minor damage. Later, the bureau said, the community and charities paid to replace windows and doors in the apartment and repair the building's roof.
However, according to the investigation, the village head, together with his deputy and the community police officer, decided to use the state compensation program for their own benefit.
"First they helped the police officer privatize the service apartment. Because the building was not declared unsafe after the shelling and its residents had already received repair aid, the officials had the village council change the apartment's status and legal address. On paper, the apartment became a separate individual house with a different number," the bureau said.
The commission members then drew up an inspection report on housing allegedly destroyed by armed aggression, which belonged to the police officer and his family members, and stated in the document that the house was ruined and unfit for living, the bureau said.
"On the basis of this report, the police officer received an eRecovery housing certificate for UAH 2.6 million, with which he bought an apartment in Mykolaiv," the bureau said.
The village head and his deputy have been served with notices of suspicion of abuse of office (Part 2 of Article 364 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), and the police officer with notice of suspicion of aiding abuse of office (Part 5 of Article 27 and Part 2 of Article 364).
All three have been suspended from their posts, and preventive measures have been chosen for them.
The bureau is taking steps to recover the damage caused to the state.
The Mykolaiv regional prosecutor's office is supervising the investigation.

Why Elon Musk Wants to Merge SpaceX and Tesla
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:45:59 UTC
17:45:59 KST

The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk, the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion, putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks, depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
Why a merger matters
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab, a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype, which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars. Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla. That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

Israeli plans to strike Iran before election raise fears of wider regional war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:45:55 UTC
17:45:55 KST

A report that Israel planned to strike Iranian civilian infrastructure earlier this month, only to be stopped by U.S. President Donald Trump, has renewed questions about the strategic justification for another war with Tehran, particularly with Israeli elections less than a week away.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday that Israel had planned to attack Iranian infrastructure on Oct. 10, including power plants, nuclear facilities and other targets associated with the Iranian government, before Trump intervened to prevent the operation.
The report has raised concerns about why Israel would consider launching another major military campaign against Iran when previous rounds of fighting have failed to topple the Iranian government or permanently eliminate its military capabilities.
Israel has spent much of the past three years engaged in intensive fighting on multiple fronts, while damage from previous confrontations with Iran and fighting along its northern and southern borders has yet to be fully repaired.
Iran, meanwhile, continues to demonstrate its ability to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, attacking vessels and affecting the global economy. Gulf states have largely absorbed the consequences without launching direct military responses.
Against that backdrop, questions remain over whether Israel has a clear strategic plan for another confrontation and what objectives a renewed campaign could realistically achieve.
Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch in the Israeli Military Intelligence Directorate's Research Division and now a senior researcher specializing in Iran and the Shiite axis at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that there was no immediate military justification for launching another war.
"There's absolutely nothing that justifies a war now, either before the elections or afterward," Citrinowicz said.
"Iran is rebuilding its strength and restoring its missile capabilities. On the nuclear front, there are no indications whatsoever that they have resumed enrichment. There are the same indications that they moved certain materials to Pickaxe Mountain, but nothing beyond that."
Pickaxe Mountain, also known as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, is a mountainous site near Iran's Natanz nuclear complex that has attracted international scrutiny over suspected underground nuclear-related construction.
Citrinowicz questioned why Iran remained capable of launching substantial missile attacks after two previous wars that Israeli officials had described as major military successes.
"We also need to understand why, after two wars against Iran, we're still seeing them launch dozens of missiles," he said. "Apparently, they're not afraid for their arsenal."
'No justification for another campaign'
Citrinowicz said the reported Israeli interest in attacking Iran's energy infrastructure appeared to rest on two possible strategic assumptions, neither of which he considered convincing.
"What is the strategic objective of another war?" he asked. "According to various reports, Israel wants to attack Iran's energy facilities for one of two reasons: Either they think that will bring down the regime, which it won't, or they want to turn Iran into a failed state. And it's clear that would lead to a very broad Iranian campaign against Israel."
He said Iran's continued military buildup did not, by itself, justify an immediate attack.
Iran has continued replacing senior officials killed in previous confrontations, including some whose successors have adopted even more hard-line positions.
Earlier this week, Mehrdad Akhlaghi was appointed Iran's new defense minister. Like his predecessors, he warned that Iranian forces remained ready to respond to threats.
But despite the rhetoric and continued rearmament, Citrinowicz said there had been no dramatic change in Iranian behavior in recent months.
He argued that Iran's efforts to rebuild its capabilities were comparable to those of other Israeli adversaries, including the Houthis in Yemen, Hezbollah in Lebanon and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq.
Another war against Iran, he warned, could reignite fighting across all those fronts.
"The point is that there is no justification requiring a military campaign at this time," Citrinowicz said. "We need to monitor the situation and see what develops. If Iran makes a breakout toward a nuclear weapon tomorrow, then we need to attack. But right now, nothing is happening."
He described the possibility of an Israeli strike just two weeks before the election as deeply troubling.
"What's happening now is sheer madness — attacking two weeks before elections. For what?" he said.
"Iran is not on the verge of developing a nuclear weapon, and with all due respect to its missile arsenal, it still hasn't returned to where it was before Operation Rising Lion and Operation Roaring Lion," he added, using the Israeli names for the previous bouts of direct fighting against the Islamic Republic.
"There is no operational or strategic need to attack now," Citrinowicz said. "There is an attempt to incorporate political considerations, and that is serious."
The former intelligence official also questioned the lasting achievements of the previous military campaigns, noting that Iran's leadership remained in power and its military continued rebuilding.
"Yes, another strike would cause damage, but the consequences for the international system would be insane," he said. "They would set the entire Gulf ablaze."
He criticized what he described as an apparent willingness to launch another campaign without first examining why earlier operations had failed to achieve their declared objectives.
"It's as if we don't care. Just attack again. But for what?" he said.
"And this is after we were promised tremendous, unprecedented achievements in two wars, that we had 'pushed the threat back for generations.' How did we push the threat back for generations if they can attack again?"
He added that Israeli officials had previously emphasized achievements against Iran's missile capabilities, yet Iranian missiles continued to pose a threat.
"The most serious thing is the mixing of political considerations," he said. "Ultimately, there is no justification for launching a campaign two weeks before elections."
US midterm elections complicate diplomatic efforts
The prospect of another confrontation also comes as Washington approaches its midterm elections in early November, a political milestone that Citrinowicz said could influence both Iranian calculations and Trump's willingness to pursue military action.
"The elections in the United States are extremely significant because the Iranians want Trump to lose," he said. "They want to demonstrate the price of confronting them to any American president: Mess with us and you'll lose the elections."
Citrinowicz said Tehran remained open to a negotiated agreement but continued to insist on conditions unacceptable to the Trump administration.
"The Iranians are prepared to return to an agreement, but the conditions they're presenting are conditions Trump will not accept," he said.
He dismissed recent reports in the Qatari newspaper Al-Araby Al-Jadeed suggesting a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
"With all due respect to the reports in Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, there is no diplomatic breakthrough whatsoever," he said.
He pointed to remarks made Tuesday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir.
According to the account, Rezaei insisted that all enriched nuclear material would remain in Iran.
"All enriched nuclear materials will remain in Iran," Rezaei said, describing them as "a central asset and national wealth of the Iranian people, intended for use within the country."
Rezaei also said Iranian officials and the public agreed that negotiations should not resume until Washington took steps to rebuild trust.
"The Iranian people and officials agree that there will be no negotiations as long as the United States does not take confidence-building measures," he said, adding that the prerequisite for restoring trust was meeting Iran's stated conditions.
Citrinowicz said the statements underscored the distance between Washington and Tehran despite those reports of diplomatic progress.
He also warned that the period between November's U.S. elections and the seating of the new Congress in January could prove especially volatile.
"I think the period between November and January is very dangerous because it's the transition between Congresses," he said. "During those two months, Trump will want to do something."
However, he suggested Trump's preferred course of action might differ substantially from Israel's reported objectives.
"Perhaps he wants to deliver a single blow, then end the whole affair and declare victory," Citrinowicz said. "I'm not sure he wants to return to the idea of toppling the regime."
He described the possibility of Israel initiating another military campaign under the current circumstances as highly irresponsible.
Israeli fighter jet activity raises escalation fears
Citrinowicz also expressed concern over a Fox News report that Israeli fighter jets had flown over Syria and Iraq toward Iran as part of a military exercise.
He warned that such activity, if accurately reported, could be interpreted by Tehran as preparation for an imminent attack, potentially provoking an Iranian response.
"If that's true, it's an extremely dangerous development," he said. "We're on the brink of war, and we're conducting a simulated strike in Iraq?"
Citrinowicz questioned the logic of staging an exercise resembling an attack on Iran during a period of heightened tensions.
"Do we want to force the Iranians to fire missiles at us?" he asked.
"There's no logic in simulating an attack on Iran at the height of tensions, other than a desire to push the Iranians into attacking us, to have them fire the first shot so we'll have an excuse to respond."
He warned that another Israeli-Iranian confrontation would almost certainly spread beyond the two countries.
"Any war with Iran will once again be a regional war," he said. "Certainly involving the Houthis, certainly the militias in Iraq, and I believe ultimately Hezbollah as well."
Citrinowicz said the regional security environment had changed in ways that could make another confrontation particularly dangerous.
He pointed to the absence of a U.S. military presence in Iraq, which he said would make it easier for pro-Iranian militias to operate, as well as the presence of Houthi elements in the country.
"We'll once again find ourselves stuck in a regional war," he said.
He also highlighted concerns about Israel's and the United States' supplies of missile interceptors, which would be essential to defending against sustained Iranian attacks.
"We know we have a problem with interceptors. That's no secret. And the Americans have a problem with interceptors as well," he said.
Those shortages, he suggested, could become particularly consequential in a prolonged conflict involving multiple fronts and repeated missile barrages.
'We cannot separate Netanyahu's political considerations from Israel's strategic interests'
Citrinowicz said his central concern was the possibility that domestic political calculations were influencing decisions with potentially far-reaching consequences for Israeli national security.
"The most serious aspect of this entire situation is that it's impossible to separate Netanyahu's political considerations from the strategic considerations of the State of Israel," he said.
"That's extremely dangerous. This would be another war with Iran."
He warned that previous confrontations had demonstrated the economic and social costs of fighting Iran, with military operations disrupting daily life and economic activity across Israel.
"We know that every war with Iran paralyzes the Israeli economy and brings activity here to a standstill," he said. "And for what? What strategic objective would this war serve?"
He argued that another campaign would be especially difficult to justify given the limited prospects of removing Iran's leadership through airstrikes alone.
"We understand very clearly that we are not going to topple this regime from the air," he said.
Rather than rushing toward another confrontation, Citrinowicz called for a thorough examination of Israel's previous campaigns, including the objectives they failed to achieve and whether additional military action would serve the country's long-term interests.
"Launching a campaign two weeks before elections is madness," he said.
"Before Israel launches a campaign for which there is currently no immediate need, we must ultimately analyze what we failed to achieve in the previous campaign and why."
He said policymakers should also consider whether military force was the only available option and whether another confrontation would advance Israel's strategic interests.
"Is the kinetic solution the only one, and will it serve the interests of the State of Israel?" he asked.
Citrinowicz emphasized that Israel should preserve close strategic coordination with Washington, describing it as the foundation of Israeli policy toward Iran.
"We certainly need to maintain strategic coordination with the United States," he said. "That's a significant issue because it's the basis of all Israeli policy toward Iran."
But he stressed that coordination with Washington should not replace an independent Israeli assessment of the risks and benefits of military action.
"With all due respect to the Americans, the State of Israel needs to examine what's right for it," he said.
He concluded that Israel should not embark on another potentially more dangerous war without first understanding why previous operations had failed to achieve their stated objectives.
"Right now, it's clear that the war's objectives were not achieved," Citrinowicz said.
"Before we analyze why they weren't achieved, we shouldn't jump into another campaign, one that could potentially be even more dangerous than the previous one, because it would be extremely violent and the Iranians are learning from every confrontation."

Russians who say they spied for Ukraine tell their story
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:45:40 BST
17:45:40 KST

Two Russian men who say they secretly worked with Ukraine’s intelligence services have given accounts of operations they claim to have carried out against military assets and personnel inside Russia, in a BBC Eye documentary for the BBC World Service, according to the BBC.
Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine premieres on BBC iPlayer and the BBC World Service YouTube channel on Monday 19 October, and airs on BBC Two on Monday 26 October at 23:00.
The Polish journalist Marcin Mamoń spent two years developing contact with a network of Russians who say they have been working covertly in support of Ukraine from inside Russia. Among them is a man the film calls Ivan, who describes himself as a patriot and says he wants Vladimir Putin’s government removed from power, arguing that supporting Ukraine’s war effort could help achieve that.
Another operative, given the name Foma and exiled in Poland, runs a network of volunteers inside Russia who carry out surveillance on senior officers that Ukraine’s military intelligence service, the GUR, is tracking.
The documentary raises the possibility that some operatives claiming to work for Ukraine could in fact be acting on behalf of Russia.
Monica Garnsey, the BBC executive producer, said: “Marcin Mamoń has used the incredible access he gained to tell a story that is not about heroes or villains, but about men who have crossed a line many will never face, and who are living with the consequences. Shadowmen asks difficult questions about acts of war, patriotism, and loyalty, and there are no simple answers.”
The BBC said the film examines the motivations of Russians who say they oppose the Kremlin and the risks they say they have taken, and that it explores the difficulty of independently verifying some of the claims made, with many of those involved unwilling to share further detail for security reasons.
Sabotage inside Russia has been a feature of the war almost since it began, and attributing any individual incident has been close to impossible from outside. Railway lines serving the front have been cut, recruitment offices burned, fuel depots set alight and military figures killed, with the GUR and the Security Service of Ukraine claiming some of it, Russian partisan groups claiming more, and Russian authorities frequently describing perpetrators as recruited over the internet for money.

2026-10-21
08:44:22 UTC
17:44:22 KST

Renewable Energy Resource Area (YEKA) tenders for wind and solar power to be held on Nov. 2-3 are expected to pave the way for around $2 billion in investment through the allocation of a total of 2,285 megawatts of capacity.
According to data from the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry, wind and solar YEKA investments aim to reduce the country’s dependence on imported energy resources and maximize the use of domestic energy sources.
On Nov. 2, a total of 1,500 MW of wind power capacity will be allocated across seven sites located in Sivas, Balıkesir, Manisa and Kütahya. On Nov. 3, 785 MW of solar power capacity will be allocated across 11 sites designated in Denizli, Ankara, Konya, Kahramanmaraş, Malatya, Diyarbakır, Mardin, Batman and Elazığ.
The projects, planned across 13 provinces, are expected to contribute to employment growth, support local economies, strengthen energy supply security and reduce dependence on energy imports.
The investments are also expected to support domestic manufacturing and supply chains for renewable energy equipment, particularly solar panels and wind turbines.
Hakan Erkan, secretary-general of the Solar Energy Industrialists and Industry Association, said the share of domestic resources in electricity generation has been increasing steadily, with the fastest growth seen in solar energy.
Noting that solar YEKA projects depend on various factors, including land conditions, transmission line lengths, fees and tender payments, Erkan said the projects are expected to attract around $500 million in investment.
He added that some of the projects could become operational in 2028, with the remainder expected to enter service by the end of 2029.
Ibrahim Erden, chairman of the Turkish Wind Energy Association, said YEKA projects support domestic equipment manufacturing while providing predictability for investors.
Erden said the 1,500 MW wind YEKA projects represent approximately $1.5 billion in investment.
“About 13 percent of Türkiye’s electricity generation in August 2026 was supplied by wind power. The local content ratio in turbines used in YEKA projects has reached 65 percent,” he said.
Erden also said the government aims to support domestic industry through YEKA projects and offer at least 2,500 MW of wind and solar capacity to investors annually.
“Such long-term targets and regular capacity allocations strengthen investor confidence and contribute to the sustainable growth of the sector,” he added.

Russia's destruction of satellites in orbit would also harm its own spacecraft – space law expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:42:00 UTC
17:42:00 KST

Russia's destruction of satellites in orbit would also harm its own spacecraft – space law expert
Anna Hurova, who holds a PhD in law specializing in space law and is a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Space Studies (Chaire Espace) at the École normale supérieure (ENS–PSL) in Paris, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"The principle of proportionality applies in humanitarian law. Even if they call a satellite a legitimate target, destroying it could cause disproportionate harm to other countries. The technical aspect must also be considered: the debris would threaten other satellites, and their owners could respond economically, politically, or in other ways," Hurova explained, commenting on Moscow's threats against Western commercial satellites that help Ukraine.
According to her, space debris would also threaten Russian satellites, forcing them to expend resources on collision-avoidance maneuvers.
Nevertheless, Moscow blocked efforts to establish a legal framework for space debris removal during negotiations on the Code of Conduct for Outer Space Activities.
"Russia objected to establishing a legal framework for this activity, arguing as follows: another satellite approaches and grabs an object – that is military activity, aggression," Hurova said.
The legal expert explained that removing a defunct satellite requires reaching an agreement and obtaining written consent from the country that owns it.
She also cited the example of Russia's destruction of one of its own satellites in November 2021, which generated a cloud of space debris.
According to Western media, on October 18, the Russian military satellite Kosmos-2612 made a dangerously close approach to Finland's ICEYE-X36 reconnaissance satellite, which provides imagery to Ukraine. Russia has repeatedly described such commercial satellites as potential military targets.

Raushan Kazhibayeva on TRC’s 30th anniversary, its media outlets and creating content about the President
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:38:51 UTC
17:38:51 KST

Raushan Kazhibayeva on TRC’s 30th anniversary, its media outlets and creating content about the President
The Television and Radio Complex of the President of Kazakhstan is marking its 30th anniversary. In an interview with Tengrinews.kz, TRC Director General Raushan Kazhibayeva spoke about how the media organization is changing, discussed Kazakhstani content and shared her views on the impact of artificial intelligence, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
- Thirty years is a considerable age for a domestic media organization. How has it changed over these three decades?
The Television and Radio Complex of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan was established by a government resolution on December 29, 1996, just before the New Year.
In its early years, the Television and Radio Complex mainly filmed official events, prepared video materials for state and commercial channels, and began filling what used to be called the “archive shelves.” At the time, production was analogue, and footage was stored on tapes. Today, we are completing the digitization of the archive, with servers and metadata offering descriptions and convenient searches replacing shelves of tapes and index cards.
By the late 1990s, TRC had begun making its first documentaries and videos, which were broadcast on Kazakhstani television channels. This new area of activity was formalized by a separate government resolution dated August 17, 1999. At the same time, TRC was transformed from a state institution into a closed non-commercial joint-stock company.
- TRC has changed its status several times over the past 30 years. Was this a search for the ideal management model?
I believe this was primarily related to changes in the country’s legislation. TRC has been a state institution, a closed non-commercial joint-stock company and simply a non-commercial joint-stock company.
Since 2019, work to develop TRC has been underway on the President’s instructions, with systematic support from the Presidential Administration of Affairs, of which TRC is a part.
- TRC is described as a presidential media resource. What meaning do you attach to this definition? Does it reflect the scale of production or new approaches to your work?
Above all, it means a systematic approach. TRC is a factory producing content about our President. And our main newsmaker is the President!
For me, a strong media system is one in which speed, editorial work, visual quality and distribution do not exist separately. They are linked by a shared responsibility for results. TRC is a cross-media company that, without false modesty, sets trends in television, international media and the digital space. We film, write and distribute content both in Kazakhstan and abroad.
Our main television outlet is Jibek Joly. Like TRC itself, Jibek Joly is a unique channel. Around a quarter of its daily airtime is broadcast live.
We were the first in Kazakhstan’s market to stop importing foreign series carrying an ideology alien to us. Their place in the broadcasting schedule was taken by our own original projects: Zhaña Uaqyt; Novoye Vremya; Taldau: Analytical Review; Bügin.Live; Senim Studiyasy; Dämdi.Life and others. Audiences have grown to love our projects, and the channel has retained its position among the country’s leading television channels.
We have accepted that one-way communication with audiences is gone for good. Today, viewers want to interact with the media outlet they have chosen. Live projects make precisely this possible. We are pleased that our audience does not watch passively but actively participates in creating content. Viewers become studio guests, can ask questions in real time and interact with presenters and show participants. In some projects, we have replaced traditional sets with live, dynamic footage from the capital’s streets.
Of course, we also remember that television remains the most widespread and accessible form of family leisure. Original shows, large-scale projects, films and animation bring thousands of viewers together every day in front of screens showing Jibek Joly.
This combination of live broadcasting, sought-after content and a balance of subjects and genres builds what matters most: viewers’ trust, which we value.
Our organization comprises six media outlets. Jibek Joly television’s work in the domestic market is complemented by a radio station of the same name, which also broadcasts in an interactive format. Listeners to our radio station, which broadcasts in Astana on 101.4 FM and is available online, also become guests in the studio and on air.
In recent years, Qazinform International News Agency has regained its status as the country’s leading news agency. Today, it ranks among the top three news outlets and has restored and expanded its network of international partners. It has become the region’s principal trusted hub, with its materials cited daily by global media from Japan to the United States.
Alongside Qazinform International News Agency, the channels under the Silk Way umbrella brand, Silk Way, Silk Way Cinema and Silk Way Prime, operate in the international information space.
These are the only international channels not only in Kazakhstan but throughout Central Asia, broadcasting abroad in six languages and reaching more than 120 countries. The channels have around 300 rebroadcasters and 22 official distributors abroad.
We also have a digital laboratory, a team of professionals of a new generation. They understand an audience that grew up with smartphones in their hands. Under the TRKLAB brand, they create vertical content, generate unique projects using AI and interact with readers across all relevant platforms. In total, we have several dozen accounts.
Our Documentary Film Center has also been modernized. For us, the center is the heart of our company, our qara shañyraq.
The team makes films for festivals, produces original content in foreign languages and was the first in the Central Asian market to release documentaries in a vertical format, an area it continues to develop.
Documentary projects in English, Chinese and French are broadcast by our foreign partners, while those in Kazakh and Russian are shown not only on national channels but also on more than three dozen regional channels.
- At the recent Astana Media Week, there was active discussion about how to make Kazakhstani content global and why translating it into a foreign language does not work. What do you think?
For us, this has been standard production practice since the launch of Silk Way. Since the revamped channel launched in 2022, all new projects for its broadcasts have been produced originally in English. We clearly understood that literal translation was a thing of the past and assembled a team of professionals who became the first in Kazakhstan and Central Asia to produce studio news and analysis in English.
In 2024, Qazinform’s English-language news moved to a global domain, qazinform.com. As the saying goes, “Content is King, but distribution is Queen.”
This year alone, materials produced by Silk Way and Qazinform have been cited by media in dozens of countries. Alongside neighboring Russia, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan, these include the United States, China, Japan, Korea, India, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Spain, Czechia, Hungary, Serbia, Bulgaria, Türkiye, Indonesia, Pakistan, the UAE, Qatar and many other countries in Europe, Asia and the Middle East, and even media in Peru, Chile, South Africa and Togo.
In total, content from our English-language media outlets, Silk Way and Qazinform, has been cited by foreign media around 6,000 times in 2026.
- Traditional television channels, news agencies and conventional media in general are often fairly conservative organizations that approach new technologies, especially artificial intelligence, with caution. How do things stand at TRC?
TRC combines the best traditions of conventional media, new media and technology, current trends and content formats, which together give us a cross-media approach and the ability to work across multiple formats.
Neural networks help us optimize routine tasks, freeing up time for creativity, and create unique content for broadcast and online platforms. The possibilities here are truly limitless.
Back in 2024, TRC was the first to make a short film in a vertical format. The capabilities of neural networks, unique at the time, allowed us to “bring to life” photographs of our President, many of which had originally been taken on ordinary photographic film.
Responsible and sensible use of AI allows us to accomplish a wide range of tasks for the public good. Last year, we used AI to create sign language interpretation for the animated series The Fixies for our broadcasts. This was our way of caring for our youngest viewers with special needs.
In addition, Jibek Joly aired 100 video lessons on digital literacy in 2025. All 100 episodes were created entirely through generation, without a single frame of live footage.
At Qazinform and in our newsrooms, AI searches for and initially processes information, transcribes audio and video, and creates images to illustrate articles. AI helps analyze large volumes of information, monitor foreign-language sources, conduct basic fact-checking and perform technical checks to ensure texts comply with the rules of the publication language.
At TRKLAB, our newsroom of a new generation, work with neural networks focuses on creating generative content and adapting materials from the news agency and television channels for a new type of reader who quickly tires of long articles and tends toward click-driven, short-form media consumption. AI helps shorten narratives and make them more concise without making them any less informative.
It is important to say that AI-based projects require substantial human involvement and are not created using just one neural network. We follow the Head of State’s principle: “Intelligent systems should not replace humans; they are intended to complement and enhance their capabilities.”
- What does “responsible and sensible use of AI” mean to you?
Our President has declared 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, and Kazakhstan is one of just five countries in the world [Editor’s note: the others are the UAE, the United Kingdom, Canada and Albania] where a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence has been established on the President’s instructions.
Meanwhile, many of our colleagues around the world are debating the future of journalism. They ask whether neural networks will replace humans and whether news journalism will become overwhelmed by synthetic content. Will we find ourselves immersed in an endless expanse of deepfakes?
We see AI as offering enormous potential and opportunities, rather than threats and scare stories. Of course, all these risks can materialize if we fail to exercise reasonable caution and approach our profession carelessly. But that is in our hands.
- Astana recently hosted the first global generative film festival, the Astana AI Film Festival. We watched the finalist entries and, we must say, were impressed. This is further evidence that Kazakhstan is one of the pioneers in adopting and using AI.
The idea for the festival belongs to Vice President Erlan Karin, while its implementation was the work of Almas Zhali and Aizatulla Khusein, young and talented leaders in Kazakhstan’s creative industry.
The festival received a total of 8,067 entries from 125 countries, amounting to more than 100,000 minutes of generative content. This is a truly world-class event with a substantial prize fund.
Without a doubt, this global project will become a regular event, as will the international televised music competition Silk Way Star, the first project by Kazakhstani creators to reach a global level. The first season attracted more than one billion viewers worldwide and was broadcast in nine countries. Citizens of 43 countries took part in the voting, while media in 60 countries cited news about the competition.
This year, together with our partners at China Media Group (CMG), we completed filming the second season in Yiwu, China. It will soon air on Jibek Joly. In China, the project is already being broadcast by two of the country’s leading television channels, CCTV 3 and CCTV 15.
The third season will be filmed in Kazakhstan next year.
- In your previous interview, you spoke about a regional television channel for Central Asian countries based on Silk Way. This October, at the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Awaza, our President emphasized the importance of creating a shared information space. How is this project progressing?
A regional channel for Central Asian countries based on Silk Way is one of our promising projects.
Today, colleagues from Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are working alongside us to provide regional content for Silk Way. We have signed several bilateral agreements with national broadcasters and the relevant authorities of partner countries.
In October, on the sidelines of the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan and the CIS Council of Heads of State in Awaza, Turkmenistan, we signed a historic agreement establishing a permanent Kazakh-Turkmen media council. This is the first document of its kind in the history of media cooperation between the two countries and in the region as a whole.
The pace of cooperation naturally varies, but it is sufficient to fill the first dedicated programming block on Silk Way devoted to Central Asia.
We continue working on a comprehensive interagency agreement between the relevant authorities of the region’s countries that would pave the way for systematic coordination and a full-fledged intergovernmental agreement. I hope we can bring this unfinished task to completion together with our colleagues at the Ministry of Culture and Information and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
- This year, Astana hosted two major events: CMG Week and the second Al Jazeera Week. On what terms do you work with the world’s largest media companies?
Today, we have 70 agreements with television and radio companies and news agencies from around the world. Our partners include Al Jazeera, China Media Group, TRT, Xinhua, Jiji Press, Kyodo, Yonhap, Aju News Corporation, Anadolu Agency, Agenzia Nova, Adnkronos, Belga News, VNA, ANI, Azertac, Petra, IRNA, WAM, Saudi Press Agency and many others.
We are also members of several international industry organizations and associations. TRC is a member of the technical committee of the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies, the Council of Heads of State and Public Television and Radio Organizations of CIS Member States, and the Interstate Information Pool. It is also an active participant in the Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation.
For our partners, TRC has become a hub for reliable and timely news from Kazakhstan and Central Asia, and this is their main reason for working with us.
To answer your question directly, we do not buy airtime or print space abroad. We have no financial relationships with any of our partners, and we have not paid for a single news story picked up by global agencies.
- In our previous conversations, you repeatedly spoke about problems in the country’s media market. You raised the near-monopoly in television advertising, weaknesses in the television audience measurement system and the need to protect domestic broadcasters. What is the situation now?
Indeed, over decades of operation, the country’s television, advertising and broader media markets accumulated numerous imbalances. Some have been eliminated through joint efforts, primarily by the regulator and market participants.
The television advertising market has become competitive, new players have emerged, and channels now have a genuine choice between advertising sales companies and the ability to negotiate terms. We have also significantly improved the television audience measurement system.
Thanks to the efforts of the National Media Association, of which TRC is an active member, audience measurement now covers the entire country, from major cities to small towns. We finally know what all Kazakhstanis watch and prefer, rather than only residents of large cities. Work is underway to integrate data from cable television operators into the audience measurement system.
- What, then, is the problem? Why are television channels complaining about falling revenues, while ratings are steadily declining? What needs attention?
The regulatory framework needs fine-tuning to protect the domestic information space in a rapidly changing market.
Today, domestic television operates under fairly strict regulation. We have requirements concerning the volume of domestic programming, language balance, and limits on the amount of advertising per day and per hour, as well as its content.
These requirements do not apply to foreign broadcasters. Yes, they do not earn advertising revenue in Kazakhstan, as this is prohibited. But they compete for our viewers’ attention while earning incomparably greater sums in their much larger home television advertising markets and receiving state support from their own countries.
There are no restrictions at all on the internet. We all watch content on YouTube, and what do we see? The number and duration of advertisements keep growing without any limits. This is despite the fact that most videos also contain advertising integrated by the creators themselves.
In practice, this means that a domestic advertiser paid the video hosting platform for an advertisement, the platform placed it, and a Kazakhstani viewer saw it, while YouTube itself and the content creator received the money. In other words, the money left Kazakhstan’s market and went abroad. Essentially, we are subsidizing content production by foreign creators while domestic producers are forced to cut costs, reduce spending on programming and face another wave of viewers leaving.
Domestic online outlets face a similar situation. We visit a foreign website and see advertisements for Kazakhstani companies. The advertiser has reached its audience, but the money has once again gone abroad, to the foreign outlet and the Google or Meta advertising network.
Numerous foreign online streaming services operating in Kazakhstan also remain outside the regulatory framework.
E-commerce platforms are a separate issue. E-commerce aggregators, which have never been media outlets, provide advertising services while producing no content for audiences. The advertising revenues of some are already comparable to the size of the entire television advertising market.
- But this is a global trend. The boundary of the information space is gradually disappearing and content is becoming a global product…
The trend is that content is becoming global while advertising money remains national. We have already discussed that trying to stop progress is impossible. We need to manage it properly, create a legal framework suited to current realities and fine-tune regulation in the interests of domestic media.
- How are you celebrating your anniversary?
We are trying to make our anniversary year beneficial to society and the industry as a whole. As you noted earlier, this year TRC organized two large-scale projects for media professionals and future journalists: CMG Week and Al Jazeera Week.
Leading professionals from two of the world’s largest media organizations spent a week sharing their experience and best practices, delivering lectures and conducting practical sessions.
From May to September, a nationwide film screening and lecture program was held in every region, allowing audiences to watch around 30 of our best documentaries free of charge on the big screen. Particular emphasis was placed on regional screenings, where, with the support of local administrations, projects about the Head of State’s activities and working people in Kazakhstan were shown. There was not a single empty seat at any screening.
Throughout the year, TRC’s senior managers delivered lectures to future journalists at the country’s leading universities, including Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University and Maqsut Narikbayev University.
An exclusive photo exhibition featuring more than 200 unique photographs of the President’s activities, along with several other large-scale events, is planned before the end of the year.
- And a final question. Working alongside our President allows you to see things that do not always appear in official coverage. Which personal qualities of the Head of State particularly impress you?
I admire his rare combination of intellectual depth and tact. The President sees issues in a broad context while always paying attention to details that may affect an individual’s life. His incredible capacity for work and exceptional breadth of knowledge cannot fail to impress.
The task of the President’s TRC creative team is to strive to meet the high standard personally set by the Head of State.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will deliver his annual State-of-the-Nation Address on October 28.

Nearly half of Dutch MPs use AI to write speeches in parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:35:52 UTC
17:35:52 KST

Nearly half of Dutch MPs use AI to write speeches in parliament
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Nearly half of Dutch MPs used artificial intelligence to help write speeches and statements delivered in parliament, according to an investigation based on the AI detection tool Pangram.
A scan of debates and committee hearings revealed that 68 of the 150 MPs from across the political spectrum used AI at least once. Most of the members admitted using artificial intelligence tools when asked by De Groene Amsterdammer and investigations website Investico.
The real number is likely to be higher because only contributions that were found to be more than 50% AI generated were included in the results.
Top of the list was former Pro MP Esmah Lahlah, who is now a member of Amsterdam city council’s executive after leaving parliament in June. The analysis found evidence of AI in her contributions to four debates on poverty and the law on jobseekers.
Lahlah said she sometimes used AI to summarise conversations she had with people during working visits. “Sometimes it was hard to condense those stories into a few minutes’ speaking time, so I used AI,” she said.
Most MPs wrote their own material for big set-piece debates such as the recent debate on the king’s speech, known as the Algemene Politieke Beschouwingen, which kicks off the parliamentary year. But more than half of contributions to committee hearings showed evidence of AI use, the analysis found.
“Rolled out by Chat”
Other frequent users included Rachel van Meetelen of the far-right PVV, who said she used it to make her statements more concise and effective. “I would never say anything in Parliament I didn’t support,” she said.
The heaviest users were right-wing parties such as Gidi Markuszower’s DNA group of former PVV MPs. Only the Socialists (SP), the animal rights party PvdD and Volt showed no use of AI at all.
Harmen Krul of the centre-right CDA also said he used AI to edit his speeches, but not generate content. “I would be dismayed if this created the impression that my contributions were rolled out by Chat,” he said.
Last month an analysis of 28,000 questions in parliament by national broadcaster NOS, again using Pangram, found that around a quarter showed stylistic features of AI.
Prime minister Rob Jetten also had to admit that he used AI to write social media posts, including personal reflections on sensitive subjects such as the mistreatment of Moluccan war veterans who came to the Netherlands in the 1950s.
He defended the practice at the time, saying: “Like three-quarters of Dutch people I sometimes use AI to make things better.”
Some MPs also dismissed the concerns raised by the latest analysis. Henk Vermeer, leader of the farmers’ party BBB, said AI was useful for small parties, after Pangram detected traces in 30% of speeches by his three MPs. “We also use calculators, mobile phones and even coffee makers,” he said.

Norway Hits Russian Banks, Crypto, and Shadow Fleet in Line With EU’s 21st Package
Norway has introduced a comprehensive new sanctions package against Russia, aligning its national measures with the European Union’s 21st sanctions package.
The updated restrictions take effect on October 21, following regulatory adjustments enacted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Pravda reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new measures establish broad economic restrictions targeting key pillars of the Russian economy.
Under the expanded framework, strict curbs apply to financial institutions, oil projects, cryptocurrency platforms, and military-industrial facilities supporting Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The measures also tighten monitoring of the shadow fleet used to transport Russian oil and expand existing restrictions across various export and import channels.
Norwegian officials stated that these policies aim to apply further financial pressure on Russia and restrict its capacity to fund ongoing aggression.
On October 8, 2026, the European Union extended sanctions against individuals and entities linked to Russia’s destabilizing activities abroad for another year, maintaining the measures until October 9, 2027, as announced by the Council of the European Union.
The restrictions applied to 80 individuals and 20 entities, subjecting them to asset freezes and travel bans, while prohibiting EU citizens and companies from making funds or economic resources available to them.
Official statements noted that the decision reflected Russia’s continued and intensified hybrid operations across Europe, which included foreign information manipulation, cyberattacks, sabotage, and interference targeting the EU, its member states, and partner countries.

Australian MP loses both legs in vehicle attack as suspect appears in court
Independent lawmaker Helen Haines is in stable condition, her husband says, as suspect charged with three offences.
Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines has had both of her legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said, as the suspected attacker appeared in court.
Doctors amputated the MP’s left leg after an attacker hit her twice with his car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They tried to save her right leg but failed to do so, he told a news conference on Wednesday.
“The good news in all this is Helen is alive, and she’s stable,” he told reporters. “That is the most important thing for our family.”
The suspect in the attack, revealed to be a 43-year-old man called Brendan Nugent, made a brief court appearance on Wednesday.
He has been charged with three crimes: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing injury and causing harm to a public official.
He was also charged with the cultivation and possession of cannabis, according to court filings.
The suspect’s lawyer said he has a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and is also recovering from a concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.
Police are still investigating the motive for the attack. Australia’s federal police commissioner Krissy Barrett said there was no intelligence suggesting any threat to Haines.
“What I can say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she told reporters.
Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in 2022 and 2025.
Attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, but concerns have been growing in recent years as online abuse and threats against elected officials have risen.

UNHCR and Vinnytsia Regional State Administration strengthen cooperation to support displaced people and regional recovery
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:34:36 EEST
17:34:36 KST

© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
Today, UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, and the Vinnytsia Regional State Administration signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen support for internally displaced people, returnees and others affected by the ongoing war, while contributing to the region’s recovery.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Vinnytsia region has provided shelter and assistance to people forced to flee their homes. Today, the region hosts around 144, 000 internally displaced people. Alongside immediate assistance, displaced people need access to stable housing, essential services, and opportunities to rebuild their lives. Through their cooperation, UNHCR and the regional administration aim to address these needs, support the communities hosting displaced people, and help families find lasting solutions.
© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
“Displaced people bring skills, experience and determination to the communities that welcome them. Practical barriers, from finding suitable housing to restoring documents and accessing services, can make it difficult to start again. By working with the Vinnytsia regional authorities, we can help remove these barriers so people can regain independence, make decisions about their future and take an active part in community life,” said Bernadette Castel-Hollingsworth, UNHCR’s Representative in Ukraine.
“UNHCR is an important partner for Vinnytsia region in supporting people affected by the war. Russia has intensified its attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure, including in our region. At the same time, Vinnytsia continues to host around 144,000 internally displaced people, for whom access to housing remains a pressing need.
The memorandum we have signed will strengthen our joint efforts to develop long-term housing solutions for people who have moved to the region because of the war, repair damaged homes and assist families affected by Russian attacks. I thank UNHCR for its partnership and readiness to continue supporting those who need it most,” said Natalia Zabolotna, Head of the Vinnytsia Regional State Administration.
© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
Housing is a central area of cooperation, especially through repairs to homes for displaced women, men, girls and boys and the search of sustainable housing solutions for people accommodated in collective sites. This year, UNHCR resumed support for home repairs for displaced people in the region, with work on 40 private homes underway. The memorandum also covers legal assistance, psychosocial support, access to social services, cash assistance, essential household items and winter support. This cooperation builds on assistance already delivered across the region. Since 2022, UNHCR and its partners have provided legal assistance to more than 44,000 people and psychosocial support to more than 30,000. Over 77,000 people received essential relief items between 2022 and 2024.
UNHCR has also supported repairs to 142 homes for displaced people in 2023–2024 and the creation of temporary housing for 14 households in Shypynky in 2024–2025. Repairs to 40 private homes currently underway are scheduled for completion by the end of 2026.
© Vinnytsia Regional State Administration
In Lukashivka, Ladyzhyn community, the QTochok pilot project will provide fully equipped homes on communal land for 10 displaced families comprising more than 50 people, with completion planned by the end of 2026. Designed for families unable to return home for the foreseeable future, the new settlement will offer long-term housing close to services and employment opportunities in nearby Ladyzhyn.
UNHCR also supports IDP Councils through strategic planning, advice and information activities. Under the memorandum, UNHCR and the regional administration will strengthen links with humanitarian, recovery and development partners and international financial institutions, helping connect emergency assistance with longer-term recovery and lasting solutions for people affected by the war.

‘People are starving’: Survivors recount horrors of Ukrainian siege (VIDEO)
Ukrainian forces have effectively laid siege to the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region, leaving civilians facing acute shortages of food, water, and medicine, residents who managed to escape have told RT.
Located on the left bank of the Dnieper River opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, the town has been largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months. Russian authorities estimate that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians remain trapped there, including elderly residents and around 15 children.
Kherson Governor Vladimir Saldo has accused Kiev’s forces of deliberately choking off humanitarian deliveries to Alyoshki by remotely mining access roads and targeting vehicles carrying food, fuel, and medicine. Strikes have also damaged the town’s energy and communications infrastructure, deepening the humanitarian crisis.
Russian forces have partially broken through the blockade by clearing some roads, but continued shelling and drone attacks hamper regular aid deliveries. Regional children’s rights commissioner Irina Kravchenko said on Tuesday that aid is reaching the town, but remains woefully insufficient.
Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik earlier described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukrainian troops of preventing civilians from fleeing and obstructing the recovery of bodies.
The crisis has also reached the highest diplomatic levels. Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, discussed the situation during a phone call earlier this month. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, has said she is in contact with US First Lady Melania Trump’s team, which has expressed willingness to help civilians.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately creating the humanitarian emergency while attempting to shift the blame onto Russia. Saldo has invited international organizations to visit Alyoshki and witness the conditions firsthand.
Residents who escaped the town have given harrowing accounts of hunger, destroyed homes, dwindling food supplies, and drones terrorizing civilians.
“The town is burning. There’s nothing left intact,” one evacuee said, describing a destroyed water pump and food prices soaring beyond residents’ reach. She claimed no food supplies have entered the town since May, leaving people “starving.” RT spoke exclusively to Alyoshki evacuees about their struggle to survive and the desperate plight of those left behind.

Council of Europe sees Ukraine gains on Roma, LGBTI rights
Ukraine

Ukraine is making significant progress in the legislative protection of Roma and LGBTI people, but gaps remain in areas such as equality, hate crime and integration, the Council of Europe's European Commission against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI) said in a new report published in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
ECRI, "recognizing the exceptional circumstances caused by Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, identifies the legislative and policy progress achieved and the gaps that remain in three main areas: effective equality and access to rights, hate speech and hate-motivated violence, and integration and inclusion," it said.
The report welcomes several positive developments, ECRI said. The Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights stepped up work on non-discrimination and strengthened cooperation with civil society.
"More training and guidance has been provided to police on investigating hate crimes, including through stronger international cooperation. New strategies and policies on Roma inclusion have been adopted, and good examples of proactive work with Roma communities have been given. ECRI also welcomes a number of political commitments made on LGBTI equality," it said.
At the same time, ECRI noted remaining problems, particularly on the situation of Roma and LGBTI people.
"Despite positive developments, some issues are of concern. Roma and LGBTI people appear to be particularly affected by hate speech, even if a decline in the overall number of hate speech cases since the start of the full-scale war is reported," it said in a press release.
According to the report, many hate incidents continue to be misclassified and not treated as such by police and prosecutors. Access to health care for LGBTI people, especially transgender people, also remains a problem. Gaps were found in school curricula on including Roma history and culture and LGBTI-related topics in a sensitive and age-appropriate way. Incidents involving allegations of racist or LGBTI-phobic misconduct by officers of the National Police, the State Border Guard Service and the Armed Forces were reported.
ECRI listed 15 recommendations for the Ukrainian authorities. Among them, the authorities should take measures to ensure access to quality education for Roma children, for example through information and awareness initiatives with Roma mediators and families. ECRI also recommended measures to combat and prevent LGBTI-phobic bullying in schools, and to improve equality and hate crime legislation by explicitly including sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, ethnic origin and skin color in the list of protected characteristics.
"ECRI stresses the need for priority implementation of two recommendations. The first says that the authorities should, in cooperation with civil society, carry out nationwide information campaigns aimed at preventing hate speech, including against LGBTI people and Roma. The second calls on the Ukrainian authorities to set up an inclusive working group to proactively identify Roma who lack proper identity documents and provide them with appropriate support. This involves further simplifying administrative procedures and, where needed, providing targeted assistance to overcome administrative barriers," it said.
The report covers the period from June 2017 to March 2026 and follows a visit to the country in September 2025. Interim monitoring will be carried out within two years of the report's publication to assess measures taken by the authorities to implement the two priority recommendations.

Can China turn national power into world leadership?
China has all the signs of world-topping national strength but whether other countries accept its leadership will depend on what’s on offer
As turbulence grows in many countries, it is tempting to ask if there is a global hegemon that can sort everything out fairly.
Our latest projections of national strength for 2027 take into account resources, territory, economic strength and military power. They still put China in first place, with its lead over other countries widening. But when might China move beyond leading the ranking to exert decisive influence over the world’s trouble spots and become a global arbiter?
To explore that question, we should first look at how states have assessed national power. Ancient rulers counted people, revenues, troops, ships and resources but these were separate assessments, not a single measure of national power.
