Expenditures by ministries and government agencies in the Ukrainian draft 2027 state budget can be reduced by UAH 161.5 billion, with the funds redirected to defense needs.
"This is the next set of our amendments to bill No. 16000," Nina Yuzhanina, a member of parliament from the European Solidarity faction, wrote on Facebook.

Instead, the released funds should be allocated exclusively to defense and strengthening the Armed Forces of Ukraine. According to party leader Petro Poroshenko, reallocating non-targeted expenditures would make it possible to direct at least an additional half a trillion hryvnias to the military.
"Our demands are specific: at least UAH 500 billion in additional funding for the military to purchase weapons and defense technologies; 30% of the military personal income tax revenue to go directly to brigades; indexation of military pay; protection of the energy sector and the economy; cancellation of non-priority and propaganda-related expenditures; fulfillment of European commitments and restoration of our allies' trust," Poroshenko said.

Universities, academies, and schools of all levels in Armenia celebrated the 26th edition of Italian Language Week Around the World, dedicated to the theme “Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian.”
The guest of honor for the Week was the Italian writer of Armenian origin, Antonia Arslan. Following Ambassador Ferranti’s introductory remarks at the opening ceremony, held at Yerevan State University, Arslan delivered a presentation on language as a creative tool, also emphasizing the importance of language for individual identity and the pain resulting from its loss or deprivation—an experience shared by many Armenians who, like her, grew up far from their homeland.
                                    
Subsequently, Antonia Arslan presented the Western Armenian translation of her book *The Book of Mush* at the Zangak bookstore in Yerevan. Ambassador Ferranti also welcomed Arslan to the Residence, along with several representatives of the Italian cultural community in Armenia from the academic, journalistic, and religious spheres. This convivial gathering provided an opportunity for dialogue and the exchange of experiences at the crossroads between Italy and Armenia, where the Italian language is playing an increasingly prominent role as a tool for connection and sharing.
                                    
Earlier in the week, Yerevan also hosted a delegation from the University for Foreigners of Perugia—which is celebrating the centennial of its founding this year—composed of Sabrina Stroppa, full professor of Italian Literature; Roberto Vetrugno, associate professor in the Department of Italian Language, Literature, and Arts in the World; and Corrado Losito, head of the university’s International Relations Office.
                                    
The delegation, accompanied by Ambassador Ferranti, signed a memorandum of understanding at V. Brusov State University with Rector Davit Gyurjinyan. The agreement between the two universities represents a step forward in academic cooperation between Armenia and Italy and aims to strengthen scientific and cultural cooperation between the two institutions, as well as to promote the teaching of the Italian language in Armenia. Finally, faculty members from the University of Perugia gave lectures to students in the Faculty of European Languages and Communication at Yerevan State University and to students in the Department of Italian Studies at V. Brusov State University.

Prince Harry on family rift: ‘Some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:06:19 UTC
17:06:19 KST

Prince Harry has once again expressed his desire to repair his fractured relationship with his older brother, Prince William, and their father, King Charles III. But his latest comments have already prompted controversy, with the Duke of Sussex's spokesperson forced to clarify that a remark about people who do not want reconciliation was not intended as criticism of any member of the royal family.
In an interview with Zach Baron for GQ, published Tuesday, October 20, Harry, 42, discussed the painful family divisions that have dominated headlines for years. Asked whether he grieves his complicated relationships with William and Charles, the prince acknowledged that he does, describing family estrangement as something many people can identify with. He said disagreements between siblings and broken relationships between parents and children frequently arise in conversations with members of the public.
Harry suggested that the intense interest in his family's troubles reflects how common such experiences are, and that people might learn something from seeing how he handles his own situation. But one comment immediately attracted attention: "And some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out." When Baron pressed him on whether he genuinely wanted reconciliation, Harry insisted that repairing relationships was his priority, saying that with everything happening around the world, "the most important thing is to reconcile."
The remark about people supposedly resisting reconciliation was widely interpreted as a possible reference to William, who has remained estranged from his younger brother. Shortly after the interview was published, however, Harry's spokesperson rejected that interpretation. In a statement reported by People, the spokesperson said the comment was "absolutely not intended as a swipe at his brother or any other member of his family." The spokesperson stressed that Harry was making a general observation rather than accusing his relatives of blocking reconciliation.
The relationship between the two princes began deteriorating around 2018, and tensions intensified after Harry and Meghan Markle stepped back from royal duties in 2020 and moved to California. Their subsequent interviews, Netflix documentary series and Harry's memoir Spare, published in January 2023, exposed deeply personal grievances about the royal family. In the book, Harry described an alleged physical confrontation with William, further damaging a relationship that had once been presented as exceptionally close.
Now, after six years in the United States, Harry and Meghan have returned to Britain with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. The family moved back in late August, and Harry told GQ that providing the children with a British education and allowing them to experience the country where he grew up were important factors in the decision. He also expressed hope that old disputes involving his family and the British press could eventually be left behind.
Harry appeared particularly determined to move beyond the bitterness of recent years. Asked whether the wounds within his family could be repaired, he acknowledged that "scars stick around forever" but emphasized the importance of letting go of past grievances. The interview, conducted in New York in late September, also explored his lifelong struggle with grief following the death of his mother, Princess Diana, and the ways that loss has shaped his relationships and approach to parenting.
There are signs that Harry's relationship with King Charles is improving. According to People, a source close to the prince described their relationship as better than it had been. Charles reunited with Harry, Meghan and their children in July, and father and son have spoken at least once since the Sussexes returned to Britain on August 26. However, those developments have not translated into progress with William, with a source close to Harry telling the magazine that the brothers remain out of contact.
Sources close to William and Kate Middleton, the Princess of Wales, say the emotional wounds behind the estrangement have not healed. One palace source recently told People that the fallout had been extremely difficult for the couple and that William's reluctance to reconnect was understandable. The assessment suggests that even if Charles is prepared to rebuild his relationship with his younger son, the Prince of Wales remains far less willing to do the same.
Royal author Russell Myers, whose book William and Catherine examines the couple's relationship and public roles, offered an even more pessimistic outlook. Speaking to People, Myers said William considers his father's relationship with Harry to be entirely Charles' decision. But Myers believes the future king has no intention of restoring ties with Harry and Meghan, whether officially or privately, describing the possibility of a relationship "in a working or private capacity whatsoever" as effectively closed.
Harry's latest interview therefore highlights the distance between his public desire for reconciliation and the reality of his relationship with William. While his return to Britain and improving ties with Charles may represent meaningful changes, the brothers' estrangement appears no closer to being resolved. For now, Harry says he wants to move forward, but there is little indication that William is prepared to join him.

The Association for Modern Trade has stressed that neither a markup nor a gross margin represents a retailer's net profit. It also argued that profit levels in Bulgaria are comparable to those across the European Union, including Germany.

Leaders of the four Quad nations will convene next month on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday.
“It’s been agreement now that we’re going to do it; we’re going to do it in Manila, at the ASEAN conference,” Rubio told Indian broadcaster CNN-News18.

The planned gathering will mark the first leaders’ summit of the diplomatic partnership since September 2024. India originally held the rotation to host the dialogue, but scheduling challenges delayed the meeting.
US President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit Manila and Shenzhen in November, attending ASEAN-related meetings in the Philippines before traveling to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting on Nov. 18-19, where he is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Europe is in trouble, and it is blaming Muslims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:02:49 UTC
17:02:49 KST

Europe is in trouble, and it is blaming Muslims
A recent European Parliament resolution shows the European mainstream is fully embracing an Islamophobic agenda.
As protests in France turned violent late last week, the French far right quickly resorted to racist language to blame the Muslim youth for the violence. Weeks earlier, when thousands of migrants tried to enter the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco, the Spanish far right spoke of an organised “invasion” by Moroccans.
United States President Donald Trump has also chimed in, claiming that this is about “Islam wanting to take over”.
While the far right’s readiness to exploit crises to fuel Islamophobia is to be expected, the idea that Islam and Muslims are to blame for Europe’s growing woes is no longer reserved for that extreme of the European political spectrum.
Last week, while student protests were heating up in France, the European Parliament quietly passed a resolution “on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network”. The text was tabled by the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), the largest group in the parliament, which European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hails from.
It passed with 381 votes in favour, 167 against and 15 abstentions. Four other groups backed the EPP almost unanimously: the far-right Patriots for Europe and Europe of Sovereign Nations, the liberal Renew Europe, and the European Conservatives and Reformists.
The Social Democrats, the Left and the Greens mostly voted against but could not stop it.
The resolution, which draws on a highly problematic report by the French government on “political Islamism”, makes a number of flawed claims that have wide-ranging implications for Muslim communities.
It defines “Islamist entryism” as “a political strategy of influence, progressive structuring, institutional penetration and ideological legitimisation”. It claims that “Islamist influence operates through a broad and fragmented ecosystem of associations, foundations and cultural, educational, religious, charitable, university, youth, anti-discrimination or social action structures”.
More specifically, it says that “diversity, equity, inclusion and anti-discrimination frameworks may be diverted as vectors of institutional legitimisation, by integrating a politicised religious identity into legitimate causes for the protection of minorities”. In other words, networks like the Muslim Brotherhood “infiltrate” European societies through anti-Islamophobia initiatives.
The resolution is not binding and European Union member states do not have to implement it. Its call to put the Muslim Brotherhood and affiliated individuals and entities on a terror list is unlikely to be implemented across Europe, given the movement’s renunciation of violence as a political tool.
However, the resolution still gives legitimacy to an ideological framework that can have grave implications for Muslim communities.
It puts under suspicion Muslim institutions and organisations that operate independently of the state and presents the inclusion of Muslim civil society in public activity as a form of infiltration.
The resolution names several organisations, including the Brussels-based European Network Against Racism (ENAR), as espousing this type of “Islamist” behaviour, and calls for blocking access to EU funding and restricting any EU-funded entity from working with them. The vague notion of a “Muslim Brotherhood network” can make guilt by association possible for almost anyone.
This can easily be weaponised by outside actors and already has been. The United Arab Emirates, for example, has funded a wide-ranging campaign in Europe and elsewhere to smear individuals and organisations as Muslim Brotherhood affiliates. Interestingly, a few months before the resolution was tabled, an Emirati ambassador participated in a conference titled “Muslim Brotherhood: A real threat to Europe” held at the European Parliament. While Emirati influence is there, the resolution itself problematises “foreign funding” that allegedly supports “Islamist entryism” from Qatar or Turkiye, another indication of the geopolitics behind the scenes.
Most importantly, the resolution frames defending Muslims against racism as part of an Islamist infiltration plot. This can directly impact initiatives and public debates that seek to address Islamophobia in European societies.
Symbolically, the resolution is a major victory for Europe’s right-wing anti-Muslim forces. It shows that the European Parliament has started abandoning any firewall against the far right as the centre right draws closer and closer to the far right. The EPP appears to have almost completely absorbed the far-right agenda but seeks to cushion it in the language of national security.
The resolution also demonstrates how European Islamophobia has evolved. The fear is no longer of the immigrants as strangers who fail to “integrate” but of the Muslims who are able to speak for themselves and defend their civil liberties.
For the centre right, this Islamophobic framework comes with political perks. Not only is it able to benefit electorally from anti-Muslim fearmongering, but it is also able to strike at those on the left who choose to reject racism and stand up for Muslim communities.
It is no surprise that the idea of “Islamo-leftism” – Islamo-gauchisme in French – is being promoted on the political scene in France. Jean-Luc Melenchon of the left-wing La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) is particularly popular among marginalised communities and a strong contender for the presidency. He is now being accused of encouraging the “rioters”, who – it is implied – are Muslim.
This dual attack on the left and on Muslims mirrors the old Judeo-Bolshevik conspiracy theory that blamed Jews for the spread of communism with the aim of destroying Western civilisation.
Today, “Islamo-leftism” serves conservatives, liberals and the far right alike as a scapegoat in their effort to complete a counter-revolution against the modest progress the West has made on tackling racism and inequality since the 1960s. Their project appears to be a fortress Europe without Muslims.
However flimsy the basis of the “Islamist entryism” resolution is, we should expect further legally dubious moves by conservative alliances in individual member states to curb Muslim agency outside state control, especially when it defends Muslim civil liberties. Meanwhile, fearmongers will keep blaming Islam for social ills and for legitimate protests against austerity, and politicians will keep directing public anger at Muslim communities to distract from their own governance failures.
What is needed now is a strong response to this conservative counter-revolution through a firm defence of civil liberties for everyone.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Seven Challenger 3 tank prototypes delivered for trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:00:23 BST
17:00:23 KST

Seven Challenger 3 prototype vehicles have been delivered for the Demonstration Phase trials programme, with an eighth in the final stages of build, and the vehicles are being used to demonstrate and assure the performance and safety of the tank in preparation for manufacture, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Correction 21/10/1990: this article originally said Challenger 3 was moving from a smoothbore gun to a rifled barrel. It is the other way round. Challenger 2 has the rifled gun and Challenger 3 has the smoothbore. The two were simply mixed up, and the text has been corrected. Thanks to the reader who pointed it out.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked how many Challenger 3 tanks have been delivered to date, following an answer given on 8 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Seven Challenger 3 prototype vehicles have been delivered to date for use in the Demonstration Phase trials programme, with an eighth prototype vehicle in the final stages of build. These vehicles are being used to demonstrate and assure the performance and safety of the Challenger 3 capability in preparation for manufacture.”
Challenger 3 takes the hull of the existing Challenger 2 and gives it a new turret, a smoothbore gun firing NATO standard ammunition, modular armour, an active protection system and a new sighting and fire control fit. Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land is building the vehicles at Telford under a contract covering one hundred and forty eight tanks, and the first prototype rolled off the production line in 2024.
The Demonstration Phase is where the design is proved before the department commits to building the rest, and the programme needs eight prototypes to run the firing, mobility, electromagnetic and safety trials in parallel.
The move from a rifled gun to a smoothbore reverses decades of British practice and was driven by ammunition supply, since the rifled 120mm round Challenger 2 fires is made for no other army in NATO and the industrial base behind it had shrunk to almost nothing. Common ammunition means Challenger 3 can draw from allied stockpiles, which matters more now than it did when the choice was first debated.
Delivery of the full fleet runs towards the end of the decade, with an initial operating capability planned for 2027 and full operating capability by 2030, and the one hundred and forty eight tanks will equip two armoured regiments inside 3rd (UK) Division.
Britain operated nearly four hundred Challenger 2 at the start of the century, and the conversion programme covers fewer than half that number.

Apple showcases upcycled found furniture and banana palm-paper lantern at Designers of Tomorrow show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Apple showcases upcycled found furniture and banana palm-paper lantern at Designers of Tomorrow show
Designers Parafernalia, Yoonjeong Lee, Salem S Charabi and Isabel Rower will celebrate “the art in the making” at technology brand Apple‘s Designers of Tomorrow exhibition at Design Miami.Paris.
The emerging designers, who have all designed furniture or lighting, were chosen by exhibition curator Rodman Primack, together with a jury that included Design Miami president Jennifer Roberts and designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
For its latest edition of the exhibition, which opens today, Apple wanted to showcase how its products are used by emerging designers in the process of creating their pieces.
“Designers of Tomorrow celebrates the process – the art in the making,” Apple said in a statement.
“Each of the designers use Apple products in a variety of ways within their creative processes, from early ideation to creation,” the company continued.
“Apple has long believed that the full potential of their products is only fully realised when put in the hands of the world’s most talented creatives.”
Among the works on show will be Egyptian-Danish designer Charabi‘s delicate lamp, made from date palm from Saqqara, limestone from the Galala Mountains and paper made from banana palms in the Nile Delta.
The theme of the exhibition this year was Design for Presence, which Charabi took into consideration by pondering “what is present?”
“A structure inspired by the date palm-cleaving methods of the qafassin, makers of boxes and trays used in the country’s souks and bakeries,” the designer said.
“A skin created by multiple layerings of banana stems, found in Beheira, in the Nile Delta of Egypt,” he continued. “A mass carved from limestone from the Galala Mountains, carrying the trace of its making through repetitive patterns.”
Seoul-based artist Lee, meanwhile, explored how objects can change their functions by using a pencil to nail paper to a surface, before taking the idea further by creating a lamp.
“For this project, I took that approach further, using wood to build a table that holds the pencil nail and paper, completing the piece as a three-dimensional lamp,” Lee explained.
“To make the table, I repeatedly stacked thin sheets of veneer to build a new, solid piece of wood – approximately 5,000 layers, perhaps more.”
Designer Rower used upcycled furniture for her piece, which she then decorated with ceramic beads.
“The chair was made using found furniture left on the curb near my studio in Brooklyn, reconstituted into a wooden armature onto which I built up layers of papier-mâché and a pulp composite containing wood glue, sawdust, and paper pulp made from shredded waste paper,” Rower said.
After spraying the surface of the chair with black paint, she glued 1,500 handmade ceramic beads to it.
The final designers taking part, Sebastián Zorrilla and Genki Matsumura of studio Parafernalia, created their design, MonoAmbiente 1, as a “landscape”.
“Its acid-etched stainless steel surfaces invite closer observation as light reveals and conceals details across them,” the designers said.
“As it unfolds, the landscape unfolds with it: rocks become stools and a table, turning a distant scene into a place for two to converse, play, or share a drink,” the designers continued.
Apple first launched Designers of Tomorrow at Design Miami.Paris last year, when it showed pieces including a table designed to look like butter.
Designers of Tomorrow takes place at Design Miami.Paris 2026 from 21 to 25 October 2026 at L’hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:56:14 UTC
16:56:14 KST

‘It’s hard for us’: Paris small businesses bear brunt of protest violence
Shopkeepers – including those from immigrant backgrounds – count losses from violence last weekend.
Paris, France – Jagged shards of glass frame the hole kicked through the window of Hassan Rashdul’s mobile phone shop near Place de la Republique, the epicentre of looting and rioting that swept this part of Paris on Saturday.
“I was crying,” Rashdul says, as he watches a CCTV livestream on his phone.
The glass countertop is shattered, the floor carpeted with broken glass. The display cases that were full of new and reconditioned mobile phones, iPads, and computers are empty. The walls where headphones, cables, phone cases and other accessories hung have been stripped bare.
“It’s really terrible,” the 32-year-old Rashdul says. “It was very, very hard for us… It’s already hard for small business owners like us. We’re not operating to keep the business going, but just to survive, really.”
Rashdul says he’s lost at least 70,000-euros ($78,600) worth of stock. His insurance won’t cover it, because loss from theft wasn’t included in his policy, though Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said the government will cover employee salaries of about 3,000 businesses across France affected by the rioting.
There will also be a “dedicated support fund” to help businesses restock, the French government has announced. Lecornu has ordered more than 200 investigators to work on catching the perpetrators of the riots and looting.
But the rioters are moving quickly: Some businesses say they found their stock being sold online within hours of being looted.
“Stolen items from this weekend are being offered for sale on certain platforms,” digital minister Anne Le Henanff said on X. “We expect these platforms to remove the listings in question without delay.”
She held a meeting with representatives of six platforms in the presence of Interior and Justice Ministry officials. According to the French commerce ministry, representatives of Vinted, Amazon, eBay, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok, as well as French online retail association Fevad, were invited.
“They will also be required to cooperate closely with state authorities so that those reselling stolen goods can be prosecuted,” Le Henanff added.
Around Rashdul’s shop, there are mini-markets, opticians, phone stores and cafes that bear testimony to the violence last weekend.
Some are boarded up. Others, where there’s nothing left to steal, have been left open and exposed to the damp October weather by their owners.
But amid his suffering, Rashdul spots a glimmer of hope.
“There’s another side to it,” he says, “a positive – local customers, people from the neighbourhood.”
These people have set up appeals on social media to secure help for shopkeepers, he says.
“They really make you want to try again,” says Rashdul. “People are helping us to rebuild our shop, to get back to work and serve this neighbourhood once again.”
But it will not be easy. It took Rashdul, who immigrated to France from Bangladesh, 10 years to build his business. He now calls himself a proud French citizen – respectful of the right to protest but also worried about the impact of violence on businesses like his, and on France as a whole.
“Even though I want to rebuild, next Saturday they’ve announced another protest,” he says. “I know we’re in a democracy and there’s a right to protest, but if that ends up in more looting, then that’s hard on France and damaging for its international reputation.”

Musk said that a merger between Tesla and SpaceX was under consideration
Kyiv • UNN
Tesla and SpaceX have formed committees to study a possible merger, but there are not yet any terms for the deal. The final decision will be made by shareholders.
Elon Musk said he likes the idea of merging Tesla and SpaceX, his two best-known companies, and that it is being actively considered. UNN reports this, citing the BBC.
Details
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a conversation with financial analysts about SpaceX's quarterly business results on Tuesday, October 20.
Although Musk said that such a merger should not be taken for granted and would require shareholder support, he said that special committees had been formed at both companies to study the move.
"The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any deal, and there is no guarantee that they will do so," Musk added. "But I think the merger has many advantages and a lot could be achieved."
With Tesla valued at approximately $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at $2 trillion, combining the two companies would become one of the largest mergers in history.
SpaceX shares rose 8% after the market closed.
The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding by offering cloud computing capacity to other technology companies, such as Anthropic and Google.
This business line became SpaceX's most profitable segment, generating $7.5 billion, according to its latest quarterly results. Starlink also recorded revenue of $5.2 billion.
However, SpaceX as a whole is not profitable and has lost $1.1 billion since the beginning of the year.
Shares of Tesla, which will publish its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after declining slightly over several weeks.
Over the past year, Musk has begun combining more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before SpaceX went public at the beginning of this year, it acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which were owned by Musk.
The recent launch of Terafab, a joint Tesla and SpaceX project to produce computer chips, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more efficient when working together, the publication notes.
On Tuesday, Musk said that a full merger of the two companies would make sense for the work each performs in chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after SpaceX's stock-market debut at the beginning of this year, said that he is not a member of either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
Elon Musk has become the world's first dollar trillionaire12.06.26, 19:39 • 38575 views
He described himself as an "interested party" as the chief executive officer of Tesla and SpaceX.
Even while commenting on the possibility of merging the two companies, Musk compared it to "tap-dancing in a minefield."
He added that shareholders would ultimately decide on the merger. At least 50% of Tesla shareholders must approve the merger, which Musk called "a fairly high hurdle to clear."
Shareholders have supported Musk's wishes before. Last year, a majority of Tesla investors approved a compensation package for Musk worth approximately $1 trillion.
Although Tesla is known as an electric-vehicle manufacturer, Musk has recently been redirecting resources there to work on robotics.
SpaceX, with its growing focus on artificial intelligence infrastructure, quickly overtook Tesla in market value when it debuted on the stock market.

‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:55:28 UTC
16:55:28 KST

‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors
French police face allegations of excessive force against student protesters, with injuries to minors deepening mistrust between authorities and youth.
Paris, France — Enzo, 17, said a police officer grabbed his arm as another struck him from behind with a baton. With his head covered in blood, he was hospitalised and needed stitches.
Eden, a 14-year-old, cannot talk right now. His jaw was smashed after a police officer fired a tear gas grenade at his face in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumone.
Mael, 16, cannot see from her right eye after being struck by a rubber-bullet launcher fired by the police.
Since mid-September, when French high school students started revolting against the education system they say has failed them, police tactics have come under scrutiny. Lawyers and protesters who spoke to Al Jazeera accused police of stirring violence and resentment, rather than seeking to de-escalate tensions.
While authorities in France have defended the police over their actions as a necessity, violence against minors will deepen the gap between the state and its citizens, experts and lawyers say.
“They are losing a generation,” said Ainoha Pascual, a lawyer at the Paris Bar. “The government is implementing a strategy of terror. Because when you maim someone, when you seriously injure someone, it means that that person, and indeed everyone around them, will not return to demonstrations.”
Demonstrations over education have morphed into a nationwide protest movement that over the weekend saw violent clashes.
‘I am still traumatised’
In the case of Enzo, videos verified by Al Jazeera show a peaceful crowd of teachers forming a chain in front of students. Police officers break through the cordon and, while advancing, use batons and pepper spray at close range. Screams of panic fill the air.
“I am still traumatised. Instead of protecting us, they are attacking us,” Enzo said.
According to his lawyer Elsa Marcel, Eden was sitting alone on a low wall looking at his phone, a few metres from the school protest, when three police officers approached him. Videos of the incident appear to show an officer striking the teenager with a baton before another officer fired a tear-gas grenade into his face. Marcel said the shot was fired from about 1.5 metres (5 feet) away, and accused officers of leaving the boy on the ground without calling emergency services. His family has filed a complaint for attempted murder.
“Within this social movement, this is unprecedented, especially considering that these are all minors,” said Mathilde Lante, Enzo’s lawyer and member of the Collective for Legal Action (CAJ).
French authorities denied that police were engaging in repression during the high-school protests, pointing to the hundreds of law enforcement personnel who had been injured.
In early October, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said there were “no instructions for restraint” given to police officers, stressing that the use of force had to remain proportionate. In early October, the Justice Ministry instructed prosecutors to pursue a rapid and firm response to violence during the protests, including considering parents’ civil liability for actions by minors.
Meanwhile, France’s police watchdog, the IGPN, has opened 36 inquiries into alleged misconduct. Nearly 6,900 people have been placed in police custody since the start of the protests, 86 percent of them minors, Interior Ministry figures show.
Such a tough stance seems to have only galvanised the protesters.
More than half a million people took to the streets over the weekend, about 100,000 in the capital Paris alone.
“We are too young to be taken seriously; we are grown up enough to be beaten up,” was one of the slogans on repeat.
On Saturday, police fired tear gas and stun grenades well before marches started, a move that critics said set the tone for what would become a tense day.
Police blocked roads to exit the square in Paris. Only a few narrow exit routes were left for people to leave the site. That meant that thousands were stuck and compressed, leading to fainting and panic attacks.
This is what experts call “la nasse”, or kettling, a controversial tactic in which officers encircle and contain demonstrators. It has long drawn criticism from rights groups over its impact on freedom of movement and the right to protest.
Allegations of police brutality over the years
The student-led protests ended up catalysing wider grievances in a country dealing with fiscal, political and now social crises. At times, the streets of Paris have been home to violence and vandalism.
On Saturday and Sunday, as night descended, groups of young people ransacked, set on fire and looted shops in riots.
“For the past three weeks, we’ve been hearing that ‘the police kill’ or ‘the police injure people’. And then, for the past two days, we’ve been asked, ‘What is the police doing?’ A very French kind of schizophrenia,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday.
This is not the first time the police have come under fire.
During the “yellow vest” protests – a period of unrest that started in 2018 over diesel price hikes and morphed into a social movement in which demonstrators wore yellow vests – officers faced criticism over their use of force, with protesters suffering serious injuries from rubber bullets and stun grenades.
In June 2023, the fatal police shooting of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk during a traffic stop in Nanterre triggered days of riots, reigniting debate over racial profiling and police violence.
Environmental activists have also accused authorities of disproportionate force, particularly during a 2023 protest against a water reservoir in Sainte-Soline, where clashes left dozens of demonstrators and police officers injured.
Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have repeatedly raised concerns about excessive force and restrictions on the right to protest.
Paolo Stuppia, a sociology lecturer at Sciences Po Paris and co-author of the book Geopolitique de la jeunesse, believes tensions between protesters and police have worsened under French President Emmanuel Macron.
“What was once reserved for the suburbs or autonomous activist groups is now being applied to everyone,” he said. “There is a climate of mistrust between protesters and police, and it is growing because police repression now affects far more people.”
‘French-style’ crowd control
Pascual, the lawyer, argued that the severity of police violence is closely linked to the use of crowd-control weapons that can cause permanent, life-changing injuries. Rubber-bullet launchers and explosive grenades have been at the centre of controversy over police tactics in the country.
“This is truly what we call ‘French-style’ crowd control – are very specific and involve the use of weapons, including weapons described as non-lethal, but which, in reality, are capable of lethal force,” she said.
Interior Minister Nunez suspended the use of stun grenades after a teenager lost his hand. But before Saturday’s marches, he said they could be used in cases of “urban violence”, adding that they were “never used when things are going well”.
On Saturday, they were used extensively.
Al Jazeera journalists at the scene saw police fire tear gas and stun grenades repeatedly, well before the march had started.
Pascual questioned whether the use of force was effective in restoring order, arguing that de-escalation could help rebuild trust between police and demonstrators.
“When you see videos of police officers deciding to put down their shields and remove their helmets, what do you see?” she asked. “The protesters opposite them stop and applaud. In France, we don’t do that.”

Liberty, equality, tear gas: no nation does mass protests quite like France
When the French take to the streets to revolt, they aren’t just venting – they’re practising centuries of political theatre
When the French fight high fuel taxes, they don yellow vests and march. When angry farmers want better pay, hundreds of them drive tractors down the Champs-Elysees. And when museum workers want better tourist management, they strike and shut down the Louvre.
Passionate public protest is as French as “La Marseillaise”, the 1792 anthem that enshrines the collective duty to fight tyranny in the country’s national identity. But this month, the most violent demonstrations in years – and tough policing – have raised concern about riots overshadowing hundreds of thousands of peaceful demonstrators marching against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
On Saturday alone, at least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings, looted stores and engulfed a historic city hall in flames. More protests could be in store.
“How can French people do this to France?” outgoing President Emmanuel Macron asked on Sunday. Nothing justifies the destruction, he added. “We all feel anger and shame.”

Unknown

2026-10-21

Aamir Latif
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
There has been no outside access to North Korean state media and official portals as nearly all of the country’s websites have been offline for over 24 hours, Seoul-based website NK News reported Wednesday.
While the cause of the nationwide outage remains unclear, the disruptions appear to be linked to issues in North Korea’s “Ryugyong-dong” network, which has historically relied on internet service supplied by Chinese provider China Unicom via IP addresses associated with Hong Kong-based network Cenbong.
Multiple websites began experiencing persistent outages simultaneously on Tuesday, including the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the Rodong Sinmun and Minju Joson newspapers, and external radio service Voice of Korea.
The websites of the official information portal Naenara, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, national airline Air Koryo and the DPRK Portal, which lists official North Korean websites, have also been down since then.
DPRK refers to North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
KCNA came back online later Tuesday but was offline for 19 of the 24 hours following the initial outage.
The other sites largely remained offline throughout, apart from brief periods of connectivity on Wednesday morning totaling approximately 10 minutes.
Pyongyang’s Silibank SMTP email server has also been offline since Tuesday morning, apart from a five-minute period of connectivity on Wednesday morning.
Russian telecommunications company TransTeleCom has also served as an alternative internet service provider since 2017, while both Chinese and Russian services have routed traffic to a secondary Philippines-based network supplementing Ryugyong-dong since 2023.
However, internet connectivity has remained at a standstill for over a day despite these alternative routing pathways.

Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.
The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.
OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

Less than a week before the elections, the four latest Knesset seat polls painted an almost identical picture: Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party led Likud in every poll, but neither bloc comes close to a 61-seat majority.
The polling average put the Zionist opposition at 51.25 seats, compared with 51 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, a near-perfect tie that leaves the Arab parties and parties hovering around the electoral threshold in a pivotal position ahead of election day.
Walla poll: Eisenkot widens lead over Likud
A Walla poll indicated a shift in momentum, although neither bloc secured a 61-seat majority. The poll also revealed significant differences in voters' confidence in their choices.
According to the poll, after Benny Gantz withdrew from the race, Eisenkot's Yashar party gained one seat, reaching 23. In contrast, Netanyahu's Likud lost one seat, falling to 19.
One of the remaining questions ahead of the elections concerns the chances of Ofer Winter's People of Israel party entering the Knesset. According to the poll, the party remains below the electoral threshold, with just 2.9% support. Meanwhile, the Reservists and Economic Party alliance, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, continued to cross the electoral threshold, winning four seats.
Despite the changes in individual parties' standings, the distribution of seats between the blocs continued to point to difficulties in forming a government. Netanyahu's bloc weakened by one seat, falling to 48 from 49 in the previous poll, while the opposition parties maintained their strength with 54 seats.
Outside the two main blocs, Hendel and Zelekha's Reservists and Economic Party alliance held four seats. The two Arab parties won 14 seats combined, up one from the previous poll.
Channel 13 poll: Opposition bloc leads Netanyahu

According to the poll, Eisenkot's party received 20 seats, while Likud won just 18.
KAN news poll: Netanyahu gains ground, three seats separate the blocs

Netanyahu's Likud also gained one seat to 21, while former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party held steady with 12 seats.
The Reservists and Economic Party alliance, led by Hendel and Zelekha, also held steady with four seats.
In contrast, Winter's People of Israel party, which won four seats in the previous poll, failed to cross the electoral threshold this time.
The most significant change between the two polls was the shift in seat distribution between the blocs. In the previous poll, Netanyahu's bloc led with 53 seats, compared with 50 for Eisenkot's bloc, a three-seat advantage for the prime minister.
Channel 12 poll: Major parties gain ground, Hendel and Zelekha fail to enter Knesset
A Channel 12 News poll put Eisenkot's Yashar party first with 24 seats, up one seat from the previous poll.
Netanyahu's Likud also gained one seat, reaching 21, leaving the gap between the two parties unchanged.
Bennett's B'Yachad party also gained one seat, rising to 14.
The Reservists and Economic Party alliance, led by Hendel and Zelekha, which won four seats in the previous poll and crossed the electoral threshold, fell to just 2.1% support, leaving it outside the Knesset.
Winter's People of Israel rose from 1.8% to 2.8% of the vote.
According to the poll, Eisenkot's bloc gained one seat, rising from 54 the 55.
Netanyahu's bloc gained two seats, rising from 49 to 51, while the Arab parties increased their combined representation from 13 to 14 seats.
Polling average: Eisenkot holds narrow lead, blocs remain nearly tied
The average of the four latest polls, conducted by Channel 12, Channel 13, KAN, and Walla, painted a fairly clear picture of the election race: Eisenkot's Yashar party leads with an average of 22.5 seats, compared with 19.75 for Likud.
Bennett's B'Yachad party ranks third with 13.5 seats, followed by the Democrats with nine, the Joint List with 8.5, and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu with eight.
On the right, Otzma Yehudit and Shas each average 7.75 seats, United Torah Judaism stands at seven, and the Religious Zionist Party at 6.75.
Ra'am averages 5.5 seats.
The Hendel-Zelekha alliance, which crosses the electoral threshold in three of the four polls, averages three seats, while People of Israel crosses the threshold in just one poll and averages one seat.
The seat distribution between the blocs also reflected an advantage for the camp opposing Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's bloc averaged 50 seats, compared with 53 for the Zionist opposition. The Arab parties averaged 14 seats combined, bringing the Zionist opposition and Arab parties to 67 seats.
Meanwhile, Hendel and Zelekha's alliance averaged three seats and is not fully aligned with either of the two blocs.
The overall picture showed Eisenkot holding a modest lead in the race to become the largest party, alongside a wider gap between the political blocs. However, it also pointed to an election in which parties hovering around the electoral threshold could significantly alter the distribution of Knesset seats.
The Hendel-Zelekha alliance and People of Israel are the most prominent examples. If they cross the electoral threshold, they could shift several seats between the political camps and change the outcome on election day.
The average is based on the distribution of seats in four separate polls and does not constitute a new poll or a forecast of the election results.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim ordered the ban "to protect government information and users' personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime," his office said in a statement on Wednesday.

A day earlier, Anwar said that the government was looking into potential security risks arising from the use of Waze, which he said "was bound to Israeli laws."

Anwar did not provide any details of the risks but recommended the use of TuJu, a domestic mapping app developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority, as an alternative.
Malaysia chief government secretary issues letter barring Waze
Malaysia's Chief Secretary to the Government, Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar, said all civil servants would now be barred from using Waze, according to a letter dated Tuesday addressed to the heads of government agencies.
The letter, reviewed by Reuters, said the directive followed a decision taken at the meeting chaired by Anwar, with the prohibition to take effect immediately.
An official with the Prime Minister's Department confirmed the letter's authenticity.
Waze, which was founded in Israel, uses satellite signals and crowd-sourced data from drivers to offer real-time traffic information. It was acquired by Alphabet-owned Google in 2013 for about $1 billion.

Two in three Ukrainians read or listen to books at least several times a month – survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:48:05 EEST
16:48:05 KST

Some 59% of Ukrainians have read or listened to books at least several times a month over the past year, according to a survey by Gradus Research commissioned by Ukraine's Ministry of Culture.
According to the survey, one in 10 Ukrainians (12%) say they read or listen to books every day or almost every day, one in five (21%) several times a week, one in four (26%) several times a month, another 22% said they read several times a year or less, 13% of respondents did not read at all in the past 12 months, and 6% found it hard to answer.
Active readers (59%) were asked why they read or listen to books. The survey showed that Ukrainians most often read to relax (69% of readers), to enjoy reading (54%), and for learning and self-development (43%).
Respondents were asked how many books they had read or listened to in the past 12 months. Some 11% (avid readers) read more than 25 books, 7% (active readers) read 13-24 books, 23% (regular readers) read 5-12 books, 37% (irregular readers) read 1-4 books, and 22% are indifferent to reading.
It is noted that during the full-scale war books have also become a way of coping: 32% of readers say reading helps reduce anxiety, 30% to recover emotionally, 28% to get through stress more easily, and one in five readers (21%) says it is easier to fall asleep with a book.
At the same time, the rest of the respondents (41%) were asked why they do not read or listen to books. Ukrainians most often do not read because they lack motivation and habit (59%), lack time and resources (53%), have no access to books (15%), because of personal and social barriers (13%), or because it is hard to find "their" book (8%).
"Some 70% of readers have had a break in reading of at least half a year in their lives. Of them, 35% returned to regular reading, and another 62% read again, though irregularly. Most often people were brought back to books by a psychological need: for rest, support and coping with stress (34% of those who returned). Another 31% returned because they saw an interesting book. A chance discovery of an interesting book is also the most common incentive to read more. It was named by 37% of Ukrainians," the Culture Ministry said.
The survey also showed that printed books remain the most common reading format. In particular, 58% of respondents said they choose a printed book, 44% an e-book, 35% an audiobook, and 3% found it hard to answer.
The comprehensive study "Reading in Ukraine: Behavior, Motivation and Engagement Tools" was carried out by Gradus Research with the support of the Believe in Yourself Foundation. It included 41 in-depth interviews (March-May 2026) and a survey of 2,200 respondents aged 14 and older (August 17-25, 2026). The survey did not cover temporarily occupied territories or areas of active combat.
As reported, Ukraine's Ministry of Culture initiated the national reading study in spring 2026. The first insights from the qualitative research were presented on May 30 at Book Arsenal.

Starlink access in Ukraine a decision for Musk, not White House, Rubio says

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against missile attacks from Russia.
The Journal cited one source saying that Musk, President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand, and two sources saying that Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown.
"I'm not aware that we knew about this decision beforehand. But that's irrelevant," Rubio told reporters during a trip to India.
"The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they'll allow it to be used at." Musk and SpaceX did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Reuters has cited two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter saying the decision ultimately came from the White House. This version was also asserted by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, but denied by the administration.
Rubio's comments are likely to intensify concerns in Washington regarding Musk's singular ability to influence US foreign policy. They also represent an apparent shift in position for the administration.
Trump has publicly said he believed neither he nor Musk was behind the slowdown. Departing for a trip to Uzbekistan and India on Saturday, Rubio had said no one ordered the slowdown, an assertion that drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties.
"I'm not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate," Rubio said at the time.
"We have nothing to do with that. I don't – the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored," Rubio said.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth also portrayed the Starlink cutoff as a commercial matter. No US official has publicly said, however, that they have pushed SpaceX to reverse any cutoffs.
"There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions," Hegseth said.
One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX's Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon.
Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield in the first place, while Zelenskiy has said that both Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine have been disrupted. REUTERS

US Restores Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine as Witkoff Heads to Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

16:42:09 KST

US Restores Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine as Witkoff Heads to Putin
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had resumed sharing intelligence on Russian strikes with Kyiv, as US special envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin following a meeting with Zelensky in Norway.
Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks, apparently restoring a service that the White House had suspended the previous week. He welcomed the resumption, saying it would help save lives.
“We are thankful that intelligence works,” Zelensky told reporters in Oslo, describing the warnings as “very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians” ahead of ballistic missile strikes.
Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg on Wednesday morning, Russian state news agency TASS reported. His visit is part of US President Donald Trump's efforts to ease a bitter dispute with Zelensky over how to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described Witkoff's discussions with Zelensky as positive and said the envoy would present their ideas to the Russian side. A US official told Reuters that Witkoff aimed to establish a route toward direct trilateral talks and broader multilateral negotiations. Axios reported that he would bring Putin an updated proposal for ending the war.
Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the discussions with Zelensky remotely and was also expected to participate virtually in the meeting with Putin, a US official told AFP. Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev was due to meet Witkoff at the airport before the talks.
The diplomatic efforts follow days of worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv. Trump has accused Zelensky of failing to pursue an end to the war and called for new Ukrainian leadership, while also criticizing Kyiv for refusing to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries.
On Tuesday, Trump again urged the Ukrainian president to agree to a deal with Moscow, saying Zelensky could have accepted terms offered during their contentious meeting in the Oval Office in February 2025.
“We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” Trump said.
Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard, an American captured by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine. It was unclear whether the request would be raised during Wednesday's meeting.
“I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens,” Trump told reporters in Washington.
The dispute escalated after Trump announced the lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He subsequently announced an energy ceasefire that Ukraine observed for several days, while Russia did not.
Washington's actions have fueled concern in Kyiv and among European and British supporters of Ukraine that the United States is increasingly favoring Moscow. US proposals for peace have largely reflected Russia's maximalist demands.
Zelensky said he had held a positive telephone conversation with Rubio earlier on Tuesday. Asked whether Ukraine was losing the war following recent US actions, he rejected the suggestion while acknowledging the cost of continued Russian attacks.
“Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It's a pity,” Zelensky said.
He also told Rubio about restrictions imposed the previous week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk's satellite internet service. The reported reduction in service speeds has hampered Ukraine's ability to conduct mid-range drone strikes against Russian battlefield positions.
Trump denied ordering the slowdown after Musk said the decision could only have come from the White House. Rubio said on Wednesday in Mumbai that Washington had not known in advance about the reduction in satellite communications speeds.
“The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk,” Rubio said.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown affecting the military-grade service.
Ukraine has also raised concerns over delays in the delivery of Patriot missile interceptors. Zelensky said he had offered to halt Ukraine's long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries, a key demand from Trump, if Washington supplied Kyiv with the interceptors.
The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriot systems purchased by other countries for Ukraine, leaving the country more exposed to Russian air attacks. Zelensky told US senators on Monday that missiles already paid for by European countries were being held up pending approval from US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Several European countries were prepared to transfer interceptors from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US authorization.
US officials have denied deliberately reducing support for Ukraine, although they have not provided a convincing explanation for the temporary interruption in intelligence sharing or the restrictions on satellite communications. Rubio said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and needed elsewhere in the world, including for the defense of the United States.
“There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” Rubio said during his visit to India.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, questioned on Tuesday whether US negotiators were acting as honest brokers in the peace process. Witkoff has met Putin repeatedly in Moscow but has visited Kyiv only once so far.
Kallas said Ukraine had resisted pressure to accept Russia's terms because of European support.
“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine had not capitulated on Putin's terms, she said, because Europe had continued to support it.
Zelensky had also told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed Washington had made a political decision to reduce assistance to Kyiv.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelensky said in Oslo, insisting that any negotiations over the country's future must include Ukrainian representatives.
He also opposed a trilateral summit proposed by Putin that would bring together the Russian president, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss a settlement for Ukraine. The Wall Street Journal reported that Zelensky would be excluded from the proposed meeting.
Trump said he was prepared to meet Putin and Xi in China next month to discuss denuclearization, adding that the talks could also address the war in Ukraine. The prospect of such a meeting has raised concerns in Kyiv that decisions about the country's future could be made without its participation.
At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. Among the victims were passengers traveling on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, where a Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of those killed was the driver of a shuttle bus traveling from the capital to a military cemetery.

Kazakhstan and Pakistan step up efforts to detect customs violations
Kazakhstan and Pakistan will strengthen cooperation in identifying and preventing customs violations under an intergovernmental agreement ratified by Kazakhstan’s Qurultay, the country’s parliament, in two readings, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to the conclusion of the Committee of the Qurultay, the agreement was signed in Islamabad on February 4, 2026. It establishes the legal and organizational framework for cooperation between the customs authorities of the two countries.
Key areas of cooperation include mutual assistance in preventing, investigating and suppressing violations of customs legislation, as well as exchanging information on export and transit declarations, including those deemed suspicious. The agreement also provides for measures to ensure confidentiality and information security.
In addition, the document allows customs officials to be sent to the partner country’s customs authorities for training, professional development and the exchange of practical experience.
Cooperation will be conducted through a request-and-response mechanism.
The implementation of the agreement is expected to strengthen bilateral cooperation in customs matters and improve the effectiveness of measures aimed at expanding economic ties and enhancing the transit and logistics potential of Kazakhstan and Pakistan.

Parliament approves liberalisation of Poland’s abortion laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:41:48 UTC
16:41:48 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.
However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.
Mamy to! Sejm przyjął dwa projekty: dekryminalizujący pomocnictwo w aborcji i przywracający aborcyjny kompromis. 
To niezbędne minimum i pierwszy krok. 
Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC
— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026
When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.
However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.
One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.
That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.
The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.
In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).
Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.
Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.
In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.
A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.
However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.
All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.
Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.
Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.
President Nawrocki joined thousands of people on the National March of Life, Poland’s largest annual anti-abortion event, which is held under the patronage of the Catholic church https://t.co/8BQEVUoMZn
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 20, 2026
Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.
However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.
He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.

A further complication is the fact that the TK is currently in crisis. The government does not recognise any of its rulings (including the 2020 abortion ruling) due to the continued presence of judges illegitimately appointed under PiS.
Meanwhile, Nawrocki and the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, have refused to accept five new TK judges appointed by the Sejm this year.
Opinion polling has consistently shown that a majority of Poles want to liberalise the abortion law.

Drone alert greets US envoy’s arrival for Putin talks
A drone threat has been announced south of St. Petersburg shortly after US President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, arrived in the city for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the Ukraine conflict. The warning comes just days after a massive Ukrainian drone barrage on the city and outskirts killed one person and injured 15 others.
Witkoff arrived at Pulkovo Airport on Wednesday morning. His motorcade headed for Constantine Palace, around 20 km southeast of St. Petersburg.
Shortly after arriving, Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko announced a UAV threat in the airspace over Luga District, around 125 km south of the venue for the talks. The governor warned that mobile internet speeds could be reduced but did not specify the number, exact location, and direction of the drones, and did not report any interceptions.
Russia’s air regulator also imposed temporary airspace restrictions around Pulkovo Airport, citing flight safety. The facility earlier received Witkoff’s aircraft from Oslo, where he met with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and European officials on Tuesday.
The alert follows Sunday’s unprecedented Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad Region. According to the Russian authorities, the strikes killed one person and injured 15, damaged residential buildings, and sparked fires at an oil terminal, oil depot, and industrial facilities.
Commenting on the raid at the time, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described it as “final manifestations of agony” of Ukraine. “The Kiev regime is fighting back [but] it cannot alter the course of history.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the Putin-Witkoff talks will center on the Ukraine conflict. This comes after the Oslo talks where the US, Ukraine, and Kiev’s Western backers discussed security guarantees, a postwar economic plan, and a broader European security architecture, according to Reuters.
