Kazakhstan’s proposal: How C5+ with the US strengthened Central Asia’s global role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:41:17 UTC
16:41:17 KST

Kazakhstan’s proposal: How C5+ with the US strengthened Central Asia’s global role
The evolution of the C5+1 format, its key achievements in strengthening cooperation between Central Asia and the United States, and its future prospects amid global geopolitical challenges were among the key topics discussed by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Kairat Umarov in an exclusive interview with Silk Way TV Channel, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
- The C5+ format has become an important mechanism for strengthening Central Asia’s cooperation with global partners. Kazakhstan played an initiating role in advancing this format as early as 2013. Could you tell us how the idea emerged and evolved into the diplomatic platform we see today?
- This is a very interesting question because, as you said, I was personally involved in the creation of the C5+ format. Even before C5+1 with the United States began, similar platforms already existed, such as Central Asia+Japan, Central Asia+South Korea, and Central Asia+European Union.
When the idea of creating a similar format with the United States emerged, we started discussing it with the State Department.
At that time, the idea was not so popular in the United States because they traditionally discussed Central Asian affairs with countries like Russia and China. The idea was to find a different way for the United States to talk directly to Central Asian ministers, without going through other countries.
Of course, this was not exclusive, and they could continue the same consultations with those countries, but it was very important to have those direct discussions and contacts with Central Asian countries. The idea was born even earlier than 2013.
It was my good friend, whom I had known for many years, Dr. Frederick Starr, who is the chairman of the Central Asia-Caucasus Institute at Johns Hopkins. He was extensively working on Central Asia and the wider region. He knows quite a bit about the history and developments.
When I was appointed ambassador to Washington in 2013 and arrived in January in Washington, D.C., I had to meet with some of my friends from previous engagements. One of the first meetings was with Frederick Starr, and he told me that he had proposed such an idea in his book: a mechanism for the US Secretary of State to meet with the foreign ministers of Central Asia. Maybe it was not exactly the same, but he was talking about this kind of interaction, and he said that nobody paid attention to it.
The idea was very topical and useful, but the US administration was not taking it forward. I said to him, "Okay, let's work together on this issue," and I proposed it to the State Department. At that time, there was a change in leadership. It was the second term of President Obama, and there was new leadership in Central Asian and South Asian affairs. Nisha Biswal became the Assistant Secretary of State, and we talked about this idea. She said, "Okay, let's look at that, but no promises." Two years later, she came back to me and said that the idea had received...
- It took two years to decide.
- It took them 2 years, I think, to consult with those who were somehow engaged in the field, so to say, at the State Department and maybe some other structures.
But the idea was to have this direct contact with Central Asian countries, and she came up with this idea. Instead of Central Asia plus US, she said, why don't we just make a shortened version, C5+1? I said, great idea. Let's just work on it.
And so, C5+1 was coined.
- More than a decade later, what are the main achievements of the C5+ format, particularly given that two U.S. presidents have met with Central Asian leaders to discuss political, economic, trade, and investment cooperation?
- So, the idea of Frederick Starr, under my personal kind of insistence with the State Department, we got this mechanism working. Now, after 2015, more than one decade has passed. It's interesting that it started as a ministerial level.
Today, it is already an institutionalized body with its own secretariat. It has different sector platforms on economy, energy, and issues, security. Lately, it was now C5+1 on minerals, rare earth minerals.
Again, there was an idea to work on the business component of it. It started with the United States Chamber of Commerce, and then it transformed itself into B5+1, a number of meetings of which were held in Astana.
From that moment on, the whole mechanism became more focused on the economy, trade and investment, connectivity, regional cooperation, AI development, and minerals. Now it has quite an extensive area of contacts and discussions.
What's interesting is that it started at the ministerial level. In 2025, it transformed into a summit meeting. It was in New York. President Trump invited all five Central Asian heads of state to the White House.
It was the first time this had been done at the White House. What's interesting, if we talk about Kazakhstan in particular, 29 agreements worth $17 billion were signed. Again, it shows that this mechanism is no longer at a nascent stage.
It's at a very active stage. Yes, now it's grown into a full-fledged mechanism of bilateral and regional cooperation with the countries of Central Asia. It's a thriving mechanism.
- Given the current geopolitical tensions and rising global conflicts, what challenges could these developments pose to the C5+ format and Central Asia’s efforts to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with its global partners?
- For me, one important thing I wanted to mention is that none of the other mechanisms we've created, like the US-Kazakhstan relationship over more than 17 years, stood the test of time.
The only one which is working and thriving today is the C5+1. We started during the Obama administration, and all the subsequent administrations supported it. Today, it has reached a much higher level. Of course, geopolitics plays its own role.
We understand that you cannot live in isolation from international issues. But it doesn't mean that we must be jeopardized by all those developments, because in the relationship between Central Asia and the US, we try to work on a positive agenda. Today, Central Asia is a region of stability and development.
So many issues are being resolved through the Coordination Council meetings among the heads of state. And it's a new development for Central Asia. Today, we are working in a very close, cooperative manner.
Of course, I gave you the figures. In general, the US presence in Kazakhstan is quite substantial. More than 600 US companies work in Kazakhstan. US investments today exceed $100 billion. Trade has also doubled in recent years, reaching $5 billion, which shows that we have so many positive things to work on. AI and digitalization, for example, are new trends in the world.
Of course, we discuss issues of stability. This is very important. It's a key issue. We're talking about threats and challenges which could pose a threat to Kazakhstan or Central Asia. Afghanistan is in a difficult situation, and we must take care of it as well. But in general, we try to discuss practical ways to cooperate to avoid and overcome those challenges through cooperation.
I think that, of course, there are some challenges and some issues. But in our discussions, we're mostly focusing today on the development agenda, regional integration, regional coordination, and connectivity.
And this is very much reflected here at the UN. At the UN, countries increasingly look at Central Asia as a united region, which is becoming a close unit, so to say. They see the countries as united in their initiatives, in what they propose, and in their willingness to build peace.
Because without peace, it's very difficult to talk about development. And if you don't work on development, you probably cannot have peace. So, these are two very interconnected things. We try to work not in a fragmented way, but with an understanding that there is a nexus between peace and security and sustainable development.
- How do you see the future of the C5+ format, particularly in light of rapid advances in digitalization and artificial intelligence? How might the mechanism evolve to address emerging opportunities and challenges?
- It's already a working mechanism. As I've said, it's digitalized. It has its own agenda, and it's working actively on the mutually beneficial issues for Central Asia and the United States. So, I see the future as the possibility through this mechanism to have a close collaboration among business circles, on economy, on artificial intelligence, on regional connectivity, which are very important for Central Asia.
That shows that this mechanism has quite a good future, because there's a lot of willingness to work, and there are some other countries, I know, that would like to have the same mechanism to work with Central Asian countries. So, it's a very promising future.
And, of course, during that time, it was not only this mechanism. For example, looking back, it was quite an interesting time for me because, during that time, we signed the agreement on a 10-year reciprocal visa regime with the United States.
There were many interesting developments during that time, and I would say it was good for Kazakhstan to start this kind of initiative, to work cooperatively with other Central Asian countries and our American colleagues on this idea. It's transforming itself, expanding, and making a lot of good starts and developments.
So, in general, to my mind, if we continue in the same way, the future is limitless. You know, there's B5+1 and the dialogue on minerals, the latest one, and I think that with every passing year, more areas are being added that could be of mutual benefit to all of us. We also have various other mechanisms, and all those mechanisms are working for the well-being of the peoples of Central Asia.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported on an interview with UN Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaaragchaa, which focused on civil society's role in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals, Kazakhstan's progress towards the SDGs, and cooperation between the United Nations and non-governmental organizations.

Egypt: End judicial harassment of Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Atallah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

16:39:26 KST

Responding to the news that Lina Atallah, editor-in-chief of independent outlet Mada Masr, has been summoned to appear before Egypt’s Supreme State Security Prosecution (SSSP) today for investigation in a new criminal case against her, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Regional Impact, Yasmine Ahmed, said:
“It is utterly disgraceful that the Egyptian authorities are once again targeting Lina Atallah for the brave and professional reporting by her team at Mada Masr. This is the sixth case against Mada Masr and its journalists in six years, illustrating the Egyptian authorities’ relentless harassment of independent journalists who challenge the state-controlled narrative.
“Lina Atallah has been bravely leading one of the few remaining independent media outlets in Egypt and should never have been targeted with these successive investigations. Egyptian authorities must immediately end all judicial harassment against her and Mada Masr staff.
“This summons is part of a wider crackdown on independent media and freedom of expression. It comes just weeks after the arbitrary arrest of six journalists at the fact-checking platform Matsadaash who are being held in pretrial detention pending criminal investigation. Instead of repeatedly subjecting journalists to unjust prosecution on unfounded terrorism-related or ‘false news’ charges, the authorities must release the Matsadaash journalists and allow journalists to investigate and report free from intimidation, harassment or fear of reprisals.”
Background
Over the past six years, Lina Atallah and her Mada Masr colleagues have faced six politically motivated prosecutions over their reporting. Most recently, on 4 August 2025, the authorities summoned Atallah for questioning on unfounded charges, including “spreading false news” and “operating a website without a license,” over an article published on 31 July 2025 about deteriorating detention conditions in Badr 3 prison. She was released on bail pending investigation. Criminal investigations against her and Mada Masr staff remain open in five cases. Mada Masr has unsuccessfully sought a license since 2018.
On the same day that prosecutors summoned Lina Atallah for investigation, President Abdelfattah al-Sisi spoke at the conference Egypt Forum 2026, saying at the government “listens, discusses, and accepts any criticism.”
The ongoing crackdown on journalists has also targeted those who took part in a sit-in at the Journalists Syndicate, which began on 3 October 2026, in solidarity with the arbitrarily detained Matsadaash journalists. On 5 October 2026, journalist Rasha Azab, a participant, was questioned over a social media post criticizing the ministry of interior. The SSSP accused her of terrorism-related charges and released her on bail of EGP 10,000. On 19 October 2026, the journalists announced they were suspending the sit-in.
At least 18 journalists were jailed in Egypt a, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Hundreds of websites remain blocked in the country, including Mada Masr, other media outlets and independent NGOs.

Rostec develops attack drones with characteristics comparable to cruise missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:38:00 UTC
16:38:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Russia’s state corporation Rostec is developing and manufacturing strike drones with performance characteristics on par with those of cruise missiles, the corporation said.
"As technology advances, the distinction between a drone, a cruise missile, and a loitering munition is disappearing. The Dan-T is already a full-fledged cruise missile in terms of its capabilities. The Rostec State Corporation is working to advance this field, and several other comparable projects are underway. These systems are becoming increasingly intelligent – all of them feature elements of artificial intelligence to one degree or another.
The next models, which we will be able to present as early as next year, will fly farther, faster, and will be considerably more advanced in terms of intelligence," Rostec said in a video presentation of its latest Dan-T aerial strike drone.
The state corporation presented this system at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026 in Egypt.
About the munition
The Dan-T is a loitering munition with a range of up to 450 km. With a weight of up to 270 kilograms and equipped with a compact turbojet engine, it can be launched from both aircraft and helicopters. The Dan-T is designed to fly in stealth mode to evade air defense systems and operates fully autonomously after launch from its carrier. The munition can approach its target at speeds of up to 500 km/h while following the terrain, thereby reducing the likelihood of interception by enemy air defense systems.
The Dan-T can be launched from Russian-designed aircraft and helicopters, including the Yak-130, MiG-29, Mi-28N, and Mi-8. It can also be integrated with foreign combat aircraft.
As Rostec told TASS, the munition’s effectiveness has been confirmed by hundreds of successful launches against enemy targets during the special military operation in Ukraine.

Witkoff in Russia for Putin meeting after ‘positive’ talks with Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:37:19 UTC
16:37:19 KST

Putin and Zelenskyy back three-way US peace talks on Ukraine
Both leaders back US-mediated negotiations targeted for next month, with talks potentially taking place in Abu Dhabi.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have both expressed support for a United States proposal to hold three-way talks to end the conflict in Ukraine.
The Kremlin said Putin conveyed his “in principle” willingness to engage in negotiations during a meeting in St Petersburg with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday.
Speaking to journalists via WhatsApp as he returned to Kyiv from Norway, Zelenskyy confirmed Ukraine’s interest in the talks, which he said should take place no later than early November.
Zelenskyy added that he had spoken with US officials following Witkoff’s discussions with Putin.
“We have received feedback that… Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams,” Zelenskyy said.
“The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that… The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November.”
Zelenskyy said Kyiv supports “any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives”.
The diplomatic effort comes as Washington pushes for an end to the war in Ukraine, which began more than four and a half years ago with Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Witkoff held talks with Putin on Wednesday after meeting with Ukrainian and European officials in Norway a day earlier.
“Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv … but there wasn’t really much substance in them.”
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned talks [with Washington and Kyiv],” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
He later told Russian state television Vesti that the talks may be held in Abu Dhabi.
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Goodwill gesture
The three-hour talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia is obviously interested in the lifting of international sanctions, and US sanctions in particular.
“The Trump administration is using economic leverage to encourage Moscow to finish this war, including the temporary lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel sales,” she said.
Putin also thanked US President Donald Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war.
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to “make a deal”. He said on Tuesday that it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”.
Putin also offered to help Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Moscow had a decades-long relationship with Tehran, which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the US to help farmers, Putin told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first trilateral meeting of its kind in history.
Oslo talks
The talks in Russia come a day after Witkoff met Ukraine’s Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway. Witkoff briefed Putin on the Oslo talks, which he described as productive and said had been characterised by “some degree of momentum”.
The prime ministers of Norway and Finland also attended the talks in Oslo. Representatives from the European Union and NATO were present. Following Tuesday’s talks, Zelenskyy said that “very, very important” intelligence from the US had been restored.
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month.
Zelenskyy has also accused Washington of slowing down the internet service Starshield, which is crucial for Ukraine’s battlefield operations. Starshield is the military-grade equivalent of Starlink – both developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
As diplomatic efforts intensify, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade long-range attacks.
At least one person was killed and two were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s western Bryansk region on Wednesday, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said on Telegram.
The Ukrainian emergency service said two people were killed in a Russian attack on a high-rise building in the Sviatoshynskyi district of the capital, Kyiv.

Nas Daily, Harvard and future of education: Jerusalem to host first international education conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:37:01 UTC
16:37:01 KST

Thousands of educators, education ministers, policymakers and technology innovators from around the world are expected to gather in Jerusalem next month for Israel's first International Education Conference, a two-day event examining how schools can adapt to rapid technological advances, social change and mounting global challenges.
The conference, scheduled for Nov. 9–10 at the Shimon Peres International Convention Center, also known as Binyanei HaUma, will feature speakers including social media entrepreneur Nas Daily, Harvard Graduate School of Education lecturer Noah Heller and leading Israeli academics, alongside education officials from countries across Europe, Asia, Africa and South America.
Organizers say the gathering is intended to address one of the most pressing questions facing education systems worldwide: how to prepare children and young people for a future increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, shifting social norms and security challenges.
The event will also seek to establish Jerusalem as an international center for educational innovation and cross-cultural cooperation, bringing together government officials, researchers, entrepreneurs, teachers and community leaders to exchange ideas and examine new approaches to learning.
Education ministers and policymakers from around the world
Education ministers from Mongolia, Montenegro, Kazakhstan, Mauritius, Eswatini and Lesotho are expected to attend, along with an education official from Colombia's Cundinamarca Department.
Other international participants will include Georgia's deputy education minister, senior education officials from Greece, Nepal and Ghana, and mayors from Estonia, Nepal and Chile.
Representatives of Jewish education systems in Australia, Finland, Russia, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Sweden and Hong Kong will also participate, reflecting the conference's emphasis on strengthening ties between Israel and Jewish communities worldwide.
The gathering will feature prominent education researchers and institutional leaders, including Rabbi Dr. David Meyer, CEO of PaJeS, an organization supporting Jewish schools; Ivo Visak, CEO of Estonia's AI Leap Foundation, which promotes the integration of artificial intelligence into education; Prof. Chen Schechter, head of Israel's MOFET Institute; and Prof. Rivka Wadmany-Shauman, vice chair of Israel's Council for Higher Education.
They will be joined by educators, researchers and innovators from additional countries to discuss how governments, schools and communities can respond to changing educational needs.
Nas Daily, Harvard lecturer among featured speakers
Among the conference's most prominent speakers is Nuseir Yassin, better known as Nas Daily, the Israeli-born Palestinian content creator and media entrepreneur who built an international following through his short-form videos.
A Harvard University graduate and founder of Nas Company, Yassin will join discussions exploring the relationship between digital media, communication and education.
Noah Heller, a lecturer on education at the Harvard Graduate School of Education whose work focuses on teaching, teacher leadership and pedagogy, will also participate.
Other speakers include Prof. Mooli Lahad, an internationally recognized expert on psychological trauma and resilience, whose work has focused on helping individuals and communities cope with crises.
Israeli participants will include entrepreneur Alon Gonen, co-founder of the online trading platform Plus500; former Education Minister Prof. Yuli Tamir; Yaffa Ben David, secretary-general of the Israel Teachers' Union; Dalit Stauber, a former director-general of the Education Ministry; and author and public intellectual Dr. Micha Goodman.
The range of speakers reflects the conference's aim to bring perspectives from technology, academia, public policy and education into a broader discussion about the future of learning.
AI, social media and teacher burnout on the agenda
Rather than focusing exclusively on educational theory, the conference will examine practical dilemmas confronting teachers, students and policymakers.
Among the central issues are the growing role of artificial intelligence in classrooms, the influence of social media and algorithms on young people, and the challenges of maintaining effective education systems during emergencies and periods of prolonged uncertainty.
Participants will also examine teacher burnout, a growing concern for education systems struggling with staffing pressures and changing professional demands.
Other discussions will address how young people can participate in shaping education policy, the relationship between academic research and classroom practice, and ways to improve cooperation between national governments and local authorities.
Questions of identity, pluralism and the relationship between Israel and Jewish communities abroad will also feature in the program.
The conference will be organized around two central themes.
The first, EduHuman, will focus on the people at the center of education, including students, teachers, families and communities. Discussions will examine human relationships, educational values and the social and emotional dimensions of learning.
The second, EduSystem, will examine the structures, infrastructure and technologies needed to help education systems meet future challenges, including the use of emerging digital tools and new institutional models.
Organizers say the two themes are intended to connect the human dimensions of education with the technological and organizational changes reshaping the field.
TEDxJerusalem to explore 'Growth in Uncertainty'
The conference's opening evening will feature an official TEDxJerusalem event under the theme "Growth in Uncertainty," bringing together speakers from education, technology, science and the arts.
The event will take place Monday, Nov. 9, at the Ussishkin Auditorium inside the International Convention Center.
Doors will open at 5 p.m., with talks scheduled from 6 to 9 p.m. The program will also include an artistic performance.
Among the speakers will be Nas Daily and Hilla Haddad-Chmelnik, an aerospace engineer and CEO of Moonshot Space who previously served as director-general of Israel's Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology.
Other participants include Dr. Liat Yakir, a biologist, author and founder of the Academy of the Science of Emotions; Or Taicher, an entrepreneur, director and founder of the collaborative singing initiative Koolulam; Dr. Nader Butto; Maayan Ben Tzion; and DJ and music producer David Abramov, known professionally as Darwish.
Actor Yadin Gellman will host the evening, which is organized by educational technology entrepreneur and TEDx license holder Daniel Kovler.
The event will explore how individuals and societies can adapt, innovate and find opportunities for growth amid uncertainty.
Innovation exhibition to showcase new approaches to learning
Beyond the lectures and panel discussions, the conference will include professional tours offering international participants a firsthand look at educational initiatives operating across Jerusalem.
An accompanying innovation exhibition will showcase companies, nonprofit organizations and educational programs developing new approaches to classroom learning, enrichment and skills development.
Exhibitors will include Nick Academy, KKL-JNF, Migvan 2002, Tiyulim B'Tzlilim, Edupedia, Dalila, Matzmichim Academy, Nitzan Association, the Biblical Museum of Natural History, Inet, Kids Speak School, HaNagar MeHaHar, Avnei HaDerech Theater, Edventure, Latet Peh Association, Makademia with Chocolate and Tomax.
The exhibition will give educators and policymakers opportunities to explore practical solutions, connect with developers and organizations, and consider how emerging educational models could be adapted to their own institutions.
Jerusalem officials seek to establish annual event
Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion said the conference reflects the municipality's efforts to position the city as an international center for educational cooperation and innovation.
"In recent years, Jerusalem has increasingly become an international center for values-based, multicultural and innovative dialogue on education," Lion said. "This reflects a clear municipal policy that places education among our highest priorities and positions Jerusalem not only as Israel's capital, but also as its education capital."
Lion said the city's education system remained a major municipal priority, with continued efforts to expand opportunities and improve educational outcomes.
"Jerusalem's education system is a tremendous source of pride for us, and we are constantly working to promote renewal, excellence and opportunities that allow every child to fulfill their potential," he said.
He described the conference as an opportunity to strengthen the city's international standing while promoting dialogue across cultures and educational traditions.
"The International Education Conference is another expression of Jerusalem's standing as a city that promotes open educational dialogue and brings together values, culture, identity and innovation," Lion said.
"I look forward to welcoming educators and policymakers from Israel and around the world, and I hope this conference will mark the beginning of an annual tradition that fosters collaboration, mutual learning and growth."
Deputy Mayor Hagit Moshe, who oversees the city's education portfolio, said Jerusalem's diverse population and extensive education system make it a natural setting for international discussions about the future of learning.
"Jerusalem is the beating heart of education in Israel," Moshe said. "The city's large and diverse education system, together with its unique mosaic of people and communities, makes it a microcosm of the world and a source of educational innovation."
Moshe said the event would bring together decision-makers and educators facing similar challenges in different countries.
"I am proud to lead Jerusalem's first conference of this kind, which will bring together education ministers, senior officials, researchers and educators from Israel and around the world to discuss today's challenges and help shape the future of learning," she said.
She added that municipal officials intend to turn the gathering into a recurring international event.
"We will work to establish the conference as an annual tradition that reinforces Jerusalem's position not only as Israel's capital, but also as an international center for educational innovation and leadership."
The International Education Conference will take place Nov. 9-10, 2026, at the Shimon Peres International Convention Center in Jerusalem. Registration, the full conference program and additional information about speakers and exhibitors are available at the conference's official website.

Poll: Yotova at 47.3%, Gyurov at 30.6%, Kostadinov with 10.3% in Presidential Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:35:00 UTC
16:35:00 KST

A survey by Market Links conducted for bTV shows President Iliaana Yotova leading Andrey Gyurov by 16.7 percentage points in the presidential race, while support for the Progressive Bulgaria (PB) party has fallen to 32% in a hypothetical parliamentary election.
Further reading: Poll: Yotova Leads Gyurov in Bulgaria’s Presidential Race
Yotova has the support of 47.3% of respondents, compared with 30.6% for Gyurov, according to the poll. The difference between the two candidates stood at 20 percentage points or more at the beginning of the campaign.
The survey was funded and conducted jointly by Market Links and bTV, covering 1,006 Bulgarian citizens aged 18 and older nationwide between October 13 and 19, 2026. The research combined face-to-face interviews with online questionnaires.
Voter turnout in the presidential election is projected at 39%, a level that would make a runoff inevitable. However, between 15% and 20% of voters typically decide whom to support at the last minute.
Kostadin Kostadinov, leader of Revival, ranks third among the presidential candidates with 10.3%, exceeding his party's result in the most recent parliamentary elections. Ivelin Mikhailov, head of Velichie, has 4.3%, followed by Radostin Vasilev of MECH with 2.8% and Ivan Hristanov with 2.3%.
Predicting turnout will be the main difficulty in the first round, Market Links director Dobromir Zhivkov said on bTV on Wednesday morning.
“Presidential elections, in general, do not generate such intense interest - especially following what I would call the 'peak' in voter turnout that we saw back in April. Currently, the engagement level among Bulgarian voters is decidedly lower; however, we are also seeing signs that are galvanizing Bulgarian citizens,” Zhivkov said.
He identified the escalation in the Black Sea as one of the issues dividing Bulgarian society and prompting citizens to take a position.
Zhivkov said the political impact of the situation could push turnout above expectations, potentially surpassing the 40% recorded in November 2021. At the same time, he noted that public dissatisfaction with the country's direction was discouraging participation, as many citizens believed Bulgaria was not moving in the right direction.
The sociologist also pointed to differences in the voter profiles of the two leading presidential tickets. Among those supporting Yotova and Kiril Valchev, 75% had also voted for Progressive Bulgaria in April. The remaining 25% represented a diverse group, including a significant share who said they had not voted previously, suggesting that new voters were being mobilized.
Gyurov and Georgi Kandev draw support from a broader range of political backgrounds, Zhivkov said, including voters who had previously supported GERB and the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS), as well as people who had not voted. However, he identified We Continue the Change-Democratic Bulgaria (PP-DB) as the core of their electorate.
In a hypothetical parliamentary election held today, Progressive Bulgaria would receive 32% of the vote, down from more than 40% in recent polling. We Continue the Change (PP) would rank second with 10.2%, ahead of GERB, which has fallen to third place with 9.6%.
The poll indicates that many voters disappointed with the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) are returning to PP. Democratic Bulgaria would receive 7.6%, DPS 5.6%, and Revival 4.4%.
The survey also found that 41% of respondents did not trust Rumen Radev's cabinet, while 36% expressed confidence in the government.
Zhivkov said PB remained well ahead of its rivals in a hypothetical snap parliamentary election, although its support could decline further by two to three percentage points.
“In other words, the results have been trending downward for several consecutive months since this cabinet took office—a trend visible across all the indicators we measure,” Zhivkov said.

S. Korea's non-regular workers hit record high amid widening wage gap
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:31:59 CST
16:31:59 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's non-regular workers hit a record high, driven by higher elderly employment, while the wage gap widened between regular and temporary workers, statistical ministry data showed Wednesday.
The number of non-regular employees totaled 8,671,000 as of August, up 103,000 from a year earlier, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
It represented the largest since relevant data began to be compiled in 2003, keeping an upward trajectory for three consecutive years since 2024.
The number of regular workers added 10,000 to 13,855,000 in the cited period, indicating that non-regular workers accounted for the vast majority of the total increase in salaried employees.
Of a combined 22,526,000 salaried workers, non-regular workers made up 38.5 percent in August, up 0.3 percentage points from a year earlier and surpassing the previous high of 38.4 percent set in August 2021.
By age group, non-regular employees aged 60 and older soared 135,000 to 3,180,000, taking up 36.7 percent of all non-regular workers. It was up 1.2 percentage points compared to the previous year.
While the number of non-regular workers climbed among those in their 30s and 50s, it declined among those aged 29 and under and those in their 40s.
The wage gap between regular and temporary workers worsened. Over the three-month period from June to August, the average monthly wage for non-regular workers rose 24,000 won (18 U.S. dollars) to 2,112,000 won (1,590 dollars).
The average monthly wage for regular workers advanced 156,000 won to 4,052,000 won, topping the 4-million-won mark for the first time.
The wage ratio of non-regular workers to regular ones dropped 1.5 percentage points to 52.1 percent. ■

China's CERES-1 rocket launches new satellite from sea
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:31:46 CST
16:31:46 KST

The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket carrying a new satellite blasts off from the waters near the city of Rizhao, east China's Shandong Province, Oct. 21, 2026. China launched a rocket from the ocean waters near the city of Rizhao in east China's Shandong Province on Wednesday, placing a new satellite into planned orbit. The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 a.m. (Beijing Time). The Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center carried out this offshore launch. (Photo by Wang Yan/Xinhua)
RIZHAO, Shandong, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China launched a rocket from the ocean waters near the city of Rizhao in east China's Shandong Province on Wednesday, placing a new satellite into designated orbit.
The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 a.m. (Beijing Time).
The Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center carried out this offshore launch.
This new satellite will be mainly used for commercial remote sensing, providing services to the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, south China, and the low-latitude regions along the Maritime Silk Road, according to the Science and Technology Daily.
The launch marked the seventh sea-based mission of the CERES-1 sea-launched carrier rocket series.
As of now, the rocket's developer Galactic Energy has successfully conducted 23 orbital launches and placed a total of 90 commercial satellites into their designated orbits, the report noted. ■

Man arrested over discovery of woman’s remains in suitcase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:31:39 UTC
16:31:39 KST

Man arrested over discovery of woman’s remains in suitcase
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A 23-year-old man has been arrested in connection with the discovery of a woman’s body in a suitcase in Amsterdam.
The victim, 29-year-old Hajar, went missing on October 4 after she was seen cycling away from the Rai area towards Buitenveldert on a bicycle with an unknown man.
Her remains were found on Saturday in a suitcase that had been dumped in the Amsteldijk. The discovery was made nearly two weeks after she disappeared and two days after police issued an appeal for information about her whereabouts.
The suspect, a Somali national of no fixed abode, was arrested on Monday evening in connection with an assault on another man in Koggeland, Noord-Holland.
According to Dutch media reports the victim of the assault was the man’s foster father, who needed hospital treatment for injuries. The suspect had lived in foster care until he was 16 years old.
He had earlier been questioned as a witness about Hajar’s disappearance after camera footage showed him with her at the Rai on October 4.
“Further inquiries led to him being identified as a suspect,” René Beukelaer, head of the prosecution service in Amsterdam told a press conference on Tuesday.
Murder of Lisa
City mayor Femke Halsema acknowledged that the death of Hajar would revive questions about women’s safety, following the murder of a 17-year-old girl, Lisa, on a cycle path in August last year. A 22-year-old asylum seeker, Chris Jude, believed to be from Nigeria, has since admitted killing her.
“It is just 14 months since the Amsterdam authorities had to inquire about the dreadful murder of a 17-year-old girl,” Halsema said.
“The fear, anger and outrage that it stirred up in our society have not been quelled, and it pains me hugely to have to sit here again, knowing that this will cause more fear for women in this city and across the Netherlands.”
Peter Holla, Amsterdam’s chief of police, said the suspect was initially treated as a witness because “there were no signs in the camera footage that he was a suspect or there was a threatening situation.”
Outstanding questions
He said police were still appealing for information from the public to answer outstanding questions, such as where Hajar was killed.
The suspect has lived in the Netherlands since the age of six and has permanent residency. He is being held in solitary detention, with contact restricted to his lawyer.
Beukelaer added there was no indication that the suspect and Hajar knew each other.
Holla said Hajar was reported missing by a family member on October 4 who said she had left home with a suitcase. The search was classed as “urgent” the following day.
Public appeal
“It was not clear at that time whether we were dealing with a crime,” Holla said.
Her photograph was circulated to the public on October 13, along with details of when she was last seen at Rai.
The family told police Hajar had spent periods of time away from home before, but always returned, Holla said.
At the start of the press conference, Halsema extended her sympathies to Hajar’s family and close friends.
“For nearly two weeks they lived between hope and fear,” she said. “A few days ago the worst possible scenario was confirmed: the 29-year-old Hajar had been violently deprived of her life.
“I ask everyone to respect the peace and anonymity of the family.”

Afghanistan harvests 5.15 mln metric tons of wheat, up 13.4 pct year on year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:31:11 CST
16:31:11 KST

KABUL, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Afghanistan has achieved a wheat harvest of 5.15 million metric tons in the current year, marking a 13.4 percent increase year on year, the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock reported on Tuesday.
The crop was cultivated across 1.97 million hectares, equivalent to roughly 68 percent of the nation's arable land, according to the report.
Despite the stronger output, national wheat demand stands at 7.09 million tons for the current year, resulting in a residual shortfall of 1.94 million tons, the report asserted.
Last year, Afghanistan produced 4.54 million metric tons of wheat from 1.89 million hectares of irrigated and rain-fed farmland. ■

Fire extinguishers stolen, emptied in streets as suspected TikTok challenge spreads in Netanya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:30:40 UTC
16:30:40 KST

Some 15 teenagers were detained for questioning in Netanya on suspicion of stealing fire extinguishers from residential buildings and emptying their contents in public areas across the city, in incidents believed to be linked to a social media challenge circulating on platforms including TikTok, police said.
Three of the teenagers, aged 14 and 15, were caught in the act and fined NIS 730 each.
The investigation was launched following reports of fire extinguishers being stolen from residential buildings and their contents being discharged in public parks, parking lots, and on roads.
Since the weekend, investigators from the youth division at the Netanya Police Station have been working alongside municipal inspectors to identify those involved.
After apprehending the three minors, investigators identified more than 10 additional teenagers suspected of similar acts. They were also detained for questioning and arrived at the police station with their parents, who were informed of the potential criminal consequences and dangers associated with their actions.
Police warn of dangers posed by missing firefighting equipment
Behind what is suspected to have become an online challenge, residential buildings are being left without firefighting equipment intended to provide an immediate response in the event of a fire.
Police warned that stealing and emptying fire extinguishers could undermine efforts to control fires and lead to serious injuries, loss of life, and property damage. Police have also questioned minors in other investigations involving suspected criminal offenses.
Police urged parents to talk with their children about the dangers of taking part in such challenges.
Building management committees were advised to secure firefighting equipment against theft while keeping it accessible for immediate use in an emergency.

====================================================================================================

A partnership guided by God: Why Trump decided to endorse Netanyahu in Israel's elections - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:30:37 UTC
16:30:37 KST

When President Donald Trump endorsed Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection as prime minister of Israel, many voices urged him not to do it.
But I believe I know why Trump made that decision. I have known Benjamin Netanyahu for nearly 50 years, and I believe Trump recognizes in him something I have witnessed for decades: courage, pragmatism, resilience, and a willingness to make difficult decisions without needing everyone’s approval.
I also believe God has a purpose for both men. My conviction began with an extraordinary encounter in Jerusalem in 1980.
A divine appointment in Jerusalem
On June 30, 1980, I sat in the office of prime minister Menachem Begin for the first time. He repeatedly asked me, “Why did you come?”
Finally, I admitted, “Mr. Prime Minister, I don’t know. All I know is that God sent me.”
He laughed and turned to his chief of staff, Yehiel Kadishai. “Shake his hand. You have finally met an honest man in this office. He knows God sent him to meet with me, but he doesn’t know why.”
Begin told me to return when God revealed the answer.
Several days later, on the Fourth of July, I was praying in Jerusalem when someone placed a newspaper outside my room. On the front page was the story of Jonathan Netanyahu, known as Yoni, and the Entebbe rescue mission. It was the anniversary of his death.
I felt a strong prompting from God: “Go and comfort the family.”
I had never met them. Nevertheless, I asked my driver to take me to the home of Yoni’s father, Benzion Netanyahu.
Benzion welcomed me inside for tea. While we were sitting together, his grieving younger son entered the room. His name was Benjamin Netanyahu.
Yoni had been his hero. Benjamin had endured the terrible responsibility of telling his parents about his brother’s death and witnessing their devastating grief.
I could see the agony in his eyes. I asked if I could pray for him and placed my hand on his shoulder.
“Jonathan loved David. You loved Jonathan. Out of the ashes of despair will come strength from God, and you will be the Prime Minister of Israel.”
He looked at me and said, “Mike, I’m not going into politics.”
After this encounter I returned to Menachem Begin’s office and explained that I had discovered why God sent me. I told Begin that Benjamin Netanyahu would one day become prime minister, and I asked him to give the young man a job in the government. He did.
I believed God had a purpose for Benjamin Netanyahu long before he became one of the most consequential leaders in Israel’s history.
Nearly half a century later, I have watched that young man’s extraordinary political journey unfold. That history shapes how I view Netanyahu, and it helps explain why I believe Donald Trump recognizes something in him that others do not.
Two leaders cut from the same cloth
Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu have remarkable similarities. Both have deep connections to American culture, and both understand the power of television and media in shaping public opinion.
Politically, both emphasize national sovereignty, security, strong borders, and the defense of their nations’ interests. Both have challenged established political elites, criticized media institutions, and portrayed themselves as outsiders fighting entrenched systems.
Both have also experienced extraordinary political comebacks. Trump returned to the presidency in 2025 after losing the 2020 election. Netanyahu returned to power after losing the premiership in 2021. Both understand what it means to be counted out and then return to the center of political power.
But I believe their greatest similarity is personal.
Neither man has a desperate need to be liked.
I have known numerous prime ministers and presidents. Many leaders are consumed by the need for approval. They want the applause, favorable headlines, and reassurance that everyone respects them.
But when the need to be liked becomes greater than the responsibility to lead, a nation pays the price.
Trump and Netanyahu have demonstrated a willingness to endure criticism rather than retreat from decisions they believe are necessary. Courage is not measured by how many people applaud you. It is measured by whether you are willing to bear the consequences of doing what is right.
Both men admire the tradition of strong leadership associated with Ronald Reagan and Winston Churchill. They understand that peace cannot always be preserved by avoiding confrontation.
The North Star: Moral clarity
The North Star for Donald Trump is moral clarity.
I believe that principle explains his endorsement of Netanyahu better than any political calculation.
No other president would have confronted Iran during a midterm election year, knowing the political risks. Trump was willing to do what he believed was right regardless of the consequences.
For decades, the Iranian regime has threatened Israel and the United States. Trump and Netanyahu opposed the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and have shared a hard-line approach to Iran’s nuclear ambitions and regional aggression. Their military cooperation against Iran has demonstrated the strategic importance of their alliance.
Trump understood that confronting a dangerous regime could carry political costs. But he also understood that ignoring threats does not make them disappear.
Moral clarity means recognizing the difference between a friend and an enemy, between a threat and an ally, and between the pursuit of peace and the appeasement of those who openly call for destruction.
That is why Trump’s endorsement matters. He described Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and an “even greater Partner for Peace”. He praised Netanyahu’s strength, bravery, and resilience despite tremendous opposition, including opposition within Israel itself.
I believe Trump endorsed Netanyahu because he sees a partner who shares his convictions, understands the stakes, and will not easily surrender under pressure.
A Partnership That Changed History
During Trump’s first term, the United States moved its embassy to Jerusalem, recognized Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, and helped broker the Abraham Accords, which established diplomatic relations between Israel and several Arab states.
These were historic decisions that challenged longstanding assumptions about the Middle East. The Abraham Accords opened new possibilities for diplomacy, trade, security, and regional cooperation.
Netanyahu played a central role in Israel’s participation, while Trump’s administration supplied the diplomatic initiative and American influence that helped make the agreements possible.
I have spent much of my life defending Israel and mobilizing Christian support for the Jewish people. I launched six billboard campaigns in Israel honoring Trump’s presidency, hosted an embassy gala, presented Trump with the Friends of Zion Hineni Award in the Oval Office, and helped mobilize millions of pro-Israel evangelical voters.
I believe Trump has been the greatest American president in history in terms of his support for Israel. I also believe God spared Trump’s life during the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. As a man of faith, I believe God can preserve a life for a purpose greater than oneself.
What the next two years could mean for history
The next two years could be among the most consequential in the history of the American-Israeli alliance.
Trump and Netanyahu have an opportunity to strengthen Israel’s security, expand the Abraham Accords, deepen regional cooperation, and pursue a more durable strategy against Iran.
Imagine a Middle East where more nations recognize that cooperation with Israel offers greater opportunities than endless confrontation. Imagine a future in which Israel can live in security and the peoples of the region can pursue peace and prosperity.
What Trump and Netanyahu could accomplish in the next two years could be written about for hundreds of years.
The stakes are enormous. Their decisions could shape regional security, the future of the Abraham Accords, the threat posed by Iran, and the relationship between America and Israel for generations.
Neither Trump nor Netanyahu appears willing to sacrifice his convictions simply to win approval. That does not make them immune to mistakes. Leadership requires accountability as well as courage. But it also requires the willingness to make difficult decisions when the consequences are uncertain and the opposition is fierce.
History does not reward leaders simply for being popular. Churchill did not become a great wartime leader by trying to please everyone. Reagan did not reshape the Cold War by avoiding every confrontation. History remembers leaders who act when the stakes are high, even when their decisions invite criticism.
Trump and Netanyahu understand that reality. Perhaps that is why they recognize something in each other that other leaders miss.
Nearly half a century ago, I prayed over a grieving young man named Benjamin Netanyahu. I could not have imagined all the battles he would face or the role he would eventually play in his nation’s history.
Years later, I stood in the Oval Office and presented Donald Trump with the Friends of Zion Hineni Award. I witnessed his commitment to Israel and his willingness to make decisions that changed the course of American-Israeli relations.
I cannot claim to know every detail of God’s plan. But I believe God can use imperfect people to accomplish extraordinary things. I believe Israel’s security matters profoundly to America, and I believe courageous leaders can change the course of history.
That is why Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu was more than a political calculation. It was an affirmation of a partnership built on shared convictions, strategic interests, and moral clarity.
Dr. Mike Evans has written 120 books and is a #1 New York Times bestselling author and Nobel Peace Prize nominee. He is the founder of the Friends of Zion Museum in Jerusalem, the Ten Boom Museum in Holland, and Churches United with Israel, one of the largest Christian Zionist networks in America.

Tunisia increases prison sentences for defendants in deadly 2023 Djerba synagogue attack - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:30:32 UTC
16:30:32 KST

Tunisia’s judicial authorities have increased the sentences and punishments for several defendants involved in the 2023 Ghriba synagogue attack on the island of Djerba.
Five defendants had been convicted and sentenced in February 2026 for the deadly May 2023 attack, led by a Tunisian National Guard officer, in which five people were killed.
Al Ain news in the United Arab Emirates and the Tunisie Telegraph reported on Wednesday that a criminal chamber of the court that specializes in terrorism cases at the Tunis Court of Appeal had increased the sentences of four defendants.
According to Al Ain, the court’s decision included increasing the prison sentence from eight to 10 years for both the fiancée of the perpetrator and the person who arranged a house for and communicated with him, while subjecting each “to administrative supervision for five years.”
It added that the court also lengthened the sentence of a third defendant from two years in prison to six. How many of these defendants had already been serving time since 2023 remains unclear.
"In the same context, the court overturned the initial ruling issued against the fourth defendant, which ruled that the case should not be heard, and decided to convict her and sentence her to six years in prison,” the Al Ain report added.
As for the Tunisie Telegraph, it noted that the Tunisian Court of Appeal had reopened the files of those involved in the attack. Al Ain provided similar information, noting that the court had revisited the case of the perpetrator’s fiancée as well as of a person who had arranged accommodation for the perpetrator and communicated with him.
Based on this report, the Tunisian National Guard member had killed his colleague “before heading toward the vicinity of the Ghriba temple and opening fire, in an incident that resulted in deaths and injuries.”
The incident “brought back to the forefront the issue of securing sensitive sites during religious and tourist visits,” Tunisie Telegraph noted.
Further, several security forces were wounded in the attack. “The attack also killed two visitors and injured others,” the news source said.
Reversal of previous decision to not hear defendant's case
The “new appellate rulings are of particular importance” because they reversed a previous decision not to hear part of one defendant’s case, the report pointed out.
“These rulings remain part of the judicial process related to determining responsibilities in the case, while the perpetrator of the attack who opened fire should not be confused with the rest of the defendants to whom the judicial authorities are responsible for the actions attributed to them,” Tunisie Telegraph reported.
It noted that the attack on the historic synagogue took place during an annual Jewish pilgrimage season. The perpetrator, it said, shot his colleague and then stole his ammunition. He then attacked the synagogue, killing three other security officers and two Jewish visitors.
The Jews who were killed included a local Tunisian and a relative visiting from France, the report added. The same site was attacked in 2002 by terrorists using a truck bombing. The attack killed 21 people and was believed to be carried out by al-Qaeda.
In May, the Associated Press noted that “the annual Jewish pilgrimage to the 26-century-old El-Ghriba Synagogue in Tunisia drew a modest but notable return of international visitors this year, worshipping together under tight security after a deadly 2023 attack disrupted the festival.”

====================================================================================================

Beneath a German lake, above a Nazi bunker: Israeli artist explores buried memory - feature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:30:32 UTC
16:30:32 KST

Clay mines inscribed with Hebrew letters and submerged in a German lake above a Nazi-era bunker are at the center of Israeli artist Yehudit Sasportas's video installation Lake of Void, which opened at Jerusalem's Tower of David Museum on October 12.
The exhibition, hosted as part of the Jerusalem Biennale, one of the world's largest platforms for contemporary Jewish and Israeli art, is expected to remain on display until the end of November.
At the opening, Sasportas, Tower of David Museum director Eilat Lieber, and exhibition curator Hillie Wurtman Moyal addressed a small audience atop the citadel's tower, discussing the significance of presenting the installation in Jerusalem, the motivations behind Sasportas's work, and the relationship between archaeology and contemporary art.
The exhibition is housed within Jerusalem's ancient citadel, home to the Tower of David Museum, which preserves and presents the stories of the people and cultures that have shaped the city.
For Lieber, hosting contemporary art in the historic structure offers a chance to add another dimension to Jerusalem's history.
"Alongside being a historical museum, we also want to host art exhibitions here, because it's another layer [of the city's history]," Lieber told The Jerusalem Post.
"It's a layer of our generation that gives more perspective and meaning to the story of Jerusalem, especially Israeli art at its best, dealing with memory."
Memory beneath the surface
Sasportas, who represented Israel at the 2007 Venice Biennale, approaches the preservation of memory differently from traditional archaeologists, Lieber explained.
"Unlike archaeologists, [...] she's creating the remains. She's connecting the memories, sounds, and she creates artifacts, trying to be the archaeologists of the future," Lieber said.
Presenting the installation inside a hall dating back approximately 800 years, to the Crusader or Ayyubid period, creates a dialogue between the ancient structure and Sasportas's exploration of memory.
"To be able to host [the exhibition] inside the original... hall... and contemporary art that thinks about memories, the past and their meaning, is important for us," Lieber said.
Rather than uncovering objects left behind by previous generations, Sasportas creates artifacts intended to preserve traces of the present for those who come after.
In Lake of Void, that idea takes the form of clay sculptures resembling land mines, each containing a concealed message.
From Germany's Black Forest to a submerged Nazi bunker
The installation draws on Sasportas's earlier work in Germany's Black Forest, where she produced hand-drawn seismographic lines inspired by recordings taken from inside more than 138 trees.
The recordings were made near the cabin of German philosopher Martin Heidegger and the approximate location of his historically charged 1967 encounter with Romanian-born poet Paul Celan.
For Sasportas, the trees became "a living archive," their sounds translated into marks made by needles and pencils on drawing paper.
The resulting drawings were rolled, sealed inside black metal boxes, and placed within the clay mines, turning recordings of the natural world into physical repositories of memory.
The mines were subsequently submerged in Lake Bant in Wilhelmshaven, Germany, a lake beneath which lies a bunker constructed during the Nazi era.
Sasportas documented their descent with underwater footage and sound recordings, making the submerging of the sculptures part of the artwork itself.
Lake of Void is set "in a place that was [formerly] a lake, but underneath that lake there was a bunker that was created during the Nazi regime," Moyal explained.
The location reflects the exhibition's broader exploration of what remains hidden beneath seemingly ordinary landscapes.
Moyal described the work as examining the "underlying layers of the unseen reality – all the stories and memories and traumas and conflicts that are beneath the ground."
By bringing these buried histories to light, Sasportas confronts the legacy of places marked by historical violence.
"She deals with traumas under the ground, but through art revealing those stories," Moyal said.
"In her work, she [Sasportas] works through art to kind of change these charged memories and create something [..] to heal these charged places."
In Mine Sentence 3/6, an underwater camera focuses on the Hebrew letters inscribed on the clay sculptures. Their combinations form words, verses, and sentences carrying "intention and meaning," according to a Tower of David Museum press release.
The work forms part of Sasportas's ongoing The Liquid Desert Project, which began in 2013.
Sending a letter to the past
Sasportas's practice frequently takes her to locations across Europe and Israel where traumatic histories have been buried, forgotten, or denied.
According to the museum, her work seeks to bring those histories back into view, using art to connect different periods.
The discovery of the bunker beneath the Banter See was particularly significant to Sasportas, who recalled being struck by the contrast between the lake's peaceful appearance and the history concealed below.
When she "realized that there is an actual underground architecture like this bunker" beneath a lake that appeared "too beautiful," she wanted to "send a letter to the past" and "be able to correspond with the collective subconscious."
Although Sasportas acknowledged that the idea might sound "very abstract" and "very poetical," she described art as a way to communicate across time.
"Through a drawing, through a sculpture, through a mute image, you’re able to correspond with different times, and I think that this defines the quality of art as a timeless thing," she said.
The sculptures remain at the bottom of the lake, forming a permanent underwater installation above the submerged bunker.
According to the museum, the work is the third of six Mine Sentence installations submerged across Europe and Israel between 2020 and 2025.
From 'ani' to 'ayin': Finding meaning in nothingness
Beyond the physical landscape, Sasportas draws on the Hebrew language to explore the relationship between identity, absence, and creation.
Central to the exhibition is the connection between ani, meaning "I," and ayin, meaning "nothingness."
In Hebrew, the two words contain the same three letters, rearranged to produce different meanings.
For Sasportas, that transformation represents an opportunity to move beyond the self and into a space of creative possibility.
"You can also move the letters for a certain... artistic practice, creative practice, spiritual practice," she said.
"The transformation from 'ani' to 'ayin' inspires me a lot, and this is the lake of void, the lake of an ayin."
Sasportas also explored another meaning of ayin through the opening of Psalm 121, Me'ayin yavo ezri, traditionally translated as "From where will my help come?"
While the verse is commonly understood as a question about the source of assistance, Sasportas also interprets it as suggesting that help can emerge from nothingness itself.
"Ayin can be like nothing, nothingness, but ayin is also a space," she said.
She explained that the distinction depends on the viewer's state of consciousness and the meanings they bring to the work.
"I'm very inspired by artistic actions that can activate within themselves those different levels of consciousness," she said.
Sasportas also connected her artistic practice to the Hebrew expression Hashem hakol bizman, which she invoked to describe trust in divine timing.
Working "from a certain space-time," she explained, allows an artist to "open up other dimensions."
For Sasportas, the ability to hold seemingly contradictory states together, the concrete and the abstract, the visible and the hidden, is central to the power of art.
"If an artwork can embrace two states, like a very concrete, recognizable one, and start losing the face slowly into more abstract, but in the same body," she said, it can "activate all dimensions simultaneously."

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said on Wednesday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court.

"The good news in all this is Helen is alive, and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said.
Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines' electorate, was charged with three offenses: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official.
Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against Nugent, court filings showed.
The suspect was restrained by members of the public at the scene before being arrested.
Haines in critical condition after rare attack on Australian official
Haines, an independent lawmaker who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, remains in critical condition.
Police are still investigating the motive for the rare attack on an elected official.
During a brief court appearance on Wednesday, the accused's lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported. His lawyer told the magistrate his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody.
There was no application for bail, and the case was deferred until February 4.
Anti-terrorism police are among the agencies investigating the incident. While police allege the attack was "targeted," they believe it was an isolated incident.
No intelligence suggested any threat to Haines, and the Australian Federal Police received no warning of imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.
"What I can say is we didn't have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon," she said.
Victoria police investigating motive for attack on Haines
Victoria state police said they could not find any direct past contact between Haines and the accused, with the motive still unknown.
"Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centerpiece of the investigation," Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said.
Bush declined to comment on the man's mental health, saying the matter was before the court.
Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery, and academia before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in both 2022 and 2025.
Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders, and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee, or attending community events with relatively little security.
However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in recent years amid rising political polarization, online abuse, and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterized Australian politics.
